items.title: Environmental scan of Indigenous resources and culturally specific tools across intensive care units in Alberta, Canada
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Indigenous Peoples in Canada are disproportionately burdened with a spectrum of health issues and consistently report lower satisfaction with their health care; nevertheless, little is known about their experiences with critical care and the support received during critical illness. We aimed to describe the current scope of critical-care-specific resources available to Indigenous patients and their families across Alberta to identify gaps and opportunities to implement actionable change to realize more equitable and culturally safe care. Source We conducted a two-phase environmental scan. Phase 1 entailed searching websites for information to support Indigenous patients, their families, and health care workers. Phase 2 facilitated 21 interviews with intensive care unit (ICU) stakeholders from across Alberta to further describe site-specific resources, services, tools, or initiatives to support Indigenous Peoples. Indigenous partners were engaged through all aspects of the project. Principal findings Our environmental scan identified a paucity of ICU-specific resources, programs, or policies to support Indigenous patients and families' navigation with critical care. We identified two national resources aimed at clinicians, rather than patients or families. Interviews with ICU stakeholders confirmed the paucity of Indigenous-specific resources. Stakeholders cited numerous barriers, including inadequate culture training, staff time constraints and burnout, physical space limits, and insufficient personnel, such as Indigenous liaisons and social workers. Conclusions Multiple gaps exist in the availability of critical-care-focused resources and supports for Indigenous Peoples experiencing critical illness in Alberta, Canada. Addressing these care gaps may improve health equity, access, and the experience for Indigenous patients and families during critical illness and further build trust and strengthen relationships with health care workers.

items.title: Postreperfusion venovenous bypass for hemodynamic stabilization in liver transplantation with hepatic outflow obstruction: a case report
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Chronic inferior vena cava (IVC) stenosis is an uncommon yet serious vascular complication that can significantly impact the success of liver transplantation. We report a case in which postreperfusion venovenous bypass (VVB) was used as a temporizing strategy to achieve hemodynamic stabilization in the setting of severe hepatic venous congestion caused by a fixed suprahepatic IVC obstruction. Clinical features A 58-yr-old male with a history of orthotopic liver transplantation complicated by recurrent IVC stenosis and end-stage kidney disease underwent a simultaneous liver and kidney transplant. Intraoperatively, dense fibrosis was encountered proximal to the suprahepatic IVC, preventing resection of the stenotic segment. Although the liver graft was successfully implanted and reperfused, severe hepatic congestion and refractory hemodynamic instability developed. Venovenous bypass was initiated to augment venous return and stabilize systemic hemodynamics. The kidney transplant was aborted owing to the patient's instability. Postoperatively, the patient initially tolerated the procedure, however, he ultimately died in the intensive care unit. Conclusions This case illustrates an unconventional postreperfusion application of VVB as a rescue measure for refractory hemodynamic instability. Given the presence of a fixed suprahepatic IVC obstruction, VVB only provided temporary hemodynamic support and did not result in graft recovery. This underscores the physiologic limitations of VVB in the presence of irreversible mechanical outflow obstruction and highlights the importance of early recognition and surgical adaptability in anatomically complex cases.

items.title: Types of adult intensive care units and admissions in Türkiye between 2018 and 2023: a nationwide cohort study
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Türkiye has one of the highest intensive care unit (ICU) bed capacities among middle-income countries but also globally. Nevertheless, little is known about the characteristics of ICUs in Türkiye, their temporal trends, and ICU admissions and readmissions. We sought to analyze the structural characteristics of all adult ICUs and the clinical profiles of ICU admissions across Türkiye. Methods We conducted a retrospective nationwide cohort study using data from the Turkish Ministry of Health National Electronic Database. We analyzed adult ICU admissions across all levels and types over 6 years (2018-2023) and documented patient demographics, comorbidities, admission diagnoses, and ICU outcomes. Results We retrieved data on 3,362,539 ICU admissions. Among 22 ICU types, mixed ICUs accounted for the highest proportion of admissions (31.4%), followed by coronary (23.7%), anesthesiology (14.3%), medical (6.1%), and surgical (6.0%) ICUs. The proportion of mixed ICU beds decreased from 44.0% in 2018 to 25.1% in 2023. Most ICU beds were in state (public) hospitals (50.8%), followed by private hospitals (34.8%). The number of ICU beds increased from 2019, with a notable rise in state hospitals after 2020. The average number of ICU admissions was 659 per 100,000 population annually. The median patient age was 65 [interquartile range, 39-91] yr, and the ICU mortality was 15.5%. The leading admission diagnoses were respiratory failure (10.1%), cerebrovascular disease (7.1%), and acute kidney injury (5.2%). Hypertension (67.5%) and coronary artery disease (44.8%) were common comorbidities, particularly in nonsurvivors. The 7-day ICU readmission rate was 3.0%. Conclusions The present comprehensive analysis of ICU admissions in Türkiye between 2018 and 2023 highlights a shift toward specialization with a decrease in mixed ICUs. The impact of ICU diversity on resource use and patient outcomes requires further evaluation.

items.title: The relationship between early warning scores at intensive care unit discharge and risk of intensive care unit readmission in adult and pediatric populations: a scoping review
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Readmission after discharge from the intensive care unit (ICU) occurs globally at a rate of approximately 1-12% and is associated with adverse patient outcomes. Despite these findings, there is no internationally accepted tool to guide or standardize decisions regarding ICU discharge. In this scoping review, we aimed to evaluate the use of early warning scores (EWSs) measured at or around the time of ICU discharge as predictors of subsequent ICU readmission in adult and pediatric populations. Source With support from a medical librarian, we searched MEDLINE®, Embase®, and the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature from database inception to December 14, 2025. We included quantitative observational and interventional studies that evaluated any EWS (e.g., National EWS [NEWS]/NEWS2, Modified EWS [MEWS], Pediatric EWS [PEWS], Rothman Index, Risk Scoring Index, or related tools) at ICU discharge, immediately prior to transfer, or immediately upon ward admission and reported unplanned ICU readmission following transfer to a hospital ward. Unplanned ICU readmissions were defined as any unplanned return to an ICU after discharge to the ward. We excluded studies in which patients were discharged to locations other than a ward (e.g., home, long-term care) or that focused solely on interfacility transfer. Screening and data extraction were performed in duplicate using a standardized template, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Principal findings The search identified 7,977 records, of which 4,824 remained after removal of duplicates. Of the articles, 58 underwent full-text review, and 20 studies met inclusion criteria. The studies were conducted across North America, Europe, and Asia and included both adult (n = 14) and pediatric (n = 6) populations. All were observational (retrospective or prospective) or pre-post intervention designs; no randomized controlled trials were identified. A range of tools were evaluated, including NEWS/NEWS2, MEWS, PEWS, the Rothman Index, the Risk Scoring Index, and several machine-learning-based EWS models. Of the 20 studies, 17 reported a significant association between higher EWS values at or near ICU discharge and increased risk of unplanned ICU readmission, while three found no significant association. Across studies, readmission rates and EWS thresholds varied, and there was considerable heterogeneity in populations, settings, and outcome time frames. The risk of bias was generally low to moderate across QUADAS-2 domains, although several studies had high or unclear risk in key areas-most commonly patient selection and index test blinding-limiting causal inference. Conclusions Most available studies report that higher EWS values at ICU discharge are associated with an increased likelihood of ICU readmission. Early warning scores may therefore serve as useful adjuncts to clinical judgement when assessing discharge readiness. Nevertheless, the current evidence base is limited by the absence of randomized or robust interventional trials, and substantial heterogeneity, which limits causal inference and the ability to determine whether EWS-guided discharge protocols improve outcomes. Further multicentre prospective studies are needed to determine whether EWS-guided discharge protocols improve patient outcomes, reduce readmissions, and optimize use of ICU resources.

items.title: Public perception of who is responsible for anesthesia-related care: a cross-sectional survey in Japan
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: PURPOSE: We aimed to assess the public perception of who is responsible for anesthesia-related hospital care tasks in Japan and examine associated factors. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional, nationwide, quota-based web survey of adults in Japan in July 2025. Of the 1,944 respondents who initiated the survey, 1,844 completed (94.9%) it, and 1,000 responses were analyzed after quota completion (ages 20-69 yr). The outcomes were attribution (yes/no) of four anesthesia-related hospital care tasks to anesthesiologists: intraoperative anesthesia, postoperative pain management, procedural sedation/analgesia (PSA), and labour neuraxial analgesia (LNA). For each outcome, we fitted multivariable logistic regression models adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics, the Health Interest Scale (HIS), Communicative and Critical Health Literacy (CCHL), board-certified anesthesiologist density, information sources, and task-matched experience, with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) control. RESULTS: Attribution was highest for intraoperative anesthesia (84.7%), followed by LNA (65.2%), PSA (37.4%), and postoperative pain management (13.5%). After FDR control, university education or higher was associated with greater attribution for intraoperative anesthesia (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.08; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.30 to 3.32), PSA (aOR, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.15 to 2.30), and LNA (aOR, 1.82; 95% CI, 1.30 to 2.55). Task-matched prior experience attributed to anesthesiologists was associated with higher attribution for intraoperative anesthesia (aOR, 3.75; 95% CI, 1.76 to 8.80) and PSA (aOR, 2.41; 95% CI, 1.34 to 4.43). Fictional media was the only information-source factor that remained significant after FDR control (intraoperative anesthesia: aOR, 2.73; 95% CI, 1.79 to 4.25; PSA: aOR, 1.90; 95% CI, 1.42 to 2.56). No factor met the FDR threshold for postoperative pain management. HIS, CCHL, and anesthesiologist density showed no consistent adjusted associations. CONCLUSIONS: Public attribution of anesthesiologists' roles in Japan varied by task. Educational attainment, task-matched experience, and information sources were more consistently associated with attribution than general health traits or workforce context, supporting the value of role-explicit, task-specific communication strategies.

items.title: Effect-site concentrations of remifentanil to suppress coughing during emergence from general anesthesia in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Remifentanil infusion titrated to effect-site concentration (Ce) is commonly used to suppress coughing during emergence from general anesthesia; nevertheless, the optimal Ce range remains unclear. We aimed to conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis to synthesize the existing evidence on the optimal Ce values of remifentanil for cough suppression during emergence. Source We performed a comprehensive literature search using PubMed®, Embase®, Web of Science™, the Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar on 27 February 2025. We included prospective studies that used the up-and-down method to estimate the effective concentrations of remifentanil in 50% of patients (EC 50 ) and 95% of patients (EC 95 ) for suppressing coughing during emergence from general anesthesia with tracheal intubation in adult patients. We excluded studies in children or patients undergoing cardiac surgery, as well as those that only compared predefined Ce targets of remifentanil to determine optimal dosing. We obtained pooled estimates using a random-effects model with inverse-variance method, and heterogeneity was quantified using the I 2 statistic. We assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias 2 tool for randomized trials and the Methodological Index for Non-Randomized Studies for nonrandomized comparative or single-arm studies. The primary outcome was EC 50 estimated using the up-and-down method, with secondary outcomes including model-based EC 50 and EC 95 estimates. Principal findings We included 22 prospective studies comprising 857 adult participants, and none were assessed as being at a high risk of bias or of low methodologic quality. Based on 28 groups and 653 participants across 17 studies, the pooled mean EC 50 from the up-and-down method was 2.0 ng·mL -1 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.8 to 2.3), with considerable heterogeneity (I 2 = 74.5%). Based on 29 groups and 693 participants across 18 studies, the model-based EC 50 was 1.9 ng·mL -1 (95% CI, 1.6 to 2.1), with considerable heterogeneity (I 2 = 96.1%). Based on 31 groups and 809 participants across 20 studies, the model-based EC 95 was 2.7 ng·mL -1 (95% CI, 2.5 to 3.0), with considerable heterogeneity (I 2 = 99.5%). Subgroup analyses revealed higher mean EC 50 values in male individuals (2.6 ng·mL -1 ) and the highest mean EC 50 in patients undergoing video-assisted thoracic surgery (2.6 ng·mL -1 ). Using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation framework, the certainty of evidence was rated as very low for all outcomes. Conclusions The identified EC 50 and EC 95 values of remifentanil for suppressing coughing during emergence from general anesthesia in adults were 2.0 and 2.7 ng·mL -1 , respectively. Patient sex and surgical type may influence the required Ce. Careful dose adjustment is recommended to avoid delayed awakening and hypoventilation, especially in cases requiring higher concentrations. Study registration PROSPERO ( CRD42024623581 ); first submitted 20 December 2024.

items.title: Video double-lumen tube intubation in a modified lateral position for unilateral video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery: a randomized controlled trial
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: PURPOSE: We aimed to evaluate and report a protocol for video double-lumen tube (VDLT) intubation in a modified lateral position and evaluate whether it shortens in-room to cut time (IRCT; defined as the time from patient entry to incision) compared with conventional supine intubation in patients undergoing elective unilateral video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS). METHODS: , mouth opening < 3 cm, Mallampati class 3-4, or anticipated difficult airway. Participants were randomized 1:1 to modified-lateral-position (Group L) or supine-position (Group S) VDLT intubation using a computer-generated sequence with sealed-envelope allocation concealment. Operators were unblinded; nonoperator staff collecting postoperative data and the outcome analyst were blinded to allocation. The primary outcome was IRCT. RESULTS: Sixty-two patients were randomized (Group L, N = 31; Group S, N = 31), and all were analyzed for the primary outcome. Mean (standard deviation [SD]) IRCT was shorter in Group L (18.1 [2.0] min) than in Group S (31.1 [3.3] min), with a mean difference (L-S) of -13.0 min (95% confidence interval [CI], -14.4 to -11.6; P < 0.001). Intubation time was similar (mean [SD], 103 [15] sec vs 97 [15] sec; P = 0.10). Video double-lumen tube malpositioning occurred in 1/31 (3%) cases in Group L vs 15/31 (48%) cases in Group S (relative risk [RR], 0.067; 95% CI, 0.009 to 0.474; P < 0.001). Sore throat within 48 h occurred in 9/31 (29%) patients in Group L vs 18/31 (58%) patients in Group S (RR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.27 to 0.94; P = 0.02). CONCLUSIONS: In patients undergoing unilateral VATS, VDLT intubation in a modified lateral position shortened IRCT. In exploratory analyses, several secondary outcomes favoured this approach. Intubation in a modified lateral position may be a feasible alternative to conventional supine position intubation in these patients. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ChiCTR.org.cn ( ChiCTR2500112254 ); first posted 21 October 2025.

items.title: Paratracheal air cysts and their associations with postoperative pulmonary complications in patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia: a retrospective propensity-score-matched study
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Paratracheal air cysts are rare benign anatomical variants. Although case reports suggest that paratracheal air cysts may lead to complications such as difficult ventilation and pneumothorax in patients whose lungs are mechanically ventilated, their association with postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) remains unclear. We hypothesized that the presence of cysts is associated with an increased incidence of PPCs. Methods In the context of COVID-19, we conducted a retrospective study of all patients undergoing surgery under general anesthesia in 2020. On the basis of the presence of paratracheal air cysts, we divided patients into two groups: the paratracheal air cyst group and the paratracheal-air-cyst‑free group. The primary outcome was the incidence of PPCs. We used propensity score matching to adjust for confounding and performed multivariable logistic regression analysis in the matched cohort to assess the association. Results Among 7,208 patients, the prevalence of paratracheal air cysts was 2.0% (141/7,208). The incidence of PPCs was 22% (31/141) in the paratracheal air cyst group and 15% (43/280) in the paratracheal-air-cyst-free group. Multivariable regression analysis showed that, after adjusting for confounders, the presence of paratracheal air cysts was associated with an increased risk of PPCs (adjusted odds ratio, 1.85; 95% confidence interval, 1.03 to 3.33; P = 0.04). Conclusions The presence of paratracheal air cysts was associated with an increased risk of PPCs. Although this association warrants cautious interpretation due to possible residual confounding and lack of data on intraoperative ventilatory settings, anesthesiologists should consider the potential perioperative implications of this anatomical abnormality during preoperative assessment.

items.title: Development and implementation of an objective framework for measuring clinician faculty research contributions in a Canadian anesthesiology department
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Given the fiduciary responsibility of an academic clinical department to ensure appropriate use of funds to support research, the Department of Anesthesia, Pain Management and Perioperative Medicine at Dalhousie University (Halifax, NS, Canada) aimed to create a framework to support the allocation of remunerated protected research time to clinician faculty members within the department. Methods A departmental Research Accountability Project (RAP) was undertaken in the context of a quality improvement initiative. The RAP initially engaged clinician faculty members in the form of a survey, interviews, and a questionnaire to provide feedback regarding current practices for evaluating protected time for research. On the basis of this feedback, a working group created a list of 151 research outputs encompassing the breadth of research-related activities and assigned scores based on their relative merit. Clinicians with protected research time completed their academic profile, and individual point allocations were calculated. Scores were then weighted by different categories (e.g., publications, grant capture, presentations), and a RAP dashboard was developed to capture research outputs, assign scores, and generate a reporting/feedback mechanism for further analysis. Results Faculty members acknowledged the importance of clinicians having remunerated protected time to carry out research; nevertheless, there was scepticism with respect to how protected research time was managed. These data were then assessed by the working group, and using the RAP metric, individual researcher reports consisting of scores and recommendations were sent to the department head for final evaluation. These reports formed the basis of the researchers' annual academic performance review and consideration for continuance. Conclusions The RAP scoring system provides an objective measure of remunerated protected research time for clinicians to assist in researcher accountability.

items.title: Evaluation of deep learning for the modified Cormack–Lehane classification in videolaryngoscopic images: a prospective observational study
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Predicting difficult intubation is still challenging, even with videolaryngoscopy. Videolaryngoscopy (VL) shows the larynx during intubation. The modified Cormack-Lehane (CL) classification grades laryngeal visibility but can vary between observers. Deep learning uses neural networks for objective, real-time airway image evaluation. We aimed to evaluate a YOLOv8-based model for object detection to automate modified CL grade classification from VL images in patients undergoing elective surgery. Methods In this prospective observational study, we developed a deep learning model using 346 VL images from 151 patients undergoing elective surgery. Two anesthesiologists classified images according to the modified CL system, and interobserver agreement was analysed using Cohen's kappa and weighted kappa. We split the data into training (80%), validation (10%), and test (10%) sets, with imbalance corrected via Albumentations augmentation. We evaluated the model results using sensitivity, specificity, and mean average precision with a 95% confidence interval (CI) and validated the model on 60 images not included in the training set. Results Interobserver agreement ranged from moderate (Cohen's kappa = 0.59; 95% CI, 0.53 to 0.66) to good (weighted kappa = 0.79; 95% CI, 0.75 to 0.84). In the test set, the overall recall rate was 0.87, and the specificity was 0.83. In the difficult intubation grades, recall and specificity were observed to be 0.79 (95% CI, 0.52 to 0.92) and 0.93 (95% CI, 0.78 to 0.98), respectively, for CL grade 2b, and 0.60 and 1.00, respectively, for CL grade 3. In the external validation data set (n = 60), the model achieved an overall accuracy of 0.767 with a recognition rate of 0.925 for clinically relevant CL grades 2b and 3. Conclusions The YOLOv8-based model showed promising performance in classifying modified CL grades, particularly for clinically relevant difficult views (CL grades 2b-3). Nevertheless, wide CIs and limited external validation indicate uncertainty. The model may be considered an auxiliary tool rather than an independent decision system and requires further validation in larger, multicentre data sets.

items.title: Voluntariness of same-day versus advance consent in low-risk clinical research: a randomized controlled trial
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose The solicitation of same-day consent for participation in clinical research is commonly prohibited by research ethics boards because of concerns about limited decision-making time and patient vulnerability. However, these concerns lack empirical support and restrict both research efforts and patient participation opportunities, particularly in medical specialties such as emergency medicine, critical care, and anesthesiology, in which clinicians and patients interact for the first time on the day of a procedure. We aimed to assess the voluntariness of research consent solicited on the day of surgery compared with consent obtained in advance. Methods We performed a prospective, noninferiority randomized controlled trial examining the voluntariness of informed consent to participate in a low-risk clinical research trial at Women's College Hospital in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. The trial design included active deception (invitation to participate in a fabricated research trial) to capture authentic measurements of participants' perceptions of any perceived coercion. Results We randomized 114 patients scheduled to undergo anterior cruciate ligament repair for recruitment into a fabricated low-risk perioperative research trial at one of two time points: at a virtual preanesthesia clinic appointment in advance of the day of surgery, or on the day of surgery. Regardless of their decision, all participants received the (same) standard of care. Overall, 71/114 patients (62%) either consented to participate in the fabricated trial or declined participation but consented to a feedback session during which perceptions of coercion were assessed. Greater participation was observed among patients approached on the day of surgery (fabricated trial, 26/58 [45%]; feedback session only, 18/58 [31%]) than in advance (fabricated trial, 17/56 [30%]; feedback session only, 10/56 [18%]). Perceived coercion, measured using two validated psychometric instruments, did not differ between patients recruited on the day of surgery and those recruited in advance. A subset of patients in each group reported modest perceptions of undue influence, but regardless of recruitment time point, these patients demonstrated their agency to decline participation. Conclusions Our findings suggest that restrictive same-day consent policies, when based on concerns regarding undue influence, may represent a structural barrier to participation in low-risk trials that lacks empirical justification. Study registrations 1) Open Science Framework ( 46twc ); first submitted 17 March 2023; 2) ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT07380035 ); first submitted 16 January 2026.

items.title: Fellowship, research, and practice preferences: an updated survey of Canadian anesthesiology residents
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: Purpose Canada faces mounting anesthesia workforce pressures, particularly in rural and smaller urban centres. Understanding residents' motivations regarding practice setting, research, and fellowship training is essential for workforce planning. We aimed to update a 2015 national survey to characterize current preferences and temporal shifts among Canadian anesthesiology residents. Methods We conducted an anonymous, cross-sectional survey of residents in accredited Canadian anesthesiology programs (November-December 2024) using Research Electronic Data Capture. Items addressed demographics, practice setting, research experience and intentions, and fellowship plans. Selected responses were compared with 2015 survey items using Chi square tests and odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals; all tests used an alpha of 0.05. Results Ninety-four residents responded (12% response rate). Most preferred academic practice (63%), and half preferred to remain at their training institution (49%). Interest in rural practice was reported by 49%. Although research participation was common during medical school (94%) and residency (83%), only 18% intended to pursue research after residency. Approximately 63% intended to pursue fellowship training. Compared with the 2015 survey, there were significant increases in intention to remain at the same institution (from 35% to 50%; P = 0.02) and residency research participation (from 69% to 83%; P Conclusions Canadian anesthesiology residents continue to favour academic practice and fellowship training, yet fewer plan to integrate research into future careers. These findings highlight opportunities for targeted mentorship, greater research autonomy, financial support, and expanded rural training pathways to align resident priorities with workforce needs.

items.title: Cardiovascular disturbances and ward hypotension after major vascular surgery: a single-centre prospective cohort study
items.containerTitle: Canadian Journal of Anesthesia/Journal canadien d'anesthésie
items.abstract: PURPOSE: Postoperative hypotension can be caused by vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, severe hypovolemia, and obstruction. We sought to estimate the effects of these causes on the incidence of hypotension after major vascular surgery. METHODS: We conducted a single-centre prospective cohort study of male and female adult patients undergoing major vascular surgery. We conducted point-of-care ultrasound and sidestream darkfield microscopy imaging to detect vasodilation, myocardial dysfunction, severe hypovolemia, and obstruction. The primary outcome was hypotension (systolic blood pressure < 90 mm Hg or a vasopressor infusion) within 24 hr of surgery. RESULTS: We recruited 100 patients, of whom 89 had data available for analysis. Hypotension occurred in 20 participants (23%), vasodilation in 30 (34%), and myocardial dysfunction in 11 (12%). Severe hypovolemia and obstruction were not observed. The adjusted marginal risk difference of hypotension was 33% (95% confidence interval [CI], 14% to 53%; P < 0.001) for vasodilation and 41% (95% CI, 3% to 79%; P = 0.03) for myocardial dysfunction. Vasodilation increased the risk of intensive care unit admission by 27% (95% CI, 8% to 45%; P = 0.006) and of requiring a vasopressor infusion by 22% (95% CI, 4% to 39%; P = 0.02). CONCLUSIONS: Vasodilation and myocardial dysfunction increased the risk of postoperative hypotension, providing insight into the mechanistic development of postoperative hypotension. The absence of severe hypovolemia was surprising. Clinicians should assess for vasodilation and myocardial dysfunction as potential preludes to postoperative hypotension, potentially using point-of-care echocardiography and sidestream darkfield microscopy.

items.title: Preoperative cognitive training for preventing perioperative neurocognitive disorders: A systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis and meta-regression of randomised controlled trials
items.abstract: Study objective Although nonpharmacological interventions are recommended for preventing perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND), cognitive training has not been explicitly advocated. Therefore, this systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (TSA) and meta-regression tested the hypothesis that preoperative cognitive training, compared with usual care, reduces the incidence of PND. Methods Eight databases and two clinical trial registries were searched for RCTs comparing preoperative cognitive training with usual care. Primary outcomes were postoperative delirium (POD), delayed neurocognitive recovery (DNR), and postoperative neurocognitive disorder. Results Thirteen RCTs with 1446 patients were identified. Preoperative cognitive training was associated with a lower risk of POD (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.36-0.77; P = 0.001; low certainty). Subgroup analysis (P for interaction = 0.01) and meta-regression (β1 1.072, 95% CI 0.006-2.138, P = 0.049) suggested an association between training format and treatment effect on POD, with a potentially greater benefit for traditional training. For DNR, the incidence was lower in the training group than in the usual care group (RR 0.66; 95% CI 0.46-0.96; P = 0.03; very low certainty), but this finding was not supported by several sensitivity analyses. No significant differences were detected between subgroups for training format, total duration, or surgery type (P for interaction = 0.06, 0.37, and 0.34, respectively), and meta-regression suggested that overall risk of bias was a potential moderator for DNR (P = 0.045). TSA suggested a potential for false-positive findings, as the cumulative Z-curves did not cross the TSA boundaries, and the required information sizes were not reached for either outcome. Conclusions Preoperative cognitive training may reduce the incidence of POD, with traditional training showing a potentially greater benefit than digital training. For DNR, the current evidence is insufficient to support a preventive effect of preoperative cognitive training, although a trend toward benefit was observed. These findings are limited by high risk of bias in several included trials and failure to reach the required information sizes in TSA, particularly for DNR, which need to be confirmed in future large-scale RCTs. Systematic review protocol PROSPERO (CRD420261293607).

items.title: Beyond objective demographics: The roles of subjective perception, state of consciousness, and language concordance in patient satisfaction
Intraoperative hypotension and postoperative acute kidney injury: Evidence and controversies
items.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) remains one of the most common serious complications after noncardiac surgery, and intraoperative hypotension (IOH) is consistently identified as a modifiable risk factor. Observational studies show a consistent, roughly dose-response association between IOH, particularly at mean arterial pressures below 60-65 mmHg, and postoperative AKI, with stronger associations in patients with limited renal reserve. Definitions of IOH vary widely, which complicates the comparison of studies and the translation of thresholds into clinical targets. Randomized trials of individualized or higher blood pressure targets have generally not confirmed a kidney-protective benefit, and pooled analyses with trial sequential analysis have not demonstrated that higher targets reduce AKI. This narrative review examines how IOH definitions evolved, summarizes the conflicting intervention evidence, and assesses the controversies that shape current practice. The review concludes that avoiding severe and sustained hypotension remains reasonable, whereas current randomized trial evidence does not support a general kidney-protective benefit of higher or individualized blood pressure targets. This conclusion is provisional and is tempered by the methodologic and causal uncertainties.

items.title: Observational study for perioperative intensive care unit (OPICU): Planned and unplanned ICU admissions, follow-up, discharge, and outcomes
items.abstract: Introduction Due to limited resources, identifying high-risk surgical patients who derive clinical benefit from Intensive Care Unit (ICU) admission is essential. Our primary aim was to characterize resource allocation and evaluate the true clinical benefit of ICU admissions using modified Wang criteria. Secondary aim is to identify independent risk factors for ICU admission; validate clinical scoring systems; and compare inter-group outcomes, including Clavien-Dindo complication rates, lengths of stay, and mortality. Materials and methods This multicenter, prospective, observational study was conducted across 75 ICUs. Adult inpatient surgery cases were categorized into four groups: planned admission (PAG), unplanned admission (UPAG), planned but not admitted (PBNAG), and emergent admission (EAG). Data included preoperative/intraoperative/postoperative(ICU) variables, modified Wang criteria, and mortality rates (ICU, hospital, 30/90-day). Results Of 55,963 preoperatively evaluated patients, 2764 (4.9%) were planned for ICU admission; 804/2764 patients could not be admitted because of limited ICU beds, remaining of 1960 patients with a planned ICU admission, 411/1960 did not require postoperative ICU care forming the PBNAG (14.8% of 2764). Overall, 1980 patients (3.09% of all cases) were admitted to the ICU (78.2% PAG, 12.5% EAG, 9.1% UPAG). POSSUM scores effectively differentiated PBNAG (lower) and EAG (higher) from PAG. ICU benefit indicators (e.g., vasopressor need, prolonged ventilation >12 h, arrest events) were significantly higher in UPAG and EAG versus PAG (p 2 (OR 2.7) independently increased UPAG risk, whereas minimally invasive surgery and regional anesthesia reduced ICU admissions. Overall ICU and 90-day mortality rates were 5.9% and 7.5%, respectively, peaking in the EAG group (18.1% and 18.9%). Conclusion Integrating modified Wang criteria, POSSUM scores, intraoperative complications, emergency status, and ASA class >2 is effective in predicting the necessity of ICU admission.

items.title: Infraorbital versus sphenopalatine ganglion block for patient-reported recovery after septorhinoplasty: A randomized controlled trial
items.abstract: Study objective To compare ultrasound-guided infraorbital nerve block with transnasal sphenopalatine ganglion block on recovery quality 24 h after septorhinoplasty. Design Prospective, randomized, patient- and assessor-blinded, parallel-group trial. Setting Tertiary training hospital; operating room and postoperative ward. Patients Ninety adults aged 18 to 65 years, ASA physical status I or II, undergoing elective septorhinoplasty; 89 were analyzed. Interventions After induction of general anesthesia, patients received bilateral transnasal sphenopalatine ganglion block (SPG group) or bilateral ultrasound-guided infraorbital nerve block (IO group), 2 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine per side. Surgical infiltration and multimodal analgesia were identical in both groups. Measurements The primary outcome was the total Quality of Recovery-15 (QoR-15) score at 24 h. Secondary outcomes were QoR-15 domains, visual analog scale pain scores, rescue morphine, nausea and vomiting, anesthetic consumption, emergence agitation, edema, ecchymosis and recovery room stay. Main results Total QoR-15 at 24 h was higher in the IO group (129.1 ± 9.4 versus 116.6 ± 11.7; mean difference 12.5 points, 95% CI 8.01 to 17.01; P = 0.001), above the prespecified minimal clinically important difference of 8. More IO patients crossed the acceptable symptom state threshold of 118 (86.4% versus 35.6%; P Conclusions Infraorbital nerve block gave better 24 h patient-reported recovery than sphenopalatine ganglion block after septorhinoplasty. Secondary findings are hypothesis-generating. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.govNCT06929429.

Short-term peripheral nerve stimulation for pain relief in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.abstract: Background Short-term peripheral nerve stimulation serves as a neuromodulation therapy that modulates neural activity to provide therapeutic benefit, particularly pain relief. This study investigated the effectiveness of short-term peripheral nerve stimulation as a minimally invasive approach for achieving pain relief. Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar from database inception till September 10, 2026, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in adults comparing short-term peripheral nerve stimulation with sham stimulation or usual care. The primary outcome was the change in average pain intensity during the implantation period. Results Eight RCTs (543 participants) were included. Compared with the control group, the intervention group showed significant reductions in average pain intensity during the implantation period at 1-4 weeks (SMD = -0.48, 95% CI = -0.71 to -0.26, P Conclusion This meta-analysis provided preliminary evidence that short-term peripheral nerve stimulation may relieve pain during the implantation period, but not all outcomes suggest sustained improvements after electrode removal. Registration prospero CRD420251243978.

items.title: Peripheral nerve block injection pressure monitoring: A systematic review
items.abstract: Study objective To determine whether injection pressure and pressure-time characteristics can discriminate potentially hazardous needle-tip locations during peripheral nerve injection. Design Systematic review of experimental preclinical studies with narrative synthesis. Setting Animal, ex vivo biological nerve, and human cadaver models of peripheral nerve injection. Interventions Needle placement and injection at intraneural, intrafascicular, perineural, or extraneural locations. Measurements CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from inception to April 28, 2026 and updated on September 19, 2026. Studies reporting opening, peak, or plateau pressure or pressure-time characteristics in relation to anatomically defined needle-tip location were eligible. Human clinical studies and non-biological bench models were excluded. Risk of bias was evaluated using SYRCLE for animal studies and a domain-based framework for cadaveric studies. Because of substantial heterogeneity in experimental models, injection techniques, and pressure definitions, meta-analysis was not considered appropriate. Main results Twenty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria: 12 animal or animal ex vivo studies and 16 human cadaver studies. Intraneural injection was generally associated with higher peak and plateau pressures than perineural injection, but substantial overlap occurred across needle locations. Importantly, low pressure did not reliably rule out intraneural injection, while elevated pressure was also observed during needle-nerve contact and fascial injection. Consequently, the commonly proposed 15-psi threshold showed inconsistent sensitivity across experimental settings. Lower thresholds, including 12 psi, appeared more sensitive in some models but have not been clinically validated. Beyond absolute pressure values, the rate of pressure rise and pressure-time curve morphology showed potential for differentiating needle-tip locations. Conclusions Injection pressure monitoring may provide a nonspecific warning of needle placement within or against a poorly compliant structure. However, preclinical evidence alone cannot establish whether it should be used routinely or whether it reduces nerve injury. No universal pressure threshold or clinically recommended injection rate can currently be defined.

items.title: Processed electroencephalogram-guided anesthesia and its impact on postoperative delirium and perioperative efficiency: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Processed electroencephalography (pEEG) provides quantitative indices for monitoring anesthetic depth and is recommended in international guidelines. Prior meta-analyses have assessed EEG-guided anesthesia but none have evaluated available evidence stratified by pEEG technology. METHODS: We performed a systematic literature review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials in adults undergoing surgical, endoscopic, or dental procedures comparing pEEG-guided with non-pEEG-guided anesthesia. Primary outcomes were anesthetic drug use (TIVA and volatile agents) and postoperative delirium (POD ≤10 days). Secondary outcomes were extubation time, wake-up time, time to orientation, and post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) length of stay. Searches (PubMed Central, MEDLINE) were conducted on 11 April 2025; the protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251067170). Random-effects models produced standardized mean differences (SMD), mean differences (MD), and risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence interval (CI). RESULTS: Eighty-seven RCTs (30,611 patients; 13,586 pEEG; 17,025 non-pEEG) were included. pEEG significantly reduced propofol use (SMD -0.42, 95% CI -0.74 to -0.10; p = 0.01) and volatile anesthetic use (SMD -1.27, 95% CI -1.88 to -0.66; p < 0.01). The risk of POD decreased by 27% (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.84; p < 0.01). Efficiency outcomes favored pEEG: extubation time (MD -2.90 min, 95% CI -3.64 to -2.16; p < 0.01), wake-up time (MD -1.83 min, 95% CI -2.42 to -1.25; p < 0.01), time to orientation (MD -4.11 min, 95% CI -6.99 to -1.23; p < 0.01), and PACU length of stay (MD -2.81 min, 95% CI -4.66 to -0.96; p < 0.01). Subgroup analyses suggested benefits were most consistently observed for BIS; estimates for Entropy and SEDLine were less precise due to fewer studies. Heterogeneity was substantial for several outcomes. CONCLUSIONS: Across 87 RCTs, pEEG-guided monitoring utilizing multiple device types improved perioperative efficiency and reduced POD compared with not using pEEG. Evidence is strongest for BIS; further well-reported trials are needed to delineate device-specific effects.

items.title: Anterior inferior psoas epimysial injection: a cadaveric feasibility study of an anterior pathway to the lumbar plexus
items.abstract: Background Posterior lumbar plexus block provides reliable anesthesia but is technically challenging and associated with risks related to deep paraspinal needle placement. Existing anterior approaches provide variable lumbar plexus coverage, and the anatomical pathways by which newer iliopsoas-based techniques reach individual plexus branches remain incompletely defined. This feasibility study evaluated whether an anterior inferior, trans-psoas injection targeting the posterior epimysium of the psoas muscle could provide a direct anterior pathway toward the lumbar plexus. Methods A cadaveric dye study was performed on four GreenMBalmed cadaver hips. Under ultrasound guidance in the supine position, 30 mL of 0.1% methylene blue was injected in a caudal-to-cranial trajectory along the posterior epimysium of the psoas. Layered dissections assessed dye spread relative to the psoas, thoracolumbar fascia, and lumbar plexus nerves. Results Cranial and anterior fascial spread was observed in all four hips, with dye tracking anterior to the quadratus lumborum and extending toward the 12th rib and perinephric region. Dense staining of the lateral femoral cutaneous and iliohypogastric nerves was seen in all hips. The femoral nerve demonstrated predominantly moderate staining, while obturator nerve involvement was variable. Minimal intramuscular staining of the psoas was observed, suggesting preferential spread along fascial planes. Conclusions Anterior inferior injection along the posterior epimysium of the psoas produced spread toward lumbar plexus regions in all four hips, in this limited cadaveric sample, suggesting this plane warrants further investigation. Clinical studies are needed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of this approach.

items.title: Cell salvage volume and hemostatic changes in cardiac surgery: A retrospective cohort study using routine coagulation and viscoelastic assessment
items.abstract: Background Intraoperative cell salvage (CS) reduces allogeneic transfusion in cardiac surgery, but the washing process removes coagulation factors and platelets, raising hemostatic concerns. The dose-response relationship between CS volume and perioperative hemostatic changes remains poorly characterized. Methods In this retrospective study of adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery with CS use, two cohorts with paired hemostatic measurements were identified: a routine coagulation cohort (primary analysis) and a viscoelastic cohort (exploratory analysis). Both cohorts were restricted to patients without coagulation-affecting blood products between measurements. Multivariable linear regression examined CS volume and absolute changes in each parameter, adjusted for surgical and patient characteristics and baseline values. Results In the routine coagulation cohort (N = 677; median CS 0.5 L, range 0.1-1.6 L), CS volume was not significantly associated with absolute changes in any parameter (all p ≥ 0.144). In the viscoelastic cohort (N = 50; median CS 0.8 L, range 0.2-3.7 L), CS volume was significantly associated with decreased functional fibrinogen clot strength (CFF MA: β = -3.31 mm/L; 95% CI: -5.53, -1.08; p = 0.004) and overall clot strength (CK MA: β = -2.93 mm/L; 95% CI: -5.73, -0.13; p = 0.041); after Holm correction for multiple testing, the CFF MA association remained significant (adjusted p = 0.031), whereas the CK MA association did not (adjusted p = 0.244). Conclusions At observed reinfusion volumes, CS was not associated with changes in routine coagulation parameters, but in the exploratory viscoelastic cohort, higher CS volume was associated with lower functional fibrinogen clot strength. These findings highlight the potential value of viscoelastic monitoring when higher volumes are anticipated.

Stellate ganglion block in contemporary anesthesia practice: perioperative applications, emerging indications, and risk management
items.abstract: Stellate ganglion block (SGB), an interventional technique that modulates sympathetic activity, has been increasingly investigated beyond traditional pain management in cardiology, neuropsychiatry, and perioperative medicine. This narrative review examines the evolving role of SGB in contemporary anesthesia practice, emphasizing that its effects may extend beyond immediate peripheral sympatholysis to longer-lasting central neural modulation. Technically, ultrasound guidance facilitates precise needle placement and low-volume injection, with improved visualization of relevant anatomy and injectate spread. Dose-finding studies have refined local-anesthetic volume and concentration, whereas continuous blockade may extend sympatholysis in selected refractory conditions. Clinically, SGB has been used in selected pain conditions, including complex regional pain syndrome and herpes zoster-related pain, and has been investigated for non-pain indications such as post-traumatic stress disorder, refractory ventricular arrhythmias, and menopausal vasomotor symptoms. In perioperative settings, SGB has been evaluated for postoperative analgesia, modulation of inflammatory responses, and potential neuroprotective effects. Risk mitigation relies on real-time ultrasound visualization of the needle tip, adjacent vascular structures, and injectate spread, together with predefined management protocols for major complications. Future research should prioritize multicenter prospective studies, standardized procedural parameters, and individualized treatment pathways to support the safe, precise, and evidence-based use of SGB across clinical settings.

items.title: Cumulative multi-threshold intraoperative blood pressure exposure patterns and postoperative mortality
items.abstract: Background Intraoperative hypotension is commonly defined as MAP Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults having non-cardiac, non-obstetric surgery using perioperative electronic health record data. Pressure-time burden and proportion of operative time were calculated across MAP thresholds from 50 to 150 mmHg. Decision-tree analysis using recursive partitioning sequentially grouped patients according to MAP exposure patterns associated with 30-day mortality. Discrimination of the multi-threshold blood-pressure-only model was compared with that of a model restricted to exposure below MAP 65 mmHg. Medication associations were exploratory. Results Among 388,407 patients, 30-day mortality was 1.49%. The multi-threshold model had greater validation discrimination than the MAP 65 mmHg model (AUROC, 0.619 vs. 0.591; ΔAUROC, 0.028; 95% CI, 0.025-0.037; p Conclusions Multi-threshold MAP exposure captured mortality-associated information not represented by exposure below MAP 65 mmHg alone, complementing this clinical threshold. The multi-threshold analysis identified groups with distinct pressure-time exposure patterns, providing a basis for hemodynamic profiling and investigation of hypotension-related outcomes. External validation is needed to assess the reproducibility and discrimination of these groups in other populations, followed by prospective studies to determine whether management informed by these patterns improves outcomes.

Long- versus medium-chain triglycerides in lipid resuscitation therapy for local anesthetic systemic toxicity: Does the length matter? A narrative review
items.abstract: Intravenous lipid emulsion (ILE) is the recommended first-line treatment for local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), particularly when cardiovascular compromise occurs. However, uncertainty persists regarding the optimal lipid formulation, specifically the comparative efficacy of ILEs containing 100% long-chain triglycerides (LCT) versus ILEs containing a 50/50 mixture of medium- and long-chain triglycerides (MCT/LCT), as well as ILEs with a 20% versus 30% lipid concentration. The primary aim of this narrative review was to compare the efficacy of 100% LCT-containing ILEs versus 50% MCT/LCT-containing ILEs by analyzing their respective mechanisms of action in experimental models of local anesthetic-induced cardiovascular toxicity, whereas the secondary objective was to compare ILEs with a 20% versus a 30% lipid concentration. The review also integrates the physiological rationale underlying lipid resuscitation and explores a mechanistically informed framework for interpreting formulation-specific effects of ILEs. A literature search of PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar was conducted from January 1998 through January 2026. Twenty experimental studies were identified-nine in vitro, one ex vivo, and ten in vivo-and qualitatively synthesized according to their principal mechanisms of action, including lipid shuttle, cardiotonic, vascular, and metabolic effects. The available experimental evidence suggests that 100% LCT-containing ILEs provide greater overall cardiovascular recovery than 50% MCT/LCT-containing ILEs, particularly through more effective lipid-shuttle activity and sustained myocardial protection. Conversely, 50% MCT/LCT-containing ILEs demonstrated greater vascular effects in several experimental models. Evidence comparing lipid concentrations was limited to 100% LCT-containing formulations and generally showed greater pharmacokinetic, hemodynamic, and survival effects with a 30% versus a 20% lipid concentration when administered at the same volume. The available evidence is derived exclusively from heterogeneous preclinical experimental models and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than practice-informing. Triglyceride composition and lipid concentration may influence distinct mechanisms contributing to cardiovascular recovery during LAST. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for exploring formulation-phenotype associations but do not establish formulation-specific treatment recommendations. Further experimental and translational studies are needed to determine whether these mechanistic findings translate into clinically meaningful benefits in patients with LAST.

items.title: Inhaled anesthetics and severe neurologic complications in individuals with Venezuelan maternal ancestry carrying the mitochondrial MT-ND4 m.11232 T > C variant: a systematic review
items.abstract: Severe neurologic injury after uncomplicated general anesthesia in previously healthy patients is rare. Since 2021, reports from South America and later from North America and Europe have described catastrophic neurologic deterioration and death after routine general anesthesia in children and adults with Venezuelan maternal ancestry. A homoplasmic mitochondrial DNA variant, MT-ND4 m.11232 T > C (p.Leu158Pro), affecting complex I of the electron transport chain, has emerged as the leading candidate susceptibility factor. This systematic review identified, appraised, and synthesized available evidence linking inhaled anesthetics, in particular sevoflurane, with severe perioperative neurologic complications in carriers of this variant and in individuals with Venezuelan maternal ancestry. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261471143), with searches of major biomedical databases, gray literature, and variant databases. The evidence describes a consistent but incompletely characterized syndrome defined by maternal Venezuelan ancestry, apparent preoperative health, predominant sevoflurane exposure, delayed emergence, and severe basal ganglia injury with frequent death. In patient-derived fibroblasts and cybrids, sevoflurane markedly suppressed complex I-dependent respiration, whereas propofol did not. Incidence, penetrance, and agent-specific risk remain uncertain. Cautious perioperative strategies that avoid volatile anesthetics appear justified.

items.title: From Microbial burden to host response dysregulation: toward host-centered precision medicine in severe pneumonia and pneumonia-associated sepsis
Which spontaneous breathing trial should be used to reproduce post-extubation respiratory effort in COVID-19-related ARDS? A multicenter randomized crossover study
items.abstract: Background Spontaneous breathing trials (SBT) guide extubation decisions in intensive care unit (ICU), predicting the respiratory effort required by the patient after extubation. Different SBTs exist and should be adapted to critical illness. Viral pneumonias such as COVID-19 combine lung injury, sepsis-induced systemic inflammation, and encephalopathy, making classification challenging. The objective was to assess which SBT could be used to reproduce postextubation respiratory effort in COVID-19-related acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) patients. Methods In this multicenter randomized crossover study, COVID-19-related ARDS patients mechanically ventilated at least 24 hours and ready for extubation underwent 3 different 15-minute SBT at random order: pressure support ventilation of 7-cmH2O with positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 0-cmH2O (PSV7PEEP0), PSV 0-cmH2O with PEEP 0-cmH2O (PSV0PEEP0) and T-piece trial. At baseline, end of each SBT, and 20 minutes after extubation, surrogates of respiratory effort were measured: esophageal pressure-time-product (PTPes), PTPes per minute (PTPes.min), swing esophageal pressure (SwingPes), and SwingPes per minute (SwingPes.min). Results Sixty measurements of respiratory effort from 12 patients were analyzed. Median PTPes.min increased from 193.8 [170.8-227.2] cmH2O.s/min at baseline to 236.6 [192.1-313.6] after extubation, with no significant differences between SBTs and postextubation. SwingPes and SwingPes.min were lower during PSV7-PEEP0 than after extubation, with median paired differences of 4.7 (95% CI 0.6-9.8) and 115.3 (95% CI 4.8-297.8), but these differences did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Conclusion No SBT modality differed significantly from post-extubation respiratory effort, suggesting that none could be excluded in COVID-19-related ARDS patients.

items.title: Anticholinergic Drug Burden and Postoperative Delirium: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Introduction Postoperative delirium (POD) is an important postoperative neurocognitive complication, and cumulative anticholinergic drug burden (ADB) may increase its risk by impairing central cholinergic neurotransmission. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to clarify the overall association between ADB scores and POD risk in adult surgical patients. Methods We searched major databases and trial registries through February 2026 for studies that assessed ADB using validated scales and reported POD outcomes in adult surgical patients. Random-effects models pooled SMDs and ORs. Prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses explored heterogeneity and robustness. Risk of bias was assessed using NOS, and evidence certainty was rated using GRADE. Results Ten reports from nine independent cohorts comprising 10,457 participants were included. Patients with POD had higher ADB scores than those without POD (SMD = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.20-0.43). Each one-point increase in continuous ADB was associated with 22% higher odds of POD (OR = 1.22, 95% CI: 1.09-1.37). Both low-to-moderate and high burden were associated with increased POD risk. In scale-specific analyses, the association was significant for ACB. The association was attenuated in studies that excluded patients with cognitive impairment. Methodological quality ranged from moderate to high, and certainty of evidence was low. Conclusions Higher ADB is significantly associated with higher odds of POD, with a graded increase in risk across burden levels. Baseline cognitive impairment appears to amplify this association. These findings support preoperative ADB assessment and medication optimization in vulnerable surgical patients, while highlighting the need for prospective head-to-head comparisons of anticholinergic burden scales. Registration PROSPERO (CRD420261294941).

items.title: Impact of additional tailored Information and music to reduce preoperative anxiety in surgical outpatients: a prospective before-after study
items.abstract: Introduction Non-pharmacological techniques have recently been developed to decrease preoperative anxiety, and music or video may be combined, as in children. This study aims to compare two additional preoperative strategies in adult outpatients. Patients and method This before-after trial was approved by the ethics committee and included adults undergoing ambulatory procedures under general anaesthesia. It compared usual care before surgery and another period with a video of the expected local journey combined with a relaxing music session. After consent, the level of anxiety was measured via the APAIS score, a repeated visual analogue scale for anxiety, and investigators collected preoperative fears. The main objective was to reduce the number of patients with significant preoperative anxiety. Secondary outcomes compared anxiety during the journey, pain, and quality of recovery after surgery. A P-value Results 99 patients were included in each period, and 194 completed the study. The intervention group showed a significant reduction in the rate of patients with significant anxiety at admission in the operating room: 23/95 (24.2%, 95%CI [16.7-33.7]) vs. 43/99 (43.4%, 95%CI [34.1-53.3]) with P = 0.005. Secondary outcomes showed no difference in anxiety after surgery, neither in length of stay nor incidence of PONV. The postoperative level of pain was also statistically reduced (P = 0.033). Conclusion The study suggests that a combined video and music strategy decreases the rate of significant anxiety in patients undergoing outpatient procedures. This low-cost strategy showed a high level of satisfaction and should be encouraged in adults. Trial registration Clinicaltrials.gov: NCT06461052.

items.title: Effect of a Tailored Educational Programme on Adequacy of Anaesthesia and Major Postoperative Complications: A Before–After Quality-Improvement Study in Intermediate- and High-Risk Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: State Entropy (SE) and Surgical Pleth Index (SPI) parameters aim to optimise anaesthetic depth and intraoperative opioid administration, but their impact on postoperative complications remains unclear. Insufficient training and limited decision support may contribute to inconsistent findings. Thus, we evaluated whether tailored training to improve SE and SPI compliance reduced major postoperative complications. METHODS: Adult inpatients undergoing intermediate- to high-risk noncardiac surgery were included in this prospective single-centre before-after study in France. The educational intervention and outcomes were based on the Kirkpatrick framework. All anaesthesia providers were invited to participate voluntarily in lectures and bedside training on SE and SPI monitoring. Training impact was assessed using a composite of major postoperative complications within 28 days as the primary outcome. Secondary outcomes included changes in monitoring practices. RESULTS: Among 1,623 eligible patients, 1,025 were included over a 13-month period (517 before and 508 after training). Of 202 eligible providers, 91 participated in the one-month training programme (45%). After training, simultaneous SE and SPI sensor use increased from 26% to 42% (P < 0.001), and combined SE-SPI compliance increased from 23% to 39% (P < 0.001). Major postoperative complications occurred in 66/517 patients (13%) before and 71/508 patients (14%) after training (P = 0.6). Multivariable and propensity score analyses showed no significant association between the intervention and the primary outcome. CONCLUSION: This training did not reduce the incidence of major postoperative complications, despite improvements in intraoperative monitoring practices. Future educational strategies should strengthen provider engagement and reinforcement to translate improved monitoring practices into clinical benefit. REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT06111248.

items.title: Procedure-specific bleeding risk assessment: a multidisciplinary expert consensus companion to the 2026 periprocedural anticoagulant management guidelines
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Periprocedural anticoagulant management requires balancing thrombotic risk against procedure-specific bleeding risk. Existing procedure bleeding risk classifications are fragmented across specialties, inconsistent in methodology, and rarely extend beyond a few procedural domains, limiting their clinical applicability. OBJECTIVE: To develop a comprehensive, standardized, procedure-specific bleeding risk classification to accompany the 2026 GIHP-SFAR periprocedural anticoagulant management guidelines. METHODS: A formal multidisciplinary consensus was conducted under the auspices of GIHP and SFAR, in collaboration with 24 surgical and interventional specialty societies. For each procedural domain, a working group performed a systematic literature review. Procedures were classified into four tiers: no bleeding risk, low bleeding risk, high bleeding risk, and very high bleeding risk. A specific category was created for procedures carrying particular contextual risk (e.g., anatomical site, patient factors, or need for reversible anticoagulation). Consensus was reached by the full expert panel. RESULTS: Twenty-four procedural domains were classified, ranging from regional anaesthesia and digestive endoscopy to cardiac surgery, neurosurgery, and ophthalmology. Each domain provides a procedure-specific bleeding risk table, with narrative supporting evidence. Procedures warranting delayed resumption of anticoagulation (≥72 hours) or use of short-acting/reversible anticoagulants are identified. The classification covers common and complex surgical scenarios, including those with limited published evidence where structured expert opinion was applied. CONCLUSION: This companion document provides clinicians with a standardized, evidence-based, procedure-specific bleeding risk framework across 24 domains to support individualized periprocedural anticoagulant decisions in daily practice.

items.title: Dysnatremia in critically ill burn patients: incidence, timing and association with kidney outcomes
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Dysnatremia is common in critically ill patients and has been linked to poor outcomes and renal prognosis. Burn patients are particularly vulnerable, but the prognostic significance of dysnatremia in this population remains unclear. METHODS: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of 1,758 burn patients admitted to a French burn center between 2011 and 2023. Dysnatremia was defined as at least one episode of hyponatremia (<135 mmol/L) or hypernatremia (>145 mmol/L) during intensive care unit (ICU) stay. The primary endpoint was the incidence of dysnatremia; secondary endpoints included major adverse kidney events (MAKE) at ICU discharge and acute kidney injury (AKI) occurrence and severity. RESULTS: Dysnatremia occurred in 56.3% of patients (n = 990), with hyponatremia in 50.5% (n = 888) and hypernatremia in 23.8% (n = 418). MAKE at ICU discharge did not differ between hyponatremic and normonatremic patients (12.6% vs. 10.9%, p = 0.304) but was sixfold higher with hypernatremia (32.3% vs. 5.4%, p < 0.001). After adjustment for age and burned total body surface area, hypernatremia was independently associated with MAKE at ICU discharge (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 4.03; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.92-5.56; p < 0.001), whereas hyponatremia was not (aHR 1.15; 95% CI: 0.85-1.55; p = 0.377). Clustering analysis identified three phenotypes: Cluster B (severe burns, worst outcomes), Cluster A (older patients, mostly hyponatremic, intermediate outcomes), and Cluster C (younger patients, mild burns, best outcomes). CONCLUSION: Dysnatremia affects over half of burn patients. Sodium disturbances should be viewed as markers of systemic severity, warranting close monitoring and preventive strategies.

Effect of age on the association between oxygen exposure and mortality in ARDS: a secondary analysis of randomized controlled trials with independent multicenter evaluation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Fractions of inspired oxygen up to 60% in patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation are commonly perceived by clinicians as safe, implying a non-linear association between oxygen exposure and mortality. Also, although it seems pathophysiologically plausible that the association between oxygen exposure and mortality may depend on age, relevant evidence in adult patients is lacking. We examined whether the association between fraction of inspired oxygen and mortality a) is non-linear and b) depends on age. METHODS: We performed a secondary analysis of individual patient-level data from six acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) Network and PETAL Network randomized controlled trials ("ARDSNet cohort"). We assessed linearity of the association between fraction of inspired oxygen and mortality along with the effect of age after adjusting for covariates, including partial pressure of arterial oxygen. We tested our findings in an independent multicenter cohort. RESULTS: In the ARDSNet cohort involving 4953 patients with ARDS, we found that the association between fraction of inspired oxygen and mortality was linear and independent of age (p = 0.655 for the interaction between fraction of inspired oxygen and age). In the independent cohort involving 559 patients with ARDS, we confirmed both the linearity of the association between fraction of inspired oxygen and mortality and the lack of effect of age (p = 0.955 for the interaction). CONCLUSION: Data from the two tested multicenter cohorts suggest that the association between fraction of inspired oxygen and mortality in ARDS may be linear and independent of age.

Dietitian involvement and nutritional care organization in intensive care and perioperative settings in France: a cross-sectional survey of healthcare professionals
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Nutrition is a key component of care for critically ill and surgical patients, but the organization of nutritional care and the involvement of dietitians in ICU and perioperative pathways remain variable. This survey aimed to describe respondent-reported nutritional care organization and dietitian involvement among healthcare professionals working in ICU and perioperative settings in France, with a focus on dietitian availability, clinical involvement, nutritional governance, and selected aspects of perioperative care. METHODS: We conducted a voluntary cross-sectional survey among physicians and dietitians working in French ICU and perioperative settings. The survey was disseminated during the French Society of Anaesthesia and Intensive Care Medicine congress, through national professional nutrition and dietetics networks, and via social media. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics. RESULTS: Overall, 147 professionals responded, mainly ICU physicians and dietitians, and most worked in university hospitals. Among respondents, dietitian availability was reported in 67% of responses, but dedicated time was frequently limited. Involvement was mainly request-based, and participation in medical meetings or ward rounds was uncommon. A medical nutrition lead was identified in 44% of responses, a written nutrition protocol in 50%, and a task-sharing protocol allowing dietitian prescription in 9%. CONCLUSION: Reported practices suggest that dietitians are available in many French ICUs and contribute to perioperative care pathways. However, access to dietetic expertise does not necessarily translate into dedicated staffing, routine multidisciplinary participation, or structured nutritional governance. Strengthening local organization through medical leadership, written protocols, and multidisciplinary collaboration may help improve the implementation of nutritional care.

Postoperative pain management: a national prospective study including 3879 patients
items.abstract: Background Postoperative pain management remains a critical issue in peri-operative medicine, but contemporary national data are lacking. Methods AlgoSFAR 2 was a prospective, multicentre and observational study, conducted in randomly selected French surgical centres. Adult patients undergoing elective surgery were included. Pain was assessed at rest and during mobilization over the first three postoperative days. Secondary outcomes included postoperative opioid consumption and multimodal analgesia strategies defined as the use of at least two non-opioid strategies such as analgesics and/or regional anaesthesia. Results A total of 3879 patients from 80 centres were analysed. While pre-operative and immediate postoperative pain levels at rest were low, pain peaked on day 1, with high interindividual variability, and 6% of patients reported severe pain. Two thirds (66%) did not need any rescue opioids postoperatively. Overall, 95% received multimodal analgesia. Conclusion These results highlight a major change in postoperative pain management in France, with broad adoption of multimodal opioid-sparing strategies. Nonetheless, a minority of patients still experience severe pain, highlighting the need for personalized management. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06487442.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Pre-anaesthetic Evaluation and Perioperative Planning: A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Preanesthetic evaluation is essential for perioperative safety, yet it remains time-consuming, heavily reliant on documentation, and vulnerable to variability in data collection, risk assessment, and clinical decision-making. The increase in surgical cases, patient complexity, and digital health records has created opportunities for artificial intelligence (AI) to assist anesthesiologists in preoperative screening, risk assessment, and perioperative planning. New AI applications in anesthesiology include machine learning models for predicting perioperative risks, natural language processing (NLP) systems for extracting key information from unstructured records, and large language model (LLM)-based tools for documentation support and structured clinical summaries. Studies indicate these systems may enhance workflow efficiency, expand preanesthetic data collection, aid ASA physical status classification, and generate structured recommendations for investigations, optimization, and anesthetic plans, all with clinician oversight. This review explores the current role of AI in preanesthetic evaluation and perioperative planning, focusing on practical uses such as automated history synthesis, investigation choices, risk stratification, preoperative orders, and personalized anesthetic decision support. It also addresses system limitations like hallucination, bias, privacy issues, lack of explainability, and medicolegal concerns. Based on current evidence, AI is best suited as a decision-support tool for clinicians rather than a standalone replacement for anesthesiologists.

Population pharmacokinetics of fibrinogen in postpartum haemorrhage during Caesarean section: a secondary analysis of the TRACES trial
items.abstract: Background In severe postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), hypofibrinogenaemia is strongly associated with bleeding severity. To correct fibrinogen depletion, various fixed dosing regimens have been evaluated, but the optimal fibrinogen dosing regimen remains unknown. To date, fibrinogen pharmacokinetics have only been studied outside haemorrhagic settings (healthy or afibrinogenaemic patients) Methods This ancillary analysis of the TRACES trial assessed fibrinogen kinetics in 142 women with PPH > 800 ml during caesarean section, among which 31 received fibrinogen replacement. Plasma fibrinogen concentrations (n = 593) were measured using the Clauss method. A population pharmacokinetic model was developed using nonlinear mixed-effects modeling. Simulations were performed to estimate loading and maintenance doses required to achieve target fibrinogen concentrations. Results A one-compartment logistic model adequately described plasma fibrinogen levels. Bleeding rate was identified as a key covariate to explain fibrinogen loss rate. Based on the estimated model, an optimised dosing regimen was derived to achieve and maintain predefined target fibrinogen levels. To achieve a target increase of 1 g.L − ¹ in plasma fibrinogen level, the required fibrinogen loading dose is at least 2.7 g for a body weight of 50 kg. To maintain plasma fibrinogen level at a target of 2 g.L − ¹ during a 1000 mL.h − ¹ bleeding rate, a fibrinogen infusion rate of 0.9 g.h − ¹ would be required. Conclusions This work supports that an individualized target-controlled fibrinogen dosing strategy is probably required to effectively correct fibrinogen levels. Integrating such models as a clinical decision support tool into a multimodal strategy that also utilizes viscoelastic testing could optimize PPH management.
