items.title: From Cohort to Outcome: Clarifying Patient Flow and Mortality After Prehospital Transfusion
Answer to Gricourt et al.
Discussing Future Treatment and Care in the ICU : Perspectives From Patients
items.abstract: Introduction Treatment in the intensive care unit (ICU) is usually predicated on curative treatment, but continuing all available treatment options may not always be beneficial for the patient or in line with their wishes. However, patients admitted to the ICU are often assessed as incapable of making decisions regarding their care; hence conversations about wishes for treatment are postponed. This study aimed to investigate the experiences of patients who participated in a conversation concerning treatment and care following ICU discharge based on the Danish version of the Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment (ReSPECT) form. Method Semi‐structured telephone interviews were conducted with patients who had a conversation about future treatment and care with an intensivist using the ReSPECT form during an ICU admission between November 2024 and July 2025. Relatives who participated in the conversation and were present during the interviews were asked to elaborate on their experiences of the conversation's timing and how they felt about participating in the conversation. Data was analysed using content analysis. Results Nineteen patients were included in the study, of whom 15 patients (83%) participated in a telephone interview. Two themes were identified: Timing of the conversation and Clarifying goals of care and options . Based on these, four sub‐themes were identified, two for each theme: Too soon, but not much later ; Wishes in accordance ; Hard, but necessary and Communicating in an understandable manner . Most patients were satisfied with having had a conversation about future treatment and care. Patients found the conversation relevant and necessary. The intensivists were praised for their communication skills and their ability to know and explain recommendations for future treatment and care. However, most patients believed that the conversation was conducted too soon after recovering from intensive care. They would have preferred to have had the conversation later during their admission. Conclusions Most participating ICU patients found a conversation about future treatment and care relevant but preferred it to be held after ICU discharge. Future research should investigate the benefits of incorporating intensivists in these conversations in general wards. Editorial Comment In this prospective study, former ICU patients were interviewed and asked about their experiences and opinions regarding a structured ReSPECT discussion that had been conducted in the end of their ICU stay. The goal of that interview was advance care planning, involving the patients and their family members. This study reports a qualitative analysis of interviews conducted at least 4 weeks later. Two main themes and four subthemes were identified. Almost all patients remembered having had the discussion, but the content was less clearly remembered. ICU physicians’ communication skills were appreciated. The study assesses a function of our daily work from patient and family perspective, and discusses important issues such as optimal timing of the advance care planning.
items.limitations: However, the difficulty in finding suitable patients is a limitation. And as described in the introduction, patients are often assessed as incapable of informed decision‐making due to reduced or altered consciousness. This assumption was also supported by the fact that most project sites had trouble finding eligible patients for this study. Therefore, the participants cannot be assessed as representatives of the ICU patients most in need of ACP. Furthermore, the physicians themselves defined ‘severe comorbidities’ with no explicit definition making room for a substantial subjective interpretation of the term ‘severe comorbidities’ and assessing patients eligible for participation. Also, not having former ICU patients and relatives included in the research process is a limitation. Considering the research question, their views and input would have been valuable when designing the study and would have strengthened the study's ability to capture relevant and meaningful data. In future studies, this would be recommendable. Most of the patients in this study were content to have had a conversation about future treatment and care and found it relevant and necessary. The intensivists were praised for their communication skills and their ability to explain recommendations for future treatment and care.

items.title: Attitudes Towards Clinical Research in Acute Illness—A Population‐Based Survey in Sweden
items.abstract: Background To investigate the attitudes of the Swedish population towards participation in research and preferences regarding legally authorized representative when a participant is unable to give informed consent. Methods A national survey conducted by a Swedish analysis and research company on a representative sample of the Swedish population on two occasions (2020 and 2023). The questions were based on the prerequisite that the respondents could not provide informed consent on their own. The questionnaire included two scenarios: one allowing time to consult a legal representative (non‐emergency) and one where research had to start immediately, before consulting a legal representative (emergency). Results In total, 2086 respondents were included in the analysis. A majority were positive to participate in both non‐emergency (81% [1690/2086]) and emergency research (82% [1714/2086]) in situations where they would be unable to provide informed consent. Next of kin was preferred as a surrogate decision maker in 81% (1686/2086) of respondents and less than 1% (11/2086) preferred an unrelated legal representative such as an attorney. Conclusion This study shows that in a representative sample of the Swedish population there is a positive attitude towards research in the acute setting and in critical illness, even in situations when a potential participant cannot receive information and provide informed consent and that a next of kin is the preferred legally authorized representative. Editorial Comment This article reports results of a national survey from Sweden, where it shows that, among Swedish citizens, there appears to be broad acceptance of allowing family members to act as surrogate decision‐makers in informed consent decisions for study participation among acutely critically ill patients who cannot perform consent themselves. At this point in time, Swedish law does not allow this.
items.limitations: Our study has several limitations worth commenting. First, the respondents were presented with hypothetical scenarios and questions, although based on real world scenarios, and it is not certain that the responders would have the same view when being exposed to an authentic situation, as it might be difficult to imagine oneself and a relative in such a situation. However, a high rate of consent to continue in the research projects among survivors in recent critical care randomized clinical trials, performed in Sweden, where a deferred consent approach was used suggests that the results are valid also in authentic situations. The questions in our survey might also be biased towards certain answers even though the questions were formulated to be as neutral as possible and reviewed by several persons outside the study. We performed two surveys, 2 years apart and the fact that the first survey was distributed in the middle of the Covid‐19 pandemic when the public debate encompassed critical illness and clinical research may have affected the results. Another limitation is that we have not corrected analyses for multiplicity. In conclusion, this study shows that in a representative sample of the Swedish population there is a positive attitude towards research in the acute setting and in critical illness, even in a situation when a potential research participant cannot receive information and provide an informed consent. The study indicates that the preferred legally authorized representative is a close relative.

items.title: Characteristics and Outcomes After General Anaesthesia in Elderly Patients: A Nationwide Cohort Study
items.abstract: Background Elderly patients are more frail and have a higher burden of comorbidity, which could influence the risk of complications after anaesthesia. The aim of this study was to describe the elderly patient population undergoing general anaesthesia in Denmark. Methods This was a national registry‐based observational cohort study of adult patients (≥ 18 years) undergoing general anaesthesia in Denmark in 2020 and 2021, with a primary focus on patients 80 years and above. Patient and procedure characteristics of interest were age, sex, BMI, ASA classification, Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, comorbidities, type of procedure, and class of priority. The primary outcome of interest was 30‐day mortality. Secondary outcomes included acute kidney injury within 7 days, length of hospital stay, and number of days in the ICU. Results A total of 453,133 cases of general anaesthesia in 328,951 unique patients in Denmark during 2020 and 2021 were included in this study. Of these, 25,955 (8%) patients were 80 years of age and above. Elderly patients undergoing general anaesthesia were of higher ASA classification, suffered from a higher degree of comorbidity measured by Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, had a lower proportion of elective procedures and a higher proportion of expedited and urgent procedures. Mortality for all patients at 30 days was 1.5% ( n = 4814). While mortality was low for cases aged between 18 and 65 years, 30‐day mortality increased for each year after 65 years of age even after adjusting for covariates. Mortality was especially high for patients with high Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, high ASA classification, and for non‐elective procedures. Conclusion In this nationwide registry‐based cohort study, we described the elderly patient population undergoing general anaesthesia in Denmark. We found that 30‐day mortality increased for each year after 65 years of age even after adjusting for covariates. Editorial Comment This large cohort study from Denmark assesses perioperative case factors including age, comorbidity and more, then describing different risk levels for 30 day mortality, particularly with advanced age.
items.limitations: The findings of our study need to be interpreted in the context of some limitations. First, not all hospitals reported all cases of general anaesthesia to the database in 2020 and 2021, and our data were collected during the COVID‐19 pandemic. The generalizability of our results may be affected by these factors. However, as discussed in our related works, data completeness is estimated to be high and did not vary substantially between 2020 and 2021. In addition, COVID‐19 related mortality and capacity strain was low in Denmark compared to other countries.

items.title: Serious Adverse Events in Adult ICU Patients: A Substudy of the PATIENCE Cohort
items.abstract: Introduction Prokinetic agents are used to enhance upper gastrointestinal motility, but adverse events related to these agents are poorly described. We aimed to provide detailed epidemiological data on predefined serious adverse events ( SAEs ) in a cohort of adult intensive care unit ( ICU ) patients with and without prokinetic treatment. We hypothesised that all predefined SAEs would occur in both patients treated and those not treated with prokinetic agents, and that a higher number of SAEs would occur among patients treated with prokinetic agents for more than three consecutive days. Methods This substudy of the inception cohort study “Prokinetic agents in adult intensive care unit patients” included acutely admitted adult ICU patients. The prokinetic agents assessed (exposures) were erythromycin, metoclopramide, domperidone, and prucalopride. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients experiencing at least one episode of five pre‐specified SAEs during ICU stay (cardiac arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, vomiting with aspiration, diarrhoea, extrapyramidal symptoms). Secondary outcomes were (1) proportion of patients experiencing each SAE , (2) the proportion of patients experiencing any of the SAEs after prokinetic treatment stratified by longest consecutive treatment duration, (3) time from index ICU admission to first SAE and (4) time from prokinetic initiation to first SAE . All analyses were descriptive, summarising SAE proportions and timing overall and according to prokinetic exposure. Results Among 1440 adult ICU patients, 710 SAEs occurred in 354 patients (24.6%), most commonly cardiac arrhythmias (199/1440, 13.8%). Across the exposure groups, the proportion of patients experiencing one or more SAEs ranged from 23.0% to 42.5%. Among patients treated with prokinetic agents for > 3 consecutive days, 14/59 (23.7%) experienced a SAE , which was similar to the proportion observed among patients not receiving prokinetic agents (291/1.253, 23.2%). Most SAEs occurred on median Day 2 after ICU admission and on median Day 3 after prokinetic initiation. Conclusion One in four adult ICU patients experienced at least one SAE , with cardiac arrhythmias being the most frequent. Among patients receiving prokinetic agents, the proportion experiencing one or more SAEs ranged from 23.0% to 42.5% across treatment groups. The findings from this study may help inform the design of a future clinical trial. Editorial Comment This analysis presents reported serious adverse event observed in an ICU trial cohort assessing gastrointestinal prokinetic drug effects. Serious adverse events were reported frequently in both the drug treatment groups and the comparison (no prokinetic drug) group. Types of serious adverse events reported are presented.

items.title: The Effect of Perioperative Video Interventions on Postoperative Pain Control: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Introduction Postoperative pain is a major cause of suffering and is linked to serious complications, including delayed wound healing, increased cardiovascular risk, delayed rehabilitation, and chronic postsurgical pain. Modifiable psychological factors influence pain outcomes, and preliminary evidence suggests video interventions can reduce preoperative anxiety and improve patient satisfaction. We hypothesized that video interventions could improve postoperative pain control. Therefore, the aim of the current systematic review was to summarize all previous research and investigate the effects of perioperative video interventions on pain levels and/or analgesic consumption. Methods The review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024596389) and followed the PRISMA Guidelines. We searched PubMed, EMBASE, CINAHL, Academic Search, and the Cochrane Central register of controlled trials from inception to October 2025 for randomized controlled trials in adult surgical patients. Trials assessing any perioperative video interventions reporting on postoperative pain intensity and/or analgesic consumption were included. Data was extracted independently by two authors, and data synthesis was qualitative due to significant heterogeneity. Risk of bias was assessed using the Revised Cochrane risk‐of‐bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2). Results Forty‐four trials were included. Of the 42 trials assessing pain, 11 (26%) reported significantly lower pain in the intervention group. Of the 19 trials measuring analgesic consumption, eight (42%) reported significantly lower consumption in the intervention group. Only two trials demonstrated a benefit for both co‐primary outcomes. Significant improvements in secondary outcomes, including anxiety, physical function, and satisfaction, were reported in 26 trials. Most trials were judged as having a high risk of bias. Conclusion The current systematic review suggests that perioperative video interventions may improve acute postoperative pain control, although effects are inconsistent across trials. Future research should focus on identifying patient and intervention characteristics that predict efficacy to guide clinical implementation. Editorial Comment This trustworthy systematic review presents an overview of current research findings for application of perioperative video‐based treatments as part of managing postoperative pain. While this approach shows promise, more definitive evidence may be needed to justify more widespread implementation.

items.title: Propofol in Exhaled Air and Plasma During Paedfusor Target‐Controlled Infusion in Children
items.abstract: Background Target‐controlled infusion (TCI) algorithms for propofol are widely employed, but inter‐individual variability in achieved plasma concentrations highlights the likely potential value of real‐time monitoring. This prospective observational study evaluated the Exhaled Drug Monitor (Edmon) for online estimation of exhaled propofol concentrations ( C A ) as a proxy for plasma propofol concentrations ( C P ) in children. We also explored the relationships between Paedfusor‐estimated concentrations ( C E–P ) and C P , and between C P and Bispectral Index (BIS). Methods Children undergoing propofol‐based anaesthesia with the Paedfusor TCI model had continuous recordings of C A (parts per billion [ppb]) and C E–P , with BIS values available in a subset of patients, as electrode placement was sometimes incompatible with the surgical field. Four arterial blood samples were obtained to determine C P . Linear mixed‐model analyses were employed to assess the relationships between variables. Results Twenty‐six children aged 3–10 years were included. During maintenance of anaesthesia at a TCI target concentration of 3.0 μg mL −1 , C A lagged behind C P by 4 min. At this delay, the slope (gain) for estimation of C P from C A was 0.36 μg mL −1 ppb −1 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.08 to 0.64, p = 0.015) and the intercept (offset) 1.16 μg mL −1 (95% CI −0.52 to 2.84, p = 0.16), RSquare 0.63. The pooled median absolute performance error based on samples obtained at 20 and 30 min after induction was 8.8% for the Edmon and 13.5% for the Paedfusor. C P was 19%, 16% and 1% higher than Paedfusor predictions at 20 min, 30 min and end of surgery, respectively. In an exploratory analysis, BIS values decreased by 4.8 for each 1 μg mL −1 increase in C P . Conclusion This exploratory study demonstrates that online monitoring of exhaled propofol during surgery is feasible in children. The Edmon provided estimates of C P comparable with those of the Paedfusor algorithm during maintenance of anaesthesia, but its use is limited by a complex setup and a 4‐min time lag relative to plasma concentrations. Editorial Comment In this study, propofol infusion in children using a target‐controlled infusion was performed, and propofol concentration in exhaled air was sampled intermittently and measured. This assessment demonstrated practical feasibility aspects of this sampling and measurement along with challenges for clinical application. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04150432): URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04150432?term=NCT04150432&rank=1

items.title: Development, Implementation and Mixed‐Methods Evaluation of a Multicomponent Peer‐Support Programme in an Anaesthesiology Department
items.abstract: Background Healthcare professionals working in anaesthesiology are exposed to frequent emotionally challenging situations. Many well‐being initiatives focus on individual coping or support after major events, whereas less attention has been given to organisationally embedded support for everyday work‐related challenges. We aimed to describe the development, implementation, uptake and staff experience of a department‐wide peer‐support programme. Methods We conducted a single‐centre, uncontrolled pre–post mixed‐methods implementation and evaluation study in a university hospital anaesthesiology department. Kern's six‐step approach guided development and implementation of a multicomponent programme comprising education about well‐being and psychological safety, leadership modelling, local change champions, structured collegial conversations and brief team defusing. Evaluation combined pre‐ and post‐intervention surveys, implementation/process data and post‐intervention group interviews. Survey outcomes across five dimensions—well‐being, coping, teamwork, psychological safety and patient safety culture—were exploratory. Results Approximately 80% of staff were trained in structured collegial conversations; 55% of post‐intervention respondents reported participating in at least one structured collegial conversation and 35% in at least one defusing. Across the five survey dimensions there was no consistent pattern of change. In exploratory analyses, the proportion of respondents with coping scores in the highest quartile increased from 31.3% to 42.0% (OR 1.59, 95% CI 1.08–2.34), while the proportion reporting ‘being new’ as a source of emotional burden decreased from 14.0% to 6.8% (OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.23–0.86). Group interview participants described a shared language for discussing challenging experiences, increased attention to colleagues' support needs and value in the structured listening approach. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the uncontrolled design and multiple exploratory outcomes. Conclusion A multicomponent peer‐support programme was implemented with substantial staff participation in an anaesthesiology department. The study provides evidence about implementation, uptake and staff experience, but does not establish that the programme caused improvements in well‐being or organisational culture. Leadership engagement, local champions and integration into existing departmental structures appeared important to implementation. Editorial Comment The present study describes the implementation of a departmental peer‐support programme addressing everyday emotional challenges in anaesthesiology. Substantial participation and positive qualitative accounts suggest that structured conversations can be integrated into clinical practice. However, inconsistent survey findings and the uncontrolled design preclude strong conclusions about effectiveness.

items.title: A Survey of Clinician‐Reported Management of Hypernatremia in the ICU
items.abstract: Background Hypernatremia is frequent in the intensive care unit (ICU) and is associated with adverse outcomes. Despite its prevalence, robust evidence to guide treatment is lacking, and global practice patterns are largely unknown. We investigated global treatment preferences and clinicians' willingness to enroll patients in a randomized trial to inform its feasibility. Methods This international cross‐sectional online survey comprised 20 primarily closed‐ended questions, using five‐point Likert‐scale responses, across four themes: treatment method, threshold, correction rate, and opinion on a proposed trial. Respondents considered a clinical vignette of hypernatremia developing before or during ICU admission, excluding dehydration and chronic causes. It was distributed to ICU physicians worldwide. Results The survey was sent to 3053 ICU physicians in 17 countries, with 1051 respondents, yielding a response rate of 34%. Of respondents, 74% were consultants, and 26% were residents. The mean ICU experience was 14 years. Increasing free water intake via enteral route was the most frequently reported treatment strategy (80% reporting “often” or “always”). Moderate hypernatremia (plasma sodium 151–156 mmol/L) was the most frequently reported threshold for initiating correction (533/892, 60%). 45% (396/888) preferred a correction rate of 8–12 mmol/L/day, and 41% (366/888) of < 8 mmol/L/day, with the remainder having no correction rate target or correction rate target of > 12 mmol/L/day. 74% (654/882) reported no barriers to enrolling eligible patients in the proposed trial. Conclusion Among ICU physicians, correction of hypernatremia is mostly achieved by increasing free water intake using hypotonic fluids, predominantly via the enteral route. Most clinicians initiate treatment once hypernatremia reaches a moderate level, aiming for a correction rate of < 12 mmol/L/day. Most clinicians expressed willingness to enroll eligible patients in the proposed trial. Editorial Comment This survey study aimed to sample physician preferences for treatment of hypernatremia when on their way to or in the ICU. This study sampled respondents in many countries, and based on different phases of treatment and assessment, as well as participant willingness for a future treatment trial.

items.title: Inter‐Individual Variation in LUNG Mechanics Assessed by the Non‐Invasive PEEP ‐Step Method During Laparoscopic and Robotic Surgery Indicates Need for Individualized Ventilatory Settings
items.abstract: Background During laparoscopic surgery, abdominal carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) insufflation in the supine position and with head‐down tilt for robotic surgery increases abdominal pressure and pushes the diaphragm cranially. This causes a decrease in end‐expiratory lung volume and in lung and chest wall compliance. These effects can be counteracted by the application of PEEP. Our study aimed to measure lung and chest wall mechanics during laparoscopic surgery using a non‐invasive method (PEEP‐step method) and to determine the optimal PEEP level for each patient. Methods Thirty‐two patients scheduled for abdominal surgery participated in this observational study with pneumoperitoneum. Fourteen patients underwent surgery for pelvic conditions in head‐down position and 18 in supine position. Data from the ventilator was collected and analysed with a dedicated software, which calculated lung compliance and transpulmonary pressure from a two‐step PEEP increase. Measurements were performed after induction, after pneumoperitoneum in supine/tilt head‐down and before emergence. Results Lung and chest wall compliance decreased during CO 2 insufflation with high individual variation, and we observed a≈90% increase in transpulmonary driving pressure. After CO 2 ‐desufflation, lung and chest wall compliance returned to near baseline levels on a group level. However, 19 patients had a remaining reduction in lung compliance, six with 20%–50%. Optimal PEEP level calculated by the software was twice the clinical routine level. Conclusions The study found substantial individual variation in lung compliance during laparoscopic surgery in patients without evident lung disease. This variability does not align well with respiratory system compliance. The findings highlight the need for individualized ventilator settings based on lung‐ rather than respiratory system mechanics. The PEEP‐step method may be a non‐invasive, real‐time bedside tool to identify patients who would benefit from higher PEEP to preserve lung volume and possibly prevent postoperative complications. Editorial Comment Laparascopic surgical conditions can affect lung mechanics, though not always predictably. This study examined how a test of higher or lower PEEP directly after anaesthesia induction might inform PEEP optimization in the same cases undergoing laparoscopic surgery. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04484727, 2022‐05‐01)

items.title: Streamlining the Evidence‐to‐Practice Pathway With Computerised Decision Support in Anaesthesiology and Critical Care: A Qualitative Study of Clinician and System‐Level Interest Holder Perspectives Across Five Scandinavian Countries
items.abstract: Background Implementing evidence‐based recommendations in anaesthesiology and critical care remains challenging due to guideline, workflow and contextual barriers. Guideline‐based computerised clinical decision support systems (CDSS), embedded in structured pathways linking international guidelines to Scandinavian‐endorsed recommendations and delivered via electronic health records, may help strengthen the evidence‐to‐practice pathway. This study aimed to explore perceived barriers and facilitators to their use. Methods This qualitative study interviewed 10 clinicians (anaesthesiologists and intensivists; specialists and non‐specialists; < 40 and ≥ 40 years; male and female) and nine system‐level stakeholders (hospital and health authority representatives) from Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. We integrated endorsed international guidelines into a CDSS providing patient‐specific reminders linked to recommendations, as well as shared decision‐making tools and decision‐analytic components. Using a simulation application, participants explored the CDSS in a demo electronic health record. Through a framework analysis based on the GUIDES checklist, we categorised perspectives as barriers, facilitators or suggestions. Results Clinicians and system‐level interest holders expressed broad interest in this multifunctional CDSS to support evidence‐based, patient‐centred care and appreciated the collaborative international pathway facilitated by digital tools. Key themes included the challenges hospitals face in translating international guidelines into up‐to‐date, locally adapted guidance. Artificial intelligence (AI) was perceived as having the potential to both enhance and challenge traditional CDSS. Opportunities were identified to strengthen shared decision‐making for major decisions through the proposed system. Finally, participants highlighted the potential value of using a decision‐analytic tool to prioritise reminders, although the tool was considered conceptually challenging in its current form and would require clearer presentation before being applied in CDSS. Conclusions This prototype study indicates support for a multifunctional CDSS. Building on the barriers and facilitators identified in this study, interviewees advocated for real‐world evaluation with particular attention to sustainable implementation. Editorial Comment This study aimed to describe how ICU clinicians experience interaction in a simulated electronic health record where there were chosen elements of decision support based on international treatment guidelines incorporated into the simulation. Participants were interviewed for their perceptions of what types of decision support might be most helpful to support their clinical work in future patient information and management systems.

items.title: Biomarkers in Patients With Acute Ischaemic Stroke Undergoing Thrombectomy Compared With Controls: A Pilot Study
items.abstract: Background Detection of cerebral ischaemia is challenging in patients who are anaesthetised, sedated or have reduced levels of consciousness, as neurological examination is difficult or even impossible to assess. Furthermore, as some patients cannot be transported for radiology, for example during surgery, a reliable blood biomarker for detecting acute cerebral events would be of considerable clinical value. We aimed to compare levels of brain injury biomarkers glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light chain (NfL), and total tau (tau) in patients with acute ischaemic stroke (AIS) undergoing endovascular thrombectomy under general anaesthesia or sedation to controls undergoing non‐cerebral surgery under general anaesthesia. These biomarkers were chosen because previous studies have demonstrated their potential as blood biomarkers of acute cerebral injury and ischaemic stroke. Methods In this prospective, observational pilot study, conducted at the Sahlgrenska University Hospital, Gothenburg, Sweden, between 2021 and 2024, GFAP, NfL, and tau were analysed using the Simoa Neurology 4‐plex assay, before thrombectomy or surgery and at 2‐ and 24 h thereafter. Results Blood samples from 21 patients with AIS and 19 controls were analysed. GFAP concentrations in patients with AIS increased significantly from baseline to 24 h (median 301.0 → 1443.0 pg/mL; p = 0.001) and were higher than in controls at all time points ( p < 0.01). In the controls there was no significant increase in GFAP from baseline to 24 h ( p = 0.449). NfL and tau increased significantly in patients with AIS ( p = 0.001 and 0.002) but also in the controls ( p = 0.001 and 0.047). Conclusion GFAP and NfL concentrations were higher in patients with acute ischaemic stroke than in surgical controls at all sampling time points, whereas tau differed only after 24 h. Unlike NfL and tau, GFAP did not increase significantly in controls, suggesting that it may be less influenced by anaesthesia and surgery. These findings support further evaluation of GFAP as a potential biomarker of acute cerebral injury in perioperative and critical care settings. Editorial Comment A biomarker of ischaemic cerebral injury could be attractive to support treatments to protect brain health during anaesthesia and surgery. In a pilot study, glial fibrillary acidic protein emerged as a potential candidate as it was increased in patients undergoing endovascular thrombectomy for large‐vessel ischaemic stroke compared to anaesthetised patients undergoing non‐cerebral surgery. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03919370

items.title: Correction to “Ephedrine for Reducing Onset Time of Rocuronium in Elderly Patients: A Randomised Study”
Avoidance Versus Use of Neuromuscular Blocking Agents for Optimising Video Laryngoscopy‐Assisted Tracheal Intubation—A Systematic Review With Meta‐Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis
items.abstract: Background Tracheal intubation during anaesthesia carries risks, and difficult intubation can lead to severe complications. Neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) are widely recommended to improve intubation conditions, but they have potential adverse effects. Video laryngoscopy is widely used, yet evidence on the role of NMBAs in this setting is sparse. We aimed to assess whether avoidance versus use of NMBAs affects first‐pass success and intubation conditions during video laryngoscopy in adults. Method Randomised controlled trials ( RCTs ) comparing avoidance versus use of NMBAs for tracheal intubation in adults during video laryngoscopy were included. The primary outcome was failed first‐pass intubation, as defined by the individual trials. Secondary outcomes were failed intubation, adverse effects ( AEs ) and serious adverse effects ( SAEs ), and acceptable intubation conditions. Furthermore, trial sequential analysis ( TSA ) was undertaken. Results 9483 records were screened. Eight RCTs (744 participants) met the inclusion criteria. The primary outcome was extractable from seven trials (690 participants). Individual trial estimates showed either no clear effect or an increased risk of failed first‐pass intubation when NMBAs were avoided. We found a statistically non‐significant RR: 1.81 (95% CI: 0.93–3.55, p = 0.08, Cochran's Q = 12.0, p = 0.04, I 2 = 58%, D 2 = 74%, TSA adjusted RR: 1.77, TSA adjusted 95% CI: 0.48–6.50, GRADE = very low certainty of evidence) comparing avoidance versus use of NMBAs. TSA showed that the trial sequential monitoring boundaries were not crossed, and the required information size of 2334 was not achieved. Conclusion The effect of avoidance of NMBAs for facilitating video laryngoscopy‐assisted tracheal intubation in adult patients is uncertain (very low certainty), and the required information size was not reached. Editorial Comment This systematic review assessed trial evidence concerning whether or not muscle relaxant use is related to first pass failure in intubation attempts using video laryngoscopy. Evidence to date does not support a clear conclusion on whether avoidance of muscle relaxants in this context is beneficial or not, at least for first pass intubation success, though the evidence has very low certainty for this question.

items.title: Digital Versus in‐Person Pre‐Anaesthetic Assessment and Postoperative Outcomes in Low‐Risk Patients: An Observational Study
items.abstract: Background Pre‐anaesthetic assessment is essential for identifying perioperative risk and optimising patient safety. Digital alternatives, including video consultation and structured electronic health record ( EHR ) review, may improve efficiency, but comparative evidence regarding postoperative safety remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate postoperative outcomes across pre‐anaesthetic assessment through EHR review, video consultation, and in‐person assessment. We hypothesised that patients selected for digital pre‐anaesthetic assessment within a structured triage system would have similar low 30‐day rates of major postoperative complications compared with in‐person assessment. Methods We conducted a single‐centre cohort study at Copenhagen University Hospital—Rigshospitalet, Denmark, including adult patients undergoing elective otorhinolaryngologic, oral, or maxillofacial surgery. Patients underwent pre‐anaesthetic assessment by one of three modalities: in‐person consultation, EHR review, or video consultation. The primary outcome was a composite of major postoperative complications within 30 days, including all‐cause mortality, intensive care unit admission, bleeding requiring transfusion, infection requiring antibiotics, or hospital readmission. A multivariable generalised linear model with a log‐link function was used to estimate adjusted relative risks (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results A total of 862 patients were included (in‐person n = 300; EHR review n = 300; video consultation n = 262). Patients in the in‐person group were older and had a higher comorbidity burden. Using in‐person as reference, neither video consultation nor EHR review showed a significantly different risk of major postoperative complications. Hospital readmission was lower in both digital groups in pairwise comparisons with the in‐person group. Results were consistent across sensitivity analyses, including inverse probability weighting and win ratio analysis. Conclusion Patients selected for digital pre‐anaesthetic assessment had low rates of major postoperative complications. However, substantial baseline differences between groups indicate that assessment modality was strongly linked to clinical triage and baseline patient risk, thereby limiting direct comparison between pathways. Thus, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence or non‐inferiority between pathways. Editorial Comment Preoperative anesthesia assessment is managed in different ways, based on local preferences logistics and resource availability, and perceived perioperative risk for complications. This study assessed this process for planned surgery in section at a university hospital. Those during a number of recent years chosen for in‐person preoperative assessment (for any reason) were compared to those who had some form of digital assessment chosen by the anesthesia personnel. The selection process for in‐person preoperative assessment seemed to identify those who had a higher chance of a major postoperative complication.

items.title: Predicting Gastrointestinal Complications After Cardiac Surgery From Mean Arterial Blood Pressure Under a Data‐Driven Threshold for Hypotension: Protocol for an Advanced Database Study
items.abstract: Background Hypotension during cardiopulmonary bypass may increase the risk of gastrointestinal complications due to insufficient splanchnic autoregulatory capacity. We hypothesize that both duration and level of blood pressure below a data‐driven threshold during cardiopulmonary bypass are associated with the risk of gastrointestinal complications. Methods Patients who underwent cardiac surgery at Copenhagen University Hospital, Rigshospitalet, during 2018–2022 will be included if they underwent on‐pump valve surgery, coronary artery bypass grafting, and/or surgery on the ascending aorta. The primary outcome is major gastrointestinal complications within 30 days, defined as acute intestinal ischemia, abdominal surgery, bowel perforation, or gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Secondary endpoints are serious gastrointestinal complications, delayed recovery of bowel function, cholinesterase inhibitor administration, and 30‐day mortality. The exposure is the exposure to lower blood pressure, calculated as the product of the duration and level of blood pressure below a data‐driven threshold. To identify the optimal threshold, we split the population in a training (75%) and validation cohort (25%). In the training cohort we will identify the threshold with the highest area under the receiver operating curve for the primary outcome. The selected threshold will then be applied to quantify the exposure to lower blood pressure for each patient. Patients will be grouped using a modified Youden's index (weighing sensitivity 80%) as a cutoff for high versus low exposure to lower blood pressure, and association with the study endpoints will be determined in the validation cohort. Conclusion Under the assumption of pressure‐dependent perfusion outside of an autoregulatory plateau, the exposure to blood pressure below a threshold might reflect the risk of gastrointestinal complications more accurately than point measures or averages. The results from this study may lead to relevant hypotheses for prospective testing.

items.title: Anaphylaxis: Early history and when did anaesthesia get involved?
Building sustainable resilient health systems: The Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists statement on desflurane
items.abstract: Climate change is recognised as a public health emergency requiring urgent and decisive action. The adverse effects on the environment from delivering healthcare are well established, and identifying areas for positive change that are under our direct control as anaesthetists is imperative. Desflurane, a volatile anaesthetic gas, has significantly greater negative environmental and financial impacts, with little benefit to patient safety or quality of care, compared with clinically equivalent alternatives. In this context, the Australian and New Zealand College of Anaesthetists released a statement on desflurane in 2024 to provide balanced guidance for reducing desflurane consumption based on current evidence and expert consensus opinion. This article summarises the background for the statement and presents the ‘ANZCA Statement on Desflurane’ verbatim.

items.title: Media Review: Resuscitation and the origins of intensive/critical care medicine TrubuhovichRonald V. Resuscitation and the origins of intensive/critical care medicine. Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society: Melbourne, Australia, 2025; 224 pp. ISBN: 978-1-876980-85-6.
The DayCOR clinical quality registry: Recording patient-reported measures in day care anaesthesia
items.abstract: Day case surgery is changing, with older and sicker patients presenting, new procedures occurring and many previously inpatient procedures converted to day-stay. The impact of these changes and additions, especially the management of elderly patients, was assessed using a digital survey of patient-reported measures commencing in March 2018. Running initially in two hospitals, spreading to include a large group of Private Hospitals in Melbourne, the survey was offered to all patients attending the facilities, following an introduction of the survey process in patient admission papers with consent obtained on the day of surgery. A 15-question digital questionnaire was sent to each consenting patient by text and email 24 h post-discharge. The patient could opt out at that stage by not opening the message; 242,025 adult patients responded (response rate of 84%), with 4.5% opting out and 9% failing to complete the survey. An ‘Alert,’ generated digitally for any problem identified in the response, was emailed to the treating anaesthetist and to an oversight group comprised of an anaesthetist, a nurse and an administrator to facilitate appropriate action and early resolution. This digital survey saves the staff costs associated with initiating individual patient contact and fully satisfied the requirements for patient-reported outcome measures and experience measures. As well as early indication of the patient’s postoperative course, confirmation of the ability to manage the elderly patient and the reliability of transferring inpatient procedures to day case management were indicated.

items.title: Safety and efficacy of volatile sedatives in critically ill patients receiving mechanical ventilation: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Volatile sedatives are increasingly utilised for sedation in critically ill patients receiving invasive mechanical ventilation. Despite numerous randomised controlled trials and observational studies comparing volatile sedation to intravenous sedation, questions regarding its safety and efficacy persist. A systematic search was performed in PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Web of Science databases for studies published up to July 2025. The analysis included randomised controlled trials and observational studies that compared the use of volatile sedation with intravenous sedation in patients admitted to the intensive care unit for mechanical ventilation. Eligible studies involved adults aged ⩾18 years, requiring mechanical ventilation, and utilising either volatile or intravenous sedatives. They also needed to report at least one outcome of interest: incidence of delirium, mortality, intensive care unit length of stay, or duration of mechanical ventilation. From 3182 identified publications, fifteen studies were included in the systematic review. Volatile sedation was not associated with a significant difference in the incidence of delirium compared to intravenous sedation (risk ratio 0.72; 95% confidence interval 0.38–1.34), mortality (risk ratio 0.97; 95% confidence interval 0.80–1.17), intensive care unit length of stay (mean difference 0.28 days; 95% confidence interval −1.74 to 2.30), or duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference −37.20 h; 95% confidence interval −78.60 to 4.20). Volatile sedation was not associated with significant differences in mechanical ventilation duration, delirium incidence, intensive care unit length of stay, or mortality compared to intravenous sedation. Further large-scale, high-quality randomised trials are needed to clarify its clinical benefit in critical care settings.

items.title: Prognostic significance of nucleated red blood cells in trauma patients
items.abstract: Nucleated red blood cells are early erythroid precursors typically confined to the bone marrow. Their appearance in peripheral blood reflects stress erythropoiesis and has been linked to hypoxia and systemic inflammation. While nucleated red blood cells have prognostic value in sepsis and critical illness, their significance in trauma remains poorly understood. This study aimed to evaluate the prognostic value of nucleated red blood cells during the first 10 days in the intensive care unit following severe trauma, and their association with 30-day mortality. We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study including 1636 adult trauma patients admitted to the Reims Level-1 Trauma Center between January 2019 and March 2025, recorded in the TraumaBase © registry. Nucleated red blood cell counts were measured daily for the first 10 intensive care unit days. K-means clustering identified four nucleated red blood cell phenotypes based on temporal patterns. Outcomes included 10- and 30-day mortality, incidence of acute respiratory distress syndrome, septic shock, mechanical ventilation, and length of stay. Survival analyses used Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age, Injury Severity Score, Simplified Acute Physiology Score II, and the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment, and propensity-weighted regression assessed dichotomised nucleated red blood cell status. Nucleated red blood cells were detected in 221 patients (13.5%). Phenotype classification revealed: transient early nucleated red blood cells (phenotype 1), single peak (phenotype 2), multiple intermittent peaks (phenotype 3), and persistent elevation (phenotype 4). Phenotype 2 was associated with reduced 10-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 0.06, 95% confidence intervals 0.01–0.46), while phenotype 4 exhibited markedly increased mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 9.6, 95% confidence intervals 2.23–41.4, P < 0.001). Nucleated red blood cell+ patients had higher risks of acute respiratory distress syndrome, septic shock, mechanical ventilation, and 30-day mortality. Kaplan–Meier curves confirmed significant differences in survival across phenotypes (log-rank P < 0.001). Nucleated red blood cell presence, particularly persistent elevation, identifies trauma patients at higher risk of adverse outcomes. Routine, daily nucleated red blood cell monitoring may serve as a simple, low-cost prognostic tool in intensive care unit trauma care. Prospective studies are needed to validate these findings and integrate nucleated red blood cell dynamics into risk stratification.

items.title: Methadone to manage pain in pregnancy at Te Toka Tumai Auckland City Hospital: A retrospective observational analysis
items.abstract: Pain during pregnancy is common, yet evidence-based management remains limited. While non-pharmacological treatments are first-line, severe pain may necessitate pharmacological intervention. Methadone is well studied for opioid use disorder, but its role in acute pain management during pregnancy is less defined. This retrospective observational study examined pregnant patients prescribed low-dose methadone for pain management between January 2022 and December 2023 at a tertiary multidisciplinary pain service. Patients receiving opioid substitution therapy were excluded. Data on methadone dosing, pain scores, maternal side effects, and neonatal outcomes were analysed. Twenty-three patients were identified, with 22 included in the analysis. The mean gestation at methadone initiation was 29.7 weeks (standard deviation 5.1), and the median starting dose was 5 mg per day (interquartile range 2.5 to 5). Pain severity decreased significantly: the proportion reporting severe pain at rest fell from 82% to 14% at 48 hours (absolute risk reduction (ARR) 68%, number needed to treat (NNT) 2), and the proportion reporting severe pain with movement fell from 95% to 32% (ARR 64%, NNT 2), with sustained improvement at 4 weeks. Side-effects included sedation (14%) and nausea (23%) and were generally well tolerated. Among 19 neonates, no cases of neonatal abstinence syndrome were observed. Six required neonatal intensive care unit admission, but none for opioid withdrawal. These findings suggest that low-dose methadone, when used within a closely monitored multidisciplinary setting, may provide effective pain relief in the pregnant patient without significant neonatal harm. However, this high level of oversight may limit generalisability to other care settings. Further research is warranted to guide safe implementation and optimise dosing.

items.title: Anaesthesia, anthropology, and colonialism in the Pacific – An unusual case report
items.abstract: Nikolai Miklouho-Maclay was a renowned Russian ethnologist who spent most of his life in the Pacific and was one of the first Europeans to live among and study the Melanesian people of Papua New Guinea. He is regarded as one of the first scientific anti-racists. New Guinea at this time was one of the remotest places on earth and had little contact with Europeans, mainly occasional missionaries and explorers. In September 1871, Maclay landed at Garagassi Point, Astrolabe Bay, on the north coast of New Guinea. Travelling with him were two assistants: Ohlsen – a Swede, and Boy – a young Samoan. Boy then proceeded to become very ill and his constant groaning was silenced only when Maclay administered morphia. Maclay was threatened by the local indigenous tribal people who wanted his belongings. They knew his two companions were possibly dying and Maclay tried to appear normal despite being ill with malaria. On the night of 13 December, Maclay poured chloroform onto cotton wool and held it over Boy’s airway – he died soon after. Maclay, as an anthropologist, wanted a Polynesian brain for study. Despite Ohlsen’s protests, Maclay removed part of Boy’s forehead and scalp but then abandoned this as he did not have a container to hold a brain. Maclay had promised Prof Karl Gegenbaur of Germany that he would obtain a ‘dark man’s’ larynx, tongue and related muscles, which he resected. Maclay came to Australia in 1878, becoming a prominent member of the Australian scientific community.

items.title: Universal videolaryngoscopy and intubation outcomes in anaesthesia trainees: A subanalysis of the multicentre VIDEOLAR-SURGERY trial
items.abstract: Tracheal intubation is a core procedural skill in anaesthesia training. Videolaryngoscopy provides improved glottic visualisation and shared airway views, but its effect on trainee-performed intubations in routine clinical practice remains uncertain. This subanalysis of a prospective, multicentre, non-randomised before-and-after study evaluated whether adopting videolaryngoscopy as the universal first-intention device improved intubation performance among anaesthesia trainees. Eight hospitals in Northwest Spain contributed 1801 trainee-performed intubations (857 before and 944 after intervention). During the non-intervention phase, direct laryngoscopy with a Macintosh blade was used, whereas the McGrath MAC videolaryngoscope was systematically adopted during the intervention phase. The primary outcome was easy intubation, defined as first-attempt success, Cormack–Lehane grade I–IIa view and no adjunct use. Easy intubation occurred more frequently with videolaryngoscopy (83.1% vs 69.3%; p < 0.001). First-attempt success (87.9% vs 77.0%; p < 0.001) and favourable glottic visualisation (91.5% vs 84.9%; p < 0.001) were also higher. Adjunct use, operator change and complications were reduced. Improvements were consistent across both junior and senior trainee groups. Universal videolaryngoscopy was associated with improved overall intubation performance among anaesthesia trainees in routine operating room practice. These findings suggest that videolaryngoscopy may be a valuable tool to support airway management training and improve intubation conditions in clinical practice.

items.title: Book Review: Resuscitation and the origins of intensive/critical care medicine TrubuhovichRonald V, Resuscitation and the origins of intensive/critical care medicine. Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society: Melbourne, VIC, Australia, 2025; 224 pp. ISBN: 978-1-876980-85-6.
items.abstract: Chapter 7 recounts the events of 'Bjørn Ibsen's Day', 27 August 1952, when he adapted a manual anaesthetic system for treating polio breathing failure, which markedly reduced the epidemic's mortality rate from c.87% to c.11% in the last 18 seriously ill polio patients.See:• In the beginning.The 1952-1953 Danish epidemic of poliomyelitis and Bjørn Ibsen.Crit Care Resusc.

items.title: Intraoperative methadone: Proceed with caution
items.abstract: In recent years, there has been increasing interest in the use of a single dose of intraoperative intravenous methadone to improve postoperative pain relief. In Australia, concerns have been expressed about this practice, specifically the potential risk of harm from opioid-induced ventilatory impairment (respiratory depression). In this paper, the current evidence for potential benefits and harms is reviewed. While benefits are said to include improved pain relief and lower additional opioid requirements after surgery, the evidence is conflicting and the clinical significance remains uncertain. There have been no significant safety issues reported in published studies; however, the evidence is limited. This paper therefore begins with a focus on some of the original clinical pharmacology studies of methadone to explain the basis of concerns regarding a potential increased risk of opioid-induced ventilatory impairment and the calls for a more cautious approach. Differences in Australian acute pain management practices (e.g., national prescribing guidelines recommending age-based initial doses of shorter-acting opioids which allow significantly higher doses and a shortened dose interval for younger patients with acute severe pain) compared with other countries may also influence the validity of some of the conclusions that have previously been made regarding efficacy and safety.

items.title: A retrospective cohort study of a midodrine protocol for the prevention of post-operative hypotension for lower limb arthroplasty and emergency hip fracture surgery
items.abstract: Hypotension is a common post-operative complication that is associated with morbidity and mortality. There has been growing interest in the use of midodrine (oral alpha-1 adrenergic vasopressor agent) to increase systolic and mean arterial blood pressure in a variety of clinical applications. Our institution developed a 48-h midodrine protocol in 2020 for patients undergoing elective lower limb arthroplasty and emergency hip fracture fixation. The aim of this retrospective, single-centre metropolitan tertiary hospital cohort study was to evaluate the efficacy of the protocol in reducing the incidence and severity of perioperative hypotension (SBP <110 mmHg) within the first 24 h following surgery compared to the pre-protocol period (primary outcome). Secondary outcomes included frequency of hypotension 24–48 h post-operatively, bradycardia, incidence of MET calls and unplanned critical care admission. In total, 328 patients were identified for inclusion in the pre-protocol group and 298 in the protocol group. Introduction of the midodrine protocol was not associated with a significant difference in the incidence of the primary outcome. There was no statistically significant difference in the incidence of hypotension between groups post-operatively at 24 or 48 h. Of the secondary outcomes, patients receiving midodrine were more likely to be bradycardic in the post-anaesthesia care unit (43.8% vs 55.9%, p = 0.001) and at 24 h post-operatively (40.7% vs 53.8%, p = 0.003).

items.title: Bilateral thoracolumbar erector spinae plane blocks for postoperative pain relief in TRAM flap breast reconstruction: A case report
items.abstract: Post-mastectomy breast reconstruction is associated with significant postoperative pain due to the involvement of both the thoracic recipient site and the abdominal donor site. Effective analgesic strategies are essential to optimise recovery, reduce opioid exposure, and support enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) pathways. We report the perioperative analgesic management of a patient undergoing mastectomy with immediate breast reconstruction using a pedicled transverse rectus abdominis myocutaneous (TRAM) flap. A multimodal regional anaesthesia strategy based on bilateral multilevel thoracolumbar erector spinae plane blocks (ESPB), supplemented by a serratus anterior plane block, was employed to address wide thoracoabdominal dermatomal pain distribution. The regional analgesic approach was associated with effective postoperative pain control and minimal systemic opioid requirements during the early postoperative period. Pain scores remained low at rest and during movement, and no block-related complications were observed. This case illustrates the feasibility of combining bilateral multilevel ESPB with adjunct interfascial plane blocks as part of a multimodal analgesic strategy for pedicled TRAM flap reconstruction. While no conclusions regarding comparative efficacy or reproducibility can be drawn from a single case, this experience supports further investigation of ESPB-based approaches within ERAS pathways for autologous breast reconstruction.

items.title: Reducing bias in estimated blood volume: A robust approach to calibration of the Nadler formula
items.abstract: The Nadler formula is widely used for blood-volume estimation but exhibits systematic proportional bias that compromises clinical accuracy. A calibrated formula was developed and validated using Passing-Bablok regression. A published dataset of 90 patients with directly measured blood volumes was randomly partitioned into training and test sets. Passing-Bablok regression on the training set derived calibration coefficients, which were applied to the internal test set. Validation used Passing-Bablok regression, concordance correlation coefficient and robust Bland-Altman analysis. Five-fold cross-validation assessed generalisability. Training set analysis demonstrated significant proportional bias. After calibration, the internal test set showed elimination of proportional bias and excellent concordance with measured blood volume. Five-fold cross-validation confirmed robust and consistent performance across all data partitions. An independent external cohort of 201 healthy men showed improved agreement after calibration, once a documented haematocrit-conversion difference between the two reference methods was accounted for, supporting generalisability beyond the initial Retzlaff dataset. Passing-Bablok regression-based calibration successfully eliminated systematic bias in the Nadler formula, achieving high concordance with radioisotope-measured blood volume in internal validation. The simple linear calibration maintains clinical simplicity while addressing a critical limitation of the original formula. A preliminary external validation in an independent historical cohort of 201 men supported this generalisability; further validation in contemporary, mixed-sex cohorts is recommended before widespread clinical implementation.

items.title: Dr Mark Lidwill investigates fatal anaesthetic ether impurities in Sydney in 1915
items.abstract: In December 1915, an article was published by Dr Mark Lidwill in the Medical Journal of Australia ( MJA ), which discussed the clinical features of a series of deaths over a few months in Sydney which were regarded as very unusual following ether anaesthesia. These deaths stimulated Lidwill, at that time in general practice and a visiting Anaesthetist/Physician at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, to gather a committee of four chemists to investigate. After much work sulphur impurities from the manufacture of ether were found to be the problem though the exact compounds were not identified. This impurity could be neutralised by potassium permanganate. This problem had arisen as Australia stopped importing ether from Germany at the start of the First World War and commenced manufacturing its own ether. There was no time during wartime to expand on these investigations. This MJA article was in advance of other world anaesthetic literature addressing ether impurities until the 1920s to 1940s, none of which mentioned the MJA article. This failure to report their chemical research in detail was unfortunate, as it was some years ahead of most other interest in the chemistry of clinical complications of ether anaesthesia due to impurities. Forty years later, after Lidwill had retired, he noted more details of these deaths and the investigations that revealed the problem and its solution. These later articles and some earlier chemical investigations into contaminants of ether are discussed, and Lidwill’s research into ether impurities compared to them.

items.title: APICS 2026: The Asia Pacific Intensive Care Symposium goes to Bali
Percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy in adult intensive care: An ANZICS consensus statement
items.abstract: Percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy (PDT) is a commonly performed procedure in intensive care units; However, the high-quality evidence base guiding many aspects of its practice remains limited, resulting in variation across clinicians and institutions. This statement was drafted by a panel of experts, later reviewed by an expert working group comprising representatives from the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society and the College of Intensive Care Medicine, and endorsed by the boards of both organisations. The recommendations presented are based on the best available evidence and, where evidence is scarce, on structured expert consensus. The scope of this statement is confined to PDT in adult intensive care patients. This document reflects current practice at the time of publication and is intended to be a living document, subject to regular review to include emerging evidence and evolving standards of care. In summary, this consensus statement provides evidence-informed, expert-guided recommendations to standardise PDT practice in adult ICUs across Australia and New Zealand, while acknowledging current variability and gaps in the evidence base.

items.title: Outcomes of SGLT2-inhibitor-induced euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis in a North Queensland intensive care unit: A retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Evidence on sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i)-associated euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis (EuDKA) in the intensive care unit (ICU) and its comparison with type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM) diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is limited. This study aims to describe ICU characteristics, management and outcomes of SGLT2i-associated EuDKA, identify predictors of poorer outcomes and compare findings with T1DM-DKA. Single-centre retrospective cohort (2017–2023) of adults admitted to a Northern Queensland ICU. EuDKA was defined by plasma glucose <13.9 mmol/L plus ⩾1 of acidaemia, low bicarbonate, raised anion gap or ketonaemia, in patients with T2DM on SGLT2i. A comparator cohort comprised ICU admissions with T1DM-DKA. Demographics, precipitants, biochemistry, insulin therapy, and outcomes were extracted and analysed with non-parametric tests. Fourteen EuDKA and 31 T1DM-DKA admissions were included. EuDKA patients were older with more frequent comorbidities; First Nations Australians were over-represented. Presenting features were heterogeneous, with overlapping precipitants (commonly caloric restriction/fasting or intercurrent illness). Compared with T1DM-DKA, EuDKA had milder biochemical derangement and lower 24-h insulin dose but required longer insulin therapy and longer ICU length of stay; time to acidosis resolution was similar. In exploratory analyses, end-organ complications in type 2 diabetes were associated with longer ICU stay, while obesity and pre-admission insulin therapy were associated with prolonged acidosis duration. ICU-admitted SGLT2i-associated EuDKA differs clinically and in management from classical T1DM-DKA. Findings highlight diagnostic challenges, potential high-risk subgroups, and the need for prospective, multicentre studies to inform risk-based management in critical care.

items.title: Boerhaave’s syndrome complicated by pneumorrhachis and chemical meningitis
items.abstract: Boerhaave’s syndrome is a life-threatening condition characterised by oesophageal perforation. This report presents a case of Boerhaave’s syndrome complicated by pneumorrhachis (air in the spinal canal) and chemical meningitis. A 26-year-old male developed meningism and an agitated delirium following oesophageal rupture, with imaging confirming pneumorrhachis and cerebrospinal fluid analysis consistent with chemical meningitis. Despite a prolonged Intensive Care Unit stay complicated by encephalopathy and severe agitation, the patient made a full neurological recovery with supportive care. This case illustrates a unique pathophysiological progression and underscores the importance of early recognition, exclusion of bacterial meningitis, appropriate prognostication and multidisciplinary management of pneumorrhachis complicating Boerhaave’s syndrome.

items.title: Anaesthetic scavenging: a brief history
items.abstract: Anaesthesia and Intensive CareThe odour from a single drop of ether can be distinctly perceived all over the operating theatre. . . the surgeon, and others who have been about the patient, also smell of the ether to a lesser degree. 1 John Snow.On chloroform and other anaesthetics, 1858While John Snow recognised that ether anaesthesia resulted in detectable levels of ether in the operating room, he stopped short of attributing harm to this phenomenon.It was not until the 1920s that surgeons began expressing concerns that exposure to anaesthetic vapours was influencing their performance, causing headaches and worsening fatigue.2,3 Given all the other stressors that surgeons experienced, no direct link could be established, but air sampling revealed that low levels of ether vapour in operating rooms were ameliorated to a certain extent by improving ventilation in the theatre.4 More immediate and obvious was the risk of fires from ether permeating the theatre.These were often due to static electricity which was difficult to avoid without complex grounding measures.5 Consequently fires were frequent-usually transient, but not without risk to both patient and theatre staff.The fire risk, and the pungent smell of ether drew everyone's attention to ether pollution in the operating theatre.

items.title: Quantitative investigation of airway lumen and area changes before and after surgical tracheostomy using CT imaging: A multicentre retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Post-tracheostomy airway narrowing may be observed after decannulation, but its persistence and clinical significance remain uncertain; quantitative evidence describing post-tracheostomy tracheal changes remains limited. This multicentre retrospective cohort study aimed to quantify computed tomography (CT)-based changes in tracheal area and minimal diameter before tracheostomy and after decannulation and to characterise the longitudinal anatomical variability of post-tracheostomy airway changes. Adult patients who underwent surgical tracheostomy between 2014 and 2024 across five affiliated hospitals were reviewed. Inclusion required both pre-tracheostomy and post-decannulation CT imaging. The tracheal area and minimal diameter were measured at the narrowest axial slice between C6 and T2. Among 4660 tracheostomy patients, 300 met eligibility. Post-decannulation CT demonstrated a mean 13.6% reduction in tracheal area (−52.8 mm 2 ) and 11.2% reduction in diameter (−2.2 mm). Airway narrowing tended to be greater in patients undergoing tracheostomy for head and neck surgery. Tube sizes showed no clear pattern with airway reduction. Of 123 patients later re-intubated, 47.2% required a smaller endotracheal tube, and 12.2% needed multiple tube size attempts. Longitudinal analysis showed substantial inter-individual variability, with no clear temporal trend in recovery. In this multicentre cohort, surgical tracheostomy was followed by modest but measurable decreases in tracheal area and diameter after decannulation. These findings provide descriptive CT-based data on post-tracheostomy airway narrowing and highlight the need for further studies linking anatomical changes with functional airway outcomes.

items.title: The incidence of postoperative hypotension among non-cardiac surgical specialties: A single-centre retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Postoperative hypotension is associated with increased risk of postoperative complications and mortality. There are limited studies quantifying the incidence of this potentially life-threatening condition among different surgical cohorts. We aimed to describe and compare the incidence of postoperative hypotension in the first 48 h after leaving the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU) across different surgical specialties after non-cardiac surgery. We conducted a single-centre retrospective study at the Royal Melbourne Hospital. The primary outcome was postoperative hypotension (systolic blood pressure (SBP) <90 mmHg) within 48 h after surgery and discharge from PACU, noted on routine blood pressure monitoring or a requirement for postoperative vasopressor or inotropic support. We estimated odds ratios (OR) using mixed-effects logistic regression models to account for multiple surgical procedures within the same patient. We identified 11,634 surgeries from 17 specialties, of which 47.3% were emergency operations. The median age was 53 years (interquartile range 35–68), with 42.2% being female and 42.5% of patients on regular antihypertensive medication. The overall incidence of ward hypotension was 4.4%. Trauma had the highest rate of postoperative hypotension (27.3%), followed by thoracic surgery (11.6%). Surgical specialties that had a higher risk of hypotension included trauma surgery (OR 13.0, 95% confidence interval (CI) 3.7–46.0) and thoracic surgery (OR 3.6, 95% CI 2.3–5.5). Specialties with a lower risk of hypotension included breast and endocrine surgery (OR 0.4, 95% CI 0.2–0.7) and plastic surgery (OR 0.4, 95% CI 0.3–0.6). Postoperative hypotension is relatively common with substantial variation in incidence between surgical specialties. These findings highlight the need for heightened vigilance for hypotension in certain patients.

items.title: Translating evidence into practice: Deimplementation of routine chest radiography after cardiothoracic drain removal
A case of massive gamma-hydroxybutyrate overdose mimicking brain death
items.abstract: A 36-year-old female was brought into hospital following a massive overdose of 100 ml of gamma-hydroxybutyrate. Unlike prior case reports where ethanol was a co-ingestant with gamma-hydroxybutyrate or its precursor, gamma-hydroxybutyrate was believed to have been the only substance ingested in this case. The patient developed a severe and persistent high anion gap metabolic acidosis and required continuous renal replacement therapy. The patient developed fixed and dilated pupils early on in her clinical course and was found to have a transient loss of most brainstem reflexes on clinical examination, thus mimicking brain death. She also developed generalised tonic-clonic seizures and received midazolam and levetiracetam for seizure control. She was successfully extubated after 5 days on mechanical ventilation and was discharged home on day 11 with no neurological deficits.

items.title: Conference Proceedings of the Asia Pacific Intensive Care Symposium 2026
Patient preference for intraoperative opioid strategy and early postoperative recovery after noncardiac surgery: a prospective partially randomised patient-preference trial (the PERFECT trial)
items.abstract: Background Patient-centred care increasingly encourages patients to participate in decisions regarding their anaesthetic management. However, whether expressing a preference regarding their anaesthetic management is associated with improved postoperative recovery remains unknown. We evaluated the association between preference expression and quality of recovery after noncardiac surgery. Methods In this prospective partially randomised patient-preference study conducted at two academic hospitals, adults undergoing minimally invasive abdominal, urologic, or gynaecologic surgery received standardised information on opioid-based and opioid-free anaesthesia, co-developed with patient partners. Participants expressing a preference received their preferred strategy, whereas those without a preference were randomised 1:1 to either strategy. The primary outcome was the Quality of Recovery-15 (QoR-15) score on postoperative day (POD) 1. Results Among 220 analysed participants, 177 (80.5%) expressed a preference, and 43 (19.5%) underwent random allocation. Mean [standard deviation] QoR-15 scores on POD 1 were higher among participants expressing a preference than among randomised participants (108.8 [18.2] vs 100.8 [23.5]), with an unadjusted mean difference of 7.9 points (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.5–14.4; P =0.017). The adjusted marginal mean difference was 7.1 points (95% CI 0.3–13.9; P =0.042). Scores on the QoR-15 also remained higher on POD 2. Sensitivity analyses showed consistent effect estimates but attenuated statistical significance. Secondary outcomes, including postoperative nausea and vomiting and bradycardia, were similar between groups. Conclusions Expression of a preference regarding intraoperative opioid management was associated with better reported early postoperative patient-reported recovery. Given the non-randomised comparison and limited precision, -generating and support further investigation into the role of patient-preference expression in perioperative recovery. Trial registration The full, long-term study is pre-registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier, NCT06855641; first posted, 3 March 2025; Alexandre Joosten). https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06855641.

items.title: Diagnostic agreement between the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition criteria and Subjective Global Assessment for preoperative malnutrition in adults undergoing elective surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis
items.abstract: Protein-energy malnutrition remains frequently unrecognised, under-reported, and undertreated in surgical populations despite being associated with a higher risk of postoperative complications. This systematic review evaluated the diagnostic agreement between the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) operational criteria and the Subjective Global Assessment for identifying adults at risk of preoperative protein-energy malnutrition undergoing elective surgery. MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 5 May 2025. Substantial heterogeneity was observed across eight included studies ( n =5834) in the definitions, cut-offs, and measurement methods for GLIM phenotypic and aetiologic criteria. In six noncardiac surgical studies ( n =3999), pooled sensitivity and specificity were 76% (95% confidence interval [CI] 69–81%) and 88% (95% CI 77–94%), respectively, using a random-effects bivariate model (very low certainty of evidence). Overall diagnostic agreement was fair; thus, the GLIM criteria alone may be insufficient to make the diagnosis of malnutrition and to guide nutritional interventions without additional clinical or dietetic assessment.
