Comparative Study of Mitral Repair Techniques for Degenerative Posterior Leaflet Regurgitation
items.abstract: Objective We investigated the role of mitral valve repair (MVr) technique on outcomes after MVr for posterior leaflet prolapse. Methods Study patients were identified from the Society of Thoracic Surgeons Adult Cardiac Surgery Database (7/2014-12/2023). Cases included patients undergoing primary, non-emergency isolated MVr for moderate-to-severe mitral regurgitation (MR) due to posterior leaflet prolapse. Three repair techniques were analyzed: triangular resection, quadrangular resection, and neochord repair, with further stratification by open versus robotic assistance. The primary endpoint was early "mitral repair failure" (MRF), defined as: ≥ moderate MR on postoperative echocardiogram, valvular reintervention during the index hospitalization or within 30 days, or 30-day readmission for valvular dysfunction/heart failure. Combined operative mortality and/or repair failure (OM/MRF) as well as need for a cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) for rhythm disturbance were secondary endpoints. Multivariable logistic regression models were derived for all outcomes. Results Of 24,383 eligible MVr cases identified, OM was low (n=168, 0.7%), and 683 (2.9%) patients required a CIED. A subset of 9,433 patients with complete postoperative echocardiography, readmission, and reintervention data comprised the primary study group. MRF occurred in 379 (4.1%) of these patients. Multivariable regression showed that open quadrangular resection was associated with increased odds of both MRF and OM/MRF (MRF OR 1.50 (1.06-2.11), p=0.02; OM/MRF OR=1.43 (1.07-1.91), p=0.02) as well as need for CIED (OR 1.31 (1.05-1.64), p=0.02). Conclusions This national-scale study of MVr associated open quadrangular resection repair with increased incidence of early MRF with or without OM as well as need for CIED.

items.title: Machine learning in risk stratification of prolonged hospital stay after congenital heart surgery
items.abstract: Objectives Extended postoperative hospital length of stay after paediatric cardiac surgery places strain on hospital resources and creates emotional and financial stress for families. However, awareness of which patients will spend relatively longer in hospital remains limited. We propose two machine learning models to predict prolonged length of stay using only electronic health record data before the surgery has taken place. Methods The first model used a fixed definition of prolonged length of stay as exceeding the 75 th percentile of the entire population (17 days). The second applied diagnosis-adjusted threshold, ranging from 8 and 49 days depending on diagnosis complexity. Both models were built using XGBoost and evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROCAUC) . An additional risk stratification was developed by applying probability thresholds on the model output to define four groups based on predicted risk. Results High ROCAUC was achieved by both the fixed-threshold model (88%) and the diagnosis-adjusted model (84%). The four-group risk stratification aligned with test-set outcomes, with prolonged length of stay cases predominantly occurring in the high-risk group and rarely in the low-risk group. Conclusions It is possible to predict prolonged length of stay, either defined using a fixed threshold or a diagnosis adjusted threshold, preoperatively, with only electronic health record data as input. It is moreover possible to stratify the patients who are at highest risk of having prolonged length of stay. Preoperative knowledge of which patients are at risk of prolonged length of stay may facilitate surgical planning and improve patient and parent communication.

items.title: R1 resection for clinical stage IIIA/B non-small cell lung cancer: should we have just given chemoradiation?
items.abstract: Objective Optimal treatment for clinical stage III (cIII) non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is debated. Recent data strongly supporting the addition of immunotherapy to neoadjuvant regimens may suggest an increasing role for surgery. The objective of this study is to compare outcomes in patients with cIIIA/B NSCLC treated with definitive chemoradiation (dCRT) versus surgery with positive microscopic margins (R1). Methods The National Cancer Database (2004-2022) was used to identify patients with cIIIA/B NSCLC (excluding N3) treated with either dCRT or surgery. Margin status was evaluated. Survival in weighted groups was analyzed by Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression. Results Of 112,197 patients, 62.7%% (n=70,324) received dCRT and 37.3% (n=41,873) underwent surgery, of which 6.2% (n=2,584) had an R1 resection. The R1 group was associated with greater comorbidity (CCI1: aOR 1.17, p=0.007; CCI2: aOR 1.22, p=0.016), middle lobe disease (aOR 1.39, p=0.002) and increasing T-stage (cT2: aOR 1.57; cT3: aOR 2.47, cT4: aOR 2.51; all p<0.001). Among R1 patients, 22.9% (n=541) received neoadjuvant therapy. Adjuvant therapy rates in the R1 group were 56.2% (n=1329) for systemic therapy and 41.7% (n=1077) for radiation. After adjustment, overall survival following R1 resection was comparable to dCRT (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.97-1.10; p=0.31). Conclusions Survival after R1 resection was not significantly different from dCRT after adjustment. These findings provide prognostic context when R1 resection occurs unexpectedly. With higher pathologic response rates identified in the era of neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy, it is anticipated that patients with cIII NSCLC will increasingly be offered surgical management.

items.title: Two Tumors, Same Size, Different Prognosis: Lung Capacity Indexing Reclassifies T Category and Identifies Higher-Risk Patients in Early-Stage NSCLC
items.abstract: Introduction Tumor size is central to non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) staging, yet it remains unclear whether absolute diameter or patient-scaled metrics better predict outcomes. We evaluated whether tumor size indexed to predicted total lung capacity (pTLC) improves prognostic discrimination in early-stage NSCLC. Methods We performed a retrospective cohort study of Veterans undergoing curative-intent resection for clinical stage I NSCLC within the Veterans Affairs (2006–2020). pTLC was estimated using European Respiratory Society reference equations, and tumor size was indexed to a reference lung capacity of 6.91 L. Tumors were categorized in 10-mm increments; "upsizing" was defined as reclassification into a higher category after indexing. Associations of absolute and pTLC-indexed size with overall survival (OS) and cumulative incidence of recurrence (CIR) were assessed using Cox and Fine–Gray regression with multivariable adjustment. Secondary analyses evaluated associations between upsizing and pathologic nodal involvement. Results Among 11,713 Veterans (mean age 68), 12.2% were upsized after indexing. Both absolute and pTLC-indexed size were associated with worse OS and CIR in a stepwise fashion. pTLC-based upsizing was associated with increased risk of death (aHR 1.08, 95% CI 1.02–1.15) and recurrence (sHR 1.13, 95% CI 1.02–1.26), even after adjustment for absolute size. Upsizing was also associated with greater odds of pathologic nodal involvement (aOR 1.23, 95% CI 1.00–1.52). Conclusion Lung capacity indexing reclassifies a subset of patients into a higher tumor size category, and these patients have worse survival, higher recurrence, and more occult nodal disease than absolute diameter alone would suggest.

items.title: A Young Surgeon’s Case for Stewardship in the Structural Heart Era
items.abstract: As transcatheter therapies mature, the surgeon's role shifts from in-room safeguard to steward of technology, complex reoperation, and lifetime valve care, anchored by operative excellence. Perspective StatementThe structural heart revolution has reshaped cardiovascular care and the surgeon's role.Drawing on a trainee's path through clinical trial research toward the operating room, this note argues that surgical involvement should track each therapy's safety curve.Operative excellence, evidencebased stewardship, and collaboration will sustain surgery's relevance to patients, trainees, and health systems. items.title: Recovery Time of Diaphragm Paralysis After Congenital Heart Surgery: A Retrospective Single-Center Cohort Study
items.abstract: Objective(s): To estimate the time to recovery from diaphragm paralysis after congenital heart surgery using interval-censored survival analysis and to characterize cumulative recovery probability over 5 years. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 111 consecutive patients < 18 years who developed diaphragm paralysis after congenital heart surgery at a tertiary center in Japan (2009-2024); 110 were analyzed after excluding 1 patient without imaging follow-up. Recovery of diaphragmatic motion was the primary outcome. Because recovery was detectable only at discrete imaging assessments, interval-censored survival methods (Turnbull estimator) were used, followed by parametric accelerated failure time modeling and a Bayesian re-analysis incorporating informative priors from a comparable published cohort. Results Recovery was confirmed in 84 patients (76.4%); 26 (23.6%) were right-censored. The median recovery time was 44 days (95% confidence interval, 41-75 days). Cumulative recovery probability was 60.5% at 60 days, 74.5% at 90 days, and 84.9% at 1 year, plateauing near 85% after 2 years with a slight increase to 87.1% at 5 years. A log-logistic distribution provided the best parametric fit. The Bayesian model yielded a posterior median recovery time of 69 days (95% credible interval, 47-102 days), and sensitivity analyses yielded consistent estimates. Conclusions Diaphragm paralysis after congenital heart surgery resolves in approximately three of four patients, with most recovering within 3 months. However, approximately 15% may not recover within a clinically meaningful timeframe, supporting the need for long-term follow-up and multicenter studies to identify risk factors for non-recovery and establish generalizable recovery time estimates.

items.title: Looking Beyond: Long-Term Post-Transplant Outcomes Stratified by STS-PEDIMACS Mechanical Circulatory Support Category
items.abstract: Background The STS-PEDIMACS classifies pediatric MCS as PP, PC, IC, and Percutaneous. While the STS-PEDIMACS provides outcomes of these devices such as bridge to cardiac transplantation, it does not provide long-term outcomes of cardiac transplantation in the transplanted patients. We used the UNOS database to study the long-term outcomes of cardiac transplantation in patients bridged with MCS as per STS-PEDIMACS classification. Methods Pediatric heart transplant recipients (2004–2025) receiving pre-transplant MCS were identified from the OPTN registry and classified according to the STS-PEDIMACS system as PP (n=1,181), PC (n=234), IC (n=660), or percutaneous support (n=57). Waitlist outcomes were additionally evaluated in 1,552 registrations with MCS recorded at listing. Kaplan-Meier, restricted mean survival time (RMST), and multivariable Cox proportional hazards analyses were performed. Results IC and percutaneous recipients were older, whereas PP and PC recipients had greater pre-transplant illness severity. Among recipients with both listing and transplant MCS data available, 95.0% had the same MCS category recorded at listing and transplantation. PC support was associated with higher post-transplant morbidity and the lowest unadjusted survival. RMST analysis demonstrated a significant 5-year survival advantage for IC compared with PP (+3.0 months; p=0.017). On multivariable Cox regression, PC remained independently associated with increased post-transplant mortality compared with PP (HR 1.97, 95% CI 1.19–3.26), whereas IC and percutaneous support demonstrated comparable adjusted risk. Conclusion Post-heart transplant outcomes are largely comparable across pediatric MCS strategies; however, PC support is associated with inferior long-term survival.

items.title: Euglycemia Does Not Prevent Neuroglycopenia After Cardiopulmonary Bypass in Neonatal Swine
items.abstract: Objective Tight glycemic control in pediatric cardiac surgery is not neuroprotective and increases the risk of hypoglycemia. Cerebral glucose uptake is mediated by glucose transporter type 1 (GluT1). Even transient cerebral glucose deprivation (neuroglycopenia) can cause irreversible neurologic injury. This investigation explores plasma and cerebral glucose relationships in the neonatal brain during and after cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). Methods Fifteen piglets underwent continuous CPB (3hrs,34°C) followed by survival for 12-24hrs post-CPB. Plasma was serially collected. Dextrose was administered to prevent hypoglycemia (<50mg/dL). Cerebral interstitial fluid (CIF) microdialysate was continuously collected. CIF and plasma glucose levels were compared to baseline using one-way analysis of variance with Dunnett's correction. Western blots evaluated GluT1 expression in cortical brain tissue harvested post-CPB and from three sham animals that underwent identical procedures without CPB. Additional metabolites were quantified using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry. Results Plasma glucose increased from baseline (100±18mg/dL) during CPB and remained elevated at 1-6hrs post-CPB (136±43mg/dL, p <0.001, q =0.004 ). Glucose in CIF remained similar to baseline (20.5±11.6mg/dL) during CPB, and decreased within 1-6hrs post-CPB (10.0±13.0mg/dL, p <0.001, q =0.001). CIF glucose remained reduced relative to plasma concentrations at 7-12hrs post-CPB ( p <0.001, q <0.001), but normalized within 24hrs post-CPB as GluT1 expression increased; however, adenosine triphosphate (ATP) remained depleted in cortical brain tissue ( p =0.026, q =0.061). Conclusions Cerebral glucose transport is upregulated within 24hrs post-CPB. Euglycemia and even mild hyperglycemia does not prevent neuroglycopenia and ATP depletion in the neonatal brain post-CPB. These findings provide a plausible biologic mechanism for clinical investigations demonstrating that postoperative hyperglycemia does not adversely impact neurodevelopmental outcomes, and may be beneficial.

items.title: Determinants of Adverse Outcomes after Completion Pneumonectomy for Pulmonary Tuberculosis: A Retrospective Study
items.abstract: s Objectives Completion pneumonectomy (CP) is a rare, high-risk procedure historically associated with mortality of 3.4-24% and morbidity up to 63.7%. Most published evidence is based on the oncological cohorts, whereas predictors of adverse outcomes in predominantly tuberculosis (TB) populations remain poorly defined. We aimed to identify factors associated with adverse outcomes after CP for pulmonary TB. Methods This retrospective study included 237 patients who underwent CP between 2000 and 2024 at four Russian pulmonology centers. The primary outcome was postoperative morbidity; secondary outcomes were 30-day mortality and broncho-pleural fistula (BPF). Multivariable logistic regression was performed for morbidity and BPF. Mortality was analyzed descriptively due to few events. Results Patients were predominantly male (59.1%) with a mean age of 36.9 years; all patients underwent surgery for pulmonary tuberculosis, of which 81.3% was multidrug- or extensively drug-resistant. Postoperative morbidity was 19.4%, empyema the most common complication (13.5%), BPF occurred in 5.5%, and 30-day mortality rate was 1.3%. In the morbidity model, blood transfusion (OR 8.25) and active progressive TB (OR 2.64) were associated with postoperative morbidity. In the BPF model longer operative duration (OR 1.015 per minute), blood transfusion (OR 8.89), and bronchial tuberculosis (OR 7.72) were associated with BPF. Conclusions CP can be performed with low mortality and acceptable morbidity in selected patients at experienced centers, even for drug-resistant tuberculosis. Transfusion requirement and active progressive tuberculosis were associated with postoperative morbidity, while longer operative duration, transfusion requirement, and bronchial tuberculosis were associated with BPF.

items.title: Diaphragm Dysfunction after Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting is Associated with Increased Postoperative Morbidity
items.abstract: Objective We sought to describe the incidence, postoperative outcomes, and rate of recovery in CABG patients who develop postoperative diaphragm dysfunction (DD). Methods We retrospectively reviewed patients undergoing isolated CABG at our institution between July 2015 and May 2025. Diagnosis of DD was based on diaphragmatic elevation on routine postoperative chest X-ray and was confirmed by sniff test. Postoperative outcomes were compared between patients with and without DD using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW). Results The incidence of postoperative DD after CABG was 3.1% (111/3594), with 60 left-sided DD, 50 right-sided DD, and 1 patient with bilateral DD. Preoperative characteristics were similar between those with and without DD. Only seven patients developed DD without ipsilateral IMA harvest; all seven were right-sided DD after isolated LIMA harvest (0.3%, 7/2084). After IPTW weighting, patients with DD had longer lengths of stay (8 vs 7 days; p=0.01), as well as increased rates of postoperative pneumonia (5.7% vs 2.3%, p=0.02), reintubation (7.4% vs 2.1%, p=0.001), ICU readmission (5.0% vs 1.9%, p=0.04), and cardiac arrest (3.8% vs 1.1%, p=0.03). Early mortality was similar between groups (p=0.52). Of patients with left DD, 45% (27/49) demonstrated recovery at a median of 7.5 months (IQR 3.1-18.9), while 50% (19/38) of patients with right DD demonstrated recovery at a median of 3.6 months (IQR 3.1-33). Conclusions While the overall rate of diaphragm dysfunction after CABG surgery is low, it is associated with increased postoperative morbidity. Further investigations into DD after CABG are necessary.

items.title: Mitral Vision: Computer Vision Evaluation of the Mitral Apparatus
items.abstract: STRUCTURED ABSTRACT Objective Recently, the advent of state-of-the-art artificial intelligence (AI) has enabled novel applications of computer vision (CV). CV allows for autonomous identification and interpretation of complex inputs, following training on a large dataset. It offers an opportunity to detect and define intricate anatomy, such as that of the mitral valve and subvalvular apparatus. However, current models lack cardiac surgery-specific training. We sought to train a model to detect and segment intraoperative mitral anatomy. Methods 221 frames were collected from an institutional archive of intraoperative videos. We manually annotated regions of interest (ROIs), labeling leaflet tissue, chordae tendineae, and papillary muscles. The YOLOv26 (Ultralytics) AI model was trained to segment these anatomic structures. Evaluative metrics included per-class precision and mean average precision (mAP) at an intersection over union (IoU) of >50% across the dataset for anatomic structure detection. Results The fine-tuned model achieved an overall precision of 0.71, with a recall of 0.60. Performance differed between classes, with the strongest segmentation performance for leaflet tissue (mAP50 = 0.73). Additionally, the model proved capable of real-time implementation on live-streamed intraoperative video on a desktop supercomputer (DGX Spark), maintaining adequate detection and segmentation performance. Conclusions We demonstrate the feasibility of training an instance segmentation model to detect anatomic components of the mitral valve and subvalvular apparatus. We achieved acceptable precision and anticipate continued improvement as training is ongoing. Ultimately, we envision integration of AI-assisted "mitral vision" in the OR, with real-time mapping of intracardiac anatomy and decision-making support during valve repair procedures.

items.title: Are Bone Metastases A Contraindication? Role of Surgical Consolidation in EGFR-Mutated Stage IV NSCLC Patients Receiving Osimertinib
items.abstract: Background Prior studies suggested that osseous metastases (OM) may limit local consolidative therapy (LCT) benefits for stage IV non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, earlier cohorts were predominantly comprised of individuals lacking targetable oncogenic drivers. We evaluated the impact of pulmonary resection among EGFR -mutated stage IV NSCLC patients with OM receiving Osimertinib. Methods We conducted a single-center review of EGFR -mutated stage IV NSCLC patients with OM receiving Osimertinib from 2005-2023. Patients were stratified by pulmonary resection receipt. One-to-one propensity matching addressed demographic and clinical group differences. Outcomes were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier and multivariable Cox regression methodologies. Results 102 patients (51/group) were included, with similar median age of 60 years ( p =0.79). Median metastases were 3 (IQR:2-5) and 5 (IQR:3-8, p =0.10) for surgical and non-operative patients, respectively. Comprehensive LCT was more frequent among surgical patients (52.9% vs 15.7%, p <0.01). Among non-surgical patients, 26 (51.0%) underwent primary tumor radiation. At median follow-up of 37.9 months, median overall survival (OS) for surgical and non-operative groups were 60.2 (95% CI : 46.5-66.0) and 38.3 months (95% CI : 32.7-47.5, P =0.02), respectively. Median progression-free survival (PFS) was 31.8 (95% CI : 26.2-36.9) and 16.6 months for surgical and non-operative (95% CI : 12.2-23.9, P =0.03) patients, respectively. Pulmonary resection was independently associated with improved OS (HR=0.61, 95% CI : 0.38-0.89, P =0.01) and PFS (HR=0.72, 95% CI : 0.49-0.97, P =0.03). Conclusion Among selected patients with EGFR -mutated stage IV NSCLC and OM receiving Osimertinib, pulmonary resection was associated with improved outcomes. As such, OM alone should not preclude LCT consideration in this population.

items.title: All Strokes Aren’t Equal After Aortic Arch Surgery: Modified Rankin Score at Discharge is Associated with Long-Term Functional Outcomes
items.abstract: Objective Stroke remains a significant cause of morbidity following aortic arch surgery and is used by the STS as a key quality metric. We evaluated the utility of the modified Rankin score (mRS) to predict long-term stroke outcomes following elective aortic arch surgery. Methods A multi-institutional retrospective review was conducted of 930 patients undergoing elective hemiarch or zone 2 arch replacement at two high-volume aortic centers. Neurologic injury was graded using mRS and categorized as mild (mRS ≤2) or severe (mRS >2). Preoperative characteristics, operative variables, perioperative outcomes, and long-term neurologic outcomes were compared. Statistical significance was defined as p<0.05. Results Postoperative stroke occurred in 69 patients (7.4%). Stroke patients were older and had higher rates of diabetes, hypertension, and heart failure (p<0.05). They also experienced increased prolonged ventilation, tracheostomy, pneumonia, dialysis, in-hospital mortality, 30-day mortality (p<0.001), and readmission (p=0.02). Among stroke patients, 23 (33.3%) had mild stroke and 46 (66.7%) had severe stroke. At 3 months, complete neurologic recovery occurred in 66.7% of mild versus 30.2% of severe stroke patients (p=0.003). At 1 year, 86.7% of mild stroke patients were functionally asymptomatic compared with 50% of severe stroke patients (p=0.02). One year mortality was 52% in severe stroke patients versus 0% in mild stroke patients (p=0.003). Conclusion The modified Rankin score (mRS) effectively stratifies postoperative stroke severity and predicts long-term functional recovery and survival after aortic arch surgery. Incorporating stroke severity into surgical quality metrics may improve risk assessment and outcome reporting.

items.title: Tricuspid Valve Surgery in Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome: When and With What Outcomes?
Clinical Outcomes of Anatomy-Driven VSD Occluder Selection in Pediatric Patients: A Dual-Center Retrospective Study
items.abstract: Objective The choice between symmetric and asymmetric ventricular septal defect (VSD) occluders is primarily determined by aortic rim anatomy. However, the procedural characteristics and outcomes associated with each device when used according to this anatomy-driven algorithm have not been systematically described. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 426 pediatric patients who underwent perventricular VSD closure at two institutions over a 12-year period. Device selection was mandated by preoperative echocardiographic anatomy: symmetric occluders were used exclusively for aortic rim ≥2 mm (n=338), and asymmetric occluders for aortic rim <2 mm (n=88). Propensity score matching, inverse probability of treatment weighting were used to balance measured non-anatomical covariates. The primary outcomes were operative time, hospital stay, postoperative aortic regurgitation and arrhythmia. Results In this anatomy-driven cohort, the adequate-rim/symmetric-device pathway was characterized by a low incidence of increased AR grade, while the deficient-rim/asymmetric-device pathway was characterized by a 33% incidence of increased AR grade—all detected intraoperatively or before discharge and non-progressive on follow-up. Other complications were infrequent in both pathways. Conclusion In this anatomy-driven algorithm, each pathway had a distinct clinical profile. The adequate-rim/symmetric-device pathway carried a low burden of postoperative aortic regurgitation. The deficient-rim/asymmetric-device pathway carried an increased aortic regurgitation signal that was consistently mild, detected intraoperatively or before discharge, and non-progressive on follow-up; pre-existing aortic regurgitation did not worsen.

items.title: Machine Learning Performance and Fairness in Postoperative Atrial Fibrillation Prediction
items.abstract: Background Postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) occurs in 15-50% of cardiac surgery patients and is associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Risk scoring tools have been developed to predict POAF yet offer moderate discrimination performance. While machine learning models achieve better predictive performance, their fairness across demographic subgroups remains largely unexamined despite known racial and sex disparities in cardiac surgery outcomes. Methods We compared 9 risk scoring tools and 7 machine learning algorithms using data from 20,325 cardiac surgery patients (2010-2025), including >20% Black patients. Models used patient demographics, clinical conditions, and medications extracted from electronic health records. Performance was assessed using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC). Fairness was evaluated across race (White vs. Black/Asian/Other/Unknown) and sex subgroups using demographic parity ratio (DPR) and equalized odds ratios (EQR). Results Machine learning models outperformed risk scores in discrimination (best AUROC 0.750 versus 0.614, p<0.001) but demonstrated lower racial parity. Random forest achieved highest AUROC but lowest racial fairness (DPR 0.236-0.790, EQR 0.205-0.693), while support vector machine balanced moderate discrimination (AUROC 0.703) with better racial fairness (DPR 0.572-0.868, EQR 0.562-0.870). Racial fairness varied widely among risk scores, from near-perfect to poor. Sex-based fairness was generally higher than racial fairness for ML models but inconsistent across risk scores. Conclusions Superior predictive performance may not guarantee equitable risk score. Future development of POAF prediction models must address the performance-fairness tradeoff through bias mitigation techniques and validation in diverse populations to prevent perpetuating healthcare disparities.

items.title: Optimal Temperature Determination in a Canine Model of Hypothermic Circulatory Arrest
items.abstract: Objective Hypothermic circulatory arrest (HCA) is required for certain aortic and cardiac operations, but postoperative neurologic injury remains prevalent. There is currently no consensus on the optimal temperature. We used a canine model to investigate neurologic outcomes after HCA at 18, 24, and 28°C. Methods Eighteen canines underwent peripheral bypass followed by prolonged HCA (90 min) at 18, 24, or 28°C (n=6, 5, and 7, respectively) with antegrade cerebral perfusion at 10 mL/kg/min. After HCA, animals were rewarmed, weaned from bypass, and extubated. Over three postoperative days (POD), behavior, cognition, and biomarkers were assessed. On POD 3, brains were removed for mitochondrial function testing and neuropathology. Results There were no significant differences between groups in behavior scores on POD 1-3. However, two 28°C animals had notable neurologic deficits, with none in the other groups. Cognition, assessed by novel object recognition, was not different between groups (all p>0.1). The 28°C group had increased serum enolase levels on POD 1 and 2 (both p<0.05). There were no significant differences in cellular respiration (all p>0.15). Prominent brain damage was noted without differences in regional or global neuropathologic injury between groups (all p>0.2). Conclusions Temperatures of 18, 24, and 28°C for prolonged HCA with cerebral perfusion yielded similar results for behavior, cognition, mitochondrial function, and neuropathology in this model after excluding one 28°C animal with severe injury. Neurologic deficits (n=2) and increased serum enolase in 28°C animals suggest that continued investigation of the safety of warmer temperatures for prolonged HCA is warranted.

items.title: Totally Endoscopic Mitral Valve Repair for Barlow’s Disease: Similar freedom from re-intervention to Isolated Posterior Leaflet Prolapse
items.abstract: Structured Abstract Objectives Totally endoscopic mitral valve repair (TE-MVR) is an established treatment for primary mitral regurgitation. However, TE-MVR in Barlow´s disease (BD) might be challenging due to its complex pathology. Herein, investigation of long-term outcomes after TE-MVR for BD is conducted and results are compared to TE-MVR for isolated posterior mitral leaflet (PML) prolapse. Methods Between 2012 and 2022, out of 1055 patients, 131 patients underwent TE-MVR due to BD (group 1) and 304 patients due to isolated PML prolapse (group 2) at our center. Baseline characteristics, surgical techniques and clinical/echocardiographic outcomes up to 10 years were retrospectively analyzed. Results BD patients were younger (group 1: 53.0±13.4 vs. group 2: 59.9±10.7 years, p<0.001) and more frequently female (46.6% vs. 31.6%, p=0.002). Cross-clamp time was longer in BD (110.8±38.3 vs. 103.1±32.2 min, p=0.046), cardiopulmonary bypass and procedure times were similar. Annuloplasty ring size was larger in BD (36.3±2.6 vs. 33.0±2.7 mm, p<0.001). Repair techniques in BD consisted of: neochordae to PML (55.0%), neochordae to AML (31.3%), leaflet resection (31.3%), Alfieri stitch (14.5%); 83.8% of PML patients received annuloplasty and neochordae to PML only. 30-day mortality was similar (0.8% vs. 0.3%, p=0.510). Ten-year survival (90.3% vs. 91.9%, p=0.879) and freedom from re-operation (95.5% vs. 97.8%, p=0.433) were similar. Conclusions TE-MVR in BD is safe and durable. Despite the need for more complex repair techniques, acute and long-term outcomes as well as durability were excellent. Durability of TE-MVR in Barlow's disease beyond 10 years of follow-up should be subject to further investigations. Abstract word count : 244

items.title: Aortic Valve Replacement During Acute Type A Dissection Repair: Bioprosthetic versus Mechanical, Does it Matter?
items.abstract: Objective Aortic valve replacement (AVR) is common during acute type A aortic dissection (ATAAD) repair, but preferences regarding prosthesis choice is unclear. We compared bioprosthetic and mechanical AVR and identified factors associated with valve selection and mortality. Methods From 1/2000-1/2022, 1,311 patients underwent ATAAD repair, 345(26%) included AVR (bioprosthetic N=289;mechanical N=56). Survival and reoperation, cumulative incidence estimated valve reintervention with death as a competing risk, and multivariable models identified factors associated with valve selection and with mortality including prosthesis type. Results Bioprosthetic recipients were older (64 vs 47 years, P<.001), less often had connective tissue disorder (9% vs 21%, P=.04), more often underwent extended aortic repair (26% vs 5.4%, P<.001), and had longer bypass times (189 vs 156 minutes, P<.001). Stroke was more frequent after bioprosthetic AVR (11% vs 1.8%, P=.03); in-hospital mortality did not differ statistically (12% vs 5.4%, P=.16). Ten-year freedom from valve reintervention did not differ; competing-risk incidence of reoperation was 18% versus 24% (P=.30). Unadjusted ten-year survival was lower after bioprosthetic AVR (47% vs 66%, P<.05), but adjusted for age, presentation, and complexity, prosthesis type was not independently associated (HR 1.11, P=.72). Conclusions Worse unadjusted survival after bioprosthetic AVR during ATAAD repair was associated with age, presentation, and operative complexity rather than prosthesis type; reintervention did not differ at ten years. We prefer valve sparing when feasible, a mechanical prosthesis in young patients with heritable aortic disease when it is not, and a bioprosthesis otherwise. Valve selection is not the driver of mortality risk is ATAAD.

items.title: Does Circulatory Arrest Add Operative Risk? A Propensity-Matched Comparison of Elective Hemiarch Replacement and Isolated AVR
International Medical Graduates, Research and Residency: The Physician-Scientist Trajectory
Donor-Recipient Size Mismatch in Pediatric Heart Transplantation.
Utilization and Outcomes of Root Enlargement and Aortic Valve Replacement in the United States
The Impact of Sievers Type on Valve Degeneration in Valve Sparing Aortic Root Replacement
Evolution of Single Ventricle Assist Device Support Strategies for Stage II Physiology: A Single Center’s Decade of Experience
One Year Survival of High-Risk Patients Undergoing Coronary Revascularization
items.abstract: Background In high-risk patients requiring coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) we sought to evaluate the differential impact of comorbid and cardiovascular risk factors on perioperative versus one year survival with the hypothesis that different phenotypes of perioperative risk may portend different longitudinal outcomes and that not all high-risk features are equivalent. Methods The Society Thoracic Surgeons (STS) Adult Cardiac Surgery Database (ACSD) was used to assess all patients (n=75,385) ≥65 years of age undergoing isolated CABG with a predicted risk of mortality (PROM) greater than 4% (2012-2022). The database was linked with Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) claims data to evaluate one-year mortality. Change in risk-adjusted odds ratios for 30-day and 1-year mortality were assessed using landmark analysis to identify variables associated with early versus late mortality. Results A total of 67,376 (89.4%) patients survived 30-days of those 8,998 (13.4%) died between 30 days and one year. Liver disease and home oxygen were associated with increased mortality at both 30 days and 1 year. However, unresponsive state, prior CABG, percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) within 6 hours, cardiogenic shock, and temporary mechanical support were associated with early mortality but exhibited no significant effects at 1 year. Finally, cancer, Medicaid coverage, and dialysis were initially neutral for 30-day mortality but emerged as independent risk factors for 1-year mortality. Conclusions In high-risk CABG, prognostic determinants evolve over time. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating temporal risk dynamics into clinical decisions.

items.title: We Love Aortic Surgery, But It’s the Genes that Hold the Key to Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm Disease
Open TAR: Still the Benchmark
Lifetime Management of Aortic Stenosis: Expert Review of Evidence and Consensus Guidelines
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The 2025 European Society of Cardiology/European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery Guidelines introduced a Class I recommendation for transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) in selected patients aged 70 years or older with tricuspid aortic stenosis and suitable anatomy, while surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) remains recommended in younger low-risk patients. In patients with long expected survival, this framework requires careful consideration of valve durability, future reintervention, and patient preferences. This expert review, developed by the Italian Cardiac Surgery Working Group, examines contemporary evidence and consensus recommendations from a lifetime-management perspective. METHODS: We performed a narrative, evidence-based synthesis of randomized trials, trial-based meta-analyses, and propensity-matched real-world registries comparing transfemoral TAVI and SAVR, with primary emphasis on low-risk patients. Lower-intermediate-risk evidence was included only when directly relevant to lifetime management, durability, or reintervention. RESULTS: Evidence suggests that treatment effects are time-dependent: early non-inferiority of TAVI may attenuate with longer follow-up, particularly in patients with substantial life expectancy. Randomized durability data remain limited, whereas propensity-matched real-world registries have suggested possible higher late mortality after TAVI in younger, lower-risk populations. Reintervention after a transcatheter-first strategy may be associated with increasing technical complexity and procedural risk over time. CONCLUSIONS: This review supports appropriate application of current guidelines through a pragmatic framework for individualized, Heart Team-based decision-making. Transfemoral TAVI is often appropriate in patients with limited life expectancy or recognized high surgical risk when anatomically feasible. In patients with long expected survival, SAVR should retain a central role as an important reference strategy.

Locating the Gender Payment Gap Among Recent Cardiothoracic Surgery Graduates: A Bottom-up Analysis of Medicare Payments
items.abstract: Background Women comprise an increasing proportion of cardiothoracic surgery trainees, yet gender differences in Medicare payments persist. Whether these differences reflect clinical volume or payment for the same service remains unclear. Methods We analyzed 2024 Medicare fee-for-service data for cardiothoracic surgeons graduating from integrated residency or independent fellowship programs between 2013 and 2023. Cardiac and thoracic surgeons were analyzed separately; mixed-practice surgeons were excluded. Mixed-effects models assessed associations between surgeon gender, clinical activity, and standardized payments. Results Among 898 surgeons, women comprised 19% (n=107) of cardiac surgeons and 25% (n=84) of thoracic surgeons. Women received lower mean annual standardized payments than men in cardiac surgery ($79,524 vs $103,940) and thoracic surgery ($52,180 vs $66,474; both p Conclusions Women treated fewer Medicare patients, performed fewer services, billed fewer unique service codes, and received lower annual payments than men. The payment difference was largely attenuated after accounting for clinical activity, while payment for the same service did not differ by gender. These findings locate the Medicare payment difference primarily in clinical volume and breadth of practice rather than service-level reimbursement.

items.title: Aortic Valve Replacement in Patients 50-65 Years: A Target Trial Emulation
items.abstract: Background Guidelines favor surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) in patients aged 65 years or younger with aortic stenosis, yet many receive transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) without supportive data. We performed a target trial emulation of SAVR versus TAVI in this population. Methods Using the all-payer Premier Healthcare Database (2016-2024), patients aged 50 to 65 years undergoing isolated SAVR or TAVI within 90 days of an aortic stenosis diagnosis were evaluated. After trial exclusions, frailty and predicted risk were incorporated into a clone-censor-weight framework with inverse probability weighting. Reporting adhered to TARGET guidance. The primary outcome was the 5-year composite of all-cause mortality, stroke, valve reintervention, or heart failure rehospitalization. Results The clone-censor-weighted analysis included 18,549 SAVR and 18,549 TAVI patients, balanced across all covariates (standardized mean difference Conclusions For contemporary patients aged 50 to 65 years, the primary composite outcome favored SAVR over TAVI at 5 years, most markedly at centers with high young TAVI utilization. These data may guide heart team decision making and future trial design.

items.title: Statewide Trends in Morbidity and Mortality in Octogenarians Undergoing Isolated Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting
items.abstract: Background We sought to determine whether advanced age modifies the association between established preoperative risk factors and 30-day outcomes following isolated coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), compare temporal trends between octogenarians and younger patients, and characterize differences in perioperative outcomes between the two groups. Methods Using the Michigan Society of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgeons Quality Collaborative (The Society of Thoracic Surgeons Adult Cardiac Surgery Database), we identified 105,445 patients undergoing isolated CABG from 2006-2024. Outcomes and case volumes were assessed across four eras. Operative mortality was evaluated using mixed-effects logistic regression with hospital as a random effect. Secondary analyses used multiple imputation with hospital-clustered multivariable logistic regression to evaluate age-related effect modification for short-term mortality and morbidity. Results Octogenarians comprised 8.1% of cases (8,563/105,445). Operative mortality was higher in octogenarians (4.8%; n=413) than patients Conclusions In octogenarians, CABG remains associated with higher morbidity and mortality than in younger patients, with minimal changes in 30-day outcomes over the last 20 years. Most traditional risk factors demonstrated similar relative associations across age groups, with age-specific effects in select postoperative domains.

items.title: Looking Back to Look Ahead: Medicaid Expansion and its Effect on Stage at Diagnosis and Surgery Rates in NSCLC
items.abstract: Background Given the uncertain future and potential changes to Medicaid, we sought to evaluate the impact of the 2014 Affordable Care Act Medicaid Expansion on non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) stage at diagnosis and rates of surgery for patients diagnosed with clinical stage I disease. Methods The National Cancer Database was used to identify patients diagnosed with NSCLC between 2004 and 2022, stratified by diagnosis timing (pre- vs post Medicaid expansion) and state expansion status. Demographic, clinical, and treatment variables were compared across time periods and expansion status using chi-square tests (categorical) and t-tests (continuous). Results Among 1,585,967 patients diagnosed with NSCLC, during the study period, 37.9% (n=600,411) were diagnosed pre-expansion and 62.1% (n=982,556) post-expansion (Table 1). A notable shift toward earlier stage of diagnosis was identified in the post-expansion era: only 17.4% (n=85,351) of patients were with cIA NSCLC pre-expansion compared to 27.3% (n=243,434) post-expansion. This shift was additionally more pronounced in expansion states (28.1% [n=135,686] vs 26.2% [n=107,748], p Conclusions Medicaid expansion was associated with increased early-stage NSCLC diagnosis and surgical treatment with larger gains in expansion states, suggesting a direct effect on access and screening. As Medicaid policy evolves, continued advocacy is vital to ensure early detection and adequate care delivery for patients with NSCLC.

items.title: A Meta-Analysis of the Role of Esophagectomy in Stage 4 Esophageal Cancer
items.abstract: Background Nearly 40% of new cases of esophageal cancer are diagnosed at stage 4. Esophagectomy may offer a survival benefit in highly selected patients with stage 4 esophageal cancer. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Databases including PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched. Studies reporting survival outcomes in patients with stage 4 esophageal cancer undergoing surgical resection were included. Random-effects models were used to pool 3-year overall survival (OS) and hazard ratios (HRs). Subgroup analyses were performed based on the timing of survival measurement (diagnosis vs. surgery). Results Eleven studies comprising 608 surgical patients were included. The pooled 3-year OS was 43% (95% confidence interval {CI}, 22%-67%) when measured from surgery and 61% (95% CI, 23%-89%) when measured from diagnosis or treatment initiation, with substantial heterogeneity (I 2 >80%). Pooled HR analysis of the 2 comparative studies without gastric cancer showed better survival with surgery, although the difference was not significant (HR, 0.16 [95% CI, 0.00-6.19]); a sensitivity analysis with the gastric cancer study yielded a similar estimate (HR, 0.25 [95% CI, 0.03-2.02]). Favorable prognostic factors included R0 resection, ypM0 status, lower nodal burden, response to systemic therapy, and oligometastatic disease. Conclusions In highly selected patients with stage IV esophageal cancer, particularly those with oligometastatic disease and favorable response to systemic therapy, esophagectomy may be considered within a multimodal treatment strategy. These findings support a biologically driven, response-adapted approach to conversion surgery. Prospective studies are required to define its role.

items.title: The Society of Thoracic Surgeons 2026 Long-term Risk Models for Lung Cancer Resection
items.abstract: Background The Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) has designed and validated risk models to predict long-term survival in patients undergoing lung cancer resection. Methods Adult patients undergoing curative intent lung resection for primary lung cancer in the STS General Thoracic Surgery Database (2015-2023) were included. Vital status was ascertained through linkage to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention National Death Index and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inpatient records. The primary endpoint was mortality, truncated at 7 years with >12% remaining at risk. 70% derivation and 30% validation subgroups were utilized. Individualized survival prediction risk scores were derived using separate stratified multivariable Cox proportional hazards models for patients with and without major postoperative complications. Model discrimination was quantified by bootstrap-adjusted Harrel's C-index. Calibration was assessed visually comparing predicted and observed survival curves. Results The study included 112,756 patients across 362 STS participant hospitals, of whom 7.0% experienced a postoperative complication. Median follow-up was 3.9 years (95% CI, 3.8-4.0), during which 28,903 deaths (25.6%) occurred. Adenocarcinoma (66.0%) and stage I disease were most prevalent (68.8%). The optimism-adjusted C-index for the risk models were good for patients with [0.71 (95% CI, 0.70-0.71)] and without major complications [0.72 (0.71-0.73)]. Calibration of the model was excellent overall and in prespecified subgroups in the 30% validation set. Conclusions The STS now offers thoracic surgeons short- and long-term models for self-evaluation, quality improvement, and research. Development of public facing risk calculators will operationalize this novel resource.

items.title: Pharmacological Prevention of Cardiac Surgery-Associated Acute Kidney Injury: Why Trials Failed and a Reimagined Endpoint Framework
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cardiac surgery-associated acute kidney injury affects approximately one in four adults and is independently associated with perioperative mortality and progression to chronic kidney disease. Despite more than two decades of randomized pharmacological trials, few have met their primary endpoint. METHODS: This invited narrative review examined 33 pivotal randomized trials of pharmacological prevention published from 2004 to 2026, grouped by mechanism, and related population, intervention timing, and endpoint selection to trial outcome. RESULTS: Trials using short-term creatinine-based kidney injury endpoints produced the positive signals, whereas trials using major adverse kidney events at 90 days as the primary endpoint were negative. This divergence reflects both the low power of that composite for detecting injury prevention and unresolved biology, since no agent has shown benefit on both types of endpoint. Positive trials shared a matched mechanism, a defined population, and an aligned endpoint. Recurrent failure modes were endpoint misalignment, mismatch between population and the timing of injury, confounding by postoperative cardiac recovery, and direct drug effects on creatinine or urine output that mimic or mask injury. CONCLUSIONS: We propose a trial framework with persistent stage 2 or 3 acute kidney disease at 30 days, by Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes criteria, as the primary endpoint; preoperative albuminuria as an enrichment criterion; and attenuation of the postoperative rise in albuminuria at 30 and 90 days as a key secondary endpoint. Platform designs with biomarker-enriched enrollment could convert the next generation of trials into interpretable tests of kidney protection.

Association of Adult and Pediatric Cardiac Surgery Volumes with Outcomes of the Ross Procedure in Adults
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: There is growing interest in application of the Ross procedure for treatment of aortic valve disease; however, utilization is restricted to specialized centers. The present study evaluated the differential association of adult aortic valve surgery and pediatric cardiac surgery volumes on outcomes of adults undergoing the Ross operation. METHODS: The 2016-2022 Nationwide Readmissions Database was queried to identify all adults undergoing the Ross procedure. Hospitals were categorized as pediatric high-volume centers (pHVC, ≥75th percentile pediatric cardiac surgery volume), adult high-volume centers (aHVC, ≥75th percentile aortic valve replacement/repair volume among non-pHVC), and low-volume centers (LVC). Major adverse events (MAE) were defined as a composite of mortality, stroke, prolonged ventilation, acute renal failure, pulmonary embolism, cardiac arrest, and reoperation. RESULTS: Among 1,212 adults undergoing the Ross operation, 37.7% were treated at pHVC, 56.7% at aHVC, and 5.6% at LVC. National utilization increased from 63 cases in 2016 to 385 in 2022, with the number of performing centers rising from 14 to 37. Patients at LVC experienced the highest rates of MAE (42.1% vs aHVC 8.8% vs pHVC 3.8%, p<0.001). After risk adjustment, care at LVC was associated with a 7.7-fold increase in odds of MAE compared to pHVC (95% CI 3.0-19.7, p<0.001). Outcomes at aHVC and pHVC were comparable, although aHVC had higher rates of reoperation (4.5% vs 0.6%, p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Adults undergoing the Ross operation at LVC face worse outcomes compared to aHVC and pHVC. These findings support selective referral strategies and regionalization of care.

items.title: Safety and Feasibility of Single-Port Robotic Lung Cancer Resection: Initial United States Experience of 145 Consecutive Cases
items.abstract: PURPOSE: The da Vinci single-port (SP) robotic system was approved for thoracic surgery in the United States in July 2024. Reports of its application in lung cancer remain limited. We present the initial experience with 145 consecutive SP resections for primary lung cancer at a single institution, with an emphasis on safety and oncologic quality. DESCRIPTION: The SP robotic platform enables lung resection through a single subcostal incision, avoiding intercostal nerve injury. EVALUATION: Three surgeons performed 34 SP lobectomies, 23 segmentectomies, and 88 wedge resections (95% stage I, 5% post-induction) between 6/2025-7/2026. Perioperative outcomes, oncologic quality, and learning curve were analyzed. Median operative time was 113 minutes, estimated blood loss 10mL, and length of stay 2 days. There were 3 conversions. R0 resection occurred in 99.3% of cases. Median lymph node yield was 5 nodes. There were zero mortalities and 4.8% major complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥III). Cumulative-sum analysis identified a learning curve plateau after 23 cases. CONCLUSIONS: Subcostal SP robotic lung resection is feasible and safe with acceptable perioperative and oncologic outcomes. Comparative studies are warranted.

items.title: Surgical Timing and Physiology-Specific Outcomes in Congenital Heart Disease
items.abstract: Background In low- and middle-income countries, most children with congenital heart disease reach the operating room after the guideline-recommended window has closed. Existing analyses grade delay by chronological age or a binary early/late split and report outcomes in aggregate, not by physiology. Methods All 12,190 consecutive pediatric congenital heart operations at a single Indian tertiary center (2020-2025) were graded against national guidelines using a lesion-normalized Guideline Deviation Score, from G0 (timely) to G4 (critically delayed). Logistic regression and restricted cubic splines assessed operative mortality, morbidity, and resource utilization overall and within seven pre-specified physiological subgroups. Results Of 10,187 gradable operations, 73.7% were delayed and 34.8% critically delayed. Operative mortality was 2.1% (adjusted OR per grade, 0.88 [95% CI, 0.81-0.96]; P = .004). Fontan-stage palliation was the only subgroup with progressive morbidity increase (64% at guideline age, 85% at grade 3; P = .002), inflecting near age 12 years. Left-to-right shunt lesions showed forward morbidity accumulation (adjusted OR, 1.05 [1.01-1.09]; P = .03). Resource utilization rose with delay overall (adjusted OR, 1.04 [1.01-1.07]; P = .01) and in left-to-right shunt and transposition physiology, but fell in cyanotic and Fontan-stage groups. Conclusions Three in four children missed their guideline window. Operative mortality did not rise with delay, which reflects case-mix confounding rather than evidence that delay is safe, since the youngest and sickest children are operated first. Morbidity rose with delay in Fontan-stage and left-to-right shunt physiology. Physiology-specific grading supports surgical decision-making when a child presents late.

items.title: Impact of Mental Health Disorders on Pulmonary Resection: A Society of Thoracic Surgeons General Thoracic Surgery Medicare Linked Study
items.abstract: Background To determine the prevalence of comorbid mental health disorders (MHDs) and association with stage of diagnosis, extent of resection, and post-operative morbidity/mortality in patients undergoing operative intervention for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Methods Adults undergoing elective resection of stage I-III NSCLC were identified from the Society of Thoracic Surgeons General Thoracic Surgery Database (July 2018-June 2024) and linked to Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to determine long-term survival. Primary outcomes were stage at diagnosis, extent of resection, perioperative morbidity, and 5-year survival. Hierarchical multivariable logistic regressions estimated associations between MHDs on each outcome. Risk-adjusted survival was derived using multivariable frailty Cox proportional hazards regression. Results Among 103,263 patients, 24.4% (n=25,163) had ≥1 MHD. Prevalence of MHDs increased from 16.8% in 2018 to 28.0% in 2024 (p Conclusions The prevalence of MHDs among patients undergoing NSCLC resection nearly doubled over 6 years and was associated with an ∼20% increase in morbidity and a reduction in adjusted 5-year survival. These findings underscore the need for targeted perioperative pathways and longitudinal support to mitigate adverse outcomes in this growing population.

items.title: Beyond PaO2: From Donor Assessment to Donor Management in Lung Transplantation
Trends in Outcomes and Regional Rates of Pulmonary Thromboendarterectomy: A National Analysis
items.abstract: Background Pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE) is the guideline-recommended treatment for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). Here, we report modern-era national-level outcomes and identify regions that lack access to PTE. Methods The STS Adult Cardiac Surgery Database was queried from 2012 to 2024 for patients in the USA who underwent PTE with circulatory arrest for chronic disease. Patient characteristics, region, travel distance, area deprivation index (ADI), temporal trends (2012-2018 vs 2019-2024), and center volume (≤15/year vs >15/year) were described and evaluated for association with 30-day mortality. Multivariable logistic regression was conducted, reported as adjusted odds ratios (aORs). Results Over the study period, 4,101 PTEs were performed; 1,238 in 2012-2018 and 2,863 in 2019-2024. Between the two periods, 25 centers closed and 35 centers opened. Higher volume centers (>15 PTE/ year) had significantly lower 30-day post-operative mortality rates compared to lower-volume centers (2.6% vs. 5.5%, p Conclusions The volume-outcome relationship for 30-day mortality after PTE persists over time and there is regional variation in rates of PTE. Development of regional centers of excellence is imperative to ensure access to high-quality CTEPH treatment.
