Three Decades of Paediatric Heart Transplantation: Long-term Outcomes and the Evolving Role of Mechanical Circulatory Support
items.abstract: Heart transplantation (HTx) remains the definitive therapy for children with end-stage heart failure, while donor scarcity exposes candidates to deterioration during waiting. Mechanical circulatory support (MCS), particularly ventricular assist devices (VADs), has therefore become an increasingly important bridge to transplantation.1–5 We report the long-term experience of a single high-volume congenital heart centre over more than 3 decades, focusing on temporal changes in paediatric HTx and the evolving role of pretransplant MCS. We retrospectively reviewed 267 patients transplanted at our institution between 1988 and 2024. The cohort was defined by transplantation within the paediatric/congenital programme. Clinical, operative and follow-up data were extracted from institutional records. Overall survival was assessed by Kaplan–Meier analysis. Mechanical circulatory support before HTx was retained as a clinical variable rather than used to define the primary study groups. Mechanical circulatory support included extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and VAD support. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Justus Liebig University Giessen (AZ 94/23; July 27, 2023).

items.title: What Are the Survival Outcomes of Patients Requiring Postcardiotomy Temporary Mechanical Circulatory Support?
items.abstract: Postcardiotomy low cardiac output syndrome (PC-LCOS) remains a poorly characterized complication of cardiac surgery, often necessitating temporary mechanical circulatory support (tMCS) with resource utilization and variable outcomes. Evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, derived from retrospective, single-centre studies. Consequently, the prognosis of patients requiring postcardiotomy tMCS remains uncertain, representing a critical concern for clinicians initiating support. In-hospital survival after postcardiotomy tMCS remains ∼40% (range 15%-55%), with varying results based on clinical severity, extent and aetiology of ventricular dysfunction, type and timing of tMCS.1,2 On-support mortality accounts for ∼60% of in-hospital deaths, predominantly occurring within the first 3 days of support and associated with greater preoperative instability, severe postoperative haemometabolic compromise, cardiac arrest, bleeding, and delayed tMCS initiation.1,3 Conversely, post-weaning mortality accounts for ∼40% of deaths and is closely related to complications including re-thoracotomy, bowel ischaemia, acute kidney injury, and septic shock.1,2 Survival according to tMCS duration follows an inverted U-shaped pattern, with the highest values (49%) among patients supported for 4-7 days. Approximately 30% of patients requiring postcardiotomy tMCS remain on support for >7 days, with in-hospital survival falling to 33% and 27% beyond 7 and 10 days, respectively.4 Survival decreases in specific populations, including patients ≥70 years of age (24%-31%), those undergoing aortic surgery (26%-33%), receiving extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (overall: 33%-35%; with favourable neurological outcome: 23%-29%),5 postoperative tMCS (36%), or central cannulation (28%-32%), although these findings should be interpreted cautiously given potential selection bias.1,4 Prophylactic, preoperatively planned tMCS initiation before cardiopulmonary bypass weaning in patients at high risk of PC-LCOS has yielded promising survival rates of up to 96%.3 Despite high early mortality, survivors to discharge have a favourable long-term prognosis, with an estimated 66% 10-year survival.1

items.title: The Standstill in Cardioplegia: Have We Reached the Peak of Myocardial Protection?
David Paul Taggart (1958-2026): In MemoriamSurgeon-scientist, patient advocate, and friend
items.abstract: The death of David Paul Taggart on August 8, 2026, at the age of 68, has deprived cardiovascular surgery of one of its most original, courageous and impactful voices. It has also deprived us both of a longstanding academic partner and friend. David was an outstanding surgeon and clinical investigator, and a relentless advocate for scientific truth who put the interests of the patient above all other considerations. David Taggart was born in Glasgow on July 1, 1958 and grew up in Scotland, with his seven siblings in a close-knit family. He studied medicine at the University of Glasgow, qualifying in 1981. His postgraduate training took him through Glasgow, Paris, Newcastle and London, including the Royal Brompton Hospital, where he trained under Sir Magdi Yacoub and Mr Christopher Lincoln; he often spoke fondly of their mentorship. He received an MD with Honours in 1989 and completed a PhD at the University of Strathclyde in 2000. In 1995 he was appointed Consultant Cardiothoracic Surgeon at Oxford’s John Radcliffe Hospital; in 2004 he became Professor of Cardiovascular Surgery at the University of Oxford. During his long and happy Oxford career, Professor Taggart—often simply called “Prof” by his many students, mentees and colleagues—conducted or participated in more than 20 original studies and clinical trials and authored more than 350 peer-reviewed publications. He served as President of the Society for Cardiothoracic Surgery in Great Britain and Ireland (SCTS) from 2010 to 2012. Although he is best known as a global expert on surgical coronary revascularization, Taggart’s early research revealed a broad intellectual curiosity in numerous areas of cardiac surgical physiology and pathophysiology. He examined hypothermia and the metabolic, endocrine and acute-phase responses to cardiopulmonary bypass and investigated postoperative respiratory dysfunction, attempting to distinguish the contributions of cardiopulmonary bypass from those of bilateral internal thoracic artery harvesting. His PhD thesis explored whether antagonism of platelet-activating factor could ameliorate the myocardial, pulmonary and cerebral consequences of cardiac surgery. Later studies led by Taggart included biochemical assessment of myocardial injury, a randomized investigation of postoperative lung injury and a randomized neuroprotection trial. Even when interventions were not consistently beneficial, Taggart published those negative findings, demonstrating his firm belief in the importance of randomized trials to provide evidence for cardiac surgical procedures. In the middle of his career, Taggart began to focus on advancing the state of the art in coronary bypass surgery. His 2001 systematic review of largely observational data found a substantial survival advantage associated with bilateral rather than single internal mammary artery grafting.1 This prompted him to build a multidisciplinary collaborative team to undertake the difficult task of testing the hypothesis prospectively. The result was the Arterial Revascularisation Trial (ART), which he conceived with the late Douglas Altman, to compare mortality rates between coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) using standard single internal thoracic artery grafts versus bilateral internal thoracic artery grafts in a randomized controlled trial. The grant application for ART to the UK Medical Research Council and British Heart Foundation was successful, and £3.4 million (about 5 million US dollars at the time) was awarded to Taggart, the University of Oxford and the Clinical Trials and Evaluation Unit at Royal Brompton Hospital, London. Between 2004 and 2007, 3102 patients were randomized at 28 cardiac surgery sites in 7 countries to single or bilateral internal thoracic artery CABG surgery with vein grafts. Enrolment into the trial was consistently ahead of schedule which was a tribute to Taggart’s leadership and ability to convene a group of enthusiastic cardiac surgeons to participate in the trial. Clinical follow-up and data analysis have continued through 15 years, during which David partnered closely with Oxford cardiologist Marcus Flather to lead the analytic team. An interim 5-year report,2 the primary outcome report at 10 years3 and the most recent 15-year follow-up report4 were consistent and showed that for the intention-to-treat analysis there was no difference in mortality rates between the two strategies. For the secondary composite outcome of death, myocardial infarction and stroke there was a slight numerical advantage for the bilateral approach, but this was not statistically significant. Interpretation was complicated by important treatment crossovers: approximately 14% of patients assigned to bilateral grafting received only one internal thoracic artery, while approximately 22% assigned to single grafting received a radial artery as a second arterial conduit. David presented the 15-year ART results at the American Association for Thoracic Surgery meeting in May 2026. The intention-to-treat comparison remained neutral, whereas the as-treated analysis again associated actual receipt of multiple arterial grafts with significantly lower mortality. ART is an important trial because observational studies have consistently shown that bilateral internal thoracic artery grafts are associated with lower mortality compared to standard single internal thoracic artery grafts, but these studies are often confounded by unbalanced covariates like age and gender which may introduce bias in spite of statistical adjustments. Taggart was one of the pioneers of multiple arterial graft CABG and many of his operations included bilateral internal thoracic artery grafts carried out using off-pump techniques. He personally enrolled more than 400 patients in ART and his own results demonstrated about 15% proportional mortality reduction with the bilateral approach—an observation that he was proud of even if it did not change the trial’s overall conclusion. Taggart’s body of work included several studies of off-pump CABG. He was an investigator and co-author in the international CORONARY trial,5 the largest randomized comparison of on-pump and off-pump CABG. His subsequent ART sub-analyses clearly demonstrated that off-pump surgery can achieve excellent outcomes, but its success is highly dependent upon operator experience. In ART, low-volume off-pump surgeons performed fewer grafts, converted to cardiopulmonary bypass more frequently and had worse patient outcomes.6 He also investigated methods of improving the performance of saphenous-vein grafts. The VEST programme evaluated whether external stenting could reduce adverse remodelling, lumen irregularity and diffuse intimal hyperplasia. The first randomized study showed reduced intimal hyperplasia area at 1 year, and subsequent multicentre work demonstrated improved FitzGibbon patency classification and reduced intimal thickening at 2 years, although a definitive clinical benefit remained unproven.7 Taggart also brought his evidence-based approach to intraoperative assessment of graft quality, with the prospective, multicentre REQUEST registry, in which protocol-based transit-time flow measurement and high-frequency epicardial and epi-aortic ultrasonography were used in 1016 patients undergoing CABG. Intraoperative assessment prompted a change in the planned operative strategy in 25.2% of patients, including graft revision in 7.8% of patients. This project reflected Taggart’s belief that the technical quality of coronary bypass surgery should be objectively measured and verified rather than presumed at the conclusion of every CABG operation.8 The rise of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in the 1990s and early 2000s saw a corresponding decline in CABG numbers globally. Taggart was very concerned about this, not because he was worried about becoming an “extinct” cardiac surgeon but because he felt that patients were being sold short with incorrect treatment decisions in favour of PCI when treating symptomatic coronary artery disease (CAD). He expressed concerns that cardiac surgeons were being left out of the decision-making process, where the interventional cardiologist would often assess the patient and advise PCI treatment without wider consultation. His efforts, and the efforts of others, led to the concept of the “heart team” approach, whereby patients with advanced or complex CAD would be discussed in a multidisciplinary team meeting with cardiologists, cardiac surgeons and other experts to provide the best treatment strategy. Reports that pooled individual patient data from the randomized trials of PCI vs CABG for symptomatic CAD consistently showed survival advantages for CABG in patients with complex CAD, including diabetes. These results shaped the revascularisation guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and the European Association of Cardiac and Thoracic Surgeons (EACTS) and undoubtedly allowed patients more appropriate access to CABG. Taggart was a popular speaker on this topic at international meetings, and his command of the relevant data and his fearless ability to push back against the tide of popular opinion was legendary. Taggart’s invited Ferguson Lecture at the Society of Thoracic Surgeons meeting in 2006 bore a title that broadcast his deeply held conviction: “Coronary artery bypass grafting is still the best treatment for multivessel and left main disease, but patients need to know.”9 Taggart was also well known, even notorious in some circles, for his fallout with the EXCEL study group, which conducted a large randomized controlled trial comparing PCI versus CABG in patients with left main CAD. When the 5-year results were being analysed, Taggart pointed out that mortality rates were higher in the PCI group and felt that the manuscript should emphasize the mortality outcome, but was voted down. Taggart also felt that the Universal Definition for perioperative MI should be reported in a sensitivity analysis as prespecified, and that the difference in definition of perioperative MI had effectively tilted the composite primary endpoint in favour of PCI; this was later shown to be mathematically true.10 He ultimately resigned from the EXCEL Steering Committee and took his name off the author list. This became a widely reported issue, with the New England Journal of Medicine requesting clarifications and the BBC launching an independent investigation of the data.11 This episode underscored Taggart’s trademark determination to seek the truth for patients and ensure that information is shared transparently with the scientific and clinical community. The eventual ESC/EACTS reassessment concluded that, among low-surgical-risk patients with left-main anatomy suitable for either treatment, both CABG and PCI were clinically reasonable, while proposing Class I, Level A support for CABG and Class IIa, Level A support for PCI. This controversy did nothing to diminish Taggart’s advocacy for the multidisciplinary Heart Team approach to coronary care. His commitment to ethical partnership between cardiac surgeons and cardiologists was recognized by the leadership of Transcatheter Therapeutics Asia-Pacific (TCTAP) in granting David Taggart the Master of Masters award in 2026, the first time a surgeon has ever received this prestigious award. In 2015, Taggart and Puskas co-founded the International Coronary Congress (ICC), and subsequently the International Society for Coronary Artery Surgery (https://internationalcoronarycongress.com). Now in its 12th year, ICC is the only annual international scientific meeting entirely devoted to advancing the state of the art in surgical coronary revascularization and has been attended by more than 10 000 cumulative delegates from more than 50 countries. From the inaugural meeting in 2015, Taggart delivered numerous lectures at each ICC meeting, engaged in many collegial debates and panel discussions and earned legions of admirers and friends from among his international coronary surgical colleagues. He was especially proud of having co-founded the International Coronary Congress; Taggart was an academic globalist who viewed world-class coronary surgery as something that should be available around the world. Moreover, he was convinced that coronary surgeons in all parts of the world could best advance the state of the art in coronary surgery by working and learning together. Taggart and Puskas created and personally funded the ICC Founders’ Fellowship to help defray the costs of attendance at each annual ICC meeting for young coronary surgical trainees and junior faculty; it has now been renamed the David Taggart Memorial Founders’ Fellowship. Taggart was immediately recognizable at the ICC or any other scientific meeting in his customary Oxford shirt and denim jeans, without a jacket or tie (Figure 1). David Taggart and John Puskas at the Inaugural Meeting of the International Coronary Congress, New York City, 2015. David Taggart was a tireless educator in coronary surgery globally and travelled the world delivering hundreds of invited lectures. He was a generous mentor to dozens of trainees and hundreds of colleagues worldwide. Also with Puskas, Taggart conceived and co-edited the 2021 Oxford University Press textbook entitled “State-of-the-Art Surgical Coronary Revascularization,” the first and only major textbook devoted solely to every nuance of surgical coronary revascularization.12 Taggart had many interests outside of cardiac surgery. He had an encyclopaedic knowledge of contemporary art. He loved sailing in the Mediterranean, snowboarding in the Alps, appreciated a good pub anywhere and possessed a mischievous sense of humour. In June 2026, only weeks before his death, he married Kathleen Hargreaves, his life partner, in an elegant ceremony in the Cotswolds, England. After a Mediterranean honeymoon, Taggart lectured in Asia in July 2026. Typical of David’s self-determination, he continued to live and to work as he saw fit, without breaking stride, despite his terminal illness. David Taggart’s greatest professional legacy is not an operation, conduit, clinical trial or controversy. It is an attitude towards our profession: surgeons must generate evidence rather than merely invoke experience; difficult improvements should not be dismissed because they require advanced training; important negative results deserve publication; and allegiance to institutions, specialties and even professional colleagues must remain subordinate to allegiance to our patients. He was a genuinely honest and honourable professional colleague. He was a tremendously productive academic partner for more than 20 years for each of us and a close friend to us both. We will miss him dearly. Godspeed, David Taggart. None declared. None declared. AI was used to confirm the accuracy of references and dates.

items.title: Coronary Dominance and Variations in Right Ventricular Failure After Left Ventricular Assist Device Implantation
Congenital syphilis requiring VA-ECMO: A case report
items.abstract: Congenital syphilis (CS) is a severe infection with a rising global incidence and potentially life-threatening neonatal outcomes. We present a late preterm infant exhibiting respiratory distress, hepatosplenomegaly, and systemic inflammation. Diagnosed with congenital syphilis at 12 hours of life, targeted antimicrobial was promptly initiated. Despite maximal medical management, her clinical course rapidly deteriorated into refractory shock, severe pulmonary hypertension, and multiple organ dysfunction. This necessitated venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO). The infant underwent 7 days of VA-ECMO, 19 days of renal replacement therapy and 23 days of mechanical ventilation before successfully discharging with multidisciplinary follow-up. This case underscores the devastating potential of re-emerging congenital syphilis. It also highlights VA-ECMO as a viable rescue therapy for refractory neonatal shock, emphasizing the critical need for early referral to specialized centers.

items.title: Hemodynamic effects of a novel counter-pulsatile system for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation
items.abstract: Background and aims Mortality from heart failure is still high despite all the recent advances. Continuous-flow (CF) Veno-arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (VA-ECMO) can temporarily maintain systemic and pulmonary hemodynamics, at the cost of overloading the left ventricle (LV). A new Pulsatile Ventricular Assist Platform (pVAP) could offer a more physiological hemodynamic support. Methods 6 large porcine models of acute ischemic left ventricular (LV) failure received the pVAP in a VA-ECMO configuration. Invasive systemic and intraventricular hemodynamic measurements were taken with synchronized counter-pulsatile flow (SCPF) and CF support at the same flow rate. The measurements were compared with no support (ON vs OFF) in both modalities. Results The pVAP successfully delivered VA-ECMO in acute ischemic heart failure. The device maintained stable hemodynamics and increased the forward cardiac output (CO F ) without overloading the LV and with no change in the LV pressure-volume area (PVA). SCPF, but not CF, was associated with improved LV afterload and ventricular-arterial coupling compared to no support. Conclusion The findings suggest that the pVAP is feasible also in a VA-ECMO configuration, supporting hemodynamics with more physiological effect on effect on the LV dynamics.

items.title: Mainstreaming Cardiovascular Care for Women: From Special Population to Standard Practice

A Female-Specific Life Course Approach to the Prevention and Management of Cardiovascular Disease: A Presidential Advisory From the American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine
items.abstract: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in women, contributes markedly to healthcare expenditures, and is projected to increase substantially by 2050 if current trends continue. There is growing recognition of the complex role of sex as a biologic variable and its influence on cardiovascular health and disease. However, cardiovascular risk remains underrecognized and underaddressed in girls and women, particularly as it relates to female-specific exposure to sex hormones (both endogenous and exogenous), which are systemic modulators of cardiovascular biology. Moreover, girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care spanning specialties, including pediatrics, adolescent medicine, primary care, obstetrics and gynecology, maternal-fetal medicine, cardiology, endocrinology, hematology, and neurology. Consequently, there is a need for a unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health. To address these gaps, the American Heart Association, in collaboration with the American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine, established a Female Life Stage framework to optimize the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women. Physiologic changes in sex hormones define clinically distinct life stages (ie, perimenarche, ovarian cycling, perimenopause, postmenopause), which directly inform female-specific considerations for screening, prevention, and management of cardiovascular disease. This presidential advisory details the framework and its scientific rationale, highlights opportunities for implementation across settings, and identifies priorities for research, clinician education, patient advocacy, and policy. This framework offers a transformative opportunity to equitably improve cardiovascular health for all girls and women.

items.title: Consensus Guidance for the Female-Specific Prevention and Management of Cardiovascular Disease: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine
items.abstract: There is growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course. Dysregulation in these health domains tends to co-occur and is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease. However, healthcare for girls and women is uniquely fragmented across clinical specialties, including pediatrics, adolescent medicine, primary care, obstetrics, maternal-fetal medicine, gynecology, cardiology, endocrinology, hematology, and neurology. Furthermore, inconsistent alignment across society guidelines contributes to missed opportunities to optimize cardiovascular health. Therefore, the American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine convened a multisociety science advisory group and developed the Female Life Stage construct. This construct defines 4 distinct and clinically meaningful stages—perimenarche (S1), ovarian cycling (S2), perimenopause (S3), and postmenopause (S4)—to enable female-specific screening, prevention, and treatment considerations. In addition, this construct incorporates pregnancy as a unique modifying life event when cardiovascular risk may emerge or be unmasked (eg, adverse pregnancy outcomes). This scientific statement crosswalks major society guidelines, synthesizes the evidence, and provides consensus-based clinical guidance for each Female Life Stage and interconnected health domain (ie, hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health). We conclude with a call to action to improve clinical workflows, enhance clinician education, and address scientific and implementation gaps to improve cardiovascular health in girls and women.

items.title: One Life Course, Many Specialties: Building a System for Cardiovascular Health in Girls and Women
items.abstract: ardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in women and men, yet women remain underrepresented in clinical trials, remain undertreated, and often experience worse outcomes.Their hormonal, physiological, psychosocial, and therapeutic risks require tailored care.The 3 multispecialty publications in this issue of Circulation describe women's cardiovascular life course, guide prevention and management, and examine women's cardiovascular disease centers.Together, they establish a scientific foundation for reorganizing care around women throughout their lives.

items.title: Women’s Cardiovascular Health: From Recognition to Action
Promises to Keep: Closing the Gaps in Women’s Cardiovascular Health
Women’s Cardiovascular Health Begins in Childhood

Comprehensive Centers of Excellence for Women’s Cardiovascular Care: A Science Advisory From the American Heart Association, American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine
items.abstract: Improving cardiovascular health in women is an urgent public health priority given the persistent and pervasive gaps in awareness, prevention, and management of cardiovascular disease in this population. Advances in scientific understanding have led to increased recognition of female-specific considerations in cardiovascular disease, which informed the development of the Female Life Stage construct by the American Heart Association in collaboration with the American Academy of Pediatrics, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine. This construct integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages. However, gaps remain in operationalizing this construct and optimizing the delivery of patient-centered, interdisciplinary care among women. Over the past several decades, women’s cardiovascular centers have emerged as leaders, expanded rapidly, and elevated the recognition of cardiovascular diseases that exclusively, disproportionately, or differently affect women (eg, myocardial infarction with nonobstructive coronary arteries, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, Takotsubo syndrome). In this science advisory, we describe the current landscape of women’s cardiovascular centers and propose a national infrastructure to support the expansion of dedicated Comprehensive Centers of Excellence for Women’s Cardiovascular Care. These centers are conceptualized as interdisciplinary care models comprising 4 defining pillars: interdisciplinary clinical care, education and training, research, and community engagement. By establishing integrated pathways that span clinical disciplines, these centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research. In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.

Price Variation in Outpatient Percutaneous Coronary Intervention
items.abstract: ore than 600 000 percutaneous coronary interventions (PCIs) are performed annually in the United States. 1 Increasing procedural safety, same-day discharge pathways, and expansion of Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services reimbursement have accelerated the transition of elective PCI into outpatient settings, including hospital outpatient departments (HOPDs) and ambulatory surgical centers (ASCs).[2][3][4] Although outpatient PCI may reduce resource utilization and overall spending, little is known about how negotiated prices vary across outpatient sites of care. 2 The 2021 Hospital Price Transparency Rule requires hospitals to disclose payer-specific negotiated rates for all services and has enabled national analyses of pricing variation for cardiovascular services.5 Previous work leveraging these data has demonstrated substantial variation in commercial prices for common cardiovascular procedures, but outpatient PCI pricing remains poorly characterized.5 We used national price transparency data to quantify variation in prices for outpatient PCI across HOPDs versus ASCs and to evaluate associations between facility characteristics and negotiated commercial prices.

items.title: Optimizing US Prehospital Care of ST-Segment–Elevation Myocardial Infarction Because Time Is Life, Not Just Muscle
items.abstract: Time is muscle" in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is the foundational principle of STEMI care, but even more importantly, time is also life since mortality rises rapidly with delays beyond the "golden hour." 1 With the steep decline in in-hospital mortality for STEMI, the majority of deaths due to STEMI now occur out-ofhospital.Thus, the greatest opportunity for improving STEMI outcomes lies in reducing the interval between symptom onset and reperfusion of the thrombolytic occlusion, which can be achieved in some patients with a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor or a thrombolytic agent, and in nearly all patients with percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI).Herein, we provide five recommendations for reducing this critical time interval, ranging from patient education to pre-hospital pharmaceuticals to changes in reimbursement for pre-hospital care teams (Figure 1).

items.title: Effect of Activin Type II Receptor Signaling in Patients With HFpEF and Pulmonary Hypertension: A Critical Analysis of Biological Mechanisms and Clinical Trials
items.abstract: The totality of evidence indicates that the mechanisms underlying the increase in pulmonary vascular resistance in patients with combined postcapillary and precapillary pulmonary hypertension (CpcPH) associated with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) differ meaningfully from those responsible for the increase in pulmonary vascular resistance in patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension. CpcPH-HFpEF is a complex disorder involving the pulmonary veins, left atrium, and pulmonary arterioles, but recent evidence has highlighted a potentially central role for pulmonary venous and left atrial (LA) dysfunction. Epicardial adipose tissue occupies anatomical proximity to both structures, allowing derivative secretory products to influence their structure and function. The most well-characterized proinflammatory adipokine released from an expanded epicardial fat mass is activin A, which causes fibrosis and cardiomyocyte stiffness and senescence in underlying tissues by signaling through activin type II receptor signal transduction. Such signaling regulates pulmonary venular responses to mechanical stretch, and circulating activin A is elevated in patients with HFpEF who have enlarged LA chambers, pulmonary venous hypertension and increased pulmonary vascular resistance. The adipokine hypothesis of HFpEF identified activin A and activin type II receptor signaling as key adipokine mediators in the pathogenesis of HFpEF. Experimentally, activin A signaling promotes the development of both atrial myopathy and HFpEF, and activin type II receptor ligand traps alleviate HFpEF and ameliorate both the pulmonary vascular and left heart abnormalities in experimental models in which CpcPH-HFpEF is induced by obesity. These collective observations led to the prospective hypothesis that adipokine modulation by sotatercept would mediate benefits on the left heart in patients with CpcPH-HFpEF. These expectations were validated when the CADENCE trial showed that sotatercept decreased both pulmonary artery wedge pressures and left atrial volume index in patients with CpcPH-HFpEF, which are effects that could not explained by a decrease in pulmonary vascular resistance. Activin A released from an expanded epicardial adipose tissue promotes both pulmonary venous and left atrial remodeling and fibrosis in vivo, which (in turn) are effects that can be attenuated by an activin A decoy. The efficacy of sotatercept to slow the progression of CpcPH-HFpEF is now being tested in a phase III outcomes trial.

items.title: Cardiac Allograft Vasculopathy Demonstrated by Coronary Angiography and Histopathological Correlates
Care Pathways to Support People Living With Heart Failure
ROR2 Drives Right Ventricular Heart Failure Through Disruption of Proteostasis
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: No therapies exist to reverse right ventricular failure (RVF), and the molecular mechanisms that drive RVF remain understudied. We recently reported that the developmentally restricted noncanonical WNT receptor ROR2 (receptor tyrosine kinase-like orphan receptor 2) is upregulated in human RVF in proportion to severity of disease. Here we test the mechanistic role of ROR2 in RVF pathogenesis. METHODS: ROR2 was overexpressed or knocked down in neonatal rat ventricular myocytes and then characterized using confocal microscopy, RNA sequencing, proteomics, proteostatic functional assays, and pacing to assess contractile properties. The impact of cardiac ROR2 expression was evaluated in mice by AAV9-mediated overexpression and by AAV9-mediated delivery of short hairpin RNA to knockdown ROR2 in a pulmonary artery banded pressure overload model of RVF. ROR2 -modified mice were evaluated by echocardiography, histology, and right ventricle protein synthesis and proteasome capacity. RESULTS: In neonatal rat ventricular myocytes, we find that ROR2 profoundly dysregulates the coordination between protein translation and folding. This imbalance leads to excess protein clearance by the ubiquitin proteasome system with dramatic impacts on sarcomere and cytoskeletal structure and function. Inhibiting the ubiquitin proteasome system or restoring chaperone expression is sufficient to partially rescue ROR2-induced structural and contractile deficits in cardiomyocytes. In mice, forced cardiac ROR2 expression is sufficient to disrupt proteostasis and drive RVF, whereas conversely Ror2 knockdown partially rescues proteostasis and right ventricle structure and function in a pressure overload model of RVF. CONCLUSIONS: In sum, ROR2 is a key driver of RVF pathogenesis through proteostatic disruption and thus provides a promising target to treat RVF.

items.title: Outcomes of Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome by Subtype and Presence of Ventriculocoronary Connections: A Fetal Heart Society Multicenter Retrospective Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) is classified by anatomic subtype: mitral atresia and aortic atresia (MA/AA), mitral stenosis and aortic atresia (MS/AA), and mitral stenosis and aortic stenosis (MS/AS). The MS/AA subtype is associated with ventriculocoronary connections (VCCs). We assessed whether specific HLHS subtypes are associated with an increased risk of mortality and whether this risk is stratified by VCCs identified during fetal or postnatal echocardiography. We also assessed whether the type of neonatal intervention performed modified the risk. METHODS: We performed a multicenter retrospective cohort study of fetuses and infants <2 months old with HLHS who were admitted between January 2012 and December 2016 to participating Fetal Heart Society institutions. Clinical and demographic data were collected. Fetal and transthoracic echocardiograms from a subset of patients with MS/AA and those with suspected VCCs were reviewed. Cox proportional hazards analysis was performed, controlling for cardiac center (random effect), birth weight, genetic diagnosis, extracardiac malformation, and restricted/intact atrial septum. RESULTS: Among 16 centers, 591 patients were born alive with intention to treat. MA/AA was the most common subtype (261, 44%), followed by MS/AA (200, 34%) and MS/AS (130, 22%). Of those with MS/AA, 115 (58%) had suspected VCCs. Median follow-up was 9.0 (interquartile range: 7.0, 10.8) years. Overall transplant-free survival (TFS) was 55.6% at 5 years and 49.4% at 10 years. When comparing MA/AA, MS/AS, and MS/AA with and without VCCs (reference group: MS/AA without VCCs), MS/AA with VCCs had the lowest TFS (hazard ratio [HR], 1.69 [1.12, 2.57]; 5-year TFS, 44.7%; 10-year TFS, 40.3%). This was followed by MA/AA (HR, 1.40 [0.95, 2.05]; 5-year TFS, 54.1%; 10-year TFS, 46.6%). Survival of MS/AA without VCCs (5-year TFS, 60.4%; 10-year TFS, 56.9%) was similar to MS/AS (HR, 0.91 [0.59, 1.41]; 5-year TFS, 65.0%; 10-year TFS, 58.3%). Among those with a prenatal diagnosis of HLHS (n=532), patients with MS/AA and VCCs suspected on fetal echocardiogram had a lower TFS compared with those with MS/AA without fetal suspicion for VCCs (HR, 1.79 [1.12, 2.85]). Fetal echocardiography was used to diagnose VCCs in 33 of 103 (32%) cases with MS/AA and VCCs suspected postnatally. Of patients with MS/AA and VCCs, type of stage I palliation was not associated with TFS ( P =0.784). CONCLUSIONS: In a large, multicenter cohort of HLHS patients, the MS/AA subtype with VCCs had the lowest TFS. Prenatal diagnosis of VCCs was associated with a lower TFS. This study underscores the prognostic value of assessing for VCCs in patients with HLHS both before and after birth.

items.title: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement in Pure Aortic Regurgitation: The Randomized SEASON-AR Clinical Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: For patients with severe pure aortic regurgitation (AR) at high surgical risk, guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) is often the only available option. Transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is an established treatment for aortic stenosis and has also been evaluated in patients with pure AR. However, no adequately powered randomized trial has compared TAVR with GDMT alone in this population. METHODS: We conducted a prospective, investigator-initiated, multicenter, randomized, open-label trial in China. Patients with severe pure AR for whom surgery was considered difficult or unacceptable by the local heart team or who persistently declined surgery were randomly assigned at a 1:1 ratio to receive transfemoral TAVR with the VitaFlow system plus GDMT or GDMT alone. The primary end point was a composite of all-cause death, disabling stroke, or heart failure rehospitalization at 1 year. RESULTS: We assigned 210 patients with severe pure AR to the TAVR group (n=109) or GDMT group (n=101) at 18 centers. At 1-year follow-up, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the primary end point was significantly lower in the TAVR group than in the GDMT group (8.3% vs 24.8%; hazard ration [HR], 0.31 [95% CI, 0.14–0.66]; P =0.001), driven primarily by a reduction in heart failure rehospitalization (3.7% vs 21.3%; HR, 0.16 [95% CI, 0.06–0.47]; P < 0.001). TAVR was associated with higher rates of major or life-threatening bleeding and new permanent pacemaker implantation, most of which occurred within 30 days after the procedure. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with severe pure AR, TAVR plus GDMT significantly reduced the rate of all-cause death, disabling stroke, or heart failure rehospitalization at 1 year compared with GDMT alone despite higher 30-day rates of major or life-threatening bleeding and new permanent pacemaker implantation. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT04864145

items.title: Validation of the PREVENT-HF Risk Prediction Equation in US Veterans
items.abstract: One in four adults in the United States will receive a diagnosis of heart failure (HF) in their lifetime (1), highlighting an urgent need for expanded prevention.Accurate prediction of HF risk is critical to prioritize high-risk individuals for targeted intervention.The American Heart Association's PREVENT-HF equation is a novel HF risk prediction tool (2).However, it is unclear how well this model generalizes outside of its development cohort.This is important for populations with disproportionately high risk of HF, such as US Veterans (3).Prior validation in this population has focused on other endpoints (e.g., atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease [ASCVD]) and limited outcome ascertainment to Veterans Health Administration (VHA) data, which didn't capture diagnoses from Medicare or VHA-paid community care claims (4).To address this gap, we validated PREVENT-HF in US Veterans.

items.title: Performance of the PREVENT-HF Equations Across Heart Failure Subtypes in Community-Based and Ambulatory Healthcare Samples
items.abstract: Background: The PREVENT-HF equations estimate 10-year risk of overall heart failure (HF), inclusive of both HF with preserved and reduced ejection fraction (HFpEF; HFrEF). Given differential risk factor profiles, pathophysiology, and therapeutic strategies for each HF subtype, we sought to examine the performance of PREVENT-HF for subtype-specific risk assessment. Methods: We included data from five pooled longitudinal cohort studies (baseline exam 1989 to 2013) and two longitudinal primary-care electronic health record-based samples (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center [BIDMC], baseline 2004 to 2014; Mass General Brigham [MGB], baseline 2001 to 2018). We assessed the performance of the PREVENT-HF equations in predicting 10-year incident HFrEF and HFpEF, including model discrimination (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC]; average precision [AP]/event rate) and calibration (integrated calibration index [ICI]), in adults aged 30-79 years without prevalent cardiovascular disease or HF. Results: The pooled cohort studies included 23,652 (55% women, age 60 ± 13 years), of whom 1,232 developed HF (432 [35%] HFpEF, 522 [42%] HFrEF). The BIDMC sample included 29,815 (55% women, 50 ± 13 years), of whom 259 (1%) developed HF (133 [51%] HFpEF, 101 [39%] HFrEF). MGB included 138,999 (62% women, 52 ± 13 years), of whom 1050 developed HF (586 [56%] HFpEF, 381 [36%] HFrEF). PREVENT-HF demonstrated better discrimination for HFpEF than HFrEF across all samples: in the pooled cohorts, the AUROC for HFpEF was 0.824 (95% CI 0.807, 0.839) versus 0.789 (95% CI 0.770, 0.807) for HFrEF; in BIDMC, the AUROC for HFpEF was 0.897 (95% CI 0.874, 0.918) versus 0.833 (95% CI 0.791, 0.869) for HFrEF; in MGB, the AUROC for HFpEF was 0.864 (95% CI 0.848, 0.880) versus 0.797 (95% CI 0.771, 0.820) for HFrEF. Similar results were reflected in the AP/event rate ratios: 2.92 (95% CI 2.47, 3.54) for HFpEF compared to 2.66 (95% CI 2.33, 3.14) for HFrEF in the pooled cohorts; 8.08 (95% CI 6.12, 12.30) for HFpEF compared to 5.12 (95% CI 3.84, 8.17) for HFrEF in BIDMC; and 6.84 (95% CI 5.66, 8.28) for HFpEF compared to 4.12 (95% CI 3.37, 5.16) for HFrEF in MGB. Calibration was similar for HFpEF and HFrEF across samples. For example, in the pooled cohorts, the ICI for HFpEF was 0.041 (95% CI 0.039, 0.043) and for HFrEF was 0.038 (95% CI 0.036, 0.040). Conclusions: PREVENT-HF demonstrated excellent discrimination for both HF subtypes across community-based cohorts and real-world samples, with consistently better discrimination for HFpEF as compared to HFrEF. Given PREVENT-HF was developed to estimate overall HF risk rather than subtype-specific risk, future studies are needed to establish subtype-specific risk thresholds.

Anfinsen. 1 Dr Braunwald noted that while the lipid hypothesis had not yet gained widespread acceptance, these interactions left him convinced of the validity of the hypothesis and, consequently, the role for treatment of hyperlipidemia in patients with atherosclerosis.At the time, Dr Braunwald's research efforts continued to focus on reducing myocardial infarct size, but he resolved to revisit treatment of hyperlipidemia in the future when better therapies became available.

Long-Term Impact of Vutrisiran in Patients With TTR Amyloidosis With Cardiomyopathy: 1-Year Efficacy and Safety Outcomes From the HELIOS-B Open-Label Extension
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In HELIOS-B (A Study to Evaluate Vutrisiran in Patients With Transthyretin Amyloidosis With Cardiomyopathy), vutrisiran reduced the risk of all-cause mortality (ACM) and recurrent cardiovascular events and slowed disease progression measures versus placebo in patients with TTR (transthyretin) amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy after 33 to 36 months. We report the long-term efficacy and safety of vutrisiran from an ongoing open-label extension of HELIOS-B. METHODS: Patients who completed HELIOS-B could enroll in the open-label extension, continuing with vutrisiran 25 mg every 3 months (continuous vutrisiran) or, if previously receiving placebo, initiating vutrisiran 25 mg every 3 months (placebo/vutrisiran). Prespecified end points assessed in the open-label extension are the composite of ACM and cardiovascular events, ACM, Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire–Overall Summary score, New York Heart Association class, and NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide) and troponin I levels. Outcomes were assessed through month 48 in this analysis. RESULTS: Of 654 participants in HELIOS-B (vutrisiran, n=326; placebo, n=328), 478 completed double-blind treatment and 466 (vutrisiran, n=243; placebo, n=223) entered the open-label extension. In the continuous vutrisiran group, the risk of first cardiovascular event or ACM was reduced by 37% (hazard ratio, 0.63 [95% CI, 0.51, 0.79]; P =0.0001) and ACM by 37% (hazard ratio, 0.63 [95% CI, 0.46, 0.84]; P =0.0023) versus the placebo/vutrisiran group. Through month 48, patients in the continuous vutrisiran group had preserved health status and quality of life per Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire–Overall Summary score (least squares mean difference, 9.0 [95% CI, 5.3, 12.6]; P <0.0001) and more patients had improved or stable New York Heart Association class (odds ratio, 1.6 [95% CI, 1.1, 2.2]; P =0.0084) versus the placebo/vutrisiran group. Benefits in the continuous vutrisiran group were maintained for NT-proBNP and troponin I levels (adjusted geometric mean fold change ratios, 0.66 [95% CI, 0.58, 0.74]; P <0.0001; and 0.71 [95% CI, 0.64, 0.79]; P <0.0001, respectively) versus the placebo/vutrisiran group. Similar benefits were observed in the vutrisiran monotherapy population. No new safety signals were observed. CONCLUSIONS: Long-term vutrisiran resulted in clinically meaningful benefits across mortality, cardiovascular events, cardiac biomarkers, functional status, and quality of life in patients with TTR amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy through month 48. Patients initially treated with vutrisiran had better outcomes than those first receiving placebo, highlighting the importance of early diagnosis and treatment in TTR amyloidosis with cardiomyopathy. items.title: Targeting ALDOA Lactylation Reverses Vascular Remodeling in Pulmonary Hypertension by Disrupting Actin Polymerization and YAP Activation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Maladaptive vascular remodeling is a hallmark of pulmonary hypertension (PH), and therapeutic strategies directly targeting the pathological activity of smooth muscle cells remain limited. Metabolic and epigenetic dysregulation are established drivers of PH, and lysine lactylation has emerged as a novel posttranslational modification implicated in diverse diseases; however, its direct contribution to PH progression remains undefined. METHODS: Integrated lactylomic and proteomic profiling was performed in hypoxic human pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cells. The functional role of ALDOA (aldolase A) lactylation at lysine 42 (K42) was assessed using site-specific mutant virus and smooth muscle cell-specific inducible ALDOA knockout mice in 2 established PH models: SU5416+hypoxia in mice and monocrotaline in rats. RESULTS: We identified ALDOA as a prominent lactylation target in hypoxic pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cells, with K42 lactylation consistently elevated in primary pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cells derived from PH rodent models and human PH tissues. Mechanistically, AARS1 (alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1)-mediated ALDOA K42 lactylation enhanced its binding to γ-actin, independent of glycolytic activity. This lactylation-enhanced interaction promoted F-actin polymerization and activated YAP (Yes-associated protein) signaling via LATS1 (large tumor suppressor kinase 1) inhibition, thereby driving pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cell proliferation and phenotypic switching. Moreover, YAP/TEAD4 (TEA domain transcription factor 4)-mediated transcriptional upregulation of AARS1 established a positive feedback loop reinforcing ALDOA K42 lactylation under hypoxia. In vivo, ALDOA inducible knockout or reconstitution with the lactylation-deficient K42R (lysine 42 mutant to arginine) mutant attenuated experimental PH progression, with suppressed F-actin/YAP activation and reduced vascular remodeling. Furthermore, competitive inhibition of lactylation through β‑alanine reduced ALDOA K42 lactylation and ameliorated vascular remodeling in ALDOA-overexpressing rodent PH models. Translationally, pharmacological disruption of the ALDOA/γ-actin interaction by raltegravir suppressed cytoskeletal reorganization and YAP signaling, mitigating PH progression in both mouse and rat models. CONCLUSIONS: AARS1-mediated ALDOA K42 lactylation drives pulmonary vascular remodeling through a mechanism independent of ALDOA’s catalytic activity, promoting F-actin polymerization and YAP activation. Precision targeting of this modification selectively inhibits pathological signaling while preserving metabolic homeostasis, highlighting a translational potential for precision intervention in PH.

items.title: 2026 International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation Consensus on Science With Treatment Recommendations: Summary from the Basic Life Support; Advanced Life Support; Pediatric Life Support; Neonatal Life Support; Education, Implementation, and Teams; and First Aid Task Forces
items.abstract: This is the annual summary of the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation Consensus on Science With Treatment Recommendations ; a comprehensive review was completed in 2025. This latest summary addresses the most recent published resuscitation evidence reviewed by International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation task forces, including Basic Life Support; Advanced Life Support; Pediatric Life Support; Neonatal Life Support; Education, Implementation, and Teams; and First Aid. Members from these 6 task forces assessed the certainty of the evidence using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation criteria, and their statements include consensus treatment recommendations. Highlights from task force discussions and insights into how decisions regarding treatment recommendations were made are provided in the Justification and Evidence-to-Decision Framework Highlights sections. The task forces also listed priority knowledge gaps for further research.

items.title: Long-Term Survival After Initial Invasive or Conservative Management of Stable Coronary Disease in Patients With Advanced Chronic Kidney Disease: ISCHEMIA-CKD EXTEND
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In the ISCHEMIA-CKD trial (International Study of Comparative Health Effectiveness With Medical and Invasive Approaches–Chronic Kidney Disease), at a median follow-up of 2.2 years, the primary composite outcome of death or nonfatal myocardial infarction was similar between an initial invasive strategy (INV) compared with an initial conservative strategy (CON) in patients with moderate or severe myocardial ischemia and advanced chronic kidney disease. However, the long-term outcomes comparing the 2 strategies are unknown. METHODS: Participants in the ISCHEMIA-CKD trial were randomly assigned to either INV, involving coronary angiography and revascularization when feasible, added to guideline-directed medical therapy or to CON with guideline-directed medical therapy alone and invasive procedures reserved for failure of guideline-directed medical therapy. After the active intervention trial phase, long-term vital status follow-up was conducted through participant contact by participating sites and by health record and centralized death database searches. The primary outcome for the extended follow-up phase was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes were cause-specific mortality, including cardiovascular and noncardiovascular mortality. RESULTS: Among the 777 participants randomized (388 to INV and 389 to CON), over a median of 8 years of follow-up, vital status retention among survivors was 95%. There was a total of 429 deaths (55%). Cumulative all-cause mortality (57.4% versus 56.8%; adjusted hazard ratio, 1.05 [95% CI, 0.87–1.28]) or cardiovascular mortality (40.3% versus 38.4%; adjusted hazard ratio, 1.06 [95% CI, 0.84–1.34]) at 8 years did not differ between INV and CON. The restricted mean survival time was 1941 days (1834–2047 days) for INV versus 1990 days (1885–2094 days) for CON, with an adjusted estimated difference of −99 days (−245 to 46). The posterior probability of at least a 1 percentage point lower or higher death with INV at the 8-year median follow-up was 28% and 52%, respectively. Similarly, the posterior probability of at least a 1 percentage point lower or higher cardiovascular mortality with INV was 23% and 56%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with at least moderate ischemia and advanced chronic kidney disease, there was no significant long-term benefit of an initial INV at reducing the risk of all-cause or cardiovascular mortality compared with an initial conservative strategy. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT01985360

items.title: Can Intravenous Cangrelor Protect the Myocardium in Infarction-related Cardiogenic Shock?

Multimodality Cardiac Imaging Substudy of the DAPT-SHOCK-AMI Randomized Trial: Echocardiographic and Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Assessment of Cangrelor versus Crushed Ticagrelor in Cardiogenic Shock Complicating Acute Myocardial Infarction
items.abstract: Background: In acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS), the myocardium sustains a dual injury: ischemia of the culprit territory and global hypoperfusion from low cardiac output. Whether platelet inhibition at reperfusion affects the microcirculation, the infarct, the noninfarcted myocardium, and ventricular function, and over what time course, has not been examined with serial imaging. The prespecified multimodality imaging substudy of the randomized DAPT-SHOCK-AMI trial (intravenous cangrelor versus crushed oral ticagrelor) addressed this question. Methods: Patients at prespecified imaging sites underwent serial echocardiography (208 enrolled; evaluable examinations in 175, 120, and 99 patients in the acute phase, at 1 month, and at 1 year) and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR; 93 enrolled; 73, 68, and 63); 81 patients (40 and 41) underwent both modalities. Blinded core laboratories analyzed all studies. The primary imaging endpoint was microvascular obstruction (MVO) on acute CMR, evaluable in 60 patients; secondary endpoints were infarct size, native T1 of the global, infarcted, and remote myocardium, left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction (LVEF), global longitudinal strain (GLS), E/e', and left atrial volume, and their changes. Comparisons between the cangrelor and crushed ticagrelor arms used covariate-adjusted logistic or linear regression; the substudy was not separately powered. Results: The odds of acute MVO were lower with cangrelor (adjusted odds ratio 0.27 [95% CI 0.08 to 0.98]; P=0.023). Infarct size did not differ between the arms. At 1 year, native T1 of the remote myocardium was lower with cangrelor (adjusted mean 1114 [95% CI 1057 to 1171] versus 1171 [1115 to 1228] ms; P=0.005). Over 1 year, LVEF increased more with cangrelor on echocardiography (37.9% versus 21.7% of the acute value; adjusted P=0.046) and CMR (15.8% versus 2.1%; P=0.027), with greater improvement in GLS, lower E/e', and less left atrial enlargement; no parameter differed between the arms at 1 month. Conclusions: In AMI-CS, serial multimodality imaging characterized microvascular, tissue-level, and functional injury over 1 year. Cangrelor was associated with less acute MVO, lower remote native T1, and more complete recovery of LV function than crushed ticagrelor, without a difference in infarct size; these hypothesis-generating findings suggest differences in the microcirculation and non-infarcted myocardial injury but do not establish a treatment mechanism.

items.title: Data, Information, and Action: The Promises and Limits of AI-Enabled Electrocardiography
AI-ECG Atrial Fibrillation Detection: Unlocking Secrets in Sinus Rhythm?
AI-ECG: Gatekeeper-in-Training for Population-level Atrial Fibrillation Screening
Leveraging AI-ECG Technology for Early Notification and Tracking of AF Development (LATENT): A Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Electrocardiographic analysis aided by artificial intelligence (AI) may identify atrial electrical vulnerability during sinus rhythm. The objective of this study was to determine whether AI–enabled ECG (AI-ECG) is effective for detecting atrial fibrillation (AF), atrial flutter (AFl), or prespecified pre-AF atrial findings in a randomized trial. METHODS: In this single-center, open-label trial, 14 665 adults 40 to 85 years of age without previous AF/AFl were randomized to an AI-ECG–guided strategy or usual care. Participants randomized to AI-ECG who were then identified by AI as having a high-risk sinus-rhythm ECG in the preceding year were offered Holter monitoring for ≤7 days. Each monitored high-risk intervention participant was paired with an age- and sex-matched control selected before control ECGs underwent AI analysis. Matched controls received identical monitoring to reduce ascertainment bias. Reporting cardiologists were blinded to AI results and randomized assignment. The primary outcome was a composite of newly detected AF, AFl, or pre-AF atrial findings within 90 days. Pre-AF atrial findings comprised frequent premature atrial complexes, short runs of premature atrial complexes, or nonsustained AF/AFl. RESULTS: Among 7337 intervention and 7328 control participants, 84 (1.1%) and 78 (1.1%), respectively, were classified as high risk. Of the 84 high-risk intervention participants, 48 (57.1%) underwent monitoring, as did 48 matched controls. The primary outcome occurred in 54 intervention participants (0.74%) versus 35 control participants (0.48%; odds ratio, 1.54 [95% CI, 1.01–2.37]; P =0.046). Hypothetical reclassification of 1 intervention event to a nonevent changed the primary analysis P value to 0.057. The intervention effect on detection of the primary composite outcome differed by baseline AI-ECG risk ( P interaction <0.001): 32.1% versus 2.6% among high-risk participants and 0.4% versus 0.5% among low-risk participants. AF/AFl detection (0.3% versus 0.2%) and antiarrhythmic therapy initiation at 180 days (2.3% versus 2.4%) did not differ significantly between the intervention and control groups. Participant-reported monitoring-related adverse events, including skin reactions and discomfort, occurred in 22.9% of monitored intervention participants versus 18.8% of matched controls. CONCLUSIONS: AI-ECG–guided monitoring resulted in a modest increase in the detection of new AF, AFl, or pre-AF atrial findings. However, these findings were fragile statistically and sensitive to reclassification of 1 event. LATENT (Leveraging AI-ECG Technology for Early Notification and Tracking of AF Development) demonstrates the clinical application of AI-ECG risk stratification to guide targeted rhythm surveillance, providing a foundation for larger trials evaluating its impact on patient outcomes. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT06847932.

items.title: Clear Target, Multiple Paths: Rethinking Intensive LDL-C Lowering
Statin–Ezetimibe Combination Therapy versus Statin Monotherapy in Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: A Prespecified Secondary Analysis of the Randomized Ez-PAVE Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In a target-directed low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C)–lowering strategy, the impact of the initial treatment regimen has not been investigated in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. We compared the efficacy and safety of initial statin–ezetimibe combination therapy versus statin monotherapy within intensive or conventional LDL-C–targeting strategies. METHODS: In this prespecified second randomization of the randomized Ez-PAVE trial (Effects of Ezetimibe Combination Therapy for Patients With Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: Randomized Comparison of LDL Cholesterol Targeting <70 versus <55 mg/dL) conducted at 17 centers in South Korea, a total of 3048 patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease were enrolled between January 2021 and July 2022. Following the first randomization to either an intensive (<55 mg/dL) or conventional (<70 mg/dL) LDL-C–targeting strategy, patients underwent subsequent randomization (initial statin–ezetimibe combination therapy [n=1525] versus statin monotherapy [n=1523]) and were followed up for 3 years. Lipid-lowering therapy was adjusted according to a predefined protocol to achieve LDL-C targets. The primary end point was a 3-year composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, any revascularization, or hospitalization for unstable angina. RESULTS: The mean±SD age was 64.4±9.0 years, and 638 patients (20.9%) were female. The incidence of the primary end point did not differ between statin–ezetimibe combination therapy (128 patients [8.5%]) and statin monotherapy (119 patients [7.9%]; hazard ratio, 1.07 [95% CI, 0.83–1.37]; P =0.596). Patients who received statin–ezetimibe combination therapy achieved lower median LDL-C levels during follow-up than those who received statin monotherapy in both the intensive-targeting (53 mg/dL [interquartile range, 45–62 mg/dL] versus 62 mg/dL [interquartile range, 53–74 mg/dL]) and conventional-targeting (63 mg/dL [interquartile range, 55–73 mg/dL] versus 70 mg/dL [interquartile range, 62–81 mg/dL]) strategies. During follow-up, ezetimibe was added to the treatment regimen of 241 patients (34.3%) and 177 patients (24.8%) who initially received statin monotherapy in the intensive- and conventional-targeting strategies, respectively. The treatment effect of intensive-targeting versus conventional-targeting strategies was consistent regardless of therapy regimens without significant heterogeneity ( P interaction =0.583). The safety end points were similar between the groups. CONCLUSIONS: Within a target-directed LDL-C–lowering strategy, cardiovascular efficacy and safety did not differ significantly, whether initiated as statin–ezetimibe combination therapy or as statin monotherapy, but combination therapy facilitated achievement of a lower LDL-C target. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT04626973.

items.title: A Potential New Therapeutic Option for Exercise Intolerance in Patients with Heart Failure and Preserved Ejection Fraction
Iron Repletion in HFpEF: An Endpoint Is Not Yet an Indication
Iron Repletion in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: The IRONMET-HFpEF Randomized Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Iron deficiency is present in >50% of patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and is associated with reduced exercise capacity and survival. Whether iron repletion improves exercise capacity as objectively measured by peak oxygen uptake ( V ˙ o 2 ) is unknown. The IRONMET-HFpEF trial (Impact of Intravenous Iron Repletion on Mechanisms of Exercise Intolerance in HFpEF) sought to determine whether ferric derisomaltose (FDI) compared with placebo improves peak V ˙ o 2 in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction with iron deficiency. METHODS: This was a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial of patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and iron deficiency, defined as ferritin <100 ng/mL or <300 ng/mL with transferrin saturation <20%. Participants were enrolled between December 2021 and April 2026. Single-dose ferric derisomaltose (1000 mg; n=44) or placebo (n=21) was administered once intravenously. The primary end point was the change in peak V ˙ o 2 from baseline to 12 weeks with an analysis of covariance model including terms for treatment group, baseline peak V ˙ o 2 , and sex. Secondary end points included changes in V ˙ o 2 at the anaerobic threshold, 6-minute walk test distance, New York Heart Association class, health status assessed by the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire–Overall Summary Score, and iron biomarkers at 12 weeks. RESULTS: Among 65 randomized participants (median age, 68 years [interquartile range, 58–76 years], 72% women, transferrin saturation 16.0±7.4%, ferritin 57.8±48.9 ng/mL), 64 (98.5%) completed the study. The median baseline peak V ˙ o 2 was 12.7 mL·kg −1 ·min −1 (interquartile range, 10.6–15.8 mL·kg −1 ·min −1 ) in the FDI group and 12.2 mL·kg −1 ·min −1 (11.6–14.6 mL·kg −1 ·min −1 ) in the placebo group. At 12 weeks, peak V ˙ o 2 improved by 1.2 mL·kg −1 ·min −1 (95% CI, 0.6–1.7) in the FDI group and was unchanged (0.1 mL·kg −1 ·min −1 [95% CI, −0.7 to 0.9]) in the placebo group (least-squares mean difference, 1.1 mL·kg −1 ·min −1 [95% CI, 0.2–1.9]; P =0.02). V ˙ o 2 at the anaerobic threshold, 6-minute walk test distance, and New York Heart Association class also improved in the FDI compared with the placebo group (all P <0.05), whereas the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire–Overall Summary Score did not differ significantly between groups (FDI group, +4.4 [95% CI, −2.4 to 11.2]; P =0.20). FDI increased transferrin saturation (9.4% [95% CI, 4.9%–13.9%]) and ferritin (183 ng/mL [95% CI, 128–238]) compared with the placebo group ( P LSMD <0.001 for both). There were no serious adverse events related to FDI administration. CONCLUSIONS: In the largest trial to date of iron repletion in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction with iron deficiency, FDI improved multiple measures of exercise capacity. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT04945707

items.title: Protecting the Kidneys After Replacing the Heart: Another Role for SGLT2 Inhibitors
Dapagliflozin for Renal Protection in Heart Transplant Recipients: A Randomized Clinical Trial
items.abstract: Background: Progressive kidney disease is common in heart transplant recipients due to calcineurin inhibitor exposure and pre-existing comorbidities. Sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors may attenuate the decline in kidney function, but evidence in heart transplant recipients is limited. Methods: The DAPAgliflozin for Renal protection in Heart Transplant recipients (DAPARHT) trial is a multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial conducted at six heart transplant centers in Northern Europe. We randomized adult heart transplant recipients with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) ≥25 mL/min/1.73 m ² at least one year after transplantation 1:1 to receive dapagliflozin 10 mg or matching placebo once daily. The primary endpoint was the slope of the eGFR from 2 weeks after treatment initiation to the end of the 12-month blinded treatment period. Results: Between June 2022 and September 2025, we randomized 430 participants, of whom 217 were allocated to dapagliflozin and 213 were allocated to placebo. We included the 424 patients with at least one eGFR measurement after baseline in the full analysis set. Their mean age was 53 ± 14 years and 29& were women. The eGFR at baseline was 67 ± 22 mL/min/1.73 m 2 . The median time from transplantation was 7 (3 – 13) years. Dapagliflozin improved the chronic slope of the eGFR compared with placebo. The change in the eGFR from 2 weeks to 12 months after treatment initiation was 2.0 (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.0 – 3.1) mL/min/1.73 m 2 in the dapagliflozin group and 0.3 (95% CI -0.8 – 1.4) mL/min/1.73 m 2 in the placebo group for a between-group difference of 1.7 (95% confidence interval 0.1 – 3.3) mL/min/1.73 m ² ; p = 0.03. There were no unexpected safety signals and similar rates of adverse events, including infections, between groups. Conclusions: In heart transplant recipients, dapagliflozin, compared with placebo, improved the slope of the eGFR from 2 weeks to 12 months of treatment.

items.title: Against All Odds: A New CADENCE in Cardiopulmonary Remodeling
Effects of Sotatercept on Cardiac Structure and Function in Combined Post- and Precapillary Pulmonary Hypertension in Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction: Analysis of the CADENCE Study

Abstract P1005: Clinical Predictors of Cardiogenic Shock in Patients with Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction Admitted to the Intensive Care Unit for Sepsis - A Multicenter Discovery and External Validation Study
items.abstract: Background: Patients with Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF) admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) for sepsis are at high risk for hemodynamic collapse, as sepsis can precipitate acute-on-chronic cardiac decompensation through myocardial depression, altered loading conditions, and neurohormonal dysregulation. We sought to identify early clinical predictors of Cardiogenic Shock (CS) among HFrEF patients admitted to the ICU with sepsis. Aim: To identify predictors of ICU-acquired CS in HFrEF patients with sepsis. Methodology: We performed a retrospective multicenter cohort study using the eICU Collaborative Research Database (2014-2015) as the discovery cohort and MIMIC-IV (2008-2022) for external validation. Adult patients admitted to the ICU with concurrent HFrEF and sepsis were included, while those presenting with CS at ICU admission were excluded. Candidate predictors available within the first 24 hours of ICU admission included demographics, hemodynamics, laboratory values, illness severity, and vasopressor use. Univariate logistic regression was performed on all candidate predictors, and significant variables (P<0.10) were entered into a multivariable model. Results: The eICU-CRD discovery cohort comprised 2,452 patients (131 [5.3%] developed ICU-acquired CS). The MIMIC-IV validation cohort comprised 3,229 patients (566 [17.5%] with ICD-coded CS). ICU-acquired CS was associated with nearly twofold higher hospital mortality (44.3% vs. 22.2%; P<0.001) and more than twofold higher ICU mortality (30.5% vs. 14.0%; P<0.001) in the discovery cohort. CS patients were younger (median 68 vs. 73 years; P=0.008), more likely male (67.9% vs. 52.3%; P<0.001), and had higher illness severity (APACHE IV 83.5 vs. 68.0; P<0.001). Eight predictors independently associated with CS on univariate analysis (all P<0.05): vasopressor requirement within 24 hours (OR 1.27, 95% CI 1.13-1.44), peak troponin elevation (OR 1.25, 95% CI 1.10 -1.42), maximum serum lactate (OR 1.23, 95% CI 1.06 -1.42), APACHE IV score (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.05 -1.38), initial serum lactate (OR 1.20, 95% CI 1.04 -1.39), maximum anion gap (OR 1.16, 95% CI 1.01 -1.34), mean arterial pressure (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.75-0.99), and minimum serum bicarbonate (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.73-0.96). The composite multivariable model achieved an AUROC of 0.778 (95% CI 0.716-0.839). In a prespecified sensitivity analysis restricted to patients with documented systolic HF, discrimination improved to an AUROC of 0.836 (95% CI, 0.753-0.914). The MIMIC-IV cohort confirmed a similarly high CS-attributable mortality burden (hospital mortality 31.9%), consistent with the discovery cohort findings. Conclusion: ICU-acquired cardiogenic shock occurs in a significant subset of HFrEF patients with sepsis, is associated with substantially increased mortality, and can be predicted using early clinical and laboratory markers.

items.title: Abstract CR03: Transforming Crisis Airway Management: Clinical Applications of Distal Pharyngeal Airway Innovation: A Report of Two Cases
items.abstract: Background: Airway management failure remains one of the most consequential adverse events in clinical practice, with the potential for severe hypoxemia, cardiac arrest, and death. While traditional airway adjuncts such as oropharyngeal (OPA) and nasopharyngeal airways (NPA) serve as foundational rescue tools, their limitations underscore the need for innovative solutions. The McMurray Enhanced Airway (MEA), incorporating a distal pharyngeal airway (DPA) component, is designed to extend beyond the tongue base to the level of the epiglottis, addressing the most common anatomic site of upper airway obstruction. Cases: We present two cases demonstrating the lifesaving utility of the MEA in high-acuity airway emergencies. The first describes a 47-year-old male (BMI 46) with obstructive sleep apnea who experienced rapid oxygen desaturation to 60% during procedural sedation. Conventional jaw thrust proved ineffective; MEA insertion with Ambu bag ventilation restored oxygen saturation within 30 seconds. The second case involves a 69-year-old female in acute respiratory distress following thyroidectomy, with a postoperative hematoma causing tracheal displacement and complete obliteration of anterior neck landmarks. Sequential failed attempts with two video laryngoscopes and a supraglottic airway resulted in oxygen saturation declining to 60%. MEA placement with two-person assisted mask ventilation restored ventilation and oxygenation, bridging the patient to successful intubation via video laryngoscope with bougie. Conclusion: These cases highlight the MEA as an effective rescue device in both procedural and emergency airway settings when conventional adjuncts fail. Early access to innovative devices such as the MEA, paired with team coordination and systematic decision-making, is essential to optimizing patient safety and outcomes across diverse clinical environments.

items.title: Abstract Or007: Racial and Ethnic Differences in Time to Shock Delivery in Adult Patients with Initially Shockable In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Prior studies have reported racial and ethnic disparities in patient outcomes after in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA), where Asian, Black, and Hispanic patients experience lower survival compared to White patients. However, racial and ethnic differences in intra-arrest resuscitation have not been fully investigated. Research Question: Does the time to shock delivery differ by patients’ race and ethnicity? Objective: To evaluate the association of patients’ race/ethnicity with time to shock delivery Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of the Get With The Guidelines—Resuscitation registry, a multicenter prospective IHCA registry in the US. We included adults (age ≥ 18 years) with initially shockable IHCA from 2000 to 2025. The exposure was patients’ race and ethnicity (Asian, Hispanic, Non-Hispanic [NH] Black, NH White, and other races). The outcome measure was the time from the initiation of chest compressions to the first shock delivery. We compared the differences in restricted mean survival time (RMST) of time to the first shock delivery: the average time-to-event duration in a survival analysis model, across patients with different races and ethnicities, with and without adjustment for patient demographics (age and sex) and cardiac arrest characteristics (year, location, and witness status). Results: Among 64,572 eligible patients, 1,158 were Asian (1.8%), 3,747 Hispanic (5.8%), 11,146 NH Black (17.3%), 47,937 NH White (74.2%), and 584 patients with other races (0.9%). Median [IQR] age was 67 (56-76] and median time to the first shock delivery was 1.0 (IQR 0-3.0) minutes. Compared to NH White patients, the unadjusted RMST differences were 1.01 minutes (95% CI: -0.12 to 2.15) in Asian, 1.61 minutes (95% CI: 0.95 to 2.27) in Hispanic, 1.38 minutes (95% CI: 1.00 to 1.76) in NH Black, and 0.77 minutes (95% CI: -0.76 to 2.29) in patients with other races ( Figure 1 ). Compared to NH White patients, the adjusted RMST differences were 0.82 minutes (95% CI: -0.27 to 1.92) in Asian, 1.59 minutes (95% CI: 0.94 to 2.24) in Hispanic, 1.29 minutes (95% CI: 0.90 to 1.67) in NH Black, and 0.51 minutes (95% CI: -1.00 to 2.02) in patients with other races ( Figure 2 ). Conclusions: In this cohort of the large IHCA registry, compared to White patients, the time from the initiation of chest compressions to the first shock delivery was longer in Hispanic and NH Black patients, suggesting the presence of racial and ethnic inequalities in intra-arrest resuscitation.

items.title: Abstract P1006: Association Between History of Substance Use Disorder and Outcomes After Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Several studies have shown improved outcomes for patients who have suffered cardiac arrest (CA) secondary to overdoses on illicit substances, but little is known about the effect of chronic illicit substance use on CA outcomes. Better understanding of this growing population can lead to more tailored management. This active, on-going study aims to evaluate outcomes after CA for those with a documented history of substance use disorder (SUD). Methods: We conducted a retrospective study of patients over the age of 18 years old treated for in-hospital CA (IHCA) or out-of-hospital CA (OHCA) between 2011 and 2025 at an urban, tertiary care hospital. The primary outcome was survival after CA. Secondary outcomes were cause of death [brain death vs. cardiac death vs. withdrawal of life-sustaining care], favorable CPC at discharge, survivor disposition (home, acute rehabilitation, subacute rehabilitation/skilled nursing facility, long-term acute care, transfer to other facility, or hospice/comfort measures), and attendance of at least one follow-up appointment after discharge.
