Fisher test was used for analysis of survival, cause of death, survivor disposition, favorable CPC at discharge, and follow up after discharge. To control for co-morbidities, adjusted analysis of survival to hospital discharge was completed using logistic regression. Results: A total of 95 IHCA and OHCA subjects were included [46.3% female, median age 60 years (IQR 50-68.5)], with 65.3% surviving to hospital discharge. Of these subjects, 26.3% had a documented history of SUD. No significant association was found between history of SUD and survival to hospital discharge (unadjusted OR=1.5, CI 0.5-4.9, p=0.47). However, when controlling for additional co-morbidities, those with a history of SUD had increased odds of survival (OR=5.4, CI 1.1-35.1, p=0.05). There was no significant difference in favorable CPC at discharge (p=1.0) or follow up after discharge (p=0.56). There was no significant difference in cause of death (p=0.29) or survivor disposition (p=0.31). Conclusion: A history of SUD was associated with improved combined IHCA and OHCA survival when additional co-morbidities were controlled for. A history of SUD was not associated with cause of death, favorable CPC at discharge, survivor disposition, or follow up after discharge. These preliminary findings emphasize the importance of SUD as a chronic modifier of CA outcomes.

items.title: Abstract P1012: Blood Pressure-Targeted Balloon Deflation Facilitates the Stabilization of Systemic Perfusion and the Recovery of Multiple Organ Dysfunction After Traumatic Hemorrhage in Pigs
items.abstract: Introduction: Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) is an effective technique to control traumatic hemorrhage. However, its inappropriate balloon deflation can cause short-time collapse of systemic perfusion and further damage vital organs. In this study, we investigated the effectiveness of blood pressure (BP)-targeted balloon deflation in stabilizing systemic perfusion and protecting vital organs after traumatic hemorrhage. Hypothesis: BP-targeted balloon deflation would produce more stable systemic perfusion and better multiple organ function compared with slow or rapid balloon deflation in a porcine model of hemorrhage. Methods: Twenty-one male domestic pigs weighing 40±2 kg were utilized. Fifty percent of estimated blood volume was removed within 30 mins. Subsequently, fluid resuscitation was performed by the infusion of normal saline with 1.5 times of hemorrhage volume and then the reinfusion of 50% of the shed blood within 60 mins. Coincident with the start of fluid resuscitation, REBOA balloon was inflated to occlude blood flow at aortic zone 1 for 30 mins, and then its deflation was implemented by one of three ways: rapid (10 s), slow (10 mins), or BP-targeted deflation. In the BP-targeted group, BP was maintained at 90-139/60-89 mmHg throughout the whole balloon deflation. Results: During balloon deflation, heart rate was significantly lower and BP was significantly higher in the BP-targeted deflation group compared with the rapid and slow deflation groups. Additionally, artery lactate was lower after balloon deflation in the BP-targeted deflation group, in which the difference was significant at 90 mins and 150 mins after hemorrhage compared to the other two groups (Fig. 1). After balloon deflation, better myocardial and neurological function were observed in the BP-targeted deflation group, in which they were significantly improved compared with the rapid deflation group. Additionally, cardiac and cerebral injury biomarkers were significantly lower in the slow deflation group than the rapid deflation group; however, all of them were further significantly decreased in the BP-targeted deflation group (Fig. 2). Interestingly, renal and intestinal injury biomarkers were significantly higher in the slow deflation group than the rapid deflation group; likewise, all of them were further significantly reduced in the BP-targeted deflation group (Fig. 3). Conclusion: BP-targeted balloon deflation would facilitate to stabilize the hemodynamics and reduce lactate production, and thereby improve systemic perfusion after hemorrhage. Furthermore, it would promote the recovery of multiple organ dysfunction after hemorrhage, such as heart, brain, kidney and intestine.

items.title: Abstract Or014: High-Density Diffuse Optical Tomography Toward Peri-Arrest Cerebral Monitoring in Piglets
items.abstract: Introduction: Neurologic injury remains a major determinant of outcome after pediatric cardiac arrest, yet bedside tools for continuous, spatially resolved monitoring of cerebral physiology are limited. High-density diffuse optical tomography (HD-DOT) is a portable, noninvasive imaging modality that measures fMRI-like cerebral hemoglobin dynamics, but its feasibility in translational large-animal cardiac arrest models has not been established. We developed a piglet HD-DOT system with custom-cap and evaluated its feasibility for cerebral monitoring toward identifying optical biomarkers of neurologic recovery. Methods: We constructed a piglet HD-DOT system (685 and 830 nm) with a fiber optic cap (26 sources, 31 detectors) designed for coverage of the dorsal brain (Fig. 1A). Our protocol consists of baseline MRI followed by continuous HD-DOT imaging from baseline through cardiac arrest and resuscitation (Fig 1D); in this abstract we present preliminary feasibility data from 10-kg and 30-kg piglets. Using structural MRI, a subject-specific head model (Fig. 1C) was generated from T1-weighted MRI, and cap position was registered with MRI-visible fiducial markers. Usable measurements were defined by in-range signal intensity, stable variance, and separations <43 mm. Data were denoised and reconstructed into HbO, HbR, and HbT dynamics. Resting-state data was analyzed using amplitude of low frequency fluctuations (ALFF) to measure brain activity and functional connectivity (FC) to map brain networks. Results: In the 30-kg piglet, 94% of measurements met usable signal criteria. Spectral analysis (Fig. 2A) showed 1/f low-frequency hemodynamic power and peaks at the respiratory rate and heart, indicating successful capture of relevant physiology. Maps of ALFF with HbT contrast show strong activity throughout the cerebrum (Fig. 2B). In contrast, respiratory and pulse-band power appeared more influenced by large vessels (e.g., midline venous sinuses, Fig 2C/D)). FC clustering (Fig. 3) identified distinct functional regions, although alignment to cortical anatomy remains preliminary. Conclusions: We demonstrated the feasibility of in vivo HD-DOT cerebral monitoring in piglets. The system captured stable optical signals, detected relevant cerebral physiology, and supported reconstruction of important functional neuroimaging. Future work will include alignment to the cortical surface and analysis of data during arrest, resuscitation, and recovery.

items.title: Abstract P1014: Carotid Velocity Time Integral Indicated the Efficacy of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Predicted Return of Spontaneous Circulation in a Porcine Model of Prolonged Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: The aim of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is to optimize the hemodynamics and thereby promote return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). However, conventional hemodynamic measurements including coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) and end-tidal CO 2 (ETCO 2 ) are invasive and difficult to implement in clinical practice. In this study, we investigated the effectiveness of a novel hands-free, noninvasive, and continuous carotid doppler ultrasound in monitoring the efficacy of CPR and predicting ROSC. Hypothesis: Velocity time integral (VTI) measured by a novel hands-free, noninvasive, and continuous carotid doppler ultrasound could be a feasible alternative of CPP and ETCO 2 to indicate CPR efficacy and predict ROSC in a porcine model of prolonged cardiac arrest. Methods: A total of 48 male domestic pigs weighing 37±2 kg were utilized. The animals were subjected to 12 mins of untreated ventricular fibrillation and then 6 mins of CPR. After 2 mins of CPR, a dose of 20 μg/kg of epinephrine was given followed by the same administration at an interval of 3 mins. During CPR, invasive CPP, ETCO 2 , and carotid blood flow (CBF) were continuously monitored. In addition, noninvasive carotid VTI were concurrently measured by a novel hands-free doppler ultrasound. Results: In overall, 34 animals obtained ROSC, and other 14 animals weren’t resuscitated. During CPR, the values of CPP, ETCO 2 , CBF and carotid VTI were all significantly greater in those resuscitated animals than those non-resuscitated ones (Fig. 1). In addition, correlation analysis showed that carotid VTI was positively associated with CPP (r=0.2027, P <0.0001), and ETCO 2 (r=0.3264, P <0.0001), and CBF (r=0.7136, P <0.0001), respectively (Fig. 2). Furthermore, carotid VTI showed the comparable performance in predicting ROSC when compared with CPP, ETCO 2 , CBF (AUCs=0.8374, 0.8926, 0.9556, 0.8370, all P <0.0001), respectively (Fig. 3). Their cut-off values for predicting ROSC were 20.50, 20.50, 17.50, and 20.50 (all P <0.0001), respectively. Conclusion: Carotid VTI measured by novel hands-free doppler ultrasound could be an effective alternative of conventional hemodynamic measurements to indicate CPR efficacy and predict ROSC in a porcine model of prolonged cardiac arrest.

items.title: Abstract CR12: Difficult Weaning from Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Due to Pulmonary Artery Compression by a Chest Compression Related Mediastinal Hematoma: A Case Report
items.abstract: Case: An octogenarian woman with a history of coronary artery bypass grafting performed 34 years earlier was admitted for non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction caused by a culprit lesion in the left circumflex artery. Immediately after successful percutaneous coronary intervention, she developed cardiac arrest and underwent cardiopulmonary resuscitation followed by initiation of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (V-A ECMO) and intra-aortic balloon pump support. Diagnostic reasoning: On hospital day 2, left ventricular systolic function was considered sufficient for an ECMO weaning attempt, and V-A ECMO weaning was attempted. During ECMO clamp testing, right atrial pressure increased abruptly in association with a marked decline in systemic arterial pressure. Notably, pulmonary artery pressure remained unchanged despite the marked increase in right atrial pressure. This discordant right-sided hemodynamic response suggested extrinsic obstruction of the pulmonary artery. The pulmonary artery catheter findings prompted focused reassessment of the right-sided circulation. Echocardiography demonstrated focal compression and stenosis of the pulmonary artery, and computed tomography identified a localized anterior mediastinal hematoma compressing the pulmonary artery. Management and Outcome: Emergency surgical evacuation of the hematoma was subsequently performed, enabling successful decannulation from V-A ECMO. The patient was discharged on hospital day 46 without neurological sequelae. Discussion: This case demonstrates a rare mechanism of V-A ECMO weaning failure in which chest-compression-related vascular injury resulted in a localized mediastinal hematoma, likely confined by postoperative adhesions after prior sternotomy. More importantly, this case highlights the physiological significance of pulmonary artery catheter assessment during ECMO clamp testing. The combination of unchanged pulmonary artery pressure and elevated right atrial pressure provided an important clue suggesting extrinsic pulmonary artery obstruction rather than persistent biventricular failure. Careful interpretation of right-sided hemodynamics during ECMO weaning may facilitate early recognition of occult extracardiac causes of circulatory collapse and guide definitive intervention.

items.title: Abstract Or013: Evaluating Monogenic Ventricular Arrhythmia Risk During STEMI in a Population Cohort
items.abstract: Background: Ventricular arrhythmias (VA) remain a leading cause of sudden cardiac death (SCD) during ST-elevated myocardial infarction (STEMI). Risk stratification for VA during STEMI remains elusive. Genetic risk for malignant arrhythmias, including out-of-hospital SCD, are well established for individuals with rare, pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants in arrhythmia (AR) and cardiomyopathy (CM)-associated genes. Whether this risk extends to VA in other clinical contexts, such as during a STEMI, remains uninvestigated. Research Hypothesis: In a population genomic screening context, individuals with a rare, P/LP, AR- or CM-associated variant (G+) have higher odds of VA during a STEMI event compared to individuals without such a variant (G-). Methods: We curated a retrospective cohort of STEMI events in the Geisinger MyCode Community Health Initiative (n=230,070 with exomes and EHR). VA was determined as a composite of ventricular fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, SCD, or CPR during the STEMI encounter. P/LP status was assigned in 37 AR/CM genes according to gene-specific loss of function (LOF) or missense mechanisms based on Variant Effect Predictor and ClinVar annotations. Statistical comparisons were made with Firth’s bias-reduced logistic regression adjusted for sex, infarct location, admission LVEF, and peak troponin T, or t-test. Results: In 230,070 MyCode participants, there were 2,385 who experienced a STEMI and 441 with VA during the STEMI encounter (STEMI+VA; 17%). In 2,161 total MyCode participants with rare, P/LP genetic variants (0.9% of MyCode), 13 were STEMI without VA (0.6% of G+) and four were STEMI+VA (0.19%). Harboring a P/LP variant did not associate with VA risk during STEMI after accounting for patient sex, infarct location, and peak troponin (Odds Ratio 1.63 [0.3-6.3], P = 0.5). Variants in STEMI+VA were all LOF variants in four different genes, MYH7 , TTN , DSG2 , and ALPK3 . This was similar to variants detected in non-VA STEMI, which were identified in TTN (n=4 G+), ALPK3 (n=3), DSC2 , DSG2 , DSP , MYH7 , PLN , and SCN5A (all n=1). Age at STEMI+VA did not differ by P/LP status (G+ age 67 ± 10; G- 63 ± 13; P = 0.4), nor did LVEF at STEMI admission (G+ 48 ± 9.6%; G- 42 ± 13.5%; P = 0.4). Conclusions: Elucidating risk factors for VA during STEMI is a first step towards improving survival rates. Preliminary analyses suggest that harboring a rare, pathogenic genetic variant in AR/CM genes does not associate with increased risk of VA during STEMI. This is limited by lower yield of genetic testing in a population screening context and incomplete EHR data. It is likely that the role of genetics in STEMI+VA is multifactorial and encompasses polygenic risk and/or environmental factors that interplay with arrhythmic etiology in addition to monogenic risk from rare, pathogenic variants.

items.title: Abstract CR05: Biventricular Intracardiac Thrombi Presenting with Ischemic Stroke in Severe Nonischemic Cardiomyopathy: A Case Report and Review of the Literature
items.abstract: Background: Biventricular intracardiac thrombi are rare clinical entities associated with severe ventricular dysfunction and substantial thromboembolic risk. Simultaneous right and left ventricular thrombi complicated by ischemic stroke remain infrequently described in the literature. Case: A 43-year-old male with severe nonischemic cardiomyopathy presented with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, multifocal pneumonia, hemoptysis, and decompensated heart failure. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated severe biventricular systolic dysfunction with a large right ventricular intracardiac mass suspicious for thrombus. Transesophageal echocardiography further demonstrated a mobile tricuspid cord-associated mass concerning for thrombus versus vegetation. During hospitalization, the patient developed an acute embolic left posterior cerebral artery ischemic stroke requiring emergent mechanical thrombectomy. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated mobile intracardiac lesions involving both ventricles consistent with biventricular thrombi. The patient was treated with systemic anticoagulation and guideline-directed medical therapy with subsequent clinical stabilization. Conclusion: This case highlights the diagnostic complexity and embolic risk associated with biventricular intracardiac thrombi in severe nonischemic cardiomyopathy. Multimodality imaging was essential for diagnosis and management. Early recognition and anticoagulation remain critical to reduce catastrophic thromboembolic complications.

items.title: Abstract Or004: Cardiac Hemodynamics in Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
items.abstract: Introduction: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) with veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is increasingly being used to manage out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. However, significant debate remains regarding the hemodynamic effects of VA-ECMO. Research Questions: 1. What happens to cardiac hemodynamics upon VA-ECMO commencement in a large animal model of cardiogenic shock and cardiac arrest? 2. In humans that survive to a weaning study, how do invasive cardiac hemodynamics change when VA-ECMO flow is manipulated? Methods: We simultaneously conducted two prospective physiologic studies where we performed serial invasive hemodynamic and echocardiographic evaluations to define cardiac hemodynamics with VA-ECMO flow variations. The first study was a porcine study where we induced cardiogenic shock and cardiac arrest via coronary balloon occlusion and significant fluid loading in 60-65 kg Yorkshire pigs. The second study involved performing simultaneous left and right heart catheterization with three-dimensional echocardiography in humans cannulated for ECPR while sequentially weaning VA-ECMO flow. Serial hemodynamic comparisons were evaluated within each study using mixed effects models. Results: There were 15 animals in the porcine study (11 experimental and four controls) and 28 humans in the clinical study. In the animal study, VA-ECMO was commenced at a median of 2L/minute flow after cardiogenic shock and cardiac arrest were induced. The initiation of VA-ECMO led to reductions in left ventricular (LV) end-diastolic volume (p<0.001 for all stages of VA-ECMO support compared to measurements taken prior to cardiac arrest), LV end-diastolic pressure (p<0.001 for all stages), LV stroke work (p<0.05 for all stages), LV pressure-volume area (p<0.05 for all stages), and right atrial pressure (p<0.01 for all stages) (Figure 1). Mean pulmonary arterial pressure was not significantly different. In our clinical study, 28 humans completed the entire hemodynamic protocol at a median of 3.0 days after VA-ECMO cannulation. Reduction in VA-ECMO flow led to increases in LV end-diastolic pressure, end-diastolic volume, stroke work and pressure-volume area (Figure 2) as well as right atrial and mean pulmonary arterial pressures (all p<0.001 for lowest flow compared to baseline). Conclusions: Higher VA-ECMO flow reduces LV end-diastolic pressure, end-diastolic volume, and cardiac work both at the time of VA-ECMO commencement in an experimental model of cardiac arrest, but also in humans able to tolerate a weaning study.

items.title: Abstract Or008: The Super-Responder Phenotype: Who Recovers Neurologically After Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Despite Prolonged Resuscitation?
items.abstract: Introduction: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) time is one of the strongest predictors of outcomes in cardiac arrest patients treated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR). Yet, a subset of patients with prolonged CPR still achieve favorable neurological recovery (“super-responders”), while others do not despite shorter CPR duration. Hypothesis: There are pre-arrest and intra-arrest characteristics that distinguish ECPR super-responders from those with poor neurological outcomes. Aims: To characterize the clinical profile of the ECPR super-responders. Methods: This retrospective study included adult out-of-hospital and in-hospital cardiac arrest patients treated with ECPR at the University of Minnesota between 2015-2023. Favorable neurological outcome was defined as Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) 1-2 at discharge. Two pre-specified comparisons were performed: 1) super-responders, defined as patients with CPR duration >45 minutes and favorable CPC, versus patients with CPR duration >45 minutes and unfavorable CPC; 2) super-responders versus patients with CPR duration ≤ 45 minutes and unfavorable CPC. Pre-specified multivariable logistic regression analyses included age, presenting rhythm, ischemic cause of arrest, intermittent return of spontaneous rhythm (ROSC) and initial lactate. Results: CPR duration exceeded 45 minutes in 355 patients; 53 had favorable while 302 had unfavorable neurological outcomes (Table 1). After multivariable adjustment, younger age (p=0.001), lower initial lactate (p<0.001), intermittent ROSC (p=0.001), and ischemic cause of arrest (p=0.042) were independently associated with favorable neurological recovery (Table 2A). When comparing the super-responder cohort to the 92 patients with unfavorable outcomes despite CPR duration ≤45 minutes (Table 3), super-responders were younger (p=0.005), more likely to have shockable rhythm (p=0.001), and intermittent ROSC (p=0.007) (Table 2B). Conclusion: ECPR super-responders have a distinct clinical phenotype characterized by younger age, lower serum lactate, shockable initial rhythm, intermittent ROSC, and ischemic cause of arrest. These findings may help guide real-time resuscitation decision-making by identifying patients who may benefit from continued resuscitative efforts and escalation to ECPR despite ongoing, prolonged CPR.

items.title: Abstract Or012: The Effectiveness of Velocity Time Integral Measured by a Novel Hands-Free, Noninvasive, and Continuous Carotid Doppler Ultrasound in the Porcine Models of Traumatic and Non-Traumatic Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Hemodynamic monitoring is important for indicating resuscitation efficacy after cardiac arrest events. Artery pressure and end-tidal CO 2 (ETCO 2 ) are two feasible indicators for evaluating the hemodynamics during resuscitation; however, they are invasive and difficult to implement in the clinical setting. This study investigated the effectiveness of a novel hands-free, noninvasive, and continuous carotid doppler ultrasound in monitoring the hemodynamics during resuscitation. Hypothesis: Velocity time integral (VTI) measured by a novel hands-free, noninvasive, and continuous carotid doppler ultrasound was equally effective in monitoring the hemodynamics when compared with conventional, invasive mean aortic pressure (MAP), coronary perfusion pressure (CPP), ETCO 2 and carotid blood flow (CBF) in the porcine models of traumatic and non-traumatic cardiac arrest. Methods: Two experiments were performed in this study. In experiment 1, 10 adult pigs were averagely randomized into sham or traumatic cardiac arrest (TCA). In the TCA group, the animals were bled at a speed of 2ml/kg/min to reach an extremely low MAP (≤10mmHg), then observed for 7 mins, and finally resuscitated with 50% of the shed blood at a speed of 5 ml/kg/min. In experiment 2, 14 adult pigs were averagely randomized into control or resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA). The porcine model was established by 6 mins of ventricular fibrillation and then 8 mins of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. The balloon was inflated to occlude blood flow at aortic zone 1 during resuscitation in the REBOA group. Results: In experiment 1, the same changes of MAP, ETCO 2 , CBF, and VTI were observed during hemorrhage, cardiac arrest and resuscitation, in which all of them were significantly lower in the TCA group than in the sham group (Figs.1A-D). Correlation analysis showed that VTI was positively associated with MAP (r=0.911, P <0.001), and ETCO 2 (r=0.939, P <0.001), and CBF (r=0.952, P <0.001), respectively (Figs.1E-G). In experiment 2, the changes of CPP, ETCO 2 , CBF, and VTI were also maintained at the same trend during resuscitation, in which all of them were significantly higher in the REBOA group than in the control group (Figs.2A-D). Correlation analysis showed that VTI was positively associated with CPP (r=0.785, P <0.001), and ETCO 2 (r=0.738, P <0.001), and CBF (r=0.830, P <0.001), respectively (Figs.2E-G). Conclusion: The VTI measured by novel carotid doppler ultrasound was effective in monitoring the hemodynamics, and could become a feasible alternative of MAP, CPP, and ETCO 2 in the porcine models of traumatic and non-traumatic cardiac arrest.

items.title: Abstract P1004: Predictors of Return of Spontaneous Circulation in In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Multivariable Analysis
items.abstract: Introduction: Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) is influenced by modifiable resuscitation processes, many of which remain underexplored. This study evaluated clinical and performance predictors of ROSC, with emphasis on time-sensitive, guideline-directed measures. Methods: Adult IHCA cases from a multicenter institutional registry between January and March 2026 were analyzed. Key predictor variables included initial arrest rhythm, code duration, and adherence to key process benchmarks: CPR initiation <1 minute, defibrillation for shockable rhythms <2 minutes, and epinephrine administration <5 minutes. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of ROSC, reported as adjusted odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results: A total of 336 IHCA events were analyzed in this study after cases with missing initial rhythm or code initiation time were excluded. Timely CPR initiation was independently associated with increased odds of ROSC (OR 2.55; 95% CI 1.46-4.43; p<0.001), with higher ROSC rates when the benchmark was met (69% vs 52%). Shorter code duration was also associated with ROSC (OR 0.96 per minute; 95% CI 0.95-0.98; p<0.001), with rates declining from approximately 50-55% for durations <10 minutes to 30-35% for durations >20 minutes (Figure 1). Shockable rhythms were associated with higher unadjusted ROSC (72% vs 59%), but this association was not significant after adjustment, likely due to collinearity with defibrillation timing and limited statistical power. Neither timely defibrillation nor epinephrine administration was independently associated with ROSC. Model discrimination was moderate (AUC = 0.70) (Figure 2). Conclusions: Timely initiation of CPR was the strongest modifiable predictor of ROSC following IHCA in this single-institution cohort, underscoring the critical importance of early resuscitation efforts. Refinement of performance metrics and incorporation of rhythm-specific analyses may further improve predictive modeling and inform resuscitation strategies.

items.title: Abstract Or001: Supraglottic Airway versus Bag-Valve-Mask Ventilation Strategies: The Pediatric Prehospital Airway Resuscitation Trial (Pedi-PART)
items.abstract: Background: Prehospital airway management in children includes bag-valve-mask ventilation (BVM), supraglottic airways (SGA), and endotracheal intubation (ETI), but the optimal strategy remains uncertain. The Pediatric Prehospital Airway Resuscitation Trial (Pedi-PART) is a multistage Bayesian adaptive platform trial evaluating paramedic airway strategies. We present Stage I results comparing prehospital SGA and BVM strategies. Methods: Pedi-PART used a Bayesian adaptive platform design. Stage I included 65 EMS agencies in 10 U.S. communities and enrolled children >24 hours and <18 years with cardiac arrest, major trauma, or respiratory failure requiring airway management. Paramedics used primary-SGA (BVM with progression to SGA; odd days) or primary-BVM (BVM only; even days) strategies. The primary outcome was 30-day ICU-free days. Secondary outcomes included favorable Pediatric Cerebral Performance Category (PCPC 1-2) and safety events (hypoxia, aspiration, pneumonia, pneumothorax). Intention-to-treat analyses used Bayesian hierarchical models accounting for age and disease group. Results: Stage I ended early for futility because airway interventions delivered in practice were similar between groups. Among 1,257 patients, assignments were primary-SGA 647 and primary-BVM 610. Advanced airway attempts occurred in 43% of primary-SGA (SGA 89%, ETI 11%) and 33% of primary-BVM (SGA 81%, ETI 19%). Baseline characteristics were similar, including disease groups (cardiac arrest 42%, trauma 17%, respiratory failure 41%) and age distribution (infant 29%, toddler 32%, child 16%, adolescent 23%). ICU-free days were mean 12.4 (SD 13.9) for primary-SGA and 11.6 (13.5) for primary-BVM, difference 0.8 days (95% CI: –0.72, 2.32). Posterior probabilities were 77.2% for SGA non-inferiority and 66.3% for BVM superiority, not meeting the prespecified threshold of 97.5%. Favorable PCPC and safety events did not differ. Conclusions: Stage I of Pedi-PART ended early for futility because overlap in delivered airway interventions limited separation between assigned strategies, precluding determination of comparative effectiveness. The trial underscores practical challenges in designing and conducting prehospital resuscitation studies.

items.title: Abstract Or016: Phenotypes of Non-Ischemic Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Treated with Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
items.abstract: Introduction/Background: Mature extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) programs can improve survival in patients with refractory ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (VT/VF OHCA) by supporting visceral perfusion and allowing time to identify the inciting cause. While ischemic etiologies account for approximately 70% of refractory VT/VF OHCA, the long-term outcomes of non-ischemic causes remains poorly explored. Research Questions: 1. Among patients with refractory VT/VF OHCA treated with ECPR, are there differences in outcomes between ischemic and non-ischemic etiologies? 2.Among patients with non-ischemic refractory VT/VF OHCA treated with ECPR, are there differences in outcomes across distinct non-ischemic phenotypes? Aims: 1. Compare outcomes between ischemic and non-ischemic etiologies2. Compare outcomes among non-ischemic phenotypes. Methods/Approach: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with refractory VT/VF OHCA referred to the Minnesota Mobile Resuscitation ECPR protocol. Patients were classified as ischemic or non-ischemic based on angiographic, biomarker, and clinical evaluation. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Kaplan-Meier and adjusted survival analyses were done to compare outcomes between ischemic and non-ischemic refractory VT/VF OHCA. Results/Data: Among 412 patients, 289 (70.1%) had ischemic and 123 (29.9%) had non-ischemic etiologies. All-cause mortality occurred in 83.3% of patients after 345.7 person-years follow-up. In unadjusted Cox proportional hazard and Kaplan-Meier analyses, ischemic cause of refractory VT/VF OHCA was not associated with the hazard of all-cause mortality (HR 0.86, 95% CI: 0.69-1.08 and log-rank, p=0.19; Figure 1). In adjusted analyses, ischemic cause of refractory VT/VF OHCA was not associated with the hazard of mortality in the total cohort (HR 0.81, 95% CI: 0.61-1.08) as well as the subset of patients who survived the index hospitalization (HR 1.05, 95% CI: 0.34-3.27). Among non-ischemic refractory VT/VF OHCA phenotypes with >5 patients, patients with known genetic cardiomyopathy, illicit drug use, and arrhythmic sudden cardiac death without known cardiomyopathy had relatively better outcome (Figure 2). Conclusions: Among patients with refractory VT/VF OHCA requiring ECPR, there is a broad array of non-ischemic pathologies. These patients have comparable outcomes to patients with ischemic refractory VT/VF OHCA. However, among patients with non-ischemic refractory VT/VF OHCA, outcomes differ significantly by phenotype.

items.title: Abstract P1003: Association of Clinical Trajectories Before In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Deterioration with Patient Outcome
items.abstract: Background: Cardiac arrest is common, affecting approximately 500,000 people[MOU1] in the United States every year. The most common framework to categorizing cardiac arrest events uses the limited information available to rescuers during an out of hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), including initial arrest rhythm, whether there was bystander CPR, and whether the patient received defibrillation. In contrast, responders to an in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) have a wealth of information about the patient. Previous work by our group has identified and defined eight pre-arrest phenotypes in patients with IHCA (Table 1). Hypothesis: We hypothesized that pre-arrest clinical phenotypes of patients with IHCA would be associated with different rates of Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC). Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of IHCA events in a large academic medical center. Each IHCA event was reviewed by study team members and categorized into one or more pre-arrest phenotypes. Multinomial logistic regression was used to assess the association between each of the pre-arrest clinical phenotypes and ROSC. Results: A total of 202 patients comprised our analytic cohort. Patient demographics and comorbidities are displayed in Table 2. All patients were able to be classified into one of our previously identified arrest categories, with the most common being “No obvious preceding clinical change” (39, 19%), “Unstable Tachyarrhythmia” (41, 21%), and “Respiratory Failure (39, 19%). 33 patients (16%) met multiple pre-arrest trajectories. On univariate logistic regression, “No obvious preceding clinical change” was associated with the highest odds of ROSC (OR 3 [1.47-6.14]), with Hemorrhage, Stable/Mild Shock, and Multiple Categories having the lowest odds of ROSC (OR 0.40, 0.48, and 0.58 respectively). This association continued after correction for potential confounders (Table 3). Conclusions: We have demonstrated that our framework of pre-IHCA deterioration phenotypes can be used retrospectively to classify patients with in-hospital cardiac arrest. We found that different presentations of pre-arrest categories were associated with varied outcomes, although our findings were likely limited by small sample sizes. Future work from our group will continue to explore how these trajectory phenotypes are associated with patient outcome, whether this framework is generalizable to other sites, and whether the causes of arrest may be different between each phenotype.

items.title: Abstract P1011: Allogeneic Mitochondria Transplantation Modulates Blood and Splenic Myeloid Phenotypes After Cardiac Arrest in Mice
items.abstract: Background: Recent human studies suggest that early immunological alterations are associated with clinical outcomes after cardiac arrest (CA). Mitochondria transplantation (MTx) improves survival and neurological outcomes after CA, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We previously showed that transplanted mitochondria are rapidly taken up by circulating and splenic myeloid cells, suggesting a potential immunomodulatory mechanism. Research Questions: (1) Does CA alter circulating and splenic myeloid phenotypes? (2) Does MTx modulate these changes? Methods: Male C57BL/6 mice underwent potassium chloride-induced CA for 8 min followed by resuscitation with manual chest compressions and mechanical ventilation. Immediately after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), animals received intravenous freshly isolated mitochondria from healthy donor mice (MTx group, n=7) or respiration buffer (Vehicle group, n=8). Neurological function score (NFS; maximum, 500) was assessed at 24 h. Blood and spleen samples were collected at 1 h or 24 h post-ROSC for flow cytometry analysis of myeloid subset frequencies, absolute numbers, and surface marker expression (CD62L, CCR2, MerTK). Results: MTx improved NFS at 24 h compared with Vehicle (354 ± 46 vs. 194 ± 46, P < 0.05). CA induced time-dependent immunological changes in both groups. At 1 h, neutrophils exhibited increased CD62L expression, a leukocyte adhesion molecule involved in leukocyte rolling and trafficking (Fig. A). At 24 h, a transition toward classical monocyte-dominant inflammation occurred, characterized by increased blood monocyte CCR2 expression, a marker associated with inflammatory monocyte recruitment, and increased splenic MerTK expression, consistent with enhanced phagocytic clearance of apoptotic cells (Fig. B). MTx did not alter myeloid subset frequencies or absolute numbers in blood or spleen at either time point but modified myeloid cell phenotype. At 1 h, MTx increased CD62L expression in classical monocytes and neutrophils in blood and spleen (Fig. A). At 24 h, MTx reduced CCR2 and MerTK expression, altering the classical monocyte phenotype (Fig. B). Conclusion: CA induces dynamic phenotypic changes in circulating and splenic myeloid cells. MTx improves neurological outcomes after CA and modulates myeloid cell phenotype without altering cell numbers. These findings support a potential immunomodulatory mechanism underlying the therapeutic effects of MTx after CA.

items.title: Abstract CR04: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Detected After Initiation of Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest with Initial Shockable Rhythm: A Case Report
items.abstract: Case Presentation: A woman in her 50s with a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus was found collapsed at home from suspected, but unwitnessed, cardiac arrest by her son who subsequently started chest compressions. Emergency medical service personnel delivered a defibrillation shock; however, spontaneous circulation was not restored. After the insertion of a laryngeal tube as an esophageal obturator-type supraglottic airway device, the woman was transported to the emergency department where the laryngeal tube was exchanged for an endotracheal tube. Although spontaneous circulation was restored the patient’s hemodynamics remained unstable. Because bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation had been initiated and the initial rhythm was shockable, we initiated venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Thus, unfractionated heparin was administered before the completion of cannulation for venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Differential Diagnosis: Head computed tomography performed immediately thereafter revealed a subarachnoid hemorrhage suggestive of a rupture of a left middle cerebral artery aneurysm, corresponding to modified Fisher grade 4. Treatment and Management: On the day of presentation, following discussions with her family and medical team, venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was discontinued. Computed tomography angiography was not performed because the patient’s condition was extremely poor and no definitive intervention for the suspected ruptured aneurysm was considered feasible. Emergency coronary angiography was also not performed. Outcome: The patient eventually died on day 3 of hospitalization. Discussion/Teaching Points: Typically, unfractionated heparin is administered before the completion of cannulation to initiate extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. However, most causes of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest remain unclear when venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is initiated in an emergency setting. This means that anticoagulation may worsen intracranial hemorrhage or acute aortic syndrome if these conditions are the cause of the cardiac arrest. Therefore, following the initiation of venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, it may be worth considering anticoagulation at least after severe subarachnoid hemorrhage and acute aortic syndrome have been ruled out by emergency computed tomography. Further research is needed to evaluate the utility of this strategy in clinical practice.

items.title: Abstract CR13: Lightning Strikes Twice: Transient ST-Segment Elevation Following High-Voltage Electrocution Causing Reversible Myocardial Stunning Mimicking STEMI in 22 y/o Male
items.abstract: Background: High-voltage electrocution produces a spectrum of cardiac effects ranging from ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest to transient arrhythmias. Although myocardial stunning is a recognized consequence, ST-segment elevation after electrocution is uncommon and may mimic STEMI, potentially leading to unnecessary activation of emergent coronary angiography pathways. Case Presentation: A previously healthy 22-year-old male sustained a high-voltage electrical shock while manipulating a ladder that contacted an active power line. He collapsed immediately, and CPR was initiated by bystanders. EMS found him pulseless in ventricular tachycardic arrest and achieved return of spontaneous circulation after three defibrillations and approximately 10 minutes of downtime. Following ROSC, ECG demonstrated marked ST-segment elevation in V1-V4 with deep T-wave abnormalities and a wide QRS morphology suggestive of diffuse myocardial injury rather than focal coronary occlusion. Within minutes, these abnormalities rapidly resolved with normalization of sinus rhythm and repolarization changes. The patient remained hemodynamically stable without recurrent malignant dysrhythmias and was discharged home on hospital day 4. Discussion: Electrical injury may cause direct myocardial injury, coronary vasospasm, global myocardial stunning, and arrhythmogenesis. Although uncommon, ST-segment elevation after electrocution can closely mimic acute STEMI. Unlike ischemic STEMI, electrical-injury-related ST elevation often demonstrates diffuse precordial involvement, atypical QRS-T morphology, rapid spontaneous resolution, and absence of reciprocal ST depression. In this patient, the transient ECG abnormalities were most consistent with electrical myocardial stunning rather than acute coronary occlusion. Recognition of this pattern is important when the mechanism strongly suggests electrocution. Conclusion: This case demonstrates a reversible pattern of transient ST-segment elevation following high-voltage electrocution that mimicked STEMI but resolved within minutes. Awareness of this presentation may prevent unnecessary invasive coronary angiography and help clinicians correctly attribute ECG abnormalities to electrical myocardial injury rather than ischemic infarction. Serial ECGs remain essential in the immediate post-ROSC period after electrical injury.

items.title: Abstract P1010: Poly(ADP-Ribose) Polymerase 1-Dependent Parthanatos Contributes to Brain Injury Following Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in Mice
items.abstract: Background: Brain injury is the primary contributor to poor neurological outcomes following the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Neuronal DNA damage, an early pathological event during cerebral ischemia-reperfusion, can initiate regulated cell death after cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). Poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1)-dependent parthanatos is a distinct cell death pathway characterized by PARP1 overactivation, poly(ADP-ribose) (PAR) accumulation, and apoptosis-inducing factor/macrophage migration inhibitory factor (AIF/MIF)-mediated DNA fragmentation. However, whether this pathway is involved in post-resuscitation brain injury remains unclear. Methods: Transcriptomic analysis was performed to identify enriched biological pathways in mouse brain tissues after cardiac arrest-cardiopulmonary resuscitation-return of spontaneous circulation (CA-CPR-ROSC). To mimic ischemia-reperfusion injury in vitro , HT22 neuronal cells were subjected to oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R). DNA damage and cell death were evaluated via γH2AX immunoblotting and immunofluorescence, comet assays, and cell death staining. Furthermore, PARP1 activation, PAR expression, alongside AIF/MIF expression and nuclear translocation, were assessed using immunoblotting and immunofluorescence in both brain tissues and HT22 cells. Results: Transcriptomic analysis revealed enrichment of pathways related to DNA damage response, NAD + metabolism, and cell death in mouse brain tissues after CA-CPR-ROSC. In HT22 cells, OGD/R exposure increased γH2AX expression, enhanced DNA damage in comet assays, and promoted cell death. Subsequent analysis demonstrated elevated PARP1 activation and PAR accumulation in mouse brain tissues post-ROSC. Concurrently, AIF and MIF expression levels increased, accompanied by nuclear translocation. Consistently, OGD/R induced parallel PARP1 activation, PAR accumulation, and AIF/MIF nuclear translocation in HT22 cells. Conclusion: These findings suggest that DNA damage-associated cell death is involved in brain injury after CA-CPR-ROSC. PARP1-dependent parthanatos may contribute to post-resuscitation neuronal injury and represent a potential therapeutic target for improving neurological outcomes after cardiac arrest.

items.title: Abstract Or009: Intra-Arrest Mechanical Phenotyping with Resuscitative Transesophageal Echocardiography Identifies Prognostically Distinct Subgroups: A Multicenter rTEECoRe Network Analysis
items.abstract: Background: Current cardiac arrest algorithms classify patients by electrical rhythm despite substantial heterogeneity in intra-arrest cardiac mechanics. Resuscitative transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) identifies occult hemodynamic states during CPR, including pseudo-pulseless electrical activity (pPEA) — organized cardiac contractility despite absent pulse — and right ventricular dilation (RVD). Objective: To determine whether TEE-derived intra-arrest hemodynamic phenotypes define clinically meaningful cardiac arrest subgroups with differential ROSC rates. Methods: Prospective observational analysis of the Resuscitative TEE Collaborative Research (rTEECoRe) Network (NCT04972526). Adults with non-traumatic cardiac arrest undergoing resuscitative TEE were included. pPEA was defined as organized biventricular contractility despite absent pulse; RVD as RV:LV end-diastolic area ratio >0.6. Four phenotypes were assigned: pPEA+/RVD–, pPEA+/RVD+, pPEA–/RVD–, pPEA–/RVD+. ROSC was modeled with multivariable logistic regression (covariates: arrest location, age, sex, presenting rhythm; reference: pPEA+/RVD–). Results: Of 552 evaluations (426 OHCA, 126 IHCA; median age 64 years [IQR 51-73], 69% male; analytic N=517), pPEA–/RVD– predominated (379/552, 69%). Relative to pPEA+/RVD– (ROSC 45/77, 58%; reference), ROSC was lower for pPEA–/RVD– (33%; OR 0.37, 95% CI 0.22-0.61, p<0.001) and pPEA–/RVD+ (41%; OR 0.48, 95% CI 0.23-0.97, p=0.044). Both lower-ROSC phenotypes were pPEA–; RV dilation did not independently stratify outcome within either pPEA stratum. pPEA+/RVD+ was small with an imprecise estimate (16/22; OR 1.68, 95% CI 0.60-5.21). Results were consistent in the OHCA-only model (pPEA–/RVD– OR 0.22, 95% CI 0.11-0.39, p<0.001). pPEA and RVD were each more prevalent in IHCA than OHCA (29% vs 17%; 29% vs 12%). Among pPEA+ evaluations with assessable compression location (N=73), LVOT/aortic root targeting was associated with lower ROSC (OR 0.37, 95% CI 0.13-0.99, p=0.047). Conclusions: Organized contractility (pPEA) identified by TEE associated with differential ROSC independent of presenting rhythm; RV dilation did not independently stratify outcome. In an exploratory pPEA+ analysis, compressions targeting the LVOT/aortic root rather than the left ventricle were associated with lower ROSC — an effect not seen overall. These findings support TEE-derived physiologic subgrouping as a framework for individualized resuscitation strategies and interventional trials.

items.title: Abstract CR08: When Stimulants Meet Opioid Therapy A Case of Severe QT Prolongation
items.abstract: Case Presentation: A 40 year old patient with polysubstance use disorder on methadone maintenance therapy presented to the emergency department for evaluation of a right eye abrasion. Medical history was notable for a ventricular fibrillation (VF) cardiac arrest two years earlier attributed to cocaine use. During the emergency department stay, the patient developed VF cardiac arrest. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after 30 minutes of resuscitation. Urine toxicology was positive for cocaine and methadone. EKG demonstrated marked QT prolongation with a corrected QT interval (QTc) of 697 ms. After admission to ICU, patient developed recurrent polymorphic ventricular tachycardia consistent with torsades de pointes (TdP). Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a moderately dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 30-35%, distal anterior and apical hypokinesis, and grade I diastolic dysfunction, consistent with stress induced cardiomyopathy. Differential Diagnosis: The differential diagnosis included methadone induced acquired long QT syndrome, cocaine induced ventricular arrhythmia, congenital long QT syndrome, and ischemic heart disease. Congenital long QT syndrome was considered less likely given the absence of family history and normalization of QTc following stabilization. Ischemia was also considered unlikely due to previously normal coronary angiography. The final diagnosis was acquired long QT syndrome with recurrent TdP and VF secondary to the combined electrophysiologic effects of methadone and cocaine. Treatment and Management: The patient was admitted to ICU for continuous monitoring. Recurrent TdP was treated with intravenous magnesium sulfate. Persistent QT prolongation and two additional cardiac arrests prompted initiation of continuous lidocaine and isoproterenol infusions to suppress ventricular arrhythmias and prevent pause-dependent TdP. Serial EKGs were obtained throughout hospitalization. Outcome and Follow Up: Ventricular arrhythmias resolved with treatment, and no further episodes of TdP occurred. QTc improved from 697 ms to 450 ms. Antiarrhythmic infusions were discontinued without recurrence of arrhythmias. The patient recovered clinically and was evaluated for implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement pending reassessment of left ventricular function and QT stability. Teaching Points: Methadone and cocaine can independently prolong ventricular repolarization and increase the risk of malignant arrhythmias. This case highlights their potential synergistic effects, resulting in extreme QT prolongation, recurrent TdP, and multiple VF arrests. Early recognition, aggressive management with magnesium and heart rate augmentation, and careful monitoring of patients receiving methadone who continue stimulant use are essential to prevent life-threatening complications.

items.title: Abstract Or005: Time Dependent and Complementary Prognostic Value of Serial MRI and CT After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: High-specificity neuroprognostication after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is essential to avoid self-fulfilling withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy, but the complementary and time-dependent roles of serial brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) remain unclear. Methods: In this retrospective cohort, adult comatose OHCA survivors underwent MRI and CT within 6 h after return of spontaneous circulation (ultra-early) and at 72-96 h (delayed). MRI was assessed using visual diffusion-weighted imaging high-signal intensity (DWI HSI) and ADC-R(450), a volumetric diffusion burden metric; CT was assessed using gray-to-white matter ratio (GWR). The primary outcome was poor neurological outcome at 6 months (Cerebral Performance Category 3-5). AUCs were compared using DeLong's test, stratified by revised Cardiac Arrest Syndrome (rCAST) grade. Results: Among 111 patients, 61 (55.0%) had poor outcomes. Prognostic performance was time-dependent. Delayed DWI HSI showed the highest discrimination (AUC 0.93), followed by delayed ADC-R(450) and delayed GWR (AUC 0.88 each), all exceeding their ultra-early imaging (AUC 0.71-0.79). The gain from delayed imaging was greatest in grade 2, the intermediate-risk subgroup, where delayed imaging outperformed ultra-early imaging for diffusion-weighted imaging high-signal intensity (0.92 vs 0.69; P less than 0.001) and gray-to-white matter ratio (0.78 vs 0.56; P=0.01), whereas ADC-R(450) remained similar (0.77 vs 0.75; P=0.78). A combined delayed DWI HSI plus ADC-R(450) model achieved an AUC of 0.96 with 0% false-positive rate at 87% sensitivity. Conclusions: Neuroimaging-based prognostication after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest varies by timing, modality, and severity of hypoxic-ischemic brain injury. Delayed qualitative and quantitative diffusion markers provided complementary prognostic information, especially in intermediate-risk patients. These findings support serial multimodal imaging and warrant external validation.

items.title: Abstract P1008: Long-Term Stored Artificial Oxygen Carrier HbV Preserves Circulation and Suppresses Arrhythmogenesis After Hemorrhagic Shock During Pneumonectomy
items.abstract: Perioperative hemorrhagic shock (HS) is a fatal complication of thoracic surgery. We previously demonstrated beneficial effects of the artificial oxygen carrier liposome-encapsulated hemoglobin vesicles (HbVs) in a rat HS model after total pneumonectomy. A major advantage of artificial oxygen carriers is long-term shelf life. Since Phase I clinical trials of HbV have been successfully completed, verification of long-term storage efficacy is essential for future clinical application. Although physicochemical stability of HbV for more than 2 years has been reported, in vivo efficacy after prolonged storage has not been confirmed. Therefore, we investigated whether long-term stored HbV (LS-HbV; >2.5 years, mean 32±2 months) could restore circulation and suppress arrhythmogenesis in a rat HS pneumonectomy model using optical mapping (OMP) with Langendorff perfusion (N=96). Immediately after pneumonectomy, repetitive 50% blood withdrawal and resuscitation procedures were performed. Animals were randomly assigned to sham (NL), 5% albumin (ALB), HbV (stored for short-term < 6 months), LS-HbV, and washed red blood cell (wRBC) groups. OMP analyses, including electrophysiological induction of lethal ventricular arrhythmias (SVT/VF), were performed. Ventricular arrhythmias (PVCs/NSVTs), blood chemistry (ALT, AST, CPK, creatinine, troponin I, lactate), and tissue HIF1α expression in the heart, lung, liver, kidney, and spleen were evaluated. Pneumonectomy increased right ventricular pressure, aggravating circulatory impairment and arrhythmogenic substrate formation. After resuscitation, systemic blood pressure was preserved in the HbV, LS-HbV, and wRBC groups, but not in the ALB group (Fig. 1). SVT/VF inducibility and spontaneous PVCs/NSVTs were increased in the ALB group but suppressed in the HbV, LS-HbV, and wRBC groups (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2). Action potential duration dispersion (APDd), an index of lethal arrhythmogenicity, was significantly lower in the HbV, LS-HbV, and wRBC groups than in the ALB group (11±4, 14±3, 12±4 vs. 24±4 ms, P<0.01), indicating preservation of electrical homogeneity (Fig. 2). ALT, CPK, troponin I (Fig. 3), and lactate levels were significantly elevated only in the ALB group (ALT: 28±8, 29±9, 24±6 vs. 72±6 U/L; CPK: 241±61, 261±55, 154±76 vs. 732±175 U/L; lactate: 0.8±0.2, 0.8±0.1, 1.1±0.1 vs. 2.6±0.6 mmol/L; all P<0.01). HIF1α staining in the heart, liver, and kidney was prominent only in the ALB group, whereas minimal staining was observed in the HbV, LS-HbV, and wRBC groups (Fig. 3). In conclusion, HbV retained excellent in vivo efficacy after storage exceeding 2.5 years. LS-HbV preserved systemic circulation, reduced tissue hypoxia, and suppressed lethal ventricular arrhythmias following HS after total pneumonectomy. The prolonged shelf life of HbV may provide an important translational advantage for emergency and perioperative medicine.

items.title: Abstract P1016: Cortical Repolarization as a Potential Indicator of Cerebral Perfusion Adequacy During CPR in a Swine Cardiac Arrest Model
items.abstract: Introduction: There is currently no method to reliably monitor the adequacy of cerebral perfusion during CPR. Ischemic depolarization occurs when brain oxygen delivery is inadequate to maintain neuronal membrane ion gradients. Repolarization can occur if adequate reperfusion is achieved prior to irreversibly injury. Utilizing a newly developed technique to monitor cortical DC potential, we tested the hypothesis that CPR can generate adequate cerebral perfusion to reverse cortical ischemic depolarization (CID) during cardiac arrest. Methods: Yorkshire swine (n=11, weigh 48.7 (7) kg) were anesthetized, intubated, and instrumented for continuous intra-arterial blood pressure and common carotid blood flow monitoring. Following bilateral craniotomy, subdural platinum electrodes were placed over the right and left cortex and connected to an OpenBCI Cyton board and graphical interface unit for continuous unfiltered full-spectrum monitoring of cortical DC potential. After baseline measurements, VF cardiac arrest was electrically induced and left untreated for 4,5 or 8 minutes followed by mechanical CPR a minimum of 5 min prior to defibrillation attempts or epinephrine administration. Results: Cortical depolarization after induction of cardiac arrest began in all animals with mean (SD) onset time of 16.2 (5) seconds. The average maximum shift in cortical DC potential during untreated cardiac arrest was -25.5 (15) mV. After initiation of CPR, complete repolarization occurred in 10 out of 11 animals. The mean time from CPR onset to complete repolarization was 90.3 (47) sec. Animals with complete repolarization had 29 (11) % baseline carotid blood flow during first 5 min of CPR compared to 15 % in the animal without complete repolarization. Conclusion: These experiments demonstrate for the first time the feasibility of monitoring cortical ischemic depolarization and repolarization in a large animal cardiac arrest model and provide the first direct evidence that CID can be reversed with CPR. Our results are consistent with published rodent global ischemia studies reporting that 20-40% baseline cerebral perfusion is required for cortical repolarization. Real-time monitoring of cortical DC potential is a promising strategy to determine the adequacy of cerebral perfusion during CPR.

items.title: Abstract CR09: Intact Survival After Massive CO 2 Embolism During Laparoscopic Surgery and Multiple In-Hospital Cardiac Arrests
items.abstract: Case presentation: A 64-year-old female presented with suspected appendicitis for laparoscopic appendectomy. Following uneventful induction of general anesthesia, abdominal access was attempted via Veress needle inserted at Palmer's point because of a prior lower midline laparotomy. Shortly after initiation of CO 2 insufflation, end-tidal CO 2 abruptly decreased and the patient developed pulseless electrical activity (PEA) cardiac arrest (CA). Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was initiated. After 8-10 minutes of CPR, three doses of epinephrine, and defibrillation for subsequent ventricular fibrillation, return of spontaneous circulation was achieved. Intraoperative trans-esophageal echocardiography (TEE) demonstrated extensive gas within both ventricles and hepatic vasculature, highly concerning for massive CO 2 embolism. A central venous catheter was placed, and small amount of gas was aspirated. Repeated TEE demonstrated a reduction in intracardiac gas burden. The procedure was aborted, and the patient was transferred for consideration of hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT). Differential Diagnosis: CO 2 embolism, anaphylactic shock, sudden cardiac death, tension pneumothorax, hemorrhagic shock, anesthetic complication, myocardial infarction, and pulmonary embolism. The temporal relationship to insufflation, abrupt decrease in end-tidal CO 2 , and TEE visualization of intracardiac gas supported massive CO 2 embolism. Treatment and Management: Management included immediate cessation of insufflation, CPR, left lateral positioning, TEE-guided diagnosis, and central venous aspiration. During HBOT preparation, the patient suffered recurrent PEA arrests secondary to bilateral pneumothoraces requiring emergent chest tube placement. Imaging subsequently demonstrated splenic injury with active hemorrhage. Exploratory laparotomy revealed a through-and-through splenic laceration, likely from Veress needle placement, requiring splenectomy. Her course was further complicated by ARDS, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, and delayed splenic bed hemorrhage requiring embolization. Outcome and Teaching Points: The patient was discharged home after 19 days with intact neurologic function and recovery of cardiac function. This case highlights the importance of vigilance during routine laparoscopic procedures. Catastrophic CO 2 embolism should be immediately considered when abrupt cardiovascular collapse follows insufflation, with “mill-wheel murmur" on auscultation. TEE can facilitate diagnosis. Standard central catheters are too short to allow effective aspiration. While HBOT is well established for arterial air embolism and neurologic injury, its role in isolated CO 2 embolism is less certain because CO 2 is highly soluble and rapidly reabsorbed. Favorable outcomes are still possible when rare causes of CA are rapidly identified and treated.

items.title: Abstract CR10: The Pause Before the Arrest: Sinus Arrest as a Warning Sign of RCA In-Stent Thrombosis Leading to Cardiac Arrest and VA-ECMO-Supported Shock
items.abstract: Case Presentation: A 51-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease, diabetes, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and prior proximal right coronary artery (RCA) drug-eluting stent presented after presyncope. Initial testing showed negative troponin and new inferior T-wave inversions. She became unresponsive during a 7.5-second sinus pause, requiring temporary transvenous pacing and leadless pacemaker placement for presumed sick sinus syndrome. Two days later, she again became unresponsive and hypotensive while ventricularly paced at 40 beats/min. ECG showed new anterolateral ST elevations, and echocardiography revealed right ventricular (RV) dilation and dysfunction. Differential Diagnosis: Pulmonary embolism, pacemaker malfunction, bradyarrhythmia-mediated shock, acute coronary syndrome, and RV infarction were considered. CT angiography excluded pulmonary embolism. Coronary angiography showed acute in-stent thrombosis of the prior RCA stent with normal left coronary circulation, establishing RCA STEMI with RV infarction as the diagnosis. Treatment and Management: Before percutaneous coronary intervention, she developed polymorphic ventricular tachycardia arrest requiring defibrillation. She underwent emergent RCA PCI. Given biventricular failure and refractory cardiogenic shock, veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation was initiated. Outcome and Follow-Up: After PCI and mechanical circulatory support, she stabilized and was decannulated. Her course was complicated by pneumonia-related respiratory failure requiring antibiotics and tracheostomy. She was transferred to the floor for recovery and disposition planning. Teaching Points: Sinus arrest may reflect ischemia of the sinoatrial nodal artery, particularly in RCA disease. Although chronic coronary disease has been proposed as a contributor to intrinsic sinus node dysfunction, acute sinus arrest during progression to critical coronary obstruction remains less well described. For resuscitation teams, new sinus dysfunction with ischemic ECG changes should be viewed as a pre-arrest warning sign of evolving coronary occlusion rather than attributed only to intrinsic conduction disease. Earlier recognition may accelerate coronary evaluation and prevent progression to STEMI, arrest, and shock.

items.title: Abstract Or006: Airway Opening Index Impact on the Association Between End-Tidal Carbon Dioxide and Survival During Pediatric Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
items.abstract: Introduction: End-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO 2 ) is associated with pediatric IHCA outcomes and is used as a marker of cardiac output during CPR, but is likely impacted by airway patency and ventilation. Aim: To determine if airway patency, defined by Airway Opening Index (AOI), impacts the relationship between ETCO 2 and survival. Hypothesis: The association between ETCO 2 and survival will differ in patients with closed vs open airways. Methods: Retrospective cohort study of pediatric IHCA data from the ICU-RESUS trial. Patients with invasive mechanical ventilation and evaluable capnography waveforms (used to determine ETCO 2 and AOI) were included. AOI quantifies chest compression-induced capnogram oscillations to assign airway opening: lower amplitude oscillations indicate closed airways (low AOI) and high amplitude oscillations indicate open airways (high AOI). Events were classified as having open or closed airways based on a previously defined AOI threshold (0.35) associated with outcomes in this cohort. Within each AOI group, outcomes (survival to discharge and achievement of age-based diastolic blood pressure targets (DBP; >/=25 mmHg for <1 year old or >/=30 mmHg for >/=1 year old) were compared between patients with high (>/=20mmHg) and low (<20 mmHg) ETCO 2 using Fisher’s exact tests. Cubic spline analyses evaluated the association between ETCO 2 as a continuous variable and outcomes. Results: Of 99 included patients, 46 (46%) had closed and 53 (54%) had open airways. In the closed airway group, 30/46 (65%) patients had high ETCO 2 and this subset more frequently survived to hospital discharge (16/30 [53%] vs 3/16 [19%]; P =0.03) and attained DBP thresholds (30/30 [100%] vs 12/16 [75%]; P =0.01). In the open airway group, 22/53 (42%) patients had high ETCO 2 ; there was no difference in survival (15/22 [68%] vs 20/31 [65%]; P =1.00) or attainment of DBP thresholds (20/22 [91%] vs 27/31 [87%]; P =1.00) between patients with high vs low ETCO 2 . Figure 1 shows the relationship between ETCO 2 and survival within the closed and open airway groups. Conclusion: In patients with airway closure during CPR, high ETCO 2 was associated with better hemodynamics and survival, suggesting that ETCO 2 is reflective of perfusion and associated with outcomes. However, this was not observed in patients with open airways, suggesting that intra-arrest ventilation modifies this relationship. These findings have important implications for the use of ETCO 2 as a physiologic monitor during CPR. Figure 1 Legend: Relationship between ETCO 2 and survival to hospital discharge in closed and open airway groups. a. Spline analysis of the relationship between event-level median ETCO 2 and survival to hospital discharge in events with closed airways (AOI<0.35). b. Spline analysis of the relationship between event-level median ETCO 2 and survival to hospital discharge in events with open airways (AOI>/=0.35).

items.title: Abstract Or015: Age-Stratified Accuracy of 911 Dispatch Recognition of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Early 911 recognition of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) enables rapid resource deployment and timely bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). Pediatric OHCA is uncommon and may present differently from adult OHCA, but age-stratified dispatch accuracy is not well described. We evaluated OHCA dispatch recognition across all ages and compared adult and pediatric performance, with additional review of pediatric false-negative and false-positive dispatches. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed Seattle Fire Department dispatch-linked EMS patient records from 2018 through 2025. Dispatch protocol directed telecommunicators to ask whether the patient was conscious and breathing normally regardless of age. If neither was present, telephone CPR instructions would be given. Treated OHCAs were classified by age and by whether arrest occurred before first unit arrival. Positive recognition was defined as assignment of an OHCA-specific dispatch code before first unit arrival. The primary outcomes were sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value, calculated overall and stratified by adult and pediatric incidents. Pediatric false negatives underwent structured review of dispatch and EMS records. Pediatric false positives were categorized by final clinical impression, age group, sex, and transport disposition. Results: Among 807,740 dispatched incidents, 3,842 OHCAs occurred before EMS arrival. Telecommunicators recognized 2,897, corresponding to sensitivity of 75.4% (95% CI, 74.0%-76.7%) and specificity of 98.0% (95% CI, 98.0%-98.0%). Among the age-linked incidents, adult incidents (n=478,125), sensitivity for the 3755 OHCA cases was 75.2% (95% CI, 73.8%-76.6%) and specificity was 97.5% (95% CI, 97.4%-97.5%). Among pediatric incidents (n=19,173), sensitivity for the 87 OHCA cases was 83.9% (95% CI, 74.8%-90.2%) and specificity was 98.0% (95% CI, 97.8%-98.2%). Of the 14 pediatric false negative cases, the majority involved childbirth (n=6) or respiratory arrest presentations (n=5). Among 377 pediatric false positive cases, the most common final clinical impressions were febrile seizure (26.5%), drug overdose (16.4%), respiratory distress (15.6%), and nonfebrile seizure (12.5%). Conclusions: OHCA-specific dispatch codes were highly specific for OHCA recognition in both adult and pediatric EMS responses. Sensitivity was higher for pediatric than adult OHCA. These findings identify dispatch quality improvement targets and may inform development of machine-learning-assisted triage for rare pediatric arrest presentations.

items.title: Abstract P1007: Emergency Granulopoiesis Drives Neutrophil Accumulation in Multiple Organs After Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Recent studies suggest that the immune response to post-cardiac arrest syndrome (PCAS) contributes to varied clinical outcomes. The systemic inflammatory response is a major feature of PCAS known to contribute to multi-organ failure and increased circulatory innate immune cells. PCAS patient data indicates an accumulation of immature neutrophils in circulation post-cardiac arrest (CA). It remains unclear whether circulatory granulocyte populations are associated with the accumulation of immune cells in different tissues. We employed a mouse model of cardiac arrest to analyze the immune cells in peripheral circulation and multiple organs. We hypothesize that neutrophil accumulation in circulation is a key driver of multi-organ failure after cardiac arrest. Methods: Experimental cardiac arrest was induced with potassium chloride in male and female C57BL/6J mice, 12-14 weeks old, n=15 per group. Resuscitation was achieved after epinephrine and CPR resulted in return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Groups included uninjured and 24-hours post-ROSC. Multiparametric flow cytometry analysis was performed on peripheral blood, brains, hearts, livers, lungs, and spleens of mice to quantify neutrophils identified as CD11b + /Ly6G + . Immature (CD101 - ) and mature (CD101 + ) neutrophils were identified within the neutrophil population. Circulatory brain injury marker Neuron-Specific Enolase (NSE) was measured via ELISA on isolated plasma. Results: Circulating neutrophils were significantly increased in ( p <0.001) post-CA. The number of neutrophils increased in the lungs, liver, spleen, heart, and brain ( p <0.05) post-CA. The ratio of CD101 - to CD101 + neutrophils significantly increased in the blood, lungs, liver, spleen, and heart (p<0.05) post-CA. The ratio of circulating CD101 - to CD101 + neutrophils was strongly associated with neutrophils accumulated in the lungs (r=0.540, p =0.018), liver (r=0.420, p =0.071), and brain (r=0.588, p =0.074) after cardiac arrest according to Pearson and Spearman correlation analyses and non-parametric t -tests. The ratio of circulating CD101 - to CD101 + neutrophils was associated with elevated plasma NSE levels (r=0.390, p =0.035). Conclusions: Increased concentrations of circulatory CD101 - neutrophils were associated with increased neutrophil infiltration to multiple organs and increased neuronal death post-CA. This data indicates a connection between circulatory CD101 - neutrophils and multi-organ failure following resuscitation from cardiac arrest. Mobilization of a heterogenous neutrophil population suggests that emergency granulopoiesis drives the neutrophil response, potentially contributing to infiltration to tissues and multi-organ failure. This model can be further used to assess the functional contribution of emergency granulopoiesis to the immune response to cardiac arrest.

items.title: Abstract P1015: The Effects of Partial Aortic Balloon Occlusion on the Outcomes of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in a Porcine Model of Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) has been proven to increase the perfusion of heart and brain and thereby improve the outcomes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). However, its complete occlusion would simultaneously cause distal ischemia and therefore aggravate post-resuscitation reperfusion injury. In this study, we investigated the effects of partial REBOA occlusion on CPR outcomes in a porcine model of cardiac arrest (CA). Hypothesis: Partial REBOA occlusion would produce equal hemodynamics during CPR and milder multiple organ injury after resuscitation when compared with its complete occlusion. Methods: A total of 21 male domestic pigs weighing 38±2 kg were used in this study. The animals were subjected to 6 mins of CA and then 8 mins of CPR. During CPR, they were randomized to receive complete (100%), partial (85%), or no (control) REBOA occlusion. For those animals treated with REBOA occlusion, aortic balloon was inflated to occlude blood flow at aortic zone 1 throughout the whole CPR procedure. Results: During CPR, coronary perfusion pressure and end-tidal CO 2 were maintained at an even level in the two REBOA occlusion groups, and both of them were significantly greater than that in the control group. Consequently, the rate of return of spontaneous circulation, duration of CPR, and number of defibrillations were better in the two REBOA occlusion groups than in the control group (Fig. 1). After resuscitation, myocardial dysfunction was equally significantly improved, and cardiac and cerebral injury were significantly alleviated in the two REBOA occlusion groups compared to the control group. Most importantly, neurological dysfunction and cardiac and cerebral injury were all significantly milder in the partial occlusion group than in the complete occlusion group (Fig. 2). Additionally, post-resuscitation renal and intestinal injury were significantly reduced in the two REBOA occlusion groups compared with the control group. Likewise, both of them were further significantly decreased in the partial occlusion group compared to the complete occlusion group (Fig. 3). Conclusion: During CPR, partial and complete REBOA occlusion could produce the equally effective hemodynamic effects. In addition, partial REBOA occlusion could further alleviate post-resuscitation multiple organ injury compared with its complete occlusion.

items.title: Abstract CR07: Phenotype-Driven Treatment for Recurrent Idiopathic Ventricular Fibrillation
items.abstract: Case Presentation: A 16-year-old male received CPR and 3 AED shocks during resuscitation from ventricular fibrillation (VF) arrest at night. An evaluation including serial ECGs, echocardiograms, and chest CT did not identify cardiac findings. Whole genome sequencing (WGS) revealed only a variant of uncertain significance in a gene unlikely to be associated with his phenotype ( CSRP3 c.175A>G, p.Lys59Glu). Exercise stress testing and cardiac MRI were not performed due to a previously retained bullet with associated spinal injuries. He had no ectopy or arrhythmia during the initial hospitalization. An ICD was implanted, and nadolol was started empirically. After >3 months without arrhythmia, he began having spontaneous, asymptomatic VF episodes over 15 months with no definitive triggers. Nearly all of the >600 VF episodes terminated spontaneously; 6 were terminated with ICD shocks. Management: During the time of recurrent VF events, flecainide, verapamil, and nadolol were prescribed in various combinations. He was admitted for additional evaluation. An EP study was negative for accessory connections, epinephrine infusion did not elicit phenotype, and mapping of both ventricles showed physiologic voltages. Hemodynamics and septal biopsy were normal. However, a procainamide challenge induced isolated monomorphic PVCs that progressed to non-sustained oligomorphic ventricular tachycardia with a short PVC coupling interval, similar to his non-sustained VF (Figure 1). No Brugada pattern was elicited. In addition, his outpatient flecainide history identified more VF events during flecainide therapy (0.83 vs. 0.63 events/day, p<0.01, Figure 2). With a working diagnosis of a sodium channel abnormality, despite normal WGS evaluation, he underwent a left cardiac sympathetic denervation and was prescribed quinidine and nadolol. The VF episodes persist but have decreased in frequency and duration. Differential Diagnosis: While this remains idiopathic VF, a genotype elusive sodium channelopathy is in the differential. In an attempt to further elucidate a sodium channel abnormality, we are currently performing long-read trio genome sequencing on a research basis. Teaching Points: The evaluation of idiopathic VF should continue after the initial hospital discharge. This is particularly important with atypical arrhythmia substrates, such as this case with frequent, usually self-terminating VF. This patient’s arrhythmic response to procainamide increased concern for a sodium channelopathy leading to a potentially beneficial treatment change.

items.title: Abstract Or010: Cerebral-Systemic Metabolic Uncoupling After Cardiac Arrest: A Time-Resolved, BBB-Corrected Paired Serum-CSF Study
items.abstract: Introduction: After cardiac arrest, whether cerebral and systemic metabolic trajectories recover in parallel after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) or diverge into distinct compartmental phases within the same patient remains unclear. We assessed early cerebral-systemic coupling using paired serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples with blood-brain barrier (BBB) correction. Methods: Adult comatose survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated with post-resuscitation care were prospectively enrolled. Paired serum and CSF were obtained every 2 h during the first 24 h after ROSC, and analyses focused on the 6-24 h window (Figure 1A). Glucose, pyruvate, lactate, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and albumin were measured in both compartments. CSF metabolites were corrected for BBB permeability using Qa = CSF/serum albumin: X cerebral = X CSF – Qa х X serum (Figure 1B). The primary outcome was 6-month neurological outcome. Group х time interactions were assessed for each metabolite trajectory.
