For each metabolite, per-patient uncoupling was defined as the cerebral-derived minus serum log 2 fold change (Δlog 2 FC) between the early window, 6-12 hours after ROSC, and the late window, 18-24 hours after ROSC, using the median concentration within each window (Figure 1C). Positive values indicate disproportionate cerebral worsening relative to serum, whereas negative values indicate relatively greater systemic change. Results: Thirty-two patients were included in the final analysis. Cerebral and systemic compartments showed metabolite-specific dissociation (Figure 2). For pyruvate, raw CSF concentrations did not differ by outcome over time (X CSF p=0.80), whereas BBB-corrected cerebral-derived pyruvate showed a significant group х time interaction (X cerebral p=0.03), with declining corrected cerebral pyruvate despite increasing serum pyruvate in patients with poor outcome. For LDH, corrected cerebral LDH increased approximately 10-fold over 24 hours in patients with poor outcome (X cerebral p=0.005), whereas serum LDH remained stable (p=0.44). Lactate separated in both compartments (serum p=0.008; X cerebral p=0.03), and glucose showed no significant interaction in either compartment. The composite lactate/pyruvate ratio (LPR) showed visually larger CSF separation than serum, but the interaction was not significant in either compartment (serum p = 0.38; CSF p = 0.28; Figure 3A). Δlog 2 FC was greater in poor outcome for pyruvate (p = 0.03) and LDH (p < 0.001), but not glucose (p > 0.99) or lactate (p = 0.16) (Figure 3B). Conclusion: During the first 24 hours after ROSC, patients with poor neurological outcome showed cerebral-systemic metabolic uncoupling, most prominently in pyruvate and LDH trajectories, suggesting that systemic markers alone may not capture ongoing cerebral metabolic injury.

items.title: Abstract P1001: Pre-Arrest Pulmonary Function and Neurological Outcome After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Multicenter Registry Study
items.abstract: Introduction: Pulmonary function may influence outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) by affecting respiratory reserve, gas exchange, and tolerance to post-resuscitation critical illness. Small airway dysfunction may also reflect underlying cardiopulmonary vulnerability and thereby contribute to poorer survival and neurological recovery after OHCA. However, evidence regarding the association between pre-arrest pulmonary function and neurological outcome after OHCA remains scarce. Hypothesis: Pre-arrest pulmonary dysfunction is associated with worse neurological outcome at hospital discharge after OHCA. Aim: To evaluate the association between pre-arrest pulmonary function and neurological outcome in patients with OHCA. Methods: We conducted a retrospective multicenter registry-based study using data from National Taiwan University Hospital and its branches in Taiwan between 2017 and 2025. Adult patients with OHCA who had undergone lung function testing within 2 years before the index arrest were included. Baseline covariates included age, sex, witnessed arrest, bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and initial shockable rhythm. The outcomes were good neurological outcome at discharge, defined as a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 or 2. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed, and results are presented as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: A total of 310 patients were included; 75.8% were male, and the mean age was 76 ± 18 years. Witnessed arrest occurred in 52.3%, bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation in 42.3%, and initial shockable rhythm in 16.5%. Overall, 23 patients (7.4%) survived to discharge and 18 (5.8%) had a good neurological outcome. After multivariable adjustment, higher FEF75% was independently associated with lower odds of good neurological outcome at hospital discharge (adjusted OR 0.171, 95% CI 0.033-0.897; p = 0.037). Younger age (adjusted OR 0.936 per year, 95% CI 0.889-0.985; p = 0.011) and an initial shockable rhythm (adjusted OR 9.287, 95% CI 2.928-29.454; p < 0.001) were also independently associated with good neurological outcome. Conclusions: Among patients with OHCA who had prior pulmonary function testing, FEF75% was independently associated with neurological outcome at hospital discharge in the adjusted model. Given the unexpected direction of the association, further studies are needed to confirm this finding and clarify its clinical significance.

items.title: Abstract Or002: The Critical Care Burden of Heat-Related Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Implications for Climate-Preparedness
items.abstract: Background: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is a devastating cardiovascular emergency; only 30% of patients survive to hospital admission and 10% survive to discharge. Extreme heat contributes to multi-organ system failure and has been associated with increased OHCA incidence. As heat events become more frequent, heat-related OHCA (HROHCA) may represent a recurring ICU challenge. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that extreme heat is associated with increased volume of ICU admissions with OHCA, and that patients with HROHCA demonstrate distinct clinical patterns compared to other OHCA patients. Aims: We aimed to quantify temperature-associated increases in OHCA ICU admission volume and to compare outcomes, organ support, and early clinical trajectories between heat-related and non-heat-related OHCA. Methods: We performed a multicenter cohort study of adult OHCA ICU admissions across 10 U.S. health systems from 2018-2024. We linked county-level daily maximum temperature (T max ) to hospitalizations. We estimated OHCA ICU admission volume change as the relative risk (RR) of admission based on daily T max compared to days with the minimum-risk temperature using distributed lag non-linear models for lags 0-5. We defined HROHCA as warm-season OHCA admission when daily T max ≥ 95th percentile. Trajectory comparisons used summaries of hourly organ support, cumulative outcomes, and vital-sign and laboratory values in the first 72 hours of ICU stay. Results: Among 5,266 warm-season OHCA ICU admissions, 270 (5.1%) were HROHCA and 4,996 (94.9%) were non-HROHCA. OHCA ICU admission volume increased progressively at higher T max . Relative to days with a T max of 29.5 °C, the 0-5 day OHCA ICU admission volume increased 45% at 33.0 °C (RR, 1.45; 95% CI, 1.12-1.89), 65% at 34.0 °C (RR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.27-2.14), and 102% at 36.5 °C (RR, 2.02; 95% CI, 1.19-3.43). HROHCA and non-HROHCA patients had similar rates of hospital mortality, hospice discharge, ICU length of stay (LOS), and hospital LOS. In the first 72 hours of ICU stay, HROHCA patients had a 2.2 to 5.0% lower mechanical ventilation prevalence, 4.1 to 8.7% higher vasopressor prevalence, 3.4% higher continuous renal replacement therapy prevalence, 2.5 mm Hg lower systolic blood pressure, 6.0 mm Hg lower mean arterial pressure, 1.6 mmol/L higher lactate, and 2.1 mg/dL higher phosphate levels (all p<0.05). Conclusions: Extreme heat was associated with increased OHCA ICU admission volume. HROHCA resembled other OHCA overall but showed signals of greater circulatory, metabolic, and renal failure. Climate adaptation policy should include hospital and ICU capacity planning alongside traditional interventions. Health systems should consider extreme heat forecasts as signals for resource allocation, surge planning, and regional coordination to ensure that ICUs are prepared for the downstream critical care needs of a warming climate.

items.title: Abstract Or011: Sodium Lactate Improves Post-Cardiac Arrest Outcomes by Normalizing TCA Flux and Suppressing Neuroinflammation
items.abstract: Background: Cerebral energy failure and neuroinflammation contribute to postcardiac arrest (CA) neurological outcomes. The brain readily consumes lactate as a fuel, yet whether exogenous lactate can improve post-CA outcomes remains unclear. Hypothesis: Sodium L-lactate (NaLac) administration improves post-CA outcomes by restoring cerebral tricarboxylic acid (TCA) flux and attenuating neuroinflammation. Aims: To determine the effects of NaLac on cardiac arrest (CA) outcomes, TCA flux, neuroinflammation, and the singlenucleus transcriptomic landscape of the cerebral cortex following cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). Methods: Adult C57BL/6J mice underwent 9.5min potassiuminduced CA/CPR. Effects of 0.5 M NaLac (0.5 g/kg, 120-min infusion), 3% NaCl, or 0.5 M NaHCO 3 , started 30 min after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), on CA outcomes were examined by assessing 5day survival, neurological function, serial arterial lactate, 13 C 3 lactate tracing into brain TCA intermediates at 3.5 h post-ROSC, qPCR for chemokines/cytokines, and snRNAseq of cortex at 12 h post-ROSC (50,587 nuclei). Results: NaLac improved 5day survival compared to NaCl (64.3% vs. 21.4%) or NaHCO3 (50% vs. 10.0%, log-rank P<0.05 for both) and neurological function at days 1 and 3 ( P <0.05 vs. both), despite equivalent sodium load and base excess correction, respectively (Fig 1A, B). During NaLac infusion, arterial lactate in post-CA mice remained at or below baseline (≤1.2 mmol/L), whereas sham mice showed a rise to ~2.6 mmol/L, indicating enhanced lactate clearance after CA/CPR (Fig 1C). 13 C 3 lactate tracing in the brain revealed that CA/CPR promoted lactate uptake and TCA entry (Fig 2A, B) while elevated succinate/fumarate/malate M+2/M+1 ratios (indicating stalled TCA cycle), latter of which was normalized by NaLac to sham levels (Fig 2C). SnRNAseq (Fig 3A, B) identified that NaLac shifted microglial transcriptomes from a CA/CPR-induced proinflammatory/chemokine signature toward a proresolving phenotype ( Clec10a , Zbtb16 ). RT-qPCR for top differentially expressed genes from microglial pseudobulk analysis confirmed marked upregulation of chemokines and cytokines in the cortex of NaCl-treated post-CA mice, which were significantly suppressed by NaLac treatment (Fig 3C). Conclusion: NaLac improved post-CA survival independent of sodium load and pH buffering by restoring brain TCA flux and suppressing neuroinflammation. Lactate acts as a metabolic resuscitation agent coupling energy delivery with immunometabolic reprogramming after CA.

items.title: Abstract P1009: Mitochondrial Transplantation Modulates Inflammatory Microglial Transcriptomes After Asphyxial Cardiac Arrest in Rats
items.abstract: Introduction: Neurologic injury remains a major cause of disability in survivors of cardiac arrest (CA) after successful resuscitation. In addition to the initial ischemic insult, progressive brain damage occurs after reperfusion through several proposed mechanisms, including hyperactivation of inflammatory responses. Mitochondrial transplantation (MTx), a novel therapy in which donor mitochondria are systemically administered after CA, is thought to reprogram immune responses. To understand the impact of CA on resident microglial responses and their modulation by MTx, we performed the first single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis of the rat hippocampus 24h after CA and resuscitation. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that cardiac arrest leads to massive activation of inflammatory programs in hippocampal microglia, which is attenuated by MTx. Methods: We used an established model of 10-minute asphyxial CA in adult Sprague-Dawley rats, which were randomized to receive CA+vehicle (n=4), CA+MTx (n=4), or sham operation (n=3). Hippocampi were isolated 24h after operation, dissociated into single cell suspensions, and purified by fluorescence-activated cell sorting to remove dead cells (DAPI+). cDNA libraries were prepared by combinatorial barcoding followed by next-generation sequencing. Computational analyses were performed using the Seurat, DESeq2, and MsigDB packages in R. Results: UMAP visualization and Leiden clustering revealed 18 distinct clusters, corresponding to major non-neuronal populations in the hippocampus (Fig. 1). Subclustering revealed 8 distinct microglial phenotypes, whose proportions were altered between groups (Fig. 2). Differential expression testing and pathway analysis demonstrate robust microglial activation across all phenotypes after cardiac arrest, including activation of gene programs related to IL-6, IL-2, TNF-alpha, and Interferon-gamma signaling (normalized enrichment score > 1.5; FDR-corrected p-value <0.05). Strikingly, we found that microglia from MTx-treated animals displayed a reduction in apoptosis, hypoxia, and TNF-alpha signaling genesets (normalized enrichment score < -1.5; FDR-corrected p-value <0.05). Conclusions: Our results suggest that MTx after CA improves inflammatory signaling and hypoxia-resilience in microglia. Further analysis is required to validate these results biologically, but our findings are in line with the theory that systemic MTx can modulate severe inflammatory reactions.

items.title: Abstract CR11: POCUS-Guided Tenecteplase Administration During Cardiac Arrest from AHA/ACC Category E2R Pulmonary Embolism
items.abstract: Introduction: Cardiac arrest from pulmonary embolism (PE) carries extremely high mortality and requires immediate reperfusion therapy. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) can rapidly identify PE when definitive imaging is not feasible. We report successful POCUS-guided administration of tenecteplase during pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest from high-risk PE. Case Presentation: A 50-year-old woman with prior PE prescribed rivaroxaban, remote breast cancer, and medication nonadherence presented with progressive dyspnea and weakness. During transport she developed profound hypotension, bradycardia, and PEA arrest. Advanced cardiac life support was initiated with multiple rounds of cardiopulmonary resuscitation and transient return of spontaneous circulation.POCUS during pulse checks demonstrated severe right ventricular dilation, septal flattening, and McConnell sign, suggesting PE with obstructive shock. Given recurrent PEA arrest and limited vascular access, weight-based tenecteplase was administered as a single intravenous bolus followed by anticoagulation. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography subsequently confirmed a saddle PE with extensive bilateral thrombus burden (Figure 1-2).The patient required mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support. Her course was complicated by gastrointestinal bleeding, acute kidney injury, and ischemic hepatitis, all of which improved. She was ultimately extubated and discharged to rehabilitation with favorable neurological recovery. Discussion: This presentation meets criteria for AHA/ACC PE Category E2R, reflecting cardiac arrest with refractory shock requiring mechanical ventilation. A key feature of this case was the use of POCUS during active resuscitation. Right ventricular dilation, septal flattening, and McConnell sign provided rapid bedside evidence of acute right ventricular pressure overload, supporting PE as the likely reversible cause of recurrent PEA arrest when transport for definitive imaging was impractical. Tenecteplase offered important logistical advantages. Unlike alteplase, which requires infusion, tenecteplase can be administered as a single weight-based bolus, enabling rapid reperfusion without occupying vascular access needed for resuscitative medications. Emerging evidence suggests outcomes comparable to alteplase. This patient's favorable neurological recovery highlights the potential value of early POCUS-guided thrombolysis in selected patients with PE-associated cardiac arrest. Conclusion: POCUS-guided administration of bolus tenecteplase facilitated emergent reperfusion and favorable neurological recovery in a patient with PE-associated cardiac arrest.

items.title: Abstract P1013: Hydroxyzine Rescue Therapy Improves Ribosome Activity and Cardiac Outcomes in a Mouse Model of Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Cardiac arrest (CA) is a leading cause of death in the US and is associated with overwhelming mortality. There exist no widely adopted therapeutics that improve cardiac or neurologic outcomes after resuscitation in CA survivors. Recent work in the Rutledge lab has implicated reduced cytosolic and mitochondrial ribosome activity in models of CA and has explored mechanisms for rescuing ribosome activity after hypoxia/reperfusion (H/R) injury. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that hydroxyzine would rescue protein synthesis rates after H/R injury and improve outcomes in our mouse model of CA. Goals: In this study, we investigated hydroxyzine’s impact on a human peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) model of hypoxia-reperfusion (H/R) and in a murine model of CA. Methods: Using an O-propargyl-puromycin high-throughput assay with AC16 cells, a line of adult human ventricular cardiomyocytes, 3180 bioactives were screened to identify pharmaceuticals based on their ability to restore ribosome activity after H/R injury. Hydroxyzine (HDX), a clinically relevant antihistamine, was identified as a top candidate in our drug screen. We validated HDX’s effects on ribosome activity in a PBMC model after H/R using the Click-iT L-Azidohomoalanine Assay. PBMCs underwent 4 hours of hypoxia/one hour of reperfusion, and newly synthesized proteins were quantified via fluorescence microscopy. A murine model of CA was used to evaluate HDX’s efficacy as a rescue therapy. C57BL/6 adult mice were subjected to 8 minutes of asystole via direct injection of potassium chloride and revived with cardiopulmonary resuscitation. At the time of reperfusion, mice were intraperitoneally injected with either 250 μL of saline or HDX at 10 mg/kg and assessed via echocardiography, activity monitoring, and neurologic scoring over a 24-hour monitoring period. Results: In the human PBMC model, HDX-treated cells showed an increase in protein synthesis rates following H/R (Normalized fluorescence 44.5±8.6%) compared to untreated H/R challenged PBMCs (21.9±5.3%, p<0.05 by student's t-test), validating our drug screen results. In the murine model, arrest animals had reduced 1-day ejection fraction (EF; 47.4±2.9%) compared to sham mice (58.1±1.8%, p<0.05 by ANOVA), while HDX rescue therapy preserved EF (56.52±2.8%, p<0.05 vs arrest by ANOVA). Neuro scoring was similarly reduced in arrest mice at 24-hours (8.8±0.8) compared to sham animals (12.0±0.0, p<0.05 by ANOVA), with trends towards neuroprotection in the HDX animals (10.4±0.4, p=0.07) Conclusion: Hydroxyzine treatment improves global cytosolic ribosome activity and protects cardiac function as a rescue therapy after CA. Further studies are needed to explore HDX effects on neurologic outcomes in the mouse model. HDX may present a novel therapeutic intervention to improve post-CA outcomes.

items.title: Abstract Or003: Associations Between Goal-Prediction Alignment, Life-Sustaining Treatment Decisions, and Regret in Disorders of Consciousness
items.abstract: Background: After severe brain injury leads to a disorder of consciousness (DoC), surrogates’ decisions about life-sustaining treatment rely on prognostic expectations and patient goals. How alignment between expected recovery and goals influences treatment decisions and regret remains unknown. Aim: To assess the association between the goal-prediction gap, life-sustaining treatment decisions, and subsequent surrogates’ decision regret. Methods: This prospective cohort study enrolled adult patients with DoC due to acute brain injury (≤28 days); post-arrest hypoxic-ischemic brain injury comprised the majority of injuries. Surrogates and physicians independently predicted the patient’s 6-month modified rankin scale (mRS). Surrogates also defined the patient’s goal mRS (the minimum acceptable functional outcome). The goal-prediction gap was defined as the difference between the goal and predicted mRS. Surrogates’ decision regret was assessed at 6 to 12-months post-discharge, using the decision regret scale. Life-sustaining treatment decisions during admission were classified as withdrawal (WLST) or continuation (CLST). Associations between goal-prediction gap, WLST, and decision regret were assessed using logistic regression and Spearman correlation. Results: Fifty-nine patients with DoC were included (median age 55 years; 53% male), of whom 35 (59%) underwent CLST and 24 (41%) WLST. The surrogate goal-prediction gap was significantly more negative (prediction worse than goal) in the WLST compared to the CLST group (p=0.045). After adjusting for baseline mRS, the surrogate goal-prediction gap, but not the physician gap, was associated with WLST (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.13-0.78). Decision regret scores were generally low but higher among surrogates in the WLST compared to the CLST group (median 7.5 vs. 0, p=0.017). In the CLST group, a more negative surrogate goal-prediction gap was associated with greater decision regret (ρ= –0.71, p=0.047), whereas no association was observed in the WLST group. Physician goal-prediction gaps were not associated with decision regret in either group. Conclusions: The surrogate goal-prediction gap was associated with WLST decisions and decision regret, suggesting that discrepancies between a surrogate’s perceived prognosis and the patient’s goals may play an important role in both life-sustaining treatment decisions and how surrogates reflect on those decisions afterward.

items.title: Abstract P1002: Staying Alive: A Retrospective Analysis of the July Effect and In-Hospital Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Outcomes
items.abstract: Background: The "July Effect" refers to a potential deterioration in patient outcomes and hospital efficiency coinciding with the annual turnover of trainees in U.S. academic medical centers. In-hospital cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) represents a high-acuity scenario where frontline providers are often early-career trainees, yet the influence of academic-year timing on CPR outcomes has not been systematically characterized. Research Question: We hypothesized that patients requiring in-hospital CPR during Q3 (July-September) — the period of maximal trainee inexperience — would demonstrate worse outcomes compared to other academic quarters. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Nationwide Inpatient Sample (NIS, 2016-2019), identifying adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent in-hospital CPR (ICD-10-PCS: 5A12012). Patients with COVID-19 were excluded. Calendar quarters were defined as Q1 (January-March), Q2 (April-June), Q3 (July-September; reference), and Q4 (October-December). The primary outcome was all-cause in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital complications: cardiogenic shock, ventricular tachycardia (VT), and acute respiratory failure (ARF). Multivariable logistic regression was performed adjusting for age, sex, and Elixhauser comorbidities. Survey-weighted analyses used HCUP-NIS discharge weights to generate national estimates. All analyses were performed in Stata 17. Results: Among 123,253 patients requiring CPR, distribution across quarters was 24.01% (Q3 July-September), 26.65% (Q4 October-December), 25.55% (Q1 January-March), and 23.79% (Q2 April-June). Compared to Q3, Q4 had significantly higher odds of mortality (OR: 1.08; p<0.001). The likelihood of developing cardiogenic shock was lower in Q4 (OR: 0.95; p=0.04), while Q1 was associated with lower odds of acute respiratory failure (OR: 0.93; p<0.001) and ventricular tachycardia (OR: 0.95; p=0.029). No significant mortality difference was observed in Q1 or Q2. Conclusions: Contrary to the classic July Effect hypothesis, mortality was highest in Q4, not Q3. This paradox — higher mortality alongside fewer severe complications in Q4 — suggests that factors beyond initial trainee inexperience, including seasonal illness burden and evolving clinical decision-making across the academic year, may shape CPR outcomes. These findings challenge a binary framing of the July Effect and underscore the need for longitudinal quality-improvement strategies in high-acuity resuscitation care.

items.title: Abstract CR02: Management of Neonatal Cardiac Arrest in the Critical Care Transport Environment: A Case Report
items.abstract: Case Presentation: We report the case of a 2-day-old term infant delivered via cesarean section after an uncomplicated pregnancy due to a non-reassuring fetal heart tracing. Meconium-stained amniotic fluid was observed during the delivery, and the infant subsequently required escalating respiratory support due to worsening metabolic/respiratory acidosis, progressing first from non-invasive positive pressure ventilation to ultimately intubation with inhaled nitric oxide (iNO). Echocardiogram demonstrated bidirectional patent ductus arteriosus, consistent with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Despite maximal support, the patient's respiratory status worsened, and transfer to a facility with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) was initiated. Differential Diagnosis: Likely PPHN secondary to meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS), as evidenced by poor respiratory status in a neonate born with meconium-stained amniotic fluid. Echocardiographic visualization of all pulmonary veins rules out total anomalous pulmonary venous return. Meconium acts as a chemical irritant in the pulmonary system, leading to widespread inflammation and vasoconstriction. Treatment and Management: A specialized neonatal/pediatric team capable of maintaining advanced support (e.g., high-frequency ventilation, iNO, vasoactive medications) during transport was mobilized. Initial assessment by the transport team revealed oxygen saturations between 55-65% on high-frequency ventilation with iNO and FiO2 at 100%. A multidisciplinary decision was made to transport the patient emergently, with ECMO cannulation planned immediately after arrival. During transportation, the patient developed a progressive bradycardia, which required CPR. ROSC was achieved after 23 minutes of resuscitation and remained in place for the remainder of the transport. At the receiving facility, preparations were made to emergently cannulate the patient for ECMO. During setup for cannulation, the patient experienced a second cardiac arrest and was cannulated with ongoing CPR. Outcome and Follow-Up: The patient was decannulated after 8 days and subsequently extubated. Respiratory support was gradually weaned, and the patient was ultimately discharged from the NICU on room air. Teaching Points: This case highlights the unique challenges of managing a neonatal cardiac arrest in the resource-limited transport environment, as well as the instability associated with MAS and severe PPHN. Successful resuscitation of this patient during transport enabled ECMO therapy and required rapid clinical decision-making and coordinated teamwork. Although neonatal cardiac arrest during transport is associated with high mortality, positive outcomes are possible with experienced specialty transport teams and timely escalation to ECMO support.

items.title: Abstract P1017: Quantifying Hemodynamic Responses to Epinephrine Administration During Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: The 2025 AHA Pediatric Advanced Life Support guidelines recommend epinephrine every 3–5 minutes during cardiac arrest (Class IIb), yet supporting evidence remains limited and hemodynamic effects of repeated dosing are not well characterized. Epinephrine raises coronary perfusion pressure via α 1 -mediated vasoconstriction and a resulting rise in diastolic blood pressure, quantifiable by computing the pressure–time integral (PTI) of the arterial diastolic waveform. In preclinical models, PTI attenuates with subsequent doses, likely due to receptor desensitization and arrest progression. Whether this decay occurs in humans, and whether its magnitude predicts resuscitation failure, is unknown. Hypothesis: The hemodynamic response to epinephrine boluses, quantified as the PTI of arterial diastolic pressure, declines with repeated dosing during cardiac arrest, characterized by exponential decay constant k. Methods: A single-center retrospective cohort of pediatric cardiac ICU arrests (2024–2026) receiving ≥2 epinephrine doses with continuous invasive arterial monitoring were identified. For each bolus, the PTI of arterial DBP above a 30-second pre-bolus baseline was computed over the subsequent 2 minutes. An exponential decay model was fit across bolus number (ln [PTI] ~ –k х dose index) to estimate each patient's per-bolus decay. The primary outcome was failed conventional resuscitation (ECPR < 20 minutes or death). Results: Twenty-one arrests met inclusion criteria and contributed 137 epinephrine boluses. All arrests had a measurable positive PTI of the arterial DBP. Median first-dose PTI was 524 mmHg·s (IQR 291-1336) and decreased to median 172 mmHg·s (IQR 105-595) by dose 5. In 14 out of 21 arrests (67%), last dose PTI was lower than first dose. Across all arrests with at least two analyzable boluses (n=20), the per-patient decay constant did not differ significantly from zero (Wilcoxon, p=0.17). Thirteen arrests (65%) had a positive exponential decay (k > 0; median k 0.47 per dose, IQR 0.10–0.54) and seven arrests (35%) had k < 0 (median k –0.21 per dose, IQR –0.37 to –0.12), indicating no consistent dose-related attenuation. In exploratory comparisons, arrests with ROSC (n=6) had higher first-dose PTI than those with ECPR/death (n=15) (median 1444 vs 495 mmHg·s), though not significant (Mann-Whitney, p=0.095). Conclusions: In this pilot cohort of pediatric in-hospital arrests, PTI computation of invasive arterial monitoring was feasible and revealed substantial interindividual variability in hemodynamic responsiveness to epinephrine across boluses. Most patients showed attenuation of response with successive doses, but effect magnitude and decay kinetics varied widely. These findings support validation of PTI-based decay metrics in larger cohorts to assess whether kinetics can inform individual resuscitation strategy or timing of escalation to ECPR.

items.title: Abstract P1026: Stroke Subtype Differences in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Outcomes
items.abstract: Background: Stroke-related out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is a heterogeneous condition with potentially distinct clinical characteristics and outcomes according to cerebrovascular subtype. However, large-scale subtype-specific analyses remain limited. Objective: To evaluate clinical characteristics and outcomes of stroke-related OHCA stratified by cerebrovascular subtype using a nationwide Japanese registry. Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational study using the All-Japan Utstein Registry linked with EMS runsheet data from 2021-2023. Patients with OHCA who underwent resuscitation attempts or automated external defibrillator use were included. Stroke-related OHCA was identified from physician-confirmed diagnoses recorded by EMS personnel. Cerebrovascular subtypes (subarachnoid hemorrhage [SAH], intracerebral hemorrhage [ICH], ischemic stroke [IS], or other cerebrovascular disease) were analyzed when available. The primary outcome was 1-month survival, and the secondary outcome was favorable neurological outcome (CPC 1-2). Multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed to evaluate associations between cerebrovascular subtype and outcomes after adjustment for key demographic, prehospital, and resuscitation variables. SAH served as the reference category. Results: Among 412,447 OHCA cases, 9,058 stroke-related OHCA patients were identified. Cerebrovascular subtype information was available in 1,715 patients, including 829 SAH (48.3%), 440 ICH (25.7%), 88 IS (5.1%), and 358 other cerebrovascular cases (20.9%). SAH was characterized by younger age, female predominance, and a high frequency of witnessed arrest, with more than half occurring at home. One-month survival occurred in 46/829 (5.5%) SAH, 17/440 (3.9%) ICH, and 9/88 (10.2%) IS patients. Favorable neurological outcome (CPC 1-2) was observed in 7/829 (0.8%) SAH, 1/440 (0.2%) ICH, and 2/88 (2.3%) IS patients. Compared with SAH, IS showed higher adjusted odds of 1-month survival (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 4.19, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.94-9.06; p<0.001). Witnessed arrest was associated with 1-month survival in SAH (OR 11.11, 95% CI 3.86-31.95) and ICH (OR 11.06, 95% CI 2.27-53.86), but not in IS (OR 1.22, 95% CI 0.26-5.84), with a trend toward interaction across subtypes (pinteraction=0.083). Conclusions: Stroke-related OHCA demonstrates heterogeneity according to cerebrovascular subtype. SAH was the dominant subtype and frequently occurred in younger women with witnessed arrest at home, yet outcomes remained poor. These findings suggest that improving recognition and increasing witnessed response alone may be insufficient, and that strengthening dedicated transport and regional care systems for neurogenic OHCA may be necessary to improve outcomes.

items.title: Abstract P1027: Cardiac Arrest Stakeholders’ Views on Measuring Prognostication Quality in Post-Cardiac Arrest Patients: A Concept Mapping Study
items.abstract: Introduction/Background: Because a perceived poor prognosis often leads to withdrawal of life-sustaining treatments, accuracy cannot be used to evaluate the quality of clinicians’ outcome predictions for patients treated after cardiac arrest. Past research has focused on sensitivity and specificity, but other measures may be preferable. Research Question/Hypothesis: What do cardiac arrest stakeholders view as the most important ways to evaluate the quality of clinician prognostication for post-cardiac arrest patients? Goals/Aims: To identify and rank potential metrics of prognostication quality. Methods/Approach: We performed a concept mapping study, mixed-methods stakeholder engagement strategy, to both identify and rank potential metrics of prognostication quality. We purposively recruited cardiac arrest stakeholders from unique perspectives: healthcare professionals (physicians, nurses, social workers), family members of survivors, family of non-survivors, survivors, and experts in religion and ethics. We conducted three pilot focus groups to refine presentation material and prompt for comprehension and clarity across stakeholder groups. Following piloting, we performed 22 stakeholder sessions that included introductory presentation and collected individually enumerated potential measures of prognostication quality. We removed irrelevant concepts, consolidated duplicative responses, and clarified concepts. We gave this synthesized list of measures back to the same stakeholders to sort concepts based on similarity and rank them by importance. We then generated graphic representations of the results. We will present the graphic results to stakeholders, integrate feedback, and refine results as needed. Results/Data: We included 70 cardiac arrest stakeholders (18 physicians, 3 nurses, 4 social workers, 15 cardiac arrest survivors, 16 family members of survivors, 7 family members of non-survivors, 9 ethics experts, and 7 spirituality/religion experts). Participants’ median age was 48 years (IQR 40-61), 42 (61%) were female, 56 (81%) were white, and 64 (88%) were non-Hispanic. Stakeholders enumerated 443 statements (measures), which we reduced to 125 distinct concepts (Table 1). Common potential measures could be categorized into reproducibility, transparency, bias, timing, evidence and tests, care team processes and experience, reassessment of prediction, fairness and uncertainty, and ways to review prediction quality (i.e., artificial intelligence, guidelines, experts). Conclusions: Stakeholders identified numerous potential measures of prognostication quality. Many are novel and rarely used in prognostication. Some factors focus on intangible components of prognostication, whereas others, identified as highly important, could be used as key outcome measures to assess clinical practice and test prognostication interventions.

items.title: Abstract P1061: Community-Based Interventions for Bystander Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in Thailand: A Multi-Site Retrospective Cohort Study
items.abstract: Introduction: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) carries a global survival rate of ~10%, with poorer outcomes across Southeast Asia. Bystander CPR (bCPR) is a critical survival determinant, yet Thailand reports bCPR rates as low as 16%. Coordinated community-based bCPR interventions have been implemented across Bangkok and Chiang Mai, but their cumulative impact has not been formally evaluated. Hypothesis: Cumulative interventions targeting bystander training and EMS-delivered bystander support will increase bCPR receipt (primary) and improve survival to discharge (secondary). Aims: To assess the association between successive intervention periods, bCPR receipt, and survival to discharge across two Thai cities with distinct EMS systems. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Pan-Asian Resuscitation Outcomes Study (PAROS) registry. Adults with non-traumatic, non-EMS-witnessed OHCA were included (Bangkok 2018 - 2025, n = 1,282; Chiang Mai 2017 - 2025, n = 504). Bangkok intervention periods: 1) Siriraj EMS foundation started, 2) community first responder (CFR) training, 3) CFR mobile app, and 4) telephone and video dispatcher-assisted CPR (Tele-CPR). Chiang Mai intervention periods: 1) baseline, 2) CPR course pilot, 3) Kru train-the-trainer initiative, and 4) AED training. Primary outcome was bCPR receipt (standard logistic regression); secondary was survival to discharge (Firth’s penalized regression). Results: In Bangkok, the mean age was 67 years, 59% were male, 89% private locations, and 53% overall bCPR. Successive periods were significantly associated with increased odds of bCPR (aOR 3.22 [2.22 - 4.72]), rising from 42% at baseline to 73% in the Tele-CPR period. In Chiang Mai, the mean age was 62 years, 63% were male, 71% private locations, and 25% overall bCPR. No significant intervention effect was detected (range 21 - 27%; aOR 1.39 [0.86 - 2.27]). Survival to discharge was rare (Bangkok 2.9%, Chiang Mai 5.9%) with no significant intervention effect at either site, constrained by very low events-per-variable ratios (2.4 - 2.5). Conclusions: Cumulative community-based interventions were associated with meaningful improvements in bCPR in Bangkok. The absence of a detectable effect at Chiang Mai suggests that local implementation context substantially moderates program impact and warrants further investigation. These findings may inform scale-up strategies for bystander programs across Southeast Asia.

items.title: Abstract P1068: Atrial Dysrhythmias Increase Before and Can Initiate Torsade de Pointes
items.abstract: Introduction: Torsades de Pointes (TdP) is commonly preceded by premature ventricular contractions (PVC) and recent data suggests atrial dysrhythmias can initiate this sequence. This study has two goals: to confirm the common involvement of atrial dysrhythmias in initiating TdP, and to assess for an increase in atrial ectopic rhythms with QT prolongation and prior to a TdP event similar to that observed with PVCs. Methods: We previously performed a case control study of TdP including 75 patients with TdP and 150 QTc, heartrate, and age and sex matched controls. We have reviewed the ECGs and telemetry tracings preceding TdP for atrial dysrhythmias in this study. We checked for involvement of an atrial dysrhythmia in the initiation of TdP on telemetry tracings. For each patient, we also checked for an additional ECG with QTc<90% of the original index ECG, and we evaluated for the presence of PVCs or atrial dysrhythmias. The assessment for dysrhythmias was performed by one unblinded and one blinded reviewer with adjudication by a senior electrophysiologist. Proportions were compared with chi- square or Fisher's exact test as appropriate and reviewer reliability was assessed with Cohen’s kappa. Results: ECG reviewers demonstrated reliability of 0.56 to 0.91 in identifying the presence and type of atrial dyshrythmia on ECG or telemetry. Atrial dysrhythmias including bradycardia with or without heart block, atrial fibrillation, or ectopy were involved in TdP initiation in 18/49 (36.7%, 95% CI 24-52%) of cases. Premature atrial (PAC) or junctional (PJC) contractions were present in 4/75 (5.3%) and 6/150 (4.0%) of ECGs with QTc<90% of index case and control ECGs, 7/75 (9.3%) and 5/150 (3.3%) of index case and control ECGs (p=0.11 comparing index ECGs), and 10/55 (18.2%) of pre-TdP telemetry strips. Using chi-square to compare the proportion of beats that are PAC/PJC across QTc<90% case ECGs, index case ECGs, and pre-TdP telemetry, p=0.05. Conclusions: Our data support the common involvement of atrial dysrhythmias in the initiation of TdP. We observed a progressive increase in supraventricular ectopy with increasing QTc and prior to TdP similar to ventricular ectopy. Increased supraventricular ectopy prior to TdP may have a similar mechanism as PVCs and may also be useful to predict an imminent TdP event.

items.title: Abstract P1075: Reperfusion Time and Non-Fatal Morbidity in Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
items.abstract: Background: Earlier reperfusion in patients receiving extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for refractory ventricular fibrillation/ventricular tachycardia out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (rVT/VF OHCA) is associated with improved neurologically favorable survival. By giving immediate circulatory and respiratory support, it allows time to stabilize the patient and investigate and treat a potential reversible cause of cardiac arrest. Despite the demonstrated association between shorter reperfusion time and improved neurologically favorable in patients with refractory OHCA requiring ECPR, there is limited data to evaluate the association between ECPR reperfusion time and post-arrest morbidity. Research Questions: Is there an association between reperfusion time and outcomes of post-arrest morbidity including biomarkers, clinical outcomes, and resource utilization in patients with rVT/VF OHCA requiring ECPR ? Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with rVT/VF OHCA treated with ECPR between 2015-2023. We evaluated the association between reperfusion time and outcomes of non-fatal post-arrest morbidity, including biomarkers, clinical outcomes, and resource utilization. Results of adjusted regression analyses were reported as beta coefficients, odds ratios (ORs), and incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI). Analyses were adjusted for age and occurrence of bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Results: The study cohort included 332 patients with a median age of the cohort was 60.7 (50.9, 67.1) years and a majority of male patients (82.5%). Median reperfusion time was 63.0 (interquartile range: 54.0, 74.0) minutes. In adjusted analyses, every additional minute of reperfusion time was associated with greater peak lactate (Beta=1.04, 95% CI: 1.01-1.07); greater odds of chest trauma on admission chest CT (OR 1.02, 95% CI: 1.01-1.03); and prolonged intensive care unit admission stays (IRR: 1.01, 95% CI 1.006-1.02). No clinical outcome was associated with reperfusion time in the adjusted analyses. Conclusion: Longer reperfusion time, from 911 call to V-A ECMO, in patients with refractory VT/VF OHCA treated with ECPR was associated with greater metabolic derangement, CPR-related thoracic trauma and longer ICU length of stay. These preliminary findings support system-level efforts to shorten time to VA-ECMO reperfusion.

items.title: Abstract P1024: Differences in Lay Bystander Automatic External Defibrillation Application on Anatomically Male Compared to Female Manikins
items.abstract: Introduction: Bystander automatic external defibrillation (AED) use in cardiac arrest is associated with 66.5% survival at discharge; however, females are less likely than males to receive AED application from bystanders. Research Question: Is there a difference in accuracy of bystander AED application (i.e., clothing removal and placement) on male compared to female manikins? Aim: To assess full clothing removal and anatomic AED placement on male vs female manikins (primary outcomes) and male vs female participants (secondary outcomes). Methods: We conducted a randomized controlled simulation study assessing clothing removal and AED placement on male vs female manikins, hypothesizing that accurate clothing removal and AED placement would be higher on male manikins. The study population was adults (>18 yo) without recent CPR training(> 2yrs). Two clinicians (FB and FT) evaluated full clothing removal and correct anatomic AED placement. We surveyed participants on perceived self-efficacy (Likert Scale: 1 not confident at all to 4 very confident). We assessed differences using a Pearson’s chi-squared test. Results: From 4/2025 to 4/2026, we randomized 85 participants (65% female) to AED placement on either a female (54%) or male manikin. Participants were White (n=51%) with most common age range over 65 (25%). Clothing was removed more often in males (73%) compared to female manikins (25%) (p < 0.01) (Figure 1). Among women participants, clothing was removed more often on male vs female manikins (73% vs 24%, p< 0.01). Among men participants, clothing was removed more often on male vs female manikins (73% vs 27% p=0.01). There was no significant difference in correct anatomic AED placement on male vs female manikins (24% vs 18%, p=ns). Similarly, there was no difference in correct anatomical AED placement regardless of participant gender. Men were more likely to report confidence in placing an AED on males vs female manikins (56% vs 33%, p=0.02). Conclusion: In a simulated cardiac arrest scenario, clothing removal occurred more often on male compared to female manikins, regardless of participant gender. While there was no significant difference in AED placement on male or female manikins, the initial findings around clothing removal suggests that bystander training should consider addressing hesitancy and de-sexualization of women’s bodies in education and training.

items.title: Abstract P1029: Prognostic Value of an Artificial Intelligence-Derived Gray-to-White Matter Ratio on Early versus Follow-Up Brain Computed Tomography After Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: The gray-to-white matter ratio (GWR) on brain computed tomography (CT) quantifies hypoxic-ischemic cerebral edema and is used for neuroprognostication after cardiac arrest. GWR is usually measured on early CT after the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), although prior data suggest that its prognostic performance increases on later imaging. Whether this gain is reproduced with automated, operator-independent quantification rather than operator-dependent manual measurement, and across more than one follow-up window, has not been established. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed adult comatose cardiac arrest survivors who underwent targeted temperature management at two university hospitals between 2019 and 2025, with non-identical enrollment periods at the two sites. Regional Hounsfield units were measured automatically with Heuron StroCare Suite, a commercial AI software. Four predefined GWR models (basal ganglia with or without insula; bilateral mean or worse side) were computed, each on a best-anatomy slice selected by a multimodal large language model (Gemini 3.1 Pro) using a standardized prompt and on the average of eligible slices. Early CT was obtained 0-6 h after ROSC in all patients, and follow-up CT at 24-48 h in one hospital and at 72-96 h in the other. The primary outcome was the 6-month neurological outcome (CPC 1-2 vs 3-5). Results: Among 381 patients, 263 (69%) had poor neurological outcome. Single-time-point discrimination was higher on later CT: for the bilateral basal-ganglia GWR (best-anatomy slice), the AUC was 0.68 (95% CI, 0.63-0.74) on early CT (n = 381), 0.81 (0.74-0.87) at 24-48 h (n = 165), and 0.87 (0.80-0.93) at 72-96 h (n = 115). In within-patient paired comparisons of this model, follow-up CT was significantly more discriminative than early CT: the AUC increased from 0.63 (0.53-0.71) to 0.81 (0.74-0.87) on best-anatomy slices and from 0.62 (0.52-0.70) to 0.77 (0.70-0.85) on average slices between early and 24-48 h CT, and from 0.68 (0.59-0.78) to 0.87 (0.81-0.94) on best-anatomy slices and from 0.70 (0.60-0.79) to 0.87 (0.80-0.93) on average slices between early and 72-96 h CT (all P < 0.001). Findings were consistent across the other models. Conclusions: An artificial intelligence-derived GWR measured on follow-up CT was associated with substantially better discrimination of 6-month neurological outcome than GWR on early CT, as shown within individual patients. Because time point and hospital were confounded across sites, the time effect is most reliably supported by these within-patient analyses; these retrospective findings warrant prospective validation.

items.title: Abstract P1063: Continuous Chest Compressions versus Thirty-to-Two Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: The optimal ventilation strategy (asynchronous breaths delivered during continuous chest compressions [CCC] vs. 30:2 compressions-to-ventilation ratio [30:2]) during emergency medical services (EMS) resuscitation of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients remains uncertain. Hypothesis: Changing ventilation strategy from CCC to 30:2 may be associated with improved patient outcomes, through optimized oxygenation and ventilation, after adult, non-traumatic OHCA. Goals: To compare outcomes between CCC and 30:2 after an EMS agency changed strategy from CCC in 2018-2019 to 30:2 in 2022-2023 throughout the resuscitation effort regardless of airway. Methods: We conducted a registry-based retrospective cohort study of adult, non-traumatic, EMS-resuscitated OHCA at a single EMS agency. EMS protocols used guideline recommended CCC in 2018-2021 and transitioned to 30:2 in mid-2021. Both strategies were used during the entire resuscitation, regardless of airway status. We excluded cases with preexisting do-not-attempt-resuscitation orders, <5 minutes of resuscitation, unavailable monitor files, nonadherence to ventilation strategy, and missing variables. The primary outcome was survival to discharge; the secondary outcomes were return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), survival to admission, and survival to discharge with a favorable neurologic outcome (cerebral performance category score ≤2). Propensity score matching was performed at 5 minutes using age, sex, witnessed status, arrest location, bystander interventions, EMS response interval, initial rhythm, and interventions received at 5 minutes including advanced airway, number of epinephrine doses, and number of defibrillator shocks. Results: Among 1150 cases screened, 539 met inclusion criteria: 326 received CCC and 213 received 30:2. Propensity score matching yielded 207 pairs with standardized differences <0.10 for all covariates. In the matched cohort, survival to discharge was 7.7% with CCC versus 6.8% with 30:2 (odds ratio [OR], 0.86; 95% CI, 0.40-1.85; p=0.70). Rates of any ROSC (39.6% vs 43.5%; p=0.41), ROSC at emergency department arrival (24.6% vs 25.6%; p=0.82), survival to admission (26.1% vs 27.5%; p=0.74), and favorable neurologic outcome (7.2% vs. 6.3%, p=0.68) were similar. Conclusions: In this observational study, changing from a CCC to 30:2 ventilation strategy for resuscitation was not associated with significant differences in patient outcomes after adult non-traumatic OHCA.

items.title: Abstract P1072: Survival After Prehospital Return of Spontaneous Circulation Within an Expert Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation System
items.abstract: Introduction: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a leading cause of death worldwide, with low survival and poor neurological outcomes despite advances in resuscitation care. Guidelines advocate for centralization of post-resuscitation care in specialized cardiac arrest centers with 24/7 access to advanced resources and expertise for all patients with OHCA. Treatment in such centers appears to improve survival and outcome across the broader OHCA population. The Minnesota Mobile Resuscitation Consortium (MMRC) is a metropolitan-wide hub-and-spoke extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) program that directs selected patients with OHCA to three expert Cannulation Hospitals for potential extracorporeal membrane oxygenation. Research Question: Whether patients who achieve prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) benefit from care within such a system, despite not requiring cannulation, remains unknown. Aim: To describe outcomes of patients with prehospital ROSC treated within an expert cardiac arrest and ECPR program, and to compare these outcomes with those of patients treated at hospitals without similar expertise. Methods: We conducted a retrospective descriptive study of patients with VF/VT OHCA meeting entry criteria for the MMRC protocol but achieving prehospital ROSC and transported to three expert ECMO centers between September 2020 and December 2025. A case control cohort of patients transported to other hospitals in the same metropolitan area were identified from the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES). The primary outcomes were survival to hospital discharge and functionally favorable survival. Results: Ninety-four patients met inclusion criteria in the MMRC cohort and 365 in the case control cohort. Survival to hospital discharge was 79/94 (84%) and 245/365 (67%) in the MMRC and case control cohorts, respectively, p<0.001. Functionally favorable survival to hospital discharge was similar between the MMRC and case control cohorts with 67/94 (71%) and 228/365 (62%), respectively, p=0.11. Conclusion: Among patients with VF/VT OHCA who achieved prehospital ROSC, treatment within the MMRC ECPR system, even in the absence of subsequent ECMO use, was associated with higher survival to discharge with no change in functionally favorable survival compared to the cohort outside the ECPR program.

items.title: Abstract P1035: Post Cardiac Arrest Clinical Care Guideline: Standardizing Care and Optimizing Outcomes
items.abstract: Background: Survival after pediatric cardiac arrest depends on both timely resuscitation and consistent post-cardiac arrest care. Prior to this initiative, no standardized institutional guideline existed across the critical care units at Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children’s Hospital of Chicago, resulting in variability in hemodynamic management, neurologic monitoring, and care coordination. Global Aim: To develop and implement a standardized multidisciplinary clinical care guideline (CCG) for pediatric post-arrest care across critical care units and evaluate early adoption and clinical outcomes. Methods: This quality improvement initiative included pediatric and neonatal patients, including those with congenital heart disease, admitted after in-hospital or out-of-hospital cardiac arrest between April and October 2026. Patients >18 years old and neonatal delivery room arrests were excluded. A multidisciplinary team conducted a current-state analysis and literature review informed by American Heart Association pediatric post-cardiac arrest recommendations. Process mapping and fishbone analysis identified barriers to standardized care. Interventions included development of a post-arrest CCG and electronic order set focused on hemodynamic optimization, neuroprotection, continuous monitoring, and standardized documentation. The primary outcome measure was CCG utilization within 6 months of implementation, with a target adoption rate of 50%. Secondary measures included mortality and neurologic outcomes using Pediatric Cerebral Performance Category (PCPC) scores. Results: Baseline assessment demonstrated substantial variability in post-arrest management across units. Early implementation established institution-wide access to standardized recommendations and linked order sets. Infrastructure for mortality and neurologic outcome tracking, including longitudinal PCPC monitoring across critical care units, was completed, with results pending. Key lessons included the importance of focused implementation, multidisciplinary engagement, and the operational complexity of standardizing care across diverse ICU settings. Conclusions: Development of a multidisciplinary post-arrest CCG was feasible and enabled standardization of pediatric post-cardiac arrest care across a large tertiary children’s hospital. Ongoing evaluation will assess the impact on guideline utilization, neurologic outcomes, and mortality. This initiative may serve as a framework for other pediatric institutions seeking to reduce variability in post-arrest care.

items.title: Abstract P1044: Real-World Adoption of a Ventilation Feedback Device During OHCA is Feasible in a Mature EMS System
items.abstract: Introduction: Ventilation quality during cardiopulmonary resuscitation remains highly variable despite clear guidelines. Ventilation feedback devices (VFDs) have shown substantial improvements in simulated settings, but real-world implementation data remain limited. Importantly, the effectiveness of medical devices is strongly influenced by human, organisational, and environmental factors. This study aimed to evaluate real-world implementation and utilisation of a VFD during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) management in a French prehospital system. Methods: We conducted a retrospective, population-based observational study of adult OHCAs jointly managed by firefighters and Mobile Intensive Care Unit teams in the Doubs region. Cases from 2022 (pre-implementation) and 2024 (post-implementation) were analysed. The primary outcome was VFD utilisation. Secondary outcomes included ROSC, survival, and neurological status, reported descriptively and exploratorily. Results: Among 756 OHCAs, 190 (2022) and 166 (2024) met the inclusion criteria. Despite a protocol mandating its systematic use, the device was used in 48/166 (28.9%) cases. Baseline characteristics and resuscitation variables were comparable between groups. Exploratory analyses showed ROSC in 25.0% with VFD versus 16.1% without, and survival at day 30 in 10.4% versus 4.2%. Favourable neurological outcome at day 30 was observed in 10.4% versus 3.4%. Given the observational design and limited sample size, these findings should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating. Conclusion: This study highlights a discrepancy between protocol and real-world use of a ventilation feedback device during OHCA. They underscore the need to better understand implementation factors to inform future studies evaluating clinical effectiveness. Future research should incorporate robust implementation strategies and standardised ventilation parameters.

items.title: Abstract P1049: Non-Invasive Abdominal Aortic Occlusion with a Circumferential Pneumatic Band Reduces Blood Loss in Porcine Femoral Hemorrhage
items.abstract: Background: Traumatic hemorrhage due to non-compressible torso or junctional hemorrhage remains difficult to treat, especially in prehospital settings. Recent development of Abdominal Aortic and Junctional Tourniquet devices have provided an option to control abdominal or femoral hemorrhage. They are not widely available in prehospital settings. Thus, there remains an urgent need for a rapid, non-invasive, medic-deployable method to temporarily occlude the abdominal aorta and reduce ongoing hemorrhage in prehospital settings. We have developed a thoracoabdominal CPR system that incorporates a circumferential abdominal pneumatic band. Objective: We tested whether the abdominal component of a thoracoabdominal circumferential CPR device could function as an effective non-invasive abdominal tourniquet to reduce femoral blood loss in a porcine model. Methods: Following a CPR study in an instrumented 35 kg Yorkshire swine, mean arterial pressure was stabilized (60-80 mmHg) with fluid administration. After administration of heparin (5000 units), a 6F femoral catheter (1.8mm Inner Diameter, 14cm length) was used to induce controlled bleeding. Blood loss was measured over 10-second intervals with the abdominal band either deflated (control) or inflated to 4.0 PSI. Trials were performed in pseudo-randomized order (alternating blocks of control and band conditions). Six trials were completed in each condition. This was a single-animal pilot study. Results: Inflation of the abdominal band to 4.0 PSI resulted in near-complete cessation of blood loss (Figure 1) (M+_SD, 0.17 ± 0.17 cc per 10-second bleed). In contrast, control trials without band inflation produced substantial ongoing hemorrhage (6.67 ± 1.37 cc per 10-second bleed; p < 0.01). Conclusions: In this preliminary single-animal study, a circumferential abdominal pneumatic band, when used as a non-invasive tourniquet at 4.0 PSI, was associated with reduced blood loss from a femoral arterial source in a porcine model. These findings support further investigation of this technology as a rapid, medic-applicable intervention for non-compressible torso and junctional hemorrhage. Additional animal studies are indicated and ongoing.

items.title: Abstract P1053: Nurse-Led In-Situ Simulation for In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Response
items.abstract: Background: Early recognition of in-hospital cardiac arrest, prompt initiation of high-quality CPR, timely defibrillation, and effective team communication are critical determinants of survival. Although simulation is used in resuscitation education, less is known about how in-situ simulation affects nurses’ readiness compared with observed team performance in the clinical environment. Research Question/Hypothesis: We hypothesized that a nurse-led in-situ simulation program would increase nurses’ self-reported confidence in responding to in-hospital cardiac arrest, while also revealing opportunities for improvement in team-based resuscitation performance. Aim: To evaluate the first-year impact of a nurse-led in-situ simulation program on nurse confidence and observed CPR performance during simulated in-hospital cardiac arrest. Methods: We conducted a 13-month pretest-posttest study across inpatient units at a large academic hospital. Simulations were implemented on day and night shifts and facilitated by Rapid Response Team nurses using standardized shockable and nonshockable arrest scenarios followed by structured debriefing. Nurses completed confidence surveys immediately before and after participation; only matched surveys were included in analysis. Team performance was assessed during simulation using a structured facilitator tool across 7 domains: recognition/response, communication, CPR quality, defibrillation, epinephrine administration, airway management, and overall performance. Objective CPR quality measures were captured using SimPAD, including compression depth, rate, recoil, and flow fraction. Paired t-tests compared pre/post confidence scores, and Cohen’s d estimated effect size. Descriptive statistics summarized observed performance and CPR quality metrics. Results: A total of 190 matched surveys from 23 inpatient units were analyzed. Confidence increased significantly after simulation (t=-14.38, p<0.001; d=1.04). However, performance across 112 simulation events was inconsistent. Recognition/response criteria were met in 79% of events, communication in 15%, CPR quality in 48%, defibrillation in 54%, epinephrine administration in 59%, airway management in 16%, and overall performance in 38%. SimPAD metrics showed mean flow fraction 63% (SD 10%), full chest recoil 80% (SD 17%), adequate compression depth 27% (SD 27%), and adequate compression rate 65% (SD 22%). Conclusions: Nurse-led in-situ simulation was associated with substantial gains in self-reported confidence, but important deficits remained in communication, airway management, and CPR quality. These findings suggest that confidence may improve more quickly than measurable resuscitation performance and support repeated, targeted in-situ simulation as a strategy to identify and address unit-level gaps in in-hospital cardiac arrest readiness.

items.title: Abstract P1023: Sex Differences in Cardiovascular Interventions Among Survivors of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Sex-based differences in the clinical presentation of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) may influence downstream cardiovascular evaluation and treatment. Evidence on in-hospital cardiovascular interventions among patients who survive OHCA to hospital discharge remains limited. Hypothesis: Among hospital-discharge survivors after OHCA, cardiovascular diagnoses and in-hospital interventions differ between females and males. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the British Columbia Cardiac Arrest Registry linked to provincial administrative and clinical databases. Adults with EMS-treated, nontraumatic OHCA from 2011 to 2017 who survived to hospital discharge were included. Cardiovascular diagnoses and in-hospital interventions were compared by sex using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests. Results: Among 9,982 EMS-treated OHCA cases, 1,325 patients survived to hospital discharge. After excluding 47 patients with missing covariate data, the final analytic cohort included survivors: 284 females (22.2%) and 994 males (77.8%). Females were less likely than males to have documented coronary artery disease (29.6% vs 56.6%; P<0.001) or ST-elevation myocardial infarction (18.3% vs 34.0%; P<0.001). Females were also less likely to undergo diagnostic angiography (52.8% vs 74.0%; P<0.001), percutaneous coronary intervention (26.1% vs 39.6%; P<0.001), or coronary artery bypass graft surgery (1.8% vs 12.3%; P<0.001). Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement was similar between females and males (22.2% vs 25.8%; P=0.22). Conclusions: Among patients discharged alive after OHCA, females underwent fewer coronary diagnostic and revascularization procedures than males. These unadjusted findings may reflect differences in arrest etiology, clinical presentation, or treatment patterns. Further multivariable analyses are needed to determine whether sex is independently associated with post-arrest cardiovascular care.

items.title: Abstract P1041: Effective Radius of Bystander Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Alerts for Registered Healthcare Providers
items.abstract: Background: Rapid bystander CPR is an essential tool for the chain of survival; however, rates of bystander CPR (bCPR) remain low; particularly in private residences, where most OHCA events occur. Citizen first responder networks alert laypeople to public cardiac arrest events to increase rates of bCPR. Healthcare providers can register as “professional responders” (PR) allowing them to receive alerts for private locations. Increasing the alerting radius for PRs may increase engagement and bCPR. Research Question: Our primary goal was to observe the result of increasing PR alerting range in Allegheny County. We evaluated if increasing alerting range correlated with increased engagement and bCPR in private settings. Methods: Allegheny County uses PulsePoint to alert citizen first responders. We conducted a retrospective analysis of responder data collected from the PulsePoint database. Our primary outcome was increased PR responsiveness to alerts, as measured by the number of PR activations, responder engagement, and CPR initiation prior to arrival of emergency medical services. In our system, users receive alerts if they are located within a 0.25-mile radius of the OHCA event. Using PRs as a subset of users, we evaluated the impact of increasing alerting range of 0.5 miles. The increased alert range was active for 136 days, from late winter to mid-summer of 2025. We compared responder metrics from this period with the corresponding date range the year prior. Results: We observed an increase in the total number of PR activations, responder engagement, and incidents of performed CPR prior to EMS arrival. During the period with non-modified range, we recorded 37 alerts, including 12 private alerts. Only one PR responded to a private alert but did not arrive. During the period with extended range, we recorded 80 total alerts, including 46 private alerts. Nine PRs responded to the incident, and 3 performed CPR on arrival. We observed an increase in number of PR responses to incidents, and incidents of bCPR. Conclusion: Expansion of the PR alert radius increased PR engagement and bCPR delivery prior to EMS arrival in Allegheny County, though findings are limited by sample size and temporal confounding. Increasing the alerting radius of citizen first responders can enhance community engagement in incidents of OHCA.

items.title: Abstract P1059: Nurse-Led Multimodal Simulation to Improve Defibrillation Timeliness and Identify Latent Safety Threats
items.abstract: Background: Delayed defibrillation during ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VF/pVT) worsens survival outcomes. Internal review at a large academic Level I trauma center identified inconsistent compliance with the recommended ≤2-minute defibrillation benchmark during in-hospital cardiac arrest events. A nurse-led multimodal simulation program was implemented to improve defibrillation timeliness and identify latent safety threats (LSTs). Objective: To evaluate the impact of a simulation-based emergency response program on VF/pVT defibrillation performance and identification of latent safety threats. Methods: A multidisciplinary Resuscitation Committee implemented a nurse-led quality improvement initiative using in-situ mock codes, simulation center-based emergency training, and specialty airway simulations. Scenarios emphasized early recognition, activation, communication, and defibrillation within 2 minutes for VF/pVT events. In-situ mock codes also functioned as systems testing to identify LSTs and workflow gaps. Drills identified vulnerabilities including lack of emergency responder badge access, relocated emergency equipment, uncertainty regarding equipment locations, and unsafe defibrillation practices. Findings prompted workflow and safety improvements before emergencies occurred. Simulations included pre-briefing, debriefing, and learner feedback. Event review data refined training. Automated assistive writing technology was used for editorial support during abstract preparation. From July 2022 through December 2025, the program delivered 62 simulation sessions involving 582 participants across inpatient and ambulatory care settings and multiple interdisciplinary clinical teams and emergency response disciplines throughout the organization. Results: Compliance with defibrillation within 2 minutes for VF/pVT events improved from 50% in Q4 2021 to sustained 100% compliance by mid-2023, maintained through 2025. In-situ simulations identified latent safety threats and operational vulnerabilities, prompting workflow improvements and reinforcement of emergency equipment accessibility, role clarity, and safe defibrillation practices during resuscitation events. Among formal simulation participants, 100% agreed training was critical to job success and 98% rated participation worthwhile. Specialty simulation participants reported improved role clarity (81%) and increased confidence speaking up during emergencies (69%). Conclusions: A nurse-led multimodal simulation program was associated with sustained improvement in VF/pVT defibrillation timeliness and identification of latent safety threats. Integrating in-situ simulation with formal and specialty training may improve resuscitation reliability and emergency preparedness.

items.title: Abstract P1022: Age-Related Left-Digit Bias in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Left-digit bias (LDB) is a cognitive bias in which individuals are perceived differently when crossing a numerical threshold despite minimal actual differences (e.g., 59 vs. 60 years). In out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), patient age strongly influences prognostic perception and treatment decisions. A prior study did not find any evidence that age-related LDB affected outcomes for OHCA patients in Japan. However, the impact of age-related LDB on OHCA outcomes according to initial recorded rhythm is unknown. Objective: To evaluate the association between age-related LDB and outcomes after OHCA stratified by initial rhythm. Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational study using a prospectively collected OHCA registry (The Portland (PDX) Epistry). Patients were categorized into “left-digit low” and “left-digit high” groups within each age decade (e.g., 57-59 vs. 61-63 years). Propensity score matching was also performed separately within each decade using demographic and arrest-related variables, including sex, arrest location, witness status, bystander CPR, bystander AED use, EMS response interval, and calendar year. Patients were stratified by the initial recorded rhythm into shockable rhythm (VF/pVT) and, non-shockable rhythm (Asystole/PEA) cohorts. Since PEA and asystole differ substantially in prognosis and clinical decision-making, the non-shockable cohort was further subdivided into PEA and asystole subgroups. The Primary outcome was favorable neurological outcome (CPC score ≤ 2). Results: Among shockable rhythm patients, 845 propensity score-matched patients (664 patients, 332 pairs) well balanced with regards to baseline characteristics were analyzed and there was no significant association observed between being in the higher left digit group and favorable neurological survival (OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.85-1.55, p=0.36). Among non-shockable rhythm patients, 1,816 propensity score-matched patients (908 pairs) were analyzed, well-balanced for baseline characteristics after propensity matching. In this group, left-digit high patients demonstrated non-significant but lower odds of favorable neurological survival (OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.43-1.06, p=0.09). Further subgroup stratification demonstrated that the association between high left digit and lower functional survival outcomes was most apparent among patients with PEA (OR 0.46, 95% CI 0.26-0.81, p=0.001) compared to asystole (OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.85-1.55, p=0.36). Conclusions: Age-related LDB may differentially affect OHCA outcomes according to the initial rhythm subtype, with only significant associations found suggesting LDB for patients initially in PEA.

items.title: Abstract P1025: Quantifying the Impact of Age on Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Risk in Women
items.abstract: Background: While previous studies have reported an increase in heart disease and cardiovascular disease in women with age, studies that specifically examine out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) have been limited. The aim of this study was to assess the impact of age on OHCA risk in women, and compare it to men. Methods: We analyzed non-traumatic OHCA cases reported to the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES) and served by Emergency Medical Services (EMS) in Illinois from 2018-2025. Only cases with presumed cardiac etiology and in the age group of 21 and above were included. Analytic sample consisted of 12,157 women and 19,359 men. Age was divided into deciles (21-30, 31-40, 41-50, 51-60, 61-70, and 71+). We assessed the distribution of cases by age group, and by the life stages/stages of menopause transition in women, and assessed trends. While we did not have menstruation data, based on age, women 21-39 years were categorized as pre-menopause, and 40-50 as perimenopause. Results: By each decile of age, there was an incremental increase in the risk in women with 21-30 years age group contributing only 1.8% of the cases, which jumped to 4.1% in 31-40 years age group, and 8% in the 41-50 age group, and continued to rise to 49.7% in the 71+ age group (slope=8.6%, p=0.014). An increase was also noticed in men, from 2.1% in 21-30 years age group, to 36.4% in 71+ (slope=6.9%, p=0.0003) but the increase among women was more drastic (Figure). From 61-70 year to 71+ age group specifically in women there was a 122.9% increase in proportion of cases while in men the increase was by 40%. Second largest jump in the proportion was observed in women and men from 21-30 to 31-40, where in women the proportion increases by 127% and in men by 148%. When analyzed by life stages, 8.8% of the OHCA in women were in perimenopause age group compared to 5.2% in pre-menopause. Hispanic women start out with a higher proportion of cases in the pre-menopause phase (7.2% vs. 6% in Black, 4.2% in White, and 2.6% in Other, p<0.001), and maintain a higher proportion in perimenopause (10.8% vs. 10.4% Black, 6.8% in White, and 6% in Other, p<0.001). Conclusion: The risk of OHCA depends on age and life stage, but the increase in risk in women is more drastic. It perhaps is not the effect of age alone but tied with the changes in menstrual phases and transition that need to be studied further.

items.title: Abstract P1046: Analysis of Time to Shock from Real-World Out-of-Hospital AED Uses
items.abstract: Background: Early defibrillation with an automated external defibrillator (AED) is critical to survival following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). AED usability has largely been evaluated in simulated settings and evidence from real-world use is limited. This study evaluated the AED user operating time intervals for two Philips AED models used in OHCA responses. Methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted using a convenience dataset of Philips AED event records collected in Europe and the United States between 2007 and 2025. The HeartStart HS1 (Onsite/Home) is designed for use by minimally trained or lay responders, whereas the HeartStart FRx is intended for Basic Life Support (BLS) providers. Cases with at least one complete rhythm analysis were included. Time intervals and user interactions were analyzed across 497 HS1 and 688 FRx cases. Interpretation of timing differences was limited by unmeasured variations in responder behavior, including pad placement before device activation and CPR performed before pad application. Results: Following AED activation, the observed time to pad placement was significantly shorter in FRx cases than in HS1 cases (25.4 s vs. 55.9 s; p < 0.05). In FRx cases, one or more shocks were successfully delivered to 100% (236/236) of the shock-advised patients by pressing the shock button within the allowable time window. In HS1 cases, one or more shocks were successfully delivered to 98.6% (208/211) of the shock-advised patients by pressing the shock button within the allowable time window. Specifically, the mean time interval of all delivered shocks from onset of the “Shock Advised” prompt to shock-button press was also significantly shorter with FRx than with HS1 (4.9 s vs. 6.0 s; p < 0.05). The mean time to first shock was 79.3 s with HS1 and 47.0 s with FRx (p < 0.05). For the initial analysis, Figure 1 shows the AED operating time intervals from power-on to shock delivery. Conclusions: Users responded rapidly to shock advisory prompts with both AED models in real-world OHCA events. Shorter AED operating times among FRx users may reflect that they typically receive more training than HS1 users. The rare absence or delay of shock-button presses may reflect responder actions, scene-safety concerns, or other ongoing events which cannot be determined from device recordings. These findings provide practical context beyond simulation studies and may inform AED training, deployment, and design.

items.title: Abstract P1030: ICECAP Trial: Neurologic Recovery and Four Score
