items.abstract: Objective: To describe early neurologic recovery using the Full Outline of UnResponsive (FOUR) Score (FS) in a prospective randomized trial that compared durations of hypothermic temperature control (HTC) in unresponsive patients resuscitated from out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Materials and Methods: ICECAP was a multicenter randomized adaptive-allocation clinical trial conducted at 71 hospitals in the United States from 2020 to 2025. Adults with OHCA (including both shockable and nonshockable rhythms) were eligible if they were unresponsive to verbal commands, achieved rapid TH with a temperature control device, and had surrogates confirm that 96 hours of treatment without limitations would be consistent with patient’s wishes. Patients were randomized to HTC at 33 °C for 6-48 hours. FS was assessed once daily for five days. FS is a 16-point scale (best score is 16) comprising Eye (0-4), Motor (0-4), Brainstem reflexes (0-4), and Respiration (0-4) subscales. We estimated longitudinal FS trajectories for all patients and stratified by initial rhythm, survival status, and WLST status. We visualized transitions in FS subscores using alluvial plots for Day 1-2 to Day 5-6. Results: Among 1,158 patients in ICECAP, 1119 (97%) had at least one valid FS assessment. A total of 5,747 assessments were included in the longitudinal analysis, with a median of 6 (IQR 4-7) daily assessments per patient. Median age was 61 years (IQR 50-70), and 60% were male. Initial cardiac rhythms were 24% shockable. FS total scores and subscores appear to improve across all patients and by initial rhythm (Panel 1). Overall, 74% died before 90 days, and 54% had withdrawal of life-sustaining therapies (WLST). FS distribution appears to differ by rhythm type, survival status, and whether patients had WLST (Panel 2). Of the 4 subscores during daily observations, the brainstem reflexes subscore had the most transitions (Panel 3). Further analysis will be presented on the effects of HTC durations, rewarming, medications, and site variations in the FS assessment in this study. Conclusion: The distribution of FOUR score among ICECAP trial patients varied across the assessed days, with a trend toward increasing across all patients, especially among survivors. The brainstem reflexes subscore had the most transitions in the early recovery period. FS scoring for neuroprognostication and detection of relevant clinical change needs further exploration.

items.title: Abstract P1038: National Evaluation of Universal Termination-of-Resuscitation Criteria and EMS Disposition Decisions in Adult Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Objective: The American Heart Association recommends a universal termination-of-resuscitation (TOR) rule to guide emergency medical services (EMS) decisions when out-of-hospital cardiac (OHCA) arrest resuscitation is futile. However, the extent to which this rule is applied when all criteria are met is not well described. We sought to determine the national patterns of adult OHCA events meeting basic life support (BLS)/Universal TOR criteria and the association with EMS termination. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of 2023 National Emergency Medical Services Information System data to evaluate TOR cases among adults (>17 years), 9-1-1, ground, non-traumatic, cardiac arrest activations. We classified cases as meeting all BLS/Universal TOR criteria when the arrest was not witnessed by EMS personnel, no return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) before transport, and no shock was delivered before transport. We described eligible OHCA events by age, sex, incident location, urbanicity, and EMS system response, scene, and transport times. We defined termination of resuscitation using the EMS disposition category “Patient Dead at Scene—Resuscitation Attempted (Without Transport).” We then used multivariable logistic regression to examine patient, event, and system characteristics associated with termination at the scene. Results: A total of 193,644 OHCA events were identified with 92,085 (47.6%) meeting all BLS/Universal TOR criteria. Cumulatively, 86.4% met at least one criterion, with ROSC accounting for the largest reduction in cases. Among those meeting all criteria, 42,646 (46.3%) were terminated on scene and 49,439 (53.7%) were not terminated on scene. Patients in both groups were predominantly male with most arrests occurring in home/residence settings, with response, scene, and transport intervals similar across groups (Table 1). In multivariable analysis of cases meeting criteria, incidents in health-care facilities had higher odds of termination (OR 1.48, 95%CI 1.43-1.54; referent: Home/Residence). Urban (referent) areas had higher odds of termination than rural (0.78, 0.74-0.82) and suburban (0.85, 0.81-0.90). South Region (referent) had lower odds of termination than the Midwest (2.22, 2.14-2.30), Northeast (1.78, 1.70-1.82), and West (1.91, 1.83-1.98). Conclusion: Despite nearly half of all OHCA events meeting BLS/Universal TOR criteria, only about a quarter of the population have termination applied on scene. These findings suggest that TOR is underutilized in EMS practice. Further work is needed to understand the factors influencing TOR application and to support consistent, guideline-aligned decision-making across EMS systems.

items.title: Abstract P1039: Age-Specific Differences in Pediatric Traumatic Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Pediatric traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (PT-OHCA) remains relatively understudied, especially regarding age-specific epidemiology and resuscitation outcomes. Emergency medical services (EMS) play an important role in the prehospital treatment of PT-OHCA, thus, EMS data may be helpful to better describe this subset of OHCA patients. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that are clinically-relevant differences in the mechanisms of PT-OHCA, as well as differences in return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), across various age groups. Methods: We utilized a longstanding national-level database of EMS activations in the United States (NEMSIS) to perform a retrospective analysis of PT-OHCA. Inclusion criteria were any OHCA patient <18 years with an EMS-documented arrest etiology of trauma. Cases were stratified based on patient age, and we identified the most common mechanisms of injury using administrative billing codes and calculated rates of ROSC within each age group. ROSC rates were compared across age groups using two-tailed two proportion z-tests; significance was defined as p<0.05. Results: A total of 1,843 PT-OHCAs were identified. Adolescents aged 13-17 y comprised the largest proportion of cases (55.5%), followed by 0-2 y (16.9%), 8-12 y (16.4%), and 3-7 y (11.2%). Transportation-related trauma was the most common mechanism overall (38.0%), followed by firearm injuries (25.1%). Firearm injuries were highly concentrated among adolescents, with 367 of 463 firearm-related cases occurring in the 13-17-year age group. Adolescents aged 13-17 years had the lowest rate of ROSC achievement (12.6%), while younger age groups all exhibited significantly higher ROSC rates; ranging from 20.2% to 23.8% (p<.001) (Table). Conclusion: PT-OHCA demonstrates substantial variation across age groups. Adolescents accounted for the most cases and experienced a disproportionate burden from firearm-related injuries resulting in cardiac arrest. These findings highlight the importance of age-specific injury prevention strategies and may help guide future EMS protocols, public health interventions, and pediatric trauma resuscitation research.

items.title: Abstract P1045: Coronary Perfusion Pressure During Automated Thoracoabdominal Circumferential and Sternal Piston Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in a Porcine Model of Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Circumferential thoracic CPR may be superior to sternal-piston-mechanism based manual and mechanical devices. We have previously reported that circumferential CPR with abdominal counterpulsation - thoracoabdominal CPR (CTA-CPR) - may be even more effective. The LUCAS sternal piston device is the most widely used method of mechanical CPR, yet it has failed to demonstrate clinical benefit over manual CPR. CTA-CPR may have enhanced hemodynamics and a superior safety profile, but its performance versus the LUCAS has not been studied. Coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) — the aortic-to-right-atrial pressure gradient during the relaxation phase — is the hemodynamic parameter most predictive of return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Research Question: We hypothesized that CTA-CPR would generate superior perfusion pressures compared to the LUCAS. Methods: 35 kg Yorkshire swine (n=3) underwent instrumentation with aortic (AO) and right atrial (RA) pressure catheters followed by electrical induction of cardiac arrest. A six-epoch crossover protocol alternated one-minute intervals of CTA-CPR and LUCAS-CPR with 15-second no-CPR interruptions between device switches. The LUCAS piston was adhered to the sternum by hook-and-loop fastener. Endpoints were AO pressure, RA pressure, CPP (AO minus RA), and Delta-CPP (change in mean CPP from the start to the end of each device epoch). Each endpoint was measured at the end of relaxation. Standard statistics included paired t-tests. Results: Compared to LUCAS-CPR, CTA-CPR was associated with superior perfusion pressures (Figure 1, Table 1, p < 0.01). Even without epinephrine, CTA-CPR was associated with CPPs above the previously identified threshold for return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). LUCAS-CPR was not. Switching from the LUCAS-CPR to CTA-CPR was consistently associated with a relatively large increase in CPP (Figure 2). The opposite happened when switching back to the LUCAS. Conclusions: In this porcine crossover model, CTA-CPR was associated with superior AO, CPP, and Delta-CPP compared to the LUCAS. The approximately 3-fold CPP advantage and uniformly positive Delta-CPP across all epochs indicate that CTA-CPR may be clinically superior to LUCAS. These results warrant replication in a larger randomized cohort with ROSC as the primary endpoint.

items.title: Abstract P1048: Selective Cerebral Perfusion Augmentation During Cardiac Arrest Using Dynamic Aortic Occlusion: A Pilot Study
items.abstract: Introduction: Survival with intact neurologic function following prolonged pediatric cardiac arrest remains poor. Even with high-quality CPR, CBF remains substantially below baseline, and autoregulatory dysfunction risks hyperperfusion injury. Therefore, maintenance of CBF close to pre-injury ranges may limit further brain injury. Endovascular aortic occlusion (AO) augments coronary and cerebral perfusion, but complete occlusion risks distal ischemia and cerebral hyperperfusion. Titrating CPR to neurometabolic optical monitoring (NOM) measurements of cerebral oxygenation and perfusion is associated with improved outcomes. We evaluated whether NOM-directed dynamic AO (dAO) could maximize cerebral oxyhemoglobin concentrations (HbO 2 ) within a previously validated target range during CPR and further optimize systemic and cerebral perfusion. Hypothesis: dAO increases time spent within the cerebral HbO2 target and improves systemic and cerebral perfusion parameters compared with standard (AHA) CPR. Methods: Juvenile swine (8-12 kg, n=4) underwent 7 minutes of asphyxia, electrically-induced VF cardiac arrest, and then AHA CPR. 10 minutes into CPR, a previously placed Zone 1 aortic balloon was inflated and dynamically titrated to maintain HbO 2 within an individualized range. Defibrillation attempts began at 15 minutes into CPR. Outcomes were compared with a historical cohort who received AHA CPR alone (n=11). Time spent within the HbO 2 goal was calculated before and during dAO. Changes in hemodynamic and NOM metrics were evaluated using a general linear model ANOVA. Massive hemo-pneumothorax was a complication seen in both groups. These subjects were excluded from analysis, as their physiology deviated significantly from the target conditions. Results: During the first 5 minutes of dAO, the intervention group spent significantly more minutes within the target HbO 2 range than controls (4.75 vs. 3.44 p<0.05). dAO significantly increased systolic blood pressure (164.1 ± 10.6 vs 87.8 ± 6.4, p <0.05), HbO2 (46.4 ± 5.0 vs 19.2 ± 3.0, p<0.05), and StO2 % (59.1 ± 6.8 vs. 30.1 ± 4.1, p <0.05). Mean arterial pressure (61.7 ± 7.0 vs 53.2 ± 4.2, p = 0.988) and coronary perfusion pressure (18.3 ± 6.7 vs. 15.4 ± 4.1, p=1.0) also trended higher with dAO. Within group, dAO was associated with trends towards increased BP, coronary perfusion pressure, HbO2, StO2, and CBF. Markers of cerebral blood volume and CBF were not significantly increased from baseline during dAO. Conclusions: In this pilot study, NOM-directed dAO improved intra-arrest maintenance of cerebral oxygen delivery as compared to AHA CPR. Trends towards improved hemodynamics and cerebral perfusion were seen, though the small cohort was likely underpowered to reach significance. These findings support the feasibility of physiology-guided fractional AO as a neuroprotective resuscitation strategy and warrant further evaluation.

items.title: Abstract P1019: Application of Human-Derived Ventricular Fibrillation Vitality Score Measures in a Swine Cardiac Arrest Model
items.abstract: Background: Quantitative ventricular fibrillation (VF) ECG measures are associated with myocardial metabolic status and can predict resuscitation outcomes. Prior study validated the VitalityScore algorithm to predict return of organized rhythm (P-ROR) and survival (P-SUR) in human out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (CA) resuscitations based on ECGs with or without CPR. We hypothesized that the VitalityScore measures P-ROR and P-SUR can be continuously applied to a swine cardiac arrest ECG dataset to quantify the impact of CPR and epinephrine on estimated prognosis. Methods: VF VitalityScore measures were retrospectively calculated in a defibrillator ECG dataset from an 8-min untreated VF swine CA model (N=8) that subsequently received 42 min of mechanical CPR concurrent with six doses of epinephrine (0.02mg/kg) at 4-min intervals. CPR time intervals were aligned within and across subjects. Measures were calculated every second throughout each subject, and were calibrated across adjacent no-CPR and CPR intervals. To evaluate VF measure progression, we compared the starting versus subsequent median P-ROR and P-SUR values at 30-s intervals within the no-CPR and CPR intervals (signed-rank test, α=0.01). To assess potential measure differences in swine versus humans, we also compared P-ROR and P-SUR medians at VF onset in swine versus measures from a previously-published human CA cohort (rank-sum test, α=0.01). Results: Median P-ROR and P-SUR ranged from 0.45-0.75 and 0.20-0.55. During the 8-minute untreated VF interval, the median P-ROR and P-SUR declined over the initial 2 mins (with p<0.01 for decrease by 30s) followed by a 6-min plateau (Figure 1, Table 1). During the subsequent CPR and epinephrine interval, P-ROR and P-SUR initially increased for 8 mins (with p<0.01 for increase by 4 mins) before declining for the remaining 36 mins. When comparing the initial swine VF measures against those from a prior human cohort, median (interquartile range [IQR]) P-ROR was higher in N=8 swine versus in N=576 humans (0.75 [73-76] versus 0.62 [41-81] respectively, p<0.01). Similarly, initial median [IQR] P-SUR was higher in swine versus in humans (0.52 [43-65] versus 0.34 [0.16-0.68], respectively), although the difference was not significant (p=0.12). Conclusions: Our proof-of-concept study demonstrated that the deterioration of human-derived VF VitalityScore measures during untreated VF can be mitigated by CPR coupled with epinephrine in a swine CA model. The results also suggest that human-derived measures may have higher baseline values when applied in swine. Future studies will focus on the development and validation of VF measures in swine to enable mechanistic investigation and to facilitate prognostic algorithm optimization through translation from human to swine CA.

items.title: Abstract P1020: Sex Differences in Cardiac Arrest Survivorship Outcomes Among Long Term Survivors and Caregivers
items.abstract: Introduction: Female cardiac arrest (CA) survivors experience poorer survivorship outcomes by hospital discharge. Caregivers of CA survivors, who are more often female, also experience substantial burden and distress. However, sex differences in survivorship outcomes among long-term CA survivors and caregivers remain understudied. We explored whether prolonged emotional distress, quality of life (QoL), and fatigue vary by sex. Hypothesis: Long-term female CA survivors and caregivers experience more emotional distress, worse QoL, and worse fatigue compared to male CA survivors and caregivers. Methods: This is a secondary analysis of an online survey completed by members of the Sudden Cardiac Arrest Foundation between October and November 2019. We measured emotional distress (anxiety and depression - Patient Health Questionnaire-4; posttraumatic stress - PTSD Checklist-5) psychological, physical, and social QoL (WHOQOL-BREF), and fatigue (WHOQOL item 10). We conducted independent t-tests to examine mean differences in outcomes by sex, followed by separate multivariable regressions for each survivorship outcome with female sex as the main predictor, adjusted for CA location, income, time since arrest, and the Charlson Comorbidity Index. Results: Participants included 169 survivors (mean age: 50.8 years, 49.7% female, mean time since arrest: 5 years) and 52 caregivers (mean age: 48.7 years, 86.5% female, mean time since arrest: 3.5 years). Female survivors reported greater anxiety (M = 2.6 vs 1.1), depression (M = 1.8 vs 1.1), and PTSD symptoms (M = 26.5 vs 17.6) and worse physical QoL (M = 14.3 vs 15.9), psychological QoL (M = 13.5 vs 15.3), and fatigue (M = 3.1 vs 3.7), when compared to males (all p < 0.05). When controlling for covariates, female sex was associated with greater anxiety and depression (β = .21, p < 0.01), PTSD (β = .17, p < 0.05), and worse physical QoL (β = -.25, p < 0.01), psychological QoL (β = -.21, p < 0.01), and fatigue (β = -23, p < 0.01). Among caregivers, females reported greater depression (M = 1.2 vs 0.3) and PTSD symptoms (M = 25.1 vs 11.7) (both p < 0.01). Overall regression models for caregiver outcomes were not significant. Conclusions: Findings indicate that poorer survivorship outcomes endure among female CA survivors and caregivers years after CA. Future research should explore the underlying mechanisms of these sex differences. Tailored interventions to address sex-specific survivorship concerns may be warranted.

items.title: Abstract P1032: Effectiveness and Safety of Enteral Nutrition During Therapeutic Hypothermia for Patient Who Received Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
items.abstract: Background: Temperature control is a pivotal component of post-cardiac arrest care for patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Therapeutic hypothermia (TH), a subset of temperature control, may provide benefits in selected patients. Meanwhile, enteral nutrition (EN) for the patients with critical condition is advoacated. However, the effectiveness of EN during TH, remain uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate the association between EN during TH and clinical outcomes in patients with OHCA. Methods: This study was a secondary analysis of the SAVE-J II study, a multicenter retrospective cohort of patients with OHCA who received veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation and were treated with TH. The duration of TH was defined as the sum of the hypothermia and rewarming periods after ICU admission. Patients were categorized based on the timing of EN initiation during TH. The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included the incidence of infection and gastrointestinal complications, such as vomiting or ischemic colitis. Generalized estimating equations (GEE) and propensity score matching (PSM) were used to adjust for potential confounders. Results: Of the 2,157 enrolled patients, 345 were eligible for analysis (EN during TH, n = 122; EN after TH, n = 223). GEE analysis showed that initiation of EN during TH was not associated with a significant difference in survival to discharge compared with initiation after TH (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.46-1.54, p = 0.57). After PSM, 188 patients were matched (94 in each group), and conditional logistic regression analysis similarly showed no significant difference in survival to discharge between the groups (68.1% vs. 72.3%; OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.45-1.52, p = 0.54). The incidence of infection (54.2% vs. 63.8%; OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.35-1.20, p = 0.17) and gastrointestinal complications (1.1% vs. 2.1%; OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.05-5.51, p = 0.57) did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusions: Although EN during TH was not associated with improved survival to discharge among patients with OHCA, the proportion of infection and gastrointestinal complication did not differ. These findings suggest that EN during TH may be feasible without increasing adverse events. Prospective studies are warranted to determine the optimal nutritional strategy during temperature management.

items.title: Abstract P1060: Ready to Respond: A Community-Based Model for Scaling Cardiac Arrest Preparedness
items.abstract: Introduction: Despite strong evidence supporting early cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and automated external defibrillator (AED) use, bystander response to sudden cardiac arrest (SCA) remains inconsistent. Scalable, community-based education models are needed to improve confidence, preparedness, and response. Research Question: Can a centralized messaging and training framework combined with decentralized, community-delivered implementation expand reach and improve access to CPR and AED education across diverse settings? Goals/Aims The Ready to Respond initiative sought to increase access to hands-only CPR and AED training and to assess implementation reach across community, school/campus, workplace, and public settings. Methods/Approach: Ready to Respond is a national initiative developed by the Sudden Cardiac Arrest Foundation to deliver hands-only CPR and AED education during Sudden Cardiac Arrest Awareness Month (October 2025). Initially launched as a focused Training Week (October 12-18), the program partnered with H.E.A.R.T. Champions, aligned organizations, and advocates to host local events. Rather than relying on a single standardized delivery format, Ready to Respond supported adaptable, community-based implementation using centralized messaging, branding, and educational resources. Events incorporated hands-on practice with mannequins and AED trainers led by CPR instructors. Results: The campaign was implemented across 97 sites in 20 U.S. states and Canada, reaching 8,891 participants. Sites included schools/campuses, workplaces, churches, and public community locations. Host feedback was positive: 86% were very satisfied with their event, 82% reported participants felt much more confident afterward, and 90% indicated the materials provided were very helpful. Additionally, 90% reported plans to host future events. Common strengths included adaptable educational materials, strong branding consistency, flexibility across diverse settings, and engagement across a wide range of age groups from youth to adults. Reported challenges included attendance variability, weather, and event promotion. Conclusion: A centralized messaging strategy combined with flexible local implementation enabled broad dissemination of hands-only CPR and AED education. The Ready to Respond model demonstrates feasibility for scaling community-based SCA preparedness initiatives nationally while fostering strong local host engagement. Key lessons included the importance of adaptable implementation, strong community partnerships, and increased media visibility. Future efforts will expand to a month-long activation during Sudden Cardiac Arrest Awareness Month and strengthen outreach and media engagement to increase reach and participation.

items.title: Abstract P1073: Timing of Endotracheal Intubation and Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Pump-On in Patients with Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Who Received Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
items.abstract: Background: Although outcomes of patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remain poor, extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has been reported to potentially improve outcomes in selected patients with OHCA. However, it remains unclear whether priority should be given to extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) pump-on or endotracheal intubation (ETI) during ECPR implementation for OHCA patients. This study evaluated the association between ECMO pump-on prior to ETI and favorable neurological outcome for patients with OHCA who received ECPR. Methods: This study was a secondary analysis of the Japanese Association for Acute Medicine Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (JAAM-OHCA) registry between June 2014 and December 2022, a multicenter retrospective registry study. Patients with OHCA who remained in cardiac arrest on hospital arrival and underwent ECPR were enrolled. Patients with a time from cardiac arrest to ETI or ECMO pump-on exceeding 60 minutes were excluded. Patients were divided into two groups depending on whether or not they underwent ECMO pump-on prior to ETI (the ECMO-first group and the ETI-first group). The primary outcome was favorable neurological outcome defined as Cerebral Performance Category scores of 1 or 2 at 30 days. Results: Of 95,902 patients registered in the JAAM-OHCA registry, 1,003 patients were enrolled in this study. The median age was 60 (IQR, 49-69) years, 85% were male. The median time from cardiac arrest to ECMO pump-on was 49 (IQR, 43-54) minutes, and the median time from cardiac arrest to ETI was 33 (IQR, 27-40) minutes. There were 73 patients in the ECMO-first group and 930 patients in the ETI-first group. The proportion of favorable neurological outcome at 30 day was 17.8% (13/77) vs. 13.0% (121/930). Multivariable logistic regression analysis adjusted for age, sex, witnessed cardiac arrest, bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and time from collapse to ECMO pomp-on, showed that the ECMO-first group was not associated with favorable neurological outcome at 30 days (Odds ratio: 0.84; 95% confidence interval: 0.37-1.91, p = 0.69). This trend was also found even for the patients with shockable rhythm on admission (OR: 1.06; 95%CI: 0.45-2.49, p = 0.90). Conclusions: ECMO pump-on prior to ETI for patients with OHCA who received ECPR was not associated with favorable neurological outcome at 30 days.

items.title: Abstract P1043: Relationship Between Heart Rate Variability and Airway Life Saving Interventions in Prehospital Critical Care
items.abstract: Background: Previous studies demonstrated that Heart Rate Variability (HRV) measures may predict the need for life-saving interventions (LSI) in critically ill patients in the prehospital setting. Beyond simple prediction, HRV measures may guide and evaluating the effects of LSIs, although the utility and limitations in this role are not well understood. In this retrospective study, HRV measures were calculated before and after airway LSI (AWLSI) to understand the HRV signatures associated with airway management. Research Question: How does a panel of HRV measures acutely change in response to the administration of AWLSI in a prehospital cohort of critically ill patients? Methods: We included patients transported by a single large helicopter air medical service between January 2023 and May 2026 who were over the age of 18, having complete records including a continuously recorded prehospital ECG, and were received at a Level 1 trauma center in a single health system. All included patients received AWLSI (defined as BVM, oral or nasal airways, SGA, ETI, or NIPPV) and we excluded patients not meeting those criteria and those who concurrently received vasopressors. AWLSI timing was established from review of the prehospital electronic health record, which included all interventions received by the patient with timestamps. We performed analyses on 10-minute epochs before and after administration of an LSI. Pre- and post-LSI HRV measurements in the time, frequency, and complexity domains were computed in 30-second windows, averaged for each epoch, and compared with either a t-test or Wilcoxon Rank Sum test. Results: A total of 2,072 patients were included. 57.79% of patients were male; the average age of male patients was 55.36 years (18.04) and the average age for female patients was 61.44 years (17.16). Twenty-six percent of patients were injured, and 22.88% of patients were scene runs. Results of HRV analysis are shown in the table. All HRV Measures differed between the pre- and post-AWLSI periods. The direction of change was different between measures, SDNN and RMSSD decreasing, and HR decreasing. LF/HF ratio demonstrated mixed changes and Sample Entropy slightly increased. The LF/HF ratio in trauma patients had the greatest proportional change; decreasing 40.3% from pre-AWLSI (3.92) to post-AWLSI (2.34). Conclusions: We found an association between specific HRV measures and airway LSIs. Further research is necessary to determine the relationship between HRV measures and other LSI categories. Additionally, while this study did not include vasopressors due to concerns about indirect effects on HRV, further studies should examine the impact of these medications on HRV measures.

items.title: Abstract P1057: From No Pulse to Go Pulse: Resuscitation Relays in Action
items.abstract: Introduction: Maintaining competency in BLS/ACLS protocols in clinical environments is challenging due to time constraints, staffing limitations, and limited opportunities. Traditional refresher training may not adequately promote teamwork, communication, and rapid decision-making during events. To address these challenges, we developed a low-cost, gamified resuscitation relay designed to improve confidence, teamwork, and adherence to evidence-based practices. Research Questions: We sought to determine whether a team-based resuscitation relay could improve participants’ confidence, preparedness, and knowledge related to emergency response. Goals: The aim of this project was to reinforce BLS/ACLS knowledge while improving teamwork, communication, and role clarity during emergency response. A secondary goal was to demonstrate an innovative educational model that could be integrated into busy clinical workflows. Methods: This interactive session utilized a competitive relay-style simulation involving two teams of 4-5 participants. Teams rotated through stations including defibrillation, code cart setup, airway management, rhythm identification, and Code Timeout exercises. Participants earned clues at each station that unlocked the next challenge, requiring successful completion before advancing. Facilitators observed for technical accuracy, teamwork, CPR quality, role clarity, and closed-loop communication. The relay concluded with an unexpected mock code requiring integration of all previously practiced skills, followed by a structured debrief. Pre- and post-session surveys assessed participant confidence, preparedness, and knowledge. Results: Post-session surveys demonstrated significant improvements in participant confidence and knowledge. Confidence scores increased from 3.41 to 4.03 (p = 0.0001), while knowledge scores increased from 3.6 to 4.2 (p = 0.00002). Additionally, 100% of participants reported feeling better prepared to manage an emergency during the first five minutes of a code. Conclusion: The resuscitation relay is an effective, low-cost educational strategy for reinforcing BLS/ACLS competencies, teamwork, and communication among healthcare providers. The interactive format increased engagement and perceived preparedness while simulating the pressures of real clinical emergencies. This model offers a scalable approach for sustaining resuscitation readiness in busy clinical settings.

items.title: Abstract P1067: Stay SAFE: A Code Blue Prevention Mission
items.abstract: Cardiac arrests carry substantial morbidity and mortality, yet many events are preventable through early recognition of clinical deterioration and timely intervention. Sanford Bemidji Medical Center, a 118-bed rural regional hospital serving nearly 200,000 residents, identified a rise in cardiac arrests occurring on non-critical care units. Given the facility’s geographic location with the nearest higher level of care hospital being 2.5 hours away, a targeted cardiac arrest prevention initiative was launched to improve early detection and response to patient deterioration. The project aimed to reduce adult cardiac arrest events on the Medical Surgical Orthopedic (MSO) and Cardiac Care Units (CCU) by 50% without increasing arrests in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU). Success metrics included a lower mortality index (MI), a 50% increase in Rapid Response Team (RRT) activations, and at least an 80% accuracy in Modified Early Warning Score (MEWS) compliance. Interventions included development of educational posters, distribution of resuscitation recognition cards to nurses initiating RRTs, intentional code status discussions especially with changes in patient condition, and implementation of a Rapid RN assessment course to strengthen clinical judgment. The initiative achieved a 42% reduction in combined cardiac arrest events on MSO and CCU, approaching the project goal, and exceeded expectations with an over 50% reduction in ICU arrests (from 9 to 4). Although the overall MI increased slightly, this likely reflects the influence of multiple clinical variables beyond cardiac arrest mortality. MEWS adherence varied by unit: MSO achieved 88% compliance and reduced arrests from 10 to 3 (70% reduction), while CCU achieved 55% compliance and experienced an increase from 2 to 4 arrests. Increased frequency of vital sign monitoring in response to elevated MEWS scores emerged as a key driver of improvement, prompting earlier provider notification and reducing the need for RRT activation. The Rapid RN course enhanced critical thinking skills, particularly among MSO nurses. This initiative demonstrates that significant reductions in cardiac arrest events can be achieved without new technology or added cost. By leveraging existing resources, data driven insights, targeted education, and strong clinical leadership, the project fostered a culture of early recognition and proactive intervention. The outcomes highlight the potential for prevention focused strategies to significantly improve patient safety in rural and resource limited hospital settings.

items.title: Abstract P1069: Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in Patients Without Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: Clinical Characteristics and Gasps in Prevention Strategies
items.abstract: Introduction: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICD) are a cornerstone of cardiac arrest prevention in high-risk patients. However, despite established indications, many individuals who experience out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) do not have an ICD at the time of the event. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that a substantial proportion of OHCA patients without a prior ICD had characteristics that could have identified them as being at increased risk of cardiac arrest before the event. Aims: We aimed to analyze OHCA cases to characterize the clinical and paraclinical profiles of patients without a prior ICD and to assess potential gaps in the identification of individuals at high risk of cardiac arrest. Methods: Using the Paris Cardiac Arrest Center Registry and the French National Heath Database (SNDS), we identified patients who were non-ICD recipients among all cases of OHCA occurring in Paris and its inner suburbs between 2011 and 2020. Demographic characteristics, medical history, and cardiovascular investigations performed within the five years preceding cardiac arrest were retrieved from the SNDS. Results: Among 22,134 OHCA, 21,855 (98,5%) occurred in patients without a prior ICD. Their mean age was 71.5 ± 16.8 years, 13,128 (60.1%) were male, and 3,518 (19.6%) presented with a shockable rhythm. Regarding clinical trajectories before the OHCA, 7,840 (35.9%) patients underwent no substantial cardiovascular evaluation (<3 cardiovascular investigations and no diagnosis); 7,636 (34.9%) underwent limited evaluation but had at least one diagnosis (<3 cardiovascular investigations and ≥1 diagnosis), most commonly hypertension (63.4%); 650 (8.3%) underwent extensive evaluation without a diagnosis (≥3 cardiovascular investigations and no diagnosis), primarily including ECG (96.0%), echocardiography (97.1%), Holter ECG (57.2%), and exercise stress testing (46.6%); and 5,720 (26.1%) underwent extensive evaluation with at least one diagnosis (≥3 cardiovascular investigations and ≥1 diagnosis), most commonly involving ECG (98.3%), echocardiography (97.4%), Holter ECG (54.5%), and coronary angiography (42.3%), with hypertension (74.3%) and ischemic heart disease (46.7%) being the most frequent diagnoses. Conclusion: Most OHCA patients without a prior ICD had already come to medical attention before the event, suggesting that current strategies for identifying individuals at risk of cardiac arrest lack sensitivity.

items.title: Abstract P1058: Self-Efficacy as Readiness to Act Under Pressure After Emergency and Resuscitation Training in Military Police Recruits
items.abstract: Introduction/Background: Emergency and resuscitation education should measure not only knowledge and technical skills, but also perceived self-efficacy as a marker of readiness to act under pressure. Military police recruits may be required to initiate care for cardiac arrest, foreign-body airway obstruction, and traumatic bleeding before emergency medical services arrive. Research Question/Hypothesis: We hypothesized that a structured emergency and resuscitation training program would improve perceived self-efficacy among Brazilian military police recruits. Goals/Aims: To evaluate changes in domain-specific self-efficacy after emergency and resuscitation training in military police recruits. Methods/Approach: We conducted a single-group quasi-experimental pre-post study with military police recruits from Santa Catarina, Brazil. The 16-hour in-person intervention included theoretical instruction, supervised practice, simulation, and immediate feedback on basic life support, cardiopulmonary resuscitation/automated external defibrillator use, foreign-body airway obstruction, and bleeding control. Domain-specific self-efficacy was measured before and immediately after training using structured 5-point Likert-scale instruments. Paired tests were used to compare pre-post scores, and effect size was calculated as Cohen dz. Results/Data: A total of 507 recruits completed pre- and post-training assessments. Self-efficacy increased significantly after training in cardiopulmonary resuscitation/automated external defibrillator use (n=507; 3.8±1.4 to 4.4±0.9; mean difference 0.60, 95% CI 0.56-0.64; p<0.001; dz=1.18), foreign-body airway obstruction (n=503; 2.4±1.3 to 4.4±0.7; mean difference 2.00, 95% CI 1.89-2.11; p<0.001; dz=1.60), and bleeding control (n=506; 3.0±1.4 to 3.3±1.4; mean difference 0.30, 95% CI 0.25-0.35; p<0.001; dz=0.54). The largest gain occurred in foreign-body airway obstruction, while bleeding control improved more modestly. Conclusion(s): A structured emergency and resuscitation training program improved perceived self-efficacy among Brazilian military police recruits. These findings support incorporating psychological readiness as a core educational outcome for public safety first responders, alongside traditional assessments of knowledge and technical skills.

items.title: Abstract P1065: Implementation of a Durable Left Ventricular Assist Device Emergency Management Algorithm
items.abstract: Background: Recent studies disprove the misconception that chest compressions can dislodge a left ventricular assist device (LVAD). The American Heart Association supports the use of chest compressions for patients with LVADs in cardiac arrest, and for in-hospital cardiac arrests, targets cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) within one minute of determining patient non-perfusion. Despite this, clinicians may hesitate to initiate CPR on patients with LVADs. One LVAD implant center (IC) and its shared-care (SC) partner sought to address this hesitancy by requiring a provider order to initiate CPR. This yielded inconsistent emergency management (EM) and delays in CPR. Research Question: Will implementation of an EM algorithm yield time to compressions under one minute and increase confidence in CPR decision-making for clinicians responding to LVAD emergencies? Aims: To implement an evidence-based LVAD EM algorithm and measure time to CPR plus clinician confidence before and after simulation-based training. Methods: After algorithms were created for the IC and its SC partner, staff participated in online and simulation-based, classroom training. Trainees completed pre- and post-surveys about their ability to determine when to perform CPR using a Likert scale (1=not at all confident to 5=extremely confident). Four months after training, three in situ EM simulations were conducted between both organizations. The time to initiate CPR during in situ simulations was measured. Staff who participated in in situ simulations completed post-surveys immediately following and three months after events. Results: Trainees’ (n=74) mean confidence score about their ability to determine when to perform CPR improved from 3 ± 0.91 (n=74) to 4.1 ± 0.71 (n=73) after education. The mean score (n=19) after in situ simulations was 4 ± 0.82. Of the staff who participated in the in situ simulations, 84.2% had completed EM training. Three months after in situ simulations, the mean confidence score (n=3) was 4 ± 1. Time to CPR from non-perfusion determination during simulations was 35 seconds (IC), 31 seconds (IC), and <5 seconds (SC), meeting the target time of under one minute. Conclusion: Sustained improvement in confidence scores and times to CPR within target suggest the LVAD EM algorithm and simulation-based training were effective in reducing delays to CPR in patients with LVADs.

items.title: Abstract P1066: Transoesophageal Echocardiographic Assessment of Mechanical Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Positioning and Outcomes in Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: High-quality chest compressions are the cornerstone of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), yet whether mechanical chest compressions delivered by the LUCAS device consistently generate effective forward blood flow remains uncertain. Transoesophageal echocardiography (TEE) enables direct visualization of the cardiac structures compressed during ongoing CPR. We investigated the association between compression site and outcomes in patients with refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR). Methods: We conducted a single-centre retrospective observational study of consecutive adult patients with refractory OHCA admitted under ongoing mechanical CPR to the Cardiac Arrest Center of IRCCS San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Milan, Italy, and subsequently treated with ECPR. TEE was performed immediately upon hospital arrival. An expert echocardiographer, blinded to outcomes, classified the compressed structure as the left ventricle (LV) body, LV outflow tract (LVOT), aortic valve/root, or left atrium. Ideal positioning was defined as LV body compression without LVOT, aortic valve, or aortic root compression, a configuration expected to maximize forward flow. Patients were categorized as having ideal or non-ideal compression. Results: Ninety patients were included (median age 54 years, 86% male, 64% presenting with a shockable rhythm). Twenty-two patients (24.4%) had ideal compression, whereas 68 (75.6%) had non-ideal compression. Survival to hospital discharge was significantly higher in the ideal group (22.7% vs 2.9%; p=0.009). Favourable neurological outcome at six months was also more frequent (14.3% vs 2.9%; p=0.083). After multivariable adjustment, ideal compression remained independently associated with survival to hospital discharge (adjusted OR 9.28, 95% CI 1.62-53.07; p=0.012) and showed a similar, borderline-significant association with favourable neurological outcome (adjusted OR 5.42, 95% CI 0.82-35.88; p=0.079). Conclusions: Among patients with refractory OHCA undergoing ECPR, TEE-confirmed compression of the LV body, without compression of the LVOT or aortic root, was strongly associated with survival to hospital discharge. These findings suggest that the anatomical target of mechanical chest compressions may substantially influence haemodynamic effectiveness and clinical outcomes. Funded by the European Union - Next Generation EU - NRRP M6C2 - Investment 2.1 Enhancement and strengthening of biomedical research in the NHS (Project code: PNRR-POC-2023-12377193; CUP master: C43C24000420007).

items.title: Abstract P1034: Hemoglobin Trends and Transfusion Practices After Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Hemoglobin targets are absent from post-cardiac arrest guidelines. New trials suggest that patients with brain and myocardial injury, injuries common post-arrest, may benefit from liberal transfusion strategies. Trends in post-arrest hemoglobin and real-world practices remain poorly characterized. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of consecutive adult cardiac arrests at three academic hospitals. Patients who survived the initial resuscitation and had a hemoglobin value measured were included. All post-arrest hemoglobin values and red blood cell transfusions were collected through 30 days; descriptive statistics and graphical visualization were used to present hemoglobin trends and transfusion practices. Associations between hemoglobin level and in-hospital mortality were assessed with logistic regression for the initial post-arrest hemoglobin value, and time-varying Cox proportional hazards models for hemoglobin values through 30 days. Results: Of 2,634 cardiac arrests, 958 met inclusion criteria, with 152 (15.9%) out-of-hospital arrests and 806 (84.1%) in-hospital. The mean initial post arrest hemoglobin was 9.75 g/dL (SD 2.60), with hemoglobin levels declining progressively over the first 20 days post-arrest. Red cell transfusions were delivered for 369 (38.5%) patients in the 30 days post-arrest, with 1,253 total transfusions. The mean pre-transfusion hemoglobin value was 6.96 g/dL (SD 1.06). A restrictive transfusion strategy (pre-transfusion hemoglobin of < 7 g/dL) was used for 772 (61.6%) of transfusions, and a liberal strategy (pre-transfusion hemoglobin of ≥ 7 g/dL) for 481 (38.4%). Over 30 days, the highest proportion of patients transfused was in the first 48 hours. Patients with initial post-arrest hemoglobin ≥ 9 g/dL had lower in-hospital mortality (adjusted OR 0.62, 95%CI 0.46-0.84, p<0.01). In time-varying analysis, post-arrest hemoglobin through 30 days demonstrated an L-shaped association with mortality, with 95% of the total reduction in mortality hazard captured below 9.20 g/dL. Conclusions: Anemia is common after cardiac arrest, worsening in initial survivors. There is substantial variation between liberal and restrictive transfusion strategies, reflecting clinical equipoise. Clinical trials are needed to disentangle anemia as a driver versus a marker of outcomes, and test whether the risk is modifiable.

items.title: Abstract P1040: Association Between Intra-Arrest Transport Distance and Duration with Clinical Outcomes for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Substantial variation exists among emergency medical services (EMS) regarding transport of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients to hospital with ongoing resuscitation, known as intra-arrest transport (IAT), as opposed to continuing on-scene resuscitation. We sought to determine whether the transport distance and duration of OHCA who underwent IAT were associated with patient outcomes. Methods: Adult (age 18+), EMS-treated OHCAs in British Columbia, Canada treated with IAT and occurring between January 1, 2019 and November 30, 2025 were included analysis, excluding those with missing data on location or outcomes. The shortest road distance between the incident location and the receiving hospital (transport distance) and the scene departure-to-hospital arrival interval (transport duration) were computed. Multivariable logistic regression was used to determine association between either transport distance or transport duration with survival to hospital discharge or at survival to hospital discharge with favourable neurological status (defined as Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] ≤ 2), adjusting for Utstein covariates. Results: A total of 2,580 OHCAs were included, of whom 342 (13.3%) survived to hospital discharge and 302 (11.7%) survived with favourable neurological status. Transport distance (per kilometre) was not associated with survival to hospital discharge (adjusted OR 1.000, 95% CI 0.998-1.002) nor survival with favourable neurological status (adjusted OR 1.000, 95% CI 0.998-1.002). Transport duration (per minute) was not associated with survival to hospital discharge (adjusted OR 1.001, 95% CI 0.998-1.004) nor survival with favourable neurological status (adjusted OR 1.001, 95% CI 0.998-1.004). Conclusion: Among OHCA patients who underwent IAT, longer transport distances and transport durations were not associated with patient outcomes.

items.title: Abstract P1018: Hemodynamic Change During Cardiorespiratory Arrest and the Association with ROSC and Survival to Discharge: Insights from Machine Learning Using High-Fidelity Physiologic Data
items.abstract: Introduction: Cardiorespiratory arrest in the cardiac intensive care unit (CICU) carries significant mortality. High-fidelity physiologic data captured at 1-second resolution offers an opportunity to characterize intra-arrest hemodynamics and identify predictors of return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Hypothesis: Hemodynamic variables during cardiorespiratory arrest are associated with ROSC, and a machine learning classifier trained on intra-arrest physiologic data will demonstrate strong predictive performance. Methods: Single-center retrospective study of pediatric patients (<18 years) with cardiorespiratory arrest in the CICU at Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children's Hospital (January 2022-May 2025). Physiologic data were aggregated via the Sickbay platform at 1-second resolution. Variables included heart rate, arterial blood pressure, arterial saturation, end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO 2 ), cerebral and renal near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), central venous pressure, and perfusion index, summarized as time-weighted area under the curve normalized by arrest duration. Univariable comparisons used the Mann-Whitney U test. A random forest classifier was trained with ROSC as the primary outcome and survival to discharge as the secondary, evaluated by stratified 5-fold cross-validation. Results: Fifty-nine arrests were included. Median age was 11 months (IQR 3.4-42.7); median weight 7.8 kg (IQR 4.5-13.4). ROSC occurred in 38 (66.1%); survival to discharge in 30 (50.8%). Higher systolic blood pressure (median difference +36.6 mmHg, p=0.03), diastolic blood pressure (+8.4 mmHg, p=0.04), and EtCO 2 (+12.4 mmHg, p=0.01) were associated with ROSC on univariable analysis. The random forest classifier for ROSC achieved AUC 0.92, accuracy 86.5%, sensitivity 89.6%, and specificity 80.0%. Top predictors included arrest duration, epinephrine bolus count, biventricular circulatory physiology, cerebral NIRS, and mean arterial pressure. The classifier for survival to discharge achieved AUC 0.60. Conclusions: A random forest classifier trained on intra-arrest hemodynamic and clinical data demonstrates excellent discriminatory performance for ROSC prediction (AUC 0.92). High-fidelity physiologic data platforms can capture granular intra-arrest data with potential for real-time clinical decision support.

items.title: Abstract P1037: Comparison of the Updated Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA-2) Scores and Original SOFA Scores for in-Hospital Mortality Prediction in Cardiac Arrest Clinical Trials
items.abstract: Background: The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score is commonly used in critical care to quantify the severity of organ dysfunction and predict clinical outcomes. Given the evolution of critical care practices, pharmacotherapy, and medical devices, an updated SOFA score (SOFA-2) was developed to more accurately reflect contemporary interventions. We evaluated whether SOFA-2 performs better than SOFA-1 as a predictor of in-hospital mortality using data from two completed cardiac arrest trials: Thiamine as metabolic resuscitator after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (THACA) and Thiamine as metabolic resuscitator after in-hospital cardiac arrest (THICA). Research Question: Does SOFA-2, compared to SOFA-1 score, improve prediction of in-hospital mortality in cardiac arrest clinical trials? Goal: To compare the performance of SOFA-2 relative to SOFA-1 for discriminating in-hospital mortality and assess differences in organ-specific subscores between SOFA-1 and SOFA-2 in the THICA and THACA cohorts. Methods: Total SOFA scores and organ-specific subscores were calculated for both cohorts. To assess discrimination for in-hospital mortality, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was compared between SOFA-1 and SOFA-2 at baseline, 24, 48, and 72 hours using tests of equality of ROC areas. Correlation between scoring systems was assessed using Pearson’s correlation coefficient. Patients who died prior to the time point of interest were excluded from analysis at that time point. Results: Median SOFA-2 scores were significantly lower than SOFA-1 in both THACA (9.5 [7, 12] vs. 12 [9, 13], p<0.001) and THICA (11.5 [10, 13.5] vs. 12.5 [10, 14], p=0.002) (Figure 1). Lower SOFA-2 values were consistently seen across most individual organ subscores and time points, except for coagulation and a transiently higher baseline renal subscore in THICA. SOFA-2 showed comparable discrimination to SOFA-1 for in-hospital mortality at all timepoints, with the strongest discrimination at the latest time point present at 72 and 48 hours for THACA and THICA respectively (Figure 2, Table 1). Conclusion: SOFA-2 consistently yielded significantly lower total and individual organ subscores than SOFA-1 but performed similarly with regard to in-hospital mortality.

items.title: Abstract P1064: Failed Resuscitation After 30-Minute Normothermic No-Flow Cardiac Arrest in a Rabbit Asphyxial Model: A Complete ACLS Simulation with Delayed Thoracotomy Resuscitation
items.abstract: Background: The reversible time window for normothermic cardiac arrest is well established within 4-6 minutes in mammals. Outcomes and resuscitative efficacy beyond 30 minutes of complete no-flow ischemia remain poorly documented in standardized, guideline-conforming experimental models. Clinical data regarding late thoracotomy resuscitation after prolonged asphyxial cardiac arrest are limited, and the exact boundary of irreversible myocardial failure after ultra-long normothermic ischemia lacks complete temporal verification. Methods: We performed a standardized, high-fidelity asphyxial cardiac arrest model in a healthy adult rabbit. Cardiac arrest (CA) was induced at 18:30 after 2 minutes of controlled asphyxia, followed by 30 minutes of complete normothermic no-flow ischemia without any intervention. At 19:00, full guideline-compliant CPR was initiated, consisting of continuous chest compressions plus manual bag-valve ventilation for a total resuscitation duration of 62 minutes. Advanced resuscitation interventions included 15 epinephrine administrations, one amiodarone dose, and two external defibrillations. After failure of conventional ACLS protocol, delayed open-chest direct cardiac massage was performed precisely at 19:52 as a final rescue strategy. Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and electrical cardiac activity were continuously monitored. Results: No ROSC or sustainable cardiac electrical activity was observed throughout the entire 92-minute experimental procedure. Despite uninterrupted high-quality CPR, repeated vasoactive drug administration, antiarrhythmic therapy, external defibrillation attempts, and late thoracotomy resuscitation, no myocardial mechanical recovery was achieved. The 30-minute normothermic no-flow ischemic period resulted in complete irreversible cardiac refractoriness to all standard and advanced resuscitative interventions. Conclusion: In a standardized rabbit asphyxial CA model, 30 minutes of normothermic full no-flow ischemia leads to irreversible myocardial failure refractory to full ACLS care and delayed open-chest resuscitation. This complete time-stamped experimental record provides direct visual and procedural evidence for the absolute time boundary of conventional resuscitation efficacy. The findings support clinical decision-making for termination of resuscitation in out-of-hospital prolonged cardiac arrest cases.

items.title: Abstract P1074: ACLS Injuries Revealed Post ECPR
items.abstract: Introduction: ACLS involves CPR and other resuscitation procedures that may cause iatrogenic injuries but unless the patient achieves sustained ROSC to evaluate for underlying cause of arrest and possible injuries, it is difficult to quantify these potential risks. HYPOTHESIS: What are the rates and types of ACLS injuries that are found post ECPR in non-trauma patients? Methods: Review of the ECLS Registry to identify all ECPR patients that survived for sufficient time to evaluate for possible post-ACLS injuries. The EMR was further used for review of radiological studies, laboratory tests, and physician notes. Results: We identified 17 ECLS patients who survived for adequate time to evaluate for iatrogenic injures due to ACLS efforts; there were 6 additional ECPR patients who died before achieving sustained ROSC so that no post-ACLS evaluation was possible. 7W/10M; IHCA 10/OHCA 7; Avg Age 58.4 (range 32-71); Avg ECMO Run: 3.4 d; Survival to D/C 5 (29.4%); Survival to Decan 4 (23.5%); Died before off ECMO 8 (47.1%); Patients without any injuries/hemorrhage: 3 (17.6%) vs significant injuries: 14 (82.4%); Injuries found: rib fractures with associated pneumothorax (4) and hemothorax (2), hemopericardium (1), liver lacerations (3), splenic laceration (1), bladder rupture (1), arterial injury [not due to ECPR] (1), massive hemorrhage [either diffuse bleeding or not due to trauma such as UGIB] (5). Total of six patients were given thrombolytics as part of ACLS prior to ECPR initiated. Only 1 patient (5.9%) who achieved sustained ROSC had an injury due to ECPR [CFA side branch repaired]. Conclusions: A large percentage of our ECPR patients who survived cardiac arrest have iatrogenic injuries presumably due to resuscitation efforts but ECPR itself appears to result in few vascular injuries. Thrombolytic administration during ACLS appears to be associated with significant hemorrhage. After sustained ROSC is achieved after ECPR, it is important to evaluate for the cause of the primary arrest and for potential iatrogenic injuries.

items.title: Abstract P1028: Longitudinal Suppression Ratio Trajectories and Neurologic Outcomes After Pediatric Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG) provides objective measures of cerebral activity and has emerged as a promising tool for prognostication after pediatric cardiac arrest (CA). Prior studies have evaluated qEEG features at discrete time points, particularly in the first 24 hours after CA. Suppression ratio (SR), a qEEG measure of the proportion of suppressed EEG activity, may provide insight into evolving cerebral dysfunction after CA. We evaluated whether SR trajectories during the first 72 hours after return of circulation (ROC) are associated with neurologic outcomes after pediatric CA. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients ≤18 years of age who experienced in-hospital and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest admitted to Children’s Medical Center Dallas from 2020-2024, and who underwent continuous EEG monitoring within 72 hours of ROC. Continuous EEG recordings were processed using automated qEEG analysis software (Persyst Development Corporation, Prescott, AZ, USA) to obtain SR trends. Hourly mean SR values were calculated for the first 72 hours. Patients with multiple cardiac arrest events during the same admission were excluded. Favorable neurologic outcome was defined as a Pediatric Cerebral Performance Category (PCPC) score of 1-2 or no change from pre-arrest baseline. Longitudinal SR trajectories were estimated using mixed-effects models and compared by neurologic outcome at hospital discharge. Results: The cohort included 223 patients, of whom 96 (43.0%) had favorable neurologic outcomes. Baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. Patients with favorable outcomes had shorter CPR duration and higher rates of in-hospital cardiac arrest and congenital heart disease. SR trajectories diverged within the first 6-12 hours after ROC; at 12 hours, mean SR was 42.2 (95% CI 34.6-49.7) in patients with unfavorable outcomes versus 3.4 (95% CI 1.1-5.8) in those with favorable outcomes, and remained distinct through 72 hours. Predicted SR trajectories differed significantly between the outcome groups (p<0.001); SR increased over time in the unfavorable outcome group but remained low and stable in the favorable outcome group (Figure 1). Conclusion: Distinct SR trajectories during the first 72 hours after ROC were associated with neurologic outcomes following pediatric cardiac arrest. Longitudinal qEEG assessment beyond 24 hours may provide complementary prognostic information and improve characterization of evolving brain injury.

items.title: Abstract P1042: Evaluating AED Training, AED Awareness, and Preparedness Across Workplace and Public Settings Using Pulse Point AED in Allegheny County
items.abstract: Background: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate intervention with CPR and AED use. Only 40% of OHCA patients receive bystander CPR before emergency medical professionals arrive. Although approximately 10,000 cardiac arrests occur in workplaces each year in the United States, only half of individuals in workplace settings can locate an AED when needed. While previous studies have demonstrated moderate public awareness of AEDs, AED location awareness, accessibility, and operational readiness in the United States, across workplace and public settings remain understudied. Hypothesis: Workplace and public-access facilities vary in CPR/AED training requirements, employee awareness, and operational readiness to respond to out-of-hospital cardiac arrest despite the presence of registered AEDs. Methods: PulsePoint AED records in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (2024-2026), were reviewed to identify public- and private-access AED locations. Sites were contacted by phone or email to verify AED location, accessibility, and registry status. Of 88 pending AED submissions, 77 AEDs across 49 sites were successfully verified and approved. Verification was limited by unsuccessful contact attempts and the inability of some representatives to provide AED-related information. Of the 49 verified sites, 42 (85.7%) completed a survey assessing AED location awareness, employee CPR/AED training, prior AED use, and training source. Additional interviews evaluated CPR/AED training requirements. Sites were categorized as for-profit, non-profit, or government facilities, and descriptive analyses were performed. Results: Among the 42 responding sites, 92.9% had reported having at least one individual trained in CPR and AED use. Site classification included 22 non-profit facilities (52.4%), 15 for-profit facilities (38.1%), and 5 government facilities (9.5%). While most sites reported having CPR/AED-trained personnel, differences in training sources and requirements were observed across facilities with for-profit facilities more likely to require CPR/AED training than non-profit or government facilities. Four sites (9.8%) reported prior use of an AED during a medical emergency. Interviews revealed that 16 facilities required CPR/AED training, while 13 offered training only upon employee request. Although 42 sites reported having CPR-certified personnel, certification was often not required by the facility, and respondents were frequently unaware of the reason employees had obtained certification. Conclusion: Despite widespread AED availability, inconsistent CPR/AED training requirements may limit preparedness for OHCA. Standardized training and continued AED registry verification may improve bystander readiness and emergency response in the workplace and public settings.

items.title: Abstract P1052: Older Adult Perceptions on Mobility-Modified CPR Strategies
items.abstract: Background: Adults age 65 years and older are most likely to experience as well as witness an out-of-the-hospital cardiac arrest due to declining health with age and cohabitation, activities with others in the same age group, and interpersonal relationships. As the body ages, physical and cognitive changes are common that may present barriers to learning and performing proper cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) techniques. The American Heart Association and the European Resuscitation Council encourage people of all ages to learn CPR, although there are no guidelines for teaching and performing CPR for older adults that meet the needs of the aging body. Objective: We aimed to identify and categorize barriers and benefits for older adults learning and performing CPR modified for mobility limitations. Methods: We conducted a focus group (FG) among older adults, age 65 years and older, to learn their sentiments on modified training methods for learning CPR. The team leading the FG was comprisedof a CPR researcher, two aging researchers, a paramedic, and a psychologist. We demonstrated one typical training scenario of hands only CPR and three non-standard scenarios. This included: 1. Therescuer being unable to move a victim off a bed onto a hard surface; 2. The rescuer is unable to perform compressions alone, so alternatively two rescuers perform 4-Handed CPR; 3. An adjustable height manikin is used to accommodate learners who cannot kneel. The scenarios were presented to a FG of 5 older adults who did not have prior knowledge of the modified CPR techniques. Pre-prepared questions were delivered to elicit sentiments for each scenario. The 2-hour FG was recorded, autotranscribed, and manually cleaned. The transcript was coded to identify themes related to barriers, education, feedback on modifications, CPR FC strengths, and CPR FC weaknesses. Results: The composition of the FG was 2 males, 3 females, and 4 out of 5 previously trained in CPR. We found 280 identifiers (ID) in 53 themes. Of these themes, 42 could be grouped into barriers, education, feedback on modifications, CPR FG strengths, or CPR FG weaknesses. Barriers were made up of 20 themes with 105 ID; emotional was the most common ID. Education was made up of 7 themes with 39 ID; teaching suggestions were the most common ID. Feedback on modification had 5 themes with 38 ID; modification benefits being the most common ID. CPR FG strengths were made up of 6 themes with 64 ID; modification benefits also being the most common ID. CPR FG weaknesses were made up of 9 themes with 30 ID; modification barrier was the most common ID. Conclusion: The older adults in the FG vocalized barriers to learning CPR most often followed by strengths in the CPR FG. This is in line with literature that suggests older adults are willing and wanting to learn CPR, but barriers to performing CPR make this difficult to achieve emphasizing the need for mobility-modified CPR curriculum.

items.title: Abstract P1055: Knowledge Assessment of CPR Readiness in High School Students. Are Mandates Enough?
items.abstract: Background: Since 2016, Wisconsin has required CPR training for high school students as a graduation requirement. Despite widespread implementation, the extent to which students achieve and retain CPR knowledge and skills remains incompletely understood. Hypothesis: Despite statewide CPR training mandates, significant deficiencies in CPR knowledge, AED proficiency, and confidence to perform bystander resuscitation persist among Wisconsin high school students. Objectives: To assess CPR knowledge, AED familiarity, and confidence in performing bystander resuscitation among Wisconsin high school students Methods: We performed a cross-sectional, survey-based study of Wisconsin high school juniors and seniors from March through May 2026. An anonymous electronic survey was distributed through student-led social media outreach and peer-to-peer recruitment. Survey items assessed CPR training history, CPR and AED knowledge, and self-reported confidence in responding to a cardiac emergency. Responses were collected electronically and analyzed descriptively. Results: A total of 139 students completed the survey. The majority (96.3%) supported CPR education for students. Although 75.6% reported prior CPR training, only 46.7% reported confidence in their ability to perform CPR during a cardiac emergency. Knowledge deficits were identified across several CPR domains. Only 50.4% of respondents correctly identified the recommended chest compression depth, representing the largest knowledge gap observed. In comparison, 63.7% correctly identified the recommended chest compression rate and rescue breathing parameters. While 77.8% knew the location of an AED within their school, 33.1% reported not knowing how to use one. Compared with students from urban and rural schools, students from suburban schools were more likely to correctly identify the recommended chest compression rate (72.8% vs. 44.2%, p=0.002). No significant differences were observed in CPR training exposure, compression depth knowledge, AED familiarity, or self-reported confidence to perform CPR between types of school. Conclusions: Despite statewide CPR training mandates, substantial gaps in CPR knowledge, AED proficiency, and confidence to perform CPR persist among Wisconsin high school students. Although suburban students demonstrated greater knowledge of chest compression rate, overall CPR knowledge remained suboptimal across school settings. These findings suggest that current training approaches may be insufficient to ensure long-term retention and preparedness and suggest the need for unique approaches or content to improve bystander CPR competency among high school students.

items.title: Abstract P1070: Assessing Feasibility of Prehospital Critical Care Response Units for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in Southern Ontario, Canada Using Geospatial Modeling
items.abstract: Background: Prehospital critical care response units (CCRUs) that respond to out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (OHCA) and administer advanced interventions such as extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) may shorten treatment delays and improve patient outcomes. We sought to examine the feasibility of a planned prehospital CCRU program in southern Ontario, Canada and quantify potential benefit for OHCAs. Methods: We included adult (age 18+), EMS-assessed OHCAs occurring within one of three regions in southern Ontario, Canada (Toronto, Peel, Halton) between January 1, 2022 and December 31, 2023. We computed estimated response times by a CCRU crew (defined as the time between 9-1-1 call and CCRU crew arrival on scene) dispatched from one of two paramedic bases, accounting for CCRU crew availability at the time of dispatch and stand-down protocols (e.g., TOR before CCRU arrival). We defined OHCAs as ECPR-eligible if they had a CCRU response time ≤45 mins and met clinical inclusion criteria from one of three previous ECPR trials (ARREST, Prague, INCEPTION). Characteristics and distributions of CCRU response times were determined for each cohort of ECPR-eligible patients. Analyses were repeated to consider limiting CCRU availability to one base and/or to between 8:00am-8:00pm on weekdays based on potential operational constraints. Results: A total of 5,469 OHCAs were included. CCRU crews arrived on scene to 5,422 (99.1%) OHCAs with a median response time of 21.6 mins [IQR: 15.5-28.6]. The number of ECPR-eligible OHCAs was 206 (3.8%) following inclusion criteria from ARREST, 366 (6.8%) from Prague, and 106 (2.0%) from INCEPTION. Assuming CCRU availability between 8:00am-8:00pm on weekdays yielded a total of 2,315 OHCAs: CCRU crews arrived on scene to 2,257 (97.5%) OHCAs with a median CCRU response time of 22.1 mins [IQR: 15.6-29.3]. The number of ECPR-eligible OHCAs during this timeframe were 87 (3.9%) following inclusion criteria from ARREST, 142 (6.3%) from Prague, and 47 (2.1%) from INCEPTION. Proportions of ECPR-eligible OHCAs significantly differed by clinical inclusion criteria used (p<0.001) but did not differ across CCRU crew availability scenarios. Conclusion: Deployment of prehospital CCRU crews can provide timely ECPR access and may shorten delays to ECPR initiation. However, proportions of ECPR-eligible OHCAs remain relatively low.

items.title: Abstract P1021: Association Between Bystander-Patient Relationship and In-Hospital Management Among Older Patients with Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Multicenter Observational Study in Japan
items.abstract: Background: Older patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) witnessed by family members in Japan are less likely to receive bystander cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in the prehospital setting and have worse neurological outcomes than those witnessed by non-family bystanders. However, differences in in-hospital management remain unclear. Aim: To examine how in-hospital management differs according to bystander-patient relationship. Methods: Older patients (aged ≥65 years) with OHCA of cardiac origin witnessed by a lay bystander and registered in the Japanese Association for Acute Medicine Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (JAAM-OHCA) registry between 2014 and 2022 were analyzed. Patients were divided into two groups: the family member-witnessed group and the non-family bystander-witnessed group. The primary outcomes were the proportions of patients receiving extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR), intra-aortic balloon pumping (IABP), coronary angiography (CAG), percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), and target temperature management (TTM). Associations between bystander-patient relationship and in-hospital management were assessed using multivariable logistic regression models adjusted for 14 covariates available at hospital arrival. Results: Among 11,861 patients (the family member-witnessed group: 7,547; the non-family bystander-witnessed group: 4,314), ECPR was performed in 387/7,547 (5.1%) in the family member-witnessed group and 291/4,314 (6.7%) in the non-family bystander-witnessed group, with no significant difference between groups (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.89; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.72-1.08). Similarly, there was no significant difference in IABP use (383/7,547 [5.1%] vs. 314/4,314 [7.3%]; aOR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.71-1.05). In contrast, the family member-witnessed group was significantly less likely to receive CAG (780/7,547 [10.3%] vs. 669/4,314 [15.5%]; aOR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.67-0.93), PCI (415/7,547 [5.5%] vs. 380/4,314 [8.8%]; aOR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.63-0.97), and TTM (569/7,547 [7.5%] vs. 488/4,314 [11.3%]; aOR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.69-0.95). Conclusions: Older patients with family member-witnessed OHCA were less likely to receive CAG, PCI, and TTM than those with non-family bystander-witnessed OHCA. The observed differences may be partly attributable to unmeasured factors, such as arrest location (e.g., at home vs. in public place), which may affect CPR quality but were unavailable in this registry. The authors used ChatGPT (OpenAI) exclusively for English language editing and not for data analysis. The authors take full responsibility for the content of the abstract.

items.title: Abstract P1031: Spinal Intrathecal versus Direct Subdural Sodium Nitroprusside Delivery for Cerebral Resuscitation in a Porcine Cardiac Arrest Model
items.abstract: Background: Direct subdural sodium nitroprusside (SNP) delivery improves cerebral cortical microcirculation after cardiac arrest but requires cranial burr-hole placement. We compared spinal intrathecal SNP delivery directed toward the foramen magnum with direct subdural delivery in a porcine cardiac arrest model. Methods: Twenty pigs underwent ventricular fibirillation induced cardiac arrest, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and SNP administration 30 minutes after restoration of spontaneous circulation. Animals received SNP either by direct subdural intracranial delivery or by spinal intrathecal delivery with rostral catheter advancement. Cerebral cortical microcirculation, brain tissue oxygen tension (PbtO 2 ), hemodynamics, mean amplitude-integrated electroencephalography (aEEG), and serum and cerebrospinal fluid neuronal injury biomarkers were evaluated for 5 hours after treatment. Results: Baseline and pre-treatment variables were comparable between groups. Direct subdural delivery produced rapid increases in cortical microcirculation and oxygenation. Percent arteriole diameter AUC was higher in the direct subdural group than in the spinal intrathecal group (34534.1 [33026.6-49893.7] vs. 27896.8 [21112.5-33046.9] %·min; P=0.009). PbtO 2 AUC from 1800 seconds to the end of observation was also higher after direct subdural delivery (22990.7±2607.0 vs. 15927.2±1807.8 mmHg·min; P=0.039). Spinal intrathecal delivery did not reproduce the immediate cortical microcirculatory or oxygenation response during the first 30 minutes, although delayed increases in capillary perfusion and arteriole diameter were observed approximately 2 to 3 hours after treatment. Mean arterial pressure showed a significant group-by-time interaction, but total MAP AUC did not differ between groups (P=0.903). Mean aEEG amplitude tended to be higher in the direct subdural group, but aEEG AUC was not significantly different (P=0.548). Serum and cerebrospinal fluid S100B, neurofilament light chain, and neuron-specific enolase were numerically lower in the spinal intrathecal group, without significant between-group differences. Conclusions: Spinal intrathecal SNP delivery did not reproduce the rapid cortical microcirculatory and oxygenation effects achieved by direct subdural delivery. The delayed response after spinal intrathecal administration suggests possible delayed rostral drug spread. Optimization of catheter position, dose, volume, infusion rate, and timing is needed before spinal intrathecal SNP can be considered a less invasive strategy for cerebral resuscitation after cardiac arrest. Figure 1. Brain tissue oxygen tension and neuronal injury biomarkers
