items.title: Abstract P1050: The Influence of Moulage on Clinical Decision-Making in Simulated Cardiac Emergencies and Resuscitation
items.abstract: Background: Simulation-based medical education increasingly incorporates strategies to improve realism and learner immersion during high-acuity training. Moulage enhances visual and environmental fidelity, but evidence regarding its influence on clinical reasoning and decision-making during cardiac emergencies and resuscitation remains limited. Objective: To evaluate the influence of advanced moulage on clinical decision-making, diagnostic accuracy, and team performance during simulated cardiac emergencies and resuscitation training. Methods: A prospective observational simulation study was conducted with 20 healthcare professionals participating in advanced cardiovascular emergency and resuscitation training at a tertiary academic simulation center. Participants included physicians, nurses, and multidisciplinary emergency providers trained in ACLS. Teams participated in two high-fidelity simulation scenarios involving cardiac arrest and severe cardiogenic shock. Scenarios incorporated advanced moulage techniques reproducing cyanosis, diaphoresis, peripheral hypoperfusion, bleeding patterns, and progressive physiological deterioration. Primary endpoints included recognition of clinical deterioration, initiation of critical interventions, diagnostic accuracy, adherence to ACLS algorithms, and overall resuscitation performance. Results: Advanced moulage was associated with improved situational awareness and faster recognition of physiological instability. Median time to initiation of life-saving interventions decreased by 18% compared with institutional historical simulation benchmarks. Diagnostic accuracy increased from 72% to 90% in scenarios requiring differentiation between cardiogenic, obstructive, and hypovolemic etiologies. Teams exposed to enhanced realism demonstrated improved adherence to ACLS protocols and earlier escalation of critical interventions. Participants reported high immersion and realism scores (9.3 ± 0.5). Non-technical skills also improved, particularly leadership behavior and communication during resuscitation efforts. Conclusion: Advanced moulage enhanced realism, clinical reasoning, and team dynamics during simulated cardiac emergencies and resuscitation scenarios. Structured moulage techniques may improve recognition of critical illness, accelerate decision-making, and optimize adherence to resuscitation protocols. Findings support the incorporation of advanced moulage into cardiovascular simulation programs aimed at improving emergency preparedness and resuscitation performance.

items.title: Abstract P1051: Barriers to Emergency Medical Services Led Community Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Education in Allegheny County
items.abstract: Background: Community cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) education is an important strategy for improving bystander response to out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Emergency medical services (EMS) agencies are well positioned to provide CPR training, but broader economic and operational pressures may limit their ability to sustain community education programs. Research Question: How do agency-level operational capacity, resource availability, and community engagement factors affect the delivery of EMS-led community CPR education and outreach in Allegheny County? Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among EMS agencies identified from the Allegheny County EMS agency listing. Agencies were contacted using a standardized phone script, and responses were entered into a structured survey form. Respondents reported agency funding model, CPR training availability, training frequency, estimated annual CPR trainees and events, community outreach activities, and barriers to CPR education. Free-text responses were coded into standardized categories. Descriptive statistics were calculated using completed agency responses. Results: Of 32 identified agencies, 25 had usable completed responses, yielding a preliminary response rate of 78.1pct. All responding agencies reported providing community CPR training;however, delivery was most often request-based rather than routine. Nineteen agencies (76.0pct) offered CPR training occasionally or by request, while 6 agencies (24.0pct) offered regularly scheduled classes. Among agencies with usable numeric estimates, annual CPR training volume ranged from 25 to 1,000 people trained per year, with a median of 125 and mean of 232.8 trainees per agency. Reported CPR-related events ranged from 0 to 10 per year. The most frequently reported barriers were staffing availability (15/25, 60.0pct), community demand or participation (12/25, 48.0pct), equipment or supplies (7/25, 28.0pct), and funding (5/25, 20.0pct). Qualitative responses supported these findings, with agencies describing CPR training as commonly occurring “by request,” limited by lack of dedicated education staffing, variable public interest, rural or older populations, and insufficient training equipment or supplies. Conclusions: EMS agencies in Allegheny County appear broadly engaged in CPR education, but delivery is often reactive and constrained by staffing, community demand, equipment, and funding barriers. These findings suggest that EMS-led CPR education may function as a discretionary community service rather than a consistently resourced public health intervention. Shared instructor resources, centralized equipment support, coordinated outreach, and sustainable funding may improve the reach and reliability of community CPR education.

items.title: Abstract P1047: The Effect of Compression Rate on Coronary Perfusions Pressures During Circumferential Thoracoabdominal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in a Porcine Cardiac Arrest Model
items.abstract: Background: Circumferential thoracoabdominal CPR (CTA-CPR) uses synchronized pneumatic thoracic and abdominal bands to generate blood flow during cardiac arrest. It may be safer and more effective than sternal piston methods of CPR. There has been a trend toward favoring higher compression rates for sternal piston methods. However, the relationship between constriction rate and perfusion pressures during CTA-CPR has not been well characterized. We have previously reported possible improvements in pressures with increasing rates of constriction. Objective: To further evaluate the effect of constriction rates coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) during CTA-CPR in a porcine model of cardiac arrest. Methods: 35 kg Yorkshire swine (n=4) underwent instrumentation with aortic (AO) and right atrial (RA) pressure catheters followed by electrical induction of cardiac arrest. CTA-CPR was applied at target rates of 80, 100, 110, and 120 compressions per minute, then in reverse order. Each rate increment was 45 seconds in duration and the result used was the mean between the ascending and descending epochs. The primary endpoint was the end epoch CPP (aortic minus right atrial pressure at the end of the relaxation phase). Secondary endpoint was Delta-CPP (change from start to end of epoch). One-way ANOVA was used to compare outcomes across rates. Results: Pooled analysis showed no significant difference in CPP between any of the compression rates (p = 0.99). Mean CPP values were similar across all rates tested (range: 20.2-21.3 mmHg). Delta-CPP also did not differ significantly between rates (p = 0.21). In individual animals, 110/min. often was associated with higher CPPs, but this pattern was not consistent. Conclusions: In this small series of porcine studies using CTA-CPR, increasing constriction rate did not appear to be associated with improvements in CPP or Delta-CPP. These findings do not confirm our previous study. If replicated, they indicate that CTA-CPR may differ from conventional sternal piston-based methods. Larger studies are needed to define the optimal compression rate for this new type of CPR.

items.title: Abstract P1054: Emotional and Psychomotor Preparation to Perform CPR Following Hands-Only CPR Training with Standard v. Interactive Film-Based Training
items.abstract: Introduction: Emotional readiness to respond to a cardiac arrest is a critical but neglected element of CPR training. We compared emotional response and CPR performance following hands-only CPR training using either the American Heart Association (AHA) CPR in Schools curriculum or cardiacSTAR, a 30-min gamefied film-based training that immerses learners in a realistic arrest scenario. Methods: Ninth-grade students were trained using either AHA CPR in Schools (n=143) or cardiacSTAR (n=163). On the day of training, students completed emotional profile surveys and CPR skills testing. CPR skills were also tested at 3-month follow-up. Emotional responses were analyzed as binary outcomes (selected vs. not selected) using Pearson chi-square tests. CPR quality metrics were compared using Welch t-tests. Results: On the day of training, students trained with cardiacSTAR reported significantly higher levels of anxiety, anger, fear, relief, upset, and panic during the training. AHA-trained students reported more pride and determination (Figure 1). When imagining responding to a cardiac arrest, students trained with cardiacSTAR reported significantly greater anticipated negative emotions - akin to those reported by actual lay rescuers - than AHA-trained students (Figure 2). On the day of training, 31 of 149 students (20.8%) in the cardiacSTAR group and 19 of 148 students (12.8%) in the AHA group achieved high-quality CPR, defined as simultaneously attaining ≥ 70% of compressions at the correct rate AND depth, but the trend did not reach statistical significance (p=0.063). At 3-month follow-up, there was no difference between groups in percentage of students achieving high-quality CPR (cardiacSTAR 37/129 students 28.7% v AHA 34/139 24.5%, p=0.434). Conclusion: Compared with standard AHA training, cardiacSTAR elicited stronger emotional engagement during training and greater emotional preparedness for an imagined cardiac arrest, with students reporting a realistic emotional profile similar to that reported by actual lay rescuers. There was a trend towards greater CPR skill acquisition with cardiacSTAR but no difference in long-term skill retention, suggesting that emotionally immersive CPR training may influence both emotional and psychomotor learning outcomes.

items.title: Abstract P1036: Association Between Procainamide Administration and Survival in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Antiarrhythmics are an important care modality for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with a shockable rhythm. Although amiodarone and lidocaine are the recommended first-line agents for ventricular dysrhythmias during resuscitation, recent research found procainamide to better outcomes for stable ventricular dysrhythmias. As research on procainamide as a second-line antiarrhythmic for OHCA is limited. Hypothesis: Procainamide administration is associated with improved survival after OHCA. Methods: We retrospectively studied OHCAs from the TriNetX research database from 2010-2024. TriNetX is a database of electronic health record data from >100 healthcare systems in the US with >100 million patients. We included adult patients with a cardiac arrest diagnosis in the emergency department who survived to hospital admission and received an antiarrhythmic. We stratified patients based on whether they received procainamide in addition to lidocaine or amiodarone in the first 72 hours after hospital arrival. We defined our primary outcomes as survival to hospital discharge and 30- day survival. We evaluated the association between procainamide administration and each outcome using multivariable logistic regression. Analyses were adjusted for sex, race/ethnicity, hypotension, marital status, and past medical history. Results: Of 31,454 adult OHCA patients, 91 received procainamide within 72 hours and 31,363 did not. The procainamide group had a median age of 68 (IQR 56-77) compared to 66 (IQR 56-75) in the non-procainamide group and was predominantly male (70.3% vs 63.1%). The procainamide group had higher rates of heart failure (37.4% vs 27.3%), coronary artery disease (35.2% vs 30.1%), and systemic hypotension (72.5% vs 62.4%). After adjustment, procainamide was significantly associated with higher odds of survival to hospital discharge (72.5% vs 57.7%, aOR 2.03 [1.27-3.24], p=0.003) and 30-day survival (67.0% vs 52.2%, aOR 1.96 [1.26-3.06], p=0.003). Conclusion: Procainamide administration within 72 hours of OHCA was independently associated with significantly higher odds of both survival to hospital discharge and 30-day survival.

items.title: Abstract P1056: “Night Sim” in the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit: Implementing Night Shift Simulation Education to Aid in Cardiac Arrest Prevention
items.abstract: Background: In-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) occurs most commonly in an intensive care unit (ICU) setting, with a survival to discharge rate of 40-60%. Past data have revealed lower rates of survival for pediatric IHCA occurring on night shifts compared to day shifts. In many hospitals, there are less experienced staff on night shifts and there may be fewer resources available at those times. Hypothesis: Implementing a night shift simulation curriculum (Night Sim) targeted at IHCA prevention in a pediatric ICU (PICU) is feasible and staff will feel more prepared to provide interventions that may prevent cardiac arrest after completing the education. Aims: We implemented a Night Sim curriculum, paired with a cardiac arrest prevention bundle as part of a multi-center trial, focused on preventing IHCA during the night hours. Methods: A multidisciplinary team of PICU attending and fellow physicians, advance practice providers (APPs), and charge nurses designed the Night Sim curriculum. Night Sims were facilitated by PICU fellows and participants included bedside nurses, resident physicians, and APPs. Each simulation focused on a current patient deemed to be at increased risk of IHCA and provided didactic and hands-on practice for specific tasks or interventions. Each participant and facilitator completed a post-simulation survey. Results: We collected 77 total survey responses over 11 Night Sims between October 2025 and March 2026. Forty-nine nurses completed the survey and 35 (71%) reported less than 1 year of work experience in the PICU. Ninety-six percent of all respondents agreed or strongly agreed that the medical team felt more prepared to carry out interventions that may prevent a cardiac arrest event after participation in the education. Night Sims prompted a change in care plan, such as new medication to bedside or change in action plan, in 16% of survey responses. Participants commented that they valued the focus on real patients who were in the unit for the simulation. Conclusion: Night Sims are a feasible way to provide education to medical teams caring for patients who are at high risk for IHCA. Staff had a positive reception to Night Sims and felt better prepared to care for patients at high risk of IHCA. This program benefits staff at early stages of their career and does not require additional costs to implement.

items.title: Abstract P1071: Electronic Medical Record-Generated Pediatric Early Warning Score Reduces Clinical Deterioration
items.abstract: Background: Rapid response teams (RRT) are an established practice in most hospitals, with the need for both timely recognition and a highly capable response team to avoid deterioration of hospitalized acute care patients. Our institution designed a Modified Pediatric Early Warning Score (MPEWS) within the electronic medical record (EMR) to allow early identification of patients at risk for deterioration. Hypothesis: The use of an automated MPEWS score will identify high acuity patients and, when linked to EMR alerting and structured RRT, will reduce transfer to an intensive care unit (ICU) and deterioration events Aims: Aim # 1- to determine if MPEWS electronic scoring predicts ICU transfer in hospitalized pediatric acute care patients. Aim # 2- to determine if implementation of MPEWS and response to electronic triggering reduces clinical deterioration events. Methods: A retrospective observational study in a pediatric tertiary hospital was conducted with MPEWS pre-implementation 1/2023-5/2024, post-implementation 7/2024-3/2026. Acute care patients that experienced RRT activation were included; event rates were measured per 1000 acute care patient days. Highest MPEWS score per patient day was used to associate MPEWS with outcome data including RRT, transfer to an ICU, and deterioration events. Deterioration events are defined as need for transfer to an ICU and one of the following within 2 hours of RRT activation: mechanical ventilation, initiation of vasoactive infusion, chest compressions, fluid bolus therapy > 40cc/kg. Results: Total RRT activations included 3296 events: 1465 vs 1831 (pre, post MPEWS implementation). With ICU transfer as outcome, the MPEWS alert specificity was 0.93, sensitivity 0.29, AUC 0.73. The rate of RRT activations was similar 14.6 vs 14.7 RRTs/1000 acute care patient days. The percentage of RRT events that resulted in transfer to ICU and the rate of ICU transfers per 1000 acute care census days were both lower following MPEWS implementation: 809 transfers to an ICU (55%), 7.88 ICU transfers per 1000 acute care patient days compared with 905 (49%), 7.30, respectively. Deterioration events were lower comparing pre and post implementation: 82 events, 0.82 events per 1000 patient days vs 83 events, 0.66 events per 1000 patient days, with Bayesian probability of improvement 90.6%. Conclusions: Fully automated electronic MPEWS scoring identifies high-risk acute care patients, reducing deterioration events in pediatric hospitalized acute care patients. Steps to optimize scoring systems and workflow response would be helpful to prevent alert fatigue.

items.title: Abstract P1085: The Ceiling Effect of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Quality Metrics: Differentiating Prognostic Determinants of Initial Resuscitation and Neurological Recovery in In-Hospital Cardiac Arrests
items.abstract: Introduction: While high-quality CPR is critical to optimizing in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) outcomes, the prognostic limits of mechanical optimization within high-performing teams remain poorly defined. Hypothesis: We hypothesized a “ceiling effect” exists where optimal CPR eliminates mechanical variance as a deciding factor. Instead, outcomes are driven first by intrinsic physiological reserve, and subsequently by ischemic downtime. Aim: To evaluate the independent associations of CPR quality and ischemic downtime across two distinct phases: initial resuscitation versus ultimate neurological recovery. Methods: A retrospective cohort study at Sengkang General Hospital, Singapore (June 2024-May 2025) analyzed index IHCAs requiring CPR; do-not-resuscitate cases were excluded. Exposures comprised total ischemic downtime and defibrillator-measured CPR quality metrics (chest compression fraction [CCF], depth, rate, and recoil velocity).The primary endpoint was the initial ROSC, while secondary endpoints included ultimate survival to discharge and favorable neurological function at discharge (Cerebral Performance Category [CPC] 1-2). Analyses utilized serial multivariable binary logistic regressions adjusting for age and initial electrocardiogram rhythm. Results: We evaluated 96 subjects (median age 70.5 years; 63.5% male; 68.8% Chinese); 75 (78.1%) achieved ROSC, 14 (14.6%) survived to discharge, and 12 (12.5%) achieved CPC 1-2. Overall median CCF was 89%, rate was 119 bpm, and depth was 5.8 cm. Uniform AHA target adherence in CPR quality metrics confirmed a clinical ceiling effect, with CPR metrics failing to predict outcomes ( p > 0.05). Instead, predictors decoupled across the survival timeline. Younger age significantly drove initial ROSC (aOR: 0.947; 95% CI: 0.899-0.998) and favorable neurological recovery (aOR: 0.942; 95% CI: 0.888-0.999), but ceased to predict overall survival. Ischemic downtime (median 9.5 mins in survivors vs. 15.0 mins in non-survivors) acted as the dominant prognostic driver: each additional minute decreased the odds of survival by 12% (aOR: 0.877; 95% CI: 0.786-0.980) and favorable neurological recovery by 16% (aOR: 0.842; 95% CI: 0.736-0.963). Conclusion: Our study demonstrates that when teams meet AHA CPR quality guidelines, a ceiling effect exists where mechanical quality metrics cease to differentiate outcomes. Instead, survival determinants decouple chronologically: intrinsic physiological reserve (age) drives initial ROSC, whereas post-ROSC recovery depends on ischemic duration. Downtime is the dominant prognostic driver for hospital discharge, and minimizing downtime is paramount to ensuring neurologically intact survival. Consequently, protocols should shift from prolonged mechanical optimization toward rapid definitive care, reversal of underlying etiologies, and early extracorporeal CPR.

items.title: Abstract P1087: Determinants of In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest and Post-Arrest Mortality in Cardiogenic Shock
items.abstract: Background: In-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) is a catastrophic complication of cardiogenic shock, yet predictors of arrest and subsequent mortality remain poorly characterized. We evaluated the incidence, determinants, and outcomes of IHCA among critically ill patients with cardiogenic shock. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the MIMIC-IV v3.1 database. Adult ICU patients with cardiogenic shock were identified using ICD-9 code 785.51 and ICD-10 code R57.0. IHCA was identified using ICD-9 code 427.5 and ICD-10 codes I46, I46.2, I46.8, and I46.9. Laboratory, hemodynamic, and cardiovascular phenotype data were extracted from the first 24 hours of ICU admission. Prespecified Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify predictors of IHCA and predictors of in-hospital mortality among patients who experienced cardiac arrest. Model discrimination was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Results: Among 3,875 ICU admissions with cardiogenic shock, 11.4% experienced IHCA. Patients with IHCA had significantly higher in-hospital mortality compared with those without IHCA (63.6% vs. 33.4%, p<0.001). In multivariable analysis, VT/VF was the strongest independent predictor of IHCA (adjusted odds ratio[aOR]4.25,95% CI 3.36-5.39, p<0.001). Additional independent predictors included higher lactate, lower bicarbonate and lower minimum MAP. HFrEF was associated with lower odds of IHCA (aOR 0.56, 95% CI 0.44-0.72, p<0.001). The prediction model demonstrated good discrimination (AUC 0.77). Among patients with IHCA, mortality varied by phenotype and was highest among patients with HFpEF (79.5%) and lowest among those with HFrEF (53.5%). Mortality was 56.9% among VT/VF-associated arrests versus 70.2% among non-VT/VF arrests. However, in multivariable analysis, VT/VF was not independently associated with in-hospital mortality following cardiac arrest (aOR 0.91, 95% CI 0.55-1.52, p=0.71). Instead, older age, higher lactate concentration, and lower bicarbonate c independently predicted mortality following cardiac arrest. HFrEF remained independently associated with lower mortality (aOR 0.58, 95% CI 0.34-0.98, p=0.041), whereas VT/VF, acute myocardial infarction, minimum mean arterial pressure, sex, and HFpEF were not independently associated with mortality after adjustment. Post-arrest mortality model: AUC = 0.801. Conclusions: IHCA occurred in approximately one in nine ICU patients with cardiogenic shock and was associated with markedly increased mortality. VT/VF and markers of severe hypoperfusion and metabolic derangement independently predicted cardiac arrest, whereas post-arrest mortality was primarily driven by age, lactate elevation, and metabolic acidosis. Early identification of high-risk patients may facilitate enhanced monitoring and timely escalation of support.

items.title: Abstract P2008: Edaravone and Dexborneol Attenuate Neurovascular Injury and Neuroinflammatory Remodeling After Cardiac Arrest and Resuscitation
items.abstract: Background: Brain injury after cardiac arrest (CA) and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) remains a major cause of mortality and long-term neurological disability, yet neuroprotective therapies are limited. Edaravone and dexborneol injection has shown neuroprotective activity in ischemic brain injury, but its effect on post-cardiac arrest brain injury and the associated neuroinflammatory programs remain unclear. Methods: Male Sprague-Dawley rats undergoing CA/CPR were assigned to Sham, CPR, or CPR + edaravone/dexborneol groups. Survival, neurological deficit scores, grip strength, open-field behavior, and Y-maze performance were assessed after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Blood-brain barrier injury was evaluated using Evans blue/FITC-dextran leakage and western blotting for claudin-5, occludin, ZO-1, MMP2, and MMP9. Neuronal apoptosis was examined by TUNEL staining and caspase-3/cleaved caspase-3 western blotting. Cortex and hippocampus were analyzed by RNA sequencing, followed by differential expression, rescue-pattern, pathway enrichment, module-score, and STRING-based network analyses. Representative inflammatory genes and proteins were selected for targeted validation. Results: Edaravone/dexborneol improved survival and neurological recovery after resuscitation, with better grip strength, exploratory activity, and spatial recognition than untreated CPR animals. Treatment reduced vascular leakage, restored tight-junction protein expression, and attenuated MMP2/9-associated blood-brain barrier disruption. TUNEL and cleaved caspase-3 analysis indicated reduced neuronal apoptosis. Transcriptomic profiling revealed CPR-induced inflammatory remodeling in both cortex and hippocampus that was partially attenuated by edaravone/dexborneol. Enrichment and module-level analyses showed convergence on innate immune sensing, interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) programs, complement/coagulation cascades, NOD-like receptor signaling, and NF-κB-related inflammatory pathways. Shared rescue-pattern genes formed an interferon (IFN)/ISG-centered interaction cluster, including Ifit1, Irf7, Ddx58 / Rig1, Ube2l6, Gbp2, Parp9, Mx2, and Bst2 . Complement/glial-response genes, including C1qa, C1qc, C3, and Lgals3 , were also induced after CPR and attenuated after treatment. Conclusions: Edaravone/dexborneol attenuates post-resuscitation brain injury by improving neurological outcomes, preserving neurovascular integrity, reducing neuronal apoptosis, and suppressing inflammatory transcriptional remodeling. These findings support edaravone/dexborneol as a neuroprotective strategy for post-cardiac arrest brain injury and identify interferon and C3-associated complement/glial responses as testable inflammatory signatures for further mechanistic validation.

items.title: Abstract P1076: Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Re-Cannulation: Patient Characteristics, Clinical Outcomes, and Predictors of Success at a High-Volume Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Center
items.abstract: Background: Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is a rescue therapy for refractory cardiac arrest and severe shock. Although cannulation strategies are standardized, decannulation decisions remain variable. When hemodynamic collapse occurs after decannulation, emergent re-cannulation may be the only life-saving option. Outcomes after a second VA-ECMO run during the same hospitalization are poorly defined, particularly among extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) patients, a group often presumed to have especially poor prognosis. Hypothesis: A second VA-ECMO run during the same hospitalization is associated with meaningful survival to discharge. Aim: To evaluate survival and predictors of outcome after repeat VA-ECMO cannulation during the same hospitalization. Methods: This is a retrospective single-center study of patients who underwent two VA-ECMO runs during a single hospitalization between 2016-2024. Among 1,000 patients treated with VA-ECMO, 40 required emergent re-initiation after initial decannulation. Clinical characteristics, indications for re-cannulation, survival to hospital discharge and predictors of outcome at the time of re-cannulation were analyzed. Results: Survival to hospital discharge after repeat VA-ECMO was 32.5% (Table 1). The most common indications for re-cannulation were refractory cardiogenic shock (52%) and cardiac arrest requiring ECPR (40%) (Table 2). Patients re-cannulated for ECPR had survival comparable to, and numerically higher than, those re-cannulated for other indications, including refractory cardiogenic shock (44% versus 24%; p=0.29). Survivors were younger and less likely to have a history of coronary artery bypass grafting (Table 1). At the time of re-cannulation, survivors had lower serum lactate, international normalized ratio levels and higher platelet counts (Table 2). On multivariable analysis, older age and higher serum lactate were independently associated with mortality. Conclusions: Repeat VA-ECMO cannulation was associated with meaningful survival after post-decannulation hemodynamic collapse. The observation that patients re-cannulated for ECPR had outcomes similar to, and numerically better than other major re-cannulation groups, challenges the assumption that repeat ECPR is uniformly futile and suggests that carefully selected patients may still derive substantial benefit. Younger age and less severe metabolic derangement at the time of re-cannulation were associated with improved outcomes.

items.title: Abstract P1081: Do Cognitive Biases Impact Adherence to Resuscitation Guidelines in Simulated Pediatric Cardiac Arrest?
items.abstract: Introduction: Variation in outcomes after pediatric cardiac arrest may be driven by inconsistent adherence to Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) guidelines. Time to defibrillation is a key metric for patients with presenting rhythm of ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VF/pVT), and delays >2 minutes are associated with a lower likelihood of survival. Interventions to improve resuscitation performance, such as CPR coaching, may offload cognitive demands on resuscitation team leaders. Excess cognitive loading has been associated with diagnostic error due to cognitive biases. Pertinent biases include the framing bias, in which the way information is initially presented impacts clinical decision-making, and the anchoring bias, which creates overreliance on initial impressions. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that cognitive biases influence resuscitation performance in simulated pediatric cardiac arrest. Specifically, events framed as non-cardiac in origin (septic shock in an oncology patient) would result in simulation teams being slower to defibrillate shockable rhythms versus events framed with a cardiac etiology (myocarditis with ventricular dysfunction). Methods: This study is a secondary analysis of a simulation-based study conducted at a quaternary children’s hospital to evaluate the impact of room design on resuscitation practices. Simulation teams of physicians, NPs, RNs, and respiratory therapists participated in two simulations with different clinical prompts both leading to cardiac arrest with initial rhythm of pVT. Team-based performance variables were abstracted from audio and video recordings including time stamps for cardiac arrest, initiation of compressions, first dose of epinephrine (if given), and defibrillation. Chest compression quality data were collected via Zoll OneStep Electrodes. Results: For all 38 simulations, average time to defibrillation was 3.4 minutes (95% CI = 3.0-3.8 mins). In 47% of simulations, epinephrine was given before defibrillation, despite the presence of a shockable rhythm. For myocarditis scenarios, defibrillation was the first intervention 58% of the time, versus 47% of the time for septic shock, though the difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.51). In simulations where epinephrine was given first, time to defibrillation increased to 3.9 minutes (95% CI=3.1-4.7 min), versus 2.9 minutes (95% CI=2.6-3.3 min) for simulations where a shock was administered first (p = 0.011). Conclusions: Clinical framing in a simulated resuscitation may activate cognitive biases that impact adherence to PALS guidelines. Administering a dose of epinephrine as the first intervention resulted in a statistically significant delay in the time to appropriate defibrillation in simulated cardiac arrest with a presenting rhythm of pVT.

items.title: Abstract P1082: Characteristics and Outcomes of Adult and Pediatric In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Adult and pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) have historically differed in baseline characteristics, etiologies, event features, interventions, and outcomes. Advances in arrest prevention and resuscitation practices may have narrowed these gaps, but contemporary comparisons are limited. We evaluated differences in characteristics and outcomes between pediatric and adult IHCA in a large national registry in North America. Methods: Using the GWTG-Resuscitation database, we identified index IHCA events requiring chest compressions for at least 1 minute between 2015 and 2024, excluding pandemic years 2020-2022. The exposure was age group (pediatric <18 years vs adult). Outcomes included survival to hospital discharge, return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), and favorable neurological outcome (adult cerebral performance category [CPC] 1–2 or pediatric CPC 1–3). Generalized estimating equations were used for clustering by hospital and event year; pre-arrest factors were treated as mediators. Standard mean differences (SMDs) with SMD >0.1 or <-0.1 indicated meaningful differences. Results: The cohort included 161,162 adults and 3,749 children with IHCA. Adults had lower odds of survival to discharge (26% vs 46%; odds ratio [OR] 0.44, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.41-0.47), favorable neurological outcome (18% vs 33%; OR 0.52, 95% CI 0.46-0.57), and ROSC (73% vs 78%; OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.74–0.88) compared with children. Adults were more likely to present with VF/pVT (16% vs 10%, SMD -0.17), yet lower adult survival persisted after stratifying by initial rhythm: for non-shockable rhythms, survival was 22% vs 44% (OR 0.50, 95% CI 0.48–0.52), and for shockable rhythms, 45% vs 52% (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78–0.97) for adults and children respectively. Children were more likely than adults to arrest in an ICU (69% vs 38%; SMD 0.66), receive calcium during CPR (44% vs 35%; SMD 0.18), and undergo ECPR (12% vs <1%; SMD 0.50). Adults more commonly received sodium bicarbonate (55% vs 48%; SMD 0.15) and amiodarone (20% vs 5%; SMD 0.49) during CPR. Conclusion: In this large IHCA registry, adults had approximately half the odds of survival to discharge and favorable neurological outcome compared with children, despite only modestly lower odds of ROSC. These survival differences were not explained by initial rhythm and occurred in the setting of marked differences in care setting, pre-arrest support, and resuscitation practices, highlighting age-specific targets to improve outcomes. Future directions include contrasting etiology of arrest and post-arrest care practices.

items.title: Abstract P1083: Building a High-Impact Resuscitation Committee to Drive Systemwide Clinical Excellence
items.abstract: Introduction: Medical emergencies require rapid, coordinated responses to optimize outcomes; however, variability in training, role clarity, and adherence to evidence-based practices are common. To address these gaps, a multidisciplinary Resuscitation Committee was established to oversee clinical support, quality improvement, and education for a hospital’s Medical Emergency Response Team. With executive sponsorship, committee structure was designed to ensure accountability, frontline engagement, and system-level reliability. Research Questions: This initiative aimed to determine whether a structured, interdisciplinary resuscitation committee could improve guideline adherence, team preparedness, and patient outcomes. We hypothesized that a formalized committee model integrating practice, education, and quality review would enhance resuscitation performance and support sustained improvement in survival outcomes. Methods: The committee operates using a three-arm framework: Practice, Clinical Support, and Quality. The Practice arm standardizes workflows, equipment, and code processes, with continuous refinement based on real event feedback. The Clinical Support arm provides structured onboarding, simulation-based training, and annual competencies to reinforce role mastery and team dynamics. The Quality arm reviews all resuscitation events through weekly multidisciplinary debriefs and bi-monthly trend analysis, incorporating metrics such as ROSC, survival to discharge, neurologic outcomes, and adherence to AHA guidelines. Results: Committee membership grew from 10 members in 2019 to 49 in 2025, reflecting increased institutional engagement. Survival to discharge improved from 20.8% in 2017 to 29.3% in 2024, representing a 40% increase from baseline, with rates consistently above 28% in past years. The institution received the American Heart Association Get With The Guidelines-Gold Award from 2020-2025. Conclusion: A structured, interdisciplinary resuscitation committee using a three-arm model can drive measurable improvements in resuscitation performance, guideline adherence, and patient outcomes. Integrating frontline clinical staff into shared governance enables sustainable system-wide change, improved operational efficiency, and enhanced emergency response reliability. This model is scalable and replicable for organizations seeking to strengthen resuscitation systems and achieve high-level clinical performance recognition.

items.title: Abstract P2002: Artificial Intelligence Analysis to Detect Acute Coronary Occlusion During Active Ventricular Fibrillation in a Preclinical Model of Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: During ventricular fibrillation (VF), conventional ECG interpretation cannot identify acute coronary occlusion (ACO). Rapid detection of ACO during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) could facilitate targeted resuscitation and triage strategies. Hypothesis: Artificial intelligence (AI) analysis of VF waveforms can distinguish ischemic VF caused by ACO from non-ischemic VF without coronary occlusion. Methods: Female Yorkshire swine undergoing standardized VF OHCA experiments were classified as ischemic VF (I-VF) following proximal left anterior descending artery occlusion or non-ischemic VF (N-VF) induced without coronary occlusion. Lead II ECGs sampled at 250 Hz during the first 3 minutes of untreated VF were segmented into 10-second windows. Four AI models were developed: convolutional neural network (CNN), random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), and decision tree (DT). Model development used 4-fold cross-validation on 56 animals (20 I-VF, 36 N-VF) with oversampling of the minority class to address class imbalance. An independent, balanced holdout test set of 16 animals (8 I-VF, 8 N-VF) assessed generalizability. Performance was evaluated using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), sensitivity, specificity, bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals (CI), and DeLong testing. Results: The CNN demonstrated superior discrimination compared with all other models in both the development and test datasets (all p<0.05 by DeLong testing). In the development dataset, the CNN achieved an AUC of 0.93 (95% CI 0.91-0.94), sensitivity of 0.84 (95% CI 0.79-0.87), and specificity of 0.89 (95% CI 0.86-0.91). Performance remained robust in the independent test dataset, with an AUC of 0.91 (95% CI 0.88-0.94), sensitivity of 0.85 (95% CI 0.79-0.90), and specificity of 0.83 (95% CI 0.77-0.89). At a clinically relevant fixed sensitivity of 90%, specificity was 0.76 (95% CI 0.66-0.86) on the test set. Conclusions: AI-based analysis of VF waveforms can identify ACO during active VF with clinically meaningful accuracy in a porcine model of OHCA. If validated in human cohorts, this approach could support real-time triage, reperfusion decision-making, and personalized resuscitation strategies during VF cardiac arrest.

items.title: Abstract P1078: Association of Transport Difficulty with Prehospital Time and Clinical Outcomes in Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Study in Japan
items.abstract: Background: In Japan, Emergency Medical Services (EMS) personnel must obtain prior approval from the hospital before transporting a patient, which can cause refusal of admission or delays in treatment. Pediatric patients may be particularly affected because hospitals and specialists capable of managing pediatric emergencies are limited. Although transport difficulty has been associated with adverse outcomes in adults, its impact in pediatric OHCA remains unclear. Hypothesis: Transport difficulty is associated with prolonged prehospital time and worse clinical outcomes in pediatric OHCA. Methods: We conducted a retrospective nationwide, population-based study using the All-Japan Utstein Registry linked with emergency transport records from 2021 to 2023. Pediatric patients (<20 years) with OHCA were included. Transport difficulty was defined as ≥4 hospital acceptance requests before transport. Total prehospital time (emergency call to hospital arrival) was categorized into call-to-scene arrival time, scene time (scene arrival to departure), and transport time (scene departure to hospital arrival). The primary outcome was 1-month survival. Secondary outcomes were a favorable neurological outcome (CPC 1-2) and prehospital ROSC. Primary analyses compared patients with transport difficulty (≥4 requests) and those without (≤3 requests). Exploratory analyses evaluated outcomes according to the number of hospital acceptance requests. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, witnessed arrest, bystander CPR, initial rhythm, cause of arrest, population density, and regional pediatric healthcare resources, including pediatric intensive care units, pediatric core hospitals, and tertiary emergency centers. Results: Among 3,967 pediatric OHCA patients, transport difficulty occurred in 106 (2.7%) (Table 1). Patients with transport difficulty had no significant difference in call-to-scene arrival time compared to those without the difficulty (9 vs 9 min, p= 0.290) but had longer scene time (16 vs 10 min) and total prehospital time (47 vs 31 min) (both p<0.001) (Table 2). ROSC before hospital arrival (6.6% vs 8.3%, p=0.650), 1-month survival (6.6% vs 13.1%, p=0.070), and favorable neurological outcome (3.8% vs 4.8%, p=0.810) did not significantly differ between groups. In exploratory analyses, observed 1-month survival rates were 12.9% for 1 call (reference), 15.0% for 2 calls (adjusted OR 1.15 [95% CI 0.82-1.58]), 11.2% for 3 calls (adjusted OR 0.82 [95% CI 0.42-1.49]), and 6.6% for ≥4 calls (adjusted OR 0.57 [95% CI 0.23-1.23]) (Figure 1). Conclusions: Transport difficulty was associated with prolonged prehospital time in pediatric OHCA. Despite no statistically significant association, the adjusted odds ratio for survival decreased as the requests increased. Further analysis with a larger sample size is needed to clarify this association.

items.title: Abstract P1080: Early Calcium Administration During Pediatric In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Though national resuscitation guidelines recommend against routine use of calcium except in special circumstances, it is often given during pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (pIHCA) for its vasoactive qualities. While observational studies have consistently shown associations between intra-arrest calcium and increased mortality, these studies failed to account for the timing of calcium administration, leading to high risk for resuscitation time bias. Aim: To examine the association of early calcium with outcomes from pIHCA. Research Question: Is early calcium associated with decreased odds of survival to hospital discharge or ROSC? Methods: This was a single-center retrospective study including patients ≤18 years old who had a pulseless IHCA from 2013-2023. The exposure was early calcium, defined as calcium administration within 5 minutes of CPR initiation. To ensure a similar timeframe for early calcium exposure across the cohort, patients who received CPR for <5 minutes were excluded. The primary and secondary outcomes were survival to hospital discharge and sustained ROSC, respectively. Logistic treatment-effects estimation utilizing inverse-probability weighting via a propensity score was used. A regression model was used to balance the groups with covariates selected a priori based on a patient’s propensity to receive early calcium: age, initial rhythm, illness category, interventions in place before arrest, presence of hyperkalemia, and presence of hypocalcemia. Because illness category, initial rhythm, and hyperkalemia did not achieve balance after weighting, they were included as covariates in the outcome model. Results: Of 242 patients, 64 (26%) received early calcium. In the univariate analyses, patients who received early calcium were more likely to be younger, have cardiac malformations, baseline central nervous system depression, hepatic insufficiency, and vasoactive infusions in place prior to arrest (Table 1). Early calcium administration varied by event location and time of event (Table 2). The median duration of CPR was longer in the early calcium cohort (27 minutes) compared with no early calcium (19 minutes; p=0.038). For the primary and secondary analyses using weighted cohorts, there were no differences in survival to hospital discharge (aOR 0.97, 95%CI 0.5-1.87, p=0.9) or ROSC (aOR 0.54, 95%CI 0.28-1.04, p=0.065; Table 3). Conclusions: In this weighted pIHCA cohort, there were no statistically significant differences in odds of survival to discharge or ROSC between patients who did and did not receive calcium in the first 5 minutes of CPR. Further work is needed to understand various time points of calcium administration and its effect on outcomes.

items.title: Abstract P1088: Predictors and Outcomes of Post-Intubation Cardiac Arrest in Critically Ill Adults
items.abstract: Background: Cardiac arrest following endotracheal intubation is a rare but catastrophic complication in critically ill patients. Data describing its incidence, predictors, and outcomes in large ICU populations remain limited. We evaluated the incidence, risk factors, and outcomes of early post-intubation cardiac arrest (PICA) in a large critical care cohort. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the MIMIC-IV v3.1 database. Adult ICU patients undergoing endotracheal intubation were identified using procedure event records. The primary outcome was cardiac arrest occurring within 6 hours of the first recorded intubation. Secondary outcomes included cardiac arrest within 1 hour and 24 hours of intubation. Demographic characteristics, comorbidities, pre-intubation laboratory values, hemodynamic parameters, and vasopressor use were extracted. A prespecified multivariable logistic regression was performed to identify independent predictors of PICA. Results: A total of 8,463 intubated ICU stays were identified. Post-intubation cardiac arrest within 6 hours occurred in 62 patients (0.73%), including 40 arrests within 1 hour (0.47%) and 103 arrests within 24 hours (1.22%). Patients experiencing PICA had higher pre-intubation lactate levels (4.42±3.18 vs 2.98±2.70 mmol/L, p<0.001), higher heart rates (117.0±22.2 vs 104.9±23.5 beats/min, p<0.001), lower minimum systolic blood pressure (91.4±26.1 vs 105.9±25.4 mmHg, p<0.001), higher creatinine levels (2.22±1.77 vs 1.72±1.73 mg/dL, p=0.030), and higher white blood cell counts (16.7±10.5 vs 13.7±10.4 х10 9 /L, p=0.032). Heart failure (43.5% vs 30.3%, p=0.033), sepsis (53.2% vs 31.6%, p<0.001), shock (17.7% vs 6.7%, p=0.001), and pre-intubation vasopressor use (33.9% vs 22.0%, p=0.036) were more common among patients who developed PICA.Hospital mortality was substantially higher among patients with PICA compared with those without PICA (82.3% vs 28.1%, p<0.001). In multivariable analysis, higher pre-intubation heart rate (adjusted OR 1.161 per 10 beats/min, 95% CI 1.020-1.306) and lower pre-intubation mean arterial pressure (adjusted OR 0.698 per 10 mmHg, 95% CI 0.560-0.869) were independently associated with PICA. Elevated lactate (adjusted OR 1.09 per mmol/L, 95% CI 0.99-1.17) and creatinine (adjusted OR 1.12 per mg/dL, 95% CI 0.98-1.24) demonstrated modest associations that did not reach statistical significance. Conclusions: Post-intubation cardiac arrest occurred in approximately 1 in 137 intubated ICU patients and was associated with extremely high in-hospital mortality exceeding 80%. Pre-intubation tachycardia and hypotension independently identified patients at the highest risk, suggesting the hypothesis that hemodynamic optimization before intubation may be an important target for prevention.

items.title: Abstract P2005: Contrastive Language and Image Reasoning - A Novel Multimodal Deep Learning Framework for Post-Anoxic Brain Injury Prognostication
items.abstract: Anoxic brain injury (ABI) classification after cardiac arrest is critical to determining eligibility for neuroprotective therapies such as therapeutic hypothermia. Subjectivity in determining injury severity on diagnostics such as CT confound and delay accurate classification and prognostication. The current standard for objective CT-based ABI classification relies on manual gray-white matter ratio (GWR) measurement, which is time-intensive and limited by variability across CT scanners, hindering its utility for time-sensitive decision-making in the early post-arrest window. In this study, we introduce contrastive language and image reasoning with masked autoencoders (CLAIR), a novel multimodal framework integrating head computed tomography (CT) imaging with non-imaging clinical patient information through a cross-attention mechanism and contrastive learning approach to predict dichotomized cerebral performance category (CPC) score in patients after cardiac arrest. We benchmarked CLAIR against manual measurements and an automated, CT only-based masked autoencoder approach (CT-MAE) in a retrospective study of 208 patients with CT scans obtained within the first 24 hours of arrest. Manual GWR and CT-MAE achieved comparable overall discriminative performance (AUC-ROC: 0.87 and 0.80, respectively); however, manual GWR was limited by low specificity (0.54), with important implications for withdrawal-of-care decisions, while CT-MAE offered the advantage of full automation without sacrificing accuracy. Critically, neither imaging-only approach alone achieved sufficient predictive performance to independently guide clinical decision-making. In contrast, CLAIR achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.94 (CI: 0.90-0.97) when trained on multiplanar CT reconstructions combined with non-imaging clinical data, significantly outperforming CT-based imaging-only methods (p = 0.03) and surpassing the manual GWR clinical standard. To further evaluate clinical utility of CLAIR, we conducted a structured clinical assessment comparing CLAIR against two clinicians, a senior neurology resident and an attending neurointensivist, across a series of tests simulating varying levels of information availability during the post-arrest course. Clinicians assisted by CLAIR predictions made fewer prognostic errors than in their non-assisted assessments. Our results suggest that CLAIR can contribute value as a clinical assistive tool aiming at reliable ABI classification for post-cardiac arrest patients, potentially enabling more timely clinical decision-making, family counseling, and resource allocation.

items.title: Abstract P2006: Automated Classification of Shock-Refractory Ventricular Fibrillation Subtypes
items.abstract: Background: Refractory ventricular fibrillation (R-VF) out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients—pragmatically defined as those requiring ≥3 shocks—experience lower likelihood of resuscitation and survival compared to non-refractory patients. R-VF subtypes can further stratify patients by prognosis which could help guide treatment. Specifically, incessant R-VF (shocks fail to terminate VF) fare worse than recurrent R-VF (shocks terminate VF but VF recurs); hence incessant R-VF outcomes may be improved with targeted, alternative treatment strategies. However, identification of incessant R-VF has been limited to retrospective studies requiring post-hoc ECG rhythm review, challenging real-time implementation of a targeted strategy. We evaluated whether a deep learning-based rhythm classification algorithm designed for real-time use can determine shock response to classify patients by R-VF subtype as a means to consider clinical implementation of subtype-specific therapies. Objective: We evaluated automated classification of individual VF shock responses and patient-level R-VF subtypes using a “see-through-CPR” rhythm identification algorithm. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult VF-OHCA from 2006-21 from a metropolitan EMS system using continuous defibrillator ECG recordings. The gold standard annotation used a previously-published, 2-person review of immediate post-shock rhythm to determine shock-specific response (incessant vs. recurrent) and consequent patient-level classification (incessant only, recurrent only, or mixed). These annotations were compared with predictions from a previously-described deep learning rhythm classifier. Data were split into training and test sets. We selected a VF probability cut point that maximized F1 score in the training set for classifying shock-specific R-VF subtypes, and calculated accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of the automated algorithm relative to the gold standard annotations. Results: Among 1790 VF patients, median age was 62, 392 (22%) were female, 999 (56%) were refractory, and 760 (43%) survived with favorable status. Based on the gold standard annotations, R-VF shock-specific response was incessant in 35% and recurrent in 65% of shocks, producing patient-level classification of 16% incessant only, 46% recurrent only, and 37% mixed. Among the R-VF test set, the algorithm achieved a shock-specific accuracy of 93% (Table 1) and a patient-level 3-category accuracy of 88% (Table 2), with an incessant classification sensitivity of 0.81 (43/53) and specificity of 0.98 (276/282). Conclusions: An automated “see-through-CPR” rhythm identification algorithm can evaluate shock-specific rhythm response to achieve classification of R-VF subtypes including incessant R-VF, providing the potential to guide differential treatment strategies in real-time.

items.title: Abstract P1084: Relationships Among Excessive Responders & Survival of In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction/Background: Successful management of in-hospital cardiac arrests (IHCAs) depends on timely interventions, effective communication, and coordinated teamwork. Healthcare organizations commonly monitor outcomes using measures such as spontaneous circulation, survival to discharge (STD), and resuscitation guideline adherence. Review of IHCAs at a Level One Academic Trauma Center revealed variability in responder numbers. Resuscitation event critiques suggested that excessive responders during IHCAs created barriers to communication, role clarity, and overall workflow efficiency. Quality improvement efforts primarily focus on clinical interventions and documentation accuracy, with less attention given to how physical environments may influence patient outcomes during IHCAs. Research Question/Hypothesis: Is there a relationship between responder overcrowding during an IHCA and survivability? Goals/Aims: The aim of this study was to evaluate the relationship between responder overcrowding during IHCA event survival and STD. Methods/Approach: This retrospective study reviewed resuscitation event critiques from 1/1/2023 to 12/31/25. Patients who underwent an IHCA were included and those under the age of 18 years, outpatients, visitors, experienced more than one IHCA, and emergency department and operating room events were excluded. The Chi-Square Test for Independence evaluated the potential association between the number of appropriate responders (i.e., ≤ 13 responders) versus overcrowded (i.e., ≥ 14 responders) and survival of an IHCA and STD (i.e., Expired or Survived). Yates’ Correction for Continuity was reported for both outcomes. Results/Data: A Chi-Square Test for Independence indicated no significant association between survivability of an IHCA event and crowd status, χ 2 (1, n = 290 = 0.610, p = 0.435, phi = -0.055. A Chi-Square Test for Independence indicated no significant association between STD and crowd status, χ 2 (1, n = 290 = 2.934, p = 0.087, phi = -0.111. Conclusions: Although there were no significant associations between survivability of an IHCA and crowd status, this project demonstrated clinical significance. For example, qualitatively exploring emergency team responder perceptions of crowd status and the impact on IHCAs. Future research implications include additional factors that may impact survivability such as deviations from Advanced Cardiac Life Support and post-cardiac arrest care guidelines.

items.title: Abstract P1086: Shock Trajectories and Practice Variation After In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Retrospective Analysis of the Discover-IHCA Registry
items.abstract: Background: Cardiac arrest affects over 500,000 Americans annually and remains a major public health challenge. Post-cardiac arrest shock—defined as inadequate oxygen delivery to vital organs—occurs in over 70% of initial survivors and contributes substantially to mortality and organ dysfunction. While post-arrest shock following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) has been extensively studied, data on in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) is limited. Research Objectives: The objectives of this study are to characterize the epidemiology, treatment patterns, and trajectory of shock following IHCA, including progression/resolution, evaluate associations with organ dysfunction, vasopressor selection, organ support, and clinical outcomes Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of patients with IHCA using the Discover-IHCA registry. Post-arrest variables included vasoactive medication use, organ support methods, and cardiac sequential organ failure assessment score (cSOFA). The primary exposure was post-arrest shock; the primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included organ dysfunction requiring organ support, survival at 24, 48 and 72 hours. We present descriptive statistics as means or medians where appropriate. Paired comparisons between pre- and post-arrest organ support were performed using McNemars where appropriate. A covariate-adjusted logistic regression model was also developed. Results: We included 955 adult patients across 69 hospitals. Of these, 339 (35.5%) were female. The majority (42.2%) of individuals were age > 70 (Table 1). Primary respiratory causes were the most common etiology of arrest (n = 316, 33.1%), followed by primary cardiac (n = 250, 26.2%). A total of 742 patients (77.7%) experienced post-arrest shock, defined as any use of vasopressor/inotrope (n = 666, 69.7%), mechanical circulatory support (intra-aortic balloon pump/impella) (n = 30, 3.14%), or initiation of VA-ECMO (n = 46, 4.82%). Norepinephrine was the most common vasopressor (n = 709, 74.2%). Comparison of pre- versus post-arrest organ support showed significant increases in multiple interventions (Table 2). Higher weighted cSOFA burden was associated with higher odds of in-hospital death (OR =1.95, 95% CI 1.73-2.19, p < 0.001) (Figure 1). Conclusions: Over three-quarters of patients with IHCA suffer post-arrest shock. Significant increases in organ support occur after IHCA. Higher cSOFA scores post-arrest was strongly associated with in hospital death. Future analyses will explore patient centered outcomes and variations in IHCA management.

items.title: Abstract P2003: Automated Video Review of Cardiac Arrest Resuscitation Using Multimodal Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Introduction: Video review is a powerful resource in quality improvement and research of high mortality rates of out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (OHCAs). Manual review is time and resource-intensive, limiting implementation at scale. Hypothesis: Automating the video review process is feasible using Artificial Intelligence (AI). Aim: We assessed the feasibility and accuracy of Google’s Gemini AI in reviewing cardiac arrest resuscitation simulations in the Emergency Department (ED). Methods: Eight pediatric OHCA simulation videos with identical scenarios were reviewed by trained investigators and Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro model. Data points were extracted blinded to study results. Inter-rater reliability of reviewers was 0.78. Simulations included a team leader, charting nurse, medication nurse, and four research actors (CPR provider/coach, bedside nurse, airway provider). Videos were captured with a GoPro Hero 12 Black camera and compressed using HandBrake to optimize AI processing. AI was instructed to act as a clinical expert in cardiac resuscitation, tasked with reviewing technical and non-technical aspects of care. Human reviewers and AI were given definitions of each critical event, Concise Assessment of Leader Management (CALM) tool, and teamwork assessment (TEAM) tool. Technical variables included critical event timestamps (cardiac arrest recognition, compression initiation, pulse/rhythm assessment/identification). Non-technical variables included TEAM and CALM scores. Human vs AI results were compared using intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) values and Bland Altman plots. Results: AI demonstrated excellent agreement with humans on technical variables (ICC ≥0.94). A total of 142 timestamps were included, with 9 events (6.3%) discordant between human and AI. Time to critical events showed a mean difference of -2.32 seconds with limits of agreement from -12.76 to +8.12 seconds (Figure 1), reflecting expected variability across clinical actions. Non-technical variable agreement was moderate. TEAM scores showed a mean difference of 7.25 points (range 1.83 to 12.67) (Figure 2); CALM scores showed a mean difference of 1.12 points (range -7.15 to 9.40) (Figure 3). ICC for non-technical variables were poor (TEAM: 0.022, CALM: 0.31). Conclusions: AI showed excellent concordance for technical metrics but requires refinement for non-technical variables. Results support automating video analysis of cardiac resuscitation to improve efficiency and scalability.

items.title: Abstract P1077: Pediatric In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in Cardiac ICUs: Benefit of Linking AHA GWTG ® -R AND PC 4 Registries
items.abstract: Background: Significant heterogeneity exists in pediatric cardiac intensive care unit (CICU) populations that suffer in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA). While individual registries provide sizable cohorts, they lack diagnostic and procedural granularity. We propose a novel linkage of national cardiac arrest and pediatric cardiac critical care quality registries to evaluate IHCA in children with heart disease, characterize cardiac disease profiles, and identify unique outcome-related risk factors. Methods: We linked the American Heart Association’s Get With the Guidelines-Resuscitation (GWTG-R) and the Pediatric Cardiac Critical Care Consortium (PC 4 ) registries. We included medical (MC) and surgical (SC) cardiac patients < 18 years of age admitted to CICUs between 8/1/2014-2/13/2023 with an index IHCA event. Cross-referencing identified 22 centers participating in both registries (Fig. 1). Primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge (SHD). Secondary outcomes were return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), return of circulation via extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ROC), and survival with a favorable neurologic outcome (FNO) from GWTG-R, defined by pediatric cerebral performance category (PCPC) scores. A composite survival with FNO variable was created by adding neurologic complications collected in PC 4 to GWTG-R’s definition. Generalized linear mixed-effects models accounting for hospital clustering examined associations between illness categories, and within MC subgroups, with outcomes. Adjustment covariates included single ventricle (SV) and congenital heart disease (CHD) status derived from PC 4 . Results: A total of 1,012 children were evaluated (418 MC; 594 SC); 42% were infants, 27% were SV, 85% had CHD, and 51% of SC patients had STAT 4-5 operations (Table 1). IHCA cumulative incidence was 0.91% for STAT 1-3 and 4.6% for STAT 4-5. Median CPR duration was similar between groups (MC 9 [IQR 3-35] vs SC 13 [IQR 3-38] mins, p=0.10). Overall, SHD was 55%, FNO in survivors was 62%, and composite FNO in survivors was 53%. In multivariable models, MC patients had lower odds of SHD (OR 0.45 [0.32-0.62]), ROSC (OR 0.43 [0.27-0.69]) and ROC (OR 0.38 [0.24-0.58]) compared to SC groups (Table 2). Among MC cohorts, having CHD was associated with lower odds of ROSC (OR 0.35 [0.14-0.88]) and ROC (OR 0.44 [0.20-0.96]), but similar SHD versus those with structurally normal hearts. No differences in FNO or composite FNO were seen between MC and SC cohorts. Conclusion: In this linkage analysis, adjusted for covariates including SV and CHD status, MC patients had higher hospital mortality compared with SC patients. Although MC cohorts with CHD had lower rates of ROSC and ROC, SHD was similar to MC patients without CHD. This study framework enables new procedure- and complexity-specific insights not feasible in either registry alone to more accurately predict outcomes.

items.title: Abstract P2001: Generative Models for Synthesizing Cardiac Arrest Electrocardiograms With and Without Chest Compression Artifact
items.abstract: Background: ECG rhythm assessment during resuscitation of ventricular fibrillation/tachycardia (VF/VT) out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) requires CPR interruption because CPR causes ECG artifacts. Ideally defibrillators would use artificial intelligence (AI) for binary (non-shockable vs. shockable) and 3-class (asystole [ASY] vs. organized [ORG] vs. shockable [VF/VT]) ECG classification during CPR to guide diagnosis and treatment. However, algorithm development is challenged by a paucity of OHCA ECGs, particularly during CPR. Goal: We built generative AI models to synthesize OHCA ECGs with and without CPR artifact to (1) determine whether classifiers trained with synthetic (artificial) ECGs can classify real (clinical) ECGs, and (2) compare performance between classifiers trained with real vs. synthetic ECGs. Methods: We performed a retrospective study of adult VF-OHCA from 2006-2021 in a metropolitan EMS system. Patients were randomized 80%/20% for training/test. Defibrillator pad ECGs clipped into 2.5-s segments were manually labeled by CPR and rhythm (ASY, ORG, VF, VT) by expert reviewers. Using training ECGs, we first developed generative adversarial networks (GAN) and diffusion models (DM) to synthesize ASY, ORG, and VF/VT ECGs with and without CPR. Then using (1) the real training ECGs, (2) GAN-generated ECGs, and (3) DM-generated ECGs, classifiers were trained for binary (ASY/ORG vs. VF/VT) and 3-class (ASY vs. ORG vs. VF/VT) rhythm prediction. Classifiers included 1-D convolutional neural networks (CNNs) with ECG voltages as inputs and 2-D CNNs with ECG scalograms as inputs. To evaluate synthetic data utility, we compared classifiers trained with real vs. synthetic data in the test dataset using binary (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC], F1 score) and 3-class (balanced accuracy [BAC]) metrics. Results: The cohort had 2011 patients with 1.03 million ECGs (60% with CPR). Classifiers were trained on real, GAN-generated, and DM-generated datasets of 816134 ECGs each (Figure). In the test dataset of 213664 ECGs from 402 patients, classifiers trained with synthetic data had good binary performance without CPR (AUC=0.97-0.99, F1=0.78-0.87) and with CPR (AUC=0.95-0.96, F1=0.84-0.86) (Table 1), and moderate 3-class performance without CPR (BAC=65-85%) and with CPR (BAC=62-84%) (Table 2). On average, classifiers trained with real data outperformed those trained with synthetic data by an AUC of 0.019 (vs. GAN) and 0.016 (vs. DM), F1 of 0.084 (vs. GAN) and 0.081 (vs. DM), and BAC of 4.4% (vs. GAN) and 6.1% (vs. DM). Conclusions: Generative models successfully synthesized ECGs with and without CPR. Classifiers trained on synthetic data had slightly reduced performance versus those trained on real data. The results suggest potential for on-demand synthesis of OHCA ECGs, enabling AI sandboxing and development of next-generation ECG algorithms.

items.title: Abstract P1079: Hour-by-Hour Temporal Patterns in 30-Day Outcomes Following Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Nationwide Japanese Registry Study
items.abstract: Background: Previous Japanese studies have reported worse outcomes after nighttime pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). However, detailed hour-by-hour temporal patterns and their relationship to arrest etiology remain unclear. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that pediatric OHCA outcomes would exhibit distinct temporal patterns beyond conventional nighttime and that these patterns would differ according to arrest etiology. Aims: To evaluate hour-by-hour associations between emergency call time and outcomes after pediatric OHCA in Japan. Methods: We conducted a retrospective nationwide observational study using the All-Japan Utstein Registry (2005-2023). Pediatric OHCA patients (<18 years) with known emergency call time were included. Cases with transport time >120 minutes were excluded. Multivariable logistic regression models evaluated hour-by-hour associations between emergency call time and 30-day outcomes using 12:00 PM as the reference hour. Models were adjusted for year, age, sex, witnessed arrest, dispatcher-assisted CPR instruction, bystander CPR, arrest etiology, and transport time. Subgroup analyses were performed according to arrest etiology and weekday/weekend status. Results: Among 31,386 pediatric OHCA patients, crude 30-day survival was 20.9% during daytime (09:00-16:59), 15.4% during transition periods (07:00-08:59 and 17:00-22:59), and 9.1% during nighttime (23:00-06:59). In hour-by-hour adjusted analyses relative to the 12:00 PM reference hour, adjusted odds of 30-day survival progressively declined overnight and during early morning hours, reaching the lowest value at 06:00 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.30, 95% CI 0.24-0.38) (Figure). Similar temporal patterns were observed for favorable neurological survival, with the lowest adjusted odds also at 06:00 (aOR 0.29, 95% CI 0.21-0.40). An additional decline in both survival and favorable neurological outcomes was observed around 17:00. These temporal patterns were more pronounced in non-cardiac OHCA than cardiac OHCA. Patterns were similar between weekdays and weekends, and transport time did not meaningfully differ across hours of the day. Conclusion: Pediatric OHCA outcomes demonstrated distinct hour-by-hour temporal patterns not explained by transport time or weekday/weekend differences. These findings may reflect temporal vulnerabilities in pediatric arrest recognition, family supervision patterns, and operational transitions within emergency and hospital systems.

items.title: Abstract P2004: A Numerical Autopsy for Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Reclassifying Unknown Etiologies from Electronic Health Records
items.abstract: Introduction: The cause of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) often remains unknown because most patients die before comprehensive diagnostic evaluation can be performed. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that healthcare data can be leveraged to infer plausible causes that are not captured by conventional investigations. Aims: The aims of our study was to develop and assess a “numerical autopsy” framework that infer probabilistic etiologic profiles for unexplained OHCA using longitudinal healthcare data. Methods: We conducted a retrospective population based study linking the Paris Cardiac Arrest Center registry with the French National Health Insurance database. Adults with non-traumatic OHCA occurring between May 2011 and May 2020 were included. Five-year pre-arrest hospital diagnoses, outpatient drug dispensations, procedures, and registry variables were aggregated into 393 standardized features. A calibrated multiclass Light Gradient Boosting Machine model was trained on clinically adjudicated cases to predict six etiologic categories: cardiac ischemic, cardiac other, hypoxic, embolic, neurologic, and other. Cases with initially unknown etiology were reclassified only when the highest predicted probability was ≥ 50%. Results: Among 22,170 eligible patients, 3,353 had an adjudicated etiology and 18,817 remained unexplained after standard evaluation. On a held-out random test set, the model achieved a log-loss of 1.07, an overall one-vs-rest AUROC of 0.79, a F1-score of 0.37, and 63% accuracy. Temporal validation showed similar performance, with log-loss of 1.04, AUROC of 0.81, and macro F1-score of 0.36. After numerical autopsy, the proportion of unknown etiologies decreased from 84.9% to 53.1%. Ischemic etiologies increased from 7.5% to 20.2%, and hypoxic etiologies from 3.0% to 21.4%. Explainability analyses showed clinically coherent patterns, including respiratory variables among hypoxic reclassifications and cardiovascular variables among cardiac reclassifications. Conclusions: Numerical autopsy provides a scalable, uncertainty-aware approach to reclassifying unexplained OHCA using routine longitudinal healthcare data. It does not replace clinical adjudication or post-mortem investigation but may support etiologic surveillance and prevention-oriented review when conventional diagnostic information is incomplete.

items.title: Abstract P2081: When Oxygen Saturation Does Not Correct: Methemoglobinemia Complicating Severe Antifreeze Poisoning During Emergency Airway Resuscitation
items.abstract: Case Presentation: An adult woman was brought to the emergency department after intentional ingestion of three glasses of ethylene glycol-containing radiator coolant. She was pale, somnolent, dyspneic, cyanotic, and hypoxemic, prompting transfer to the resuscitation bay. Initial SpO2 was 75% with symmetric breath sounds, respiratory rate 25/min, poor perfusion, and delayed capillary refill. Blood drawn during resuscitation had a brown/chocolate discoloration. Despite non-rebreather oxygen at 15 L/min, SpO2 did not correct. Bag-mask preoxygenation with PEEP and apneic nasal oxygenation failed to raise SpO2 above 85%. Intubation was successful on the first attempt. After ventilation with FiO2 1.0, SpO2 increased only to 92%. Admission testing showed pH 7.309, lactate 10.5 mmol/L, bicarbonate 19.77 mmol/L, O2Hb 19%, COHb 6.3%, and MetHb 29.4%. Co-oximetry confirmed methemoglobinemia of 29.4-30%, with high anion gap metabolic acidosis consistent with toxic alcohol ingestion. Differential Diagnosis: Differential diagnosis included toxic alcohol poisoning, sedative intoxication, aspiration, impaired oxygen delivery, and acquired dyshemoglobinemia. Antifreeze ingestion, acidosis, cyanosis, brown/chocolate-colored blood, refractory SpO2 despite optimized airway resuscitation, and co-oximetry-confirmed methemoglobinemia supported ethylene glycol poisoning complicated by acquired methemoglobinemia. Treatment and Management: The patient underwent intubation, lung-protective ventilation, invasive monitoring, and norepinephrine. Methylene blue was indicated but unavailable. Fomepizole was also unavailable; alcohol dehydrogenase blockade was initiated with ethanol 35%. Due to persistent acidosis and ethylene glycol’s dialyzable nature, she completed three HD/SLED sessions. Outcome and Follow-Up: By ICU day 5, she was awake, oriented, extubated, oxygenating on room air, lactate-normalized, and off vasopressors. Acid-base status normalized, renal function was preserved, and the dialysis catheter was removed. She was transferred to intermediate care and discharged home with mental health follow-up. Teaching Points: In antifreeze ingestion, cyanosis, brown/chocolate-colored blood, and SpO2 that fails to correct despite high FiO2 should prompt early co-oximetry. When targeted antidotes are unavailable, optimize oxygen delivery and perfusion, block alcohol dehydrogenase, and pursue extracorporeal clearance when indicated.

items.title: Abstract P2017: Cadaveric Evaluation of Supraglottic Prehospital Ventilation Esophageal Pressure and Gastric Venting
items.abstract: Background: During prehospital airway and ventilatory emergencies including respiratory emergencies, airway compromise, and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), ventilation delivered by prehospital providers often exceeds recommended airway pressures and ventilation rates. Elevated inspiratory pressures increase intrathoracic pressure, impair venous return, and promote gastric insufflation, increasing the risk of regurgitation and aspiration. Supraglottic airway devices (SGAs) are widely used in emergency medical services because they can be placed rapidly and have high first-pass success rates. However, limited physiologic data describe how SGA design affects esophageal pressure transmission under high-pressure ventilation conditions typical of prehospital resuscitation. Hypothesis: Second-generation SGAs with dual gastric channels will reduce gastric insufflation and distention, reflected by lower esophageal pressures, compared with single-channel devices under conditions simulating cardiac arrest ventilation. Goal: This study compared esophageal pressure transmission and gastric venting among SGAs during pressure-controlled ventilation simulating prehospital cardiac arrest. Methods: In a controlled cadaveric study, fresh unfixed human cadavers were ventilated with multiple SGAs; an endotracheal tube served as the reference standard. Pressure-controlled ventilation was delivered at inspiratory pressures of 20, 30, 40, and 50 cmH 2 O to replicate prehospital ventilation extremes. Distal esophageal pressure was measured continuously through a cannula inserted through the abdominal wall into the stomach and secured in the distal esophagus. Airway placement was confirmed bronchoscopically, and airflow through gastric channels and oropharyngeal leak pathways was assessed. Results: As inspiratory pressure increased, esophageal pressure rose across all devices. Dual-channel second-generation SGAs transmitted lower esophageal pressures than single-channel and first-generation devices, indicating reduced gastric insufflation and distention under high-pressure ventilation. Conclusion: SGA design significantly influences esophageal pressure transmission during cardiac arrest ventilation. Dual-channel second-generation SGAs reduce esophageal pressurization, suggesting a mechanism to mitigate gastric distention during CPR.
