These findings have direct implications for OHCA airway strategy, supporting device selection and ventilation approaches that minimize hyperventilation and its downstream hemodynamic consequences during resuscitation.

items.title: Abstract P2030: Association of Post-Arrest Blood PCO2 and pH with Outcomes After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy is the leading cause of mortality in adults who survive out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). While post-cardiac arrest ventilation and acid-base management are important to mitigate brain injury, the optimal resuscitation targets are unknown. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that perturbations in post-resuscitation blood carbon dioxide (PCO2) and pH would adversely impact 30-day mortality after OHCA. Methods: We conducted a retrospective study of 2013-2024 data from Trinetx, a federated database of health records from >100 healthcare organizations and 100 million patients. We included adult patients with an emergency department of diagnoses of OHCA and who survived to hospital admission. Based on the mean PCO2 in the first 48 hours, we stratified patients by PCO2 (hypocapnia 30-50, normocapnia <30 and hypercapnia >50 mmHg) and pH (acidemic <7.3, normal physiologic 7.3-7.5, alkalotic >7.5). The primary outcome was 30-day death. Using Cox proportional hazards regression, we evaluated the associations of PCO2 and pH with 30-day death, adjusting for age, sex and past medical history. Results: Of 88,754 OHCA patients admitted to hospitals, we included 36,176 adults with complete data. Median age was 64 (IQR 52-74), and 13,176 (37.9%) were female. Initial PCO2s were 30-50 (66.6%), <30 (10.3%), and >50 (23.1%). Initial pHs were 7.3-7.5 (51.8%), <7.3 (46.4%), and >7.5 (1.8%). Compared with normocapnia, risk of 30-day death was higher for sustained hypocapnia PCO2<30 (aHR=1.2, 95% CI 1.2-1.3) and for hypercapnia PCO2>50 (aHR=1.2, 95% CI 1.2-1.3). Compared with normal physiologic acid-base status, risk of death was higher for acidosis pH<7.3 (aHR=1.6, 95% CI 1.6-1.7) but not for sustained alkalosis pH>7.5 (aHR=1.0, 95% CI 0.9-1.2). Conclusion: In the early post-arrest period, sustained exposure to hypercapnia, hypocapnia, and acidosis were associated with worse 30-day mortality. Post-arrest management of ventilation and acid-base status are important in the care of OHCA.

items.title: Abstract P2042: Spinal Cord Injury and Neurological Outcome in a 72-Hour Survival Rat Model of 8-Minute Ventricular Fibrillation Cardiac Arrest Resuscitated with ECPR and Immediate 12-Hour Hypothermic Temperature Control vs 2 Hour Delayed Temperature Control
items.abstract: Introduction: Ischemic spinal cord injury and strategies for its protection have received comparatively little attention in global ischemia and reperfusion research. We investigated the therapeutic effects of hypothermia on the spinal cord in our extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) rat model after 8 min of untreated ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest (VFCA) and hypothesized that immediate hypothermic temperature (HT) control (33°C for 12 hours) would reduce spinal cord dysfunction and histological damage, whereas delayed initiation of cooling after 2 hours would attenuate these protective effects after 72 hours of survival. Methods: Adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (n=39) were subjected to 8 min of VFCA and resuscitated with ECPR and drugs (epinephrine, bicarbonate, heparin). After defibrillation and restoration of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), rats were randomized into normothermic (NT) (n=16), immediate HT (n=9) and delayed HT (DHT) group (n=8). Hind leg paralysis (HLP) and urinary bladder retention (UR) were recorded and after 72h, the spine was fixed in formalin. Transverse sections of cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spinal cord (NT n=6, HT n=5, DHT n=5, Sham n=5) were embedded in paraffin. In Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE)-staining neuronal necrosis (NN) was evaluated semi-quantitatively (mild, moderate, marked). Microglia activation was assessed semi-quantitatively (mild, moderate, marked, malacia) utilizing Iba1- immunohistochemistry. Results: All animals achieved ROSC, but 8 NT animals died before the study endpoint. All surviving NT animals showed HLP. In the HT group only 2/9 animals exhibited HLP (p=0.002 vs. NT) while the DHT group showed less recovery (6/8 HLP; p=0.47 vs. NT, p=0.057 vs. HT, Sham 0/6). Urinary retention was not significantly different between groups (NT 3/8, HT 1/9, DHT 2/8, Sham 0/6). In HE-staining, 3/5 HT animals showed mild NN in the gray matter, while all animals of the NT group showed marked NN (p=0.0006 vs. Sham, p<0.0134 vs HT). Variable NN (mild to marked) was present in the DHT group. Sham animals showed physiological Iba1-expression. All VFCA groups exhibited microglia activation, reaching significance in NT (p=0.0003 vs. Sham) and DHT (p=0.0429 vs Sham). HT animals showed significantly less microglia activation compared to NT (p=0.0487). Conclusions: We found consistent NN in the spinal cords of NT rats 72 hours after 8 minutes of untreated VFCA followed by ECPR. In the HT group, these lesions were significantly reduced, correlating with improved neurological outcomes, whereas DHT group showed less pronounced protective effects. In addition, microglial responses after 72 hours of survival differed between the VFCA groups.

items.title: Abstract P2063: An Integrative Review of Thoracoabdominal Pressure Coupling During Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
items.abstract: Introduction/Background: The hemodynamic mechanism of closed-chest cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) remains incompletely defined. Cardiac and thoracic pump theories account for different components of flow, but the abdominal compartment and prone position are less integrated into current models. Research Questions/Hypothesis: We asked whether adult CPR is better explained as an interacting thoracoabdominal pressure system and whether prone positioning could alter coupling through changes in abdominal compliance, diaphragmatic force transfer, and intrathoracic pressure generation. Methods/Approach: A structured integrative review with narrative synthesis was performed. Three searches of Scopus, PubMed/MEDLINE, and CINAHL were targeted: 1) conventional CPR hemodynamics; 2) abdominal pressure, interposed abdominal compression, and thoracoabdominal interaction; and 3) prone physiology/prone CPR. Screening and full-text review were completed in Covidence. Adult human, cadaver, translational, and adult physiology-based in silico studies were eligible; pediatric studies were excluded. Results/Data: The searches yielded 587 records; 153 duplicates were removed, 434 records were screened, 139 full texts assessed, 74 excluded, and 65 studies included. The evidence base included 24 intrathoracic pressure/thoracic pump studies, 8 direct cardiac compression/intracardiac studies, 29 abdominal pressure studies, and 5 prone positioning or prone CPR studies. Across domains, CPR-generated flow was most consistent with pressure-mediated interaction among intrathoracic pressure transmission, variable direct cardiac compression, and intra-abdominal effects on venous reservoir mobilization, preload, aortic pressure, and arterial-right atrial pressure gradients. Prone CPR reports showed favorable arterial pressures, but no included study simultaneously measured intra-abdominal, intrathoracic, and arterial or intracardiac pressures in prone and supine CPR. Conclusions: Adult CPR should be conceptualized as a thoracoabdominal pressure-coupled system rather than a competition between isolated cardiac and thoracic pump models. Prone positioning may modify this system by limiting abdominal pressure dissipation and improving cranial pressure transmission during compression, while excessive abdominal constraint may impair recoil-phase refilling. The key gap is simultaneous multi-compartment pressure measurement during standardized supine and prone CPR.

items.title: Abstract P2052: Microaxial Pump Support in Ultra High Risk Pulmonary Embolism
items.abstract: Introduction: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is responsible for more than 300,000 deaths per year in the United States and is the third leading cause of death worldwide. It is well established that the presence of right ventricular (RV) dysfunction increases mortality in PE. Despite advancements in therapies for massive pulmonary embolism (PE) some patients with refractory cardiogenic shock will still require additional hemodynamic support. Such support is typically available at specialized referral centers where veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) is commonly used to stabilize cardiogenic stages (D-E) associated with PE. In this case series, we describe the use of temporary pRVAD support with a micro-axial flow pump (RP Impella Flex) following aspiration thrombectomy and or systemic thrombolysis. Purpose: We describe and report the characteristics of eight patients with ultra high-risk PE, defined as category E1 or E2 who were treated with a temporary pRVAD micro-axial flow pump for refractory cardiogenic shock. Methods: We included patients aged 18 or older who presented from 01/2024 to 12/2025 with PE who received pRVAD. IRB (IRB00144384) approved the study and waived consent. Statistical Analysis: Data from all patients evaluated by the PE Response Team during the study period were analyzed. Baseline age, sex, BMI, Charlson comorbidity index, pulmonary embolism related shock stage, RVSP, TAPSE, and RV/LV ratio were summarized for patients who received RVAD support in Table 1. Descriptive statistical methods were used to summarize baseline characteristics among the included patients. Results: Six out of 8 patients were males with mean age of 59 (95% CI 54.1-64.1), BMI of 32.5 (95% CI 26-39). All 8 patients were stage E cardiogenic shock. A total of four out of 8 patients had cardiac arrest.All patients were on multiple vasoactive medications. The NEE (norepinephrine equivalents) use mean was 4.13 mcg/kg/min (95% CI 2.46-5.29). Their RV/LV ratio mean by CT was 1.63 (95% CI 0.85-2.41) and mean RVSP of 44.9 (95% CI 55.3-54.5). Six out of 8 patients survived hospitalization. Discussion: Patients with PE in cardiogenic shock stage E—with or without cardiac arrest—remain an extremely challenging population, with reported mortality rates nearing 70%. Our findings indicate that early pRVAD intervention may provide stabilization in select scenarios, compared to the conventional practice of stabilizing patients on VA-ECMO to achieve maximal hemodynamic support. The retrospective design and limited cohort size of this study preclude any broad generalization. Conclusion: In summary, temporary pRVAD support, combined with mechanical aspiration thrombectomy, appears to be a promising strategy for managing stage E cardiogenic shock in PE. Future prospective studies with larger cohorts are warranted to refine patient selection and optimize treatment protocols.

items.title: Abstract P2065: Impact of Chest Compressions on the Accuracy of Automated Tidal Volume Estimation During Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
items.abstract: Introduction: Monitoring ventilations during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is of growing clinical interest. Estimates of inspired (V TI ) and exhaled (V TE ) tidal volumes could provide valuable information on air leakage and rescuer performance, which might eventually be incorporated into CPR feedback systems. Such estimates can in principle be obtained through numerical integration of the airway flow signal. However, chest compressions (CC) delivered during CPR sometimes induce oscillations on the flow waveform that can be misinterpreted as pseudo-ventilations by automated detection algorithms, or alter the automatically identified integration boundaries of true breaths. Therefore, the accuracy of device volume estimates may be compromised during CPR when ventilation detection is performed automatically. Aim: To assess the impact of chest compressions on the accuracy of automated V TI and V TE estimations during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Methods: OHCA episodes with defibrillator, spirometry-based volume and inspiratory flow signals, recorded after intubation and during continuous ventilation, were available. Ventilations were manually annotated from the flow signal and classified as artifact-free or as affected by CCs. For each, device V TId , V TEd and exhalation time (t e ) were obtained from the volume signal. Recalculated V TIr and V TEr were independently obtained by numerical integration of the flow signal between the manually identified ventilation boundaries. Absolute volume differences (mL) were quantified between device and recalculated values. Differences between groups were assessed with the Mann-Whitney U test. Results: A total of 25 cases were analyzed, comprising 4,312 ventilations. Median (IQR) ventilation rate was 12.6 (9.8, 16.0) per minute. Median (IQR) recalculated V TIr and V TEr were 377 (297, 478) mL and 370 (258, 469) mL, respectively. Overall median (IQR) absolute differences were 2.0 (0.6, 8.9) mL for V TI and 14.0 (5.1, 52.2) mL for V TE . Artifact-free absolute differences were 1.3 (0.5, 3.0) mL for V TI and 6.6 (3.0, 12.8) mL for V TE . CC-affected absolute differences were 5.1 (0.9, 23.9) mL for V TI and 58.1 (24.1, 106.7) mL for V TE . Differences between populations were significant ( p < 0.001). Median (IQR) t e was 1.55 (0.74, 2.05) s in CC-affected ventilations and 3.42 (2.52, 4.80) s in artifact-free ones. Conclusion: Agreement between automated and flow-based volume estimates is substantially poorer for exhaled than for inspired volumes. It also degrades substantially in the presence of chest compression artifacts. The analyzed device’s integration algorithm seems to prematurely identify the end of expiration when compressions distort the flow signal. Our results suggest that volume estimation algorithms might need to be made robust against compression-induced artifacts to provide reliable ventilation monitoring during CPR.

items.title: Abstract P2072: Association of Drainage Pressure and Pump Head Pressure with Early Hemolysis During Veno-Arterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Support: A Retrospective Study
items.abstract: Background: Hemolysis during veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (V-A ECMO) support is an important complication associated with acute kidney injury and increased transfusion requirements. Mechanical stress within the ECMO circuit is thought to contribute to the development of hemolysis; however, the association between circuit pressure parameters and hemolysis during V-A ECMO support has not been sufficiently investigated. This study examined the association of drainage pressure and pump head pressure with hemolysis in patients treated with V-A ECMO for cardiogenic shock. Methods: We conducted a single-center retrospective observational study including 23 patients who underwent V-A ECMO support between October 2022 and June 2024. Serum haptoglobin levels were measured at intensive care unit admission and at 12 and 24 hours thereafter. Hemolysis was defined as a minimum serum haptoglobin level <19 mg/dL at any of the three time points. ECMO circuit pressures were obtained from pressure monitoring values displayed on the ECMO console. Drainage pressure was defined as the pre-pump pressure, and pump head pressure was calculated as the difference between the pre-oxygenator pressure and the pre-pump pressure. Results: Twenty-three patients were included (median age, 73 years; 69.6% male). Most patients had advanced cardiogenic shock, with SCAI stage E accounting for 65.2% of the cohort (stage C, 13.0%; stage D, 21.7%; stage E, 65.2%). Hemolysis was observed in 19 of 23 patients. At 12 hours after intensive care unit admission, a visual trend was observed whereby patients with greater pre-ECMO shock severity tended to exhibit more negative drainage pressures and lower serum haptoglobin levels (Figure A). In addition, serum haptoglobin levels decreased over time from intensive care unit admission to 12 and 24 hours thereafter (Figure B). Compared with the non-hemolysis group, the hemolysis group had significantly lower drainage pressures at intensive care unit admission (–104 [–137 to –66] vs. –30 [–47 to –7] mmHg, p=0.017) and at 24 hours (–87 [–112 to –54] vs. –16 [–42 to –1] mmHg, p=0.005), as well as significantly higher pump head pressure at 24 hours (343 [298-397] vs. 188 [148-203] mmHg, p=0.003). Exploratory Firth penalized logistic regression analysis demonstrated that minimum drainage pressure (OR 0.58 per 10-mmHg increase, 95% CI 0.23-0.91, p<0.001) and maximum pump head pressure (OR 1.14 per 10-mmHg increase, 95% CI 1.01-1.37, p=0.017) were associated with hemolysis. Conclusions: More negative drainage pressure and higher pump head pressure during the early phase of V-A ECMO support were associated with hemolysis, as assessed by reduced serum haptoglobin levels. These ECMO circuit pressure parameters may serve as indicators associated with early hemolysis during V-A ECMO support.

items.title: Abstract P2074: Institutional Selection Patterns and Outcomes of ECMO Initiated After ROSC Following Pediatric OHCA
items.abstract: Introduction: Survival with favorable neurologic outcome from pediatric OHCA is poor and there are few data regarding who may benefit from extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) initiation after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). We aimed to describe institutional use of post-arrest ECMO, characterize clinical features associated with ECMO initiation, and compare outcomes between ECMO-treated patients and post-OHCA patients not treated with ECMO. Hypothesis: Children treated with post-arrest ECMO support represent a highly selected subgroup with greater post-arrest hemodynamic instability but will have similar favorable neurologic survival compared with post-OHCA patients not treated with ECMO. Methods: We performed a single-center retrospective cohort study of pediatric OHCA patients achieving ROSC, admitted to the pediatric ICU or cardiac ICU not at their neurologic baseline, and requiring invasive mechanical ventilation between 2017-2025 using prospectively collected event data. Descriptive statistics compared patients treated with post-arrest ECMO to non-ECMO treated patients. Favorable neurologic survival was defined as PCPC 1-2 or no change from baseline. Results: Among 217 OHCA patients included, 12 (5.5%) received post-arrest ECMO support. Median times from ROSC and hospital admission to cannulation were 358 (229-545) and 143 (111-353) minutes; 75% received veno-arterial ECMO. Compared with the non-ECMO cohort, ECMO-treated patients demonstrated greater post-arrest cardiopulmonary instability within 6 hours of admission, including higher vasoactive infusion score (VIS) [27.0 (5.0-52.5) vs 1.9 (0.0-10.8); p=0.002], lactate [8.1 (5.5-12.1) vs 4.7 (2.8-7.7); p=0.02], PaCO 2 [51.0 (35.3-61.0) vs 37.5 (31.6-44.5); p=0.01], and FiO 2 [60.0 (30.0-100.0) vs 43.3 (29.6-71.7); p=0.19]. All ECMO-treated patients had an initial GCS of 3T or NT. No ECMO-treated patient had pre-cannulation acute brain injury or bleed on head CT. Favorable neurologic survival was 33.3% (4/12) among ECMO-treated patients and 32.7% (67/205) among non-ECMO treated patients. Conclusion: Post-arrest ECMO after pediatric OHCA was used infrequently. Despite greater post-arrest hemodynamic instability within 6 hours of admission, ECMO-treated patients demonstrated comparable favorable neurologic survival to the broader ICU OHCA cohort. These data provide an initial description of post-arrest ECMO utilization and outcomes after pediatric OHCA. Larger multicenter studies are needed to identify patients most likely to benefit from post-arrest ECMO support.

items.title: Abstract P2083: Intersectionality of Race/Ethnicity and Sex on Survival in Adult Patients with In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Prior studies reported racial disparities in patient outcomes after in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA), where Asian, Black, and Hispanic patients experience lower survival, compared to White patients. However, it remains unknown how survival differs across the intersections of race/ethnicity and sex. Objective: To evaluate the association of combinations of patients’ race/ethnicity and sex with survival to hospital discharge after IHCA Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of the Get With The Guidelines—Resuscitation registry. We included adults (age ≥ 18 years) with an index IHCA from 2000 to 2025. The exposure was patients’ race/ethnicity (Asian, Hispanic, Non-Hispanic [NH] Black, NH White, and other races) and sex. We used a multivariable multilevel mixed-effects logistic regression model to account for confounders and clustering within hospitals and evaluated the association and the interaction between race/ethnicity and sex on the outcome of survival to hospital discharge. Results: Among 480,505 included patients (male [58.4%]; female [41.6%]), we included 5,859 Asian males (1.2%), 4,066 Asian females (0.8%), 20.413 Hispanic males (4.2%), 13,083 Hispanic females (2.7%), 60,149 NH Black males (12.5%), 53,318 NH Black females (11.1%), 191,715 NH White males (39.9%), 127,326 NH White females (26.5%), 2,568 males with other races (0.5%), and 2,008 females with other races (0.4%). The crude rates of survival to hospital discharge were 22.4% in Asian males, 20.9% in Asian females, 22.5% in Hispanic males, 23.0% in Hispanic females, 21.4% in NH Black males, 21.0% in NH Black females, 25.2% in NH White males, 24.5% in NH White females, 23.5% in males with other races, and 24.9% in females with other races. Compared to NH White males, the adjusted odds ratio (95% CIs) of survival to hospital discharge was 0.95 (0.88-1.02) in Asian males, 0.89 (0.82-0.97) in Asian females, 0.94 (0.90-0.98) in Hispanic males, 1.00 (0.96-1.05) in Hispanic females, 0.88 (0.86-0.90) in NH Black males, 0.90 (0.88-0.93) in NH Black females, 1.02 (1.00-1.04) in NH White female, 0.83 (0.75-0.92) in males with other races, and 0.93 (0.83-1.04) in females with other races ( Figure ). However, the interaction between race/ethnicity and sex was not significant (p-value for interaction = 0.19). Conclusions: In this cohort of the large IHCA registry, compared to White males, Asian females, Hispanic males, NH Black males and females, and males with other races were associated with lower odds of survival to hospital discharge, whereas the intersectionality of race/ethnicity and sex on survival was not observed.

items.title: Abstract P2013: Oxygen Without Benefit: Post-Cardiac Arrest Hyperoxia Results in Systemic Metabolic Failure Despite Preserved Arterial Oxygenation
items.abstract: Background: Oxygen administration following cardiac arrest (CA) is associated with cardiac dysfunction, brain injury, and poor survival. These injuries are driven in part by mitochondrial injury, but the metabolic consequences of post-CA hyperoxia remain incompletely understood. We hypothesized that post-CA hyperoxia produces histotoxic dysoxia — impaired cellular oxygen utilization despite adequate arterial oxygenation. Methods: In a murine model of CA, mice underwent 12 minutes of asystole followed by CPR. Beginning 30 minutes post-resuscitation, mice were exposed to 30% O 2 for 6 hours. Systemic metabolic parameters, including core body temperature, whole-body oxygen consumption (V̇O 2 ), and arterial blood gas values (pH, PO 2 , SaO 2 ) were assessed. Results: Post-CA exposure to 30% O 2 induced a systemic metabolic crisis characterized by hypothermia (35.0±0.3 vs. 37.3±0.1°C, p<0.005, n=3-4) and markedly suppressed V̇O 2 (2.1±1.0 vs. 9.1±1.3 mL/kg/min, p<0.001, n=5) compared to sham animals receiving identical oxygen treatment. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated severe acidosis (pH 6.91±0.03 vs. 7.19±0.01, p<0.001, n=8-10). Notably, arterial PO 2 and SaO 2 were preserved and did not differ from sham (p>0.05, n=8-10), indicating that metabolic injury occurred independently of arterial hypoxemia. Conclusions: Post-CA hyperoxia produced systemic hypothermia, suppressed whole-body oxygen consumption, and severe acidosis. Despite normal arterial PO 2 and SaO 2 , these findings indicate a failure of cellular oxygen utilization rather than delivery. This pattern is consistent with histotoxic dysoxia and implicates mitochondrial dysfunction as a central mechanism of post-resuscitation metabolic injury.

items.title: Abstract P2022: Functional Recovery After Cardiac Arrest Understanding Paths and Potential
items.abstract: Introduction: Survivorship after cardiac arrest includes cognitive, emotional, and physical aspects of recovery. Domain specific recovery trajectories are individualized and under-reported in the literature. Understanding recovery capacity is critical for optimizing goal setting when counseling patients and their caregivers. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of comatose cardiac arrest survivors enrolled in our single-center acute brain injury repository between 2/5/2022 and 12/11/2025. We excluded patients who died prior to hospital discharge or who had no follow up modified Rankin Scale score (mRS). Patients were followed prospectively, and mRS was determined using patient and family interviews. Patients discharged alive with at least one follow-up mRS at any of the four time-points (3-month, 6-month, one year, two years) were included in the analysis. Good outcome was defined as mRS 0-3; longitudinal mRS changes were assessed with a Sankey plot. Results: Among the 56 patients [mean (SD) age 57.7 (16.8) years] included, 89.3% (n=50) were out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. The most common arrest etiology was cardiac (n = 36, 64.3%), of which the majority (n = 26, 72.2%) had a shockable rhythm, followed by respiratory (n = 15, 26.8%). Median (IQR) length of stay was 14 (9-22) days. The most common discharge locations were home (n=31, 55.4%) and short-term rehabilitation (n=14, 25%). Median (IQR) number of mRS assessments was 2 (2-3). Good outcome increased from 23 patients at three months to 26 patients at one year. There was one patient with poor outcome at one-year (mRS 4) who improved to good outcome at two years (mRS 0). In a sub-analysis of patients with an mRS at both 3-months and 1-year (n=11), 4 (36.4%) patients with mRS 2-3 improved to mRS 0-1. Conclusion: Functional neurologic recovery following cardiac arrest varies over time. Understanding recovery trajectories and factors associated with improvement are critical to maximizing survivorship potential. Our preliminary findings convey that recovery can be delayed, and possible up to two years following arrest.

items.title: Abstract P2045: Novel Peptides Improve Cardiac Arrest Survival by Enhancing Metabolic Recovery and Mitigating Thrombo-Inflammation
items.abstract: Introduction: Cardiac arrest (CA) is a leading cause of death that affects about 650,000 people annually in the USA. The overall survival rate for out-of-hospital CA is less than 10%. Despite this public health challenge, no effective drug is available to improve CA survival. Defibrillation and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) can achieve return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Despite ROSC, patients die due to post-CA syndromes including two critical mechanisms: metabolic derangement and thrombo-inflammation. We have developed two novel peptides, TAT-PHLPP9c and M3mP6, that enhance metabolic recovery and mitigate platelet-induced thrombo-inflammation, respectively. We hypothesized that these two peptides will synergistically improve cardiac arrest survival. Methods: C57BL6 mice (retired breeder, female) underwent 8 min of KCl-induced asystole arrest. Mice were randomized to receive saline, TAT-PHLPP9c (7.5 mg/kg), M3mP6 (5 μmol/kg) or in combination of these two peptides intravenously during CPR. Cardiomyocytes H9C2 and platelets were also used. AKT phosphorylation (p-AKT), platelet aggregation, and β-thromboglobulin (β-TG), a marker of thrombo-inflammation, were measured by Western blot, Light Transmission Aggregometry (LTA), and ELISA assay, respectively. Survival (5-day) was assessed by Kaplan-Meier analysis. Results: Compared to saline, M3mP6, TAT-PHLPP9c and the combination all significantly increased survival, about 30%, 60% and 80%, respectively (n=14 mice each group). In H9C2 cells, TAT-PHLPP9c activated Akt S473 while M3mP6 alone minimally affected p-Akt S473. The combined treatment did not further increase AKT activation as compared to TAT-PHLPP9c treatment alone. In platelets, TAT-PHLPP9c enhanced p-AKT in the presence of platelet agonist thrombin and attenuated platelet aggregation, while M3mP6 inhibited p-AKT and markedly inhibited platelet aggregation. In plasma, M3mP6 reduced plasma β-TG level at 2h post-ROSC while TAT-PHLPP9c had minimal effects which was confirmed in the plasma of swine underwent PEA treated with TAT-PHLPP9c. Conclusions: TAT-PHLPP9c and M3mP6 synergistically improve cardiac arrest survival. TAT-PHLPP9c and M3mP6 likely have differential effects in different cell types. TAT-PHLPP9c-activated AKT may play a functional role in platelets that is distinct from the role of m3mP6 activated AKT via the integrin outside-in signaling pathway which stimulates platelet activation. Both metabolism and thrombo-inflammation are important targets for effective cardiac arrest treatment.

items.title: Abstract P2055: Circulating Biomarkers of Myocardial Injury, Hemodynamic Stress, and Inflammation for Predicting Sudden Cardiac Death: A Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Sudden cardiac death (SCD) is a leading cause of cardiovascular mortality and represents a keystone outcome in cardiovascular pathology, since it often occurs without warning. Existing risk stratification tools fail to identify many at-risk individuals. Circulating biomarkers reflecting myocardial injury, hemodynamic stress, and systemic inflammation may improve SCD risk prediction by capturing subclinical pathophysiology.We systematically searched PubMed, AHA Journal, BMC Journal, Sage Journal, Oxford Academic, ScienceDirect, and other major cardiology journal platforms from inception through October 2025. Primary statistical and observational studies of biomarker data, supported by Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), were evaluated to identify biomarkers most strongly associated with SCD. Biomarkers related to inflammation, stress, and myocardial injury were prioritized due to their direct role in SCD development. Eligible studies included adult populations with measurements of one or more cardiovascular biomarkers and healthy controls. Meta-analyses used random-effects models. Heterogeneity was assessed using I 2 and Cochran’s Q, publication bias with funnel plots, and Egger’s regression test. Analyses were performed in Python, and study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS).Twenty studies comprising >240,000 participants met the inclusion criteria. Populations included healthy adults and individuals with known cardiac disease. Biomarkers were grouped as myocardial injury (troponins), hemodynamic stress (BNP/NT-proBNP), and inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6). Higher troponin levels were associated with ~2.8-fold increased SCD risk (HR≈2.84, 95% CI 1.94-4.14; I 2 ≈0%). Elevated BNP/NT-proBNP showed the strongest association (HR≈4.2, 95% CI 2.2-8.7; I 2 ≈84%). CRP exhibited a modest association (HR≈1.19, 95% CI 1.09-1.29; I 2 ≈45-50%). These associations generally persisted after adjustment for demographic factors, LVEF, coronary artery disease, and other cardiovascular risk factors. Troponin and BNP/NT-proBNP remained independently predictive, whereas CRP and IL-6 primarily functioned as supportive inflammatory markers.In this meta-analysis, biomarkers of hemodynamic stress (BNP/NT-proBNP) and myocardial injury (troponins) were strong independent predictors of SCD, while inflammatory markers such as CRP provided weaker but complementary information. Incorporating troponin and especially BNP/NT-proBNP into multimodal risk stratification frameworks may improve early identification of SCD and guide future prevention strategies.

items.title: Abstract P2084: Latent Pre-Arrest Illness Phenotypes and Outcomes After Pediatric In-Hospital ICU Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (pIHCA) occurs in patients with diverse pre-existing illnesses and pre-arrest supports, but whether these characteristics form clinically relevant phenotypes is unknown. Objective: To identify pre-arrest illness phenotypes in pIHCA events and determine whether phenotypes are associated with outcomes. Methods: Retrospective cohort study of patients <18 years with CPR >1 minute in the pediatric or cardiac ICU at a single children’s hospital from 2017 to 2026. Mixed-measurement latent class analysis (LCA) was applied to age, pre-arrest diagnoses (e.g. ARDS and acute neurologic disease), and interventions (vasoactive infusions and respiratory support). The final solution was selected using Bayesian information criterion (BIC), class size, clinical interpretability, and consensus-clustering stability. The primary outcome was sustained ROSC. Secondary outcomes were ROC, survival to hospital discharge, and favorable neurologic survival. Outcome rates were compared using likelihood-ratio tests (LRT). Results: Among 659 IHCA events in 508 patients, median age was 0.8 years; medical-noncardiac (49%) and surgical-cardiac (31%) predominated. The lowest-BIC four-class solution had strong class separation (entropy 0.86; average posterior probability 0.93). Phenotypes were: 1. Chronic respiratory vulnerability (185/659, 28.1%), 2. Low-Shock cardiac vulnerability (180, 27.3%), 3. Cardiac shock (131, 19.9%) and 4. Septic Shock/Multisystem illness (163, 24.7%) (Figure 1). Sustained ROSC differed across phenotypes (93.5%, 73.3%, 60.3%, and 58.9%; LRT p<0.01). ROC was similar across the first three phenotypes but lower in septic shock/multisystem illness (94.6%, 91.7%, 89.3%, and 65.0%; p<0.01). Among index arrests (n=396), survival to hospital discharge was 76.8%, 66.1%, 51.7%, and 28.4% (p<0.001), and favorable neurologic survival was 49.5%, 45.6%, 39.3%, and 20.3% (p<0.001). Compared with chronic respiratory vulnerability, septic shock/multisystem illness had lower odds of ROSC (OR 0.11, 95% CI 0.05-0.21), ROC (OR 0.11, 95% CI 0.05-0.22), survival to hospital discharge (OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.06-0.23), and favorable neurologic survival (OR 0.26, 95% CI 0.13-0.51) (p<0.01) (Figure 2). Conclusion: Pre-arrest illness LCA identified four clinically interpretable phenotypes with distinct outcome profiles. These findings support phenotype-based approaches to pIHCA research, and future work will integrate pre-arrest physiology and response to therapies to further refine subgroups.

items.title: Abstract P2049: Simulation Training Increases Resuscitative Echocardiography Use in Cardiac Arrest but Decays Without Reinforcement: The MAINSTREAM Study
items.abstract: Introduction/Background: Resuscitative transesophageal echocardiography (rTEE) provides real-time hemodynamic guidance during cardiac arrest but requires skills beyond most emergency medicine attendings working in the Emergency Department (ED). Simulation-based deliberate practice may bridge this gap, but its real-world impact on adoption remains unknown. Research Questions/Hypothesis: We hypothesized that proficiency-based deliberate practice in rTEE would increase utilization among trained attendings, modulated by provider role. Goals/Aims: To measure rTEE adoption across three implementation eras and quantify the effect of provider role using the Capability-Opportunity-Motivation-Behavior (COM-B) framework. Methods/Approach: We conducted a pre-post study of MAINSTREAM (Measuring Adoption: Impact of Novel Simulation Training on Resuscitative Echocardiography in Arrest Management), a simulation-based rTEE curriculum (~5 hours) for non-Advanced Emergency Medicine Ultrasound trained (AEMUS-T) attendings at an academic ED. Provider roles, per COM-B "opportunity" framework, were defined as MAINSTREAM-trained ED attending designated as arrest team leader (MtL), MAINSTREAM-trained attending available in the ED (MtAv), and AEMUS-T provider (benchmark). Three eras: pre-training (AEMUS-T performed only, 9 months), post-training window (14 months), durability window (14 months). Utilization compared using Fisher's exact test and Cochran-Armitage trend testing. Results/Data: We analyzed 920 non-traumatic cardiac arrests (MtL n=162, MtAv n=355, AEMUS-T n=403) from March 2023 to April 2026. rTEE utilization increased across eras (trend OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.02-1.63, p=0.037). MtL utilization rose from 0% pre-training to 32.1% (95% CI 21.1-45.5%) during the post-training window, then declined to 17.4% (95% CI 11.5-25.6%) in the durability window (OR 2.24, p=0.044). MtL was associated with 2.58-fold higher utilization than MtAv (OR 2.58, 95% CI 1.29-5.18, p=0.010). Across the durability window, rates attenuated to 15-17% (p>0.68); the overall post-training rate of 16.0% remained nearly double the pre-training benchmark of 9.1% (p=0.017). Conclusion(s): Simulation-based deliberate practice was associated with increased rTEE utilization during the post-training window, but attenuation in the durability window indicates one-time implementation is insufficient for sustained behavior change. Within COM-B, provider role — a proxy for structured opportunity — emerged as a key modifiable driver. These findings suggest ongoing reinforcement is needed to maintain rTEE adoption.

items.title: Abstract P2069: Patterns of Cerebral Blood Flow Post-Cardiac Arrest in Pediatric Swine
items.abstract: Introduction/Background: Neurologic injury is unfortunately common in survivors of cardiac arrest. Despite restoration of native cardiac output after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), secondary brain injury may be caused and/or exacerbated by cerebral microvascular hypoperfusion. Research Question/Hypothesis: The aim of this study was to use invasive laser doppler and non-invasive magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to characterize cerebral blood flow (CBF) during recovery from cardiac arrest. We hypothesized that there would be a period of microvascular hypoperfusion in the brain after resuscitation from cardiac arrest. Methods/Approach: Prior to cardiac arrest, a fiberoptic laser doppler flow probe was implanted into the basal ganglia. Pediatric swine (4 kg) underwent 8 min of ventricular fibrillation followed by resuscitation with chest compressions, ventilation, and epinephrine administration. Defibrillation was provided at 10 min of resuscitation and every 2 min thereafter, as indicated. CBF and mean arterial pressure (MAP) were measured at baseline and continuously during 4 hours of recovery in animals that achieved ROSC. A second cohort of animals underwent brain MRI with arterial spin labeling (ASL) sequences at 4 and 48 hours of recovery. Results/Data: Eight animals underwent cardiac arrest. Five had laser doppler flow probes implanted for measurement of CBF and three underwent MRI with ASL at 4 and 48 hours of recovery. Observed patterns of microvascular CBF included brief hyperemia in the first 5-10 minutes post-ROSC, followed by hypoperfusion that reached a nadir of about 50% of the baseline value at 30 min after resuscitation ( Fig 1 ). Thereafter, CBF slowly recovered over 4 hours and neared baseline levels in some animals. Mean arterial pressure averaged 94 ±16 mmHg and remained relatively stable during this same period. Similarly, MRI demonstrated decreased CBF on ASL sequences relative to baseline at 4 hours recovery ( Fig. 2 ). At 48 hours of recovery CBF was increased as compared to baseline, particularly in anatomic areas with diffusion restriction. Conclusion: Cerebral hypoperfusion, demonstrated by both invasive CBF monitoring and on non-invasive MRI, persists several hours after resuscitation from cardiac arrest in this pediatric swine model. This may represent a therapeutic target to improve neurologic outcomes after cardiac arrest. Figure 1 . Microvascular cerebral blood flow measured by laser doppler flow probe in the basal ganglia (A) and systemic mean arterial pressure (B) during 4 hours of recovery after cardiac arrest. Figure 2 . Representative ASL sequences from an MRI obtained at baseline, 4 hours, and 48 hours recovery after resuscitation from cardiac arrest.

items.title: Abstract P2015: Hydrogen Peroxide-Induced Pyroptosis in Cardiomyocytes is Regulated by NAMPT and NAD
items.abstract: Introduction: The role of pyroptosis, a highly inflammatory form of programmed cell death, in cardiac injury following cardiac arrest is unknown. Related to pyroptosis, our prior work has shown that both oxidant injury and intracellular NAD levels result in significant cardiac injury and protection respectively. A better understanding of how oxidant stress and NAD metabolism affect cardiomyocyte injury and pyroptosis could identify new targets for cardiac arrest care. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that cardiac oxidant exposure induces NAD depletion and pyroptosis, which can be rescued by replenishment of cellular NAD. Methods: H9C2 cardiomyocytes were exposed to H 2 O 2 to create oxidative stress. Cell morphological change was observed under microscope, and cell viability was measured by CCK8 kit based on intracellular LDH activity. The expressions of GSDMD and GSDME and their N-terminal fragments were assessed by Western blot analysis. Intracellular NAD content was measured by assay kit. Results: H 2 O 2 induced a dose-dependent death of H9C2 cardiomyocytes, which plateaued at 1 mM and this death was related to NAD + depletion. H9C2 cells exhibited characteristic morphological changes of pyroptosis, such as cell swelling and rupture of the cell membrane, and release of LDH. Supplement with 1 mM NAM, a NAD + precursor, partially rescued viability in H 2 O 2 -treated cells from 54.9 ±1.7% to 81.7 ± 2.2% at 4h (p<0.01). The Nampt inhibitor FK866 (1 μM), which blocks NAD synthesis, totally nullified the protective effect of NAM on cell viability. The pan-caspase inhibitor Z-vad (100 μM) blocked the typical morphology of pyroptosis induced by H 2 O 2 . NAM also restored NAD + concentrations. To determine which gasdermin is involved in oxidant-induced cell death, cardiomyocytes were treated with 1 mM H 2 O 2 for up to 5 hrs. Both GSDME and its Asp270 cleavage N-terminal fragment were observed, and GSDME-N expression peaked after 2h exposure to H 2 O 2 . It was blocked by treatment with NAM or a caspase 3 inhibitor, but not by the NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950. Although GSDMD was cleaved after 2h exposure, there was no expression of the cleaved GSDMD (Asp275) N-terminal fragment. Conclusion: Cardiac oxidant injury, known to occur during cardiac arrest, can result in pyroptotic cell death that is mediated by caspases and can be rescued by NAD precursor treatment.

items.title: Abstract P2028: Beyond Return of Circulation: Temporal Trends in Mortality Involving Cardiac Arrest and Anoxic Brain Injury
items.abstract: Introduction: Cardiac arrest is the leading cause of cardiovascular mortality in the United States (US) with post-cardiac arrest anoxic brain injury (ABI) the leading cause of mortality among resuscitated survivors. Despite its high clinical and public health burden, national mortality trends and disparities in this subgroup of population remain largely uncharacterized. Aim: To evaluate national trends, demographic disparities and regional variations in mortality involving cardiac arrest and post cardiac arrest ABI among US adults from 1999 to 2024. Methods: We analyzed the CDC Wide-ranging Online Data for Epidemiologic Research (CDC WONDER) for death certificates (1999-2024) of adults 25 years and older, with cardiac arrest (ICD: I46) and anoxic brain injury (ICD: G93). Age adjusted mortality rates (AAMR) per 100,000 and annual percent change (APC) were calculated through join-point regression analysis. Results: Between 1999 and 2024 a total of 291,796 deaths involving cardiac arrest and ABI were reported. After an initial decline in AAMR from 4.35 in 1999 to 3.79 in 2004 (APC = –1.96%), a prolonged rise spanning two decades [APC = +3.77% (2004-2014), APC = +1.15% (2014-2021)] was observed, reaching a study peak of 6.10 in 2021. This represents a 40.2% increase from 2004 to 2021. Subsequently, AAMR declined to 4.96 in 2024 (13.8% above the 1999 baseline). Males consistently had a higher mortality than females. AAMR increased from 5.32 vs. 3.69 in 1999 to 6.21 vs. 3.90 in 2024. By 2024, female mortality had returned to near-baseline levels, whereas male mortality remained 16.7% above baseline. Non-Hispanic (NH) Black adults had the highest mortality burden with AAMR rising from 8.1 in 1999 to a peak of 12.9 in 2021. This group accounted for 59,322 total deaths, with a 2024 AAMR that remained 2.5-fold higher than that of NH Whites (10.85 vs. 4.31). NH American Indians demonstrated the largest relative increase in AAMRs (108% from 1999-2022). Region wise, the South consistently had the highest AAMR from 2013 onward, peaking at 6.99 in 2021 and was the region with highest AAMR in 2024 at 5.51. In 1999, urban areas had a higher AAMR than rural areas (4.51 vs. 3.72). However, by 2020, rural AAMR exceeded urban by 0.50-0.63 per 100,000. Although adults aged 65-74 years accounted for the largest number of deaths (74,200), crude mortality rate increased most rapidly among younger adults aged 25-34 years (+312%) and 35-44 years (+194%), while rates among adults ≥85 years declined by 47.8%. Conclusion: Between 1999 and 2024, mortality involving cardiac arrest and ABI demonstrated a sustained rise, with a peak in 2021. NH Blacks, NH American Indians, males, and residents of Southern states were disproportionately affected. The concurrent rise among younger adults warrants further investigation. These findings highlights the need for equitable post-resuscitation care and targeted policy interventions.

items.title: Abstract P2085: Adoption of the “Ten Steps” Framework for Improving In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Care: A Multinational Needs Assessment Survey
items.abstract: Background: In-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) outcomes depend on timely, coordinated systems and guideline-based care. The International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR)’s “Ten Steps Toward Improving IHCA Quality of Care and Outcomes” framework describes key IHCA best practices, but the status of these adoptions across healthcare settings is not well described. Aims: To evaluate global implementation of key IHCA best practices and identify priority areas for improvement and support. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional, web-based de novo survey of healthcare professionals (HCPs) and institutional stakeholders from June to December 2025. A multidisciplinary team of clinical and resuscitation experts developed the survey. The survey was administered via Qualtrics and disseminated through AHA communication channels to a convenience sample of national and international respondents. The data was analyzed using descriptive statistics. Results: A total of 659 responses were received from 23 countries, with the majority from the USA (91%). Respondents were predominantly healthcare workers (90%, n=543/606), and 69% had >=11 years of HCP experience. Most respondents were registered nurses (54%). The rest of the demographics are summarized in Table 1. Implementation practices are described in Table 2. Full implementation was the most frequent for presence of resuscitation response teams (69%) and guideline-based resuscitation care (66%), with lower rates in post-cardiac arrest care (52%), prevention systems (50%), person-centered culture (38%), person-centered culture (38%), patient-centered care (31%), and healthcare worker well-being initiatives (31%). The top three areas needing support included multidisciplinary mock codes (43%), resuscitation training (33%), and debriefing implementation (31%). Most respondents (87%) reported that an IHCA toolkit would be beneficial. The barriers identified primarily related to limited resources, time, and leadership support (Table 3). Conclusions: Current implementation of IHCA best practices varies across care settings with stronger adoption of acute resuscitation processes than of infrastructure, data systems, and patient care components. These findings highlight the need for comprehensive resources to strengthen IHCA systems of care globally.

items.title: Abstract P2047: Use of Rapid Cycle Deliberate Practice Simulation to Increase Resident Knowledge and Retention of ACLS Algorithms
items.abstract: Background: Annually, there are 290,000 in-hospital U.S. adult cardiac arrests; 25% survive to discharge. Simulation-based ACLS training enhances resuscitation knowledge and technical skills. Rapid Cycle Deliberate Practice (RCDP) emphasizes repetitive performance with immediate feedback and within-scenario debriefing. At our institution, internal medicine interns undergo initial (non-RCDP) simulation-based ACLS training/certification with follow-up RCDP trainings throughout the year. This study aims to see whether intern ACLS training via RCDP is associated with improvements in ACLS passing score (Kirkpatrick level 2) and self-efficacy. Methods: All incoming Internal Medicine interns at our 269-bed hospital are required to have ACLS certification prior to internship. Training sessions are facilitated in the institutional simulation laboratory by a single emergency/critical care physician with simulation fellowship training. Following ACLS training, participants completed ACLS knowledge tests and self-efficacy surveys. Similar assessments were repeated 9 months later; 80% was required to pass both the baseline and post-intervention ACLS assessments. Learners’ ACLS knowledge was assessed using a modified McEvoy scoring tool. Self-efficacy was measured using a modification of the Basic Resuscitation Skills Self-Efficacy Scale.The Student’s T test was used when 2 comparator groups were compared and p-value was set to p<0.05 Results: Resident knowledge of ACLS protocols increased statistically-significantly (p <0.0001). At baseline, only 2 of 36 residents (5.6%) achieved a passing score; post-intervention, 14 of 30 residents (46.7%) did. Despite objective improvements in knowledge (as evidenced by higher passing rates), self perceived knowledge decreased in the following domains: confidence in knowledge and guidelines, differentiating between defibrillation and synchronized cardioversion, and appropriate level of energy (Joules) for cardioversion and defibrillation. Overall intern self-efficacy demonstrated a statistically-significant decline (p <0.0059). Although some learners self-rated as “very confident” on particular domains after the first training, none were “very confident” at their follow-up evaluation. Conclusion: Simulation-based ACLS training was associated with significant improvement in resident knowledge of ACLS protocols over a 9-month period. However, overall self-efficacy significantly declined over time. Additionally, none reported feeling “very confident” on follow-up assessment despite some initially endorsing high confidence levels. These findings suggest that, while longitudinal simulation-based education employing a RDCP model may improve ACLS knowledge, it may also increase learner recognition of the complexity of resuscitation care and the limitations of their knowledge.

items.title: Abstract P2066: AED Awareness and Knowledge Gaps Between Healthcare and Non-Healthcare Workers in a Major US Metropolis
items.abstract: Introduction: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) survival depends on prompt bystander action, including automated external defibrillator (AED) use. Despite more widespread AED deployment, rates of bystander defibrillation remain low, potentially due to gaps in public awareness and knowledge. Aims: To examine differences in AED knowledge, training, perceived permissibility of use, and legal protections between healthcare workers (HCW) and non-healthcare workers (nHCW) in a major metropolitan area (New York City, or NYC). Methods: A cross-sectional survey was administered to adults residing in NYC. Inclusion criteria were participants aged ≥18 y residing in NYC. Survey questions covered topics including AED recognition, confidence in AED use, operational knowledge, prior training, awareness of AED locations, and understanding of Good Samaritan laws. Statistical comparisons used Pearson chi-square or Fisher's exact tests and significance was defined as p<0.05. Results: Among 1,211 respondents, 812 (67.1%) were male and 986 (81.4%) were aged 30-44 years. Of these, 992 (81.9%) were HCW and 219 (18.1%) were nHCW. Overall, AED awareness was 96.4% and was higher among HCW than nHCW (HCW: 97.4% vs. nHCW: 92.2%; p<0.001). Confidence in AED recognition did not differ significantly between groups (HCW: 78.9% vs. nHCW: 80.6%; p=0.845); however, operational knowledge was significantly higher among HCW (HCW: 85.1% vs. nHCW: 71.5%; p<0.001). Prior AED training was substantially more common among HCW (HCW: 90.8% vs. nHCW: 44.7%; p<0.001). 736 (60.8%) of participants correctly identified that any member of the public may use an AED; nHCW more frequently believed public access AED use was restricted to emergency personnel (nHCW: 32.0% vs. HCW: 11.0%; p<0.001). Awareness of AED locations in residential and workplace settings was lower among nHCW (nHCW: 63.0% vs. HCW: 87.6%; p<0.001). Good Samaritan law awareness was also significantly lower among nHCW (nHCW: 61.8% vs. HCW: 90.2%; p<0.001). Conclusion: Despite high overall AED awareness, critical gaps persist among nHCW in operational knowledge, training, location awareness, and legal protections. These findings underscore the need for targeted, skills-based public education and clearer messaging to advance the usage of AEDs by bystanders.

items.title: Abstract P2082: Impact of Affordable Care Act Medicaid Expansion on Survival After In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: The 2014 Affordable Care Act (ACA) Medicaid expansion reduced uncompensated care and improved hospital operating margins, particularly at safety-net hospitals, potentially improving patient outcomes. Whether the expansion was associated with improved survival after in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) is unknown. Research Question: We sought to examine if the ACA Medicaid expansion is associated with improved survival to discharge and survival with favorable neurologic outcome after IHCA. Methods: We conducted a difference-in-differences (DiD) analysis of adults (≥18 years) with IHCA in the American Heart Association Get With The Guidelines–Resuscitation (GWTG-R) registry from 2000–2024 linked to state-level Medicaid expansion status from the Kaiser Family Foundation. Exposure was a time-varying state expansion indicator (fractional in the year of expansion). Two-way fixed-effects linear probability models on hospital-year data included hospital and year fixed effects, state-clustered standard errors, and adjustment for case-mix (demographics, comorbidities, acute illness factors, arrest characteristics). Missing data were addressed with multiple imputation. Outcomes were survival to discharge and survival with favorable neurologic outcome (CPC 1–2). Results: The analytic sample included 6,285 hospital-year observations from 831 hospitals across 51 states; 40 states expanded Medicaid during the study period and 11 did not. The neurologic-outcome model included 5,922 hospital-years among survivors. ACA Medicaid expansion was not associated with a significant differential change in survival to discharge (+0.81 percentage points, 95% CI –0.66 to +2.28; p=0.28) or in survival with favorable neurologic outcome (+0.40 percentage points, 95% CI –1.45 to +2.26; p=0.67). Conclusions: In a national DiD analysis, the ACA Medicaid expansion was not associated with measurable improvements in survival or neurologic outcomes after IHCA. Improving outcomes will likely require interventions targeting in-hospital resuscitation processes and post-arrest care, not insurance coverage alone.

items.title: Abstract P2087: Patient Characteristics Associated with Pulmonary Embolism and In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Limited research has characterized pulmonary embolism (PE) as a potentially reversible cause of in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA). The incidence, associated risk factors, and characterization of PE-IHCA remain incompletely defined. Improved characterization of PE-IHCA could assist clinicians in the early identification of candidates for PE-focused IHCA resuscitation strategies. Research Questions: What is the incidence of PE in an IHCA population? What are the clinical characteristics of IHCA patients with suspected PE as a potential arrest etiology? Methods: We conducted a retrospective multicenter observational study of adult (≥ 18 y) IHCA patients within a large urban academic health system from 1/2021 - 11/2025. Pediatric and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest cases were excluded. We abstracted data by manual chart review, including demographics, clinical characteristics, vital signs, IHCA resuscitation interventions, and outcomes. CT angiogram (CTA) chest radiology reports were independently assessed by 2 expert reviewers (emergency medicine and critical care), with discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer. PE-positive cases were defined as PE identified on CTA within 7 days of IHCA and identified as a potential etiology for the IHCA. Clinical characteristics associated with PE-positive patients versus PE-negative patients were analyzed descriptively. Results: In a cohort of 1,347 unique IHCA patients, 58.7% (n=791) achieved ROSC, 15.6% (n=210) survived to discharge, 5.9% (n=79) underwent CTA, and 1.1% (n=15) had positive PE results. PE-positive patients had a mean age of 66.8 ± 13.8 years and were predominantly male (60.0%), similar to PE-negative patients (n=64). PE-positive patients were significantly more likely to have an underlying malignancy (p=0.025) or to have undergone surgery within the 30 days preceding the arrest (p=0.025). Conclusions: In this multicenter study, we found that PE-positive IHCA patients were significantly more likely to have underlying malignancies and recent surgeries compared with PE-negative IHCA patients. Further research is needed to develop strategies for early identification of PE-IHCA patients who might benefit from thrombolytics or other critical resuscitation strategies.

items.title: Abstract P2060: CPR Quality During Dental Chair Resuscitation: Impact of Surface Stability on Chest Compression Performance
items.abstract: Background: Cardiac arrest in dental offices represents a rare but critical emergency, requiring immediate initiation of high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). In many situations, resuscitation is started directly on the dental chair due to logistical challenges and delays associated with transferring the patient to the floor. However, the mechanical instability of dental chairs may negatively affect chest compression quality and rescuer performance. Objective: To compare the quality of chest compressions performed on a dental chair versus on the floor by dental students after standardized Basic Life Support (BLS) training. Methods: A quasi-experimental simulation study was conducted with 40 dental students from Centro UniversitÁrio Facens. Participants completed a standardized BLS educational intervention consisting of: 20-minute theoretical lecture10-minute instructor demonstration30-minute supervised hands-on practice using feedback-enabled manikins. Each participant performed two 2-minute chest compression tests in randomized order: CPR on a dental chairCPR on the floor. Compression quality metrics were collected using Little Anne QCPR® manikins and included compression depth, rate, recoil, and percentage of effective compressions. Results: Participants achieved acceptable compression rates in both scenarios. However, CPR performed on the dental chair demonstrated significantly lower overall compression quality when compared with the floor. Key findings included: Reduced compression depth during chair-based CPRLower percentage of complete chest recoilDecreased proportion of effective compressionsGreater rescuer instability and fatigue perception on the dental chair. The percentage of compressions achieving target depth was significantly higher when CPR was performed on the floor (84%) compared with the dental chair (68%) (p < 0.001). Conclusion: Although chest compressions can be initiated on a dental chair when immediate patient transfer is not feasible, the instability of the chair negatively impacts CPR quality. Whenever possible, transferring the patient to a firm surface should be prioritized to optimize compression effectiveness and overall resuscitation performance. Keywords: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation; Dental Emergencies; Simulation Training; Chest Compressions; Basic Life Support; Dental Education.

items.title: Abstract P2062: Rapid Restoration of Carotid Blood Flow Following Chest Compression Pause During Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Interruptions in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and chest compressions are known to impair circulation, but the time required to restore effective cerebral perfusion after a pause is still debated. Research Questions: How many chest compressions are required to re-establish carotid artery blood flow velocity following pauses during CPR? Aim: To quantify the recovery of carotid artery blood flow velocity following pauses during CPR using RescueDoppler, a continuous, hands-free pulsed-wave Doppler ultrasound system. Methods: In this out-of-hospital cardiac arrest multicenter study involving four centers, carotid artery peak systolic blood flow velocities (PSV) were measured using RescueDoppler during chest compressions. Measurements were analyzed in predefined sequences, each consisting of 10 consecutive compressions following pauses (Figure 1). The number of sequences per patient ranged from 1 to 13. We used a linear mixed-effect model in Stata version 19.5, with observations nested within sequence and patient, and allowing for autocorrelation between repeated measurements. Results: In total 33 cardiac arrest patients (men = 22; mean age 63.8 ± 16.4 years) were included. Causes were cardiac (n=14), respiratory failure (n=3), trauma (n=1), intoxication (n=1) and unknown (n=14). Initial rhythms were ventricular fibrillation (n=8), pulseless electrical activity (n=8), asystole (n=14) and unknown (n=3). A total of 116 sequences were analyzed; median CPR duration was 25 minutes (interquartile range = 13 - 49). Sequences were distributed across the resuscitation period, with 27 in the first third, 50 in the middle third, and 39 in the final third. PSV differed significantly across both patients, sequences, and compressions (p < 0.001). On average, the first compression after a pause resulted in significantly lower PSV (59.2 ± 5 cm/s [SEM]) compared to subsequent compressions (66.2 ± 5 cm/s [SEM], p < 0.001; Figure 2). There was a significant inverse relationship between pause duration and PSV during the first compression, with longer pauses associated with reduced PSV (β = –0.56, p = 0.034; Figure 3). The median pause duration was 8.4 seconds (interquartile range 3.9-14.9). Conclusions: Carotid blood flow velocity is significantly reduced at the first compression following pauses but is rapidly restored at the second compression and beyond. Longer pauses are associated with reduced carotid blood flow velocity during the first compression.

items.title: Abstract P2068: Manual Chest Compression Synchronization with External Stimuli at Varied Rates: Synchronization Proof-of-Concept
items.abstract: Background: Synchronizing compressions with native cardiac activity in pulseless electrical activity (PEA) cardiac arrest may be beneficial in increasing coronary perfusion pressures when native cardiac impulse is insufficient to generate a pulse or facilitate adequate end-organ perfusion. Through treatment at the current standard of care, survival rates from PEA in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest remain dismal at 11%. If bystander cardio-pulmonary resuscitation (CPR) can be provided with timely, high-quality chest compressions synchronized to native cardiac activity, it could improve perfusion and perhaps mortality. Research Question: We sought to evaluate the ability of individuals previously trained in CPR to respond to audio and/or visual stimuli and deliver effective chest compressions on a mannequin at a range of rates comparable to those found in PEA arrest. Methods: Ten participants with prior CPR training were included and given instruction to perform chest compressions to the standard of their prior training. Chest compressions were completed at 10 rates determined by stimuli produced by either an audio, visual, or audio/visual cue. Rates ranged from 50 to 140 beats per minute, comparable to previously reported case analysis of pseudo-PEA presentation. Each participant completed 30 seconds of manual compressions at each rate and for each of the three stimulus types, with all orders randomized. Adequate rest was allotted to negate the impact of fatigue. Synchronization of manual compressions was determined by a pressure sensor inside a standard CPR mannequin. We analyzed the difference between stimulus and compression initiation and modeled this “lag” as a function of stimulus type and rate with a mixed linear analysis. Results: There was an overall median lag of 156 ms (n=16,695, u=103,sd=247) from stimulus to onset of nearest compression across all three stimulus types. By stimulus, light showed the lowest median lag at 108 ms (n=5587, u=72,sd=280), followed by sound at 164 ms (n=5554, u=109, sd=185), and then both with 180 ms (n=5,551, u=127, sd=267). In our model, with the shortest lag stimuli light as the baseline, sound has an adjusted lag +36.1 ms (95% CI 27.1-45.1) and both stimuli have an adjusted lag +55.4 ms (95% CI 46.3-64.4). We also found that lag changes by -1.3 ms (95% CI -1.4--1.2) for every one CPM increase. We calculated that compressions would occur within the first half of the average estimated QT interval for each given stimulus rate 51% (95% CI 50-52) of the time overall. Conclusion: Manual provision of chest compressions in response to an external stimulus is feasible at rates inherent to pseudo-PEA arrest. However, based on typical QT intervals in both male and female populations, adequate synchronization without additional rate predictive stimulus timing adjustment only occurs about half of the time.

items.title: Abstract P2086: Modes of Death Following In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Single Center Study
items.abstract: Introduction: Nearly 15,00 children experience pediatric in-hospital cardiac arrest (pIHCA) in the US annually, yet limited research has investigated the reasons for death following acute survival from these events. Aims: To characterize modes and timing of death among children who achieved return of circulation (ROC) after pIHCA Methods: Single center retrospective study of children who achieved ROC after IHCA but died prior to discharge from 2013 to 2023. Modes of death were defined by either refractory organ failure leading to death without attempted resuscitation or withdrawal of life-sustaining therapies (WLST) within the following categories: neurologic, circulatory, respiratory or other comorbidities. Recurrent arrest was defined as re-arrest with attempted but unsuccessful resuscitation. Intergroup characteristics were compared using Fisher’s exact, Chi-squared and Kruskal Wallis tests. Results: Of the 122 patients included in the study, circulatory failure (n=45; 37%) and recurrent arrest (n=27; 22%) accounted for the majority of deaths, followed by neurologic causes in 20 patients (16%) and respiratory and other comorbidities in 15 patients (12%) each (p<0.001). Pre-arrest characteristics varied by mode of death, including age, race and illness category (Table 1). The only event characteristic which varied by group was exposure to ECPR, with the highest rates in the neurologic and circulatory categories (Table 2). In the post-arrest phase, procurement of brain imaging and EEG varied by mode of death, with the highest rates for both in the neurologic category (Table 3).Finally, median time to death after initial arrest varied between groups, with the longest duration in circulatory group and the shortest in the re-arrest group; (p<0.001 Table 3). Conclusions: In this single center retrospective cohort study, we found that children who died following successful resuscitation from pIHCA were most likely to die due to non-neurologic causes, indicating that pIHCA occurs in the context of complex critical illness. Therefore, pIHCA may serve as a complication of severe illness rather than the direct cause of death in many patients. These findings are in contrast with prior work in children who die after resuscitation from out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with deaths more likely related to neurologic causes from prolonged arrest. This distinction is key to interpreting long-term outcomes in pIHCA which are often influenced by factors unrelated to the arrest.

items.title: Abstract P2029: Pseudo-Subarachnoid Hemorrhage and White Cerebellum Sign Following Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Case Series
items.abstract: Background: Pseudo-subarachnoid hemorrhage (pseudo-SAH) and the white cerebellum sign are head CT findings that reflect severe hypoxic-ischemic brain injury following out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). The clinical significance and outcomes have not been systemically characterized. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that these imaging findings signify poor neurological outcomes with important implications on goals-of-care discussions and neuroprognostication. Methods: This study is a retrospective case series of all adult OHCA patients presenting to four hospitals within the University of Pennsylvania Health System (2019-2024) under IRB approval #849677. Patients that had return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) with head CT findings of pseudo-SAH and white cerebellum sign were included for this study and corresponding arrest and outcome characteristics were collected from the electronic health record into a secured REDCap database. Primary outcome included in-hospital mortality and secondary outcomes encompassed cerebral performance category (CPC) and modified Rankin Scale (mRS). Results: Thirty-five patients were identified meeting the inclusion criteria: 30 (85.7%) with pseudo-SAH and 5 (14.3%) with white cerebellum sign. Mean age 53.6 ± 17.1 years; 45.7% female; 68.6% Black or African American. Non-shockable rhythms predominated (88.6%). CT co-findings included loss of gray-white differentiation and sulcal effacement (94.3% each), diffuse cerebral edema (91.4%), and herniation (20.0%). Neuron-specific enolase (NSE), available in 11 patients (31.4%) and was elevated (median 53.7 ng/mL [IQR 46.9-120.7]). Absent pupillary reflexes at 72 hours were documented in 78.3% and absent corneal reflexes at 72 hours in 87.5%. In-hospital mortality was 94.3% (33/35) in this group of patients. Both survivors had mRS 5 at discharge (CPC 3 and CPC 4, respectively); one died within three months post-OHCA. No patients achieved good neurological outcome (CPC 1-2 or mRS 0-2). Conclusions: This is the largest cohort in the literature describing pseudo-SAH and white cerebellum sign following OHCA. This study indicates that these findings are associated with very high in-hospital mortality and poor neurological recovery in the rare case of survival. These findings may serve as an early prognostic marker guiding neuroprognostication and goals-of-care discussions.

items.title: Abstract P2036: Emergency Medical Services Perspectives on Family Life Support and Intra-Arrest Transport
items.abstract: Introduction: Intra-arrest transport (IAT) of out of hospital cardiac arrest is associated with worse patient outcomes compared to on-scene resuscitation. However, on-scene resuscitation is difficult to sustain as family distress may impact clinical decision-making, requiring a structured approach to supporting families and family presence during resuscitation. Research Questions: To what extent does family presence influence EMS clinician decision-making regarding IAT? What impact does family-focused training have on EMS clinician confidence in managing resuscitation in the presence of family members? Aims: Describe EMS clinician perceptions of how the presence of family may influence IAT decision-making. Develop and pilot a family life support (FLS) training program and evaluate its impact on EMS clinician confidence in performing pre-defined competencies. Methods: We created a FLS training program with didactic and simulation education within a single, rural EMS agency. A pre-post survey with Likert scale evaluated clinician confidence in four identified competencies. A Wilcoxon signed rank test was performed to determine significance. Rapid thematic analysis was performed on open text responses. Results: A total of 73 EMS clinicians participated; 64% reported that the presence of family members did not influence IAT decision making, 36% were somewhat influenced in their decision and 7% reported a direct influence. Five themes described how family presence influences IAT decision-making: decisions driven by protocol alone, contextual considerations, ability to communicate with the family, scene safety, and ethical beliefs regarding family perspectives. After FLS training, there was a significant improvement in EMS clinicians’ confidence in guiding a family member through a resuscitation event (4.10 ± 0.97 v 4.48 ± 0.69,p <0.001). There were no statistically significant changes in confidence in communication, leading a pause, or empathizing with family. Participants described wanting to be more inclusive of family in future resuscitations (24%,9/37), improve communication with family (49%,18/37), and implement a pause in the case of patient death (14%,5/37). Narrative responses described high perceived value in the training and a strong preference for experiential learning. Conclusion: Family presence influences some EMS clinicians’ IAT decision-making. The FLS training program improved EMS clinicians' confidence in skills to guide families through a resuscitation.

items.title: Abstract P2037: Physician-Performed Prehospital Endotracheal Intubation and Outcomes in Patients with Trauma: A Nationwide Cohort Study
items.abstract: Background: Prehospital airway management, including prehospital endotracheal intubation (PETI), is an important component of prehospital trauma care for patients with severe trauma. Previous studies evaluating the association between PETI and mortality have reported conflicting results, potentially due to variability in provider expertise, patient selection, and healthcare systems. Japan has a physician-staffed emergency medical service system, including helicopter emergency medical services (HEMS) and ground emergency medical services (GEMS), in which emergency physicians provide prehospital advanced airway management. Therefore, the aim of this study was to evaluate the association between physician-performed PETI and in-hospital mortality. Hypothesis: Physician-performed PETI would be associated with lower in-hospital mortality compared with IETI. Methods: This multicenter retrospective cohort study analyzed data from the Japan Trauma Data Bank, a nationwide trauma registry, between 2019 and 2023. Adult trauma patients (18 years or older) directly transported from the injury scene to participating hospitals by physician-staffed HEMS or GEMS were eligible. Patients with a clinical indication for endotracheal intubation defined by respiratory failure, shock, or impaired consciousness, who underwent PETI or IETI were included. Patients with cardiac arrest at the scene and those with burns were excluded.The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. Secondary outcomes included scene time and total transportation time. Inverse probability weighting (IPW) with propensity scores was used to adjust for patient demographics, prehospital vital signs, and injury severity. The association between PETI and in-hospital mortality was evaluated using IPW-adjusted logistic regression. Several subgroup analyses by intubation indication were performed to evaluate the consistency of the findings across patients with respiratory failure, shock, or impaired consciousness. Results: Among 1,253 patients (median age, 68 years; 76% male; median Injury Severity Score, 26), 370 (30%) underwent PETI and 883 (70%) underwent IETI. PETI was not associated with lower in-hospital mortality compared with IETI (37% vs 34%; adjusted odds ratio, 1.17; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.91-1.51; p=0.226). PETI was associated with a longer scene time (median difference, 9 minutes; 95% CI, 7-11; p<0.001) and longer total transportation time (median difference, 13 minutes; 95% CI, 10-17; p<0.001). Subgroup analyses across intubation indication showed consistent results. Conclusions: In this nationwide cohort of trauma patients transported by physician-staffed emergency medical services, PETI was not associated with lower in-hospital mortality compared with IETI and was associated with longer scene and total transportation times.

items.title: Abstract P2061: CPR-Induced Consciousness Detection of Carotid Blood Flow During Apparent Pulselessness Using Doppler Monitoring
items.abstract: Background: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation-induced consciousness (CPRIC) refers to signs of consciousness during chest compressions despite cardiac arrest and absence of return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Manifestations include eye opening, breathing, purposeful movements, speech attempts, or resistance to resuscitation. This can be mistaken for ROSC, leading to interruptions in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). The underlying physiology is unclear but is thought to involve cerebral perfusion from high-quality compressions. The role of intrinsic cardiac mechanical activity (ICMA) during CPRIC has not been well characterized, partly due to lack of real-time monitoring. Hypothesis: Continuous carotid Doppler monitoring during CPR detects perfusion linked to CPRIC and reveals ICMA, even without palpable pulses. Aims: To describe the relationship between CPRIC, compressions and carotid blood flow using hands-free Doppler, and assess whether continuous monitoring improves recognition of perfusion during CPR. Methods: From a multi-center study including four out-of-hospital and four in-hospital centers and 207 cardiac arrest patients, 20 (9.7 %) cardiac arrest cases were documented as CPRIC. A hands-free pulsed-wave Doppler ultrasound device, RescueDoppler, blinded to rescuers, continuously measured carotid blood flow during CPR and pulse checks. ICMA was defined as having antegrade systolic velocity with or without retrograde flow during pauses (Figure 1) or during chest compressions (Figure 2). Results: Of the 20 CPRIC cases, RescueDoppler was applied in five patients after CPRIC had been documented; and two recordings had insufficient carotid flow quality.
