Thirteen patients were included in the analysis (mean age 69 years, range 37-77). Mean BMI was 25.3 kg/m 2 (range 19.7-30.0). Cardiac arrests occurred in-hospital in 54% and out-of-hospital in 46%. At the time of CPRIC, the observed rhythm was pulseless electrical activity (PEA) in 5 (38%) of the cases, ventricular fibrillation (VF) in 1 (8%), a combination of PEA and VF in 4 (31%) and a combination of PEA and ventricular tachycardia in 1 (8%). ROSC occurred in 85% (n=11) and sustained ROSC in 54% (n=7). RescueDoppler detected ICMA, in all 13 CPRIC patients during CPR, including during compressions and/or pulse checks, despite absent palpable pulses. Conclusions: Detection of intrinsic cardiac mechanical activity by continuous carotid Doppler in all CPRIC cases, both during pauses and/or during chest compressions, suggests that CPRIC represents a state in which some underlying cardiac activity is present, rather than being solely a consequence of high-quality chest compressions. This provides a physiological explanation for consciousness despite absent palpable pulses and highlights the potential role of real-time decision-making during CPR.

items.title: Abstract P2076: Behavioral Characteristics of Foreign Body Airway Obstruction: Analysis of Publicly Available Online Videos
items.abstract: Introduction: Foreign body airway obstruction (FBAO) is a life-threatening event. Early bystander intervention improves survival and neurologic outcomes. However, previous studies have shown that many patients do not receive timely bystander intervention, and the reasons for this remain unclear. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that publicly available online videos of real-world FBAO events could provide clinically meaningful information into individual behaviors and bystander interventions. We further hypothesized that patients with FBAO do not consistently exhibit the universal choking sign, defined as placing one or both hands in front of the neck. Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational study analyzing publicly available YouTube videos. Real-world FBAO cases were identified using search keywords in four languages (English, Spanish, Japanese and Korean). We included cases of all ages and stratified them into infants (<1 year of age), children (1-12 years), and adults (>12 years). Two investigators independently screened each video for eligibility and extracted data. Videos were excluded if the event was not a real FBAO case (e.g., training or simulation video) or if video quality was insufficient for evaluation. Results: Of 334 videos screened, 75 cases met inclusion criteria and were analyzed, including 21 infants (28%), 21 Children (28%), 31 adults (41%) and 2 unknown (3%). Thirty-one cases (41%) captured the entire FBAO event from onset to resolution with no infant cases. The universal choking sign was observed in 12 of 31 fully captured cases (39%). When stratified by age group, the sign was more frequently observed in adults than children (10/22, 45% vs. 2/8, 25%) with no statistically significant difference between groups (Fisher’s exact test, p=0.42). As the initial bystander intervention, back blows were the most commonly performed maneuver in infants (20/21, 95%) and children (13/21, 62%), whereas abdominal thrusts were most frequently used in adults (23/31, 74%). Conclusion: Online media provided clinically relevant information on real-world FBAO events that would otherwise be difficult to study. The universal choking sign was observed in only approximately one-third of fully captured cases and was less frequently seen in children than in adults, suggesting that bystander recognition may be particularly challenging in the younger victims. These findings may help inform future resuscitation education and FBAO recognition strategies.

items.title: Abstract P2018: Effects of Positive-End Expiratory Pressure on Capnography and Hemodynamics During Mechanical Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in Swine
items.abstract: Introduction: During CPR, chest compressions induce oscillations in the capnogram that can be quantified as the Capnogram Oscillation Magnitude (COM) and the Airway Opening Index (AOI). These metrics are hypothesized to reflect airway patency and effective ventilation. Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) may modulate capnographic waveform morphology during CPR, though the relationship between PEEP, COM, AOI, and hemodynamics remains poorly understood. Aim: We examined the effect of titrated PEEP on capnographic waveform morphology, including COM, AOI, and peak end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2) during mechanical CPR in a pilot study using a swine model of ventricular fibrillation (VF) cardiac arrest. Methods: Four swine underwent 8 minutes of untreated VF followed by 60 minutes of mechanical CPR. Animals were intubated and ventilated at 10 breaths/min with fraction of inspired oxygen of 1.0. PEEP was sequentially titrated across 6-minute epochs of 0, 5, and 10 cmH 2 O in repeated cycles during CPR. 6 doses of epinephrine (0.02 mg/kg) were administered beginning at minute 14 and repeated every 4 minutes. Continuous capnography and aortic blood pressure were recorded throughout. A custom MATLAB algorithm was used to calculate COM and AOI. Results: Across 4 animals, we observed that stepwise increases in PEEP from 0 to 5 to 10 cmH2O were associated with longer time to peak ETCO2 within ventilation cycles (Figure 1). We observed no overall changes in aortic pressure or ETCO2 with PEEP titrations, but these did gradually decrease over the course of resuscitation (Figure 2). Conclusion: In this preliminary swine model of cardiac arrest, increasing PEEP appeared to influence capnographic waveform morphology during mechanical CPR, particularly the time to peak ETCO2 after a ventilation. Aortic blood pressure and overall ETCO2 remained largely stable during stepwise PEEP titration, but decreased over the course of resuscitation. This association may indicate that at higher PEEP levels cardiac output exceeds ventilation, resulting in the prolonged time to peak ETCO2. Ongoing analysis will quantify the dose-dependent effects of PEEP on ventilation metrics (AOI, COM, and peak ETCO2), along with indicators of cardiac output (aortic blood pressure and the area under the capnography waveform curve). These findings may inform PEEP as a modifiable ventilation parameter during CPR to optimize airway management and resuscitation outcomes.

items.title: Abstract P2034: Identifying Precision Resuscitation Endophenotypes Using Pre-Arrest and Post-ROSC Biomarker Trajectories
items.abstract: Introduction: While ACLS has optimized CPR, post-ROSC care lacks targeted interventions for endophenotypes. Precision resuscitation requires moving beyond static baseline risk. By leveraging EMR data to quantify dynamic trajectories of immuno-metabolic biomarkers from pre-arrest to post-ROSC, we characterized active physiological shifts to identify treatable in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) endophenotypes. Methods: This IRB-exempt study (January 2020-January 2026) evaluated adult patients undergoing CPR for IHCA within 48h of admission who achieved ROSC and survived in the ICU for >24h. Sequential clustering integrated Elixhauser Comorbidity Categories with pre-arrest biomarkers. Within derived clusters, Boosted Tree models quantified the variance explained (VE%) for a composite outcome (CO) (Hospice DC or Hospital Mortality) using delta ( D) (pre-IHCA to post-ROSC/ICU Day 1) of 22 biomarker predictors. Results: Among 435 patients, five distinct clinical endophenotypes were identified with divergent clinical profiles, host support requirements, and survival rates (Table 1). Boosted tree modeling demonstrated cluster-specific risk was driven by biological mechanisms (Figure 1): Cluster 1 (Immune Mobilization; n=239, 55%): A predominant, intermediate-risk phenotype with variance heavily driven by the acute mobilization of immature myeloid lineages ( D Promyelocytes, Myelocytes, and Metamyelocytes). Cluster 2 (Cardiorenal Frailty; n=103, 24%): An elderly cohort characterized by valvular and renal multimorbidity, where outcomes were primarily dictated by acute protein-vascular shifts ( D Albumin and D Platelet Count). Cluster 3 (Vascular/Capillary Leak; n=19, 4%): A high-mortality, low-support phenotype uniquely driven by microvascular barrier degradation and capillary leak ( D Albumin/Creatinine Ratio). Cluster 4 (Metabolic Exhaustion; n=58, 13%): A younger, lower-mortality cohort where outcome variance was almost exclusively explained by bioenergetic failure and altered anaerobic pathways ( D Lactate/Glucose and D Glucose/Albumin Ratios). Cluster 5 (Endothelial Collapse; n=16, 4%): A hyper-acute, high-risk phenotype presenting with dense baseline CHF and hepatic disease, exhibiting severe, symmetrical immuno-metabolic disruptions and profound endothelial degradation ( D Albumin x Platelet Product and D Neutrophil/Albumin Ratio). Conclusions: Coupling structural multimorbidity with functional biomarker trajectories operationalizes treatable traits. This approach allows standard ACLS pathways to be enhanced by targeted, phase-specific interventions. Transitioning targeted therapies into the immediate post-ROSC window could rescue specific bioenergetic (Cluster 4) or endothelial collapse (Cluster 5) phenotypes before secondary reperfusion injury becomes irreversible.

items.title: Abstract P2058: Optimal Duty Cycle During CPR: Clinical Rationale and Preclinical Validation
items.abstract: Introduction: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) aim to provide blood flow during cardiac arrest by simulating the cardiac cycles of systole and diastole with compression of the chest (systole) effecting cardiac output and decompression (diastole) with elastic recoil of the chest allowing cardiac filling and coronary artery perfusion, a vital parameter during CPR, since it is linked to return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Although guidelines call for a 50% duty cycle (percent compression), it is acknowledged that this recommendation is not based upon high quality evidence. A normal healthy heart spends about twice as long in diastole compared to systole, i.e. a 33% duty cycle. Similarly, during manual CPR compression time tends to be shorter compared to decompression time. In a clinical study in adults with out of hospital cardiac arrest the mean duty cycle observed during resuscitation was 39% and there was a 43% survival to hospital discharge, 37% with good neurological outcome. Physiologically, the optimal duty cycle would maximize coronary perfusion time (diastole/decompression), without negatively influencing cardiac output (caused by systole/compression). Time in systole and compression may be as low as 33% (normal cardiac cycle) and 39% (manual CPR high-performing system), respectively, without negatively influencing ejection. This study hypothesizes that a 40% duty cycle is more optimal (improving coronary blood flow without compromising peak arterial pressure) than the 50% duty cycle recommended by guidelines. Methods: Hemodynamic response to a LUCAS®3 (Jolife AB/Stryker) modified to deliver a 40% duty cycle was compared to standard LUCAS®3 (50% duty cycle) on nine swine (36.5-40kg) in cardiac arrest. Ventricular fibrillation was induced and left untreated for six minutes followed by mechanical CPR for 23 minutes alternating between the two duty cycles (Figure A). Arterial and venous pressure were measured, and the sum of their difference during decompression was calculated as an estimate of coronary perfusion, since perfusion is determined by both perfusion pressure and perfusion time (Figure B). Results: Coronary perfusion was 19% higher during 40% duty cycle compared to the standard 50% duty cycle (p<<0.001). The increase in perfusion during 40% duty cycle is due to the prolonged perfusion time obtained during decompression (Figure C). There was a 2% improvement in peak arterial pressure (p<0.001) with 40% duty cycle compared to 50% duty cycle, indicating that ejection is not negatively influenced by the shorter compression (Figure C). Conclusion: Coronary perfusion increased significantly with shorter compression (40%) and longer decompression (60%) than current guideline recommendation without compromising arterial pressures. The potential impact of improved coronary perfusion with this 40% duty cycle warrants further study to confirm its impact on ROSC.

items.title: Abstract P2033: An Exploratory Evaluation of Blood Pressure, Vasoactive Support, and Hemodynamic Index After Pediatric Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Post-arrest hypotension, typically defined by the lowest systolic blood pressure (SBP), is associated with mortality after pediatric cardiac arrest. However, many post-arrest patients require vasopressors and inotropes, and prior analyses have not accounted for SBP together with vasoactive support intensity. Research Question: Among children after cardiac arrest, is Vasoactive Inotropic Score (VIS) and a derived ratio of VIS to SBP associated with mortality, and does incorporation of VIS improve outcome discrimination beyond SBP alone? Aim: We aimed to 1) create a composite term to account for both SBP and VIS called Hemodynamic Index (HI; a calculated ratio of simultaneously measured SBP to VIS) and 2) explore the relationship between SBP, VIS and HI and mortality after pediatric cardiac arrest. Methods: We retrospectively reviewed children < 18 years who initially survived IHCA and OHCA lasting > 1 minute cared for in our single-center pediatric intensive care unit with pathway-guided SBP targets. We collected lowest percentile-corrected SBP and peak VIS in multiple time intervals (0-24, 0-48- and 0-72 hour epochs post-arrest). We created 3 equations to calculate HI in this exploratory analysis (Figure 1). Outcome was hospital mortality. For this preliminary analysis, we performed univariate analysis to determine association of each predictor with mortality. To assess prediction of SBP, VIS and HI for mortality, we calculated unadjusted areas under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC). Results: Of 793 patients, IHCA occurred in 63%, and mortality in 38%. Median age was 1.8 (IQR 0.4-8.0) years, and arrest duration was 7.4 (IQR 2-21) minutes. On univariate analysis, VIS and HI were associated with increased odds of mortality (p<0.001, Table 1). VIS demonstrated the strongest precision-recall performance for mortality (AUPRC 0.622 at 0-24 h, 0.634 at 0-48 h, and 0.642 at 0-72 h), followed by HI 1 and HI 2, while HI 3 showed weaker discrimination. SBP showed only modest improvement over the mortality prevalence baseline, indicating limited discriminative utility. Conclusions: In this exploratory single-center analysis of children after cardiac arrest, peak VIS was more strongly associated with mortality than SBP alone or the derived HI models. Further work is needed to refine composite hemodynamic measures and to determine if accounting for the interaction between blood pressure and vasoactive support improves hemodynamic assessment after pediatric cardiac arrest.

items.title: Abstract P2051: Obsessed with Failure: Scaling VHA's Standardized Mock Code Training Program
items.abstract: Introduction/Background: The Veterans Health Administration (VHA), the largest integrated healthcare system in the United States with 1,380 facilities, continues to face persistently low in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) survival rates of 18-20%. Because real code events are low-frequency but high-risk, structured simulation offers a critical opportunity to strengthen clinical performance and system reliability. Research Question/Hypothesis: Standardizing mock code training and system-level assessment across a highly variable national health system will improve identification of latent safety risks and promote targeted quality-improvement actions. Goals/Aims: To develop, implement, and scale a standardized VHA-wide mock code program with unified data collection, a shared educational structure, and a systematic approach to risk identification using a modified Healthcare Failure Mode and Effect Analysis (HFMEA) Hazard Scoring Matrix. Methods/Approach: Beginning in 2020, the VHA Resuscitation Education and Innovation (REdI) program implemented a hybrid mock code curriculum grounded in high-reliability organization principles. Participating facilities engaged in a virtual collaborative learning environment followed by onsite simulation and evaluation. Contributive factors were scored using a modified HFMEA matrix to assess system vulnerabilities and recommend mitigation strategies. Data from local training events were entered into a national database for descriptive analysis. Results/Data: To date, more than 50% of VHA facilities have adopted the standardized REdI Mock Code Program (RMCP). Over 500 mock code events have been documented and analyzed. Preliminary review of descriptive data revealed the five most common national latent safety risks, including recurrent system-level, workflow, and communication vulnerabilities. Inferential statistical analyses will be presented to compare hazard scoring patterns across facility complexity levels. Conclusion: A scalable, standardized mock code training program with integrated HFMEA-based risk scoring is feasible across a large, complex national health system. Early findings demonstrate consistent identification of high-impact latent safety risks, providing actionable insights for both local and enterprise-level quality-improvement initiatives.

items.title: Abstract P2073: Effects of Delayed Treatment with Moderate Therapeutic Hypothermia in a 72-Hour Survival Rat Model of 8-Minute Ventricular Fibrillation Cardiac Arrest Resuscitated with eCPR
items.abstract: Introduction: The effects of global ischemia-reperfusion injury on the brain have been widely studied in cardiac arrest animal models, and moderate therapeutic hypothermia (MTH) remains a promising treatment. However, its mechanisms are still unclear, and benefits seen in animals have not fully translated to humans, possibly because target temperature is reached too late after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Methods: Male Sprague Dawley rats (Charles River Laboratories) with a weight between 450-800g were subjected to 8 minutes of ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest (VFCA) and resuscitated with extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (eCPR) (n=33). Sham-operated animals (n= 6) served as controls. After ROSC, animals were randomized into three groups: Normothermia (NT, n=16), Immediate MTH with 33 ± 0.5 °C for 12 h (HT, n=9), and delayed MTH with cooling initiation 2h after ROSC following 33 ± 0.5 °C for 12 h (dHT, n=8). Over the course of 72 hours animals were evaluated using the Neurologic deficit score (NDS) and Overall performance category (OPC) daily. Then brains of five animals per group were fixed in formalin, embedded in paraffin and stained with hematoxylin and eosin. Neuronal necrosis was assessed semi-quantitatively in the hippocampal CA1 region. Results: Survival after 72h was 100% in both MTH groups (immediate: 9/9; delayed: 8/8) compared to 50% in the NT group (8/16), with all sham animals surviving to the study endpoint (6/6).At 72 hours, NDS scores differed significantly across groups (Kruskal-Wallis: p < 0.001). Both HT and dHT groups demonstrated significantly lower NDS scores compared to NT controls (p < 0.001 and p < 0.001, respectively). Importantly, HT showed superior neurological recovery compared to dHT(p = 0.020). OPC scores at 72 hours likewise differed significantly across groups (Kruskal-Wallis: p < 0.001). Both MTH groups demonstrated significantly improved OPC compared to NT controls (HT: p < 0.001; dHT: p = 0.002), with HT achieving superior outcomes compared to dHT (p = 0.022). Neither sham animals nor MTH groups showed neuronal necrosis in the hippocampus, while all NT animals exhibited marked neuronal necrosis. Conclusion: In this VFCA eCPR model, MTH showed clear beneficial effects, but delaying cooling by just two hours markedly reduced its neuroprotective and overall benefit. Interestingly, the histological findings only showed a significant difference between NT and HT+dHT, not between HT and dHT.

items.title: Abstract P2038: Prehospital Endotracheal Intubation and Outcomes in Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study
items.abstract: Introduction: Pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is a high-acuity, low-occurrence event with persistently poor survival and neurologic outcomes. Optimal airway management during pediatric OHCA remains uncertain, as high-quality evidence comparing endotracheal intubation (ETI) with less invasive alternatives such as bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation or supraglottic airway (SGA) devices is limited. Hypothesis: Prehospital ETI is associated with improved outcomes compared to non-ETI airway management. Aims: To evaluate the association between prehospital ETI and clinical outcomes in children with OHCA. Methods: We performed a single-center retrospective cohort study of subjects aged 30 days to 18 years with OHCA transported by emergency medical services (EMS) to the only quaternary pediatric emergency department serving a large metropolitan area with over 50 EMS agencies . Patients with tracheostomy or cricothyroidotomy were excluded. Subjects were stratified by final airway management strategy prior to ED arrival: prehospital ETI versus non-ETI airway management (BVM and/or SGA without ETI). Patient demographics, arrest characteristics, and prehospital interventions were compared using Kruskal-Wallis and chi-square analyses. Primary outcomes were return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival to hospital discharge (SHD). Multivariable logistic regression was used to evaluate associations between ETI and outcomes, adjusting for age, initial rhythm, and witnessed arrest status. Results: Among 203 included patients, 40 (20%) underwent prehospital ETI. The cohort was predominantly infants (median age 0.7 years, IQR 0.2 - 4.3), with mostly unwitnessed arrests (75%) and non-shockable rhythms (94%). Patients receiving ETI were older (median age 2.5 vs 0.4 years, p<0.001) and received more epinephrine doses (median 4 vs 2, p<0.001). Unadjusted outcomes were numerically higher in the ETI group, including ROSC (32.5% vs. 26.4%) and SHD (12.5% vs. 8.0%). However, after adjustment, ETI was not independently associated with ROSC (aOR 1.32, 95% CI 0.57-2.91) or SHD (aOR 1.56, 95% CI 0.44-4.85). Shockable initial rhythm was independently associated with both ROSC (aOR 5.98, 95% CI 1.54-29.5) and SHD (aOR 5.54, 95% CI 1.26-23.3), while witnessed arrest was associated with ROSC (aOR 2.42, 95% CI 1.14-5.07). Conclusion: In this single-center cohort of pediatric OHCA, prehospital ETI was not independently associated with improved ROSC or survival to hospital discharge. Patients undergoing ETI demonstrated characteristics suggestive of greater arrest severity, raising the possibility of residual confounding by indication. These findings underscore the need for multicenter studies and improved physiologic characterization of pediatric OHCA to better define optimal airway management strategies.

items.title: Abstract P2040: Hemodynamic Characterization of a Novel Perfused Cadaver Cardiac Arrest Model
items.abstract: Background: Cardiac arrest is a highly morbid condition, affecting nearly 350,000 Americans annually, with survival rates of 10% despite decades of research. Resuscitation research has traditionally relied on animal models, but animal models differ from humans in thoracic anatomy, chest wall compliance, and the absence of clinically relevant comorbidities, limiting translatability to human cardiac arrest. Human cadavers offer superior anatomical fidelity, but they have been limited by the absence of circulation. Perfused cadavers have shown promise in trauma simulation, but no prior model has demonstrated continuous pulsatile perfusion with a beating-heart circuit across cardiac arrest states. Research Question: Can a perfused human cadaver with a beating-heart cannulation circuit simulate hemodynamic states of cardiac arrest and CPR? Aims: To develop and characterize a novel perfused cadaveric cardiac arrest model capable of generating physiologically plausible hemodynamic data across three resuscitation states: beating-heart baseline, simulated cardiac arrest, and active CPR. Methods: Five human cadavers were prepared by MaxFi Surgical Simulations using the enviroPC® perfusion system with SimBlood® synthetic blood. A beating-heart cannulation circuit was established via left atrial appendage cannulation and jugular venous reservoir, enabling pulsatile aortic flow. Ultrasound-guided 20-gauge artery catheters were placed in the right carotid. Hemodynamic data were recorded via PowerLab (AD Instruments) across three sequential states: pump-ON (beating-heart), pump-OFF (simulated arrest), and manual midline mid sternum chest compressions (CPR). One cadaver was mechanically ventilated via a 7.0 ET tube in volume control with 6 mg/kg at PEEP of 5 cmH2O. Results: The beating-heart model generated pulsatile arterial waveforms (mean systolic 40.35 ± 10.1 mmHg, diastolic 35.5 ± 11.6 mmHg, MAP 37.1 ± 11 mmHg). Pump cessation produced loss of pulsatile morphology with residual pressurization of 24.9 ± 2.23 mmHg, consistent with cardiac arrest hemodynamics. Manual CPR generated aortic pressures of systolic 56.9 ± 11, diastolic 25.5 ± 6.5, MAP 38.4 ± 5.4 mmHg, which demonstrates a significant increase from cardiac arrest baseline (p=0.0008, ANOVA). Pump on vs Pump off was also significantly different (p = 0.04, ANOVA). The ventilated cadaver demonstrated respiratory variation on arterial tracings. Conclusion: To our knowledge, this is the first cardiac arrest model utilizing a continuously perfused human cadaver with a beating-heart cannulation circuit. The model reproducibly and recognizably transitions through beating-heart, arrest, and CPR states while generating physiologically plausible hemodynamic waveforms and preserving human thoracic anatomy and chest wall mechanics. This model represents a promising platform for future resuscitation research.

items.title: Abstract P2043: Recombinant Heme Protein Without Vasoconstriction for Resuscitation and Improved Oxygen Delivery in Hemorrhagic Shock and Asphyxiation
items.abstract: Introduction: Hemorrhagic shock remains a leading cause of preventable death. Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning is the most common human poisoning but there is no antidote. We have engineered the Regulator of CO Metabolism (RcoM) heme protein to include just the heme-binding domain truncate as an intravenous therapeutic which shows no vasoconstrictive effects, a major limiting toxicity for hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers. We have previously shown the efficacy of RcoM as a CO antidotal therapy to reverse CO binding to hemoglobin. We have produced RcoM in multiple microbial expression systems at grams scale to facilitate in vivo testing. Hypothesis: We anticipate RcoM can serve as platform therapeutic as a blood substitute and as a CO poisoning antidote. Goals: The goals of the study are to: 1) assess the biochemical features of engineered RcoM as an oxygen delivery agent; and, 2) assess the tolerance and efficacy of intravenous RcoM in an animal model of hemorrhagic shock. Materials and Methods: We assessed biochemical features of engineered RcoM using UV-visible spectroscopy methods. We used a murine model of traumatic-hemorrhagic shock utilizing anesthetized mice with a 2cm abdominal incision and left femoral artery and vein catheterization. Mice underwent 30-minute controlled bleeding to a target blood pressure of 25 to 40 mmHg, shock maintained for 30 minutes, and then treatment by lactated Ringer solution (LR), 2mM stroma-free hemoglobin (sHb), or 2mM RcoM at volume equal to removed blood, and monitored for 30 minutes. We also assessed RcoM safety profile at 48 hours. Results: RcoM shows an autoxidation rate of 0.015 min -1 and a P50 of 4.2 mmHg. In our hemorrhagic shock model, there was no difference in the ratio of shed blood volume to the total blood volume between groups and no difference for the baseline MAP between LR (83.5±5.7 mmHg), sHb (87.4±3.0 mmHg) and RcoM (82.3±1.9 mmHg; p = 0.2931). Post-resuscitation MAP was significantly higher for RcoM (67.0±6.3 mmHg) and sHb (60.4±16.0 mmHg) compared to LR (25.9±21.4 mmHg, p = 0.0029). There was no difference between Rcom and sHb in the post-resuscitation mean arterial pressure (MAP). RcoM was well tolerated. Conclusion: This study demonstrates that resuscitation with engineered RcoM improves MAP in a murine traumatic hemorrhagic shock model. In addition to the previously reported ability of RcoM to reverse CO toxicity, these data suggest the potential application of intravenous RcoM as a non-globin artificial oxygen carrier for hemorrhagic shock.

items.title: Abstract P2077: Cardiac Arrest Following Prehospital Rapid Sequence Intubation: Etomidate versus Ketamine
items.abstract: Introduction: The optimal induction strategy for rapid sequence intubation (RSI) during emergency airway management remains unclear. Two commonly-used medications include etomidate and ketamine. Relatively little research has examined potential differences between the two medications specifically in the prehospital setting for intubations performed by emergency medical services (EMS). Hypothesis: Differences in the proportion of post-intubation cardiac arrest will exist for prehospital RSI by EMS stratified by induction agent (etomidate vs. ketamine). Methods: We used a nationally-representative sample of EMS activations from 2000+ EMS agencies throughout the United States (ImageTrend Collaborate) to examine ground EMS activations in 2025 involving adult (≥18 years) patients where an intubation was performed and either ketamine or etomidate was documented as being given. We evaluated raw proportional differences in documented cardiac arrest incidence across induction method. Results: A total of 5195 cases with prehospital RSI and documented administration of either ketamine or etomidate met inclusion criteria. Ketamine (3552/5195, 68.4%) was more commonly used than etomidate (1643/5195, 31.6%). Cardiac arrest was documented more often in patients who received ketamine (246/3552, 6.9%) compared with etomidate (89/1643, 5.4%) (p=0.04). Conclusions: Our retrospective analysis of prehospital RSIs reveals ketamine may be associated with a higher rate of post-intubation cardiac arrest, mirroring findings from a recent in-hospital trial. Our findings are limited by potential inconsistent EMS documentation and an inability to ascertain whether a documented cardiac arrest can be attributed to induction medication strategy. Further research is needed to better define the optimal induction strategies for prehospital RSI.

items.title: Abstract P2027: Association of Institutional Protocol Availability with Management Practices in Post-Anoxic Status Epilepticus: An International Survey
items.abstract: Introduction: Post-anoxic status epilepticus (PASE) occurs in approximately one-third of comatose cardiac arrest (CA) survivors and is associated with high mortality. Although emerging evidence suggests favorable outcomes are achievable in a subset of patients, management is challenging and therapeutic nihilism may persist. In the absence of established management protocols, seizure monitoring and treatment practices may vary widely. Objective: To assess whether institutional protocol availability is associated with variation in management and electroencephalography (EEG)-based prognostication practices for PASE following CA. Methods: A cross-sectional Qualtrics survey was designed and approved for international dissemination (IRB #202300051) with assistance of professional societies between 2024-2026 to clinicians involved in PASE management. Responses were analyzed using question-specific denominators due to incomplete surveys. Exploratory protocol comparisons used Fisher exact tests. Results: Among 154 respondents, 27/95 (28%) reported having an institutional protocol, 61/95 (64%) reported no protocol, and 7/95 (7%) were unsure. Among those with protocols, 4/18 (22.2%) practiced in the United States, compared to 26/43 (60.5%) without protocols (p=0.011). ICU-based practice was less common among respondents with protocols versus without protocols (11/18 [61.1%] vs. 38/43 [88.4%], p=0.030). Continuous EEG use was higher among protocol respondents but non-significant (25/27 [92.6%] vs. 46/60 [76.7%], p=0.132). Monitoring all patients after return of spontaneous circulation was more common among respondents with protocols (10/27 [37.0%] vs. 10/60 [16.7%], p=0.053). The clearest differences were in EEG-based prognostic interpretation. Protocol respondents more often rated generalized periodic discharges within 24 hours as highly important for unfavorable prognosis (11/18 [61.1%] vs. 14/53 [26.4%], p=0.011). After 24 hours, they more often rated burst suppression as highly important (17/18 [94.4%] vs. 34/53 [64.2%], p=0.015). Escalation patterns were similar across groups, though intravenous non-anesthetic anti-seizure medications were selected less often, as first-choice therapy by respondents with protocols than those without protocols (7/23 [30.4%] vs. 29/58 [50.0%], p=0.140). Perceived benefits of early aggressive treatment were similar (3/18 [16.7%] vs. 8/53 [15.1%], p=1.000). Conclusion: PASE is largely managed without institutional protocols. Protocol availability was associated with differences in EEG-based prognostic interpretation, while treatment strategies and perceived benefits of aggressive treatment were similar. This suggests the key gap in PASE care may lie less in aggressive treatment and more in how clinicians interpret EEG patterns that guide prognostic judgment.

items.title: Abstract P2032: Analgosedation and Time to Awakening After Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Analgesia and sedation are key components of post-cardiac-arrest care and facilitate temperature control; however, limited data describe their safety. We evaluated the association between time to awakening (T2A) and cumulative dose of analgosedation (AS). Methods: We performed a retrospective, cohort study of adults with non-traumatic in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) or out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) between January 2021 and November 2025 at three Seattle, WA hospitals. Patients who awoke prior to 24 hours were excluded. The primary exposure was cumulative AS dose given during comatose hours in the first 96 hours of hospitalization. Cumulative doses were normalized to patient weight and number of comatose minutes. The primary outcome was T2A, with awake defined as a Glasgow Coma Scale-Motor score of 6. The secondary outcome was achieving wakefulness. Outcomes were adjusted for covariates (age, sex, Charlson Comorbidity Index, OHCA vs IHCA, seizures within the first 96 hours, shock on admission) and were analyzed using Cox regression and logistic regression, respectively. A time-varying coefficient was used for propofol due to a proportional hazards violation. Results: Of 855 eligible adults, 26 (3%) received barbiturates or dexmedetomidine and were excluded. Of the remaining 829, 141 (17%) awoke. Higher cumulative benzodiazepine exposure was associated with slower T2A (HR=0.37, 95% CI 0.17-0.83, p=0.015) and decreased chance of awakening (OR=0.19, 95% CI 0.07-0.51, p=0.001). Higher cumulative propofol exposure was associated with faster T2A, and this association was time-dependent, showing strongest effect at 6 hours (HR=6.45, 95% CI 2.46-10.44, p=0.0015) and attenuating by day 7 (HR=2.01, 95% CI 1.47-2.55, p<0.0001); it was also associated with an increased chance of awakening (OR=4.33, 95% CI 3.21-5.84, p<0.001). Opioid exposure was not significantly associated with T2A (HR=1.05, 95% CI 0.95-1.16, p=0.343) or chance of awakening (OR=1.24, 95% CI 0.99-1.56, p=0.061). Conclusions: In non-traumatic OHCA and IHCA, higher cumulative benzodiazepine exposure was associated with longer T2A and lower overall chance of awakening, whereas higher cumulative propofol exposure was associated with faster T2A and higher chance of awakening. Opioid exposure was not significantly associated with awakening metrics. Given the observational nature of this study, these findings cannot definitively establish causality, and confounding may remain where patients with greater illness severity required higher AS doses.

items.title: Abstract P2075: Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Preserves Cerebral Mitochondrial Function After Refractory Cardiac Arrest in Rats
items.abstract: Introduction: Mitochondrial dysfunction severely impacts neurological recovery after cardiac arrest (CA). While extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) improves cerebral blood flow post-CA compared to conventional cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CCPR), its impact on brain mitochondrial function, critical for neuronal survival, is unknown. This study addresses this gap. Research Question: Does ECPR preserve cerebral mitochondrial function more effectively than CCPR after refractory asphyxial CA due to superior circulatory support? Aim: Our primary goal was to compare the effects of ECPR and CCPR on brain mitochondrial respiratory capacity in the cerebral cortex and hippocampal CA1 following refractory asphyxial CA in rats. Methods: Male Wistar rats underwent refractory asphyxial CA. CCPR consisted of chest compressions, ventilation, and epinephrine administration, whereas ECPR utilized veno-arterial extracorporeal circulation to restore systemic perfusion. Resuscitation with CCPR or ECPR began 20 minutes after asphyxia initiation. Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) was defined as a sustained MAP ≥ 60 mmHg. Cardiac function by echocardiography was monitored at 30 and 60 minutes post-ROSC. At 60 minutes post-ROSC, high-resolution respirometry was used to assess mitochondrial oxygen consumption in permeabilized brain cortical and hippocampal CA1. Results: ECPR achieved a higher ROSC rate than CCPR (83.3 % [5/6] vs. 42.3 % [11/26]). ECPR significantly improved cardiac function post-ROSC. At 60 minutes post-ROSC, fractional shortening (FS) was higher in ECPR (49.9 ± 4.8 %) vs. CCPR (22.8 ± 7.9 %; P < 0.01, Fig 1a). Stroke volume (SV) was also significantly preserved in ECPR at 30 and 60 minutes post-ROSC (at 60 min: ECPR 0.53 ± 0.13 ml vs. CCPR 0.19 ± 0.08 ml; P < 0.05, Fig 1b). Pyruvate/malate stimulated oxidative phosphorylation was significantly lower in both cortex and CA1 in the CCPR group when compared to the Naive group (Cortex: Naive 1.00 ± 0.16, vs. CCPR 0.83 ± 0.13, CA1: Naïve 1.00 ± 0.16, vs. CCPR 0.76 ± 0.21, both P < 0.05) (Fig 2a) and further uncoupling maintained reduced oxygen consumption in the CCPR group (CA1: Naive 1.00 ± 0.18, vs. CCPR 0.78 ± 0.14, P < 0.05) (Fig 2b). Conclusions: ECPR improved ROSC rate and cardiac function while preserving cerebral mitochondrial function compared with CCPR following refractory CA. These findings suggest that ECPR may mitigate early mitochondrial injury in vulnerable brain regions after CA.

items.title: Abstract P2088: Early Identification of Mortality Risk After In-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Using Pre-Arrest ICU Data
items.abstract: Background: Early identification of mortality risk after in hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA) may inform ICU decision making, post arrest triage, and allocation of critical care resources. However, robust prognostic approaches based solely on routinely collected pre arrest electronic health record (EHR) data remain limited. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the MIMIC IV ICU database, identifying 393 adult patients with documented IHCA using a structured ICU cardiac arrest event marker. We excluded patients with pre existing do not resuscitate or do not intubate orders, a primary admission diagnosis of cardiac arrest or respiratory arrest, or evidence of transfer from out of hospital cardiac arrest. Analyses were restricted to the first qualifying IHCA. The primary outcome was in hospital mortality. Candidate predictors were derived exclusively from the 72 hours preceding arrest and included demographics, laboratory values, vital signs, interventions, and derived physiologic scores. Sparse features were excluded, and missing values were median imputed. Feature ranking was performed using training data only to minimize leakage. Multiple predictive models were internally validated using subject level train/validation/test splits with repeated resampling. Results: The cohort had a median age of 69 years (IQR 57-80), and 54.7% were male. Overall, 272 of 393 patients (69.2%) died during the index hospitalization. Across resampling experiments, the best performance was achieved by a random forest model, with a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.77 (95% CI, 0.66-0.87). Predictor importance was consistently dominated by markers of metabolic and hemodynamic instability, with markers shown in Figure 1. Discrimination was strongest among patients with overt pre arrest physiologic deterioration and more limited when survivors and non survivors demonstrated overlapping pre arrest profiles. Conclusions: In this retrospective ICU cohort, routinely collected pre arrest EHR data provided moderate but clinically meaningful prognostic signal for in hospital mortality following IHCA. Prognostic information was driven primarily by metabolic derangement, escalating hemodynamic support, and organ dysfunction. While these findings support the potential role of pre arrest EHR based risk stratification, predictive performance remains insufficient for stand alone clinical deployment, underscoring the need for further refinement and external validation.

items.title: Abstract P2009: Hydrogen Gas Inhalation Enhances Transfusion-Based Resuscitation Efficiency and Attenuates Organ Injury After Hemorrhagic Shock
items.abstract: Background: Hemorrhagic shock and resuscitation cause ischemia-reperfusion injury, endothelial glycocalyx degradation, vascular dysfunction, and organ injury. Although transfusion is essential, strategies that improve resuscitation efficiency and reduce blood product requirements are needed. The effect of hydrogen gas (H 2 ), which has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, during transfusion-based resuscitation remains unknown. Hypothesis: H 2 inhalation would reduce transfusion requirements without compromising hemodynamic or metabolic recovery and would attenuate endothelial and organ injury. Methods: Twenty male Sprague-Dawley rats underwent pressure-controlled hemorrhagic shock. Blood was withdrawn to maintain mean arterial pressure at 30-35 mmHg for 60 minutes, followed by shed-blood transfusion over 60 minutes to achieve predefined hemodynamic targets. Animals were randomized to control gas or 1.3% H 2 gas inhalation, which was initiated 15 minutes before resuscitation and continued throughout resuscitation. Hemodynamics, arterial blood gas variables, lactate, transfusion volume, and plasma syndecan-1 were evaluated during the acute resuscitation phase. Animals were followed for 24 hours, after which blinded histopathological scoring of kidney, small-intestinal, and liver injury was performed. Results: Shed blood volume was similar between the H 2 and control groups (10.8 vs 10.4 mL; P=0.64), whereas transfused blood volume was significantly lower with H 2 (4.7 vs 6.9 mL; P<0.02). Despite receiving less transfusion, H 2 -treated rats maintained post-resuscitation hemodynamics and arterial blood gas parameters comparable to controls throughout the acute observation period, indicating that reduced transfusion did not compromise circulatory stabilization. Lactate did not increase after resuscitation in the H 2 group, and lactate normalization occurred more frequently with H 2 than with control gas (67% vs 38%; P=0.23). Plasma syndecan-1 after resuscitation was lower with H 2 , consistent with attenuated endothelial glycocalyx shedding (900 vs 1140 pg/mL; P<0.01). H 2 also reduced renal tubular injury (Paller score, 4 vs 9; P<0.01) and intestinal mucosal injury (Chiu-Park score, 0.5 vs 4; P<0.01). Liver injury scores were lower with H 2 , although the difference was not statistically significant (2.0 vs 6.5; P=0.24). Conclusions: H 2 inhalation improved transfusion-based resuscitation efficiency by reducing transfusion requirements while preserving hemodynamic stability and lactate clearance. Attenuation of endothelial glycocalyx shedding and kidney and intestinal injury suggests that H 2 may be a promising, resource-sparing adjunct for hemorrhagic shock resuscitation.

items.title: Abstract P2012: Nicolas Segond M.D. Ph.D.
items.abstract: Introduction: The potential impact of Resuscitative Endovascular Balloon Occlusion of the Aorta (REBOA) during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) remains controversial. Little is known about the potential survival benefit of REBOA combined with head-up cardiopulmonary resuscitation (AHUP-CPR). Research question: The primary study objective was to compare the 24-hour survival after conventional (C) CPR+REBOA, AHUP-CPR alone, or AHUP-CPR+REBOA. Additional survival and hemodynamic outcomes were assessed. Methods: This was an experimental, prospective, controlled, randomized study. After isoflurane anesthesia, preparation and induction of ventricular fibrillation (VF), Yorkshire pigs were randomized in three groups: C-CPR+REBOA, AHUP alone and AHUP+REBOA. After 10 minutes of untreated VF, 18 minutes of C-CPR or AHUP-CPR (combination of an impedance threshold device, active compression-decompression and progressive head and thorax elevation) was provided. REBOA was inflated after 15 min (Figure 1) of CPR. Using Kaplan-Meier and a log-rank tests, 24-hour survival was compared between groups. Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC), and favorable neurologic function at 24 hours (FN-24, defined as a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 or 2) were assessed. Decompression aortic blood pressure (DBP), coronary perfusion pressure (CorPP), end-tidal CO2 (EtCO 2 ) and cerebral oximetry (rSO 2 ) before (14min) and after (17min) REBOA inflation were measured. Results: With 10 pigs per group, ROSC rates were 20% with C-CPR+REBOA, 60% with AHUP alone, and 90% with AHUP+REBOA (p = 0.008), respectively. Differences in 24h survival were also significantly different between groups (0% C-CPR+REBOA, 30% AHUP alone, and 30% AHUP+REBOA; log-rank p = 0.008; Fig. 2). Median (Q1; Q3) survival times were 0 h (0; 0) with C-CPR+REBOA, 4.25 h (0.0; 19.5) with AHUP alone, and 7.5 h (6.0; 20.0) with AHUP+REBOA (p = 0.002). FN-24 was 0% with C-CPR+REBOA, 30% with AHUP alone and 30% with AHUP+REBOA (p = 0.15).Detailed hemodynamic data are presented in Table 1. Before REBOA inflation (14 min of CPR), EtCO2 differed significantly among the three groups (p < 0.001). After REBOA inflation (17 min of CPR), DBP, CorPP, and EtCO2 differed significantly among the three groups (p = 0.04, p = 0.03, and p < 0.001, respectively). Conclusion: In this preclinical study, AHUP-CPR alone or with REBOA, significantly increased 24-hour survival rate and hemodynamics compared with C-CPR+REBOA.

items.title: Abstract P2044: Immunologically Distinct Endotypes Identified in Human Subjects Following Successful Resuscitation After Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Emergent evidence suggests that immune and inflammatory responses contribute to clinical polymorphism of post-cardiac arrest (post-CA) syndrome. We performed a temporal analysis of immune cell subpopulations in the peripheral circulation of CA subjects and applied clustering analysis to identify post-CA endotypes characterized by specific immune patterns. Methods: Multiparametric flow cytometry analysis was performed on fresh whole blood from 154 subjects at 6, 12, 24, 48, 72, and 168 hours after resuscitation following CA. A gating strategy to identify immune patterns was created using samples from 14 healthy donors. A hierarchical clustering approach was used to detect distinct immune patterns. Functional properties of granulocytic leukocytes, including production of myeloperoxidase (MPO) and neutrophil elastase (NE), generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), phagocytic activity, and phagocytosis-induced cell death (PICD), were examined in vitro using freshly isolated immune cells. Platelet-free plasma was analyzed with ELISA. Clinical parameters were extracted from Epic and EMS run-sheets. Results: Two immunologically and clinically distinct endotypes of nearly equal prevalence were identified using probabilistic clustering. The first endotype is associated with a predominance of CD10ˉ over CD10 + neutrophils, reduced expression of mature neutrophil markers, increased circulating granulopoiesis factors, e.g. G-CSF and IL-8, and increased levels of neutrophil primary granule enzymes, MPO and NE, indicative of emergency granulopoiesis (EG) induction. The second endotype, while also associated with elevated white blood cell and neutrophil counts, is characterized by a predominance of mature CD10 + neutrophils, suggestive of increased steady state granulopoiesis (SSG). The EG endotype is associated with a slightly longer time to return of spontaneous circulation ( p=0.013 ), metabolic acidosis at admission ( p<0.001 ), and higher prevalence in females ( p=0.004 ). We observed increased circulating neuron-specific enolase ( p=0.013 ), indicative of neurological injury severity, and higher mortality ( p=0.005 ) in the EG group. No differences in the incidence of pneumonia or infection-associated neutrophil subsets were found between endotypes. Mechanistically, EG and SSG neutrophils are characterized by similar levels of MPO and NE production. However, EG neutrophils exhibit reduced capacity to generate ROS, decreased phagocytic activity, and increased resistance to PICD compared with SSG. Conclusion: These data point to the potentially damaging roles of emergency granulopoiesis and immature CD10ˉ neutrophils, which are characterized by prolonged survival, in post-CA patients. Immunoprofiling of circulating leukocytes may inform the optimization of endotype-specific anti-inflammatory therapies to treat post-CA syndrome.

items.title: Abstract P2048: What Level of Expertise is Necessary to Generate ACLS Training Test Questions: Pre-Med Students vs. Artificial Intelligence?
items.abstract: Introduction: In-hospital cardiac arrest carries high mortality despite standardized ACLS training. Educators face increasing time constraints in developing assessment tools for ACLS training. Two possible solutions to this problem are using pre-medical students or using artificial intelligence to generate test questions. This study compared the quality of pre-medical student-generated ACLS test questions vs. AI-generated ACLS test questions, testing the hypothesis that AI-generated questions are non-inferior to student-generated questions. Methods: Ten pre-medical students created ACLS questions following predefined criteria, while an AI model (Northwell’s Artificial Intelligence Hub) generated comparable questions. A blinded ACLS-certified physician evaluated questions on the qualities of Alignment, Clarity, Cognitive Level, and Question Design using a standardized rubric (Likert scale: 1 = poor quality, 5 = excellent). Student’s T-test and Chi-square analysis were used to compare the quality of questions on different rubric domains within each arm (student vs. AI) and within one domain (eg, question Clarity) between arms. The Student’s T test was used when 2 comparator groups were compared (eg, Clarity of student-generated vs. AI-generated questions) within one arm. The ANOVA test was used when comparing more than 2 comparator groups (eg, Alignment vs. Clarity vs. Cognitive Level) within one arm. Statistical significance was set as a priority at p <0.05. Results: Both student-generated and AI-generated questions were of high quality. AI-generated questions achieved the maximum score in the domains of Alignment, Clarity, and Question Design, but fell short of perfect scores in the domain of Cognitive Level (8 of 50 questions were less than 5). Student-generated questions achieved less-than-perfect scores in each domain. No significant difference was found in overall mean question scores between groups (students = 4.79, AI = 4.81; p = 0.9). However, AI-generated questions had significantly-greater Clarity (students = 4.8, AI = 5; p = .0461), while Alignment, Cognitive level, and Question Design showed no significant differences. Conclusions: AI-generated questions demonstrated overall quality comparable to those generated by pre-medical students, supporting the potential role of AI as a scalable tool in ACLS educational assessment development. Further studies are warranted to evaluate additional AI platforms and determine optimal integration of AI in medical education assessment design.

items.title: Abstract P2020: Adolescent and Young Adult Survivors’ and Parent Co Survivors’ Lived Experiences of Pediatric Out of Hospital Cardiac Arrest Survivorship
items.abstract: Background: Survival following pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) has improved, yet there is a paucity of research about the long-term outcomes and experiences of survivors and their families. Understanding their experiences will help shape survivor- and co-survivor-centered interventions and outcomes that focus on long-term recovery and well-being. Research Question: What is the lived experience of adolescent/young adult survivors (AYA) of OHCA and their parent co-survivors in survivorship? Aims: This study primarily sought to: (1) gain a deeper understanding of AYA survivors’ and their parents’/legal guardians’ perceptions of life after a CA in survivorship and (2) understand how survivors’ and co-survivors’ needs have changed over time since arrest. Methods: The study was conducted at a large pediatric healthcare system in Southern California using a qualitative phenomenological design. Participants were recruited using purposive, snowball, and convenience sampling. Eligible AYA were aged 10 to 24 years, English-speaking, experienced OHCA between ages 10-18, survived greater than 6 months post-arrest, and were able to verbally articulate their experiences. Parents/legal guardians of eligible AYA were also invited to participate. Each participant completed two semi-structured interviews between October 2025 and March 2026, which were audio-recorded and transcribed. Data were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis informed by the hermeneutic circle. Coding was performed independently by two researchers, resolving discrepancies through consensus. Recruitment continued until thematic saturation was achieved. Results: Nine participants, including both survivors (n=3, 33.3%) and co-survivors (n=6, 66.6%), participated. Survivors were aged 18 to 24 years, and co-survivors were aged 40 to 59 years. Four (44.4%) self-identified as Hispanic or Latino. Five (55.5%) identified as White, two (22.2%) as Asian, and two (22.2%) as Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander. Among participants, four (44.4%) preferred “she” as their gender pronoun, three (33.3%) preferred “he,” and two (22.2%) preferred not to state. Five overarching themes about survivorship were identified: survivorship (a) is a new normal, (b) means being there, (c) is a physical embodiment, (d) means letting go, and (e) is what meaning we want to give it. Survivors emphasized challenges with self-concept and social reintegration, which is critical in their development stage. Parents described persistent anxiety, adjustment challenges, and advocacy burdens. Both groups highlighted discordance between acute care received and long-term support. Conclusions: AYA survivors of OHCA and their parents experience enduring psychosocial and functional impacts. Findings underscore the need for structured, family-centered, and individualized support throughout survivorship.

items.title: Abstract P2021: Temporal Trends in Hospitalization and Survival After Out of Hospital Cardiac Arrest: Insights from the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES)
items.abstract: Background: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) remains a major public health challenge, with persistent variation in outcomes across demographic and clinical subgroups. Evaluating recent trends in hospitalization and survival may identify disparities and inform targeted improvements in resuscitation systems of care. Methods: We conducted a retrospective trend analysis using the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival (CARES) from 2019-2024. We evaluated temporal changes in (1) proportions of hospitalized OHCA patients across demographic and clinical characteristics and (2) survival to hospital discharge stratified by hospitalization-related factors.Generalized linear models with a Poisson distribution and log link were applied separately for each subgroup, with calendar year modeled as a continuous predictor and population at risk included as an offset. Deviance-based corrections accounted for overdispersion. Annual percentage changes with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated, with p<0.05 indicating statistical significance. Results: Significant shifts in OHCA hospitalization patterns were observed. The proportion of hospitalized female patients declined by 0.60% per year (95% CI, –0.76% to –0.45%; p<0.0001), while male hospitalizations increased by 0.37% per year (95% CI, 0.28% to 0.46%; p<0.0001). Hospitalizations among Black patients decreased modestly (–1.30% per year; 95% CI, –2.56% to –0.03%; p=0.045), whereas Hispanic/Latino patients demonstrated a substantial increase (4.94% per year; 95% CI, 2.17% to 7.79%; p=0.0004).Clinically, the proportion of patients achieving sustained return of spontaneous circulation declined (–2.58% per year; 95% CI, –4.41% to –0.72%; p=0.0066), while hospitalizations without sustained ROSC increased modestly. The proportion pronounced dead in the emergency department decreased significantly (–6.26% per year; 95% CI, –10.24% to –2.10%; p=0.0035).Despite these shifts, no subgroup demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in survival to discharge. Overall survival increased by 1.54% per year (95% CI, –2.18% to 5.39%; p=0.42), with similarly non-significant findings across arrest characteristics and hospitalization factors. Conclusions: From 2019 to 2024, OHCA hospitalization patterns shifted across demographic and clinical subgroups, with persistent disparities and declining sustained ROSC. Despite these changes, survival to hospital discharge has not significantly improved. These findings highlight ongoing inequities and underscore the need for targeted, system-level interventions to improve OHCA outcomes.

items.title: Abstract P2041: Hemodynamic Effects of Intramuscular Epinephrine During Cardiac Arrest: A Porcine Study
items.abstract: Background: Early epinephrine administration is associated with improved survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but difficult intravenous access may delay its delivery. Intramuscular (IM) epinephrine may offer a rapid alternative delivery route, but its hemodynamic efficacy remains uncertain. We evaluated the dose-dependent hemodynamic effects of IM epinephrine during cardiac arrest. Methods: In a randomized controlled porcine model, anesthetized and intubated adult swine (~50 kg) underwent 7 minutes of ventricular fibrillation followed by CPR. Study drug was administered IM at 12 minutes of arrest; hemodynamics were recorded for the subsequent 9.5 minutes. Animals received placebo (0.1 mL/kg saline IM), low-dose epinephrine (0.1 mg/kg IM), or high-dose epinephrine (0.2 mg/kg IM). Outcomes were changes in systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and coronary perfusion pressure (CPP). We analyzed hemodynamic trajectories with baseline-adjusted linear mixed-effects models with treatment-by-time interactions and random animal-level effects. Results: We included 26 swine: placebo (n=8), low-dose epinephrine (n=10), and high-dose epinephrine (n=8). Baseline characteristics were similar across groups. SBP trajectory was greater for high-dose epinephrine than placebo (1.09 vs -0.75 mmHg/min, difference 1.84 mmHg/min, p<0.001). DBP trajectory was greater for high-dose than placebo while declining with placebo group (0.45 vs –0.23 mmHg/min, difference +0.67 mmHg/min, p=0.027). CPP trajectory was greater for high-dose than placebo, but the difference was not significant (0.75 vs 0.03 mmHg/min, +0.72 mmHg/min; P=0.097). SBP, DBP and CPP trajectories did not differ between low-dose and placebo. Conclusions: High-dose epinephrine is associated with stronger hemodynamic response than placebo. Intramuscular epinephrine may be a viable option in resuscitation of OHCA.

items.title: Abstract P2080: Improved Airway Confirmation Practices During CPR Using a Plan-Do-Study-Act Methodology
items.abstract: Background: AHA guidelines recommend advanced airway placement either via endotracheal intubation (ETI) or placement of a supraglottic airway during CPR Airway placement verification is a patient safety standard reducing the risk of esophageal intubation, airway displacement, or delays in ventilation. A review of CPR performance metrics showed frequent noncompliance with this standard. While patients undergoing ETI during cardiac arrests had consistent verification of airway placement, documentation and verification were significantly less common in patients with a pre-existing airway prior to the cardiac arrest. Methods: A multidisciplinary QI project was initiated to create consistent verification practices for airway placement, raise awareness among staff, and ensure availability of equipment for airway verification. The goal was to increase the verification of placement of new and pre-existing airways, and to improve conformity with national standards. A Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) methodology was utilized to address specific issues associated with non-conformity. Cycle 1: Plan: To raise awareness of current guideline requirements Do: To increase awareness via mock codes, unit-based huddles, and regular competency reviews. Study: Evidence of improved knowledge of guideline requirements. Act: Capnography availability identified as a barrier to compliance Cycle 2: Plan: To standardize equipment access procedures Do: To increase availability of color capnograms and obtain quantitative capnography capable defibrillator devices Study: Evidence of improved confidence in ability to comply with guidelines Act: Monitor equipment availability via regular inspections, and delegate accountability to designated departments to ensure continued availability Cycle 3: Plan: To reinforce consistency and maintain achievement levels Do: Multidisciplinary mock codes, real-time auditing, immediate post-event debriefing, and regular didactic reinforcement with housestaff and nursing. Study: Evidence of improved interdisciplinary communication, role identification, and protocol adherence Act: Increase frequency of multidisciplinary simulation training Results: Detailed in attached Run Chart Conclusion: A multidisciplinary QI project utilizing three PDSA cycles successfully improved compliance with endotracheal tube verification during CPR events.

items.title: Abstract P2056: Between-Site Variability in Clinical Outcomes Within the Influence of Cooling Duration on Efficacy in Cardiac Arrest Patients (ICECAP) Trial: Institutional Variability and Relationship with Enrollment Volume
items.abstract: Introduction: Previous studies have found substantial site-to-site variation in clinical outcomes among resuscitated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients. The Influence on Cooling duration on Efficacy in Cardiac Arrest Patients (ICECAP) trial was a pragmatic study of the duration of therapeutic hypothermia in patients with ROSC following OHCA. Objectives: We aimed to quantify the between-site variation in all-cause 90-day mortality in the ICECAP trial. Methods: This was a secondary analysis of patients enrolled in ICECAP, describing variation in the post-resuscitation care process and outcomes stratified by site enrollment (low: 1-10, medium: 11-30, high: >30 enrolled patients), with a primary endpoint of all-cause 90-day mortality. Between-site variation in outcomes was quantified using a mixed-effects logistic model with site included as a random intercept and summarized using the median odds ratio (MOR). Fixed effects included age, initial rhythm, sex, resuscitation circumstances (bystander-identified and initiated CPR, bystander-identified EMS-initiated CPR, EMS-witnessed or bystander-identified), time from arrest to ED arrival, and first temperature on ED presentation. Results: A total of 1158 patients were enrolled in ICECAP: median age of 61 (50-70), 458 (40%) were female, 448 (38.7%) were Black/African American race, 601 (51.9%) received bystander CPR, and 208 (17.9%) presented with a shockable initial rhythm. Median time from arrest to ED arrival was 39 min (30-51), and arrest to cooling device initiation was 151 min (113-195). All-cause 90-day mortality occurred in 862 (75%) patients, whereas across low (n=38), medium (n=23), and high (n=10) enrollment sites, the outcome occurred in 115 of 141 (81.6%, 95% CI: 74.4-87.1%), 312 of 417 (74.8%, 95% CI: 70.4-78.7%), and 435 of 600 (72.5%, 95% CI: 68.8-75.9%) respectively. In the adjusted mixed-effects model, residual between-site variation was modest, with an MOR of 1.19 (95% CI: 1.00-1.61). Conclusion: We observed higher unadjusted 90-day mortality at lower enrolling sites than at higher enrolling sites. After adjustment for patient and arrest-level characteristics, residual between-site variation was modest (MOR 1.19), suggesting that, on average, selecting two individuals from two sites would yield a 19% difference in mortality odds. These findings support consideration of site characteristics and enrollment volume in the design, conduct, and analysis of future cardiac arrest trials.

items.title: Abstract P2070: Incidence and Prognostic Implications of Thrombus in Patients Receiving Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation for Refractory Ventricular Tachycardia/Ventricular Fibrillation Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Thrombus formation is a feared complication of veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) treatment in patients requiring extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Research Questions: What are the incidence, subtypes, and prognostic implications of clinically detected incident thrombi in patients receiving ECPR for refractory ventricular tachycardia/ventricular fibrillation (rVT/VF) OHCA? Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study in patients with rVT/VF OHCA requiring ECPR. All patients were treated with a standardized anticoagulation strategy as per our previously published ECPR protocols. The primary objective was to determine the frequency and anatomic distribution of clinically detected incident thrombi during VA-ECMO support or within 7 days after the VA-ECMO treatment course. The secondary objectives was to evaluate the association between any incident thrombus and in-hospital mortality. The results were reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results: During 2015-2023, 418 patients were referred to our program for ECPR for rVT/VF OHCA (median age 60.8 years, 79.9% male, 78.7% witnessed, 69.1% ischemic cause of VT/VF OHCA). In this cohort, 63.6% (266/418) had an unloading device during the VA-ECMO run, with the vast majority being an intra-aortic balloon pump (260/266). There were 33 patients who were diagnosed with 40 incident thrombi (24 arterial and 16 venous). The presence of any thrombus was not statistically associated with in-hospital survival in unadjusted analyses (OR 1.59, 95% CI: 0.75-3.22) or after adjustment for adjustment for history of heart failure and presence of unloading device (OR: 1.87, 95% CI: 0.87-3.86). Conclusion: In a high-volume ECPR program using standardized anticoagulation, clinically detected incident thrombi occurred in approximately 8% of patients treated for rVT/VF OHCA. Arterial thrombi, particularly left ventricular thrombi, were the most common subtype. Incident thrombus detection was not statistically associated with in-hospital survival.

items.title: Abstract P2078: Airway Management Strategy Varies by Race/Ethnicity in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Racial and ethnic disparities in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) treatment and outcomes are well documented. Advanced airway management is a key component of prehospital resuscitation, with endotracheal intubation (ETI) and supraglottic airway (SGA) placement representing the two most commonly used strategies. Despite ongoing debate regarding their comparative effectiveness, little is known about whether their utilization differs across racial/ethnic groups and whether such differences are associated with clinical outcomes. Hypothesis: Significant racial/ethnic differences exist in the utilization of advanced airway management strategies during OHCA and that these differences may be associated with variation in return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) rates. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of a longstanding nationally-representative registry of emergency medical services (EMS) activations (NEMSIS). Adult patients (≥18 years) with OHCA occurring prior to EMS arrival with documented race/ethnicity and attempted advanced airway placement (ETI or SGA) were included. Airway management strategy utilization and rates of ROSC were compared among White, Black, and Hispanic/Latino patients using two-tailed two-proportion z-tests, with statistical significance defined as p<0.05. Results: A total of 58,551 OHCA cases met inclusion criteria; 59.6% (n=35,809) underwent ETI and 40.4% (n=24,252) underwent SGA placement. ETI was more frequently performed in White patients (59.6%) compared with Black (56.4%) and Hispanic/Latino (56.3%) (p<0.05). Across all racial and ethnic groups, ETI was associated with higher ROSC rates than SGA placement. Within the ETI group, ROSC was achieved more frequently among White patients (30.1%) compared to Black (26.3%) and Hispanic/Latino patients (28.5%) (p<0.05). Within the SGA group, White patients also had significantly higher ROSC rates (24.5%) compared with Black patients (21.9%) (p<0.05), while ROSC rates were comparable between White and Hispanic/Latino patients (23.6%). Conclusions: In this national EMS cohort, White patients with OHCA were more likely to receive ETI than Black or Hispanic/Latino patients. Black patients experienced lower ROSC rates regardless of airway strategy, while Hispanic/Latino patients demonstrated lower ROSC rates following ETI but not SGA placement. These findings suggest that airway management disparities may reflect broader inequities across the OHCA chain of survival.

items.title: Abstract P2007: Data-Driven ECG Features for Prediction of Out-of-Hospital Rearrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Recurrent cardiac arrest (rearrest) affects up to half of patients who achieve return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) and is associated with worse outcomes. Predicting rearrest may enable preemptive EMS interventions. Evidence to date indicates clinical ECG features provide modest, time-dependent prediction of rearrest, performing better as rearrest approaches, potentially too late for intervention. Machine learning-based feature extraction may capture ECG signatures not detected by clinical measures. Goal: We evaluated a data-driven approach for rearrest prediction using ECG waveform data. Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult OHCA patients treated by urban Emergency Medical Services (EMS) between 2018 and 2024 who achieved ROSC. We developed and evaluated a machine learning model to predict rearrest using a 5-minute ECG segment spanning the 6 to 1 minute period before rearrest. Patients were randomized 80/20% into training and test sets. ECGs were divided into 15-second segments and transformed into scalograms ( Figure 1 ). Principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to the training data, and the top 20 principal components (measured by variance captured) were used as inputs to an XGBoost classifier. Hyperparameters were optimized using a grid search with 10-fold cross-validation. To provide a comparative baseline versus the data-driven model, a clinical model was also developed using heart rate, heart rate variability, and QRS duration as inputs for logistic regression. Performance was evaluated by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Results: Of the 1,247 OHCA patients who achieved ROSC, 526 (42%) experienced rearrest. The AUROC of the data driven model and the clinical model were 0.48-0.65 and 0.49-0.74, respectively. The data-driven model demonstrated relatively stable predictive performance across the entire evaluated pre-rearrest ( Figure 2 ). In contrast, the clinical model showed greater temporal dependence, with AUROC values improving as rearrest approached. At earlier timepoints, the data-driven approach’s AUROC point estimates exceeded the clinical model’s, whereas the clinical model AUROC point estimates were higher closer to rearrest. Conclusion: Rearrest prediction did not differ between machine learning versus clinical ECG measures, though these models differed with regard to time-dependent prediction. Machine learning-based feature extraction may complement conventional ECG models to predict impending rearrest, enabling earlier and more robust identification of patients at risk.

items.title: Abstract P2023: Hospital Readmission and Mortality in Cardiac Arrest Survivors Discharged with Favorable Neurologic Outcome
items.abstract: Introduction: Even among cardiac arrest survivors discharged with favorable neurologic outcomes, the risk of subsequent cardiac and non-cardiac complications, hospital re-admission, and mortality remains substantial. A better understanding of the causes and predictors of post-discharge re-admission and death is essential to developing targeted follow-up strategies, optimizing long-term recovery, and improving cardiac arrest survivorship. Methods: We performed a retrospective analysis of cardiac arrest survivors enrolled in a single center cardiac arrest recovery program (CARP) between 1/19/2024 and 5/9/2026. The CARP program follows all in-hospital (IHCA) and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients from index hospitalization admission to discharge, at which point those who awaken and were following basic commands were enrolled. Enrollment included an evaluation for psychological and cognitive symptoms, as well as post-discharge neurology clinic appointment (on average three months post-discharge). Amongst enrolled patients, hospital re-admissions and mortality occurring prior to post-discharge neurology clinic visit were tracked. Results: Of 105 enrolled patients, 34 (32.4%) underwent hospital readmission. The median [interquartile range] time from index cardiac arrest discharge to re-admission was 16 [8-99.8] days. Eight (7.6% of all patients, 24% of re-admitted patients) died at a median of 71.5 [20-160] days from index hospital discharge. The most common cause of death was withdrawal of life sustaining therapy (50%, n=4), followed by recurrent arrest without ROSC (25%, n=2). Amongst those who survived the readmission, the median [IQR] length of stay was 4 [2-10] days and the most common admission diagnoses included cardiopulmonary dysfunction (n=13, 38.2%) and neuropsychiatric symptoms (n=11, 32.4%). Patients requiring readmission were more likely to have suffered an IHCA, were younger, had longer length of stay, and were less likely to be discharged home (Table 1). Conclusion: Cardiac arrest survivors experience a heightened risk for readmission and mortality, even after discharge with good neurologic outcome. The most common causes for readmission were cardiopulmonary and neurologic symptoms. Further work to help identify those at highest risk for readmission and to evaluate the impact of a nurse navigator on readmission rate and mortality should be prioritized.

items.title: Abstract P2031: National Income-Based Disparities in Post-Arrest Care After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Low-income patients experience worse outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Little is known about disparities in post-arrest hospital care that may contribute to these outcome disparities. We sought to identify income-based disparities in post-arrest care. Hypothesis: Lower income patients have worse hospital outcomes and receive post-arrest care less often. Methods: We retrospectively analyzed the 2019-2022 National Emergency Department Sample, a national claims database. We included adult patients who survived to admission and excluded those with missing data. We stratified patients based on their household income quartile. We defined outcomes as post-arrest care, survival to discharge, and discharge to home (a surrogate for a good neurologic outcome). Using ordinal logistic regression, we evaluated the association between decreasing income quartile and outcomes with the top income quartile defined as the reference. We adjusted the analyses for age, sex, and race. Results: Of 359,652 OHCAs, 198,785 survived to admission. We included 188,627 patients; 32,534 from the top, 40,661 from the 2 nd , 49,751 from the 3 rd , and 65,681 from the lowest income quartile. Discharge to home rates for each group were 19.6% for 1 st , 19.1% for 2 nd , 17.9% for 3 rd , and 16.4% for 4 th income quartiles. Decreasing income was associated with decreased odds of left heart catheterization (OR 0.81 [0.77-0.85]), percutaneous coronary intervention (OR 0.85 [0.81-0.89]), ventricular assist device (OR 0.77 [0.71-0.83]), automatic implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement (OR 0.85 [0.81-0.89]), extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (OR 0.55 [0.45-0.68]), coronary artery bypass graft (OR 0.84 [0.75-0.94]), echocardiography (OR 0.85 [0.76-0.95]), central line placement (OR 0.93 [0.89-0.97]), arterial line placement (OR 0.86 [0.79-0.97]), therapeutic hypothermia (OR 0.70 [0.56-0.86]), survival (OR 0.90 [0.87-0.93]) , and survival with discharge to home (OR 0.87 [0.83-0.90]). Decreasing income was not associated with decreased odds of Head CT, electroencephalogram, body CT, or do not resuscitate orders. Conclusion: Decreasing income was associated with decreased odds of cardiac procedures, resuscitative procedures, and OHCA outcomes. Our findings suggest that income-based disparities in post-arrest care exist and warrant further investigation.

items.title: Abstract P2035: Optimizing Transport Timing in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest with Refractory Ventricular Fibrillation: A Secondary Analysis of the DOSE-VF Trial
items.abstract: Background: For refractory ventricular fibrillation (rVF), two strategies have been studied in separate clinical trials: intra-arrest transport (IAT) to Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (ECPR) and Double Sequential External Defibrillation (DSED). However, some systems have both treatments available, and the optimal time to stop DSED and start IAT to ECPR remains unclear.
