Aim: We aimed to describe the probability of prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) with ongoing DSED in patients still pulseless at three time points in the resuscitation and the proportion of pulseless patients already undergoing IAT at these times. Methods: We included patients randomized to DSED in secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial who did not have prehospital termination of resuscitation, vector change shocks prior to DSED, or a missing time of fourth defibrillation. We calculated the probability of prehospital ROSC at or beyond minute 5, 10, and 15 post-fourth defibrillation (first randomized DSED shock) in those still pulseless and the proportion already undergoing IAT. Results: Of 125 patients, 118 were included after applying exclusion criteria. Of these 118 patients, 58 (49%) achieved prehospital ROSC with 53/58 (91%) occurring on scene. At minutes 5, 10, and 15 post-fourth-defibrillation the probability of ROSC with continued resuscitation was 32/96 (33%), 16/80 (20%), and 7/71 (10%) respectively. At these same time points, the proportion of pulseless patients undergoing IAT was 2/96 (2%), 10/80 (13%), and 23/70 (33%) were actively undergoing IAT. Conclusions: The optimal timing of IAT in a system providing both ECPR and DSED may be from minutes 10-15, as the proportion of patients who will get ROSC falls below 10% at 15 minutes post-fourth-defibrillation; however, 32% of patients were receiving IAT at this timepoint, potentially underestimating the yield of continued on-scene resuscitation.

items.title: Abstract P2053: Association Between Splenic Volume, Lymphocyte Fraction, and Neurological Outcomes After Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: A dynamic reduction in splenic volume is followed by immunosuppression and secondary brain injury in animal models of cardiac arrest. The multiple roles of the spleen are garnering increased attention in the context of acute illnesses. Lymphopenia following clinical cardiac arrest is associated with poor neurological outcomes. However, it remains unclear whether splenic volume correlates with lymphopenia and neurological outcomes after clinical cardiac arrest. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that a reduced splenic volume after the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) precedes lymphopenia and is associated with poor neurological outcomes. Aims: This study aims to clarify the association between splenic volume and neurological outcomes following cardiac arrest. Methods: This single-center retrospective study included adult patients who underwent computed tomography (CT) after ROSC and were admitted to the intensive care unit between March 2016 and March 2026. We investigated patient characteristics, treatments during and after resuscitation, blood lymphocyte fraction (percentage of white blood cells), splenic volume immediately after ROSC and within one year prior to arrest, and modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scores at 30 days (0-3: favorable; 4-6: poor). Splenic volume was calculated using CT volumetry. Results: Among 158 patients (median age, 70 years; 111 males [70%]; 84 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests [53%]; 45 cardiogenic arrests [28%]), 40 patients (25%) achieved a favorable neurological outcome. Splenic volume demonstrated positive correlations with height and weight, and a negative correlation with age. Paired splenic volumes were obtained for 55 patients, of whom 8 (15%) achieved favorable neurological outcomes. Post-ROSC splenic volumes were significantly smaller than pre-arrest volumes (median 82 [interquartile range 60-176] vs. 109 [84-188] mL; p<0.001). Furthermore, BMI-adjusted splenic volume was significantly smaller in patients with poor outcomes compared to those with favorable outcomes (3.7 [2.5-5.9] vs. 5.0 [3.3-6.8] mL/BMI; p=0.03). There was no significant difference in the lymphocyte fraction between patients with poor and favorable neurological outcomes immediately after ROSC (19.3% [7-32] vs. 19.5% [6-37]; p=0.88). However, at 24 hours post-ROSC, the lymphocyte fraction was significantly lower in patients with poor neurological outcomes compared to those with favorable outcomes (4.6% [2-8] vs. 9.1% [4-14]; p=0.006). Conclusions: A reduction in splenic volume, as determined by CT scan immediately after ROSC, preceded lymphopenia and was associated with poor 30-day neurological outcomes. Splenic volume may serve as an early imaging biomarker for poor neurological outcomes.

items.title: Abstract P2057: Incidence and Outcomes of Overdose-Associated Out of Hospital Cardiac Arrest in a Large US-Based Clinical Trial Network
items.abstract: Introduction: Despite recent reductions in US-based overdose death, drug overdose remains the leading cause of death in persons 18-44 years of age. Victims of overdose who experience cardiac arrest are a largely understudied population. To date, randomized clinical trials in cardiac arrest outcomes have actively excluded this patient population. The Influence of Cooling Duration in Cardiac Arrest Patients (ICECAP) trial was the first prospective randomized clinical trial in out of hospital cardiac arrest to include patients with overdose-associated cardiac arrest. Objective: To describe the population with overdose associated OHCA in the ICECAP Trial and compare their outcomes to those with other etiologies of arrest. Methods: All study participants from the ICECAP trial were analyzed in a planned a priori secondary analysis. Enrollments between April 2020 and June 2025 were assessed for etiology of arrest. Patient and arrest characteristics as well as initial laboratory results and outcomes were compared via the following two distributions; overdose vs. non-overdose; and overdose vs. cardiac vs. respiratory. Results: Among 71 participating hospitals, 1158 patients were enrolled into the ICECAP trial and 24.4% (n=283) of the study participants experienced an overdose-associated OHCA. When compared to the non-overdose cohort, overdose patients were younger [50 yrs (IQR 34,60) vs. 65 yrs (IQR 55,73)], male [65.4% (185) vs. 58.8% (493)] and more commonly Black [42.8% (121) vs. 37.8% (317)] and/or Hispanic/Latino [13.1% (37) vs. 8.5% (71)] (Table 1). The overdose cohort received less layperson CPR (48.4% vs. 53.6%), less AED use (11.3% vs. 16.4%), and presented with predominantly non-shockable rhythms at EMS/ED arrival (83.0% vs. 69.6%) (Table 2). Of note, 6.7% of persons in the overdose cohort presented with STEMI on initial EKG. Patients with overdose experienced slightly worse neurologic recovery versus those with non-overdose defined as a modified Rankin Score of 0-3 (15.2% vs. 18.0%); though no difference was appreciated in unadjusted 90-day mortality (75.6% vs.75.1%) for overdose versus non-overdose victims in the ICECAP trial (Figure 1). Conclusion: In this descriptive secondary analysis of the ICECAP participants who experienced OHCA due to overdose, overdose-associated OHCA victims were younger, Black and Hispanic, Male persons who received less bystander CPR and AED application. Overall survival outcomes were similar however, there is trend towards slightly worse neurologic recovery. Further study in this patient population is necessary to examine the role of neuroprotective strategies, variability in neuro-prognosis and use of withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy and to identify targets to improve outcomes in this growing population of younger adults.

items.title: Abstract P2064: Building-Level Determinants of AED Accessibility in New York City Residential Housing
items.abstract: Introduction/Background: Bystander automated external defibrillator (AED) use is associated with higher rates of survival and better functional outcomes in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Although most OHCA occurs at home, AED access in residential areas remains low. Dense urban settings like New York City (NYC) have unique built environments in which commercial and residential spaces overlap, and residential buildings range from single-family homes to multi-unit high-rise structures. These unique features may influence AED access, but this relationship is poorly characterized. Aims: We aimed to quantify AED proximity within 15m and 100m of residential buildings in NYC by building-level characteristics, and evaluate the independent association between these characteristics and AED proximity. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that high-rise and mixed-use buildings, which are likely closer to commercial centers, would have greater odds of having an AED within 15m and 100m compared to low-rise and residential-only buildings. Methods: We used the NYC AED Inventory to identify AED locations, the NYC Primary Land Use Tax Lot Output (PLUTO) dataset to characterize buildings, and NYC Census Tract Data to identify neighborhood co-variates for each building included in the analysis. All buildings with at least one residential housing unit were included and stratified by height (low-, mid-, and high-rise). Building use type was classified using PLUTO land use codes. QGIS was used to identify AEDs within 15m and 100m of each residential building. Descriptive statistics were used to characterize AED proximity by building feature, and multivariable logistic regression adjusting for neighborhood-level covariates was used to identify building features independently associated with AED proximity. Results: Of 766,246 residential buildings, 98.8% were low-rise and 92.7% were residential-only. Overall, 0.6% and 3.0% of residential buildings had an AED within 15m and 100m, respectively. We found that 0.5% and 0.9% of low-rise compared to 17.2% and 24.4% of high-rise buildings had an AED within 15m and 100m, respectively. High-rise buildings independently had higher odds of having an AED within 15m (17.57 [14.72-20.87], p<0.001) and 100m (OR 13.09 [11.24-15.19], p<0.001) compared to low-rise buildings. Mixed-use buildings independently had higher odds of having an AED within 15m (OR 1.70 [1.57-1.84], p<0.001) and 100m (OR 1.90 [1.79-2.01], p<0.001) compared to residential-only buildings. Conclusion: AED proximity to NYC residential buildings is low overall. Low-rise and residential-only buildings have significantly lower AED proximity than mixed-use and high-rise buildings, suggesting that current AED placement may not align with population need. Future AED deployment and redistribution efforts should prioritize residential neighborhoods to improve OHCA survival.

items.title: Abstract P2014: Pharmacological Inhibition of cGAS Attenuates the Early Post-Resuscitation Transcriptomic Inflammatory Response in a Porcine Model of Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Objective: Post-cardiac arrest syndrome (PCAS) is characterized by a rapid, dysregulated inflammatory response that exacerbates organ injury and undermines recovery. Extracellular vesicle-encapsulated mitochondrial DNA has recently been identified as a potent stimulus of post-resuscitation immune cell activation via the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) pathway. Whether pharmacological cGAS inhibition can attenuate the post-resuscitation inflammatory response in vivo is unknown. Accordingly, we tested the hypothesis that cGAS inhibition attenuates the early post-resuscitation transcriptomic inflammatory response in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) after cardiac arrest. Methods: Swine (n=14) underwent 7 minutes of ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest and subsequent resuscitation. After return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), animals were randomized to receive a small molecule inhibitor of cGAS (G140; 0.1 mg/kg IV; n=7) or vehicle (n=7) at 15 minutes post-ROSC. PBMCs were isolated at baseline and 4 hours post-ROSC for bulk RNA sequencing. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified using DESeq2 (adjusted p<0.05). Results: PBMCs from vehicle-treated animals exhibited 3,145 DEGs at 4 hours post-ROSC compared with baseline, reflecting widespread transcriptomic activation. G140-treated animals exhibited only 719 DEGs (77% reduction vs. vehicle; Figure, A ). Expression of cGAS itself was unchanged, consistent with pharmacological inhibition of enzymatic activity rather than gene expression. However, TBK1, the kinase immediately downstream of STING that phosphorylates IRF3, was significantly downregulated in G140-treated animals (log 2 FC=–0.39, p_adj=0.04). Additional genes within the cGAS-STING and innate immune signaling pathways were suppressed in G140- vs. vehicle-treated animals, including NLRP3, IL-15, TNFRSF11A, CCL14, and CCL21 ( Figure, B ). Conclusion: Systemic cGAS inhibition with G140 administered shortly after ROSC markedly attenuates the early post-resuscitation transcriptomic inflammatory response in porcine PBMCs. These findings support cGAS-STING as a tractable therapeutic target and provide rationale for further evaluation of cGAS inhibition as a targeted immunomodulatory strategy in PCAS.

items.title: Abstract P2024: Longitudinal Trend in 1-3 Month Functional Outcomes in the ICECAP Trial
items.abstract: Introduction: Functional outcomes after out-of-hospital-cardiac-arrest (OHCA) are often measured using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at a single time point, typically 90 days. While useful, this approach may miss meaningful changes in recovery that occur earlier in the post acute phase. Discharge location, whether home, a rehabilitation facility, a skilled nursing facility, or long term acute care, reflects a patient's recovery status, anticipated needs at the time of hospital discharge, and potentially with subsequent recovery trajectories. Methods: We performed a secondary analysis of ICECAP trial participants who completed mRS assessments at Day 90. We defined functional trajectories as improved when the Day 90 mRS was lower than at Day 30, stable when there was no change, or worsened when the Day 90 mRS was higher than Day 30. Outcomes were also grouped as favorable (mRS 0-3) or unfavorable (mRS 4-5), with changes examined by discharge location. Results: Among 1158 patients (median age 61 years, 40% female, 76% nonshockable rhythm), 276 had a documented discharge location with mRS assessed at Day 90. Discharge locations included home (53%), rehabilitation facility (18%), skilled nursing facility (12%), and long-term acute care (14%). Recovery trajectories varied substantially across discharge settings. Among patients discharged home, 57/146 (39%) improved, 52/146 (35.6%) remained stable, and 37/146 (25.3%) worsened between Day 30 and Day 90. Among patients discharged to rehabilitation facilities, 25/50 improved (50%), 19/50 remained stable (38%), and 6/50 worsened (12%). Those discharged to skilled nursing facilities had more mixed trajectories, 11/33 improved (33.3%), 18/33 remaining stable (54.5%), and 4/33 worsening (12.1%). In contrast, patients discharged to long term acute care were largely unchanged, with 31/38 stable (81.6%). Detailed recovery trajectories are shown in Figure 1. Conclusions: Functional recovery after OHCA continues to evolve between Day 30 and Day 90. Discharge location is associated with different recovery patterns and may offer early insight into a patient’s trajectory. These findings emphasize the importance of looking beyond a single 90 Day endpoint and suggest that discharge disposition can provide useful prognostic context.

items.title: Abstract P2059: Metronome Use During Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest in the Emergency Department: Impact on CPR Quality
items.abstract: Background: Metronomes have demonstrated improved adherence to AHA chest compression rate in simulation; however, evidence supporting their effectiveness in real-world pediatric cardiac arrest is limited. Goal: Determine the association between the use of an audible metronome and adherence to the AHA-recommended compression rate during cardiac arrests in a pediatric emergency department (ED). Hypothesis: The use of an audible metronome is associated with better adherence to the AHA-recommended compression rate in pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in the ED. Methods: This is a retrospective review of pediatric OHCA at a single pediatric ED from January 2025 to March 2026. Metronome use was defined as audible metronome activation for >50% of the arrest based on video review of ED care. CPR quality metrics were evaluated via a defibrillator with accelerometer feedback. The primary outcome was the percent of compressions adherent to the AHA-recommended rate of 100-120 per minute during the ED portion of event. Secondary outcomes evaluated adherence to AHA depth, chest compression fraction (CCF), longest pause, return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), and survival to hospital discharge (SHD). Continuous CPR quality metrics were compared using the Wilcoxon rank sum test. Clinical outcomes were compared using the Fisher’s exact test. Results: Forty-seven patients with pediatric OHCA were included, 27 without and 20 with metronome use. Median age in each group was 0.6 and 1.4 years, respectively. The median percent of compressions adherent to AHA-recommended rate in the ED was higher with a metronome (90%) than without (75%, p<0.001). The median percent of compressions adherent to AHA-recommended depth was higher in the metronome group, although did not meet statistical significance (35% vs. 44%, p=0.3). CCF and longest pause were similar in both groups. There was no significant difference in ROSC or SHD. One patient in each group was still hospitalized at the time of analysis. Conclusions: An audible metronome during pediatric OHCA was associated with a higher percent of compressions adherent to the AHA-recommended rate in the pediatric ED. While we found no difference in clinical outcomes, we were limited by sample size. Our findings support the use of an audible metronome as a low-cost intervention to improve adherence to AHA chest compression rate guidelines in a pediatric ED.

items.title: Abstract P2071: Kidney Donation Outcomes After Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation
items.abstract: Introduction: Extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) has improved survival significantly in refractory cardiac arrest in recent years, yet mortality remains high. When ECPR does not achieve patient survival, organ donation may be pursued. The 2025 American Heart Association Guidelines recognize ECPR patients as a potential source of donor organs, however data on transplant recipient outcomes is limited. Hypothesis: Kidneys donated from ECPR donors have comparable short- and long-term function as those from non-ECPR donors and thus have the potential to expand the donor pool. Aims: To assess short- and long-term outcomes in kidney transplant recipients from ECPR versus non-ECPR donors. Methods: In this retrospective study, ECPR and non-ECPR donors from the University of Minnesota and their corresponding recipients were identified between 2016 and 2023. Donor and recipient baseline characteristics, transplant variables and post-transplant outcomes were compared between groups. Primary outcomes included graft failure and patient mortality. Secondary outcomes included serum creatinine at discharge and at 6-, 12-, 24- and 36-month follow-up. Results: Overall, 23 ECPR donors and 24 non-ECPR donors were identified, donating kidneys to 39 and 45 recipients, respectively. Recipients were transplanted across multiple regions, with 41% (16/39) of ECPR and 49% (22/45) of non-ECPR recipients residing in Minnesota. Donor age was similar between groups, and ECPR donors had significantly higher serum creatinine at the time of organ procurement (p=0.002) (Table 1). Recipients had similar baseline characteristics (Table 2). Recipients from ECPR donors had significantly higher creatinine at discharge and at 6-, 12-, and 36-month follow-up, though graft failure rates were low and not significantly different between groups (5% versus 7%, p=1.0). Mortality rates were similar (p=0.62), and no deaths were attributable to graft dysfunction. Median follow-up was shorter in the ECPR group (Table 3). Conclusion: Kidney recipients from ECPR donors had consistently higher creatinine, however, they had similar graft and patient survival with those from non-ECPR donors. These findings show that in cases when patient recovery is not feasible, organ donation can extend the benefit of ECPR from one individual to multiple recipients per donor, across geographic regions.

items.title: Abstract P2079: Tidal Volume Leak Associated with Different Airway Devices During CPR
items.abstract: Background: High-quality ventilation should be provided during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). The 2025 AHA guidelines recommend targeting visible chest rise with an estimated tidal volume of 5-7 mL/kg in adults. Until recently, objective measurement of ventilation quality during OHCA has been largely unavailable, limiting comparisons between airway strategies. The EOlife™ device (Archeon Medical) provides in-line monitoring and real-time feedback on parameters such as air-leak presence, delivered tidal volume, and ventilation rate. Study Aims: The primary aim was to compare ventilation delivery with bag-valve mask (BVM), BVM with oropharyngeal airway (OPA), supraglottic airway (SGA), and endotracheal tube (ETT) during OHCA. Hypothesis: We hypothesize that advanced airways (SGA, ETT) deliver higher tidal volumes (Vt) and have lower air leaks than BVM with or without OPA during 30:2 CPR cycles performed by EMS clinicians. Methods: This prospective observational study examines ventilations delivered during 30:2 CPR cycles by a single fire-first response agency serving a population of 550,000 in the Portland, Oregon, metropolitan area. Enrollment spanned June 2025 to April 2026. Adult (age >18 years), non-traumatic OHCA patients who had ventilation guided by the EOlife™ were included. Cases without EOlife™ use, ROSC before EOlife™ use, and age <18 years were excluded. The primary outcomes were Vt and air leak volume. Ventilatory parameters were recorded breath-by-breath by the EOlife™ and exported as CSV files. Airway type was manually annotated from case records. Chest compression artifacts were filtered, and the first and second ventilations within each 30:2 CPR cycle were identified using previously published criteria. Descriptive statistical (median, IQR) comparisons were computed across ventilation categories and airway type. Results: Overall, 2903 non-passive ventilations were examined from 24 patients (Table). Median Vt were 307 mL (BVM), 315mL (OPA), 421mL (i-gel), and 444mL (ETT). BVM had the largest median air leak of 175mL, compared with OPA (83mL), i-gel (59mL), and ETT (24mL). Among all devices, the first ventilation had a median air leak of 36 mL, compared with 124 mL for the second ventilation in the 30:2 cycle. The EOlife™ target Vt of 400-500mL was reached most often with i-gel (40.3%), followed by ETT (36.9%), OPA (24%), and BVM (16.2%). Conclusions: Among OHCA cases with EOlife™ use, BVM ventilation with or without an OPA was associated with greater air leak and lower Vt than advanced airways, suggesting that manual ventilation remained difficult even with real-time feedback. The observed air leak was also higher during the second ventilation during 30:2 CPR, which may be related to the resumption of chest compressions.

items.title: Abstract P2010: Neurophysiological and Molecular Remodeling in the Hippocampus Following Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Introduction: Brain injury is a major contributor to post-cardiac arrest (CA) morbidity and mortality, yet the synaptic and molecular mechanisms governing these outcomes remain poorly understood. We have previously shown that Dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1), a regulator of mitochondrial fission, is activated in the heart immediately following resuscitation and is an important determinant of myocardial function. Drp1 is also critical for maintaining normal synaptic function, but its relationship to post-CA neurophysiology is unknown. Here, we evaluated acute post-CA changes in synaptic physiology and Drp1 expression at the CA3-CA1 synapse of the hippocampus, a region with well-characterized ischemic vulnerability and a central role in activity-dependent plasticity, at 3 and 7 hours (h) post-CA. Methods: In an established murine model of CA, we characterized the neurophysiology of the CA3-CA1 synapse using field electrophysiological recordings, at 3h and 7h post-CA to characterize the input-output relationship, paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) and short-term and long-term potentiation (PPF). We also evaluated changes in total Drp1 and Drp1 phosphorylation, and total CaMKII and CaMKII T286 phosphorylation, in the hippocampus and in the heart, at 3h and 7h post-CA. Results: In the hippocampus, we observed impairment in baseline transmission as seen in the input-output curve at the CA1-CA3 synapse (p<0.05) as well as in synaptic functions, such as short-term potentiation (p<0.01) and long-term potentiation, LTP (p<0.0001) at both 3h and 7h post-CA, congruent with loss of postsynaptic function. Additionally, paired-pulse facilitation (PPF) was only impaired at 7h post-CA (p<0.05), indicating the generalization of injury to presynaptic sites. We also measured total Drp1 and Drp1 phosphorylation at these timepoints, and our results demonstrate that inactivating Drp1-S637 phosphorylation is downregulated in the heart (p<0.05) at 3h and 7h post-ROSC. However, in the hippocampus, activating Drp1-S616 phosphorylation is upregulated only at 7h (p<0.01), indicating increase in mitochondrial fission markers at 3h and 7h in the heart but only at 7h in the brain. We also evaluated total CaMKII protein and CaMKII T286 phosphorylation in the hippocampus at both timepoints, and saw a decrease in total CaMKII protein (p<0.05) at 3h and 7h post-ROSC. Conclusion: Post-CA injury in the hippocampus is dynamic and progressive in the hours following resuscitation, in contrast to the more acutely injured heart. These findings demonstrate that the brain and heart follow unique post-CA timelines, suggestive of distinct windows of organ specific opportunity for therapeutic intervention.

items.title: Abstract P2050: Enhancing Pediatric Cardiac Arrest Documentation via Video Based Education
items.abstract: Introduction: Effective code documentation is essential to evaluate cardiac arrest events identifying high quality CPR and opportunities for improvement. Previous education included passive review of code documentation which continued to result in incomplete documentation. The purpose of utilizing a simulated educational forum was to improve code documentation compliance for effective evaluation of actual code outcomes versus small group education sessions in which key information was incomplete or lacking. Research Questions/Hypothesis: Allowing registered nurses to practice code documentation utilizing a video simulation of a pediatric cardiac arrest event would improve code documentation comprehensive and adherence. Methods/Approach: Code documentation forms completed between 2024 to present were collected and analyzed to assess documentation completeness. The review identified several key data elements that were consistently missing from the records. To improve compliance and support accurate evaluation of actual code outcomes, a simulated educational forum was developed. An interprofessional team created and recorded a 6-minute mock cardiac arrest event, incorporating a visual timer to assist the designated documenter. Results/Data: During six sessions, 45 out of 73 (62%) registered nurses served as real-time documenters during the simulated arrest event. The code document contains 29 potential data points which include multiple medication options and fill in medications administrations. For the purposes of this project, 21 data points integral to successful documentation were reviewed with 15 out of 21data points noting improvements. There were significant documentation improvements in the following categories: time, rhythm, blood pressure, time to chest compressions, pulse and rhythm checks, airway confirmation, IV fluids, infusions, and precipitating events. Conclusion: The hands-on educational methodology over passive instructional review demonstrated effectiveness of the approach as evidenced by the documentation outcomes. While not all categories demonstrated improvement, future simulated educational sessions will focus on these areas while maintaining compliance in the categories that demonstrated improvement.

items.title: Abstract P2019: Mental Health Outcomes After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Population-Based Cohort Study Comparing Adult Survivors with Other Critically Ill Patients
items.abstract: Background: Psychiatric morbidity is common after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), yet whether survivors carry excess risk relative to other critically ill patients or instead share post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) mechanisms remains unclear. Hypothesis: OHCA survivors experience excess new-onset mental health and addictions (MHA) risk compared with matched critical illness survivors, beyond what is explained by pre-existing psychiatric history and sociodemographic vulnerability. Methods: Population-based retrospective cohort study (ICES, Ontario, Canada; 2007-2022). Adults surviving ICU admission for non-traumatic OHCA were matched to non-OHCA critical illness survivors by age (±3 years) and admission date (±3 days). Primary outcome: time to first new-onset MHA diagnosis within 15 years of discharge, from validated physician-coded inpatient, emergency department (ED), and outpatient records. We fit flexible parametric (Royston-Parmar) survival models with death as a competing risk and used logistic regression to compare inpatient versus outpatient care intensity, adjusting for sex, comorbidities, prior healthcare use, and neighbourhood marginalization. Results: Among 6,034 OHCA survivors matched to 16,461 controls (mean follow-up 4.7 years), 2,740 OHCA survivors (45.4%) received a new MHA diagnosis: anxiety/mood (33.9%), substance-related (7.8%), and psychotic disorders (2.7%); 20.0% required inpatient psychiatric admission. Incidence peaked within six months post-discharge. Composite MHA hazard was similar between cohorts (aHR 0.95; 95% CI 0.89-1.02). OHCA survivors had lower hazards for outpatient anxiety/mood (aHR 0.91), psychotic (0.74), and behavioural disorders (0.62); any inpatient psychiatric admission (0.85); inpatient mood disorders (0.69); and deliberate self-harm (0.73). The strongest predictor of new MHA outcomes was pre-existing psychiatric diagnosis (aHR 2.22; 95% CI 1.97-2.49); high pre-arrest ED use, younger age, female sex, and residence in racially marginalized or high-density neighbourhoods also independently predicted risk. Conclusions: Contrary to our hypothesis, OHCA survivors did not exhibit excess MHA risk versus matched critical illness survivors and showed lower hazards across several subcategories, suggesting shared post-ICU rather than arrest-specific psychiatric mechanisms. Nevertheless, nearly half developed a new MHA diagnosis, concentrated in the first six months and driven chiefly by pre-existing psychiatric history. These findings support integrating OHCA survivors into unified post-ICU mental health pathways, with early screening and targeted outreach for those with prior psychiatric diagnoses, high ED use, or residence in disadvantaged communities.

items.title: Abstract P2046: Practice Makes Progress: Longitudinal Trends in Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Skills
items.abstract: Objective: The Resuscitation Quality Improvement (RQI) program utilizes high frequency, low dose resuscitation training as a strategy to improve cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) skills and retention. However, longitudinal performance across variable CPR activities such as ventilation or chest compressions remains poorly described. Our objective was to evaluate longitudinal CPR performance for a RQI program with baseline (no feedback) and quarterly skills assessments (with feedback). Methods: We performed a longitudinal retrospective analysis from a RQI program implemented across multiple clinical sites in a large academic healthcare system. We defined CPR performance across four activities: adult compressions, adult ventilations, infant compressions, and infant ventilations. We evaluated competency for participants through repeated quarterly assessments over 5 years. Using mixed-effects regression models accounting for repeated measures, we examined session number (time), CPR activity type, and their interaction to assess differences in improvement, and estimated average predicted performance over time to illustrate trends. Results: We included 803,775 assessments (baseline: 45,646; skills: 758,129) from 16,797 participants. At baseline, overall competency improved consistently by 6.2 percentage points per session (95%CI: 4.7 to 7.7). Compared to adult compressions, adult ventilation demonstrated no difference. The highest predicted infant performance was observed for ventilation (96.4%) and the lowest for compressions (90.5%). Interaction effects demonstrated rate of change differed by activity type (Figure 1A). When evaluating quarterly skills sessions (with feedback), all activities showed high and improving performance, with an additional 3.0 percentage point gain per session (2.1 to 4.2) (Figure 1B). Adult and infant ventilation skills improved faster than compression skills over time. Predicted performance remained high across all activities with feedback (pairwise p<0.001). Conclusions: Quarterly RQI training with feedback was associated with consistently high CPR performance that progressively improved over time. This study is limited by observational design and potential confounding by unmeasured differences in prior experience/training. Although baseline performance varied by activity, feedback was associated with progressive improvement across all skills suggesting a strong reinforcement effect.

items.title: Abstract P2054: Probability of a Favorable Outcome for Each Minute of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation in Patients Without a Return of Spontaneous Circulation After Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Previous studies have shown that a longer duration of cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) before the return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) was associated with poor outcomes for patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). However, most prior work focused on overall resuscitation duration and had not fully addressed a clinically relevant, time-updated question. Research Questions: Among patients who remain without the ROSC for each minute of ongoing CPR, what is the probability of subsequently achieving favorable outcomes? Aims: Our objective was to quantify the time-dependent probabilities of favorable outcomes as a function of CPR duration, defined as the interval between the start of chest compressions and the first ROSC or termination of resuscitation, in patients with OHCA. Methods: This was a secondary analysis of a nationwide, hospital-based, prospective database of the Japanese Association for Acute Medicine OHCA Registry between June 1, 2014, and December 31, 2022. Our outcome measures were 30-day survival and a favorable neurological outcome 30 days after OHCA occurrence. A favorable neurological outcome was defined as a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1 or 2. We estimated the time-dependent probabilities of subsequently surviving to 30 days or having a favorable functional outcome if patients, pending the first ROSC at each minute, received further CPR beyond the time point, assuming that all decisions on the termination of resuscitation were accurate. Results: Among 41,933 analyzed patients, 13,661 (32.6%) achieved a ROSC with a median interval of 38 (interquartile range 27-48) minutes of CPR duration whereas 28,272 (67.4%) patients did not achieve ROSC with a median interval of 56 (46-68) minutes of CPR duration. Of these, 1,561 (3.7%) patients had a favorable neurologicaloutcome 30 days after OHCA occurrence. The time-dependent probabilities of survival and a favorable functional outcome among patients, pending ROSC, for one minute’s duration of CPR were 6.3% (2,625/41,930) and 3.7% (1,558/41,930), respectively. The probabilities decreased over time and were <1% for survival at 36 minutes and <1% for a favorable functional outcome at 22 minutes’ duration of CPR. Conclusions: Using a nationwide multicenter registry, we quantified the time-dependent probabilities of patients’ outcomes for each minute of CPR duration. The findings indicate the likelihood of favorable outcomes in patients pending the first ROSC.

items.title: Abstract P2011: Automated Endovascular Aortic Occlusion Mitigates Cerebral Ischemia and Eliminates Rearrest in a Porcine Model of Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Traditional cardiac arrest resuscitation relies heavily on high-dose epinephrine to achieve return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and on continued vasopressors to support hemodynamics after ROSC. Despite high doses of vasopressors, many patients continue to re-arrest after ROSC and have substantial cerebral ischemia. We evaluated whether automated, titratable endovascular partial aortic occlusion to offset epinephrine requirements could mitigate secondary injury, eliminate post-ROSC rearrest, and preserve cerebral perfusion compared to standard vasopressor-based management. Methods: Ventricular fibrillation was induced in 20 anesthetized Yorkshire swine. Following a 5-minute no-flow injury phase, mechanical CPR and automated Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS)-guided resuscitation were initiated. Animals achieving ROSC were randomized to automated critical care for 12 hours (Control, n=10) or endovascular perfusion augmentation for critical care (EPACC, n=6) for 6 hours, followed by an additional 6 hours of automated critical care. Automated critical care used MAP, CVP, fluid responsiveness, lactate, and urine output as input variables for determining the need for weight-based crystalloid boluses and titration of epinephrine and vasopressin. Automated aortic balloon-augmentation created a goal blood pressure gradient of 10 mmHg across the balloon within Zone 1 of the descending thoracic aorta. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed on all surviving animals at 12 hours after ROSC. Results: A total of 12 animals survived to MRI evaluation (EPACC, n=6; Control, n=6); 4 control animals expired early due to re-arrest. Automated balloon support achieved a 100% survival rate and eliminated rearrests, compared with 40% early mortality and a significant rearrest rate in the control group (p = 0.03). While macro-hemodynamics (mean arterial pressure, carotid blood flow) and total epinephrine and fluid requirements were comparable between groups, laser Doppler flowmetry demonstrated significantly higher cerebral microvascular perfusion in the EPACC group during the first hour after balloon deflation (p < 0.05). MRI revealed smaller cerebral infarct volumes and superior sum ASPECTS in the EPACC group compared to Controls (Figure 1, p < 0.05). EPACC animals exhibited a minor, non-significant increase in peak creatinine. Conclusions: Automated, dynamic endovascular aortic occlusion successfully bridged the post-ROSC "hemodynamic cliff," preventing rearrest and significantly reducing cerebral infarction. These data demonstrate that second-to-second automated titration of afterload provides neuroprotection and preserves micro-perfusion during the early post-ROSC phase.

items.title: Abstract P2016: Physiological Effects of a Flow-Modulating Device During Prolonged Manual Ventilation in a Swine Model
items.abstract: Introduction: In austere settings, prolonged bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation may be required before advanced airway support is available. Excessive inspiratory flow, elevated airway pressures, and inconsistent tidal volumes during sustained manual ventilation increase the risk of lung injury and provider fatigue. Sotair is a flow-modulating accessory designed to improve ventilation safety during prolonged manual ventilation. Hypothesis: We hypothesized that Sotair would improve ventilation safety by limiting excessive inspiratory flow, airway pressure, and tidal volume delivery while maintaining physiologic stability compared to ventilation with a sham device. Methods: Twenty-two juvenile domestic swine (mean weight 52 ± 4 kg) were enrolled and assigned to 6-hour (n=8) or 24-hour (n=14) ventilation cohorts in a non-survival model of prolonged manual overventilation. Animals underwent intubation, invasive hemodynamic monitoring, hourly arterial blood gas sampling, and prolonged manual ventilation with a BVM system using either an active Sotair or sham device. Respiratory rate was titrated to end-tidal CO 2, and sham ventilation was delivered with forceful manual respirations to model excessive ventilation conditions. Airway flow, peak airway pressure, and tidal volume were continuously recorded, and gross lung injury was assessed at necropsy. Longitudinal physiologic data were analyzed using generalized estimating equations and mixed-effects regression models. Results: Twenty-one animals were analyzed after protocol violation: 8 in the 6-hour cohort (4 sham, 4 Sotair) and 13 in the 24-hour cohort (7 sham, 6 Sotair). Across 124,350 breaths over 360 observation hours, Sotair significantly reduced average inspiratory flow (–46.63 L/min), peak airway pressure (–33.04 cmH 2 O), and tidal volume (–312.52 mL) compared with sham ventilation (all p<0.001). In the 24-hour cohort, Sotair was associated with improved oxygenation stability, including higher ABG-derived arterial oxygen saturation at 24 hours compared with sham (+3.34%, p=0.031), lower continuous pulse oximetry-derived oxygen saturation coefficient of variation (1.73% vs 4.26%, p<0.0001), and lower partial pressure carbon dioxide coefficient of variation (12.01% vs 15.29%, p<0.0001). Gross lung injury scores did not differ significantly between treatment groups overall, although injury severity was greater in 24-hour than in 6-hour animals independent of device assignment (p=0.003). Conclusions: Flow modulation using Sotair reduced excessive inspiratory flow, airway pressure, and tidal volume during prolonged manual ventilation while maintaining physiologic stability. Although gross injury outcomes were not significantly different between groups, these findings support further evaluation of Sotair as a low-resource adjunct for prolonged field care and austere settings.

items.title: Abstract P2067: Association of Serum Magnesium Measured During Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation with Initial Shockable Rhythms in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Magnesium (Mg) is not currently recommended for routine use in shockable rhythms such as ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, except in cases of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. The clinical studies supporting this recommendation are more than 20 years old, and contemporary evidence is limited. In addition, no clinical study has evaluated serum Mg concentrations during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). Therefore, we conducted an observational study to examine the association between serum Mg levels measured during CPR and the occurrence of initial shockable rhythms in patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA). Hypothesis: This study aimed to test the hypothesis that lower serum magnesium concentrations measured during CPR are independently associated with a higher likelihood of presenting with an initial shockable rhythm Methods: We performed a single-center, retrospective analysis of prospectively collected data from 1,506 OHCA patients treated between June 2016 and December 2024. Blood samples were obtained early during CPR in the emergency department. Associations between Mg levels and the presence of an initial shockable rhythm were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression analysis. Results: A total of 1,458 patients had serum Mg levels measured during CPR. In univariable analysis, gender, age, no-flow time, witnessed arrest, public-location arrest, serum Mg concentration, and presumed cardiac etiology were significantly associated with the presence of an initial shockable rhythm (Table 1). In multivariable analysis, serum Mg concentration remained independently associated with an initial shockable rhythm odds ratio 0.455, 95% confidence interval 0.294-0.704, p < 0.001). When serum Mg levels were categorized into quartiles, the proportion of patients with an initial shockable rhythm decreased significantly with increasing Mg levels (p < 0.001; Figure 1). Conclusion: Serum Mg concentration measured during CPR was independently associated with the presence of an initial shockable rhythm in OHCA patients, and higher Mg levels were associated with a lower proportion of initial shockable rhythms. These findings suggest that Mg levels during CPR may be related to the likelihood of presenting with an initial shockable rhythm.

items.title: Abstract P2039: Impact of Esmolol Administration on Outcomes in Shock-Refractory Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
items.abstract: Background: Shock-refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is associated with poor survival. The beta-blocker esmolol may improve OHCA outcomes by mitigating catecholamine-mediated myocardial stress. Hypothesis: The addition of esmolol to emergency medical services (EMS) protocols is associated with improved patient outcomes in shock-refractory OHCA. Methods: We conducted a retrospective study of adult (age≥18), non-traumatic OHCA cases who received ≥7 shocks treated by dual-advanced life support single tiered EMS systems in the Portland, OR region from 2018-2023. Esmolol was added to protocols on January 1, 2022, for use after the 7th shock, following failure of standard therapy (epinephrine, amiodarone, and alternative defibrillation strategies). The primary outcome was survival to discharge; secondary outcomes were return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) at hospital arrival, survival to admission, and favorable outcome (cerebral performance category score ≤ 2). We used mixed effects logistic regression adjusting for age, sex, arrest location, witness status, initial rhythm, bystander interventions, timing elements (call to EMS arrival, 1st defibrillation, 1st epinephrine, 1st amiodarone, and 7th defibrillation), and clustering by county. Sensitivity analyses included restricting post-implementation cases to those receiving esmolol (as-treated), exclusion of COVID-era controls (2020-2021), and using propensity score matching for cases receiving esmolol to controls. Results: A total of 227 patients met criteria (147 pre- and 80 post-esmolol implementation [65% received esmolol]), unadjusted outcomes were similar: ROSC 15.0% vs 17.5% (p=0.62), survival to admission 26.5% vs 33.8% (p=0.25), survival to discharge 10.9% vs 11.2% (p=0.93), and favorable outcome 10.9% vs 11.2% (p=0.93) for controls and esmolol periods, respectively. Adjusted analyses showed no significant association with ROSC (aOR 1.95, 95% CI 0.80-4.77), survival to admission (aOR 1.71, 95% CI 0.89-3.29), survival to discharge (aOR 1.25, 95% CI 0.47-3.31), or favorable outcomes (aOR 1.25, 95% CI 0.47-3.31). The as-treated analyses, the analyses excluding COVID-era controls, and propensity matched analyses for cases receiving esmolol (n=46) matched to controls (n=46) were similarly not significant. Conclusions: The addition of esmolol for the management of shock-refractory OHCA after failure of standard therapy in this EMS system was not associated with differences in patient outcomes.

items.title: Myocardial Responses to Eplontersen in Transthyretin Amyloid Cardiomyopathy: The CARDIO-TTRansform CMR study
items.abstract: Background: Transthyretin-lowering therapies target the underlying cause of transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), but their effects on myocardial amyloid burden and cardiac remodelling remain incompletely characterized. We evaluated the myocardial effects of sustained transthyretin suppression with eplontersen using serial multiparametric cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR). Methods: This CMR study was a pre-specified, international, prospective study embedded within the randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 CARDIO-TTRansform trial. Participants underwent CMR at baseline and planned assessments at weeks 25, 49, 97, and 140. The primary imaging analysis evaluated longitudinal changes in CMR parameters using mixed models for repeated measures. Myocardial amyloid regression and progression were defined as ≥5 percentage-point decreases and increases in extracellular volume (ECV), respectively. All other patients were considered stable. Results: We enrolled 120 participants with baseline and ≥1 follow-up CMR assessment (eplontersen, n=58; placebo, n=62; mean age, 76.7±6.5 years; 95% male; baseline stabilizer, 12.5%). At week 140 eplontersen resulted in lower ECV, compared with placebo (least-squares mean difference [95% CI], –6.7 percentage points [ –8.7 to –4.7]; P<0.001) and lower native T1 ( –25.9ms [–41.7 to –10.2 ]; P=0.002) and left ventricular mass (–19.1g [–28.0 to –10.2]; P<0.001). Eplontersen also increased left ventricular ejection fraction (+5.1% [1.8–8.3]; P=0.002), right ventricular ejection fraction (+4.6% [0.6–8.7]; P=0.03), and left ventricular global longitudinal, circumferential, and radial strain and right ventricular longitudinal strain (all P<0.05), compared to placebo. At week-140, myocardial amyloid regression occurred in 12.5% receiving eplontersen versus 0% receiving placebo, whereas progression occurred in 12.5% versus 76%, respectively. Conclusions: Sustained transthyretin suppression with eplontersen resulted in substantially lower myocardial ECV and favorable changes in cardiac structure, biventricular systolic function, and myocardial deformation compared with placebo in a cohort of patients mostly not on background stabilizer at baseline. These findings provide randomized evidence that lowering circulating transthyretin modifies myocardial disease progression in ATTR-CM and support serial multiparametric CMR for characterizing myocardial treatment response.

Off-Pump versus On-Pump Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting in Prefrail and Frail Patients: 30-Day and 1-Year Outcomes From the FRAGILE Randomized Trial
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Frailty is associated with worse outcomes after coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). However, the comparative effectiveness of off-pump CABG (OPCAB) versus on-pump CABG (ONCAB) in prefrail and frail patients remains uncertain. METHODS: This multicenter, randomized, open-label trial enrolled patients ≥60 years of age classified as prefrail or frail, randomized 1:1, between January 2018 and December 2024. The primary outcome was a 30-day composite of death, myocardial infarction, stroke, renal failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome, or reoperation for bleeding. Secondary outcomes included ventilation time, intensive care unit and hospital stay, transfusion requirements, completeness of revascularization, surgical wound infection at 30 days, and neurocognitive function preoperatively and at 1 year. Analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle; relative risks with 95% CIs were estimated. RESULTS: A total of 508 patients were included (OPCAB, n=258; ONCAB, n=250; median age, 68 years [interquartile range, 65.0–73]; 30.5% female). The primary composite outcome occurred in 28 patients receiving OPCAB (10.9%) and 40 patients receiving ONCAB (16.0%; relative risk, 1.47 [95% CI, 0.94–2.31]; P =0.09). Surgical wound infection was more frequent with ONCAB (20 [8.0%] versus 9 [3.5%]; P =0.04). No significant differences were observed in neurocognitive or quality of life outcomes at 1 year. Estimated 1-year survival probabilities were 96.1% and 92.8% in the OPCAB and ONCAB groups, respectively ( P =0.099). CONCLUSION: In prefrail and frail patients undergoing CABG, OPCAB and ONCAB resulted in similar rates of the primary composite outcome. No significant differences between OPCAB and ONCAB were found in neurocognitive outcomes. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov ; Unique identifier: NCT02338947.

items.title: Generation of Human Cardiomyocytes With Adult-Like Metabolism by a Chemically Defined Medium for Mitochondrial Disease Modeling
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)–derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC cardiomyocytes) as a model for cardiac disease have become increasingly important, bolstered by the Food and Drug Administration’s initiative to promote novel alternative methods for biomedical research. A key limitation of metabolically immature iPSC cardiomyocytes is their limited ability to accurately recapitulate mitochondria-dependent pathologies, such as Friedreich ataxia–associated cardiomyopathy. Adult cardiomyocytes are characterized by a high density of interfibrillar mitochondria, abundant respiratory complexes (I–V) that form supercomplexes, and efficient utilization of fatty acids to drive mitochondrial respiration. These unique metabolic structures and functions are largely missing in iPSC cardiomyocytes. Further, whether iPSC cardiomyocytes can efficiently utilize fatty acids for respiration in the presence of glucose, a unique adult feature, remains unclear. METHODS: We developed a chemically defined, 11-component maturation medium (MM11) designed using a bioinformatics-guided strategy that identified high-fidelity transcriptional markers of adult cardiac metabolic maturity. Human iPSC cardiomyocytes were treated with MM11 for 2 weeks and evaluated at the molecular, structural, and functional levels, with an emphasis on mitochondrial maturity. We benchmarked our results with isolated primary adult human cardiomyocytes. Last, we tested whether this method could enable us to more accurately model Friedreich ataxia cardiomyopathy. RESULTS: MM11 treatment increased expression of metabolic pathways, including mitochondrial respiration and fatty acid metabolism, at the transcript and protein levels. Ultrastructural analyses revealed the formation of interfibrillar mitochondria and mitochondrial respiratory supercomplexes, a feature never shown in previous reports. Functionally, MM11-treated iPSC cardiomyocytes exhibited substantially increased oxidative phosphorylation and a metabolic preference for fatty acid utilization in the presence of physiologic substrates, as determined by oxygen consumption assays and 13 C isotope tracing. CONCLUSIONS: MM11 promotes robust metabolic maturation of human iPSC cardiomyocytes, enabling sophisticated mitochondrial architecture and substrate utilization. These metabolically matured cardiomyocytes more faithfully model mitochondria-dependent cardiac pathologies, including ischemia-reperfusion injury and Friedreich ataxia cardiomyopathy, improving the use of iPSC cardiomyocytes for mechanistic studies of human heart disease.

items.title: Cardiovascular Health Promotion for US Veterans: Current State, Gaps, and Strategies: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association
items.abstract: US veterans represent a large and diverse population with distinctive demographic characteristics, comorbidity profiles, and social determinants of health shaped by military service. These factors contribute to a high burden of cardiovascular risk and low attainment of ideal cardiovascular health. At the same time, the Department of Veterans Affairs, which operates the nation’s largest integrated healthcare system, provides a unique infrastructure for delivering population-level cardiovascular disease prevention for veterans. Understanding its successes and ongoing challenges can inform broader strategies across all health systems for promoting health among veterans. This scientific statement applies the American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 framework, expanded to include mental health and substance use, to evaluate veteran cardiovascular health. For each domain, we review guideline recommendations, barriers to achieving optimal health, and major Veterans Affairs programs such as Patient Aligned Care Teams, the MOVE! Weight Management Program for Veterans, Whole Health, telehealth-based interventions, and integrated mental health and substance use disorder services. Across domains, veterans receiving Veterans Affairs care often achieve outcomes that are equal to or better than those of their non–Veterans Affairs counterparts, reflecting the strengths of the system in coordinated, team-based care and research-driven implementation. Despite substantial progress, opportunities remain to improve veteran lifestyle behaviors, metabolic health, lipid and blood pressure control, engagement in mental health and substance use care, and detection and management of sleep disorders. Addressing these challenges at the Veterans Affairs will require continuing to expand care access, enhancing digital data integration, tailoring interventions to high-risk subgroups, and strengthening implementation strategies to improve uptake and engagement across Veterans Affairs services.

items.title: Abstract P1060A: CPR Training Perception and Willingness to Act: A Cross-Sectional Survey of Pre-Medical Students
items.abstract: Introduction/Background: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) is critical step for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survival. Pre-medical students represent an unstudied and high-potential bystander population, yet predictors of post-training CPR willingness remain poorly characterized. Hypothesis: Pre-medical students from a public university in Argentina perceiving CPR training as highly important would demonstrate greater willingness to perform CPR after course completion. Methods: Prospective, cross-sectional study post mandated CPR-course survey of all pre-medical students (full cohort 2026) at Universidad Nacional de La Matanza, Argentina. The educational program comprised a 3-hour, theoretical-practical course led by university instructors in accordance with the 2025 AHA guidelines. Variables included demographics, prior CPR exposure (awareness, prior formal course, real-life CPR performance), perceived training importance (Likert 1-5), post-course CPR willingness (Likert 1-5; high=4-5). Real-life CPR performance was operationally defined as the delivery of chest compressions with or without the use of an automated external defibrillator (AED). Bivariate analyses used chi-square and crude odds ratios (OR, 95%CI). Two multivariable logistic regression models identified independent factors associated to: Model 1: high post-course CPR willingness and model 2: prior real-life CPR performance. Results: 448 students responded (mean age 21.9±5.5 years; 70.8% female). Prior awareness of CPR was high (94.9%); 32.1% had completed a prior formal CPR course; only 6.5% had performed CPR in a real-life emergency. Perceived importance was: 96.2% rated 5/5. High post-course CPR willingness was reported by 67.2%. In bivariate analysis, maximum importance perception was associated with high willingness to render CPR in real life (OR=3.07, 95%CI:1.14-8.23, p=0.020), as was prior formal CPR course (OR=1.82, 95%CI:1.16-2.84, p=0.008). In multivariable analysis (Model 1), maximum importance perception independently predicted high willingness (adjusted OR=2.96, 95%CI:1.07-8.22, p=0.037). For real-life CPR performance (Model 2), prior formal CPR course (adjusted OR=5.24, 95%CI:2.06-13.36, p<0.001) and older age (adjusted OR=2.18 per SD, 95%CI:1.63-2.92, p<0.001) were the sole independent predictors. Gender was not associated with either outcome. Conclusions: Perceiving CPR training as maximally important independently predicted greater willingness to perform CPR post-course. Prior formal CPR training was the strongest predictor of real-life CPR performance. These findings support early, repeated CPR training in medical curricula and emphasize framing instruction within clinical relevance to enhance motivation and real-world application. These cross-sectional associations warrant confirmation in longitudinal studies.

items.title: When Causal Is Not Enough
Contents
Full Issue PDF
Interpreting High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin in Clinical Practice and Emerging Directions
items.abstract: High-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) assays have solved the problem of detecting myocardial injury and, in doing so, created the problem of classifying it. Abnormal troponin concentrations are now known to be common across a wide spectrum of cardiac and systemic disease, and the central challenge of contemporary practice is no longer whether myocardial injury can be detected, but whether it can be correctly classified. Misclassification occurs in both directions and with real consequence: nonischemic myocardial injury is frequently mislabeled as secondary myocardial infarction (MI), contributing to the overdiagnosis of MI, and chronic myocardial injury, which carries a risk of subsequent MI or cardiovascular death approaching that of primary MI, is routinely dismissed once infarction has been excluded. This narrative review argues that accurate classification cannot be delegated to an algorithm and instead requires integrated, context-aware interpretation grounded in 4 domains: 1) the analytical and biological properties of hs-cTnI and hs-cTnT, including assay-specific and sex-specific thresholds, clearance kinetics, and sources of analytical interference and false-positive results; 2) the capabilities and limitations of guideline-endorsed serial testing, including the European Society of Cardiology 0/1h and 0/2h algorithms, point-of-care platforms, and artificial intelligence-based decision support; 3) rigorous application of the Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction, in particular the distinctions between myocardial injury, necrosis, and infarction, and between diagnosis and risk stratification; and 4) recognition of the non-acute coronary syndrome conditions-chronic kidney disease, heart failure, sepsis, tachyarrhythmias, pulmonary embolism, takotsubo syndrome, and others-in which troponin elevation is expected rather than anomalous. We provide explicit bedside guidance for the situations that clinicians find most difficult, including suspected secondary MI, the observe zone, and troponin elevation without a dynamic pattern. Finally, we review emerging understanding of troponin biology, clearance, proteolysis and fragmentation, macrotroponin, antitroponin autoantibodies, and extracellular vesicle-associated troponin, which may eventually allow the assay itself to carry more of the interpretive burden. Until then, that burden rests with the clinician.

items.abstract: Background Patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) at high bleeding risk (HBR) are also at increased risk of ischemic events, making the optimal antiplatelet therapy challenging. Whether HBR identifies patients who may benefit from upfront aspirin omission at the time of primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains unclear. Objectives In this study, we sought to evaluate whether HBR modifies the effect of aspirin omission in STEMI patients undergoing primary PCI. Methods The PREMIUM trial randomized patients with STEMI before primary PCI to low-dose prasugrel monotherapy or dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with aspirin plus prasugrel. In the DAPT group, patients meeting Academic Research Consortium (ARC) for HBR criteria were permitted to discontinue aspirin at 3 months, whereas non-HBR patients were intended to continue DAPT for 12 months. This post hoc analysis assessed the primary outcome of a 12-month composite of all-cause death, stroke, or myocardial infarction and the major secondary outcome of Bleeding Academic Research Consortium type 3 or 5 bleeding according to HBR status. Results Among 2,189 patients, 786 (35.9%) met ARC-HBR criteria. HBR patients had higher rates of the primary outcome (16.2% vs 6.2%; HR: 2.68; 95% CI: 2.05-3.52) and the major secondary outcome (10.9% vs 4.9%; HR: 2.28; 95% CI: 1.65-3.14). The primary outcome occurred with monotherapy vs DAPT in 18.0% vs 14.5% of HBR patients (HR: 1.29; 95% CI: 0.91-1.82) and 7.4% vs 5.0% of non-HBR patients (HR: 1.55; 95% CI: 1.01-2.37; P for interaction = 0.51). The major secondary outcome occurred in 9.2% vs 12.5% of HBR patients (HR: 0.71; 95% CI: 0.46-1.11) and 3.8% vs 6.1% of non-HBR patients (HR: 0.62; 95% CI: 0.38-1.00; P for interaction = 0.67). Conclusions ARC-HBR identified patients with a substantially higher overall risk after primary PCI for STEMI, but did not identify a subgroup with a more favorable treatment effect of upfront aspirin omission. Clinically meaningful treatment-effect modification cannot be excluded, owing to limited precision. These findings do not support using HBR status alone to guide upfront aspirin omission and should be interpreted in the context of the low-dose prasugrel regimen used in Japan. (Prasugrel Monotherapy Following Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention for ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction [PREMIUM; NCT05709626]).

items.abstract: Background Current guidelines recommend echocardiographic surveillance every 1-2 years for patients with moderate aortic stenosis (AS). Ongoing randomized trials are evaluating transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) for patients with moderate AS and at-risk features associated with rapid progression or poor outcomes. The prevalence and prognostic impact of these features in clinical practice are unknown. Objectives To determine the prevalence and prognostic impact of at-risk features in real-world clinical practice among patients with moderate AS. Methods We analyzed deidentified data from 14,859,523 patients at 48 US institutions (egnite Registry; IRB exempt). Patients with moderate or severe AS per echocardiographic assessment (ACC/AHA guidelines) identified on or after January 1 , 2022, were included. At-risk features for moderate AS (PROGRESS trial criteria) included valve-related symptoms, left ventricular ejection fraction <60%, diastolic dysfunction grade ≥2, stroke volume index <35 mL/m , atrial fibrillation, or elevated natriuretic peptide. Outcomes were 2-year mortality, hospitalization with heart failure, aortic valve replacement (AVR), and progression to severe AS (Kaplan-Meier for mortality; Aalen-Johansen with death as a competing event for the others). Results Among 53,994 patients with at least moderate AS, 35,343 (65.5%) were moderate, and 18,651 (34.5%) were severe. Among patients with moderate AS, 27,815 (78.7%) had at least 1 at-risk feature. At 2 years, the cumulative mortality for patients with moderate AS without at-risk features, moderate AS with at-risk features, and severe AS was 9.0% (95% CI, 8.1–9.9), 20.1% (95% CI, 19.5–20.7), and 23.5% (95% CI, 22.7–24.3), and hospitalization with heart failure was 21.9% (95% CI, 20.7–23.2), 44.6% (95% CI, 43.8–45.3), and 54.8% (95% CI, 53.9–55.8), respectively (p value <0.0001 for both). With follow-up censored at AVR, progression to severe AS at 2 years was similar with and without at-risk features (28.2% vs 26.3%). Conclusions In this large real-world cohort, the vast majority of patients with moderate AS had at-risk features and experienced worse clinical outcomes, with 2-fold higher risks of mortality and hospitalization with heart failure than those without at-risk features, despite similar progression to severe AS. These findings support risk-based stratification of moderate AS and investigation of strategies to reduce adverse events in patients with at-risk features.

Single vs Double ProGlide Devices for Access Site Closure after Transfemoral Aortic Valve Replacement
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite advances in transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), access-site vascular complications remain an important source of procedural morbidity. The conventional double-ProGlide strategy may increase the risk of access-site stenosis and other vascular complications, particularly in patients with challenging iliofemoral anatomy. Retrospective studies have suggested that a single-ProGlide strategy may offer an effective alternative, but this strategy has not yet been evaluated in a randomized trial. OBJECTIVES: This trial aimed to determine whether a single-ProGlide strategy could offer a simpler alternative to the conventional double-ProGlide strategy without increasing vascular complications. METHODS: The SINGLE-CLOSURE trial was a prospective, multicenter, open-label, randomized trial conducted at 25 centers in China. Patients aged ≥65 years scheduled for transfemoral TAVR were assigned 1:1 to single-ProGlide or double-ProGlide closure for the main access site. The primary endpoint was the in-hospital composite of Valve Academic Research Consortium (VARC)-3-defined access-site or access-related major and minor vascular complications. RESULTS: A total of 876 patients were randomized. In the modified intention-to-treat population, the primary endpoint occurred in 57 of 436 patients (13.1%) in the single-ProGlide group and 65 of 430 patients (15.1%) in the double-ProGlide group, meeting the prespecified criterion for noninferiority (risk difference: -2.2%; 95%: -7.0% to 2.6%; P = 0.013; noninferiority margin: 3.19%). Access-related major vascular complications occurred in 2 patients (0.5%) in the single-ProGlide group and 6 patients (1.4%) in the double-ProGlide group. Among the secondary endpoints, individual components of the primary endpoint, access-related bleeding, time to hemostasis, and all-cause mortality were similar between groups. Access-site stenosis was numerically less frequent with the single-ProGlide strategy (5.0% vs 7.9%), whereas additional closure devices might be used more often (2.5% vs 0.9%). CONCLUSIONS: A single-ProGlide strategy was noninferior to conventional double-ProGlide closure for the composite of VARC-3-defined access-site or access-related vascular complications after transfemoral TAVR. Primary endpoint events were predominantly minor vascular complications.

items.title: Percutaneous Transcatheter Mitral Valve Replacement for Symptomatic Mitral Regurgitation
items.abstract: Background Transcatheter mitral valve replacement (TMVR) is an approved treatment option for select high-risk patients with symptomatic mitral regurgitation (MR). The main cohort of the ENCIRCLE trial, evaluating fully percutaneous transseptal TMVR with the SAPIEN M3 system, demonstrated 13.9% mortality, significant MR reduction, and improved functional and health status outcomes at 1 year. Objectives We report 2-year outcomes from the main cohort of the ENCIRCLE trial. Methods Eligible symptomatic patients with ≥3+ MR who were not suitable for surgery or transcatheter edge-to-edge repair underwent TMVR with the SAPIEN M3 system. Independent study oversight included an echocardiographic core laboratory and a clinical events committee. Endpoints included the nonhierarchical composite rate of all-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalization (HFH) as well as clinical, echocardiographic, functional, and health status outcomes. Results A total of 299 patients were treated, with 2-year follow-up data available for 202 of 210 eligible patients (96.2%). Mean age was 75.5 ± 9.3 years, 50.8% were men, and the mean Society of Thoracic Surgeons Predicted Risk of Mortality score for mitral valve replacement was 6.6% ± 4.1%. At 2 years, MR reduction was sustained, with MR ≤1+ in 97.0% patients (P Conclusions The 2-year results of the ENCIRCLE trial demonstrated durable near MR elimination with sustained improvements in functional and health status outcomes in surviving patients. These findings support transseptal TMVR as a therapeutic option for carefully selected patients with symptomatic MR. (The ENCIRCLE Trial [ENCIRCLE]; NCT04153292).

items.limitations: Certain limitations merit consideration. First, the training label was an expert-reader assignment of a prominent epicardial fat depot extracted from routine clinical reports, which is more specific than sensitive. Report-negative studies were labeled negative, and external cohorts lacked report labels (MIMIC-IV echocardiography reports are not available); we therefore used CT-derived EAT as the quantitative reference standard. Clinical reports flag overt accumulation rather than applying a standardized echocardiographic threshold for epicardial adiposity. The continuous biomarker score nevertheless tracks a graded spectrum of severity, as supported by its correlation with CT-quantified EAT and its graded associations with cardiometabolic biomarkers and newly documented disease.

Right Heart Dysfunction in Valvular Heart Disease
items.abstract: Right ventricular (RV) dysfunction is an important determinant of clinical outcomes across a wide range of cardiovascular pathologies. As the prevalence of valvular heart disease (VHD) increases with the aging population, the intersection between RV function and VHD will become all the more relevant for proper risk assessment, treatment selection, and prognostication. Even though RV dysfunction may not always be attributed to VHD, we aim to give clinicians, researchers, and regulators a deep understanding of how patients with VHD should be evaluated for RV dysfunction and treated when RV dysfunction coexists with VHD. We begin with a discussion of the epidemiology and diagnostic evaluation of RV dysfunction in patients with a variety of VHD subgroups, including right-side (ie, associated with the tricuspid valve) and left-side (ie, associated with the mitral and aortic valves) VHD. Attention is also given in that section to contemporary methods and evolving techniques for identifying and phenotyping different forms of RV dysfunction in patients with VHD. No single imaging test practically or comprehensively captures all degrees and forms of RV dysfunction in patients with VHD; therefore, the discussion emphasizes integrating evidence from different imaging modalities and hemodynamic assessments. The second component of the review discusses how RV dysfunction affects therapeutic options, including medical, transcatheter, and surgical therapies for VHD. The focus of the discussion is on the interplay between RV dysfunction in patients with right-side VHD, namely tricuspid regurgitation (TR). Unlike left-side VHD, where RV dysfunction is a marker of overall disease severity but does not necessarily indicate futility or nonresponse to therapy, right-side VHD and TR-associated RV dysfunction identifies a subset of patients where intervention may precipitate even worse RV function. The nuances of these interactions between ventricular and valvular function are the emphasis of this section, and we aim to provide a framework for understanding RV function in the context of these different forms of VHD. Finally, the review concludes with an eye to the future, discussing the ways in which RV dysfunction can be identified and managed with the use of novel techniques. This discussion is increasingly relevant as RV dysfunction and VHD frequently coexist, and accurate identification is critical to matching the right treatment for the right patient.
