items.abstract: Background Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is increasingly used as an alternative to oral anticoagulation for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. Its comparative effectiveness and safety in patients at a high risk of both stroke and bleeding remain uncertain. Objectives We evaluated the efficacy and safety of LAAC vs contemporary medical therapy in a high-risk population using individual participant data from randomized trials. Methods Bibliographic databases and trial registries through August 5, 2026, were searched for randomized trials comparing percutaneous LAAC with contemporary medical therapy in populations with a trial-level mean CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score ≥4. A 1-stage common-effect analysis used Cox models stratified by trial and adjusted for age, sex, CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score, and HAS-BLED score. Both primary outcomes were time to first stroke, systemic embolism, or cardiovascular/unknown death (efficacy) and time to first major bleeding (safety). A flexible time-varying Cox model was used for major bleeding. The protocol was submitted to PROSPERO (CRD420261335972). Results CLOSURE-AF (Left Atrial Appendage CLOSURE in Patients With Atrial Fibrillation Compared to Medical Therapy) and PRAGUE-17 (Left Atrial Appendage Closure vs. Novel Anticoagulation Agents in Atrial Fibrillation) contributed 1,290 participants (647 assigned to LAAC and 643 to control). Median age was 77.3 years (Q1-Q3: 71.4-81.9 years), and 809 participants (62.7%) were men. The primary efficacy outcome occurred in 142 LAAC participants (21.9%) and 133 control subjects (20.7%) (adjusted HR: 0.98; 95% CI: 0.77-1.24; P = 0.842). Major bleeding occurred in 86 LAAC participants (13.3%) and 80 control subjects (12.4%) (adjusted HR: 1.03; 95% CI: 0.75-1.39; P = 0.874). The treatment effect on major bleeding varied over time (P for treatment-by-time interaction Conclusions In high-risk patients with atrial fibrillation, no statistically significant difference was detected between LAAC and contemporary medical therapy for the primary efficacy outcome or major bleeding. The major bleeding hazard varied over time, with higher early and lower later conditional hazard estimates; however, a cumulative bleeding benefit was not demonstrated by 3 years. Long-term randomized data are needed to improve the precision of later treatment-effect estimates.

items.title: Left Atrial Appendage Closure or Anticoagulation for Atrial Fibrillation
items.abstract: Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has emerged as an alternative to long-term anticoagulation for preventing stroke or systemic embolism in selected patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) based on several randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that collectively enrolled >7,000 participants. In this JACC Evidence Review, we interpret the major RCTs as distinct experiments, clarify what each can and cannot establish, and offer a phenotype-based framework for interpreting the evidence. The most recent RCTs, OPTION, CLOSURE-AF, and CHAMPION-AF, have prompted efforts to pool the evidence into a single summary estimate. However, these trials are not one coherent evidence base; they are distinct clinical experiments that asked different questions. They differ in patient phenotype, comparator, device generation, postprocedure antithrombotic regimen, endpoint construction, and follow-up duration. Study-level meta-analysis of published reports remains methodologically valid for estimating the broad direction of effect of a device class, but when the component trials differ materially in patient phenotype, comparator, and outcome construction, the pooled estimate does not map to a common patient group or treatment decision. Patient eligibility as well as thromboembolic and bleeding risk varied markedly across trials. In addition, device technology has progressed, and comparators have evolved from warfarin to direct oral anticoagulants. Heterogeneity and insufficient details also exist about the antithrombotic therapy regimen in LAAC arms and adjunct antiplatelet therapy in control arms. Methodological issues further complicate interpretation, including the use of bleeding events (ie, the putative ancillary benefit of LAAC compared with anticoagulation) within composite endpoints tested for noninferiority, varying noninferiority margins, analytical approaches that may undermine the interpretation of noninferiority, and exclusion of periprocedural bleeding from primary safety endpoints in some trials. Finally, the standard of care for anticoagulation in AF has evolved, obviating concomitant aspirin use in stable individuals on therapeutic anticoagulation, thereby reducing bleeding risk compared with that of the control arm of LAAC RCTs. For most anticoagulation-eligible patients, anticoagulation remains the preferred first-line strategy. LAAC is a reasonable option when long-term anticoagulation is unsafe or unsustainable provided that procedural risk, adjunct antithrombotic feasibility, surveillance needs, and competing mortality are carefully considered. RCT evidence in this latter population is limited, and RCTs in other populations have features that limit their support for LAAC as an alternative to anticoagulation. Because LAAC and anticoagulation offer different types of risk, aligning the most applicable evidence with patient values through shared decision-making is central to care.

items.title: When and How to Consider Left Atrial Appendage Closure as a Management Option for Patients With Atrial Fibrillation
Antithrombotic Therapy Management After Left Atrial Appendage Closure
items.abstract: Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure is increasingly used for stroke prevention in patients with atrial fibrillation, particularly when long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC) is unsuitable. Although postprocedural antithrombotic therapy is necessary to prevent device-related thrombosis (DRT), it may increase bleeding and attenuate the benefit of avoiding long-term OAC. Uncertainty over the optimal antithrombotic strategy persists, with available randomized trials being small and heterogeneous. Direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) monotherapy and dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) are 2 common early strategies. In ANDES, DRT was numerically less frequent with DOAC than with DAPT (1.5% vs 4.1%). In ADALA, low-dose apixaban was associated with greater net benefit than DAPT (HR: 0.19; P = 0.02), although enrollment was prematurely stopped. A meta-analysis of randomized trials found significantly lower DRT with DOAC than with DAPT (risk ratio: 0.17). Current guidelines endorse regimens largely based on device-specific trial protocols or low-certainty evidence. During the initial postimplantation period, antithrombotic therapy should primarily aim to support device healing and prevent DRT, with treatment intensity tailored according to risk profile, concomitant indications, patient preferences, and the feasibility of imaging follow-up. Reassessment at 45 to 90 days should guide de-escalation once adequate device healing has been confirmed, with no fixed treatment stop date. In the absence of device-related complications, long-term OAC or DAPT should be continued only for concomitant indications, whereas continuation of single antiplatelet therapy or complete withdrawal of antithrombotic therapy should be individualized according to thrombotic and bleeding risk. Finally, definite or probable DRT generally warrants OAC, when feasible; in contrast, treatment decisions should not be based solely on the presence or size of a peridevice leak. This review critically appraises the available evidence and guideline recommendations and discusses how treatment intensity and duration may be tailored over time according to evolving thrombotic and bleeding risks.

items.abstract: Background Women sex is an established, nonmodifiable risk factor for adverse outcomes in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has been proposed as an alternative to oral anticoagulation (OAC) for stroke prevention in patients with AF; however, there are limited data on sex-based outcomes of LAAC following catheter ablation. Objectives This study sought to compare outcomes of LAAC vs OAC after AF ablation in men and women. Methods Patients with AF and CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc ≥2 in men and ≥3 in women were randomized 1:1 to either ablation + LAAC or ablation + OAC. The primary safety endpoint was nonprocedural major or clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding at 36 months. The primary efficacy endpoint was a composite of all-cause death, stroke, or systemic embolism at 36 months. Results The study included 1,053 men and 546 women. LAAC and OAC demonstrated comparable primary efficacy events in men (HR: 0.96; 95% CI: 0.56-1.65; P = 0.88) and women (HR: 0.81; 95% CI: 0.41-1.62; P = 0.55), with no treatment-by-sex interaction (P interaction = 0.71). Procedural complication rates were similar at 2.3% in men and 3.7% in women with only 1 pericardial effusion in each group, not related to the index LAAC procedure. At 36 months, the primary safety endpoint was significantly lower in the device group among men (HR: 0.34; 95% CI: 0.23-0.50; P Conclusions In this prespecified analysis of the OPTION (Comparison of Anticoagulation With Left Atrial Appendage Closure After AF Ablation [OPTION]) trial, stroke, systemic embolism, and mortality outcomes were not significantly different between LAAC and OAC following AF ablation in either men or women. Compared with OAC, LAAC demonstrated a greater magnitude of major and clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding reduction in men as compared with women. (Comparison of Anticoagulation With Left Atrial Appendage Closure After AF Ablation [OPTION]; NCT03795298).

Left Atrial Appendage Closure in Patients Considered Unsuitable for Oral Anticoagulation
items.abstract: Background Oral anticoagulation (OAC) use in atrial fibrillation is suboptimal due to real or perceived bleeding risks. Left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is an alternative to OAC, but pivotal trials used OAC comparators. Objectives The study sought to assess the long-term safety and effectiveness of LAAC in patients deemed unsuitable for OAC. Methods The ASAP-TOO trial was a multinational randomized trial of patients with atrial fibrillation, CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc (congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75 years, diabetes mellitus, prior stroke or transient ischemic attack or thromboembolism, vascular disease, age 65-74 years, sex category) score ≥2, and OAC unsuitability; target enrollment was 888 patients. Patients were assigned 2:1 to LAAC with a Watchman device or control treatment-single antiplatelet therapy or no therapy. Device patients received dual antiplatelet therapy for 3 months and aspirin through 12 months. The primary effectiveness endpoint was ischemic stroke or systemic embolism; the primary safety endpoint was death, ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, or 7-day device/procedure-related events requiring major intervention. Results Enrollment stopped early because of slow accrual, accentuated by the COVID-19 pandemic: only 481 patients were randomized (320 LAAC, 161 control treatment) and withdrawal was significant (7.8% LAAC, 24.2% control treatment), with disparate follow-up durations (median 876 days and 440.1 total patient-years of follow-up for control patients; median 1,768 days and 1,154.6 total patient-years of follow-up for LAAC patients), reducing statistical power. Patients were 75 ± 8 years of age, the CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score was 4.6 ± 1.7, and 34% had prior intracranial/subdural hemorrhage. Implantation success was 97.8%. Only 31 of the 101 planned primary effectiveness events occurred, fewer than the 34 events required to trigger the first planned interim analysis. The primary safety endpoint occurred in 1.0% of implant-attempted patients, meeting the prespecified performance goal (P Conclusions In this prematurely terminated and underpowered trial, LAAC implantation was successful, with acceptable safety. Long-term estimates with LAAC were numerically favorable for thromboembolism but imprecise, while early bleeding was increased with the mandated antiplatelet regimen. These findings should be interpreted as exploratory and integrated with contemporary evidence and shared decision making. (Assessment of the WATCHMAN Device in Patients Unsuitable for Oral Anticoagulation [ASAP-TOO]; NCT02928497).

items.abstract: Background Whether age affects the comparative treatment effect of immediate complete revascularization (CR) vs staged CR during the index admission in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction and multivessel disease remains unknown. Objectives This study aimed to assess how age influences clinical outcomes in patients with with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction and multivessel disease randomized to immediate or in-hospital staged CR. Methods This is a secondary analysis of the OPTION-STEMI (Optimal Timing of Fractional Flow Reserve-Guided Complete Revascularization for Non-Infarct-Related Artery in ST-Segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction with Multivessel Disease) trial, which included 994 patients randomized to immediate or in-hospital staged CR. The primary endpoint at 1 year, defined as a composite of all-cause death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or any unplanned revascularization, was analyzed according to age and CR strategy. Results A significant interaction was found between age, as a continuous variable, and CR strategy for the primary endpoint (interaction P = 0.015). The HR for the primary endpoint was initially higher in the staged CR arm until approximately 67 years, after which it increased steadily in the immediate CR arm. In the binary analysis, a significantly higher incidence of the primary endpoint was observed in the immediate CR arm compared with the staged CR arm in patients ≥70 years (45 of 202 [22.3%] vs 29 of 210 [13.8%]; HR: 1.68; 95% CI: 1.06-2.69; log-rank P = 0.029), but not in patients Conclusions This post hoc analysis of the OPTION-STEMI trial demonstrates that older patients experience significantly worse clinical outcomes with immediate CR than with in-hospital staged CR. These findings suggest that age modifies the treatment effect of the CR strategy and warrant confirmation in adequately powered trials (Timing of FFR-guided PCI for Non-IRA in STEMI and MVD [OPTION-STEMI]; NCT04626882).

items.title: Complete, But Not All at Once
Snare-Guided Repositioning of a Vascular Plug Device for Device-Related Hemolytic Anemia
Impact of Recurrent Mitral Regurgitation Following Mitral Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair on Long-Term Outcomes
items.abstract: Background Residual mitral regurgitation (MR) after mitral transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER) is a major determinant of outcome. However, the prognostic impact of recurrent mitral regurgitation (recMR) after initially successful M-TEER remains unclear. Objectives This study aimed to evaluate the association between recMR after successful M-TEER and long-term mortality across degenerative mitral regurgitation (DMR) and functional mitral regurgitation (FMR). Methods This retrospective cohort included 461 consecutive patients with MR undergoing successful M-TEER (residual mitral regurgitation ≤2+ at discharge) between 2008 and 2021. recMR was defined as ≥1-grade increase in mitral regurgitation severity at follow-up compared with discharge. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality. Results Among 461 patients with MR undergoing M_TEER (mean age 75.0 ± 9.1 years; 60.7% male [280 of 461]; 29.3% [135 of 461] had DMR), recMR occurred in 31.7% (146 of 461) (FMR in 31.9% [104 of 326]; DMR in 31.1% [42 of 135]). The median follow-up time was 3.44 years (Q1-Q3: 1.51-3.99 years). In a 12-month landmark analysis, absence of recMR was associated with improved survival (log-rank, P = 0.0088). At 4 years, all-cause mortality was 44.8% (95% CI: 38.7%-50.3%) in patients without recMR and 56.3% (95% CI: 47.2%-63.9%) in those with recMR. In multivariable Cox regression, recMR independently predicted higher mortality (HR: 1.43; 95% CI: 1.06-1.93; P = 0.019). The survival difference was significant in patients with DMR (log-rank, P = 0.014) but not with FMR (P = 0.11). Conclusions recMR is common and independently associated with increased mortality after M-TEER, with a more pronounced effect in patients with DMR. Identification of patients at risk may inform closer surveillance and timely reintervention.

items.title: Dynamic Common Iliac Vein Compression by the Adjacent Intestine Revealed by Intravascular Ultrasound
Morphology-Dependent Dose-Response of Intravascular Lithotripsy on Coronary Calcium Fracture
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intravascular lithotripsy (IVL) uses ultrasonic acoustic pressure waves to modify calcification to enable optimal balloon and stent expansion in calcified lesions. However, the dose-response relationship for creating fractures within calcified lesions of different calcium morphologies is unknown. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to evaluate the dose-dependent effects of IVL on calcium fracture overall and in the setting of calcification arc <180° vs ≥180°. METHODS: Micro-computed tomography images were acquired before and after 10, 20, 40, 60, 80, and 120 pulses of IVL treatment (Shockwave Medical) in an ex vivo study of 5 cadaveric human hearts (15 coronary lesions). A total of 30 cross-sections of micro-computed tomography (2 sections per lesion) were analyzed for this study. RESULTS: Cumulative fracture occurrence increased progressively with the number of IVL pulses delivered, with fractures observed in 33% of sections after 10 pulses, 50% after 40 pulses, and 60% after 120 pulses. Calcification arc ≥180° exhibited a higher fracture occurrence compared with arc <180° (P = 0.028). After adjustment for pulse number, calcification arc ≥180° was associated with significantly higher fracture counts compared with arc <180° (rate ratio = 6.1, P = 0.003). CONCLUSIONS: Fracture occurrence following IVL increased with cumulative pulse delivery and differed significantly according to calcification concentricity. Calcification arc ≥180° demonstrated a higher and earlier likelihood of fracture occurrence than arc <180°, independent of pulse number. These findings establish a clear dose-dependent relationship between IVL pulse delivery and fracture formation and highlight calcification concentricity as a key determinant of fracture response.

items.title: Pulmonary Index of Microcirculatory Resistance
Two-Year Outcomes of the Prospective THRILLER Registry on Popliteal and Infrapopliteal Endovascular Interventions for CLTI
items.abstract: Background Over 70% of patients with chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) present with below-the-knee disease, and there is a growing trend towards endovascular revascularization. Objectives The Dutch Chronic Lower Limb-Threatening Ischemia Registry (THRILLER) aimed to provide real-world data on outcomes after popliteal and infrapopliteal endovascular revascularization to guide revascularization strategies. Methods This prospective multicenter registry included consecutive CLTI patients undergoing popliteal or infrapopliteal endovascular revascularization in seven Dutch hospitals. Primary outcomes were limb salvage and amputation-free survival (AFS) at 24 months, estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Results Between February 2021 and December 2023, a total of 1,119 interventions in 1,060 limbs (938 patients) were included, treating 551 popliteal, 1,352 tibial, and 239 pedal lesions. The median follow-up was 43.6 months (Q1-Q3: 35.5-52.7 months). Overall, 78.4% (831/1,060) of the limbs were Rutherford 5 and 8.1% (86/1,060) were Rutherford 6; 41.3% (382/926) were WIfI (Wound, Ischemia, and foot Infection) stage 4. Technical success was achieved in 92.3% (1,033/1,119). Limb salvage and AFS decreased significantly after technical failure and with increasing WIfI stage and Rutherford category. Compared to Rutherford 5, Rutherford 6 limbs had significantly worse limb salvage (HR: 3.07; 95% CI: 1.89-4.99; P Conclusions Endovascular revascularization for popliteal and infrapopliteal disease in patients with CLTI is safe and effective in preventing limb loss and mortality at 2 years, although patients with Rutherford 6 limbs face significantly worse outcomes, particularly in the first 3 months.

items.title: Calcium Fracture Detection by Optical Coherence Tomography Versus Intravascular Ultrasound Following Intravascular Lithotripsy
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Calcium fracture is a metric used to assess lesion preparation success. We have shown previously that optical coherence tomography (OCT) misses approximately half of these fractures. Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) is the most commonly used intravascular imaging modality. The sensitivity of IVUS for detecting calcium fractures after intravascular lithotripsy (IVL) is unknown. OBJECTIVES: This study sought to assess the frequency and characteristics of calcium fracture observed on IVUS in comparison to OCT and gold standard micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) using heavily calcified coronary artery cadaveric vessels. METHODS: In an ex vivo study of 5 cadaveric hearts (15 coronary lesions), OCT, IVUS, and micro-CT were obtained before and after IVL coronary artery treatment. Fracture detection rates and appearance patterns were compared across modalities. Receiver operating characteristic analyses evaluated OCT-measured fracture width thresholds for IVUS detectability. RESULTS: Compared with micro-CT, OCT and IVUS significantly underestimated fracture occurrence, but OCT demonstrated higher detection sensitivity than IVUS (P < 0.05 by McNemar's test). Narrow linear nondisplaced fractures identified on OCT were frequently undetectable on IVUS or appeared as subtle hyperechoic shadows. Fracture width was strongly associated with IVUS detectability; fracture width >115 μm on OCT were identified by IVUS with excellent diagnostic performance (area under the curve: 0.99 [95% CI: 0.98-1.00], sensitivity 100%, specificity 92%). CONCLUSIONS: OCT and IVUS underestimate the occurrence of IVL-induced calcium fractures compared with micro-CT, with IVUS demonstrating lower sensitivity than OCT. IVUS detectability is strongly dependent on fracture width. Absence of visible fracture on either OCT or IVUS does not exclude calcium modification.

items.title: Beyond Procedural Success
Periprocedural Pulmonary Hypertension and Outcomes After Mitral Valve Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair
items.abstract: Background Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is common in patients undergoing mitral valve transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (M-TEER), but the prognostic significance of periprocedural PH changes remains uncertain. Objectives This study sought to evaluate the association between periprocedural PH patterns and clinical outcomes after M-TEER and to identify predictors of residual and new-onset PH. Methods The OCEAN-Mitral registry prospectively enrolled 3,764 patients with severe mitral regurgitation treated with M-TEER. Among 3,484 patients with paired echocardiographic tricuspid regurgitation pressure gradient (TRPG) data, PH was defined as TRPG >31 mm Hg. Patients were classified as having no PH, normalized PH, new-onset PH, or residual PH according to pre- and postprocedural PH status. The primary endpoint was 2-year cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of residual and new-onset PH. Results No PH was observed in 1,432 patients (41.1%), normalized PH in 763 (21.9%), new-onset PH in 298 (8.6%), and residual PH in 991 (28.4%). The 2-year incidence of the primary endpoint differed significantly across groups (17.6%, 18.1%, 27.2%, and 27.6%, respectively; P 50 mm Hg, and tricuspid annular dilation predicted residual PH, whereas residual mitral regurgitation and postprocedural transmitral gradients >5 mm Hg predicted new-onset PH. Conclusions Periprocedural PH dynamics provide robust risk stratification after M-TEER, identifying low-risk patients with PH normalization and high-risk subsets with residual or new-onset PH, requiring closer surveillance and procedural optimization. Registration Treatment and Prognosis of Heart Valve Registry; UMIN-ID: UMIN000023653.

items.title: Safety and Effectiveness of a Novel Laser-Based Intravascular Lithotripsy System for Coronary Calcium
items.abstract: ObjectivesThis study evaluated the safety and effectiveness of a novel laser- and optic-based quad-emitter IVL system in severely calcified de novo coronary lesions. MethodsFRACTURE was a prospective, multicenter, single-arm trial. The primary safety endpoint was 30-day freedom from major adverse cardiac events (MACE; composite of cardiac death, myocardial infarction, or target vessel revascularization). The primary effectiveness endpoint was procedural success (successful stent delivery with a final residual stenosis <50% and freedom from in-hospital MACE). Both endpoints were evaluated against prespecified performance goals. An optical coherence tomography (OCT) substudy was performed. ResultsA total of 420 patients (mean age: 71.2 ± 9.01 years; 74.0% male) were enrolled. Median calcified length was 34.4 mm (Q1-Q3: 21.3-52.5 mm). Among 106 patients with OCT, at the site of maximum calcification, the calcium arc was 271.89° ± 77.35° and the median thickness was 0.88 mm (Q1-Q3: 0.72-1.11 mm). OCT confirmed calcium fracture in 67% of lesions; the median minimal stent area was 6.51 mm2 (Q1-Q3: 4.85-7.78 mm2), and stent expansion was 94.2% ± 19.4% at the site of maximum calcification. The primary safety endpoint of 30-day freedom from MACE was 93.3% (373/400; with lower bound of 95% CI of 90.8%, exceeding the 86.2% performance goal [P < 0.0001]). The primary effectiveness endpoint of procedural success was 93.7% (374/399; with lower bound of 95% CI of 91.3%, exceeding the 85.8% performance goal [P < 0.0001]). ConclusionsThe quad-emitter IVL system is a safe and effective option to modify severe calcified coronary lesions and facilitate stent implantation. Registration: (Modification of Coronary Calcium With Laser Based Intravascular Lithotripsy for Coronary Artery Disease [FRACTURE]; NCT06181240)

Paradoxical 1-Year Improvement in Right Ventricular Function After Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Replacement
Sirolimus- Versus Everolimus-Eluting Stents With Contemporary PCI in Three-Vessel Disease: The Multivessel TALENT Randomized Noninferiority Trial
items.abstract: Background Contemporary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has improved outcomes in three-vessel disease (3VD). However, the Supraflex Cruz sirolimus-eluting stent (SES) has not been compared with the SYNERGY everolimus-eluting stent (EES) in this setting. Objectives We compared the performance of the Supraflex Cruz SES and the SYNERGY EES in patients with de novo 3VD undergoing contemporary PCI. Methods We randomized 1,548 patients to the Supraflex Cruz SES (n=774) or the SYNERGY EES (n=774). Patients were selected after Heart Team discussion incorporating the SYNTAX Score II. Contemporary PCI included angiography-derived physiology, intravascular imaging optimization, CTO expertise, and short DAPT followed by prasugrel monotherapy. The primary endpoint was the 1-year patient-oriented composite endpoint (POCE: all-cause death, any stroke, any myocardial infarction, or any revascularization), estimated by Kaplan–Meier in the intention-to-treat population. The non-inferiority margin was 4.28%. Results Median follow-up was 367 days (IQR, 362–372). At 1 year, POCE was 15.23% (95% CI, 12.87–17.96) with Supraflex Cruz SES and 14.51% (95% CI, 12.20–17.21) with SYNERGY EES. The risk difference was 0.72 percentage points; the one-sided 95% upper confidence bound was 3.71%, below the margin (P non-inferiority=0.025). Myocardial infarction occurred in 10.07% (95% CI, 8.14–12.43) versus 8.14% (95% CI, 6.41–10.33), revascularization in 6.40% (95% CI, 4.86–8.40) versus 6.81% (95% CI, 5.22–8.87), and stent thrombosis in 1.31% (95% CI, 0.71–2.43) versus 1.08% (95% CI, 0.54–2.14). Conclusions In patients with 3VD undergoing contemporary PCI, the Supraflex Cruz SES was noninferior to the SYNERGY EES for 1-year POCE. Clinical Trial Registration NCT04390672

items.title: Fully Retrievable Self-Expanding Short-Frame Valve for Aortic Regurgitation
Prognostic Impact of Discharge Transprosthetic Tricuspid Gradient After Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Replacement
items.abstract: Background Although transprosthetic gradients are established prognostic markers after left-sided valve interventions, the prognostic significance of discharge tricuspid gradient (dTVG) after transcatheter tricuspid valve replacement (TTVR) remains unclear. Objectives This study sought to evaluate the association between dTVG and clinical outcomes after TTVR and identify high dTVG determinants. Methods TRIPLACE (Global Multicenter Registry on Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Replacement) is an international, multicenter TTVR registry. A discharge landmark analysis was performed, excluding patients with in-hospital mortality, lack of TTVR technical success, missing dTVG, or unavailable follow-up at any time point. Endpoints included all-cause mortality and the composite of all-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalization. The optimal dTVG cutoff was identified through quartile-based survival analysis and confirmed by log-rank maximization. Multivariable Cox models were developed using cross-validated candidate variable selection. Results Among 526 patients, 474 were included. Median follow-up was 208.5 days (Q1-Q3: 54-474 days). A data-driven dTVG cutoff of 3.5 mm Hg identified 122 of 474 patients (25.7%) with high dTVG. dTVG ≥3.5 mm Hg was associated with higher 1- and 3-year mortality (HR: 2.07; 95% CI: 1.14-3.75; P = 0.017 and HR: 2.07; 95% CI: 1.24-3.48; P = 0.006, respectively) and composite endpoint events (HR: 1.99; 95% CI: 1.31-3.03; P = 0.001 and HR: 1.96; 95% CI: 1.33-2.88; P 2 increase; 95% CI: 0.71-0.88). Conclusions Elevated dTVG after TTVR independently identifies patients at increased risk of adverse outcomes. A 3.5 mm Hg threshold may support postprocedural risk stratification, whereas inner valve diameter represents a potentially modifiable determinant of elevated dTVG. (TRIPLACE [Global Multicenter Registry on Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Replacement]; NCT06033274).

items.title: One Lesion, Two Perspectives
Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve-in-Valve and Valve-in-Ring Implantation: the TRIVIR registry
items.abstract: Background Transcatheter tricuspid valve-in-valve (TViV) and valve-in-ring (TViR) procedures are increasingly used; however, data on clinical outcomes, valve performance, and symptomatic improvement remain limited. Objectives To evaluate a real-world multicenter cohort undergoing transcatheter TViV and TViR procedures. Methods We conducted an international multicenter registry including patients undergoing TViV/TViR procedures. The TRIVIR Registry evaluated all-cause mortality and a composite endpoint (CE), defined as all-cause mortality, heart failure (HF) hospitalization, and tricuspid bioprosthesis degeneration during follow-up. Results Between 2012 and 2025, 75 patients underwent TViV (n=62) or TViR (n=13) across 16 centers using Sapien (88%) or Myval (12%) valves. Median follow up was 1.86 years (IQR 0.10-2.59). Mean age was 62±13 years, and 69% were women. NYHA class III–IV decreased from 72% at baseline to 13% at 1-3 months and remained low during follow-up. No 30-day deaths occurred, while periprocedural complications occurred in 24% of procedures, mostly minor (17.3%). At 3 years, the Kaplan–Meier estimates of all-cause mortality and CE were 35.6% and 42.9%, and the cumulative incidences of HF hospitalization and tricuspid bioprosthesis degeneration were 16.6% and 11.4%, respectively. Patients who died had markers of advanced disease, including higher NT-proBNP levels, greater diuretic requirements, more frequent pacing/CRT implantation, and higher procedural complication rates. Conclusions TViV/TViR represents a viable treatment strategy and provided sustained symptomatic improvement in high-risk patients. Patients who died exhibited a more advanced clinical profile, highlighting the importance of appropriate patient selection, early referral, and treatment in experienced centers.

items.title: Renal Outcomes With Staged Versus Concomitant PCI and TAVR
Extrinsic Left Main Coronary Compression Caused by Delayed Periaortic Hematoma After Aortic Valve Replacement
Targeted Transcatheter Mitral Edge-to-Edge Repair for Dynamic Systolic Anterior Motion After Mitral Valve Repair
Thirty-Day Outcomes of a Dedicated Transcatheter Occlusion Device for Paravalvular Leak Closure: The PARADIGM Study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Paravalvular leak (PVL) is a complication of surgical valve replacement and is associated with poor prognosis. Percutaneous device closure offers a less invasive alternative to repeat surgery. OBJECTIVE Evaluate the Amplatzer Valvular Plug III (APVL3) for PVL closure after surgical implant of a mechanical or bioprosthetic valve. METHODS PARADIGM is a prospective, multicenter, single-arm study assessing transcatheter PVL closure. The primary endpoint was a composite of safety and effectiveness measures evaluating the implant success, PVL reduction ≥2 grades on exit from the procedure, procedural mortality, and device-related reinterventions through 30 days. Descriptive safety and performance endpoints were evaluated at 30 days. RESULTS A total of 200 patients were enrolled across 24 sites in the United States, Europe, and Canada. Average age was 67.7+/-11.5 years, 58.5% were male, and 70.0% had a mechanical valve. Median(IQR) logistic EuroSCORE was 5.2(3.2,10.3), median(IQR) STS PROM was 2.9%(1.4,5.4), and 53.1%(104/196) were NYHA class III/IV. Heart failure was the primary indication for PVL closure (89.5%), and 65.0% were treated for mitral PVL. Successful implantation was achieved in 96.0%(192/200), with no procedural mortality. The primary endpoint was met in 94.0%(188/200), exceeding the performance goal(P<0.0001). The 30-day procedural success was 77.3%(140/181). At 30 days, mortality was 2.0%(4/200,95%CI:0.5-5.0), hemolytic anemia occurred in 3.5%(7/200,95% CI:1.42%,7.08%), 95.7%(156/163) had mild or less PVL, 82.7%(143/173) were NYHA class I/II, and KCCQ-OS improved by 15.7(12.6,18.8) points. CONCLUSION PARADIGM met its primary endpoint, with favorable short-term outcomes. The results support this transcatheter device as a promising therapeutic option for PVL closure. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04489823

items.title: Posterior Leaflet Restoration for Secondary Mitral Regurgitation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Secondary mitral regurgitation (MR) contributes to morbidity and mortality in patients with symptomatic valve disease. Although transcatheter edge-to-edge repair is beneficial, many patients remain suboptimal candidates. Posterior leaflet restoration (PLR) provides a prosthetic coaptation surface via an adaptive coaptation element that inflates during systole and deflates during diastole to facilitate leaflet coaptation. OBJECTIVES: This study aims to evaluate the safety and feasibility of PLR using the MRace implant (Polares Medical, Inc). METHODS: Early Feasibility Experience of Posterior Leaflet Restoration to Reduce Mitral Regurgitation Using the MRace Implant in Georgia and Brazil (EXPLORE MR) enrolled 78 symptomatic patients with severe secondary MR (≥3+), stratified post hoc by left ventricular end-diastolic volume: nonseverely enlarged left ventricle (NSELV) (N = 46) and severely enlarged left ventricle (SELV) (N = 32). The primary endpoint was 30-day mortality; secondary endpoints were MR reduction and functional outcomes. RESULTS: The implant was successfully deployed in 96.2% of patients. All-cause mortality at 30 days was 6.4%. MR ≤2+ was achieved in 93.8% of patients at 30 days and was sustained in 90.6% at 1 year. Patients with NSELV showed better results in MR ≤1+ at every time point (94.4% at 30 days, 89.5% at 1 year) compared with the SELV group (79.3% and 69.2%, respectively). The NSELV subgroup demonstrated better functional recovery, with NYHA functional class I or II rising from 8.7% to 84.2%, vs a more attenuated response in the SELV group (15.6%-76.9%). The 6-minute walk test improved in the paired NSELV cohort (Δ +93.9 m), but not in paired patients with SELV (Δ -7.8 m). Kaplan-Meier 1-year all-cause mortality was 29.5% overall and was better in patients with NSELV (19.4%) than in SELV (41.7%). CONCLUSIONS: PLR with the MRace implant achieves substantial MR reduction and meaningful functional improvement, most pronounced in patients without severely enlarged left ventricles. (XPLORE MRace [BR]: Early Feasibility Experience of Posterior Leaflet Restoration to Reduce Mitral Regurgitation Using the MRace Implant [EXPLORE MRace]; NCT06113354).

items.title: TECTONIC CAD
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Severe coronary calcification complicates percutaneous coronary intervention by limiting lesion compliance and impairing stent expansion. OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the safety and effectiveness of the SonicForce Coronary Intravascular Lithotripsy System (Abbott Vascular) in severely calcified de novo coronary lesions. METHODS: TECTONIC CAD intravascular lithotripsy investigational device exemption (NCT06885177) was a prospective, multicenter, single-arm study of 335 patients at 40 U.S. CENTERS: The primary safety endpoint was 30-day target lesion failure, defined as cardiac death, target-vessel myocardial infarction, or clinically driven target lesion revascularization. The primary effectiveness endpoint was procedural success. Each endpoint was tested against a prespecified performance goal. A prespecified optical coherence tomography (OCT) substudy evaluated calcium modification and stent expansion. RESULTS: , with stent expansion of 95.9% ± 18.6%. Calcium fracture was identified in 62.5% (50 of 80) of lesions after intravascular lithotripsy and 66.3% (53 of 80) after stenting. CONCLUSIONS: TECTONIC CAD met both prespecified coprimary safety and effectiveness endpoints, demonstrating low 30-day target lesion failure and high procedural success. OCT demonstrated calcium fracture and favorable stent expansion at maximum contiguous calcium.

items.title: Rotational Atherectomy Plus Intravascular Lithotripsy Versus Intravascular Lithotripsy Alone for Coronary Calcified Nodules
items.abstract: Background Optimal lesion preparation for coronary calcified nodules (CNs) and intravascular lithotripsy (IVL) pulse delivery for severe calcification remain uncertain. Objectives This study sought to evaluate phenotype-specific calcium modification in severe calcification with and without CNs. Methods In this single-center randomized trial using a new-generation coronary IVL catheter, patients with optical coherence tomography-defined CNs (Cohort A) were assigned 1:1 to rotational atherectomy (RA) plus IVL or IVL alone; patients with severe calcification without CNs (Cohort B) were assigned 1:1 to maximum or operator-determined IVL pulses. Primary endpoints were minimum stent area (MSA) at the CN site in Cohort A and at the maximum calcium arc site in Cohort B. Results Among 120 patients, 66 (55%) were in Cohort A (33 per group) and 54 (45%) in Cohort B (27 per group). MSA at the CN site was 7.41 ± 2.12 mm 2 with RA plus IVL vs 6.23 ± 1.55 mm 2 with IVL alone (mean difference: 1.18 mm 2 ; 95% CI: 0.27-2.09; P = 0.012). In Cohort B, MSA at the maximum calcium arc site was 5.50 ± 1.19 mm 2 with maximum IVL pulses vs 5.56 ± 1.45 mm 2 with operator-determined IVL pulses (mean difference: -0.06 mm 2 ; 95% CI: -0.78 to 0.67; P = 0.873). Conclusions RA plus IVL increased final stent area vs IVL alone in CN lesions, whereas maximum IVL pulses did not significantly increase final stent area compared with operator-determined pulses in severe calcification without CNs. These findings warrant validation in larger multicenter trials with clinical endpoints. (Coronary Calcified Nodule Management With Rotational Atherectomy Plus Shockwave Intravascular Lithotripsy vs Intravascular Lithotripsy Alone: A Prospective, Randomized Trial [NODULE-SHOCK]; ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07000045).

items.title: 1-Year Safety and Effectiveness of a Next-Generation Dual-Seal Left Atrial Appendage Occluder
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) is a stroke prevention alternative for patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) intolerant to long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC). The next-generation dual-seal device was designed to improve operator ease of use while maintaining effective LAAO of the predicate device. OBJECTIVES: The purpose of this analysis was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of a next-generation device through 1 year. METHODS: VERITAS is a single-arm, prospective, global, multicenter study. Patients with nonvalvular AF with an increased thromboembolism risk seeking a nonpharmacologic alternative to OAC were enrolled. One-year descriptive endpoints are provided, including mortality, neurological events, major bleeding, and device-related complications. One-year cardiac imaging was assessed for peridevice leak and device-related thrombus (DRT). RESULTS: Complete left atrial appendage (LAA) closure (0 mm leak) was observed in 91.1% (95% CI: 87.9%-93.7%) of patients by either transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) or cardiac computed tomography and 96.3% (95% CI: 93.2%-98.2%) by TEE alone. The cumulative DRT rate was 3.3% (95% CI: 2.0%-5.3%) with only 0.4% (95% CI: 0.1%-1.5%) deemed clinically relevant. One-year key clinical outcome rates are as follows: all-cause mortality: 3.9% (95% CI: 2.4%-6.3%); cardiovascular mortality: 1.9% (95% CI: 0.9%-3.8%); major bleeding: 6.6% (95% CI: 4.5%-9.2%); ischemic stroke or systemic embolism: 1.8% (95% CI: 0.8%-3.3%); pericardial effusion requiring intervention: 0.9% (95% CI: 0.3%-2.1%). No (0%) device embolization occurred. Median follow-up was 365 days (IQR: 349-380 days). CONCLUSIONS: The VERITAS study results support the 1-year safety and effectiveness of the next-generation device. (Abbott Medical-VERITAS Study; NCT06707688).

items.title: 3-Year Comparison of Sirolimus- Versus Paclitaxel-Coated Balloon Angioplasty in Femoropopliteal Artery Disease
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sirolimus-coated balloons (SCBs) have emerged as alternatives to paclitaxel-coated balloons (PCBs), but randomized comparative data beyond 2 years are lacking. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to compare patient-reported outcomes, effectiveness, and safety through 3 years in symptomatic femoropopliteal artery disease. METHODS: SIRONA was a prospective, multicenter, randomized controlled trial comparing SCB angioplasty with a PCB strategy. Patients were randomized 1:1 after successful predilation. Prespecified 3-year outcomes included walking capacity, health-related quality of life, clinically driven target lesion/vessel revascularization (cdTLR/cdTVR), mortality, major amputation, and amputation-free survival. RESULTS: Among 482 randomized patients (SCB, n = 238; PCB, n = 244), 96.3% had intermittent claudication; 3-year follow-up was completed by 76.5% and 79.6%, respectively. Changes in patient-reported walking distances did not differ between-groups. Three-year freedom from cdTLR was 88.2% (95% CI: 83.1%-91.9%) versus 80.2% (95% CI: 74.1%-85.0%; HR: 0.60, 95% CI: 0.36-0.97; nominal log-rank P = 0.03). Post-hoc analysis suggested time-varying treatment effects (treatment-by-period interaction P = 0.006), with separation after the first year. Freedom from cdTVR (HR: 0.78, 95% CI: 0.50-1.21; nominal P = 0.27) and amputation-free survival (HR: 1.09, 95% CI 0.57-2.09; nominal P = 0.79) did not differ. CONCLUSIONS: Through 3 years, no between-group differences were observed in walking capacity and health-related quality of life or clinical safety outcomes between SCB angioplasty and the PCB strategy. Three-year freedom from cdTLR was higher with SCB angioplasty, with treatment effect that varied over time. Given the exploratory, nonmultiplicity-adjusted 3-year analysis, the cdTLR difference requires confirmation.

Cardiac Damage and Clinical Outcomes in Symptomatic Severe Aortic Stenosis Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The extent of cardiac damage in patients with aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with worse clinical outcomes. OBJECTIVES: This study sought to investigate the clinical impact of cardiac damage using the updated criteria incorporating the echocardiographic probability of pulmonary hypertension. METHODS: This post hoc subanalysis of LANDMARK trial, which randomized 768 patients with severe AS to the Myval transcatheter heart valve (THV) series or to contemporary THVs (Sapien and Evolut series), used updated cardiac damage classification: stage 0, no cardiac damage; stage 1, left ventricular damage; stage 2, left atrial or mitral valve damage; stage 3, pulmonary artery or tricuspid valve damage; and stage 4, right ventricular damage. The impact of cumulative cardiac damage, defined as meeting all criteria for stages 1 to 4, was also assessed. The primary endpoint was 1-year all-cause mortality. RESULTS: Cardiac damage stages were assessed in 596 patients (stage 0, n = 36; stage 1, n = 88; stage 2, n = 284; stage 3, n = 84; stage 4, n = 104), with a mean age of 80.2 (5.7) years and a mean Society of Thoracic Surgeons score of 3.3% (2.4%). One-year mortality was 0%, 1.1%, 4.7%, 7.2%, and 20.4% in stages 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4, respectively (log-rank P < 0.001). The area under the curve for predicting 1-year mortality was 0.739. Patients with cumulative cardiac damage had the highest mortality (23.6%). In the multivariable analysis, stage 4 was independently associated with higher 1-year mortality. CONCLUSIONS: The updated cardiac damage staging stratified 1-year mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement, highlighting the importance of comprehensive echocardiographic assessment in severe AS. (LANDMARK Trial: a Randomised Controlled Trial of Myval THV [LANDMARK]; NCT04275726).

items.title: Is Bilateral Occlusion Mandatory?
Transcatheter vs Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement for Isolated Native Aortic Regurgitation
items.abstract: Background Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is well established for aortic stenosis, while its application for isolated native aortic regurgitation (AR) was previously off label and technically challenging. Comparative data between TAVR and surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) are limited. Objectives The aim of this study was to compare patient characteristics and outcomes of off-label TAVR vs SAVR among patients with isolated native AR. Methods Using the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Medicare Provider Analysis and Review database, patients ≥65 years of age who underwent TAVR or SAVR for isolated native AR (2017-2023) were identified. Propensity score matching (1:1) was performed to evaluate short- and long-term outcomes. Fine-Gray models accounted for death as a competing risk, reported as subdistribution HRs (SHRs). Results Among 9,859 patients, 1,742 propensity score-matched pairs were included, with balanced baseline characteristics (mean age 75.8 years vs 75.7 years; female sex 517 of 1,742 [29.7%] vs 528 of 1,742 [30.3%]). In the matched cohort, TAVR was associated with shorter hospitalization (OR: 0.33; 95% CI: 0.28-0.39; P Conclusions In this analysis, TAVR was associated with shorter hospitalization and comparable 5-year survival as SAVR, although pacemaker and long-term reinterventions rates were higher.

items.title: Prosthesis–Patient Mismatch and Patient-Centered Outcomes After TAVR
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prosthesis-patient mismatch (PPM) after transcatheter aortic valve replacement has been widely studied for its association with clinical outcomes, but its effect on patient-reported health status remains less defined. OBJECTIVES: This study sought to evaluate the association between PPM severity and health status through 3-year follow-up after transcatheter aortic valve replacement. METHODS: This post hoc analysis of the SCOPE I (Safety and Efficacy of the ACURATE Neo/TF Compared to the SAPIEN 3 Bioprosthesis) randomized trial categorized patients according to PPM severity using Valve Academic Research Consortium-3 criteria. Endpoints included survival and patient-reported health status, with an integrated outcome defined as being alive with good health status (Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary score ≥75 without a decline of >10 points from baseline). RESULTS: Among 662 patients, moderate and severe PPM occurred in 184 (27.8%) and 69 (10.4%), respectively. All-cause mortality at 1 and 3 years was 7.0% and 20.5%, with no differences across PPM categories. Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire Overall Summary score was similar through 1 year but lower at 3 years in patients with severe vs no PPM (median 71.1 vs 83.9; P = 0.027). Fewer patients with severe PPM were alive with good health status at 3 years (30.6% vs 49.4%; P = 0.021). In multivariable analysis, severe PPM was associated with a lower likelihood of the integrated outcome (OR: 0.51; 95% CI: 0.27-0.96; P = 0.036), but this association was no longer statistically significant after adjustment for 30-day mitral regurgitation (OR: 0.59; 95% CI: 0.30-1.15; P = 0.121). CONCLUSIONS: Among survivors, severe PPM was associated with a lower likelihood of good health status at 3 years. This association was attenuated after accounting for 30-day residual mitral regurgitation, suggesting a possible contributory role. Given the post hoc design, the findings are hypothesis-generating.

items.title: Mavacamten for Refractory Dynamic Intraventricular Obstruction After Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
The Right-Sided Substrate for Sudden Cardiac Death
Prevalence and Consequences of Guideline-Directed Indications for Aortic Valve Replacement in the EARLY TAVR Trial
items.abstract: BackgroundThe current American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association valvular heart disease guidelines were published before several recent trials that provide greater support for early intervention in patients with asymptomatic severe aortic stenosis (AS). ObjectivesThis study sought to investigate the prevalence and clinical impact of American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Class II recommendations for AVR in the EARLY TAVR trial. MethodsThe EARLY TAVR trial randomized patients with asymptomatic severe AS to transfemoral transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance (CS) with conversion to TAVR based on development of ACC/AHA Class I indications. Patients in the intention-to-treat cohort were stratified by presence of a Class II indication for AVR at randomization. The primary endpoint of the present analysis was the composite of all-cause death, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization. Interaction tests were performed to assess whether the treatment effect differed by level of guideline recommendation. Timing of conversion to AVR in the CS group according to the presence/absence of Class II indications was also assessed. ResultsOf the 901 patients randomized to TAVR (N = 445) and CS (N = 446), 636 (70.6%) patients had no guideline recommendation, and 265 (29.4%) had at least1 1 Class II recommendation for AVR at the time of randomization. At a median follow-up of 3.8 years, patients with a Class II indication for AVR experienced higher rates of the primary endpoint (Class II: 24.5% vs no recommendation: 14.5%; HR = 1.78; 95% CI: 1.30-2.44; P < 0.001) and were more likely to have acute valve syndrome at the time of conversion. Compared with CS, the relative benefit of early TAVR on the primary endpoint was similar regardless of the presence or absence of a Class II guideline recommendation (HR = 0.62; 95% CI: 0.37-1.02 vs 0.61; 95% CI: 0.40-0.92; Pinteraction = 0.96). ConclusionsAmong patients in the EARLY TAVR trial, Class II indications for AVR were present in almost one-third of patients at baseline. The benefit of early TAVR was consistent regardless of the presence or absence of Class II indications. These findings support the strategy of early TAVR over CS in asymptomatic patients with severe AS, independent of guideline indications. Clinical Trial Registration: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03042104; Unique Identifier: NCT03042104

Development of a Quantitative Contrast CT-Based TAVR-Risk Score to Reliably Predict Deformation in Bicuspid Aortic Valves
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) calcification affects clinical outcomes by causing transcatheter heart valve (THV) deformation after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR). However, a computed tomography (CT)-based scoring system for grading BAV calcification severity and predicting THV deformation has not been established. OBJECTIVES: This study sought to develop a cardiac CT-based BAV TAVR-risk score for grading BAV calcification severity and predicting THV deformation. METHODS: This single-center retrospective study included consecutive patients with BAV who underwent TAVR using contemporary balloon-expandable valves between January 2016 and December 2024 and who had preprocedural and postprocedural CT imaging. The BAV TAVR-risk score integrated calcification severity and distribution across valve leaflets, raphe, annulus, and left ventricular outflow tract, quantified using a fixed HU-850 threshold of detection on contrast-enhanced CT scans. Score thresholds were derived by receiver operating curve analysis with Youden index optimization. Patients were categorized into low-, intermediate-, and high-risk score groups. RESULTS: Among 321 patients (median follow-up: 1,825 days; Q1-Q3: 765-1,825 days), 56 (17.4%) were classified into the high-risk score group. Both underexpansion and eccentricity of the THV occurred in 49 of the 321 patients (15.3%) and were predominantly observed in the high-risk score group. However, in the low-risk score group, 149 of 155 patients (96.1%) demonstrated no underexpansion or eccentricity of the THV. A high BAV TAVR-risk score independently predicted both underexpansion and eccentricity of the THV (OR: 89.13; 95% CI: 35.02-226.83; P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: This CT-based BAV TAVR-risk score provides a systematic method to precisely quantify BAV severity which reliably predicts THV deformation for BAV patients with contemporary balloon-expandable valves and may help guide decision-making in this challenging population.

items.title: Prognostic Impact of Paravalvular Regurgitation in Patients With Severe Low-Flow, Low-Gradient Aortic Stenosis Undergoing TAVR
items.abstract: Background Paravalvular regurgitation (PVR) is a frequent complication after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and may influence clinical outcomes in patients with high-gradient aortic stenosis. However, its prognostic relevance in patients with low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis (LFLG-AS) undergoing TAVR remains incompletely elucidated. Objectives This study sought to evaluate the prognostic significance of PVR severity in patients with LFLG-AS undergoing TAVR with current-generation prostheses. Methods This multicenter registry-based cohort study included consecutive patients with LFLG-AS undergoing TAVR from January 2019 to December 2024 at 17 high-volume Italian centers. PVR severity was classified using a 5-class grading scheme and stratified as Results A total of 1,358 patients were included. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed lower event-free survival among patients with ≥2+ PVR at discharge compared with those with Conclusions In this large, real-world study of patients with LFLG-AS treated with current-generation TAVR devices, PVR ≥2+ was independently associated with worse clinical outcomes after discharge, regardless of LFLG-AS subtype.

items.title: A decade-long device–valve interaction: severe aortic regurgitation after residual ventricular septal defect closure
items.abstract: A NTI1008"49-year-old woman underwent tetralogy of Fallot repair at age 16, including closure of a 25 mm intracristal ventricular septal defect (VSD) and right ventricular outflow tract reconstruction. Sixteen years later, a postoperative residual VSD was closed transcatheterly. Eleven years after device implantation, echocardiography showed mild-to-moderate aortic regurgitation (AR), which progressed to severe over 2 years, while the ascending aortic diameter increased from 38 to 45 mm despite 6-month surveillance. At the current admission, three-dimensional transoesophageal echocardiography showed the occluder impinging on the non-coronary and right coronary cusps at the commissure, restricting cusp motion and producing severe AR on colour Doppler (Panel A). Computed tomography confirmed protrusion into the aortic valve complex (Panel B). At surgery, both cusps were markedly thickened and firmly adherent to the occluder at the commissure (Panel C). The protruding portion of the device and adherent cusp tissue were excised (Panel D), followed by mechanical aortic valve replacement (Panel E). Recovery was uneventful, with normal prosthetic function at 1 month.

items.title: When platelets are under pressure: an angiotensin II-TGF-β axis in hypertensive patients leads to receptor PAR4 overexpression
items.abstract: Angiotensin II-TGF-β1-Smad2 signalling promotes PAR4 overexpression and platelet priming in hypertension. The schematic depicts the proposed mechanism by which an angiotensin II-high hypertensive phenotype drives megakaryocyte reprogramming and platelet hyperreactivity. In normosensitive individuals and in hypertensive patients without increased angiotensin II signalling, TGF-β1, Smad2 activation, and platelet PAR4 expression remain unchanged, resulting in quiescent platelets. In contrast, increased angiotensin II signalling promotes TGF-β1/Smad2 activation in megakaryocytes, leading to increased PAR4 expression in newly generated platelets. PAR4-high platelets display increased platelet activation markers and are associated with enhanced thrombotic risk. Valsartan, through angiotensin II type 1 receptor blockade, attenuates this pathway and may reduce PAR4-dependent platelet activation in this specific hypertensive phenotype.

items.title: Clonal haematopoiesis across the cardiovascular–kidney–metabolic continuum: from risk marker to therapeutic target
Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction and an update on lipoprotein(a) and inflammation
items.abstract: For the podcast associated with this article, please visit https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/pages/Podcasts. This Issue starts with an ESC Guidelines article entitled ‘Fifth Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction (2026): On behalf of the Joint European Society of Cardiology (ESC)/American College of Cardiology (ACC)/American Heart Association (AHA)/World Heart Federation (WHF) Task Force for the Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction Endorsed by the European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS), and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) Affirmation of Value by the Society for Cardiovascular Angiography and Interventions (SCAI)’, by Nicholas Mills from the University of Edinburgh, UK, and colleagues. The authors of this very much-awaited Fifth Universal Definition provide an updated, pathophysiology-based classification of Myocardial Infarction that standardizes the diagnosis, improves clinical care, promotes research, and defines disease coding.1 The Issue continues with a focus on dyslipidaemias. In a State of the Art Review article entitled ‘Lipoprotein apheresis in the era of new lipid-lowering therapies’, Francesco Sbrana from Fondazione Toscana Gabriele Monasterio in Pisa, Italy, and colleagues aim to review the current role of lipoprotein apheresis (LA) in managing severe lipid disorders, particularly homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (HoFH), and to highlight its benefits, current challenges, and potential future clinical applications.2 HoFH is a rare and severe genetic disorder characterized by extremely elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels from birth, resulting in a very high risk of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and aortic outflow obstruction from both the aortic valve and supravalvular aortic stenosis. During the 1960s, in a pioneering way, LA was used to treat children with HoFH. Over the years, LA has evolved into increasingly selective methods, which have been used in paediatric HoFH since the 1990s. Today, LA is able to selectively remove atherogenic apoB100-containing lipoproteins from the blood: the main component of LDL-C, very LDL-cholesterol, and lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)]. LA has demonstrated protective effects in the endothelium and microcirculation, prevention of the development of new aortic and coronary lesions in HoFH, reducing the incidence of major cardiovascular events, and proving helpful in subjects who fail to reach the LDL-cholesterol target or who have elevated Lp(a) levels in secondary prevention. Although advances in pharmacological therapies (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin Type 9 inhibitors, antisense oligonucleotides, and siRNA-based treatments) have expanded the options for lipid management, LA remains a safe therapeutic approach for patients with severe lipid disorders, including HoFH, to reduce their cardiovascular risks. Currently, to put LA into perspective, some obstacles need to be overcome, including: (i) the underdiagnosis of HoFH and high Lp(a) levels; (ii) therapeutic inertia resulting from the use of new lipid-lowering drugs with partial achievement of lipid targets; and (iii) availability of qualified LA centres and practitioners. Further prospective studies may prove useful to identify other therapeutic scenarios for LA, such as renal disease, diabetic foot ulcer, peripheral arterial disease, pre-eclampsia, macular degeneration, or sudden sensorineural hearing loss. In these clinical settings, prospective, randomized clinical trials are therefore warranted. In a State of the Art Review article entitled ‘Homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: insights from the Global HICC Registry’, Willemijn Schonck from the University of Amsterdam in The Netherlands, and colleagues outline the rationale, structure, and objectives of the HoFH International Clinical Collaborators (HICC) and highlights the key contributions of this global initiative to date in advancing the full clinical spectrum from diagnosis to outcomes in patients living with HoFH.3 To address the global paucity of observational data, the HICC registry was established. To date, over 950 HoFH individuals from 45 countries have been included. The median age at diagnosis was 12 years, and untreated LDL-C levels were markedly elevated (median 14.7 mmol/l). At diagnosis, 9% had ASCVD or (supra)aortic valve disease, and despite the widespread use of lipid-lowering therapy (LLT), only 4% achieved guideline-recommended LDL-C goals. Early initiation of LA was associated with greater LDL-C reductions and delayed ASCVD onset. Cardiovascular burden remains substantial, with a median age at death of 37 years. No sex differences were observed in age or clinical characteristics at diagnosis, treatment patterns, or timing of ASCVD, although the usual sex gap in cardiovascular disease onset was absent. Profound global disparities persist, including limited genetic screening, restricted access to LLT, and earlier onset of major adverse cardiovascular events in non-high-income countries. Reproductive care for women remains highly variable and understudied. The HICC aims to guide global stakeholders in improving clinical outcomes for individuals with HoFH through earlier diagnosis, equitable access to advanced therapies, and broader inclusion of underserved regions. By generating evidence from routine clinical care and patient-reported data, identifying gaps in care, and fostering international collaboration, HICC seeks to advance a more equitable and effective global approach to HoFH management. There is growing interest in Lp(a).4–13 Current guidance recommends better LDL-C control in patients with elevated Lp(a), as Lp(a)-lowering therapies are unavailable. Whether risks attributable to Lp(a) are mitigated in patients with CAD who achieved LDL-C < 55 mg/dl remains unknown. In a Fast Track Congress article entitled ‘Lipoprotein(a) and residual cardiovascular risks in Japanese patients with coronary artery disease who achieve guideline-recommended low-density lipoprotein cholesterol goals’, Yu Kataoka from the National Cerebral and Cardiovascular Center in Suita, Japan, and colleagues investigate whether elevated Lp(a) levels contribute to cardiovascular outcomes in Japanese patients with coronary artery disease (CAD) and to what extent lowering LDL-C < 55 mg/dl mitigates this risk.14 A multicentre retrospective observational study analysed 1581 Japanese patients with CAD. Risk of major cardiovascular events (MACE) was compared according to Lp(a) levels (<30, ≥30 and <50 mg/dl, and ≥50 mg/dl) and amongst LDL-C strata (<55 mg/dl vs ≥55 mg/dl) 8 weeks after PCI. During the 5.1-year observation amongst patients with LDL-C ≥ 55 mg/dl (n = 1069), MACE occurred in 21% with risk of MACE increasing with Lp(a) levels (3.9, 7.9, and 11.0 events per 100 person-years for <30, ≥30 and <50 mg/dl, and ≥50 mg/dl, log-rank P < .001). Amongst those with LDL-C < 55 mg/dl (n = 512), the proportion with MACE was lower overall (4.3%, P < .001). However, elevated Lp(a) levels still identified those at higher risk of MACE (1.4, 4.7, and 7.5 events per 100 person-years in Lp(a) < 30, ≥30 and <50 mg/dl, and ≥50 mg/dl, P < .001). The standardized 5-year MACE rate was over two and five times higher in patients with Lp(a) ≥ 30 and <50 mg/dl and ≥50 mg/dl compared with Lp(a) < 30 mg/dl. The ROC analyses identified Lp(a) ≥ 28 mg/dl as the threshold for MACE (AUC = .68, P < .001). The authors conclude that whilst lower achieved LDL-C attenuates in part the risk from Lp(a), elevated Lp(a) levels still associate with worse cardiovascular outcomes. The Lp(a) threshold amongst Japanese patients with CAD at risk of recurrent events appears lower than in Caucasian populations which merits further evaluation. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Florian Kronenberg from the Medical University of Innsbruck, Austria.15 The author notes that from a clinical practice perspective, the data strongly support routine measurement of Lp(a) at least once in all adults, as recommended by recent ESC/EAS and US recommendations, and particularly in Japanese and other East-Asian patients in whom risk thresholds appear lower. In those with elevated Lp(a), clinicians should pursue long-term intensified LDL-C lowering and systematically address all modifiable risk factors, recognizing that such measures attenuate but do not abolish Lp(a)-mediated risk, as also demonstrated in the Japanese study. These recommendations are strongly supported and extended to Japanese practice by Kataoka et al.: achieving LDL-C < 55 mg/dl was associated with lower standardized 5-year MACE rates across all Lp(a) categories compared with remaining above this threshold. Even in patients with high Lp(a), lowering LDL-C into the guideline-recommended range attenuated, although it did not eliminate, risk. These observations are consistent with the concept that LDL-C and Lp(a) confer largely independent risks, and that lowering LDL-C is necessary but insufficient when Lp(a) is markedly elevated. We are now just a short time away from the results of the first outcome trial of a potent, specific Lp(a)-lowering therapy. Until now, we have only been able to speculate on the potential clinical consequences of these therapies. The first outcome studies will hopefully clarify what Lp(a) levels are required for study inclusion and whether there are heterogeneities in the results across different subgroups. This will help us design future Lp(a)-lowering programmes that are globally inclusive rather than anchored to thresholds derived from White populations alone. Inflammation plays a key role in atherothrombosis and markers of inflammation predict cardiovascular events.10,16–19 An elevated level of either interleukin-6 (IL-6) or high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP) is associated with poor cardiovascular outcomes after acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Whether the prognostic information provided by hsCRP and IL-6 is independent and complementary after ACS is unclear. In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein prognostic value following acute coronary syndrome’, Johan Wouter Jukema from Leiden University Medical Center in The Netherlands, and colleagues aim to determine whether baseline levels and changes in IL-6 and hsCRP, individually or together, independently predict MACE and death after acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in statin-treated patients.20 The ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trial compared alirocumab with placebo in post-ACS patients on optimized statin therapy. In post-hoc analyses, the relation between log-transformed hsCRP and IL-6 levels and risk of MACE and all-cause death was assessed in proportional hazards models. A total of about 11 800 patients had baseline hsCRP and IL-6 data; 1306 had a MACE primary endpoint and 458 died. Median hsCRP, IL-6, and LDL-C were 1.54 mg/l, 5 pg/ml, and 86 mg/dl, respectively. hsCRP and IL-6 had moderate correlation (r = 0.52). In models for one biomarker adjusted for the other biomarker, treatment assignment, age, sex, diabetes, LDL-C, and time since index ACS, hsCRP was a significant independent predictor of MACE (P < .0001) and IL-6 was not (P = .21); both independently predicted death (P < .0001 for hsCRP and P = .0003 for IL-6). Relationships did not depend on treatment (all Pinteraction > .25). When dichotomized at 2 mg/l (hsCRP) and 5 pg/ml (IL-6), risks of MACE and death were significantly elevated when both, but not when one marker was elevated (Figure 1). Inflammasomes are key signalling platforms that detect noxious stimuli and activate the highly pro-inflammatory cytokine, IL-1β, which stimulates elaboration of IL-6 by inflammatory cells and CRP by the liver. When dichotomized at conventional thresholds (5 pg/ml for IL-6; 2 mg/l for hsCRP), MACE and death following ACS were significantly higher only when both biomarkers were elevated. ACS, acute coronary syndrome; CI, confidence interval; CRP, C-reactive protein; hsCRP, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein; IL, interleukin; MACE, major adverse cardiovascular events; NLRP3, nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat-containing pyrine receptor 3.20 The authors conclude that in patients with recent ACS, hsCRP independently predicts MACE, while both hsCRP and IL-6 predict death. Together, the two markers provide complementary prognostic information. hsCRP conveys independent information on inflammatory risk beyond that provided by IL-6. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Erik Stroes and Maxim Annink from the University of Amsterdam in The Netherlands.21 The authors highlight that the study by Jukema et al. makes a strong case for rethinking how we assess inflammatory risk after ACS. The observation that combined rather than individual biomarker elevation drives MACE risk is itself an argument against relying on any single inflammatory marker. This is supported by recent work by Nurmohamed et al. showing that targeted proteomics can identify inflammatory proteins predictive of MACE even in patients with low CRP levels, pinpointing pathways that CRP misses altogether. Just as lipid risk assessment has evolved from LDL-C alone towards integrated evaluation including Lp(a) and triglyceride-rich remnants, inflammatory risk stratification should move towards multi-marker panels that capture the diversity of proatherogenic inflammatory pathways. Such panels could help select patients for emerging and probably costly anti-inflammatory therapies, aligning treatment intensity with individual pathobiology. The goal is not a single number that summarizes inflammation, but a profile that guides precision, and perhaps intensity, of the intervention. As anti-inflammatory cardiovascular therapies progress from proof-of-concept to clinical implementation, translating the optimal inflammatory signature into scalable, actionable tools will be an important next step. In a Clinical Research article entitled ‘Cholesterol-lowering therapy from childhood/adolescence and long-term outcomes in familial hypercholesterolaemia: the SAFEHEART study’, Antonio Vallejo-Vaz from the University of Seville, Spain, and colleagues assess the long-term impact of contemporary management of FH on LDL-C and cardiovascular events.22 Evidence supporting initiation of cholesterol-lowering medication (CLM) in childhood to lower this cumulative cholesterol burden and cardiovascular sequelae is sparse. SAFEHEART is an observational prospective cohort study including children/adolescents (age <18 years) with genetically confirmed heterozygous FH (FH-Ch), their non-affected children and adolescents’ relatives (non-FH-Ch), and FH parents (FH-P). Impact of CLM, LDL-C burden, and cardiovascular events were assessed. Overall, 348 FH-Ch, 165 non-FH-Ch, and 288 FH-P were included (50% female; median untreated LDL-C: 5.46, 2.63, and 7.19 mmol/l, respectively). Median follow-up was 12.4 years. At follow-up, 84% FH-Ch, 4.2% non-FH-Ch, and 95% FH-P were receiving CLM. FH-Ch started therapy at a median age of 14.5 vs 36 years in their FH-P. Latest on-treatment LDL-C was 3 mmol/l in FH-Ch and 2.44 mmol/l in FH-P; LDL-C among non-FH-Ch (not on CLM) was 2.72 mmol/l. By age 30–40 years, median LDL-C burden over life was 5909 and 10 207 mg/dl*years among FH-Ch and FH-P, respectively. By age 39 years, the rate of cardiovascular events was 0.0%, 0.3%, and 5.2% among non-FH-Ch, FH-Ch, and FH-P, respectively. The authors conclude that treatment of FH from childhood/adolescence reduces the cumulative LDL-C burden compared with later onset treatment from adulthood in affected parents and permits attainment of LDL-C levels close to non-FH individuals; this finding is associated with the observation of a reduction in the cardiovascular risk of young FH patients. These findings support FH as a paediatric condition requiring early-life detection and treatment. The manuscript is accompanied by an Editorial by Archna Bajaj and Marina Cuchel from the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA.23 The authors highlight that in the SAFEHEART registry there were differences reported in the treatment of young female patients compared with males. Intense lipid-lowering treatment, defined as treatment that would be expected to decrease LDL-C by at least 50%, was present in 61% of males from the HeFH children/adolescents group, but only in 50% of females, highlighting a gap that needs to be addressed, particularly as females are often undertreated over their lifetime due to required interruption of lipid-lowering treatment for periods of pregnancy and lactation. In summary, while great strides have been made in the diagnosis and treatment of HeFH patients, aided by the development of novel LDL-C-lowering therapies in recent years, there still remains a considerable gap in improving the management of such patients across real-world settings.
