items.title: Creating space for a third valve: bioprosthetic valve fracture facilitating TAVI-in-TAV-in-SAV
items.abstract: An 88-year-old woman presented for redo transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) after degeneration of a transcatheter balloon-expandable aortic valve within a prior surgical bioprosthesis. She had undergone surgical aortic valve (SAV) replacement in 2007 with a 23-mm SJM Epic valve. Structural valve degeneration led to valve-in-valve TAVI in 2020 (20-mm Edwards SAPIEN 3, Panel A) via transapical access due to iliofemoral tortuosity. Despite technically successful implantation and semi-compliant post-dilatation, gradients remained elevated and further increased during follow-up, accompanied by moderate paravalvular leakage (PVL) (Panels B–C; Supplementary data online, Videos S1–S2) and worsening symptoms including dyspnoea on minimal exertion. Given the small surgical bioprosthesis (true internal diameter of approximately 19 mm) and high surgical risk, the Heart Team decision was made in favour of bioprosthetic valve fracture (BVF) followed by transfemoral TAVI-in-TAV-in-SAV using a supra-annular prosthesis. The SJM Epic valve was fractured using a 22-mm Atlas Gold non-compliant balloon, confirmed by an abrupt drop in inflation pressure at ∼14 atm (Panel D; Supplementary data online, Video S3). Bioprosthetic valve fracture also resulted in marked expansion of the S3 frame permitting implantation of a 26-mm Medtronic Evolut FX+ followed by post-dilatation using the 22-mm non-compliant balloon (Panel E). Final aortography and echocardiography showed marked reduction in PVL, preserved coronary flow (Panel F; Supplementary data online, Video S4), and a mean gradient of 9 mmHg.

items.title: Correction: Peri-aortic fat to assess cardiovascular aging using an AI-driven radiomic biomarker
Giant aortic aneurysm in a child with a lethal arteriopathy due to a novel mutation in the FBLN4 gene
items.abstract: A lethal inherited arteriopathy syndrome associated with a novel, homozygous mutation (D203A) of the EFEMP2 (FBLN4) gene was discovered in an ethnically unique cohort of 22 infants from Kerala, India.1 EFEMP2 encodes fibulin-4 that has been identified as a critical determinant of elastogenesis. This connective tissue disease is characterized by a severe vascular phenotype with gross dilatation, elongation, tortuosity and narrowing of elastic arteries, in addition to cutis laxa, joint hyperlaxity and typical facial features.2 Although classified under Autosomal Recessive Cutis Laxa 1B in OMIM, this particular syndrome has a far more lethal outcome than other inherited arteriopathy syndromes including Arterial Tortuosity Syndrome, Loeys-Dietz Syndrome and Marfan Syndrome. In an expanded cohort of 63 patients, the median age at death is 15 months. Our current patient, an isolated survivor, a 14-year-old girl presented with symptoms of dyspnoea on exertion. She was diagnosed with the above-mentioned mutation 5 years ago and was on follow-up for the ascending aortic aneurysm. Her current CT aortogram and 3D reconstruction revealed a dilated ascending aorta of maximum diameter of 12 cm and occupying almost the entire left hemithorax. Due to the mass effect, there was complete left bronchus compression at its origin with a fully collapsed left lung (Figure A–D). The abdominal aorta, arch vessels and intracranial arteries showed a tortuous course consistent with the disease. She underwent ascending aorta and arch replacement using a dacron graft and had an uneventful recovery and is doing well at 2 years follow-up (Figure E and F).

items.title: Clonal haematopoiesis and the cardiovascular–kidney–metabolic continuum
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Clonal haematopoiesis and cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome: a cohort study’, by A. Chang et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag655 and the discussion piece ‘Defining CKM progression by a cardiovascular endpoint: a built-in circularity’, by A. Kazory and A. Koratala, https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag857. We thank Drs Kazory and Koratala for their thoughtful response to our recent report on clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) and cardiovascular–kidney–metabolic (CKM) syndrome.1 The authors note that development of clinical cardiovascular disease (CVD) was used to determine progression to Stage 4 CKM. However, Stage 4 was not an outcome definition created for our study; clinical CVD defines Stage 4 within the established CKM staging framework. Now codified in multi-society guidelines,2 the CKM syndrome framework conceptualizes CKM as a continuum culminating in clinical CVD at Stage 4. Accordingly, evaluating whether an exposure is associated with transition from Stages 0–3 to Stage 4 is consistent with the framework itself. We respectfully wish to clarify that this does not create ‘built-in circularity.’ Clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential does not contribute to the definition of CKM stage or the Stage 4 outcome; rather, our analysis asked whether baseline CHIP was cross-sectionally associated with CKM stage and prospectively associated with transition to a prespecified CKM stage. That CHIP has previously been associated with CVD informs the interpretation of this finding, but does not make the analysis circular.

items.title: Defining cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic progression by a cardiovascular endpoint: a built-in circularity
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Clonal haematopoiesis and cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome: a cohort study’, by A. Chang et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag655 and the discussion piece ‘Clonal haematopoiesis and the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic continuum’, by A. Chang and M. C. Honigberg, https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag858. We read with interest the study by Chang et al. examining the association of clonal haematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) with cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome.1 The authors provide an important analysis linking CHIP, inflammatory proteomic signatures, and adverse cardiovascular outcomes. However, we question whether these longitudinal findings truly demonstrate CKM progression or largely reflect the already established association between CHIP and cardiovascular disease (CVD). The primary longitudinal outcome was progression from CKM stages 0–3 to stage 4. Yet, stage 4 is defined by the development of clinical CVD, such as coronary artery disease or heart failure. Thus, among participants without CVD at baseline, ‘progression to CKM stage 4’ essentially meant developing CVD. This is important because CHIP is already known to be tightly associated with several cardiovascular outcomes.2 Therefore, showing that CHIP predicts a composite of cardiovascular events does not necessarily mean that it predicts progression of the broader, multi-component CKM syndrome. The magnitude of the reported associations further reinforces this concern. The strongest associations were observed for specific cardiovascular outcomes: spliceosome and JAK2 CHIP were associated with heart failure with hazard ratios (HRs) of 2.62 (95% CI 2.01–3.41) and 2.79 (95% CI 1.58–4.91), respectively, and JAK2 CHIP was associated with peripheral artery disease with an HR of as high as 3.80 (95% CI 1.81–7.98). Interestingly, the signal became substantially weaker when examined within the broader CKM construct: non-DNMT3A CHIP was associated with progression to stage 4 with an HR of 1.24 (95% CI 1.17–1.31), while any CHIP had an HR of only 1.13 (95% CI 1.09–1.17); its cross-sectional association with greater CKM severity was only minimal (OR 1.04; 95% CI 1.01–1.08). This striking dilution suggests that the apparent CKM-level signal is largely inherited from its cardiovascular component rather than reflecting an independent multi-component CKM phenomenon.

items.title: Weekly Journal Scan: PREMIUM evidence that aspirin omission in STEMI patients undergoing primary percutaneous coronary intervention is unjustified and unsafe
items.abstract: Comment on ‘Aspirin Omission at the Time of Primary Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in STEMI’ which was published in The New England Journal of Medicine, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2606997. DAPT with low-dose aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor remains the default treatment strategy for 12 months after an acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in patients without high bleeding risk.2 Its rationale extends beyond the prevention of stent thrombosis, as the simultaneous inhibition of thromboxane A2- and adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-dependent platelet activation reduces also recurrent atherothrombotic events arising from non-target lesions in the coronary circulation and other vascular territories.3 However, evidence from randomized trials and meta-analyses has challenged the need for a uniform DAPT strategy, suggesting that shorter DAPT regimens, particularly in appropriately selected patients at low ischaemic risk, may reduce bleeding without compromising protection against ischaemic events.4–7 The STOPDAPT-3 trial found that immediate aspirin omission with prasugrel monotherapy at the time of PCI in 6002 Japanese patients with ACS or HBR did not reduce major bleedings and was associated with an excess of early coronary events, including stent thrombosis.4 Of note, in the control group, DAPT was maintained for the first month after PCI, followed by aspirin monotherapy, thus testing aspirin withdrawal specifically during the period of highest thrombotic risk rather than a long-term aspirin-free strategy. The NEO-MINDSET trial, in which aspirin was stopped as early as 2 days after PCI for ACS, failed to demonstrate non-inferiority and showed numerically more death, MI, stroke, and a three-fold higher incidence of stent thrombosis.5

items.title: Micro- and nanoplastics in acute coronary thrombosis: exposure, enrichment, or a dual mechanism?
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Micro- and nano-plastics in the coronary circulation and air pollution exposure in ischaemic heart disease presentation’, by P. Paolisso et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag447 and the discussion piece ‘Coronary micro- and nanoplastics in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: antecedent exposure or post-thrombotic enrichment’, by J. Qin et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag800. We thank Qin et al.1 for their thoughtful commentary on our study of micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) in the coronary circulation across the spectrum of coronary artery disease. The authors raise two principal points: whether the proximal-to-peripheral gradient observed in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) reflects antecedent exposure or post-thrombotic enrichment and whether smoking confounds the association between MNPs and acute coronary thrombosis. We welcome the opportunity to clarify these issues. We agree that our cross-sectional, single-timepoint sampling design cannot definitively separate focal accumulation preceding plaque rupture from secondary enrichment occurring after thrombotic occlusion. We emphasize that this local mechanism cannot alone account for our findings. Indeed, our most robust finding was not the concentration gradient itself but the markedly different rate of patients with detectable MNPs across the three groups, highest in STEMI, intermediate in chronic coronary syndromes, and lowest in controls, a binary difference in presence vs absence that local stasis or thrombus-related sequestration at a single occlusion site does not readily explain. Moreover, we deliberately used peripheral arterial blood, sampled at the vascular sheath and remote from the culprit lesion, as the reference compartment for this comparison to avoid confounding from local thrombus formation and flow disruption at the site of coronary occlusion. Peripheral arterial MNP concentrations were also significantly higher in STEMI than in chronic coronary syndromes or controls, a systemic difference that stasis or thrombus-related sequestration at the occlusion site cannot explain.2 We therefore view antecedent exposure and post-thrombotic local enrichment not as competing explanations but as plausibly coexisting phenomena: a higher systemic MNP burden predisposing to atherothrombotic events, superimposed on focal concentration once coronary flow is disrupted. The design proposed by the authors—comparing polymer burden and composition across peripheral blood, upstream and downstream coronary blood, aspirated thrombus, and plaque tissue from the same patient—is precisely the direction we are now pursuing, building on prior work demonstrating MNPs within coronary and peripheral thrombi and within atherosclerotic plaque itself.3–6

items.title: Coronary micro- and nanoplastics in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction: antecedent exposure or post-thrombotic enrichment?
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Micro- and nano-plastics in the coronary circulation and air pollution exposure in ischaemic heart disease presentation’, by P. Paolisso et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag447 and the discussion piece ‘Micro- and nanoplastics in acute coronary thrombosis: exposure, enrichment, or a dual mechanism?’, by R. Marfella et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag803. We read with interest the study by Paolisso et al., who quantified micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) in paired peripheral and coronary blood samples from patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), chronic coronary syndromes, and angiographically normal coronary arteries. The paired sampling design, rigorous contamination controls, and complementary analytical methods are important strengths. However, the spatial gradient observed in STEMI permits an alternative interpretation.1 In STEMI, MNP concentrations were highest in coronary blood sampled upstream from the culprit occlusion before lesion crossing (Tube B), followed by downstream coronary blood after lesion crossing (Tube C) and peripheral arterial blood (Tube A). This pattern may reflect focal accumulation before plaque rupture, but all samples were obtained after a TIMI 0/1 thrombotic occlusion had formed. Markedly reduced flow and stasis near the occlusion, prolonged residence of circulating particles, or incorporation into thrombotic material could also produce secondary enrichment. Plastic polymers have been detected in coronary thrombi from patients with myocardial infarction and in thrombi retrieved from coronary, cerebral, and deep venous sites. These observations establish that thrombi can contain plastic particles, but not whether the particles promoted thrombosis or became incorporated during clot formation. The proximal-to-peripheral gradient should therefore be regarded as lesion-associated enrichment rather than evidence that focal deposition necessarily preceded the acute event.1–3

items.title: Cortisol in cardio-kidney-metabolic disease
items.abstract: Despite guideline-directed therapy, many patients with cardio-kidney-metabolic (CKM) disease remain uncontrolled due to therapeutic inertia, adherence barriers, and underrecognized secondary causes. Hypercortisolism, ranging from mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) to overt Cushing syndrome, is an increasingly recognized contributor. MACS is associated with a 2.5-fold higher risk of cardiovascular death and increased prevalence of hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and kidney impairment. Cortisol excess promotes muscle insulin resistance, hepatic gluconeogenesis, β-cell dysfunction, sodium retention, and vascular remodelling, worsening glycaemia and blood pressure, leading to poor CKM outcomes. Recent prospective studies suggest that hypercortisolism is more prevalent than previously suspected in selected CKM phenotypes, including 24% in patients with difficult-to-control T2DM in CATALYST and 27% in patients with resistant hypertension in MOMENTUM. The overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test remains the diagnostic test of choice. Therapeutic strategies include adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors, glucocorticoid receptor antagonists, and pituitary-directed therapies in selected cases, while surgery remains the first-line treatment for surgically remediable disease. This review summarizes the epidemiology and mechanisms linking cortisol excess to CKM dysfunction, and also highlights the need for clinical trials, standardized diagnostic thresholds, and assays to enable integration of cortisol-targeted therapies into management pathways to mitigate residual CKM risk. This review will serve as a practical guide for cardiologists to manage a potentially reversible contributor to poor CKM control.

items.title: Extensive type B aortic dissection with Michels type IX hepatic arterial anatomy causing acalculous gangrenous cholecystitis
items.abstract: A 36-year-old man with hypertension presented with a 3-day history of abrupt-onset back and chest pain, followed by abdominal pain. Computed tomography angiography demonstrated an acute Stanford type B aortic dissection (Panel A, arrowheads) extending from the proximal descending thoracic aorta to both common iliac arteries, with multiple re-entry tears and severe ostial compromise of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) (Panel A, red arrow). Three-dimensional reconstruction showed a replaced common hepatic artery arising from the SMA (Michels type IX anatomy1; Panel B, blue arrows), rendering the entire hepatobiliary arterial inflow SMA-dependent. The gallbladder was markedly distended without visible calculi (Panel C, asterisk). Angiography confirmed non-opacification of the SMA origin and poor distal perfusion. Endovascular aortic repair involved three overlapping stent grafts and supra-aortic branch reconstruction. Subsequent SMA stenting restored visceral flow (see Supplementary data online, Figure S1). Persistent abdominal pain and gastrointestinal bleeding prompted immediate laparoscopy. Moderate bile-stained ascites was present. The small bowel and colon were viable, but the gallbladder was gangrenous, measuring 10 × 8 × 6 cm, with focal bile leakage (Panel D). Laparoscopic cholecystectomy was performed. The opened specimen showed haemorrhagic mucosal necrosis without gallstones (Panel E), and haematoxylin and eosin staining confirmed haemorrhagic necrosis with acute inflammation (Panel F). Michels type IX anatomy is rare, occurring in 2.96% of 5002 patients.2 Here, the variant rendered cystic arterial perfusion SMA-dependent; SMA malperfusion from the type B dissection therefore caused acalculous gangrenous cholecystitis despite viable bowel. Clinicians should consider gallbladder ischaemia in this setting.

items.title: Acquired ventricular septal defect in the setting of a catecholaminergic storm
items.abstract: A 58-year-old man was admitted to the cardiac intensive care unit following an episode of chest pain and severe hypertension (277/110 mmHg) during haemodialysis. Electrocardiography showed intermittent left bundle branch block, and high-sensitivity troponin I peaked at 27 582 ng/L. A loud holosystolic murmur was noted the following day. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a 15 mm ventricular septal defect (VSD; Figure A, Supplementary data online, Video S1), while cardiac catheterization confirmed a significant left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs 2.2) with normal coronary arteries (see Supplementary data online, Video S2). Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed no late gadolinium enhancement (Figure B). Given marked blood pressure lability and recurrent hypertensive crises, secondary causes were investigated. Plasma metanephrines were elevated, and 18F-DOPA positron emission tomography identified a right adrenal lesion consistent with pheochromocytoma (white arrow; Figure C), which was surgically resected, resulting in blood pressure control. At follow-up, signs of left ventricular volume overload and rising pulmonary pressures prompted consideration of VSD closure. Owing to comorbidities, the Heart Team favoured a percutaneous approach with surgical backup. Patient-specific three-dimensional printing enabled detailed characterization of the tortuous VSD trajectory and its relationship with adjacent structures, particularly its proximity to the right ventricular free wall, informing device type, size, and delivery strategy (Figure D, Supplementary data online, Video S3). Percutaneous closure was successfully performed using a dedicated VSD occluder under fluoroscopic and transoesophageal echocardiographic guidance (Figure E–1F, Supplementary data online, Video S4). The post-procedural course was uneventful. At 2-month follow-up, there was significant clinical and haemodynamic improvement (Qp:Qs 1.2). To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of an acquired VSD associated with pheochromocytoma.

items.title: Weekly Journal Scan: rethinking factor XIa inhibition after acute coronary syndromes
items.abstract: This comment refers to ‘Milvexian with Antiplatelet Therapy after Acute Coronary Syndrome Event’, published in the New England Journal of Medicine; https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2608717. FⅪa inhibitors were developed around a very attractive -though not novel- therapeutic proposition: pathological thrombosis might be reduced while largely preserving physiological haemostasis, potentially dissociating efficacy from safety.2,3 LIBREXIA ACS tested this hypothesis in a contemporary ACS setting and prompts consideration of what this strategy of anticoagulation may offer to patients receiving intensive antiplatelet therapy. Moreover, most patients had undergone revascularization during the index hospitalization and were receiving guideline-directed medical therapy. The rationale for adding an oral anticoagulant in this intensively treated population rests on the persistence of high levels of thrombin generation and FⅪ despite effective platelet inhibition. This concept had found clinical support in the results of the ATLAS ACS 2–TIMI 51 trial, in which low-dose rivaroxaban added to antiplatelet therapy reduced cardiovascular death, MI, or stroke, at the cost of increased major and intracranial bleeding.4 FⅪa inhibition with milvexian offered the theoretical possibility of preserving this antithrombotic benefit with less interference with physiological haemostasis.

items.title: AI algorithms and external validation: promises, pitfalls, and a practical blueprint
items.abstract: External validation involving the testing of a frozen AI model on independent data from other sites, populations, time periods, or devices provides the clearest estimate of intended-use setting performance when those external data are deployment-representative of the expected population, measurement processes, and clinical workflow. It yields realistic estimates of discrimination and calibration, exposes shortcut learning and distribution shift, quantifies clinical utility through decision-analytic measures, and reveals subgroup disparities requiring mitigation. Yet common pitfalls undermine credibility: quasi-external splits with hidden relatedness; spectrum and prevalence mismatch; site, workflow, and hardware effects; label noise and reference-standard drift; analytic flexibility and selective reporting; small, underpowered samples; reliance only on the area under the curve; unreported threshold tuning; and leakage. A practical blueprint emphasizes pre-registration; representative, multi-site cohorts spanning geography, time, and acquisition; prevention of patient and temporal overlap; comprehensive evaluation of discrimination, calibration (including calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, and calibration plots), and net benefit with confidence intervals; pre-specified subgroup and fairness audits; transparent labelling procedures and uncertainty analyses; principled sample-size calculations; and minimal, well-documented model updating (recalibration before revision). Finally, external validation should connect to post-deployment governance via drift detection, performance triggers, and change-control plans, complemented by site-specific local evaluation to ensure safety and reliability across diverse clinical environments. When executed to these standards, external validation transforms promising prototypes into dependable clinical tools, clarifying where a model performs, where it fails, and what adaptations are necessary for safe, equitable, and sustainable use. This framework links statistical evaluation to clinical use, model updating, and post-deployment monitoring.

items.title: A rare cause of syncope
items.abstract: A 52-year-old woman presented with syncope 6 months earlier. Ambulatory electrocardiography revealed sinus arrest, leading to a diagnosis of sinus node dysfunction and implantation of a right atrial leadless pacemaker. Subsequently, she developed palpitations and transient visual disturbances. A right ventricular Aveir leadless pacemaker was implanted (Panel A; Supplementary S1), but symptoms persisted, predominantly after physical activity. Ambulatory electrocardiography showed a pacing burden of 0.23%, 3123 premature atrial contractions, and 40 premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) with two morphologies. Device interrogation revealed no malfunction. Echocardiography showed no significant structural disease or systolic dysfunction. Exercise electrocardiography documented non-sustained ventricular tachycardia coinciding with syncope (Panel B). At rest (heart rate, 72 beats/min; LVEF 60%), exercise stress echocardiography showed limited mobility of the atrial leadless pacemaker without definite tricuspid-valve interaction (Supplementary S2). With increasing workload and heart rate above 90 beats/min, excursion of the free end progressively increased. At peak exercise (heart rate, 131 beats/min; LVEF 72%), the free end intermittently contacted the septal tricuspid leaflet, coinciding with increased PVC frequency (Panels C and D; Supplementary S3).

items.title: Oral anticoagulation and cognitive outcomes in atrial fibrillation and Alzheimer’s disease: considerations for longitudinal analyses
Prevalence-dependent thresholding and the safety of ruling out left main disease
items.abstract: This commentary refers to ‘Standard clinical and stress ECG variables to exclude left main and left main-equivalent disease: the MASTER study’, by M. De Carlo et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag464 and the discussion piece ‘Prevalence-dependent thresholding and the safety of ruling out left main disease’, by M. De Carlo et al., https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehag860. De Carlo et al. report a clinical and exercise electrocardiographic model intended to defer coronary angiography or coronary computed tomography angiography in patients with suspected chronic coronary syndromes. At an assumed 5% prevalence of left main coronary artery disease (LMCAD) and a 1:100 misclassification cost ratio, the negative predictive value was 98.2%.1 Their Discussion further states that a lower LMCAD prevalence would increase both sensitivity and negative predictive value, making adoption more advantageous. That interpretation is not supported by the supplementary analyses: after prevalence-dependent threshold selection, the higher negative predictive value at 0.9% prevalence was accompanied by lower sensitivity. At 5% prevalence, optimism-adjusted sensitivity and negative predictive value were 85.3% and 98.2% at the 1:100 ratio and 74.4% and 97.7% at 1:50.1 At 0.9% prevalence, Supplementary Table 7 reported sensitivities of 64.5% and 63.0%, with a negative predictive value of 99.5% under both ratios.1 The Mayo Clinic validation showed the same pattern: sensitivity fell from 87.2% to 79.5% at 1:100 and from 84.6% to 69.2% at 1:50, despite higher negative predictive values.1 These estimates imply that the proportion of affected patients missed increased from 14.7% to 35.5% at 1:100 and from 25.6% to 37.0% at 1:50. A lower prevalence reduces the absolute number of false negatives per 1000 patients, but it does not reduce the probability of missing LMCAD among patients who have the disease.

items.title: An uncontainable ‘ball’ in the heart: a giant right sinus of Valsalva aneurysm
items.abstract: An ‘uncontainable ball’ was found swinging relentlessly within the heart of a 38-year-old previously healthy woman presenting with a three-day history of chest tightness. Auscultation identified a 3/6 blowing murmur over the aortic area. Laboratory tests revealed elevated high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (43.4 pg/mL), NT-proBNP (4198.0 pg/mL), D-dimer (16 311 ng/mL), INR 1.7, and marked leukocytosis (WBC 20.82 × 109/L, neutrophil 84%). Hepatic and renal functions were severely impaired (ALT 1263 U/L, AST 1005 U/L, urea 10.20 mmol/L), with mildly elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (7.45 mg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography unveiled the culprit—a giant (5 × 3 cm), thin-walled, ball-like aneurysm of the right sinus of Valsalva (Panels A and B; Supplementary data online, Videos S1 and S2). With every heartbeat, this ‘ball’ tumbled unrestrictedly between the right atrium and right ventricle, hammering the tricuspid valve and generating severe tricuspid regurgitation. Aortic CTA confirmed a contrast-filled saccular structure adjacent to the right coronary sinus with an ill-defined superior margin (Panels C and D), alongside multiple pulmonary emboli in the left lower lobe pulmonary artery and its branches, bilateral pleural effusions, and massive ascites. Given the critical condition, emergent surgery was performed after informed consent. Preoperative transoesophageal echocardiography re-identified the same uncontainable ‘ball’ with a 0.8 cm neck, continuous blood filling, and a 0.9 cm rupture on the right atrial side (Panels E and F; Supplementary data online, Videos S3–S5). 3D transoesophageal echocardiography clearly shows the aneurysm and the rupture site at the right atrial side (Panel G). Intraoperative findings confirmed a thin-walled aneurysm communicating between the aortic sinus and the right atrium (Panels H and I; Supplementary data online, Video S6). The procedure was completed uneventfully.

items.title: Transcatheter aortic valve implantation vs surgical replacement in low-risk aortic stenosis: time-dependent late mortality in a pooled analysis of trials
items.abstract: The expansion of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) to low-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS) has been driven by randomized trials reporting favourable early outcomes and non-inferiority to surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR), through early and intermediate follow-up.1 However, longer-term assessment is essential for patients with a longer life expectancy, in whom durability, reintervention risk, and survival are central to treatment selection.2 Recently released extended follow-up data from pivotal lower-risk trials have raised concerns that the early advantages of TAVI may attenuate over time, with emerging signals related to late mortality, valve durability, and reintervention.3–5 However, these trials were underpowered to evaluate all-cause mortality as an individual endpoint. Moreover, conventional time-to-event analyses may obscure clinically important time-dependent differences between two treatment strategies exhibiting non-parallel patterns of early and late risk. We therefore conducted a pooled reconstructed time-to-event analysis of randomized low-risk trials with extended follow-up of up to 7 years.

items.title: Obesity, frail obesity, and outcomes after durable left ventricular assist device implantation: a pooled analysis of the MOMENTUM 3 trials
items.abstract: Background and Aims Obesity in patients supported by left ventricular assist devices (LVADs) is linked to excess mortality and haemocompatibility-related events. Whether this association persists with the fully magnetically levitated HeartMate 3 (HM3) pump is unknown. This analysis tested outcomes with obesity and the additive influence of co-existing frailty (‘frail obesity’) in the contemporary era. Methods The study pooled 2200 HM3 recipients from the MOMENTUM 3 pivotal randomized trial (n = 515) and Continued Access Protocol (n = 1685). Obesity was defined as body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m2 and frailty by a 40-item Rockwood cumulative-deficit frailty index (FI), with clinically relevant frailty defined as FI ≥0.325 (moderate–severe frailty); BMI was excluded from the FI to avoid mathematical coupling. The primary endpoint was survival to transplant, recovery, or 24 months of support free of disabling stroke (modified Rankin score >3) or pump replacement reoperation. Results Obese patients (n = 887, 40.3%) were younger, less often with ischaemic aetiology, and more frequently women, but more often had diabetes and hypertension, than non-obese patients. Unadjusted 2-year outcomes were similar between groups (freedom from the primary endpoint: 75.1% vs 77.1%, log-rank P = .34; survival: 79.9% vs 81.2%, P = .57). After covariate adjustment, obesity was independently associated with a higher risk of the primary endpoint (hazard ratio [HR] 1.30, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07–1.58) and all-cause mortality (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.10–1.67), as well as heart failure hospitalization, infection, and arrhythmia, but not stroke, bleeding, or early right heart failure. Frailty affected 67.3% of obese recipients (571/849) and was associated with a higher adjusted risk of the primary endpoint (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.09–2.10), overall mortality and non-haemocompatibilty-related morbidity endpoints. The obesity-by-frailty interaction was not significant for either the primary endpoint (P = .436) or mortality (P = .215), indicating additive rather than synergistic risk; frail–obese patients nonetheless carried the highest absolute risk of any subgroup. Frailty improved by at least one severity class by 6 months in 75.9% of frail–obese patients, and improvement was associated with better survival (adjusted HR 0.14, 95% CI 0.07–0.26). Conclusions In the HM3 era, obese and non-obese recipients had similar unadjusted 2-year outcomes; however, after adjustment for baseline case-mix, obesity was independently associated with a higher risk of both the primary endpoint and all-cause mortality, together with heart failure hospitalization, infection, and arrhythmia. Frailty was independently associated with adverse outcomes across nearly all endpoints and was highly prevalent among obese recipients; the combination of obesity and frailty was additive but not synergistic, with frail–obese patients carrying the highest absolute risk. Frailty, however, proved substantially reversible after LVAD support, and its improvement was associated with markedly better survival. Obesity and frailty should therefore be assessed together, rather than through BMI thresholds alone, with recognition that frailty status is dynamic after implantation and that improvement in frailty is associated with markedly better survival.

items.title: Heart failure therapy in congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries: effect on right ventricular function and survival
items.abstract: Background and Aims The aim of the study was to assess the effect of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) on cardiac function, neurohormonal activation, and mortality in adults with congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries (cc-TGA) presenting with systemic right ventricular (RV) systolic dysfunction. The study hypothesis was that GDMT use (assessed using the GDMT score) was associated with improved cardiac function (higher RV free wall strain [RVFWS]), less neurohormonal activation (lower N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide [NT-proBNP] levels), and lower mortality. Methods GDMT score, RVFWS, and NT-proBNP levels were assessed at baseline and 1-year follow-up. GDMT uptitration was assessed using ΔGDMT (GDMT at 1-year minus GDMT at baseline). Improvements in RV systolic function and neurohormonal activation were defined as a relative increase in RVFWS of >20% and a relative decrease in NT-proBNP levels of >20%, respectively. Results Of 213 patients (age 43 ± 15 years; 54% male), baseline GDMT score was 1.97 ± 1.27, and ΔGDMT score was 0.74 ± 0.39. Baseline RVFWS was −18 ± 5%; 25% had improved RV systolic function. Baseline NT-proBNP was 369 (142, 1004) pg/mL; 56% had improved neurohormonal activation. Higher baseline GDMT score and ΔGDMT score were associated with improvement in RV systolic function and neurohormonal activation. Overall, 34 (16%) patients died, and higher baseline GDMT score and ΔGDMT score were associated with a lower risk of mortality and of the composite adverse event endpoint (heart failure hospitalization, death, and heart transplantation). Clinical benefits of GDMT use were observed only in patients with moderate/severe RV systolic dysfunction, and not in patients with mild RV systolic dysfunction. Conclusions GDMT use was associated with improved outcomes in patients with moderate/severe RV systolic dysfunction.

items.title: Heart failure therapy for congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries: a new paradigm for congenital heart disease?
Atherosclerotic plaque healing: mechanisms and clinical relevance
items.abstract: Atherosclerotic plaque healing is a dynamic biological mechanism that occurrs after plaque disruption and represents an endogenous reparative response within the atherosclerotic lesion. This process unfolds through three partially overlapping phases: endogenous thrombus lysis, granulation tissue formation, and re-endothelialization. Through the coordinated interaction of circulating cells, vascular wall components, and soluble mediators, plaque healing promotes fibrous repair and structural stabilization of the disrupted plaque. For many years, plaque healing remained primarily a histopathological observation described in post-mortem studies. The advent of high-resolution intracoronary imaging, particularly optical coherence tomography, has enabled in vivo visualization of the characteristic layered morphology of healed plaques, providing direct clinical confirmation of these early pathological findings. These observations have significantly improved our understanding of the clinical significance of plaque healing. Healed plaques are more frequently observed in patients with chronic coronary syndromes, supporting the concept that healing contributes to plaque stabilization. At the same time, recurrent cycles of plaque disruption followed by repair may lead to progressive luminal narrowing, thereby contributing to the long-term progression of coronary atherosclerosis. This review provided an updated overview of the clinical significance and implications of healed plaques in coronary artery disease, the mechanisms underlying plaque healing, and examines emerging intracoronary and non-invasive imaging modalities that allow their in vivo identification.

En bloc heart-lung transplantation in the modern donor era: Dual-organ recovery and preservation challenges
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Combined heart-lung transplantation remains a rare but essential therapy for selected patients with end-stage cardiopulmonary disease that cannot be addressed by isolated heart or lung transplantation. Modern donor allocation, increasing recipient acuity, donation after circulatory death, and longer transport distances have made graft preservation a critical determinant of whether scarce en bloc grafts can be used safely. Unlike isolated organs, the intact heart-lung bloc presents competing preservation requirements: the heart and lungs differ in ischemic tolerance, optimal storage temperature, perfusate chemistry, airway management, and tolerance of pressure and volume during recovery. Across conventional static cold storage, controlled hypothermic transport, regulated airway-pressure devices, 10°C storage, and emerging donation after circulatory death recovery pathways, this review integrates contemporary approaches for donation after brain death and donation after circulatory death while distinguishing direct en bloc evidence from single-organ extrapolation. The evidence base remains observational and constrained by procedural rarity. Future progress will require multicenter preservation-specific data collection and graft-specific systems that treat the heart-lung bloc as an integrated physiologic unit rather than as 2 isolated organs transported together.

items.title: Resource Utilization and Forecasting in Heart Failure Patients with Durable Left Ventricular Assist Devices
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Heart failure patients treated with durable left ventricular assist devices (LVADs) require significant resource utilization. Patient volume and contact points based on implant volume remain poorly quantified. We retrospectively reviewed 268 patients implanted with a durable LVAD at a single, experienced center from 2011 through 2022 and recorded survival, telephone encounters, office visits, and all-cause hospitalizations. Telephone encounters peaked at 10.4 per patient-month and declined to approximately 5 after 24 months; 66% were anticoagulation-related. Office visits peaked at 3.0 per patient-month and declined to approximately 0.7 after 18 months. Hospitalizations decreased from 2.7 per patient-year in year 1 to approximately 1 by year 5. Five-year survival with HeartMate 3 (HM3) was 61.4%. Applying HM3 survival to constant annual implant volumes yielded estimated 5-year censuses of 39, 96, and 193 surviving patients for 10, 25, and 50 annual implants, respectively. These findings may inform LVAD program capacity and staffing.

items.title: Association Between Elevated Donor-Derived Cell-Free DNA and Donor-Specific Antibodies in Heart Transplantation: Antibody-Mediated Rejection and Long-Term Outcomes
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Background Donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA) and donor-specific antibodies (DSA) are both used for non-invasive surveillance after heart transplantation (HT). Whether DSA provides incremental value beyond dd-cfDNA for detecting antibody-mediated rejection (AMR) and predicting outcomes is uncertain. Methods In this single-center retrospective study of adult HT recipients with paired dd-cfDNA and DSA results (September 2019 to December 2024), biopsies within 30 days of sampling were paired for analysis. Significant rejection was defined as acute cellular rejection (ACR) grade ≥2R and/or AMR (pAMR ≥1). Associations were modeled among biopsy-paired samples using patient-clustered generalized estimating equations, and mortality using time-dependent Cox and Bayesian joint models. Results We analyzed 2,856 dd-cfDNA/DSA pairs from 287 recipients, of which 763 were biopsy-paired. Elevated dd-cfDNA was more frequent in DSA-positive samples (19.3% vs 10.5%; p = 0.006). Among biopsied samples, AMR was associated with DSA (OR 5.93, 95% CI 1.82-19.26) and elevated dd-cfDNA (OR 6.21, 95% CI 2.07-18.60). Relative to negative concordance, the risk of significant rejection was similar with isolated DSA-positivity (OR 3.83) and isolated dd-cfDNA-positivity (OR 3.80) and was highest with double-positivity (OR 15.70, 95% CI 4.71-52.30). Adding DSA with MFI ≥4,000 to dd-cfDNA increased the AUC for AMR from 0.73 to 0.84 (p = 0.03). Among 15 deaths, dd-cfDNA, but not DSA, was associated with mortality (HR 2.12, 95% CrI 1.24-3.39). Conclusions dd-cfDNA and DSA carried similar, additive information for rejection, with double-positivity identifying the highest-risk phenotype. In exploratory analyses, DSA at MFI ≥4,000 added to dd-cfDNA for AMR, and dd-cfDNA was the only marker associated with mortality.

items.title: Donor-Recipient Sex Mismatch is Associated with Severe Primary Graft Dysfunction after Heart Transplantation
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The association between sex and primary graft dysfunction after heart transplantation (HT) remains unclear. We evaluated whether recipient sex and donor-recipient sex matching are associated with severe primary graft dysfunction (PGD) in a contemporary, multicenter cohort. METHODS: We analyzed data from the International PGD Consortium comprised of adult HTs from 2010 to 2024 across 14 centers. Associations between sex-related variables and severe PGD were assessed using multivariable logistic regression, and adjusted for ischemic time, pre-transplant durable left ventricular assist device (LVAD), dialysis, congenital heart disease, and predicted heart mass (PHM) ratio. RESULTS: Among 3,994 recipients, 1,030 (25.8%) were female. Female recipients were younger (54 vs. 57 years) with fewer comorbidities, and less frequently bridged on a durable LVAD (19.8% vs. 29.1%). Although female recipients had a lower incidence of PGD than male recipients (7.1% vs. 9.4%), recipient sex was not independently associated with PGD after multivariable adjustment. Female donor to male recipient sex mismatching had the highest PGD incidence of 11.5% and was associated with a 43% increase in the odds of severe PGD (p=0.030). While sex-mismatch was associated with an increased incidence of PGD, size mismatch by PHM ratio was not an independent predictor. CONCLUSION: In this large international registry, donor-recipient sex mismatch, specifically among male recipients of female donor hearts, was independently associated with severe PGD, even when appropriately size matched. These findings inform risk stratification for development of severe PGD after HT.

items.title: Waitlist outcomes of multiorgan heart transplant candidates
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In recent years, the number of patients undergoing simultaneous multiorgan heart transplant (MOT) has increased significantly. However, there is no unified policy for MOT allocation, allowing Organ Procurement Organizations to individually determine priority for match runs across all organ types. We evaluated if heart transplant (HT) candidates listed simultaneously for a kidney or liver are at a disadvantage on the waitlist. METHODS: Adult HT candidates registered with the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients between 2019 and 2023 were included. Candidates were waitlisted statuses 1-6 within the heart allocation system in order of medical urgency. The primary outcomes were transplantation and removal from the waitlist for death or clinical deterioration, estimated with cumulative incidence functions for the first-year after listing, stratified by both waitlist status and type of organ listing. Rates of transplantation and removal from the waitlist at 1 year were reported. Using cox proportional hazards models, cause-specific hazards of transplantation and removal, holding waitlist status constant were estimated. RESULTS: Of 20,588 HT candidates, 9.3% were heart kidney (HK) and 1.4% were heart liver (HL) candidates. Irrespective of status, heart-alone candidates had higher cumulative incidence of transplant (70.6% vs. 67.9% HK, p < 0.01; vs. 63.6% HL, p < 0.01), and lower cumulative incidence of removal from the waitlist for death or deterioration (5.3% vs. 10.3%, p < 0.01); vs. (10.4%, p < 0.01). In adjusted analysis and stratified by candidate listing center, MOT listing was significantly associated with lower likelihood of transplant (HK: HR 0.71, 0.68-0.75; HL: HR 1.13, 1.09-1.17), and a significantly higher risk of delisting due to death or deterioration (HK: HR 2.08, 1.81, 2.39; HL: HR 2.45, 1.75, 3.42). Hemodialysis-dependent HK candidates experienced the highest cumulative incidence of death or deterioration at 1 year (13%) compared to non-hemodialysis dependent (8.7%, p < 0.01) and heart-alone (5.3%, p < 0.01) candidates, but similar to HL candidates (10.4%, p = 0.32). CONCLUSION: MOT candidates, especially HK, had worse waitlist outcomes with lower rates of transplantation and higher incidence of removal from the waitlist compared to heart-alone candidates. These outcomes demonstrate a need for MOT allocation based on criteria more reflective of medical urgency.

items.title: Cell and Gene Therapy in Lung Transplantation: From Experimental Promise towards Clinical Translation
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Lung transplantation (LTx) remains the only definitive therapy for selected patients with end-stage lung disease, yet outcomes are limited by early ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) and primary graft dysfunction (PGD), and by chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) as the leading cause of late graft failure. These entities share overlapping injury and repair pathways, including alveolocapillary barrier disruption, microvascular dysfunction, innate immune activation, and maladaptive remodeling, which remain incompletely controlled by current perioperative management and systemic immunosuppression. This review summarizes cell and gene therapy approaches in LTx and frames these strategies around the IRI/PGD-to-CLAD continuum. Stromal cell therapies, regulatory immune cell approaches, and cell-free or cell-derived products such as extracellular vesicles and mitochondrial transfer are discussed, with emphasis on route, dose, persistence, and the graft microenvironment as determinants of biological activity. Gene modulation strategies and delivery platforms relevant to the lung, including viral vectors, lipid nanoparticles, and virus-like particles, are outlined, together with preclinical gene therapy strategies targeting IRI and allograft rejection. Ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) is highlighted as a practical window for organ-confined delivery and early mechanistic assessment prior to implantation. Key translational considerations are outlined, including product characterization and potency, clinically interpretable dosing, and the need for harmonized endpoints and pharmacodynamic readouts to improve comparability across studies.

items.title: Structural determinants of regional lung transplant listing rates in metropolitan France: A national ecological panel study
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Regional lung transplant listing rates in metropolitan France range from 2.4 to 11.4 new listings per million inhabitants per year across individual region-years, and from 4.7 to 8.3 when averaged over 2016-2023. We examined how geographic access, chronic respiratory disease burden, pulmonologist workforce composition, and socioeconomic deprivation relate to new waitlist inscriptions. METHODS: Ecological panel study of 12 metropolitan French regions (2016-2023; 96 region-years). The outcome was annual new lung transplant listings per million inhabitants. Predictors were population-weighted distance to the nearest authorised transplant centre (and binary centre presence), office-based and hospital-salaried pulmonologist density, chronic respiratory disease prevalence, and the European Deprivation Index (EDI). We used pooled ordinary least squares with year fixed effects, Driscoll-Kraay (DK) and small-sample cluster-robust standard errors. RESULTS: In the primary model, listing rates were higher with transplant programme presence (β = +0.86 listings/million/year; 95% DK CI 0.53-1.20), hospital-salaried pulmonologist density (β = +0.066; 95% DK CI 0.02-0.11), and lower socioeconomic deprivation (EDI β = -0.085; 95% DK CI -0.15 to -0.02). Office-based pulmonologist density was associated with listing rates unadjusted but attenuated after adjustment for centre presence, consistent with geographic co-location. With cluster-robust standard errors accounting for correlation within regions, the estimates were unchanged but all confidence intervals included zero. CONCLUSIONS: Inequalities in access to lung transplant listing in France may be in part driven by transplant programme distance, limited hospital-embedded pulmonology, and socioeconomic deprivation. These structural barriers are likely shared by other centralised, single-payer transplant systems. Additional studies using patient-level data to confirm these findings are needed to support interventions targeting these mechanisms.

items.title: Introducing an ELSA-IE approach to accelerate the translation of innovative technologies in lung preservation: The LifeLUNG project
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Despite significant advances in ex vivo machine perfusion and innovation in graft modulation, successful translation of preclinical research into clinical practice is limited by the lack of multi-disciplinary exchange early in the research pipeline. LifeLUNG is a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Doctoral Network funded by the European Union that aims to improve long-term outcomes in lung transplantation by leveraging ex vivo lung perfusion platforms to genetically modify donor lungs to modulate immune responses, reduce injury, and prevent graft rejection. LifeLUNG introduces an ELSA-IE approach, integrating Ethical, Legal, and Social Aspects research, Implementation science, and health Economics with preclinical research to navigate translational uncertainties and reduce the risk of late-stage innovation failure. By fostering the continuous exchange of insights and challenges among researchers, patients, and health systems, LifeLUNG aims to accelerate the responsible and clinically viable translation of lung transplantation innovations.

items.title: Not All PVR Reductions Are Created Equal: Lessons From the CADENCE Trial
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: The CADENCE trial evaluated sotatercept in combined post- and pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension associated with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (CpcPH-HFpEF). We analyzed the pathophysiological implications of the observed pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) reduction.A hemodynamic comparison was conducted contrasting the mechanistic effects of sotaercept with conventional pulmonary vasodilators.In CADENCE, PVR and pressure reductions occurred without marked cardiac output augmentation, contrasting with flow-mediated recruitment typical of traditional vasodilators. Sotatercept-induced PVR reduction may reflect true vascular reverse remodeling rather than vasodilation, underscoring the need to discriminate resistance reduction mechanisms in CpcPHHFpEF.

items.title: Utility of Donor-Recipient HLA Matching in Heart Transplantation in the Era of Extended Donor Organ Preservation: A Multi-Institutional Analysis
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Closer human leukocyte antigen (HLA) match between the donor and the recipient leads to better outcomes after kidney transplantation. Since extended donor preservation is now possible in heart transplantation (HT), we examined the possible impact of prioritization of HLA matching in HT. METHODS: We included single organ HT recipients reported to the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) transplanted in 2010-2019. Outcomes included survival, treated rejection and development of cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) across 5 and 10 year follow-up after transplant. We examined associations between matches at A, B, DR, DPB, DQA, DQB and DPA loci and the outcomes in univariable and multivariable analyses. RESULTS: There were 5176 patients in the 5Y cohort with a median of 9 (IQR 8; 11) HLA mismatches and 9118 patients in the 10Y cohort with a median of 6 (IQR 5; 7) HLA mismatches. In adjusted analyses, there was no significant association between donor-recipient HLA match and mortality, treated rejection or CAV in the 5Y cohort. In the 10Y cohort, HLA mismatch was a risk factor for mortality (HR 1.06, CI 1; 1.12, p=0.047) and treated rejection (HR 1.13, CI 1.07;1.2, p<0.001) in adults. Among pediatric patients, HLA mismatch conferred a nominally higher risk of mortality (HR 1.14, CI 0.97; 1.34, p=0.121) and treated rejection (HR 1.08, CI 0.96;1.21, p=0.226). CONCLUSIONS: We show that the current impact of donor-recipient HLA match on post-HT outcomes is relatively small. While novel organ preservation techniques may make HLA matching feasible, our data do not support its adoption into future iterations of the HT allocation system.

items.title: On generative artificial intelligence in scientific writing
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Scientific communication - the dissemination of ideas, hypotheses, and discoveries - is fundamental to advancing human knowledge and to ensuring public access to new knowledge as it is generated. Growth in the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific communication has been explosive, likely driven by high uptake among an adept userbase with demanding schedules, making the efficiency gains attractive. The rapid uptake of AI is creating disruptive changes in the way scientific communication happens, affecting the methods by which abstracts, manuscripts, figures, presentations, and funding proposals are generated, and in many cases impacting the final product. In this perspective piece, we reflect on the rapidly changing landscape of AI use in scientific communication with attention to the potential immediate and long-term risks. The inherent unauthorized secondary use of the data used to train AI models raises questions about credit and plagiarism in academia. Fabricated references have proliferated in the scientific literature resulting from "hallucinations" by AI models. Meanwhile, each use of an AI model comes with an incremental risk to the environment at an already perilous time. More abstractly, AI use in scientific communication risks the process itself becoming iterative, prioritizing summation while diminishing insights that fuel the scientific engine. Finally, the friction that AI models remove from writing may risk removing an essential part of the process of scientific thinking, particularly for the next generation of scientists. While we acknowledge that AI is here to stay, we feel an element of caution is warranted in its implementation, to help preserve science and its dissemination as a fundamentally human endeavor.

items.title: Harnessing Lung-Kidney Crosstalk: A Novel Ex Vivo Platform for Donor Lung Rehabilitation
items.containerTitle: The Journal of Heart and Lung Transplantation
items.abstract: Background The lack of perfusate metabolic homeostasis during ex vivo lung perfusion (EVLP) may impair lung physiology or stability and limit the application of advanced donor lung therapies. There is evidence that additional organ support during EVLP can improve graft preservation and transplant outcomes. We hypothesized that incorporation of a kidney into an EVLP circuit would maintain perfusate homeostasis and improve lung preservation and metabolic activity. Methods A novel circuit was developed to allow simultaneous normothermic perfusion of lungs and kidney in parallel. Donor pig lungs underwent 12 hours of cellular EVLP (EVLP, n=5) or combined cellular ex vivo lung-kidney perfusion (EVLKP, n=5). Lung function was assessed hourly and inflammatory cytokines, edema formation, hemolysis, histologic injury, and kidney performance were evaluated. Results Simultaneous lung and kidney perfusion achieved target pulmonary and renal perfusion parameters with stable hemodynamics. EVLKP demonstrated trends of higher compliance, lower inspiratory pressure and pulmonary vascular resistance. Perfusate lactate concentration in EVLKP was markedly lower (P Conclusions Combined ex vivo lung-kidney perfusion is safe and feasible in a large-animal model for prolonged lung perfusion. EVLKP improved perfusate homeostasis compared with EVLP alone, which is associated with trends of improvement in lung physiologic parameters. These findings suggest that kidney-derived metabolic and biological support may provide benefits beyond perfusate filtration and highlight the potential importance of organ-organ crosstalk during ex vivo perfusion.
