Flow dynamics and systemic arterial stiffness distinguish bicuspid aortic valve aortopathy from heritable thoracic aortic disease
items.abstract: Aims Bicuspid aortic valve-associated aortopathy (BAVA) and heritable thoracic aortic disease (HTAD) share clinical manifestations but may represent distinct pathophysiological entities. We aimed to compare morphological and haemodynamic profiles between both groups using cardiovascular magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) and non-invasive systemic haemodynamic assessment. Methods and results A total of 185 patients (111 BAVA, 74 HTAD) were prospectively enrolled. CMR 4D-flow assessed aortic distensibility (ADCMR), pulse wave velocity (PWVCMR), global wall shear stress (WSSCMR) and energy loss (ELCMR). Oscillometry assessed systemic PWVM, augmentation index (AIxM) and systemic vascular resistance (SVRM). Composite adverse aortic events (AAE) comprised acute aortic syndrome, cardiovascular death or guideline diameter-based indication for surgery over 42.1±17.6 months. BAVA showed greater tubular ascending aorta and sinotubular junction dilation, ascending aorta WSSCMR (0.42±0.18 vs 0.28±0.12 Pa, p=0.020), ELCMR (19.8±8.4 vs. 12.3±6.1 mW, p<0.001) and ADCMR (6.1 ± 3.5 vs. 4.8 ± 2.9 ×10−3 mmHg−1, p=0.023), yet lower systemic stiffness than HTAD (PWVM 6.2±1.7 vs 7.8±2.1 m/s; AIxM 12.1±7.6 vs 18.4±9.2%; both p<0.001). AAE rates were similar. In exploratory aetiology-specific analyses, ascending aorta WSSCMR was associated with events in BAVA (HR 8.92, 95% CI 2.85-27.95) and systemic PWVM in HTAD (HR 2.16, 95% CI 1.30-3.57). Conclusion BAVA and HTAD show distinct morphological and haemodynamic phenotypes: BAVA with focal dilation, elevated WSSCMR/ELCMR and preserved systemic function; HTAD with reduced local distensibility and greater systemic stiffness. These aetiology-specific predictors are exploratory and require external validation.

items.title: Liver radiomics on routine cardiac CT identifies hepatic stress states that predict heart failure
items.abstract: Aims Heart failure (HF) prevention remains limited because early multisystem cardiometabolic dysfunction is not captured by conventional risk tools. We evaluated whether liver radiomic phenotypes derived opportunistically from coronary artery calcium computed tomography (CAC-CT) identify imaging-defined hepatic stress states associated with incident HF. Methods and results We analysed 59 237 individuals undergoing CAC-CT (CLARIFY: 46 028; Houston Methodist: 13 209). Liver regions were segmented and radiomic features extracted to derive a Liver Radiomics Score (LRS). The model was trained in a CLARIFY derivation cohort (Dtr, n = 9205), validated in a hold-out cohort (Dts, n = 36 823), and externally evaluated in Houston Methodist (Dext, n = 13 209). The mean follow-up was 1411 days (SD 760.1) in the pooled Dtr and Dts cohorts (1144 HF events) and 470 days (SD 596) in Dext (212 HF events). Continuous LRS was associated with incident HF [Dts: hazard ratio (HR) 1.63, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.52–1.74; P < 0.001; Dext: HR 1.04, 95% CI 1.01–1.07; P = 0.004] and remained significant after multivariable adjustment in Dts. Increasing LRS quartiles showed progressively adverse hepatic, haemodynamic, and cardiometabolic profiles and higher HF risk. Among 17 806 Dts participants with PREVENT data, adding LRS modestly improved discrimination across CAC- and PREVENT-based models (P < 0.001) and improved reclassification metrics (7-year net reclassification improvement up to 0.25; including integrated discrimination improvement up to 0.015). High LRS identified elevated risk in low-risk groups: among participants with CAC=0, high LRS conferred ∼2.5-fold higher 5-year HF incidence, and ∼2.9-fold in PREVENT-low individuals. Conclusion In this large multicentre cohort, liver radiomics from CAC-CT captured hepatic stress states linked to HF risk and modestly improved risk stratification beyond CAC and PREVENT scores.

items.title: Whole-body diffusion-weighted magnetic resonance imaging in systemic sarcoidosis
Prevalence of Angiographic Coronary Artery Disease in Systolic Heart Failure Without Infarct-Pattern Late Gadolinium Enhancement: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.abstract: Aims Rest late gadolinium enhancement cardiovascular magnetic resonance (LGE-CMR) identifies infarct-pattern scar but does not assess coronary anatomy. We estimated the prevalence of angiographic coronary artery disease (CAD) among adults with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) or otherwise unexplained left ventricular systolic dysfunction without infarct-pattern LGE. Methods and results MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched to 27 July 2026. Eligible studies provided separable scar-negative denominators and corresponding angiographic CAD counts from invasive coronary angiography (ICA). Scar-negative was defined as the absence of subendocardial or transmural LGE in a coronary distribution. Random-effects logit meta-analysis used restricted maximum likelihood and Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals. Twenty-two reports representing 20 studies included 2,236 paired LGE-CMR and ICA. 818 patients had infarct-pattern scar, and 1,418 were scar-negative. Eight studies contributed 44 CAD cases among 468 scar-negative patients for ≥50% stenosis, giving a pooled prevalence of 10.8% (95% confidence interval [CI] 7.4–15.4). Five studies contributed 19 CAD cases among 271 scar-negative patients for ≥70% stenosis, giving a pooled prevalence of 7.6% (95% CI 4.4–12.6). Seven studies contributed 33 CAD cases among 679 scar-negative patients for high-risk-pattern CAD, giving a pooled prevalence of 4.9% (95% CI 2.2–10.6) and a 95% prediction interval of 0.8–24.8%. These strata represented different study subsets and were not nested. Conclusion Among selected adults with HFrEF or otherwise unexplained LVSD who underwent paired LGE-CMR and ICA, absence of infarct-pattern LGE did not exclude angiographic CAD. Further coronary assessment should be considered when resolving that uncertainty would alter diagnosis or management.

items.title: Long-term prognostic value of sequential coronary CT angiography and quantitative PET in suspected chronic coronary syndromes: a multicentre study
items.abstract: Aims The long-term prognostic value of a guideline-recommended selective sequential anatomical-functional imaging strategy using coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) followed by quantitative [15O]H2O positron emission tomography (PET) remains uncertain. We evaluated its long-term prognostic value in patients with first symptoms suggestive of obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD). Methods and results In this multicentre European cohort, symptomatic patients first underwent CCTA and were selectively referred to quantitative [15O]H2O PET in cases of suspected obstructive stenosis (≥50%). Patients were stratified according to CCTA findings and PET-derived ischaemia (normal CCTA; non-obstructive CAD on CCTA; obstructive CAD on CCTA without ischaemia; obstructive CAD on CCTA with ischaemia). The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), and hospitalization for unstable angina (UA). Adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) were calculated. Among 3918 patients (61.0 ± 9.8 years; 54.3% female) with a median follow-up of 5.1 [3.8–8.0] years, 278 (7.1%) experienced the primary endpoint. aHRs increased stepwise across CCTA-PET categories. Compared with normal CCTA, non-obstructive CAD and obstructive CAD without ischaemia were associated with a higher risk of the combined primary endpoint [aHR 1.89, (95% CI: 1.23–2.91), P = 0.004; aHR 3.20, (95% CI: 1.95–5.25), P < 0.001]. Among patients with obstructive CAD on CCTA, PET-derived ischaemia further increased the risk of the primary endpoint [aHR 1.55, (95% CI: 1.05–2.30); P = 0.029], but not when excluding UA from the composite endpoint [aHR 1.37, (95% CI 0.90–2.07); P = 0.141]. PET-derived ischaemia primarily predicted events within the first year, while obstructive CCTA findings remained associated with long-term hard outcomes. Conclusion A sequential strategy combining CCTA and quantitative [15O]H2O PET provides robust and incremental long-term risk stratification. While PET-derived ischaemia refines prediction of short-term and symptom-driven events, CCTA-derived CAD remains the principal determinant of long-term hard outcomes.

items.title: Tricuspid inflow E-wave velocity for the assessment of severe or greater tricuspid regurgitation: derivation and external validation of threshold values
items.abstract: Aims Current guidelines include tricuspid inflow E-wave (>100 cm/s by pulsed-wave Doppler) as a semiquantitative criterion for diagnosing severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR), despite limited supporting evidence. We assessed its diagnostic performance for identifying severe or greater TR, deriving and externally validating practical thresholds. Methods and results Tricuspid inflow E-wave velocity was measured by pulsed-wave Doppler in consecutive patients with at least mild TR between December 2024 and February 2026. Among 178 patients (77±13 years, 65% women), TR was mild in 44, moderate in 61, severe in 44, massive in 15, and torrential in 14. Mean tricuspid E-wave velocity was 56±16 cm/s and increased with TR severity: 47±8, 50±10, 62±16, 67±13, and 77±21 cm/s for mild, moderate, severe, massive, and torrential TR. Only three patients had E-wave velocity >100 cm/s (one with severe and two with torrential TR). Using multiparametric echocardiographic grading as the reference standard, the >100 cm/s threshold showed 5.5% sensitivity, 100% specificity, and kappa 0.25 for severe or greater TR. As a continuous variable, E-wave velocity discriminated severe or greater TR with an AUC of 0.81. A lower threshold of 52 cm/s yielded 81% sensitivity and 67% specificity, whereas 47 cm/s provided 90% sensitivity and 43% specificity. External validation resulted in 94% sensitivity and 47% specificity. Conclusion The guideline-recommended threshold of >100 cm/s is highly insensitive for detecting severe or greater TR. Lower cut-offs, particularly 47 cm/s, may be useful for screening to trigger a comprehensive multiparametric assessment.

Standards Defining Echocardiography Core Laboratory (ECL) in Clinical Practice and Research
items.abstract: Echocardiography is extensively utilized in both clinical practice and research due to its accessibility. Echocardiography core laboratories (ECLs) adhering to societal guidelines offer superior readings and interpretations compared with the on-site assessments by reducing measurement variability and enhancing study precision. In the present work, we aim to define minimum standards for clinical echocardiography laboratories and research ECLs based on recommendations from the American Society of Echocardiography and the European Association of Cardiovascular Imaging, as well as on expert opinion and our experience in European countries. Accurate acquisition of high-quality images is crucial for ensuring reproducibility, repeatability and reliability of the echocardiographic measurements. In addition to the commonly used workstations, an academic ECL must also possess the necessary capacities and skilled personnel to conduct sophisticated research projects. Personnel should hold advanced certification in echocardiography, indicating postgraduate training and experience beyond the basic cardiovascular ultrasound education. They should be capable of designing, performing, and interpreting complex echocardiography studies. Reproducibility of the ECL should be validated using a small, randomly selected sample, preferably in the early analytic phase. ECL readings and interpretations are superior to site-reported measurements and serve as the gold standard in observational studies and clinical trials. To ensure internal validity, an academic ECL should continuously evaluate/report reproducibility, repeatability and reliability. ECL should be formally acknowledged and accredited by an international scientific imaging society.

Liver Extracellular Volume in Patients With Tricuspid Regurgitation
items.abstract: Background Liver extracellular volume (L-ECV), a novel cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) parameter of systemic venous congestion, might help to stratify tricuspid regurgitation (TR) patients at higher risk, but its role in this context is unexplored. Objectives The aim of this study was to assess the incremental prognostic relevance of L-ECV in a large TR cohort. Methods Data were collected from patients with TR referred to CMR between 2019 and 2024 who had parametric mapping analysis for L-ECV quantification. The primary endpoint was the composite of all-cause mortality and heart failure (HF) hospitalization, under medical management. Results In 462 patients included (median age: 67 years; 43% female), median left ventricular ejection fraction was 51% (Q1-Q3: 40%-59%), median tricuspid regurgitant fraction was 21% (Q1-Q3: 14%-33%), and median L-ECV was 31% (Q1-Q3: 28%-35%). When dividing the cohort according to median L-ECV value, patients with high L-ECV (≥ median) showed worse baseline status with more clinical and imaging signs of right HF and (after a median follow-up of 2.1 years) poorer survival free from the primary outcome (P Conclusions In our large real-world TR cohort, L-ECV appeared as a novel, powerful CMR marker of right HF with an independent and incremental prognostic value to stratify patients with TR at higher risk of events.

Multimodality Imaging Across the Lifespan in Repaired Tetralogy of Fallot
items.abstract: Repaired tetralogy of Fallot (rTOF) is a common condition encountered across pediatric and adult congenital heart disease clinics. Although childhood survival is excellent, patients remain at risk for late complications, including exercise intolerance, arrhythmias, heart failure, and sudden death. Residual lesions, most notably pulmonary regurgitation and right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, drive progressive right and secondary left ventricular remodeling, often necessitating repeat interventions such as pulmonary valve replacement. Multimodality imaging is central to management, enabling risk stratification and informing the optimal timing of reintervention. This State-of-the-Art Review summarizes the current state of the art in multimodality imaging for rTOF across the lifespan, highlighting established and emerging techniques. The authors discuss the roles of 2- and 3-dimensional echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance, strain and exercise imaging, ultrafast ultrasound, and advanced cardiac magnetic resonance methods in characterizing ventricular function, remodeling, mechanics, flow dynamics, fibrosis, stiffness, and electromechanical interactions. The authors explore developments in image-based machine learning and computational modeling that support patient-specific intervention planning and personalized care.

CT-Based Deep Learning Assessment of Aortic Valve Fibrosis and Calcification
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Computed tomography angiography (CTA) enables assessment of aortic valve tissue composition, providing insights into disease progression and helping predict outcomes in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis (AS). The authors aimed to develop a deep learning system for CTA-based quantification of aortic fibrotic and calcific tissue, validate its agreement with expert manual analysis and histopathology, and evaluate its value for outcome prediction. METHODS: This international, multicenter study included 1,674 patients who underwent CTA at 9 sites. A deep learning model based on the nnU-Net architecture was trained in 468 patients and applied to an external test set of 1,206 patients, including 29 with valve histology and 12 with serial CTA. In 1,165 patients with clinical outcomes, prognostic value was assessed adjusting for clinical, echocardiographic, and procedural covariates. RESULTS: ) had a 2-fold higher risk of death (aHR: 2.0; P < 0.001), whereas patients with dense calcific tissue attenuation (>885 HU) had a 1.5-fold higher risk of death. CONCLUSIONS: Deep learning enables rapid quantification of aortic valve fibrotic and calcific tissue from CTA, demonstrating excellent agreement with both expert CTA and histological assessments. Quantitative analysis of aortic tissue composition provides additional prognostic value for all-cause mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement in multicenter external evaluation.

items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Characteristics of future culprit lesions according to artificial intelligence-guided quantitative computed tomography (AI-QCT) are unknown. OBJECTIVES: The authors aimed to characterize and derive thresholds to predict future culprit lesions from coronary computed tomography angiography using AI-QCT. METHODS: A total of 2,169 patients/13,772 lesions undergoing coronary computed tomography angiography at Turku University Hospital, Finland, (derivation) and 553 patients/3,948 lesions from Amsterdam University Medical Center, the Netherlands, (validation) were analyzed with AI-QCT. Lesions from vessels undergoing early revascularization were excluded. Lesion-level total plaque volume (TPV) and noncalcified plaque volume (NCPV) thresholds were derived and externally validated to predict lesion-level and patient-level acute coronary syndrome (ACS). RESULTS: : adjusted HR: 5.11; 95% CI: 2.49-10.46; P < 0.001) with consistent results in the validation cohort. CONCLUSIONS: were derived to predict future culprit lesions and associated with increased rates of lesion-level and patient-level ACS in 2 independent cohorts.

items.title: Multivessel Assessment by Angiography-Derived Index of Microcirculatory Resistance in Patients With Nonobstructive Coronary Artery Disease
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Current guidelines recommend testing for coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD) in the left anterior descending coronary artery, and it is unclear whether multivessel assessment can improve the diagnostic yield and prognostic value of CMD. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic and prognostic implications of multivessel CMD assessment using angiography-derived index of microcirculatory resistance (angio-IMR) in patients with nonobstructive coronary artery disease (NOCAD). METHODS: Angio-IMR was measured in all 3 major coronary arteries in 439 patients with NOCAD. Single-vessel assessment was defined as angio-IMR measurement in the left anterior descending coronary artery only. Multivessel assessment was defined as angio-IMR measurement in all 3 major coronary arteries. The primary endpoint was major adverse cardiovascular events, comprising a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, and hospitalization for heart failure. RESULTS: Multivessel assessment identified more patients with CMD than single-vessel assessment (46.7% vs 24.1%; P < 0.001). During a median follow-up period of 4.3 years, an increased number of vessels with CMD was associated with a higher risk for major adverse cardiovascular events after adjustment for diabetes mellitus, smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and history of myocardial infarction (adjusted HR: 1.963 per vessel; 95% CI: 1.513-2.548; P < 0.001). Multivessel assessment showed superior prognostic performance compared with single-vessel assessment when added to a clinical risk factor model (area under the curve: 0.751 vs 0.707; P = 0.034). CONCLUSIONS: Multivessel assessment by angio-IMR improved the diagnostic yield of CMD and added incremental prognostic information compared with single-vessel assessment in patients with NOCAD.

Post-market device experience reports of dorsal root ganglion stimulation: a 10-year retrospective analysis of the FDA MAUDE database
items.abstract: Background Dorsal root ganglion stimulation is an established therapy for focal neuropathic pain, including complex regional pain syndrome. Post-market adverse event data spanning the full post-approval decade are lacking. Methods We retrospectively analyzed dorsal root ganglion stimulation-related U.S. Food and Drug Administration Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) reports (January 2016–May 2026). Records underwent multi-stage deduplication, combining a blinded manual review by four independent investigators with a custom two-stage algorithmic protocol to merge complex residual duplicates. Thematic analysis was performed using NVivo V.15. Results Following deduplication, 10 532 reports were included. 10 334 were reported as serious injuries. Among reports with documented sex (n = 4796), 60.2% were female. Age was reported in 4329 records, and the median was 44 years (IQR: 36–50). The USA contributed 88.4% of geographically identified reports. Most reported patient-related issues were “inadequate pain relief” (n=7135), followed by “failure of implant” (n=781), “implant pain” (n=548), and “cerebrospinal fluid leakage” (n=274). “Migration” was the most prevalent device problem code (n=2426), followed by “high impedance” (n=1560), “therapeutic or diagnostic output failure” (n=1167), and “fracture” (n=1160). Implant-year data were right-truncated. Conclusion Reported dorsal root ganglion stimulation events are dominated by lead migration, impedance abnormality, and fracture frequently co-presenting with persistence of symptoms. These patterns support engineering attention to lead fixation and structured hardware surveillance within routine follow-up. Because MAUDE lacks denominator data, results are signal generating. Prospective registries with implant-level denominators are needed to define true complication rates and distinguish hardware failure from programming-related efficacy loss.

items.title: Reporting of commercial involvement and the direction of stated conclusions in the neuromodulation-for-pain literature: a meta-research study of 896 publications
items.abstract: Background Efficacy in neurostimulation for chronic pain rests on patient-reported outcomes, which admit no external verification, so procedural transparency substitutes for it. The sponsorship effect is established for drugs and barely characterized for devices. Methods Meta-research study of 896 publications (1995–2025, 155 journals) on neurostimulation for pain, 712 of them primary studies, coded under a prespecified schema with a verbatim quotation per field. The primary exposure was industry sponsorship, analyzed where the funding source was determinable; authors9 declared ties were entered both separately and in the same model; a four-level hierarchy of commercial involvement was secondary. Undeterminable sources were never scored. Firth penalized logistic regression related exposure to a favorable stated conclusion, whose coding was re-applied independently and by two human coders. Results A disclosure statement was locatable for 80.6% of publications; 38.5% stated no funding source, and of 239 declaring industry funding, 69.5% described the sponsor9s role nowhere. Sponsorship was associated with a favorable conclusion (OR 4.03 (95% CI 2.42 to 6.85); n=333), persisting after adjustment for reporting quality (3.90) and among randomized trials (5.59 (95% CI 2.25 to 14.71)). With both exposures in one model, sponsorship gave 5.19 (95% CI 2.81 to 9.85) and authors’ ties 0.95 (95% CI 0.48 to 1.87). The hierarchy reached 7.36 (95% CI 2.68 to 23.44) where the sponsor had an active role. Sponsored studies were better reported, not worse (ρ=+0.23); outcome misclassification was non-differential. Conclusions The association lies with funding and the sponsor9s described role, not with the authors9 declared ties the disclosure system captures. This design does not establish causation.

items.title: Prevalence and intensity of chronic postsurgical pain after cranial surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and non-randomized studies
items.abstract: Background/Importance Estimates of chronic postsurgical pain (CPSP) after cranial surgery vary widely, and the prevalence and severity remain uncertain. Objectives To synthesize the literature and estimate the prevalence and intensity of CPSP after cranial surgery. Evidence reviews We searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and Web of Science up to April 2026 for randomized and non-randomized studies reporting CPSP (pain lasting ≥3 months) after cranial surgery. We performed random-effects meta-analysis and assessed the certainty of evidence using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach. Findings 76 studies (13 740 patients) were included. Most studies evaluated tumor resection (54 of 76; 71%), and most patients underwent craniotomy (10 813 of 13 740; 79%). The median follow-up was 28.8 months (range 3 months to 16 years). Moderate-certainty evidence from 67 studies (10 607 patients) showed the pooled prevalence of CPSP at any severity is probably 27.4% (95% CI 20.8% to 34.6%; 95% prediction interval (PI) 0% to 85.8%). Moderate-certainty evidence from six studies that reported pain intensity (233 patients) showed the average pain intensity among patients who developed CPSP is probably 5.8 (95% CI 4.6 to 7.0; 95% PI 1.79 to 9.76) on a 0–10 Numerical Rating Scale (NRS). Moderate-certainty evidence from 24 studies (4328 patients) showed the prevalence of moderate-to-severe CPSP (≥4/10 on a 0–10 NRS) is probably 16.7% (95% CI 12.8% to 20.9%; 95% PI 2.3% to 39.4%). Low-certainty evidence from 13 studies (3281 patients) suggests the prevalence of severe CPSP (≥7/10 on a 0–10 NRS) may be 5.9% (95% CI 3.0% to 9.8%; 95% PI 0% to 25.5%). Conclusions Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that CPSP probably affects approximately one in four patients after cranial surgery. Approximately one in six patients probably experience at least moderate pain (moderate certainty), and 1 in 17 may experience severe pain (low certainty). These findings underscore CPSP as a common complication after cranial surgery and highlight the need for prevention and management strategies. PROSPERO registration number CRD42024505270.

items.title: C2 suboccipital plane block (SOB-C2) for cervicogenic headache: a cadaveric study
items.abstract: Background and aims Cervicogenic headache is mediated by nociceptive input from upper cervical structures, including the C1–C3 spinal nerves, cervical joints, suboccipital muscles, and associated myodural bridges. The C2 dorsal root ganglion (DRG) represents an important convergence site within this nociceptive network. The suboccipital plane block targeting the C2 DRG (SOB-C2) has been described as an approach to these structures. This cadaveric study investigated the spread of injectate following SOB-C2 and determined whether the technique encompasses the suboccipital triangle and its neurovascular contents. Methods Bilateral ultrasound-guided SOB-C2 injections were performed in two unembalmed adult cadavers, yielding four hemispecimens. With the cadavers in the prone position, a needle was advanced in-plane from lateral to medial to a position deep to the obliquus capitis inferior muscle. A 2 mL of saline containing India ink was injected into each specimen. 1 hour after injection, layered anatomical dissection was performed to assess the distribution of injectate relative to the C2 DRG, suboccipital triangle, vertebral artery and C1–C2 joint. Results A tissue plane deep to the obliquus capitis inferior muscle was consistently identified in all four hemispecimens. Injectate staining consistently involved the deep surface of the obliquus capitis inferior muscle and its associated myodural bridges, the C2 DRG, and the floor of the suboccipital triangle, including the posterior atlanto-occipital membrane and underlying dura. The contents of the suboccipital triangle, particularly the vertebral artery were consistently stained. The posterior capsule of the C1–C2 joint was also stained in all specimens. The suboccipital nerve could not be reliably distinguished because of extensive staining within the triangle. Conclusions In this cadaveric study, the SOB-C2 injection consistently spread beyond the C2 DRG and myodural bridges to encompass the suboccipital triangle, including the vertebral artery with its surrounding sympathetic plexus, as well as the posterior capsule of the C1–C2 joint. These findings suggest that SOB-C2 may influence multiple anatomical structures implicated in cervicogenic headache. Further clinical and imaging studies are warranted to determine the clinical significance of this spread and to characterize the safety profile of the technique.

items.title: Assessment of preoperative gastric content with ultrasound in patients taking GLP-1 receptor agonists: an observational, multicenter, cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) delay gastric emptying, and there have been incidents of pulmonary aspiration in patients who had followed standard preoperative fasting instructions while on GLP-1 RA therapy. As the use of GLP-1 RAs is rising, we aim to compare the preoperative gastric contents of elective surgical patients taking GLP-1 RAs with those not taking these medications. Secondary objectives were to study the association of the indication, dose, time since last dose, and hours of fasting with gastric content. Methods This cross-sectional, multi-center study included elective surgery patients taking weekly GLP-1 RA medications for all indications, and those not taking them. All patients underwent standardized bedside gastric ultrasound preoperatively. Statistical analysis included χ2 or Fisher’s exact testing, Mann-Whitney U testing, and a multivariable logistic regression of full stomach on GLP-1 RA users, controlling for potential confounders where data were available. Results A total of 354 patients were enrolled from August 29, 2023, to January 31, 2025. A total of 307 patients were analyzed, 151 in the GLP-1 RA group, and 156 in the non-GLP-1 RA group. The occurrence of a full stomach was not significantly different between groups (13.9% vs 10.3%, p=0.38). Adjusted regression analysis also did not show a significant difference in fullness between groups (p=0.61). Patients in the GLP-1 RA group had a significantly longer solid fasting time than the non-GLP-1 RA group (median (Q1, Q3): 18.5 (13.5, 25.45) vs 15.98 (14.27, 17.55) hours; p=0.002). Treatment indication, time since last dose, and duration were not significantly associated with the occurrence of full stomach. Conclusions This study found no difference in the occurrence of full stomach in elective surgical patients taking GLP-1 RAs compared with the non-GLP-1 RA group. A longer solid fasting time in the GLP-1 RA group may have contributed to this finding. Our results also indicate that longer fasting times alone may not eliminate the risk of full stomach in patients taking GLP-1 RAs. Trial registration number NCT06003985.

items.title: Fluid dynamics of local anesthetic spread: a hypothesis-generating review
items.abstract: Background Fascial plane blocks (FPBs) have gained popularity for perioperative analgesia due to their simplicity and low complication rates, yet the anatomical and fluid-dynamic determinants of their injectate spread remain incompletely understood. A possible reason, so far largely unexamined, is that the biomechanics of fascial tissue and the fluid dynamics of injected solutions are poorly understood. Objective To introduce a theoretical, hypothesis-generating biophysical framework describing how fascial geometry, the viscoelastic properties of hyaluronan (HA)-rich fascial extracellular matrix, and injection parameters might influence spread of local anesthetics (LAs). None of the mechanisms discussed has been studied in patients receiving FPB, and the framework is offered as a research agenda rather than guidance for practice. Evidence review PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar were searched from inception to May 2026 for work on fascial geometry, HA, LA spread, and fluid mechanics of narrow and porous media. Because the mechanisms of interest have not been investigated in regional anesthesia, evidence was also drawn from biomechanics, tissue engineering, porous-media flow, Hele-Shaw cell research, and ophthalmic anesthesia (sub-Tenon block). Sources were selected for conceptual relevance with no formal assessment of study quality or risk of bias. Findings Two conventional modes of fluid propagation are distinguished: pressure-driven bulk-flow hydrodissection, initiating the initial anatomical distribution, and concentration-driven diffusion, acting later over a shorter distance. Hydrodynamic interfascial pattern-forming instabilities—of which viscous fingering is the best characterized—are proposed as a hypothesis, not as a third transport mechanism but as a pattern the advancing front may adopt during pressure-driven flow. In laboratory Hele-Shaw systems, a branched, fingering front fills a compartment with less work than a blunt front, but whether this occurs in living fascia is unknown. HA behaves as a non-Newtonian viscoelastic matrix whose rheology could modulate spread. Its postmortem degradation may contribute to the discrepancy between cadaveric and in vivo injectate patterns. Conclusions Recognizing HA as a dynamic functional matrix rather than merely a passive conduit for LA provides a theoretical explanation for the variability of FPBs. A strategy incorporating slow injection, warmed LA solution, real-time pressure monitoring, and the adjunctive use of hyaluronidase may promote more homogeneous distribution in experimental settings, but requires clinical validation.

items.title: Social determinants of health and outcomes after spinal cord stimulation: a retrospective cohort study
items.abstract: Background and objectives Social needs may influence longitudinal care after spinal cord stimulation (SCS), but their relationship to trial and post-implant outcomes is uncertain. We examined associations between cumulative social determinants of health burden and SCS outcomes. Methods We retrospectively studied adults identified through chart review of SCS-related procedure records at three centers in a single health system from 2021 to 2024. Five electronic health record social-need domains (transportation, food, housing, utilities, and intimate partner violence) were assessed and patients were grouped as having 0, 1, or ≥2 positive domains. Outcomes included trial-to-implant conversion, post-implant pain and response, longitudinal pain, adverse events, and documented loss of efficacy. Results Among 407 patients, 322 had 0 positive domains, 55 had 1, and 30 had ≥2. Trial-to-implant conversion was similar across groups (78.0%, 80.0%, and 76.7%; p=0.925). Among 317 patients with post-implant pain data, sustained response occurred in 51.6%, 47.7%, and 21.7% (p=0.023). In adjusted analysis, patients with ≥2 positive domains, compared with those with no documented social needs, had 75% lower odds of achieving ≥50% pain relief at last follow-up (OR 0.25, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.75), pain scores 1.26 points higher (95% CI 0.45 to 2.08), and pain relief 14.13 percentage points lower (95% CI −23.68 to −4.58). In an exploratory full-cohort analysis, period-adjusted probabilities of documented ≥50% relief were 55.1%, 42.1%, and 33.3% (p=0.003). Conclusions Patients with multiple documented social needs had substantially worse post-implant outcomes despite similar SCS trial-to-implant conversion. While these observational findings identify an association with longer-term SCS outcomes, they do not establish that social needs necessarily cause reduced SCS efficacy.

Surgical wound infiltration with liposomal bupivacaine admixture as an adjunct to intrathecal morphine for post-caesarean analgesia: a randomised, double-blind controlled trial
items.abstract: Background Intrathecal morphine is the gold standard for post-caesarean analgesia, but it lasts only 18-24 h. Whether wound infiltration adds benefit in patients receiving intrathecal morphine remains controversial. This study evaluated the opioid-sparing efficacy of wound infiltration with a liposomal bupivacaine-bupivacaine hydrochloride admixture as an adjunct to intrathecal morphine. Methods In this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 188 patients undergoing elective caesarean delivery with intrathecal morphine (100 μg) received either wound infiltration with liposomal bupivacaine (266 mg) plus bupivacaine hydrochloride (100 mg), or saline placebo. All patients received standardised multimodal analgesia including scheduled non-opioid analgesics and hydromorphone patient-controlled analgesia. The primary outcome was cumulative opioid consumption (oral morphine milligram equivalents) at 48 h. Results With treatment, 48-h opioid consumption was significantly lower (12.60 mg [IQR 6.30-15.80] vs. 15.75 mg [IQR 9.45-25.50]; Hodges-Lehmann estimate -3.05 mg, 95% CI -5.9 to -1.4; P = 0.002). Secondary outcomes also favoured treatment: 24-h opioid consumption (6.30 vs. 9.45 mg; P Conclusions In women undergoing scheduled caesarean delivery, wound infiltration with a liposomal bupivacaine-bupivacaine hydrochloride admixture significantly reduced postoperative opioid consumption and improved pain scores. It may be an effective opioid-sparing adjunct to intrathecal morphine.

items.title: The role of central nervous system sensitization in obstetric pain: A focused review
items.abstract: Obstetric pain conditions are clinically significant but often underrecognized complications of pregnancy and childbirth. Central nervous system sensitization (central sensitization) refers to the amplification of neural signaling in the central nervous system leading to pain hypersensitivity and offers a mechanistic framework for understanding acute and persistent obstetric pain. Central sensitization does not, however, act in isolation. It is initiated and sustained by ongoing input from sensitized peripheral nociceptors, potentially associated with pain amplification and persistence. This focused review synthesizes the neurophysiological mechanisms which may underlie sensitization in the peripartum period and examines the main obstetric pain conditions in which sensitization has been implicated, including pregnancy-related lumbopelvic pain, labor pain and persistent postpartum pain after vaginal delivery, persistent perineal pain, and chronic postcesarean pain. We also discuss psychological factors including anxiety, depression, pain catastrophizing, and fear of childbirth, as potential active modulators of central pain processing rather than merely coexisting conditions. These factors may represent modifiable targets for prevention, mitigation, and management. Key evidence gaps include the absence of obstetric-specific validation for clinical assessment tools such as the Central Sensitization Inventory, and limited prospective data linking intraprocedural nociception to postprocedural pain sensitization. Addressing these gaps through rigorously designed peripartum studies is essential for developing targeted, mechanism-based strategies to prevent and treat obstetric pain.

Maternal and fetal anesthetic management during in utero embolization for fetal vein of Galen malformation: a case series
items.abstract: Background In utero embolization for fetal vein of Galen malformation is a novel ultrasound-guided transuterine, transcranial fetal neurointervention. We describe the anesthetic management for this procedure. Methods We conducted a retrospective case series of the anesthetic management of patients undergoing in utero vein of Galen malformation embolization at a fetal surgery program. Maternal and fetal anesthetic techniques and perioperative complications were assessed using descriptive statistics. Results Nine patients underwent attempted embolization. Combined spinal-epidural anesthesia was employed in all cases, with conversion to general anesthesia in one. Fetal anesthesia consisted of intramuscular fentanyl, rocuronium, and atropine. Complications included fetal bradycardia and emergent delivery. Conclusions Fetal vein of Galen malformation embolization can be performed under combined spinal-epidural anesthesia with general anesthesia in reserve. Direct fetal anesthesia provides analgesia and immobility. Multidisciplinary maternal-fetal anesthetic coordination and preparedness for emergent delivery are essential. These findings provide guidance for anesthetic management of this novel procedure.

items.title: Development and validation of a Polish version of Obstetric Quality of Recovery-10 (ObsQoR-10-Polish)
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The Obstetric Quality of Recovery-10 is a patient-reported outcome measure designed to evaluate early global postpartum recovery. No Polish version exists, and most prior validations excluded women with high-risk pregnancies. METHODS: In this prospective single-center cohort study at a tertiary referral center for placenta accreta spectrum, the Polish translation was administered at 24, 48 and 72 h postpartum. The primary aim was a psychometric evaluation at 24 h (structural validity, convergent validity against the EuroQol five-dimension index and visual analogue scale, internal consistency, test-retest reliability, floor and ceiling effects). The secondary aim was to explore univariable associations with obstetric and anesthetic variables. RESULTS: Of 800 eligible women approached, 441 consented, with data from 410 analyzed. Internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha 0.90), test-retest reliability (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.85) and convergent validity (r = 0.77 and 0.69) were good, and a modified one-factor model fitted acceptably. At 24 h, 1.5% of women had a maximum score. Scores at 24 h were higher after vaginal compared with cesarean delivery (77.8 vs. 67.0; P < 0.001), higher after spinal compared with general anesthesia for cesarean delivery (68.6 vs. 51.0; P = 0.011), lower with increasing perineal injury severity (53.0 vs. 81.5; P = 0.001) and with placental pathologies (60.7 vs. 72.6; P = 0.003), and lowest in placenta accreta spectrum (42.4; n = 5). DISCUSSION: The Polish Obstetric Quality of Recovery-10 is reliable and demonstrated known-groups validity across the obstetric risk categories represented in this cohort. Associations in high-risk subgroups were unadjusted and require confirmation.

items.title: Multidisciplinary Risk Assessment Outcomes Are Associated With 30‐Day in Hospital Complications Following Pediatric Scoliosis Surgery: Evaluation of a Three‐Tiered Traffic‐Light Triage System at Great Ormond Street Children's Hospital
items.abstract: Background Scoliosis surgery is complex and associated with significant morbidity. Accurate risk assessment is essential for appropriate resource allocation and improved care. Risk factors for developing complications have been identified; however, structured frameworks to support preoperative assessment are limited. Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH) uses a three‐tier multidisciplinary team (MDT) traffic‐light system to triage patients based on well‐defined risk factors and expert clinical judgment. Aim We aimed to describe complications following scoliosis surgery at GOSH and evaluate the relationship between preoperative MDT traffic‐light assessment and outcomes such as complication rates, operative times, and length of stay. Method A retrospective hospital file review was conducted for all patients presenting to GOSH for primary scoliosis surgery between January 2019 and December 2023. Institutional approval was obtained, and the need for ethical approval was waived. Preoperative risk is quantified by the MDT using a three‐tier traffic‐light system categorizing patients as low (green), intermediate (amber), and high‐risk (red). Outcomes including 30‐day in‐hospital complications, operative time, and length of stay were analyzed in relation to preoperative MDT traffic‐light score. Results Of 350 eligible patients, 337 had a documented preoperative MDT traffic‐light assessment. Low‐risk patients comprised 43.6% ( n = 147/337), intermediate‐risk 49.3% ( n = 166/337), and high‐risk 7.1% ( n = 24/337). Major complications occurred in 2% ( n = 3/147) of low‐risk patients compared with 50% ( n = 12/24) of high‐risk patients, corresponding to an adjusted odds ratio of 11.4 ([95% CI 1.98–65.4], p = 0.006). High‐risk patients also had significantly longer operative times (381 min vs. 320 min, p < 0.001) and length of stay (12 days vs. 5 days, p < 0.001) when compared to low‐risk patients. Conclusion Patients classified as high‐risk by the MDT demonstrated an increased odds of developing major complications, longer operative time, and extended length of stay when compared to low‐risk patients. Similar structured tools, with local adaptations, may be valuable in other centers to support preoperative assessment, shared decision making, and guide resource allocation.

Fidget and Sensory Toys for Anxiety and Emotional Regulation in Children: A Scoping Review With Implications for Pediatric Perioperative Care
items.abstract: Background Non‐pharmacological interventions are essential to reduce procedural anxiety in pediatric care. Fidget and sensory toys are widely used for distraction and self‐regulation, yet evidence on their effectiveness remains fragmented. This scoping review mapped the evidence on fidget and sensory toys across general pediatric settings, with a focus on perioperative outcomes—such as anxiety, distress, and pain—to highlight relevant gaps in care. Methods This scoping review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the PRISMA‐ScR guidelines. Searches were conducted in MEDLINE/PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Cochrane CENTRAL, complemented by trial registries, gray literature, citation tracking, and reference screening. Studies involving children (0–18 years) evaluating fidget or sensory toys in any setting were eligible. Two independent reviewers performed study selection and data extraction. Findings Fifteen studies published between 2017 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. Fidget spinners were the most frequently investigated device ( n = 9), followed by stress balls ( n = 3). Studies were conducted in educational ( n = 8) and healthcare settings ( n = 7). Educational studies generally reported limited or no benefits for attention, engagement, behavior, or academic performance. In contrast, healthcare studies generally suggested reductions in anxiety, pain, fear, and procedural distress, although findings were heterogeneous, and outcome measures varied substantially. Conclusions Current evidence does not support the routine use of fidget toys to improve attention or academic performance in educational settings. Evidence from healthcare and procedural settings suggests that fidget and sensory toys may be feasible distraction tools for selected pediatric patients, but evidence is insufficient to support routine perioperative use. Further high‐quality randomized controlled trials are needed to establish standardized intervention protocols and identify the pediatric populations and clinical settings most likely to benefit.

items.title: Neonatal Spinal Anesthetic LAST : Case Unproven
Preoperative Oral Esketamine for Perioperative Comfort in Children Undergoing Adenotonsillectomy: A Randomized, Double‐Blind, Dose‐Finding Study
items.abstract: Background Pediatric adenotonsillectomy often causes preoperative anxiety, venous cannulation pain, and emergence agitation. Esketamine has multimodal properties, but the optimal oral dose for children is unknown. This study evaluated oral esketamine at 1, 2, and 3 mg/kg for perioperative comfort. Methods In this randomized double‐blind trial, 99 children (ASA I–II, 1–6 years) received oral 10% glucose (control, n = 26) or esketamine 1 mg/kg (EK1, n = 26), 2 mg/kg (EK2, n = 23), or 3 mg/kg (EK3, n = 24) 30 min before anesthesia. Primary outcomes: Ramsay Sedation Scale (RSS) and FLACC pain score at venous cannulation, and PAED score at 15 min after extubation. Secondary outcomes: remifentanil use, postoperative FLACC (2–48 h), sleep quality, and adverse events. Results All esketamine doses improved sedation and analgesia at cannulation (overall p < 0.001), with largest effect at 3 mg/kg. Median RSS (IQR): control 1.00 (1.00–2.00); EK1 2.00 (1.75–3.00, p = 0.028); EK2 2.00 (1.00–3.00, p = 0.049); EK3 3.00 (2.00–3.37, p < 0.001). FLACC scores: control 6.00 (3.00–7.00); EK1 2.50 (1.00–4.00, p = 0.016); EK2 2.00 (0.00–4.00, p = 0.001); EK3 0.00 (0.00–1.75, p < 0.001). PAED score at 15 min was lower in EK2 than control (5.00 [2.00–10.00] vs. 10.00 [6.00–12.00], p = 0.048). Remifentanil consumption was reduced in EK3 (120.00 [80.00–159.50] vs. 240.00 [160.00–315.00] μg, p = 0.001). Postoperative pain at 2–6 h was lower in EK2 and EK3 ( p < 0.05), persisting to 48 h in EK3 ( p < 0.05). Sleep quality improved in EK3 at 24 h ( p = 0.023) and 48 h ( p = 0.032). Adverse events did not differ significantly. Conclusions Preoperative oral esketamine (1–3 mg/kg) enhances perioperative comfort in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy. The 2 mg/kg dose offers the best balance of efficacy and safety, while 3 mg/kg provides superior analgesia and opioid sparing.

items.title: Ultrasound‐Guided Supraclavicular Brachiocephalic Vein Cannulation in Pediatric Patients With Hematological Disorders: A Retrospective Comparative Study
items.abstract: Background Central venous access is indispensable for clinical management of pediatric patients with hematological disorders, including chemotherapy administration, blood product transfusion, and critical rescue. Repeated venipuncture attempts, procedural failure, postoperative catheter malposition, and cannulation‐related complications can substantially disrupt subsequent treatment courses and compromise therapeutic efficacy. Aims This retrospective study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and safety of ultrasound‐guided brachiocephalic vein (BCV) cannulation, with the goal of optimizing central venous catheterization protocols, reducing procedure‐related adverse events, and improving the efficiency and safety of treatment via central venous access in pediatric patients. Methods This retrospective study included 580 children (303 subclavian vein [SCV], 277 BCV) who underwent ultrasound‐guided central venous catheterization between January 2021 and December 2024. We compared first‐attempt success rate, overall success rate, procedural duration, intraoperative adverse events, postoperative complications, and catheter malposition. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to improve comparability between the groups with respect to measured baseline covariates. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent risk factors. Results After IPTW, the BCV approach was associated with a higher first‐attempt success rate (OR = 1.72, 95% CI: 1.05–2.81; risk difference [RD] = 0.119, 95% CI: 0.015–0.222) and a higher overall success rate (RD = 0.091, 95% CI: 0.013–0.168). The mean procedural duration was 6 min shorter in the BCV group (95% CI: −9.5 to −2.5). The BCV approach was independently associated with lower odds of intraoperative malposition (OR = 0.096, 95% CI: 0.037–0.249), postoperative malposition (OR = 0.34, 95% CI: 0.16–0.74), and perioperative complications (OR = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.08–0.94). Multivariable regression analysis showed that catheterization approach was independently associated with catheter malposition. Conclusions Compared with SCV, ultrasound‐guided BCV cannulation is associated with higher success rates, shorter procedural duration, and fewer malpositions and complications. This technique may offer particular benefits for children with hematological disorders.

items.title: Intravenous Lidocaine in Children: French Practice, Barriers to Use, and the Need for Pharmacokinetic Data
Comparing Subglottic Ultrasound and Distal Phalanx Width for Pediatric Endotracheal Tube Sizing in a Predominantly School‐Aged Pediatric Cohort: A Prospective Study
items.abstract: Background Accurate endotracheal tube (ETT) sizing is essential in pediatric airway management to optimize ventilation and reduce complications. Traditional methods, including age‐based formulas and distal phalanx width (DPW), may lack precision. Subglottic ultrasound (US) has emerged as a promising tool, but its predictive accuracy compared with DPW remains unclear. This study aimed to compare accuracy, agreement, diagnostic performance, and clinical applicability of subglottic US versus DPW for predicting optimal ETT size in children, while recognizing that the enrolled cohort was predominantly school‐aged. Methods In this prospective observational study, pediatric patients aged 0–12 years undergoing elective or emergency intubation were assessed. Pre‐intubation measurements included subglottic transverse airway diameter by ultrasound (ACUSON Juniper, microconvex probe, 5–10 MHz) and DPW by digital calipers. Predicted ETT sizes were compared with the final clinically accepted cuffed ETT inner diameter confirmed by leak testing and cuff pressure optimization. Agreement was evaluated using Bland–Altman analysis and intraclass correlation coefficients, while diagnostic performance was defined a priori as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), likelihood ratios, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Logistic regression identified predictors of good ETT fit. Results Among 160 patients, the median age was 8.8 years (IQR 7.0–10.5), indicating predominance of older children. Ultrasound‐predicted ETT size showed a stronger correlation with actual size ( r = 0.479, p < 0.001) than DPW ( r = 0.248, p = 0.002). Ultrasound predictions had narrower Bland–Altman limits of agreement, although ultrasound measurement is operator‐dependent. DPW showed poor sensitivity (5.9%) but high specificity (99.3%) for identifying underfit ETTs, with limited overall discrimination (ROC AUC = 0.53). Only subglottic diameter was a significant predictor of good ETT fit. Conclusion Subglottic ultrasound showed better agreement with clinically accepted ETT size than DPW in this predominantly school‐aged pediatric cohort. These findings support the potential role of ultrasound as an adjunct to pediatric airway assessment, but conclusions should be interpreted cautiously in infants and younger children because they were under‐represented. Standardized measurement protocols and operator training are needed before broad implementation.

items.title: Individualizing Pediatric Central Venous Access
Effects of Different Measures for the Treatment of Arterial Hypotension on Cerebral Oxygen Saturation During Pediatric General Anesthesia: An Observational Pilot Study
items.abstract: Background Intraoperative hypotension is a common complication in pediatric anesthesia. The definition of hypotension and treatment strategies are heterogeneous. The association of these treatments with cerebral regional oxygen saturation, measured by near‐infrared spectroscopy, is insufficiently characterized. Aims The study explores whether changes in cerebral regional oxygen saturation, mean arterial pressure, and heart rate differ after the administration of an isotonic fluid bolus, noradrenaline, adrenaline, or cafedrine/theodrenaline for perioperative hypotension in children. Methods This single‐center, observational pilot study included children aged 18 years or younger undergoing noncardiac surgery who developed hypotension requiring treatment. The choice of the intervention was at the discretion of the attending anesthetist and guided by an internal guideline. Cerebral regional oxygen saturation, mean arterial pressure, and heart rate were recorded for 8 min after the first intervention and analyzed relative to the value immediately before treatment. Groups were compared using the area under the curve of these changes and linear mixed‐effects models. Results Forty‐six patients were analyzed. Cerebral regional oxygen saturation immediately before treatment did not differ from the pre‐induction baseline. Cafedrine/theodrenaline was the only treatment associated with a sustained increase in cerebral regional oxygen saturation, with a significantly higher area under the curve than noradrenaline ( p = 0.017), adrenaline ( p = 0.017), and fluid administration ( p < 0.001), which was confirmed by mixed‐effects models. Only cafedrine/theodrenaline was associated with an increase in heart rate. Changes in heart rate were significantly correlated with changes in cerebral regional oxygen saturation (Spearman's ρ = 0.376, p = 0.010), but not with changes in mean arterial pressure. Conclusions Cafedrine/theodrenaline was associated with a sustained increase in cerebral regional oxygen saturation, heart rate, and blood pressure. Noradrenaline, adrenaline, and fluid administration were associated with unchanged or decreasing cerebral regional oxygen saturation. Randomized controlled studies are required to confirm these findings.
