Long-Term Mortality in Sepsis Survivors: A Population-Based Study During 15 Years
items.abstract: Objectives: To evaluate long-term mortality among sepsis survivors in Catalonia over a 15-year period and to identify factors associated with increased mortality within 2 years after hospital discharge. Design: Retrospective population-based cohort study. Setting: Acute-care hospitals in Catalonia, Spain. Patients: Adult and pediatric patients hospitalized with sepsis between 2005 and 2019 identified using the International Classification of Diseases , 9th Revision, Clinical Modification and International Classification of Diseases , 10th Revision, Clinical Modification codes for infection and acute organ dysfunction. Patients who died during hospitalization, were transferred to another facility, or represented readmission episodes were excluded. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Data were obtained from the Catalan Minimum Basic Dataset of Acute-Care Hospitals, with longitudinal follow-up through the Central Registry of Insured Persons. Comorbidities were assessed using the Charlson comorbidity index. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used to identify predictors of long-term mortality. Among 296,554 hospital admissions for sepsis, 237,075 patients (79.9%) survived to hospital discharge. Of these, 42% died (99,571) within 2 years. Long-term mortality increased significantly with age, ranging from 5.8% in patients younger than 15 years to 62% in those older than 84 years ( p < 0.0001), and with comorbidity burden (21%, 38%, 51%, and 67% for Charlson index 0, 1–2, 3–4, and ≥ 5, respectively; p < 0.0001). Neoplasia (hazard ratio [HR], 2.011), liver cirrhosis (HR, 1.562), and dementia (HR, 1.304) were the comorbidities most strongly associated with mortality. Longer hospital stays were also associated with increased mortality. A progressive decline in long-term mortality was observed during 2017–2019. Conclusions: Long-term mortality among sepsis survivors remains high, with more than 40% dying within 2 years after hospital discharge. These findings support the need for structured post-sepsis care strategies focused on high-risk patients, improved continuity of care, and prevention of long-term sepsis-related complications.

items.title: Shortening the Family Satisfaction in the ICU (FS-ICU): Development and Validation of a 12-Item Family Satisfaction Survey for Adult ICUs
items.abstract: Objectives: To develop and validate a shorter Family Satisfaction in the ICU (FS-ICU) questionnaire that reduces survey length while preserving content and psychometric performance for quality improvement and benchmarking. The FS-ICU survey assesses family perceptions of care, communication, and decision-making and has been translated into multiple languages with implementation across diverse health care systems internationally. In a province-wide electronic implementation in Ontario, more than 40% of initiated surveys were incomplete, suggesting that survey length may limit practicality for large-scale quality improvement and benchmarking. Design: Multistage study using provincial FS-ICU survey data and an independent multicenter validation dataset for item reduction, psychometric evaluation, agreement testing, and external validation of a shortened questionnaire. Setting: A 12-member expert working group, convened for a Critical Care Services Ontario initiative, used provincial web-based data from adult ICUs across Ontario to develop a shorter version, FS-ICUshort. External validation was applied to FS-ICUshort using a separate multicenter Canadian revised FS-ICU dataset. Participants: A 12-member expert working group led by Dr. Daren K. Heyland, including administrative staff, ICU clinical staff, patient experience specialists, and quality improvement specialists from Ontario, used provincial FS-ICU rollout data. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Using empirical criteria and expert ratings, the FS-ICU was reduced from 29 to 12 items: seven in the satisfaction-with-care domain (FS-Care) and five in the communication and decision-making domain (FS-DM). FS-ICUshort showed high internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.93 for FS-Care, 0.86 for FS-DM, and 0.94 for total). Confirmatory factor analysis supported a two-factor structure with better fit than a single-factor model. Scores from FS-ICUshort closely matched full FS-ICU, with mean differences less than or equal to 1.1 points on a 0–100 scale and intraclass correlations of 0.97–0.99. External validation replicated these results. Conclusions: The 12-item FS-ICUshort maintains the core content and psychometric quality of the original FS-ICU while significantly reducing length, supporting routine use in ICU family experience measurement and benchmarking.

items.title: Association Between the Neutrophil:Lymphocyte Ratio After Hospitalization for Sepsis and Long-Term Outcomes: A Population-Based Cohort Study
items.abstract: Objectives: Long-term outcomes after sepsis survival remain poor. No clinical laboratory tests are in use for stratifying long-term risk after sepsis, limiting the development of secondary prevention. The peripheral blood neutrophil:lymphocyte ratio (NLR) reflects innate and adaptive immune cell balance, and may reflect an immune milieu which is associated with long-term risk after sepsis. Accordingly, we evaluated the association between the NLR in the weeks after sepsis hospitalization discharge—a time when patients are routinely seen in post-ICU clinics—and long-term outcomes. Design: Population-based cohort study. Setting: Ontario, Canada, 2010–2020. Patients: Adults discharged alive from a sepsis hospitalization. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: The exposure was the first outpatient NLR—derived from the complete blood count—measured 15–90 days after sepsis discharge. Among 37,250 survivors with available NLR, the median (interquartile range [IQR]) time-to-measurement was 34 days (22–54 d), and the median NLR was 2.7 (1.8–4.2). Within 1 year, 17,732 patients (47.6%) were rehospitalized or died (median [IQR] time-to-event, 82 d [27–185 d]). The frequency of rehospitalization or death increased across increasing NLR quartiles: 34.2%, 41.5%, 50.3%, and 64.4% ( p trend < 0.001). Compared with the lowest quartile, adjusted hazard ratios (95% CI) were 1.24 (1.18–1.29), 1.54 (1.48–1.62), and 2.25 (2.15–2.35) across higher quartiles. For most patients, NLR after sepsis returned to its patient-specific presepsis ambient level, which was itself prognostic. Conclusions: Among sepsis survivors, outpatient NLR measured 15–90 days after discharge is strongly associated with 1-year risk of rehospitalization or death. As a simple, widely available biomarker, the NLR may support early postsepsis risk stratification and inform development of secondary prevention strategies.

items.title: The Post-Sepsis Neutrophil: Lymphocyte Ratio: A Population Signal in Search of Individual Meaning
Circulating Cell-Free Mitochondrial DNA, Delirium, and Long-Term Cognitive Impairment in Critically Ill Adults With Sepsis: A Prospective Cohort Study
items.abstract: Objectives: During sepsis, circulating cell-free mitochondrial DNA (ccf-mtDNA) is released and elevated due to cell injury, augments the immune response, and may contribute to organ dysfunction. Delirium is common and deleterious during sepsis, but little is known about the relationship between mitochondrial injury and delirium during sepsis. We sought therefore to examine associations between ccf-mtDNA and delirium and other clinical outcomes during sepsis. Design: Multicenter, prospective cohort study. Setting: Medical and surgical ICUs in university and community hospitals in Nashville, TN. Patients: Four hundred eighty patients with sepsis plus shock and/or acute respiratory failure. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: We measured ccf-mtDNA in plasma collected on multiple days (study days 1, 3, and 5) during sepsis and assessed participants bid for delirium and coma using the validated Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU and Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale. We then assessed survivors’ cognitive function 3 and 12 months after hospital discharge using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status. During sepsis, the adjusted odds of delirium were 7% lower for individuals at the 75th percentile of ccf-mtDNA compared with those at the 25th percentile (odds ratio [OR], 0.93; 95% CI, 0.86–0.99; p = 0.048). ccf-mtDNA was marginally associated with in-hospital mortality (hazard ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.99–1.20; p = 0.08), but was not associated with coma (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.90–1.05; p = 0.31) or 3-month (beta, 0.23; 95% CI, –1.58 to 2.05; p = 0.80) and 12-month (beta, –0.36; 95% CI, –2.13 to 1.42; p = 0.69) cognitive outcomes. Conclusions: In this multicenter, prospective cohort study, higher levels of ccf-mtDNA were associated with lower odds of delirium, a result that contradicted our hypothesis. This provocative finding should be interpreted cautiously until replicated and explained by future studies.

items.title: Normocapnia Versus Mild Hypercapnia During Lung Protective Ventilation in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: A Target Trial Emulation
items.abstract: Objectives: This trial emulation aimed to answer the question: Among patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) who receive lung protective ventilation with low tidal volume, is normocapnia through an increase in respiratory rate associated with lower mortality than mild hypercapnia? Design: Target trial emulation. Setting: Hospitals of the ARDS Network and Prevention and Early Treatment of Acute Lung Injury (PETAL) Network. Patients: Patients with ARDS enrolled in seven ARDS Network and PETAL Network randomized controlled trials. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: A target trial was emulated, assigning participants in a 1:1 ratio to normocapnia (target Pa co 2 35–45 mm Hg) or mild hypercapnia (target Pa co 2 50–55 mm Hg) for 4 days following the initiation of lung protective ventilation. The primary outcome was 90-day in-hospital mortality. Of 5367 potentially eligible subjects, 292 patients were assigned to normocapnia and 292 to mild hypercapnia. Separation in Pa co 2 values was preserved over the 4-day period of emulated intervention. Both groups had median pH greater than or equal to 7.33. Bicarbonate levels, driving pressure, tidal volume, and dead-space fraction did not differ clinically significantly between groups, while median respiratory rate was 33.0 breaths/min in the normocapnia vs. 28.0 breaths/min in the mild hypercapnia group ( p < 0.001). Death within 90 days occurred in 84 of 292 patients (28.8%) in the normocapnia group and in 84 of 292 patients (28.8%) in the mild hypercapnia group (log-rank p = 0.842). This result persisted in subgroups such as older (≥ 65 yr) and obese (body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m 2 ) patients. Conclusions: Among patients with ARDS who received lung protective ventilation, normocapnia through an increase in respiratory rate was not associated with lower mortality than mild hypercapnia. As this finding is derived from a trial emulation, it should be interpreted cautiously given the potential for significant residual bias.

items.title: Alarm Fatigue Across Critical Care Domains: Comparative Insights and Independent Predictors From a Cross-Sectional Multicenter Survey Study
items.abstract: Objectives: Alarm fatigue, the desensitization to excessive false alarms, threatens patient safety and staff performance across critical care domains. It is unclear whether alarm fatigue differs between hospital departments. This study compared alarm fatigue among staff in the ICU, cardiac telemetry ward (CTW), and operating room (OR), and, secondarily, identified its independent determinants. Design: Cross-sectional, multicenter survey study. Setting: ICUs, a CTW, and ORs. Patients: A total of 514 healthcare professionals working in the ICU, CTW, and OR. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Alarm fatigue was assessed using the Dutch-translated Charité Alarm Fatigue Questionnaire, which includes alarm stress and alarm coping subscales. Participants also rated their self-perceived alarm fatigue on a 1–10 scale and the percentage of perceived false alarms. Telemetry staff reported the highest self-perceived alarm fatigue (B = 0.65; 95% CI, 0.06–1.24; p = 0.032) and perceived false alarms (B = 0.77; 95% CI, 0.23–1.30; p = 0.005), while OR staff reported the lowest (B = −1.01; 95% CI, −1.59 to −0.43; p < 0.001). Second, physicians (B = −0.13; 95% CI, −0.25 to −0.01; p < 0.031) and less experienced staff (< 3 mo; B = −0.34; 95% CI, −0.68 to −0.01; p = 0.046) reported lower alarm fatigue. Conclusions: Alarm fatigue varied significantly across departments and professions, being highest in telemetry staff and lowest among physicians and less experienced personnel. Targeted department-specific interventions and longitudinal research are necessary to mitigate alarm fatigue and enhance patient safety.

items.title: Characterization of Urgent ICU Consultations in the Evaluation of Processes of Care and the Outcomes of Children in Hospital (EPOCH) Randomized Clinical Trial
items.abstract: Objectives: Urgent ICU consultation is intended to elicit advice and consider ICU transfer. Our objective was to describe the nature and outcomes of ICU consultations across a global cohort. Design: This is a secondary analysis of patients with one or more ICU consultations. A care episode was defined as consecutive urgent ICU consultations until an ICU admission or at least 2 weeks without an urgent ICU consultation. We describe consultation outcomes for the last care episode. Late escalations were defined by a Children’s Resuscitation Intensity Scale score greater than 2. Setting: Twenty-one centers participating in the Evaluation of Processes of Care and the Outcomes of Children in Hospital (EPOCH) cluster-randomized trial. Patients: There were 4288 urgent ICU consultations in 3625 care episodes for 3000 patients with a median (interquartile range) age of 25 months (5–99 mo). Interventions: In the parent EPOCH trial, hospitals were randomized to Bedside Pediatric Early Warning System or usual care; no intervention was assigned in this secondary analysis. Measurements and Main Results: The outcomes of the 3000 last care episodes were in-consultation death in three (0.1%) and urgent ICU admission in 1477 (49.2%). Among 3000 first, 400 second, and 68 third consultations, the proportions of ICU admission were 42%, 44%, and 47%. The proportions of ICU admissions that were late escalation were similar across groups: 18% for first and second urgent ICU consultations, and 25% for third urgent ICU consultations. among patients having a second urgent ICU consultation, patients who had received resuscitation interventions in their first urgent ICU consultation (and remained on the ward) had more frequent resuscitation events (23.2% vs. 3.4%, p < 0.01) and had a similar frequency of late escalation (31.8% vs. 15.6%, p = 0.07) and ICU admission (51.1% vs. 43.1%, p = 0.40) compared with patients without resuscitation in their first urgent ICU consultation. Conclusions: Urgent consultation to the ICU is common during pediatric hospitalization. Repeated ICU consultation was associated with a similar frequency of late escalation. Resuscitation measures were provided in one of 12 ICU consultations where patients were not admitted to ICU and were a risk factor for late escalation in subsequent consultations.

items.title: The Effect of Guanfacine on Delirium in Surgical and Trauma ICU Patients: A Pilot Randomized Clinical Trial
items.abstract: Objectives: To evaluate the feasibility of conducting a randomized controlled trial investigating guanfacine for ICU delirium, including assessment of recruitment, retention, protocol adherence, and data completeness, while estimating treatment effects to inform future trial design. Design: Single-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial conducted from November 2020 to February 2023. Setting: Surgical and Trauma ICUs at the University of Alabama at Birmingham Hospital. Patients: One hundred critically ill adults with Confusion Assessment Method-ICU-confirmed delirium randomized 1:1 to guanfacine or placebo. Interventions: Patients received 2 mg guanfacine or matching placebo nightly for up to 14 days, or until ICU discharge or delirium resolution. Measurements and Main Results: Primary feasibility outcomes included protocol adherence (target ≥ 90%), retention (target ≥ 80%), recruitment rate (target ≥ 2 patients/mo), and data completeness (target ≥ 95%). Most feasibility targets were achieved: protocol adherence was 100%, retention was 100%, and data completeness was 100%. Recruitment was significantly impacted by COVID-19 pandemic disruptions, achieving 0.9 patients/wk during active recruitment periods. For clinical outcomes, in unadjusted analyses, median delirium and coma-free days were higher with guanfacine than placebo (2 [interquartile range [IQR], 0–6] vs. 1 [IQR, 0–4]; p = 0.02); however, this association was not statistically significant after adjustment for prespecified baseline covariates. ICU and hospital length of stay and duration of mechanical ventilation did not differ significantly between groups. No hemodynamic differences or safety concerns were observed. Conclusions: This pilot study successfully supports feasibility for a definitive trial, with excellent protocol adherence, adequate retention, and preliminary signals that warrant further evaluation. Although adjusted analyses were not statistically significant, the observed unadjusted difference in delirium and coma-free days and favorable safety profile support progression to a multicenter trial informed by these pilot estimates.

items.title: Composite Endpoints in Critical Care Delirium Trials
items.abstract: Delirium is an abnormal mental status, commonly occurring among critically ill patients, in which a person’s attention and awareness change acutely. Delirium is associated with negative outcomes, including death. Furthermore, a longer duration of delirium is associated with long-term cognitive impairment in survivors of critical illness. Hence, there is a need for novel interventions that reduce the duration of delirium; however, measuring and analyzing “duration of delirium” as an endpoint in randomized trials is challenging due to the episodic nature of delirium and the competing events of coma and death, which can bias analyses of duration of delirium. Given these challenges, delirium trials have adopted one of two composite endpoints: delirium- and coma-free days, defined as the number of days alive without delirium or coma for both survivors and nonsurvivors, and an alternative composite that ranks death as the worst state and orders days alive without delirium or coma among survivors. To date, these composite endpoints have not been rigorously evaluated. Hence, herein we use data from the Maximizing Efficacy of Targeted Sedation and Reducing Neurologic Dysfunction (MENDS) trial to motivate the use of composite endpoints in critical care delirium trials, discuss how to define the effect of treatment on each composite endpoint and their clinical interpretability, and present a method for visualizing how the treatment effects accrue over the course of follow-up. Based on these analyses, we provide practical recommendations for the use of composite endpoints in critical care delirium trials, which could be extended to other randomized trials that rely on similar composite endpoints.

items.title: Low Physical Activity and Reported Barriers Among Survivors of Critical Illness: A Mixed-Method Study
items.abstract: Objectives: To examine physical activity levels in survivors of critical illness across 6 months, and to understand the barriers and facilitators of physical activity. Design: Prospective, longitudinal, convergent mixed-methods study. Setting: Functional testing laboratory. Patients: Adults admitted to the ICU for at least 72 hours with acute respiratory failure or sepsis. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Patients wore an accelerometer starting at hospital discharge, at 3- and 6-month follow-up to quantify daily step counts. At 6 months, physical function and patient-reported outcomes were collected in-person, with a subset of participants completing semi-structured interviews. Eighty-two patients were enrolled, with 67 (82%) having physical activity data with median age of 60 years (interquartile range [IQR], 52–66 yr), 54% male, and ICU stay 9.0 days [IQR, 5.8–17.0 d]. The median daily steps were 1358 (IQR, 742–2799) in 50 patients at baseline, 2305 (IQR, 1081–3898) in 54 patients at 3 months, and 2826 (IQR, 1609–4781) in 44 patients at 6 months. Higher comorbidity burden and earlier measurement associated with lower step counts. At 6 months, patients walked a mean of 344 ± 169 meters on the 6-minute walk test and reported being sedentary a median of 300 min/days (150–480 min/d). Eleven participants completed interviews, yielding three themes: 1) “a marathon, not a sprint”: the extended ICU recovery trajectory; 2) engagement in physical activity is highly regulated by personal context; 3) value-driven and motivation-informed physical activity decisions. Mixed-methods integration demonstrated that qualitative themes expanded upon quantitative findings to explain nonlinear recovery patterns, contextualizing persistent sedentary behavior, and revealing that motivational and behavioral gaps are not captured by accelerometry. Conclusions: Survivors showed gradual improvement in daily steps over 6 months yet remained below recommended activity levels. Survivorship and attrition biases may lead to overestimation of step counts, further warranting larger studies. Integrating quantitative and qualitative data reveals modifiable contextual factors that may inform the design of pragmatic physical activity interventions.

items.title: Evaluation of Sequential Organ Failure Assessment-2 Performance Across Demographic Subgroups: An External Validation Using MIMIC-IV
items.abstract: Objectives: To evaluate the discrimination and calibration of the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA)-2 score for ICU mortality across demographic subgroups defined by age, sex, race and ethnicity, primary language, and insurance status. Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting: Single academic medical center in the northeastern United States (Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA), using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care-IV database (version 3.1), 2008–2022, a dataset external to the SOFA-2 development cohort. Patients: Adult patients (≥ 18 yr) with at least one ICU admission. The first ICU admission of the first qualifying hospitalization per patient was analyzed. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: First-day SOFA-2 scores were calculated from the worst values recorded during the first 24 hours of ICU admission across six organ systems, with ICU mortality as the primary outcome. Discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and calibration using intercept and slope, with subgroup differences in AUROC estimated by bootstrap resampling. Among 64,015 ICU patients (mean [ sd ] age, 64.6 [17.1] yr; 56.1% male; 66.1% White), overall AUROC was 0.77 (95% CI, 0.76–0.77). Discrimination declined significantly with age: AUROC, 0.85 (0.83–0.87) for ages 18–44 years vs. 0.72 (0.70–0.73) for ages 75 or older (ΔAUROC, −0.14 [95% CI, −0.16 to −0.11]), with systematic underprediction in older patients. Discrimination was significantly decreased among non-English speakers (ΔAUROC, −0.04) but did not differ across documented racial/ethnic groups. Patients with missing demographic information had markedly higher mortality than the overall cohort rate of 7.2% (14.1% for missing race/ethnicity; 23.1% for missing language). Conclusions: SOFA-2 demonstrated good overall performance but with clinically meaningful variation across subgroups, particularly with age and language. Patients with missing demographic data experienced markedly higher mortality. These findings argue for routine equity evaluation as a complement to traditional validation of clinical prediction tools.

items.title: National Early Warning Score 2-Guided Sepsis Hour-1 Bundle Care for Adults With Suspected Sepsis in the Emergency Department: A Hybrid Type 1 Effectiveness-Implementation Stepped-Wedge Randomized Controlled Trial Pilot Study (NEWS-1 TRIPS)
items.abstract: Objectives: To increase the uptake of the Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle, we implemented a novel sepsis care model (National Early Warning Score [NEWS]-1 care), in which the Hour-1 Bundle is objectively triggered by a high NEWS-2 (≥ 5). We aimed to determine the feasibility of a full-scale type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation trial of this model. Design: A pilot type 1 hybrid trial, comprising a stepped-wedge cluster randomized controlled trial and mixed-methods implementation evaluation with staff focus group interviews and an anonymous survey guided by the Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance framework. Setting: Four emergency departments in Hong Kong. Patients: Adult patients of 18 years or older with a clinical diagnosis of infection requiring hospitalization and a NEWS-2 greater than or equal to 5. Interventions: Implementation of the Hour-1 Bundle when NEWS-2 was greater than or equal to 5. Measurements and Main Results: The primary outcome was the feasibility of a full-scale hybrid trial, evaluated based on 14 progression criteria. Preliminary clinical effectiveness and safety were assessed, alongside implementation barriers and facilitators. During the implementation phase, compliance with lactate, blood culture, and antibiotics increased significantly. All progression criteria were met, except for suboptimal overall bundle compliance (56.1%). Exploratory intention-to-treat analysis (standard care group, n = 102; NEWS-1 group, n = 98) showed no significant between-group difference in 30-day all-cause mortality (standard care group, 3.9%; NEWS-1 group, 9.2%; absolute risk difference, 5.3%; 95% CI –1.6% to 12.1%); in-hospital, 90-day all-cause, or sepsis-related mortality; need for mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, intensive care, or surgery; or ventilator-free days and adverse events. Implementation evaluation identified 15 barriers and 13 facilitators. Conclusions: The effectiveness of NEWS-1 care remained uncertain, though adverse events were rare. A full-scale hybrid stepped-wedge trial is feasible but requires a much larger sample size. Real-world implementation barriers and facilitators should be considered in sepsis management guidelines.

items.title: New-Onset Atrial Fibrillation in Critically Ill Patients: A Systematic Review of In-Hospital and Post-Discharge Outcomes
items.abstract: Objectives: This systematic review and meta-analysis determines the incidence of new-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) in critically ill patients, risks of post-discharge systemic thromboembolism, anticoagulation therapy, and the proportion diagnosed with AF post-discharge. Data Sources: A search of registered databases (PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and CINAHL) was performed from inception to April 20, 2026. Study Selection: Eligible studies included critically ill patients (≥ 18 yr old) who developed NOAF during admission to general ICUs or high-dependency units. NOAF was defined as AF in patients without prior history of AF. Data Extraction: Data were independently extracted from full-text versions of included studies by nonblinded reviewers. Data Synthesis: A Bayesian meta-analysis was conducted on 54 studies (367,896 patients) with a random-effects model using R (Version 4.3.3). Pooled incidence of NOAF in critically ill patients was 10.6% (95% credible interval [CrI], 8.6–12.9%). Absolute risk of post-discharge systemic thromboembolism was 7.1% (95% CrI, 4.5–11.0%), changing to 6.9% (95% CrI, 4.2–11.6%) after age and sex adjustment. Evidence from six studies reports that critically ill patients with NOAF had 1.94 times (95% CrI, 1.23–3.29) higher relative risk of systemic thromboembolism post-discharge than patients without NOAF, rising to 2.01 (95% CrI, 1.54–2.80) with adjustment. Absolute and relative risk are evaluated with follow-up durations ranging from 1.5 months to 5 years, with variable anticoagulation exposure. Anticoagulation rates were low: 32.9% in-hospital (95% CrI, 14.6–57.9%) and 35.9% post-discharge (95% CrI, 19.7–55.9%). On follow-up, 23.9% (95% CrI, 13.9–38.5%) of critically ill patients with NOAF were subsequently diagnosed with AF. Conclusions: Our review suggests that NOAF during critical illness is associated with significantly increased risk of post-discharge systemic thromboembolism and subsequent AF diagnosis. However, rates of anticoagulation initiation remain low, highlighting the need for improved risk stratification and targeted strategies post-discharge.

items.title: The Impact of Hospital Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation Volume and Its Distribution Across ICUs on Adult Patients’ Outcomes: An Analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization Registry
items.abstract: Objectives: Research from a prior era of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) found that higher hospital ECMO volume was associated with higher survival rates, but it did not examine whether distributing ECMO volume across multiple ICUs affected this relationship. Design: Retrospective analysis of the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) registry. Setting: ECMO centers contributing to the registry. Patients: Adult patients required ECMO support from 2012 to 2023. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: We analyzed adult patients from the ELSO registry (2012–2023), adjusting for hospital factors and case mix using multivariable hierarchical logistic regression. The main outcome was in-hospital mortality. Hospital experience was measured by the annual number of adult ECMO cases and total ECMO hours. Volume-outcome associations were modeled for all centers and by total adult ICUs per center. We included 115,849 adults on ECMO across 495 hospitals. Model estimates showed small decreases in mortality odds with higher annual case counts (odds ratio [OR], 0.98; 95% CI, 0.97–0.99 per 10-case increase) and ECMO hours (OR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.99–1.00 per 1000 hr increase). Hospitals with one ICU had a median of 10 cases (interquartile interval [IQI], 3–25 cases), while those with four or more ICUs had a median of 50 (IQI, 28–91). Adjusted mortality was higher in centers delivering ECMO across four+ ICUs compared with one ICU (OR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.06–1.31), the annual case model (OR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.06–1.26), and the annual ECMO hours model. Higher volume was associated with a reduction in the odds of mortality for hospitals with four+ ICUs compared with those with one ICU (OR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.96–1.00 per 10 cases and OR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.99–1.00 per 1000 hr). Conclusions: Higher hospital ECMO volume is associated with reduced mortality. Hospitals with more adult ICUs that perform ECMO may experience higher mortality, which may be explained by increased patient complexity and is offset by the higher center volume. More research is needed to better understand the optimum design of ECMO centers.

items.title: A Telemedicine Intervention for Spontaneous Awakening and Breathing Trials in Small and Large ICUs
items.abstract: Objectives: To evaluate the effect of a tele-critical care (TCC) daily audit-and-feedback intervention on spontaneous awakening trial and spontaneous breathing trial protocol compliance. Design: Pre-post quality improvement study. Setting. Single health system composed of 14 hospitals in the Midwestern United States. Patients: A total of 8909 patients of 18 years or older receiving mechanical ventilation via endotracheal tube for more than 1 calendar day between October 01, 2022 and September 20, 2024. Interventions: Daily in the early afternoon, TCC nurses reviewed mechanically ventilated patients to determine whether a spontaneous awakening trial and spontaneous breathing trial had occurred. They contacted the bedside nurse if no trial had occurred and no weaning exclusion criteria were noted during a manual chart review. Measurements and Main Results: The coprimary outcomes were the proportion of ventilator days during each ventilator episode with documentation of spontaneous awakening trials and spontaneous breathing trials. Linear mixed effects models were used to examine the effect of the intervention on each outcome stratified by ICU size (large ≥ 15 beds or small < 15 beds). Spontaneous awakening trial documentation improved over time throughout the entire period, but the rate of improvement increased significantly after the telemedicine intervention (preintervention slope: 0.2% increase per 30 d; 95% CI, –0.2% to 0.6% and postintervention slope: 1.4% increase per 30 d; 95% CI, 1.0% to 1.9%; p < 0.001 for intervention-time interaction). The telemedicine intervention was associated with a step increase in spontaneous breathing trial documentation in small ICUs (absolute increase, 12.8%; 95% CI, 8.7–16.9%) but not in large ICUs (absolute increase, –0.1%; 95% CI, –1.8% to 1.6%; p = 0.02 for intervention-ICU size interaction). Conclusions: The telemedicine intervention was associated with increased spontaneous awakening trials and spontaneous breathing trials selectively in small ICUs. Telemedicine may have promoted practice standardization in small ICUs where exposure to ventilated patients was infrequent. Local ICU characteristics may impact the effectiveness of TCC interventions.

items.title: Structured Patient and Family-Centered Rounding in the ICU is Associated With Increased Family Confidence in Staff Compassion and Perceived Quality of Information Shared
items.abstract: Objectives: Determine whether inviting families to participate in structured, multidisciplinary rounding in the ICU can lead to improved quality of information shared and greater overall confidence in the care delivered to patients. Design: Pre- and postimplementation observational study based on surveys provided by the Society of Critical Care Medicine—Patient-Centered Outcomes Research Institute initiative. Setting: Academic teaching hospital with 21 medical (closed unit) and 25 surgical (open unit) ICU beds. Subjects: Family members and care providers of critically ill adults of 18 years and older. Interventions: Families and clinicians were surveyed before and after implementation of a quality initiative to promote greater patient and family-centeredness in daily ICU rounds, using a structured and scripted rounding template. Additional information was gathered regarding provider attitudes toward the incorporation of families in rounds. Measurements and Main Results: In pre-and postintervention periods, 36 and 28 families were surveyed in the MICU, and 44 and 42 families were surveyed in the SICU, respectively. In pre-and postintervention periods, respectively, 53 and 48 clinicians were surveyed in the MICU, and 46 and 28 clinicians were surveyed in the SICU. Clinician perceptions improved favorably in the MICU, with statistically significant improvements falling under the category of family welcoming, presence, and participation in decision-making; less so in the SICU. Family perceptions improved in almost all parameters in the MICU, with statistical significance achieved in perceived interest in patient needs, control of agitation and pain, and consistency and honesty of information shared. Similar patterns were observed in the SICU but did not reach statistical significance. Conclusions: Structured, multi-disciplinary rounding with regular inclusion of family members and bedside nurses was associated with significantly greater family confidence in the quality and honesty of information shared, and an increase in perceived compassion in the care provided by ICU staff. Clinician perceptions regarding family inclusion on rounds were generally positive.

items.title: Global Prevalence of Obstetric Causes of Critical Illness in Pregnancy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Objectives: To determine the prevalence, risks, and outcomes of obstetric causes of critically ill pregnant women admitted to the ICU. Data Sources: We searched the PubMed, Scopus, Embase, Ovid, and ScienceDirect databases up to May 15, 2026. STUDY SELECTION: We included studies reporting primary data on critically ill pregnant and postpartum women (up to 48 d post-delivery) admitted to an ICU, with relevant obstetric risk factors and maternal outcomes. Data Extraction: Two reviewers independently performed data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment using the adapted Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. The pooled prevalence was estimated using a random-effects model with 95% CIs. Data Synthesis: Of the 3,735 total records, 50 studies met the eligibility criteria, encompassing 7,756,232 women receiving obstetric care in tertiary hospitals across 20 countries, with 49,299 ICU admissions. Globally, 1.0% (95% CI, 0.8–1.3%) of pregnant and postpartum women experience critical illness and require admission to an ICU. The frequency varies according to the country’s income levels, with the highest in low-income countries (4.1%) and the lowest in high-income countries (0.5%). Notably, 72.3% of ICU admissions were attributed to known obstetric causes, primarily obstetric hemorrhage (23.3%) and hypertension in pregnancy (26.9%). Nearly 33.3% of ICU patients required either respiratory or transfusion support, and the maternal mortality rate among ICU-admitted obstetric women was 8.5%. Conclusions: Nearly one in 100 pregnancies require admission to intensive care due to critical illness, and nearly three-quarters of these admissions were due to direct obstetric causes, with high maternal morbidity and mortality. Obstetric hemorrhage and hypertensive disorders account for the majority of ICU admissions. Strengthening obstetric care in resource-limited settings through the expansion and optimization of intensive care services is essential for improving maternal and neonatal outcomes and reducing preventable morbidity and mortality.

items.title: Neurological Outcomes of Rhythm Transitions in Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest With Initial Nonshockable Rhythms: A Nationwide Population-Based Study
items.abstract: Objectives: To evaluate the prognostic implications of rhythm transitions between asystole and pulseless electrical activity (PEA) in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients with initial nonshockable rhythms. Design: Nationwide population-based observational study. Setting: Nationwide OHCA Registry of South Korea, managed by the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency. Patients: Consecutive adult (≥ 18 yr old) OHCA patients with nonshockable rhythms from January 1, 2016 to December 31, 2021. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Patients were categorized into four groups based on rhythm changes during cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR): asystole-to-asystole (A–A), asystole-to-PEA (A–P), PEA-to-asystole (P–A), and PEA-to-PEA (P–P). The primary outcome was good neurologic outcome at hospital discharge, defined as a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1–2. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to adjust for measured confounding. In the primary IPTW model, weighted risks of good neurologic outcome were 0.101% in A–A, 0.231% in A–P, 0.384% in P–A, and 0.874% in P–P. Compared with A–A, the odds of good neurologic outcome were higher in A–P (odds ratio [OR], 2.28; 95% CI, 1.78–2.93; risk difference [RD], 0.130 percentage points), P–A (OR, 3.80; 95% CI, 3.01–4.80; RD, 0.283 percentage points), and P–P (OR, 8.70; 95% CI, 6.98–10.83; RD, 0.773 percentage points). Compared with A–P, P–A had higher odds of good neurologic outcome (OR, 1.66; 95% CI, 1.39–1.99; RD, 0.153 percentage points). Conclusions: Asystole conversion to PEA during CPR was associated with a better neurologic outcome than persistent asystole. Although transitioning from PEA to asystole was associated with lower odds of a good outcome compared with persistent PEA, it was associated with a better outcome than A–P transitions. Recognizing these patterns may provide prognostic context beyond a single rhythm assessment.

items.title: The Impact of Early Changes in Albumin Levels on Long-Term Kidney and Mortality Outcomes in Patients With Acute Kidney Injury Undergoing Continuous Kidney Replacement Therapy
items.abstract: Objectives: To investigate the association between early changes in the levels of serum albumin during continuous kidney replacement therapy (CKRT) and long-term dialysis dependence and mortality in patients with acute kidney injury who survived for 90 days or more days after CKRT initiation. Design: A multicenter retrospective cohort study. Setting: Eight university-affiliated tertiary hospitals in South Korea participating in the LINking health medical records, biospecimens, and biosignals in Korean patients with Acute kidney injury consortium cohort. Patients: The study involved 1087 adult patients with acute kidney injury who survived for 90 or more days after CKRT initiation between January 2017 and June 2022. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Based on albumin levels at CKRT initiation and on day 7, patients were categorized into the persistent, resolved, new-onset, and no hypoalbuminemia groups. A composite of progression to end-stage kidney disease and all-cause mortality within 365 days was the primary outcome. The composite outcome occurred in 33.4% (363/1087) of the patients. The adjusted odds ratio (aOR) for the primary outcome was significantly higher in all groups when compared with the no hypoalbuminemia group (persistent: aOR, 2.64; 95% CI, 1.73–4.04; p < 0.001; resolved: aOR, 2.27; 95% CI, 1.38–3.75; p < 0.001; new-onset: aOR, 1.68; 95% CI, 1.06–2.68; p = 0.028). No hypoalbuminemia group was associated with the most favorable prognosis, whereas persistent hypoalbuminemia was associated with the worst outcomes. Conclusions: During CKRT, early albumin level changes are associated with long-term kidney failure and mortality risk. Persistent hypoalbuminemia predicts the worst outcomes. Even in patients without baseline hypoalbuminemia, early decline in albumin is associated with worse prognosis.

items.title: Dynamics of Mitochondrial Structure, Biogenesis and Function in Skeletal Muscle of Critically Ill Patients
items.abstract: Objectives: To define the timing and phenotype of mitochondrial ultrastructural remodeling and electron transport chain (ETC) function in skeletal muscle during early critical illness. Design: Secondary analysis of a prospective observational study with serial muscle biopsies. Setting: Adult ICU. Patients: Thirty-three mechanically ventilated ICU patients (median age, 49 yr; 27% women) with Sequential Organ Failure Assessment greater than or equal to 9 on three consecutive days; skeletal muscle biopsies of the vastus lateralis muscle at ICU day 5 ( n = 29) and day 15 ( n = 22). Healthy subjects served as controls. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: Vastus lateralis biopsies were analyzed by electron microscopy with stereology, quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR), Western blotting, and spectrophotometric ETC enzyme assays (reported per tissue weight and normalized to citrate synthase [CS]). Intact mitochondrial profiles were reduced vs. controls (fold change vs. controls: day 5, 0.24 [0.18–0.34]; p = 0.039 and day 15, 0.20 [0.16–0.33]; p = 0.011) and disturbed profiles increased (day 5, 5.62 [3.20–7.17]; p < 0.001 and day 15, 5.20 [3.67–6.36]; p = 0.001), with reduced volume density of intact mitochondria (day 5, 0.33 [0.20–0.49]; p = 0.009 and day 15, 0.32 [0.21–0.50]; p = 0.005). Inner mitochondrial membrane surface-to-volume ratio was reduced at day 5 (0.69 [0.49–0.89]; p = 0.022) and remained unchanged at day 15. Complex III tissue activity was reduced at day 5 (85.6 [22.1–133.3] vs. 151.4 [100.5–205.0]; p = 0.015) and day 15 (50.5 [36.0–69.8]; p = 0.001), remaining reduced after CS normalization (day 5, 0.83 [0.34–1.49]; p = 0.040 and day 15, 0.87 [0.65–0.93]; p = 0.007). Complex IV activity remained reduced before and after CS normalization at both time points (all p < 0.001). CS activity declined by day 15 (56.3 [52.7–65.1] vs. 95.6 [80.1–133.0]; p = 0.001 and day 15 vs. day 5; p = 0.041). qRT-PCR and Western blot supported reduced ETC components and altered biogenesis signaling. Conclusions: Skeletal muscle mitochondrial ultrastructure is altered by ICU day 5 and remains abnormal at day 15, with persistent complex III/IV dysfunction after CS normalization. These findings define an early sustained mitochondrial remodeling phenotype in skeletal muscle during critical illness.

items.title: Language Concordance in Critical Care: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Objectives: Language barriers are associated with differences in care delivery processes and outcomes in critical care settings, with differences despite language assistance services. Less is known about outcomes associated with language concordant care. Language concordance is a linguistic match between a patient’s preferred language and the language used by their care team. We undertook a systematic review to examine the measurement and impact of language concordant care delivery during critical illness, inclusive of the critical care recovery period after hospitalization. Data Sources and Study Selection: A systematic review was conducted in PubMed, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Embase, and Cochrane of English-language publications from database inception to March 3, 2026. Studies that investigated adults in critical care and post-ICU recovery clinic settings that included measurement of language concordance were included. Study quality was evaluated by the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist. Data Synthesis: Of 1,682 unique records identified, 11 were eligible for inclusion (128,181 total patients; mean [ sd ] age, 68.4 [17.9 yr]; 72,872 [56.9%] male and 55,082 [43.1%] female). Six studies assessed clinical decision-making. Reported outcomes included code status changes, family conferences, communication complexity, delirium, length of stay, mechanical ventilation, and mortality. Due to significant heterogeneity in study analyses and reported outcomes, data were not pooled for quantitative analysis. Conclusions: Current evidence suggests that language-concordant care may influence clinically meaningful processes of critical care, warranting interventional studies to guide care delivery recommendations.

items.title: Association of Care Intensity With Survival and Long-Term Cost-Effectiveness in Sepsis Without Initial Organ Support After Emergency Admission: A Multicenter Cohort Study in Japan
items.abstract: Objectives: To identify subgroups of patients hospitalized for community-acquired sepsis without initial organ support who may derive survival and cost-effectiveness benefits from ICU or high-dependency care unit (HDU) admission. Design: Retrospective cohort study. Setting: A 140-hospital Japanese database (April 2016–March 2024). Patients: Adults admitted via emergency ambulance for community-acquired sepsis not requiring extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, mechanical ventilation, catecholamines, or renal replacement therapy before or on the antimicrobial-initiation day. Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: We compared ICU and HDU admissions, each vs. general ward (GW) admission, balancing patient characteristics using overlap propensity-score weighting. In-hospital mortality was estimated as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% CIs using modified Poisson regression. Cost-effectiveness was measured by the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) in 3-year costs per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Among 28,211 patients (GW, 18,349; HDU, 8,706; ICU, 1,156), ICU and HDU admissions were not associated with lower mortality overall (HDU vs. GW; RR, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.92–1.06 and ICU vs. GW; RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 0.92–1.22). However, HDU admission was associated with lower mortality among patients with Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score greater than or equal to 6 (RR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.75–0.99) or Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score less than or equal to 12 (RR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.71–0.92). Under the Japanese (50,000 USD/QALY) and U.S. (100,000 USD/QALY) thresholds, ICU and HDU admissions were not cost-effective overall (ICERs > 200,000 USD/QALY). However, the HDU subgroup with GCS score less than or equal to 12 (ICER, 47,738 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 45,918–49,558) was cost-effective under both thresholds, and that with SOFA score greater than or equal to 6 (ICER, 55,319 USD/QALY; 95% CI, 52,018–58,624) met the U.S. threshold. Conclusions: ICU or HDU admission was not associated with survival or economic benefits overall, whereas HDU subgroups (SOFA score ≥ 6 or GCS score ≤ 12) were associated with lower mortality and better cost-effectiveness. These findings may help optimize resource allocation.

items.title: A Guytonian Atlas of Venous Return in Septic Shock: Reconstruction of Hemodynamic States
items.abstract: Objectives: To reconstruct venous return physiology across published studies of septic shock and characterize the distribution of circulatory states represented in the literature. Design: Exploratory physiologic reconstruction study. Setting: Secondary analysis of published hemodynamic observations. Patients: Adult patients with septic shock reported in studies containing sufficient information for reconstruction of mean circulatory filling pressure analogue (Pmca) and related parameters including venous return driving pressure (VRdP) and resistance to venous return (RVR). Interventions: None. Measurements and Main Results: A total of 150 observations were available. Median Pmca, central venous pressure (CVP), VRdP, and RVR were 17.3 mm Hg, 9.0 mm Hg, 7.9 mm Hg, and 1.04 mm Hg/min/L, respectively. Empirical quartiles identified four recurrent circulatory phenotypes: reduced filling pressure/gradient, preserved venous return, elevated venous pressure, and high-resistance venous return. The preserved venous return pattern demonstrated the highest median cardiac output (CO), whereas the high-resistance pattern exhibited the lowest flow despite comparable filling pressures. In exploratory adjusted analyses incorporating available vasopressor exposure and fluid-therapy context, VRdP remained strongly associated with CO (β, 1.03 L/min/mm Hg; 95% CI, 0.80–1.25; p < 0.001). When Pmca and CVP were entered separately, Pmca was positively associated with CO (β, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.79–1.25; p < 0.001), whereas CVP was inversely associated with CO (β, –1.03; 95% CI, –1.26 to –0.80; p < 0.001). Conclusions: Published hemodynamic observations in septic shock occupy distinct Guytonian phenotypes characterized by different combinations of circulatory filling pressure, venous pressure, and RVR. Reconstruction of venous return geometry may provide a physiologic framework for interpreting circulatory heterogeneity in septic shock.

items.title: Reduced desaturation-based detection of sleep apnea events in self-identified Black individuals across two cohorts
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Rationale Pulse oximetry may overestimate oxygen saturation in individuals with darker skin pigmentation, potentially reducing detection of desaturation during sleep-disordered breathing. Objectives To assess racial/ethnic differences in desaturation-based obstructive event detection and cardiovascular risk, and evaluate heart-rate response as an oximetry-independent marker for risk stratification. Methods We analyzed participants without cardiovascular disease in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis(MESA) and Sleep Heart Health Study(SHHS). We modeled desaturation-based AHI relative to airflow-defined AHI and examined AHI-ΔHR6, defined by respiratory events with a heart-rate increase ≥6 beats/min. Adjusted Cox models evaluated associations with a composite outcome, major adverse cardiovascular events or all-cause mortality(MACE/mortality). Measurements and Main Results Black participants had 21% and 20% lower proportions of airflow-defined events meeting the ≥4% desaturation criterion than White participants in MESA (ratio 0.79[95% CI,0.68–0.93]; p = 0.003) and SHHS (0.80[0.68–0.94]; p = 0.008), respectively. No other racial/ethnic group showed a lower proportion of airflow-defined events meeting desaturation criteria than White participants. AHI-ΔHR6 event detection was similar between Black and White participants in both cohorts. In Whites participants, desaturation-based events were associated with MACE/mortality in MESA but not in SHHS, while desaturation-based AHI measures were not significantly associated with MACE/mortality in Black individuals in either cohort. In contrast, AHI-ΔHR6 was associated with MACE/mortality in MESA (HR 1.33[1.09–1.63];p=0.006) and SHHS (1.26[1.02–1.55]; p = 0.033). Conclusions Desaturation-based scoring identified a lower proportion of reduced flow events in Black than White participants, whereas heart-rate-response-based event detection was similar across groups, suggesting oximetry-related under-detection in individuals with darker pigment.

items.title: Therapeutic Targeting of the Macrophage YTHDC1/TIGAR/NF-κB Axis Mitigates Pulmonary Hypertension
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Rationale Immune dysregulation is a pivotal driver of pulmonary hypertension (PH) pathogenesis, yet therapeutic targeting of inflammation has yielded limited clinical success. Although cytosolic RNA-binding proteins are known to regulate immune responses in PH, the specific role of the nuclear m⁶A reader YTHDC1 remains undefined. Objectives To elucidate the function of macrophage YTHDC1 in orchestrating inflammatory vascular remodeling during PH. Methods Expression profiles of YTHDC1 and TP53-induced glycolysis and apoptosis regulator (TIGAR) were evaluated in human and rodent PH specimens. The mechanistic and therapeutic roles of this axis were assessed using myeloid-specific knockout mice and pharmacological inhibitors (YL-5092, 5Z-7-oxozeaenol) across hypoxia-, SU5416/hypoxia-, and monocrotaline-induced PH models. Measurements and Main Results In patients with idiopathic or connective tissue disease-associated PAH, YTHDC1 and TIGAR expression levels were elevated in pulmonary and circulating macrophages, correlating with disease severity. In murine models, myeloid-specific deletion of Ythdc1 or Tigar conferred profound protection against hypoxia- and SU5416/hypoxia-induced PH. Mechanistically, hypoxia upregulated Ythdc1, which directly bound and stabilized Tigar mRNA. The subsequent accumulation of Tigar protein operated non-enzymatically via a specific domain (residues 152-161) to interact with Tak1, thereby activating the NF-κB cascade, augmenting pro-inflammatory cytokine release, and driving pulmonary artery smooth muscle cell proliferation. Pharmacological inhibition of YTHDC1 (YL-5092) or disruption of the TIGAR-TAK1 interaction (5Z-7-oxozeaenol) effectively attenuated vascular inflammation and mitigated PH progression in diverse rodent models. Conclusions The macrophage YTHDC1/TIGAR/NF-κB signaling axis acts as a critical determinant of inflammation and vascular remodeling in PH, representing a potential biomarker and therapeutic target for this disease.

items.title: The Future of AI in Critical Care: An Exploration in Ten Parables
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: We cannot know how artificial intelligence (AI) will ultimately change critical care, only that it is driving substantial change quickly. Through ten parables, we describe plausible benefits, harms, and trade-offs involving prognosis, monitoring, liability, research, clinical work, data governance, education, and triage. These parables are not predictions. They are intended to help clinicians, institutions, and regulators envision a range of potential scenarios and think broadly about which applications to pursue, which risks to consider, and which rules to establish before AI systems become entrenched. Each parable reveals how the outlook for AI in critical care is characterized by uncertainty. This includes uncertainty about what a single prediction means for the patient in front of us, how an application built and tested in one setting performs in another, accountability frameworks, professional practice and learning, patient privacy and autonomy, and more. Within each parable we try to keep visible what current evidence already supports and what remains speculative. We close with a set of questions designed to focus that speculation among the interested parties who will shape the future of AI in critical care.

items.title: Clinician-guided digital CBT-I improves sleep quality and apnea severity in patients with co-morbid insomnia and OSA: A Double-Blind, Randomized Clinical Trial
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Rationale Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the accepted first-line treatment for insomnia, but its scalability and safety in patients with co-morbid insomnia and obstructive sleep apnea (COMISA) remain unclear. Clinician-guided digital CBT-I (D-CBT-I) is a potential treatment option that may address these limitations in COMISA. Objective To evaluate the effectiveness of clinician-guided D-CBT-I versus sleep hygiene education (SHE) in patients with COMISA. Methods This randomized trial (n = 88) compared clinician-guided D-CBT-I (6 weekly online sessions: sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, relapse prevention) with SHE alone. Blinded outcome assessments were conducted at baseline, posttreatment (6 weeks), and 3-month follow-up. Primary outcomes were Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores at posttreatment and 3-month follow-up. Secondary outcomes included daytime sleepiness, sleep parameters, OSA severity, neurocognitive function, and adverse events. Measurements and Main Results At 3-month follow-up, intention-to-treat analysis showed significantly greater improvements with D-CBT-I versus SHE on ISI (−9.5 vs. −4.0 points; d = −1.18, P = 0.001) and PSQI (−4.9 vs. −1.8 points; d = −0.87, P = 0.001); D-CBT-I also reduced subjective sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale; -3.4 vs. -1.0 points; d = -0.68, P < 0.001). At posttreatment, D-CBT-I reduced the apnea–hypopnea index (attended in-laboratory polysomnography; −6.0 vs. +2.0 events/h; d = -0.64, P = 0.019). Although transient increases in ESS occurred at weeks 2-4, no functional impairment or sleepiness-related adverse events were reported. Additional benefits were observed in metacognition and executive function. Conclusion Clinician-guided D-CBT-I improved insomnia and OSA severity, and enhanced cognitive function in COMISA patients. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry; NO.: ChiCTR2500099854; URL: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=267457

items.title: Lung Allograft Function After Primary Graft Dysfunction in the Lung Transplant Outcomes Group Cohort
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Rationale Primary graft dysfunction (PGD) after lung transplant is associated with increased mortality. Whether PGD increases mortality via long-term effects on allograft function is poorly understood. Objective Evaluate the association of PGD with potential lung function and chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD). Methods We included lung transplant recipients enrolled in an 8-center prospective cohort study from 2007-2018. PGD was defined by ISHLT criteria. Linear mixed effects and logistic regression models evaluated the association between PGD and maximum potential forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) and whether Global Lung Function Initiative defined (GLI) predicted FEV1 was attained, respectively. Flexible parametric survival models evaluated the association between PGD and CLAD, accounting for confounding and mortality as a competing risk. Measurements and Main Results Among 2419 recipients, 510 had PGD. Recipients with PGD had lower maximum potential FEV1 (-311 ml, 95% CI -245 to -377 ml) and were less likely to achieve GLI-predicted FEV1 (probability difference -12.5%, 95% CI -17 to -8%). 930 recipients developed CLAD (405 obstructive, 525 restrictive) over median (IQR) 5.9 (3.0-8.0 years). The 5-year cumulative incidence of CLAD did not differ by PGD (cumulative difference: -2.2%, 95% CI - 6.4% to 1.9%). This association was not modified by age, sex, BMI, pretransplant diagnosis, or transplant type. PGD was not associated with a difference in cumulative incidence of obstructive or restrictive CLAD (cumulative difference -1.2% and -0.8%, respectively). Conclusion PGD is associated with reduced lung function and lower likelihood of achieving GLI-predicted maximum potential lung function but not CLAD.

items.title: Pragmatic trial of a self-directed intervention for weight loss in obstructive sleep apnea (POWER)
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Rationale Self-directed lifestyle interventions may improve access to weight loss care in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), but effectiveness in routine practice is unknown. Objective Test whether a proactively delivered self-directed lifestyle intervention improves weight and sleep-related quality of life versus usual care. Methods POWER enrolled patients with OSA and body mass index of 30-45 kg/m2, recruited from Veteran Affairs (VA) sites nationwide, and randomized participants to a self-directed intervention based on the Diabetes Prevention Program with video-based sessions, readings, and regular coaching reminders or usual care. Co-primary outcomes were change in Functional Outcomes of Sleep Questionnaire (FOSQ) and clinical weight in kilograms (kg) from baseline to 12 months post-randomization. Given two primary outcomes, we defined significance at p = 0.025. Measurements and Main Results This trial randomized 696 participants. Mean age was 56.2 years (SD 12.2), with 19.7% identifying as female. Clinical weights at 12 months were available for 81.9% of intervention and 83.6% of control participants. Unadjusted weight declined 2.1 kg (SD 6.8) in intervention and 0.9 kg (SD 5.9) in control (adjusted between-group difference: -1.1 kg, 95%CI -2.0, -0.1; p = 0.037). FOSQ measures were available at 12 months for 78.2% of intervention and 90.5% of control participants. From baseline to 12 months, unadjusted FOSQ improved 1.4 (SD 2.7) points in intervention and 0.9 (SD 2.9) points in control (adjusted between-group difference: 0.6 points, 95%CI 0.2, 1.0; p = 0.001). Conclusion and Relevance Among participants with OSA and obesity, a self-directed lifestyle intervention did not improve weight loss and led to improvements in sleep-related quality of life that are of limited clinical importance. Trial Registration Clinicaltrials.gov NCT05104450, registered 10/19/2021

items.title: Dupilumab is associated with improved lung functions in patients with COPD and type 2 inflammation: a post hoc analysis of the BOREAS and NOTUS trials
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Rationale Type 2 inflammation is present in 20%-40% of patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Objective To perform in-depth analyses of the efficacy of dupilumab on lung function parameters in patients with COPD and type 2 inflammation. Methods In BOREAS (NCT03930732) and NOTUS (NCT04456673), patients with COPD and type 2 inflammation were randomized to dupilumab 300 mg (n = 938) or placebo (n = 936) subcutaneously every 2 weeks for 52 weeks. Measurements and main results Dupilumab versus placebo improved pre-bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1; least squares mean difference: 83 [95% confidence interval (CI): 53-112] mL; P < .0001), post-bronchodilator FEV1 (71 [41-101] mL; P < .0001), pre-bronchodilator forced vital capacity (FVC; 64 [26-102] mL; P = .0009), post-bronchodilator FVC (41 [3-79] mL; P = .0341), post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC (0.016 [0.010-0.022]; P < .0001), and forced expiratory flow 25%-75% of FVC (78 [45-111] mL/s; P < .0001) at week 12 and sustained to week 52. Improvements in pre-bronchodilator FEV1 were observed regardless of smoking status or the presence of co-existing emphysema; greater improvements were observed in patients with higher baseline eosinophil counts or fractional exhaled nitric oxide. Dupilumab versus placebo achieved >100 mL improvements in pre-bronchodilator FEV1 at week 12 (42.2% vs 31.1%) and week 52 (36.9% vs 31.2%), with a similar proportion for post-bronchodilator FEV1 at weeks 12 and 52. Conclusions Dupilumab treatment resulted in early and sustained improvements across multiple spirometric lung function parameters in patients with COPD and type 2 inflammation.

items.title: As-needed inhaled corticosteroids in asthma: an Official American Thoracic Society clinical practice guideline
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Background Inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-containing reliever therapy has demonstrated efficacy in improving asthma outcomes when compared to short-acting beta2-agonists (SABA) alone but remains underutilized. The purpose of this guideline is to provide recommendations surrounding the use of combination ICS-formoterol or ICS+SABA (in combination or separate inhalers) as reliever therapy across the asthma severity spectrum in adolescents and adults. Methods The American Thoracic Society clinical practice guideline panel evaluated six research questions in the PICO format addressing the use of ICS-containing reliever therapy across National Asthma Education and Prevention Program (NAEPP) asthma treatment steps 1-5. The methodology team conducted systematic literature reviews and GRADE assessments, which the panel utilized to inform the recommendations for each specific PICO and overall. Recommendations In patients at NAEPP steps 1 and 2, the panel made strong recommendations for the use of as-needed-only ICS-SABA or ICS-formoterol over SABA-only therapy, and conditional recommendations over scheduled ICS + as-needed SABA. In patients at NAEPP steps 3-5, the taskforce made a strong recommendation for the use of maintenance-and-reliever therapy (MART) with ICS-formoterol over scheduled ICS-LABA plus as-needed SABA. In patients at NAEPP steps 3-5 who are using scheduled maintenance ICS-LABA, the panel made a conditional recommendation for use of ICS+SABA reliever over SABA reliever. In considering these recommendations, the panel valued the importance of preventing severe exacerbations and considered the risk of SABA-only treatment, as well as ICS and systemic corticosteroid (SCS) exposure. Conclusions This clinical practice guideline, informed by systematic reviews and GRADE-based appraisals of PICO-framed evidence, makes these evidence-based recommendations for the safe and effective use of ICS-containing reliever therapy in asthma.

items.title: Development and Validation of a Pre-COPD Score to Predict Incident COPD
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Rationale The ability to predict progression from a pre-disease state in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), pre-COPD, to overt COPD remains limited. Objective To test the hypothesis that development of COPD can be predicted by characterizing pre-COPD and creating a simple pre-COPD score. Methods We identified individuals without airflow obstruction, defined as pre-bronchodilator (BD) forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1)/forced vital capacity (FVC)≥0.70 and ≥lower limit of normal, from the Copenhagen General Population Study (CGPS)(N = 14,506), Copenhagen City Heart Study (CCHS)(N = 8673), and Genetic Epidemiology for COPD (COPDGene) Study(N = 2982). A pre-COPD score was developed in CGPS by assigning 1 point to each of smoking history≥10 pack-years, active smoking, any respiratory symptom, asthma, and pre-BD FEV1/FVC 0.70-0.75, and 4 points for pre-BD FEV1<80% predicted, indicating presence of Preserved Ratio Impaired Spirometry (PRISm), with external validation in CCHS and COPDGene. Participants were followed for 5-10 years for incident COPD, defined as pre-BD FEV1/FVC<0.70 and FEV1<80% predicted. Measurements and Main Results During follow-up, COPD developed in 669 individuals (4.6%) in CGPS, 685 (7.9%) in CCHS, and 367 (12%) in COPDGene. In CGPS, 10-year incidence was 1.5% in the low-risk, 9.3% in the intermediate-risk, 24% in the high-risk, and 42% in the very high-risk category. Corresponding 5-year incidences were 3.7%, 7.3%, 12%, and 25% in CCHS, and 4.1%, 5.3%, 13%, and 31% in COPDGene, respectively. The pre-COPD score demonstrated good discrimination with areas under curve of 0.88 in CGPS, 0.76 in CCHS, and 0.81 in COPDGene. The pre-COPD score was also associated with exacerbations. Conclusions The pre-COPD score is useful in predicting the onset of COPD with clinically relevant discrimination in three cohorts with different risk profiles.

items.title: Optimizing Sepsis Time Zero Definitions Through Associations between Antibiotic Timing and Mortality
items.containerTitle: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine
items.abstract: Rationale Sepsis performance measures require operational definitions of “time zero”, but SEP-1’s heterogeneous organ dysfunction criteria may not all identify patients vulnerable to harm from antibiotic delays. Objectives To determine which SEP-1 organ dysfunctions identify patients in whom antibiotic delays are associated with increased mortality. Methods We analyzed adults with suspected infection using electronic health record data from 145 U.S. hospitals (2018-2023). We estimated associations between antibiotic timing (1-3 vs. 0-1h and 3-6 vs. 0-3h) and in-hospital mortality for each SEP-1 organ dysfunction criterion, alone and in combination: hypotension, elevated lactate, respiratory failure, renal dysfunction, hyperbilirubinemia, thrombocytopenia, and coagulopathy. We used inverse probability weighting to adjust for baseline and time-varying confounders. Measurements and Main Results Among 1,849,729 encounters with suspected infection, 624,416 had ≥1 organ dysfunction and received antibiotics within 6h of time zero. Antibiotics at 1-3 vs. 0-1h were associated with higher mortality when time zero was defined by hypotension (aRR 1.07; 95% CI, 1.03-1.10) or lactate ≥4.0mmol/L (aRR 1.10; 1.05-1.15), but not for other dysfunctions alone or in combination. Among patients without hypotension or lactate ≥4.0mmol/L, antibiotics at 3-6 vs. 0-3h were only associated with higher mortality in patients with acute respiratory failure (aRR 1.11; 1.05-1.18). Conclusions Mortality associations with antibiotics beyond 1 hour were most evident when sepsis time zero was defined by hypotension or lactate ≥4.0mmol/L, and with antibiotics beyond 3 hours when defined by acute respiratory failure. These findings could inform refinements to sepsis time zero definitions to better guide antibiotic urgency and performance measurement.
