Effect of discontinuing antihypertensives on perioperative hypotension in older patients before non-cardiac surgery: multicentre, randomised, double blind, controlled trial
items.abstract: Objective To determine whether discontinuing versus continuing angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) on the morning of surgery reduces perioperative hypotension in older patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery. Design Multicentre, randomised, double blind, placebo controlled trial. Setting Five tertiary teaching hospitals in China, November 2020 to December 2023. Participants 2036 older patients (60-80 years) using ACE inhibitors or ARBs for at least two weeks and scheduled for non-cardiac surgery under general anaesthesia. Interventions Patients were randomised to receive their usual ACE inhibitor or ARB or a placebo in identical capsules on the morning of surgery. Main outcome measures The primary outcome was the incidence of perioperative hypotension (mean blood pressure <65 mm Hg or a =30% decrease from baseline requiring treatment). Secondary outcomes included duration of hypotension, requirement for a vasopressor, intraoperative fluid volume, postoperative hypotension, and 30 day complications (neurocognitive disorders, major cardiocerebral events) or mortality. Results 2012 patients (mean age 68.8 years; 54.4% male) completed the study: 1004 were included in the antihypertensive group and 1008 in the no antihypertensive group. The incidence of perioperative hypotension was lower in the no antihypertensive group (314/1008, 31.2%) versus antihypertensive group (457/1004, 45.5%): adjusted odds ratio 0.52 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.43 to 0.63); absolute risk difference -14.4% (95% CI -18.5% to -10.1%); P<0.001. The duration of hypotension and requirement for a vasopressor were both reduced in the no antihypertensive group: adjusted mean difference -1.3 minutes (95% CI -1.8 to -0.8 minutes) and 28.5% v 41.1%; adjusted odds ratio 0.54 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.66). Intraoperative fluid volume, postoperative hypotension, 30 day complications, and mortality did not differ significantly between groups. Conclusions Discontinuing ACE inhibitors or ARBs on the morning of surgery in older patients with hypertension statistically significantly reduced perioperative hypotension and the requirement for vasopressors without increasing 30 day complications or mortality. This simple strategy provides high certainty evidence for preoperative drug management in this patient population. Trial registration Chinese Clinical Trial Registry NCT2000039376 .

Effect of intensive blood pressure control on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes: prespecified analysis of secondary outcomes of BPROAD randomised controlled trial
items.abstract: Objective To evaluate the effect of intensive compared with standard treatment of systolic blood pressure (SBP) on cognitive outcomes and brain structures in adults with type 2 diabetes. Design Multicentre, open label, outcome assessor masked, randomised controlled trial. Setting 145 clinical centres across seven geographical regions in China. Participants 12 821 adults aged ≥50 years with type 2 diabetes, raised SBP, and increased cardiovascular risk, of whom 12 434 without probable dementia at baseline were included in this cognitive ancillary study. Further assessments were performed annually and at the end of study. Interventions Participants were randomly assigned to receive intensive treatment targeting SBP <120 mm Hg or standard treatment targeting SBP <140 mm Hg for up to five years. Main outcome measures The primary cognitive outcome was a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment. Secondary cognitive outcomes included all cause dementia, mild cognitive impairment, changes in cognitive functions, and changes in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics. A subset of participants underwent brain MRI at baseline (n=862) and at the end of study (n=605) to assess changes in white matter lesion volume and total brain volume. Results 6219 participants were assigned to receive intensive treatment and 6215 to receive standard treatment. Baseline mean age was 63.7 years, and 5567 (44.8%) participants were women. After one year, mean SBP was 121.6 mm Hg in the intensive treatment group and 133.2 mm Hg in the standard treatment group. During a median follow-up of 3.8 years, the primary cognitive outcome of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment occurred in 747 participants (3.69 events per 100 person years) in the intensive treatment group and 783 participants (3.89 events per 100 person years) in the standard treatment group (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.86 to 1.06; P=0.38). In the MRI substudy (428 intensive treatment v 434 standard treatment), the intensive treatment group had a smaller increase in white matter lesion volume compared with the standard treatment group (between group difference −0.09 inverse hyperbolic sine (asinh) transformed cm 3 , 95% CI −0.15 to −0.02; P=0.01). Conclusions Over a median of about four years, no statistically significant difference in incidence of a composite of all cause dementia or mild cognitive impairment was observed among adults with type 2 diabetes receiving standard treatment of SBP (target <140 mm Hg) and intensive treatment (target <120 mm Hg). Intensive treatment was, however, associated with a reduction in the accrual of cerebral white matter lesion volume. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03808311 .

Effects of plastic exposure on human health
items.abstract: Plastic pollution is a critical environmental and public health challenge, with growing evidence linking human exposure to microplastics, nanoplastics, and associated chemicals to adverse health outcomes. This review summarises current knowledge on the health effects of plastic exposure, addressing both established findings and critical knowledge gaps. We examine human exposure to plastics and associated health risks based on available clinical and epidemiological evidence. Additionally, we explore chemicals associated with plastic, including their potential as carcinogens and disruptors of endocrine and immune function. Recognising the urgent need for preventive measures, we examine emerging strategies for reducing plastic burdens, including global regulatory efforts like the United Nations Plastics Treaty and proposed public health guidelines. By integrating current evidence, this review aims to provide a foundation for advancing research and informing strategies to mitigate health risks associated with plastic.

items.title: Surgical Margin and Risk of Local Recurrence in Children and Young Adults With Nonrhabdomyosarcoma Soft Tissue Sarcoma
items.abstract: Importance The extent of negative margin necessary to achieve a high rate of local tumor control in children and young adult patients with nonrhabdomyosarcoma soft tissue sarcomas (NRSTS) is unknown. Objective To evaluate the impact of negative margin extent on local tumor control in children and young adult patients with NRSTS undergoing R0 resection as part of risk-adapted multimodality treatment. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter prospective clinical trial was conducted at Children’s Oncology Group (COG) member sites from February 2007 through February 2012. Analysis was performed on the final dataset June 30, 2018, with a median follow-up of 6.2 years. Reviewers of margin status/extent were blinded to local control outcomes. Patients included 266 eligible/evaluable individuals younger than 30 years with nonmetastatic NRSTS who were enrolled in the COG ARST0332 trial and underwent upfront or delayed R0 resection as part of treatment. Patients who underwent an amputation or did not receive protocol-specified radiotherapy were excluded. These data were analyzed from January 2023 through July 2026. Intervention Risk-adapted treatment included 3 patient groups with upfront or delayed surgery with or without radiation therapy with or without ifosfamide/doxorubicin chemotherapy, based on the extent of initial resection, surgical margin status, tumor size, and histologic grade. Main Outcomes Cumulative incidence of local recurrence based on treatment approach and surgical margin extent and outcomes after local recurrence. Results Of 266 patients (median age 13.7 [range, 2.1-27.6] years; 138 female [52%] and 128 male [48%]) who underwent upfront (n = 207) or delayed (n = 59) R0 resection, 132 had measured surgical margins: 1 mm (n = 56), 2 to 5 mm (n = 50), or 6-mm or larger (n = 26). The 5-year cumulative incidence of local recurrence overall was 4.4%. Local recurrence occurred in 10 of 178 patients treated with surgery alone (5.6%) and 2 of 88 patients treated with surgery and chemoradiotherapy (2.3%). Among the 132 patients with measured surgical margins, the 5-year cumulative incidence of local recurrence was 4.9% for 1-mm margins, 2.0% for 2- to 5-mm margins, and 0% for 6-mm or larger margins. Local recurrence occurred in 10 of 178 (5.6%) patients with tumors smaller than 5 cm treated with margin-negative surgery alone, 1 of 29 (3.4%) patients with tumors larger than 5 cm treated with margin-negative surgery followed by chemoradiotherapy, and 1 of 59 (1.7%) patients with initially unresectable disease treated with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy. Five of 12 patients with local recurrence were alive without further disease progression. Conclusions and Relevance In this study, the local recurrence rate after R0 resection among children and young adult patients treated with risk-based therapy for nonmetastatic NRSTS was low, and some patients underwent successful salvage therapy with durable long-term disease control. Wider (&gt;1 mm) negative margins further decrease local recurrence risk. Close surgical margins may be adequate in some clinical settings, particularly in the context of chemoradiotherapy, according to a risk-adapted approach. Trial Registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT00346164

items.title: Error in Figure 2
Rethinking Risk in Ventral Hernia Repair—Sex as a Signal, Not a Cause
Comparison of Outcomes Between Men and Women Undergoing Ventral Hernia Repair
items.abstract: Importance Sex-based differences in ventral hernia repair (VHR) outcomes remain incompletely characterized. Objective To compare short-term clinical outcomes, recurrence through 3 years, and patient-reported outcomes between female and male patients undergoing VHR. Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study included patients undergoing VHR from January 2012 through December 2023, with follow-up through 3 years. Data were from the Abdominal Core Health Quality Collaborative (ACHQC), a prospective, multi-institutional clinical registry. Participants were adults undergoing primary or incisional VHR whose data were recorded in the ACHQC database. Data analysis was performed from May to September 2026. Exposures Sex (female vs male). Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes included 30-day wound morbidity, comprising surgical site infection (SSI), surgical-site occurrence (SSO), and SSO requiring procedural intervention (SSO-PI), readmission, and length of stay. Secondary outcomes included pragmatic recurrence at 30 days, 1 year, 2 years, and 3 years and patient-reported quality of life and pain. Multivariable logistic regression assessed associations between sex and outcomes. Results Among 31 358 patients, 14 303 (45.6%) were female and 17 055 (54.4%) were male. Women were younger than men (mean [SD] age, 55.0 [14.6] vs 56.5 [13.0] years, respectively) and had higher body mass index (mean [SD], 32.1 [7.6] vs 31.7 [5.9], respectively). Women presented with more complex hernia phenotypes, including higher rates of incisional, recurrent, and larger hernias. Compared with men, women experienced higher 30-day readmission (483 [3.4%] for women vs 428 [2.5%] for men), SSI (370 [2.6%] vs 284 [1.7%], respectively) SSO (1323 [9.2%] and 1286 [7.5%], respectively), and SSO-PI (517 [3.6%] vs 434 [2.5%], respectively; all P &lt; .001), with no differences in reoperation or mortality. Female sex was independently associated with higher odds of SSI (odds ratio [OR], 1.40; 95% CI, 1.17-1.67) and SSO-PI (OR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.04-1.40) after incisional hernia repair. Clinical outcomes and recurrence were similar at 1 year; however, women had higher recurrence at 2 years (444 [19.3%] vs 406 [15.7%] men) and 3 years (351 [20.9%] vs 320 [17.6%] men). Women reported worse baseline quality of life and pain but greater improvement after 1 year. Conclusions and Relevance This study found that women undergoing VHR presented with greater hernia complexity and experienced higher early wound morbidity and increased late recurrence, while achieving substantial patient-reported benefit. These findings may inform sex-specific risk stratification and counseling, although further studies with more longitudinal follow-up are needed.

items.title: Emergency General Surgery Verification—Which Differences Matter?
Diagnosis and Management of Acute Cholangitis
items.abstract: Importance Acute cholangitis (AC) is a potentially fatal biliary tract infection most commonly caused by gallstones. While modern-day treatments with antibiotics and biliary decompression have drastically decreased mortality rates, AC still requires prompt intervention. Observations Diagnosis of AC traditionally relied on the presence of the Charcot triad, which has since proven to incompletely capture the complexity of this condition. Modern-day diagnosis, severity grading, and management guidelines provide a more holistic approach. Tokyo Guidelines (TG) are widely used, though newer guidelines, namely the BILE criteria, have recently emerged. These criteria include demonstration of inflammation, cholestasis, and biliary obstruction. Ultrasound is first-line imaging modality with computed tomography or magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography often used for diagnostic dilemmas. Treatment is dependent on severity, though guidelines generally recommend early decompression (most commonly with endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography [ERCP]) for moderate to severe cases. The optimal timing of biliary drainage remains unclear, with mixed evidence from observational studies and no universal definition of what constitutes “early” vs “urgent” drainage. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy should be performed during index hospitalization, when possible, with multiple studies demonstrating lower morbidity and mortality rates when compared with interval procedures. The prognosis of AC is favorable if treated swiftly and appropriately; in turn, mortality rates increase with severity and delays in diagnosis. Conclusions and Relevance AC can be challenging to diagnose and the precise timing of biliary drainage and cholecystectomy is debated. This comprehensive review reflects the most recent evidence and recommendations on severity grading, resuscitation, and timing of ERCP and cholecystectomy to assist clinicians who manage these complex patients.

items.title: The Next Question in Postoperative Opioid Stewardship
items.abstract: This Viewpoint addresses the question of whether surgical opioid stewardship should involve consideration of the type of opioid agent used for postoperative prescriptions in addition to considering the quantity of tablets prescribed.

items.title: Improving Quality Through the Emergency General Surgery Verification Program
items.abstract: Importance The Emergency General Surgery Verification Program was designed and launched in 2023 by the American College of Surgeons to standardize and improve EGS care through 43 standards that support hospital structure, care processes, and outcome surveillance. Objectives To evaluate the association between EGS verification and hospital length of stay (LOS), acute kidney injury (AKI), and 30-day mortality and to assess whether changes in care processes contribute to effects. Design, Setting, and Participants This quasi-experimental difference-in-differences cohort study with staggered adoption used data from the ACS National Surgical Quality Improvement Program EGS Targeted Dataset. Patients with operatively managed EGS diagnoses from July 1, 2023, through December 31, 2024, at 50 control and 5 verified hospitals were evaluated. Data were analyzed from July 2025 through February 2026. Exposure Hospital EGS verification status. Main Outcomes and Measures Primary outcomes were mean LOS, 30-day mortality rate, and AKI rate. These were calculated adjusted and unadjusted. Average treatment effects on the treated were estimated with hospital-clustered bootstrap standard errors. Results The final cohort included 21 858 patients at 55 hospitals. Median (IQR) patient age was 53.2 (36.5-68.5) years, and 12 366 patients (56.6%) were female. Prior to verification, verified hospitals treated higher-acuity patients and had higher predicted mortality and AKI rates. Verification was associated with absolute reductions in LOS (−1.31 days; 95% CI, −1.95 to −0.67), AKI (−1.23 percentage points; 95% CI, −2.00 to −0.46), and mortality (−1.63 percentage points; 95% CI, −2.55 to −0.71), corresponding to relative reductions of 19.7%, 29.0%, and 28.8%, respectively. These results held after risk adjustment and Bonferroni correction. Verification was also associated with improved care processes, including increased admission to surgical services (74.8% to 85.7%; P &lt; .001), decreased failure of nonoperative management (25.5% to 19.0%; P &lt; .001), and shorter time to operation (−10.7 hours; P &lt; .001). All processes were independently associated with improvements in all 3 primary outcomes. Conclusions and Relevance In this cohort study, early adoption of ACS EGS verification was associated with clinically meaningful reductions in LOS, AKI, and 30-day mortality among participating hospitals. These findings demonstrate the EGS verification likely drives systems-level improvements in emergency surgical care, which may be partially explained by improvements in performance on hospital process measures.

items.title: Error in Affiliations
Addressing the Issue of Laparoscopic Deskilling—Reply
Scaling Telesurgery—Safety, Equity, and Governance
items.abstract: This Viewpoint discusses the technical feasibility of remote surgery and the challenges that prevent routine expansion and proposes standards for evidence, accountability, training, and local capacity.

items.title: Addressing the Issue of Laparoscopic Deskilling
Manually Abstracted vs Electronic Health Record Data for Risk Adjusting Hospital Postoperative Mortality
items.abstract: Importance National surgical quality improvement (QI) programs rely on manual data abstraction to produce hospital-level risk-adjusted outcomes, and while electronic health records (EHRs) could provide an efficient platform for automating data collection of model covariates, the robustness of this approach has not been explored. Objective To evaluate whether risk adjustment using EHR data performs similarly to manually abstracted model covariates for characterizing hospital-level 30-day postoperative mortality. Design, Setting, and Participants This is a national, hospital-level comparative effectiveness study using data from the Veterans Affairs Surgical Quality Improvement Program (VASQIP) and the VA Corporate Data Warehouse (CDW, a repository of national VA EHR data) to compare risk adjustment strategies within a national surgical QI program. VASQIP records were matched to patients’ corresponding CDW record. VASQIP variable correlates were created using VA EHR data. Patients aged 18 years or older who underwent a noncardiac operation at a VA facility from January 1, 2016, to September 30, 2020, with a record in VASQIP were included. Data were analyzed from April 2025 to September 2025. Main Outcomes and Measures The primary outcome was 30-day postoperative mortality. Quarterly observed to expected (OE) ratios were calculated using either EHR or manually abstracted (ie, VASQIP) variables as model covariates and compared to ascertain whether hospital performance was concordantly identified using these different risk adjustment strategies (ie, risk adjustment performed with the same variables but from different data sources). Results Among 386 157 unique patients who underwent 460 585 noncardiac operations at 113 VA facilities, mean (SD) age was 62.9 (13.4) years and 43 781 patients (9.5%) were female. Correlation in OE ratios was strong ( r = 0.98; 95% CI, 0.98-0.98). Across all quarters of data (n = 2111), 2096 hospital quarters (99.3%) were concordantly identified. Among quarters in which hospitals were identified as having higher-than-expected mortality after risk adjustment with VASQIP data (n = 42), 34 (81.0%) were concordantly identified after risk adjustment with parsimonious EHR data. Conclusions and Relevance In this comparative effectiveness study, risk adjustment with EHR data was shown to perform similarly to manually abstracted data for characterizing hospital performance in 30-day postoperative mortality. The use of EHR data for risk adjustment could facilitate automation of data extraction, increase programmatic efficiency, and improve the timeliness of data provision to stakeholders for QI efforts.

items.title: JAMA Surgery
Prior Biliary Drainage Procedure Is a Near-universal Risk Factor for Postoperative Hepatic Abscess After Liver Resection
Out in the Match
items.abstract: Objective: To explore LGBTQ+ general surgery resident experiences during the Match process. Summary Background Data: General surgery (GS) applicants negotiate the residency match process through the lens of their identities, but little is known about LGBTQ+ applicant experiences. This study explored how current LGBTQ+-GS residents navigated their identity and evaluated programs for psychological safety and belonging during the Match. Methods: This qualitative study utilized semistructured interviews with current US LGBTQ+-GS residents recruited using purposive and snowball sampling from Oct to Dec 2025. Interviews focused on LGBTQ+ identity, experiences throughout medical school, recruitment, and residency, and how psychological safety was assessed. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using a deductive-inductive approach to identify themes. Results: Of 17 participants, mean age was 30.7±1.8 years, and most identified as male (52.9%) and White (76.5%). Five themes were identified: (1) Participants strategically disclosed identity: disclosing as a “ litmus test ” to filter for identity-affirming programs or concealing identity in fear “ that’s the reason why I don’t get ranked .” (2) Participants relied on subtle micro-signals to indicate psychological safety (eg, pronouns, pride symbols). (3) Participants scrutinized the manner and tone of responses to LGBTQ+-related questions in addition to the content. (4) Representation of LGBTQ+ residents/faculty reduced belonging uncertainty. (5) Participants “used geography as a proxy for acceptance , ” weighing regional sociopolitical climates when assessing their potential to thrive. Conclusions: LGBTQ+ trainees assessed a variety of micro- and macro-signals to evaluate residency programs. Residency programs can design their programs around these signals to enhance recruitment of LGBTQ+-GS applicants.

items.title: Surgeon Perspectives on Disclosure of Artificial Intelligence in the Operating Room
Endoscopic Classification of Fundoplication Integrity Predicts Pathologic Reflux
items.abstract: Objective: We aimed to validate individual endoscopic parameters against clinical and functional testing and to build a simple classification of fundoplication integrity. Summary Background Data: Endoscopy is the main tool to assess the gastroesophageal valve after antireflux surgery (ARS), but existing classifications are complex and have never been validated against objective pathophysiologic data. Methods: This was a single-center, two-phase cohort study of adults undergoing endoscopy, high-resolution manometry (HRM), and reflux monitoring after ARS. Retroflexed videoclips were reviewed blinded to functional results. In the development cohort (2018–2024), endoscopic parameters were tested against pathologic GERD (Lyon 2.0 criteria); those correlating with reflux were included in the classification and the population was stratified according to the number of impaired mechanisms (0–3). In the second phase, the classification was validated prospectively (2024–2026). Results: Of 122 patients, 73 formed the development and 49 the validation cohort. Three parameters were associated with pathologic GERD: intrathoracic valve, disrupted valve, and visible hiatus. Clinical, manometric, and reflux metrics worsened stepwise with the number of impaired mechanisms, and pathologic GERD rose from 11.8% to 37.5% to 85.7%. The new classification discriminated pathologic GERD with an area under the curve of 0.860 in the development and 0.870 in the validation cohort (0.869 overall). Conclusions: A simple endoscopic classification based on valve location, disruption, and hiatal opening reliably identifies fundoplication failure and correlates with symptoms, manometric features, and reflux burden.

items.title: Reappraising Liver Transplantation for Combined Hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma
items.abstract: Objective: To determine whether liver transplantation (LT) confers durable oncologic benefit in combined hepatocellular-cholangiocarcinoma (cHCC-CCA) and to identify predictors of recurrence that may guide transplant candidacy. Background: cHCC-CCA is a rare primary liver malignancy with aggressive biological behavior. LT has traditionally been contraindicated due to concerns regarding recurrence. We evaluated long-term outcomes of LT versus liver resection (LR) and compared LT outcomes for cHCC-CCA with those for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Methods: Patients with cHCC-CCA who underwent LT or LR between 2010 and 2024 were identified from a prospective database. Survival outcomes, recurrence patterns, and risk factors for recurrence were analyzed. Outcomes of LT for cHCC-CCA were additionally compared with HCC. Results: A total of 79 patients underwent LT (diagnosed on explant) and 32 underwent LR for cHCC-CCA. 5-year overall survival (OS) and recurrence-free survival (RFS) were superior following LT compared with LR (OS: 89.9% vs. 65.6%, P =0.007; RFS: 84.8% vs. 53.1%, P =0.001). This benefit was maintained for tumors within UCSF criteria [overall survival (88.7% LT vs. 65.6% LR, log rank P 0.014) and RFS (89.8% LT vs. 51.6% LR, P <0.001)]. Among LT recipients, OS for cHCC-CCA was comparable to HCC (89.9% vs. 86%, P =0.721). Within the LT cohort, macrovascular invasion (HR 25.01, P =0.003) and poor tumor differentiation (HR 7.29, P =0.004) independently predicted recurrence. Conclusion: In carefully selected patients, cHCC-CCA within UCSF criteria can achieve transplant outcomes comparable to HCC. Macrovascular invasion and poor tumor differentiation are major predictors of recurrence and may inform candidate selection for LT.

items.title: Hospital-level Variation in Medical Debt After Acute Traumatic Injury
items.abstract: Objective: To determine whether the treating hospital contributes to patients’ medical debt following injury. Summary Background Data: Trauma patients often have little or no choice in where they receive care. However, variation in hospital billing and collection practices, and their association with patient medical debt, remains poorly characterized. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adult trauma patients hospitalized from January 2019 to December 2020 at 29 Level I and II trauma centers within a statewide quality collaborative. Trauma registry data were linked to quarterly consumer credit reports from 12 months preinjury through 18 months postinjury. The primary outcome was change in medical debt in collections from baseline to months 9–18 postinjury. Hierarchical mixed-effects models with empirical Bayes shrinkage and reliability adjustment estimated risk-adjusted hospital-level changes, adjusting for demographics, injury severity, and treatment intensity. Hospitals were classified as outliers if 95% confidence intervals for observed-minus-expected differences excluded zero. Results: Among 20,613 patients (mean age 63 y; 49% female; 82% non-Hispanic White), mean change in medical debt was $314 (SD $3464). Four hospitals (14%) were high outliers, generating $365–$566 more debt per patient than expected, while 4 (14%) were low outliers, generating $292–$676 less. Low-outlier hospitals cared for younger, lower-income, and higher-risk patients yet produced less debt than predicted. Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses. Conclusions: Substantial hospital-level variation in postinjury medical debt persists after adjustment for clinical and demographic factors. Billing, financial assistance, and collection practices may represent modifiable targets to reduce financial hardship after trauma.

items.title: Surgeon Perspectives on Pregnancy Loss
items.abstract: Objective: To voice surgeons’ experiences with pregnancy loss during training and identify current gaps in support structures within training programs. Summary Background Data: Previous literature emphasizes the prevalence of pregnancy loss among female surgeons, frequently reporting a rate of more than double that of the general population. Despite this, little has been done to voice the personal experiences behind this data and to identify solutions to support trainees through these events. Methods: Semistructured focus groups and individual interviews were conducted between June and August of 2025. Surgeons within 5 years of general surgery residency graduation and current surgical fellows and general surgery trainees who identify as female and as having had a pregnancy loss during surgical training were recruited through targeted social media platforms. Transcripts were individually coded, and emerging codes were iteratively refined into themes related to the pregnancy loss experience and gaps in support resources. Results: Participants described the multidimensional impact of pregnancy loss during general surgery training. Mental health, physical, and professional impacts were pervasive. Five barriers to seeking support were identified: burden to colleagues, privacy concerns, reputation concerns, guilt and isolation, and rigidity of training. Facilitators to seeking support, though fewer, were greatly beneficial. These thematic categories informed critical gaps in general surgery program support structures and important components of a pregnancy loss policy designed to reduce stigma, promote trainee well-being, and mitigate attrition from the field. Conclusions: This study highlights the pregnancy loss experience among current and former general surgery trainees and uses these experiences to propose necessary support structures to be implemented within training programs.

items.title: Cirrhosis Regression After Metabolic Bariatric Surgery in Patients With Compensated MASH Cirrhosis
items.abstract: Objective: To evaluate histologic cirrhosis regression after metabolic bariatric surgery (MBS) in patients with compensated metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) cirrhosis. Summary Background Data: Cirrhosis in MASH has traditionally been considered irreversible. Although MBS improves steatohepatitis and fibrosis in noncirrhotic MASH, its impact on established cirrhosis remains uncertain. Methods: This retrospective study included adults with biopsy-proven compensated MASH cirrhosis who underwent MBS at Cleveland Clinic from 2004 to 2024 and had paired baseline and follow-up liver biopsies. The primary outcome was regression from NASH Clinical Research Network (NASH CRN) stage 4 to stage 3 or lower. Fibrosis was also assessed using modified Ishak staging and the Beijing classification. Results: Thirty patients were included; 22 (73%) were female, median age was 54.2 years, and median baseline body mass index was 43.7 kg/m². The median (IQR) biopsy interval was 6.2 (2.0–9.2) years, median body weight reduction was 31.8 (21.4–40.4) kg, and median total weight loss was 23.9% (18.0%–30.5%). Cirrhosis regression occurred in 33% of patients using NASH CRN staging and in 40% using modified Ishak staging. Regressive fibrosis features were identified in 60% of patients using the Beijing classification. Significant improvements were also observed in steatosis, lobular inflammation, and hepatocyte ballooning. Conclusions: MBS was associated with histologic cirrhosis regression in a substantial proportion of patients with biopsy-proven compensated MASH cirrhosis. More detailed histologic frameworks identified additional fibrosis improvement and regressive remodeling, suggesting that compensated MASH cirrhosis may be reversible after sustained metabolic intervention.

items.title: Bariatric Surgery as a Rescue Strategy After Semaglutide or Tirzepatide
items.abstract: Objective: To evaluate 2-year weight loss after bariatric surgery among adults with intolerable adverse effects or inadequate weight loss with semaglutide or tirzepatide. Summary Background Data: Semaglutide and tirzepatide are effective obesity medications, but intolerance and inadequate weight loss are common, creating uncertainty about next-step therapy. Methods: This retrospective cohort included adults with BMI ≥35 kg/m² undergoing Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) or sleeve gastrectomy (SG) at Cleveland Clinic hospitals from 2018 to 2024. Electronic health record and dispensing data classified preoperative semaglutide or tirzepatide exposure and response. The primary outcome was estimated 2-year total body weight loss (TBWL), stratified by procedure and type 2 diabetes (T2DM) status. Results: Among 4929 patients, 4661 had no prior exposure (comparator group), 61 discontinued semaglutide or tirzepatide because of intolerable adverse effects, and 207 had inadequate weight-loss response. Before surgery, estimated 2-year medication-associated weight change was a 1.4% gain in the intolerance group and 1.5% TBWL in the inadequate-response group. After surgery, 2-year TBWL in the intolerance group was 27.9% and 22.7% after RYGB and 20.1% and 21.6% after SG among patients without and with T2DM, respectively. Corresponding estimates in the inadequate-response group were 35.8%, 27.4%, 14.3%, and 14.2%. For comparison, corresponding 2-year TBWL estimates in the comparator group were 33.3%, 28.7%, 23.6%, and 19.9%. In adjusted analysis of the inadequate-response group, RYGB was associated with greater 2-year TBWL than SG (32.7% vs. 17.8%; difference, 14.9 percentage points [95% CI, 13.1%–16.7%]). Conclusions: Bariatric surgery was associated with clinically meaningful 2-year weight loss after semaglutide or tirzepatide intolerance or inadequate response, with RYGB potentially offering greater benefit after inadequate response.

items.title: Sociobehavioral Comorbidities and Outcomes After Colectomy in a National United States Veteran Cohort
items.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the independent association between sociobehavioral comorbidities (SBCs) and complications after colectomies in a national Veteran cohort. Background: SBCs are determinants of health outcomes, and Veterans represent a high-vulnerability population. However, the relationship of SBCs with postoperative complications remains understudied, and current surgical risk models underestimate risk among patients with significant SBC burden. Methods: We conducted an observational study of Veterans undergoing elective colectomy included in the Veterans Affairs Surgical Quality Improvement Program (VASQIP). Structured data from the Veteran Health Administration Corporate Data Warehouse were used to identify 6 SBC phenotypes (mental health disorder, suicide risk, substance use, social isolation, housing instability, and food insecurity) across 3 preoperative ascertainment windows: ≤90 days, ≤365 days, and lifetime. The outcome was any 30-day VASQIP-defined postoperative complication. Multilevel logistic regression estimated associations between SBCs and complications. Results: Among 38,188 Veterans undergoing colectomy between 2009 and 2025, the median age was 66 years; 5% were female; 30% were non-white; and 48% had cancer. Mental health disorder, social isolation, or substance use were each associated with an 8%–40% increase in the odds of a complication across all ascertainment windows. Within the most proximal window, risk of complication increased as SBC burden increased: 16% increased odds with 1 SBC (aOR 1.16, 95% CI: 1.09–1.23) and 80% increased odds with 4–6 SBCs (aOR 1.80, 95% CI: 1.32–2.36). Conclusions: In a national Veteran cohort, SBCs were associated with postoperative colectomy complications. The strongest associations were observed with SBCs ascertained within the 90-day window, and the odds increased in a dose-response relationship with increasing SBC burden.

items.title: Metro-Pancreas Stratifies Survival After Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy and Surgery for Resectable Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract: Objective: To assess the prognostic utility of the Metro-Pancreas framework in resectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAT) and resection. Summary Background Data: Upfront surgery and NAT are options in anatomically resectable PDAC. Metro-Pancreas combines tumor size and CA 19-9 to stratify prognosis after upfront resection, but its applicability after NAT is unknown. Methods: We analyzed 623 patients with nonmetastatic, anatomically resectable PDAC who underwent NAT followed by resection from 5 institutions (2016–2024). Metro-Pancreas classification ( IN/OUT ) was determined by tumor size and CA19-9 levels. Treatment response followed NCCN 2026 definition based on radiologic and biochemical changes. Postoperative disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) were evaluated. Results: At diagnosis, 263 patients (42.2%) were Metro-Pancreas OUT and had shorter postoperative DFS (13.3 vs. 16.7 mo; P =0.003) and OS (29.5 vs. 34.8 mo; P =0.006) than Metro-Pancreas IN patients. After NAT, 71.9% of OUT patients were reclassified as IN , while 5.0% of initially IN patients became OUT . Among baseline OUT patients, 35.7% had significant response, 46.0% had minimal response, and 18.3% had progression. Prognostic separation was greater at Metro-Pancreas restaging (DFS: 7.7 vs. 17.3 mo; OS: 15.8 vs. 36.7 mo; both P =0.001). Patients reclassified from OUT to IN had postoperative DFS and OS comparable to those initially IN ( P =0.806 and P =0.631, respectively). Conclusions: Among patients undergoing resection after NAT, Metro-Pancreas stratified prognosis at diagnosis and more effectively at restaging. Reclassification from OUT to IN was associated with favorable postoperative survival, supporting dynamic prognostic reassessment in the neoadjuvant setting.

items.title: Adjuvant Hepatic Arterial Infusion Pump Chemotherapy Without Systemic Therapy After Repeat Local Treatment for Patients With Liver-only Recurrence of Colorectal Cancer
items.abstract: Background: Approximately 30% of patients develop liver-confined recurrences after local treatment for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM), which may be reduced by adjuvant therapy. Hepatic arterial infusion pump (HAIP) chemotherapy delivers high-dose liver-directed chemotherapy. Objective: To investigate adjuvant HAIP chemotherapy without systemic therapy in patients with resectable liver-confined recurrence after prior local treatment of CRLM. Methods: This multicenter, single-arm phase II trial enrolled patients with resectable recurrent CRLM across 3 centers in the Netherlands. Patients with prior or present extrahepatic disease were excluded. Adjuvant HAIP with floxuridine was administered up to 6 cycles. The primary endpoint was hepatic disease-free survival (hDFS) estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with a prespecified efficacy boundary of 36 months. Results: Forty-five patients underwent local treatment followed by adjuvant HAIP chemotherapy without systemic therapy. Twenty-eight patients(62%) were treated for a first recurrent CRLM, and 17 patients for a second or higher. Twenty-five patients (56%) had ≥3 CRLM. All patients started HAIP chemotherapy, with a median of 6 cycles (interquartile range: 4 to 6). After a median follow-up of 38.7 months (95% CI: 33.0–42.3), the median hDFS was 16.5 months (95% CI: 9.1–25.8). The median progression-free survival was 14.0 months (95% CI: 7.7–23.0), and the 3-year overall survival was 71% (95% CI: 58%–87%). Initial recurrence included the liver in 23 patients (51%). HAIP implantation-related complications (Clavien–Dindo grade ≥3) occurred in 4 patients (9%), and HAIP chemotherapy-related complications (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events grade ≥3) occurred in 6 patients (13%). Biliary sclerosis occurred in 4 patients; 3 required stent placement. Conclusion: Adjuvant HAIP chemotherapy without systemic therapy did not achieve the hypothesized hDFS in patients undergoing repeat local treatment for recurrent CRLM.

items.title: Does the SOUND Trial Apply to Patients With Invasive Lobular Carcinoma?
The Future of Robotic Surgery Will Require Collaboration and Thoughtful Leaders
Shifts in Professional Medical Organizations’ Gender-Affirming Care Position Statements Between 2023 and 2026: A Cross-Sectional Study
Commentary on “Implementation of an Enhanced Recovery Protocol Attenuates Disparities in Pediatric Surgical Care”
Clinical Impact in Pancreatic Cancer Trials
Beyond Diameter: The Next Era of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Risk Assessment
Primary Tumor Biology, Recurrence and Survival After Colorectal Liver Metastasis Resection: The BIO-CRLM Study
items.abstract: Objective: To evaluate whether integrated primary tumor biology, combining primary tumor location and RAS/BRAF status, defines recurrence phenotypes and survival trajectories after liver resection for colorectal liver metastases (CRLM). Summary Background Data: Selection for resection remains largely morphology-based, although tumor biology strongly influences post-hepatectomy outcomes. Primary tumor site and RAS/BRAF status are individually prognostic, but whether their integration identifies distinct post-resection trajectories is unclear. Methods: An international multicenter cohort of patients undergoing liver resection for CRLM between 2017 and 2023 was analyzed. Integrated biology was defined a priori as left-sided-wild-type, right-sided-wild-type, rectal-wild-type, left-sided-RAS-mutant, right-sided-RAS-mutant, rectal RAS-mutant, and BRAF-mutant disease. Primary outcomes were recurrence-free survival (RFS) and overall survival (OS). Secondary outcomes included early recurrence, disseminated first recurrence, and first recurrence phenotype. Results: Among 3162 patients from 44 centers, 2415 (76.4%) developed recurrence and 1342 (42.4%) died. Integrated biology was independently associated with both RFS and OS (global P <0.001 for both). Compared with left-WT tumors, the highest mortality risks were observed in BRAF-mutant disease [hazard ratio (HR): 2.68, 95% CI: 2.02–3.57, P <0.001] and right-RAS-mutant disease (HR: 2.32, 95% CI: 1.94–2.79, P <0.001). Integrated biology was also associated with early recurrence, disseminated first recurrence, and first recurrence phenotype. Rectal-RAS-mutant tumors had the strongest association with lung-only recurrence [relative risk ratio (RRR): 3.38, 95% CI: 2.22–5.13, P <0.001] and disseminated recurrence (RRR: 2.57, 95% CI: 1.86–3.55, P <0.001) relative to liver-only recurrence. Conclusions: Integrated primary tumor biology identifies clinically distinct post-hepatectomy disease trajectories after CRLM resection. Combining primary tumor site with RAS/BRAF status may support preoperative counseling, surveillance planning, and trial stratification.

items.title: Postpancreatectomy Mortality (PPM) Following Minimally Invasive Pancreatic Surgery Is Mainly Driven by Pancreatectomy-Specific Complications
items.abstract: Background: Postpancreatectomy mortality (PPM) remains relatively unexplored after minimally invasive pancreatic surgery (MIPS). The International Study Group for Pancreatic Surgery (ISGPS) recently proposed a consensus definition and classification of PPM based on root-cause analysis. We aimed to assess the applicability of this classification and characterize mechanisms of PPM following MIPS. Methods: This study retrospectively analyzed consecutive patients undergoing MIPS enrolled in the Italian IGoMIPS registry (October 2019–July 2025). All PPM events were reviewed and attributed specific PPM types using structured root-cause analysis according to ISGPS criteria. Multivariable logistic regression identified predictors of PPM, and PPM type distributions were compared across procedures. Results: Out of 3590 patients, the PPM rate was 2.7%. Specifically, PPM occurred in 5.9% following minimally invasive pancreatoduodenectomy (MIPD), 0.8% following left pancreatectomy (MILP), and 4.8% following total pancreatectomy (MITP), while no PPM events occurred after parenchyma-sparing resections. Increased age and American Society of Anesthesiology Physical Status (ASA-PS) ≥3 independently predicted PPM. Root-cause analysis showed that most PPM followed cascades of multiple pancreatectomy-specific complications, predominantly postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF) and postpancreatectomy hemorrhage (PPH). PPM 2 accounted for approximately two-thirds of deaths, particularly after MIPD and MITP, whereas PPM 1 and PPM 3 accounted for 13.3% and 15.3%, respectively. Conclusions: Mortality after MIPS predominantly occurs after a cascade of pancreatectomy-specific complications rather than technical failure or isolated medical events. Centers performing MIPS should invest in strategies to mitigate POPF and PPH and minimize failure to rescue once they occur.

items.title: An anti-inflammatory melanocortin fusion polypeptide augments whole blood resuscitation of hemorrhagic shock in a rodent polytrauma model
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Severe trauma induces a cytokine storm that is associated with impaired resuscitation and recovery. We investigated the impact of AQB-565, an anti-inflammatory melanocortin fusion polypeptide, as a novel treatment adjunct for whole blood resuscitation of hemorrhagic shock using a rat polytrauma shock model. METHODS: Hemorrhagic shock with polytrauma was induced in 64 Sprague-Dawley rats. The rats were randomized to receive one of four intravenous treatments at 15 minutes posthemorrhage (T15): saline control, AQB-565, tranexamic acid (TXA), or combined AQB-565+ TXA. The rats were given autologous transfusion of shed whole blood at 60 minutes and as needed thereafter to achieve mean arterial pressure (MAP) of 60 mm Hg for up to 3 hours. Survival, hemodynamics, cytokine profiles, and hemorrhage volumes were compared between groups. RESULTS: There was a significant overall effect of treatment group on MAP (two-way rmANOVA p =0.02) that coincided with blood transfusion. MAP was significantly increased at T105 with AQB-565+TXA versus saline control ( p =0.046). Inflammatory plasma cytokines, including interleukin-6, were significantly decreased with AQB-565 versus control groups (ANOVA p values ≤ 0.01). Seventeen (26.6%) rats died before 3 hours. There was a trend towards increased survival for treatments containing AQB-565 versus controls that was not statistically significant (Kaplan-Meier log rank p =0.06). CONCLUSIONS: A melanocortin pathway-activating polypeptide suppressed inflammation and improved hemodynamic response to whole blood transfusion in this hemorrhagic shock model.

items.title: Timing matters: Delayed surgery increases mortality for blunt hollow viscus injury
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Immediate surgical exploration is recommended for suspected hollow viscus injury (HVI) following blunt trauma. However, diagnostic uncertainty can lead to delayed operative management. We aimed to evaluate if delayed bowel resection/repair (DBR), defined as ≥8 hours after emergency department arrival, was independently associated with increased mortality in blunt trauma patients. We also sought to identify risk factors associated with DBR. METHODS: The Trauma Quality Improvement Program database (2017-2024) was queried for admitted adults with blunt abdominal trauma (abdomen abbreviated injury scale grade ≥2) who underwent bowel resection/repair. Patients who were transferred from another facility or died within 8 hours were excluded. Patients undergoing early bowel resection <8 hours (EBR) were compared with patients undergoing DBR (≥8 h). Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between DBR and mortality, controlling for age, severe head and thoracic injury, intubation within 1 hour of arrival, injury to the small bowel, colon, or rectum, and blood transfusion within 4 hours. RESULTS: Of 33,728 patients undergoing bowel resection/repair, 16,010 (47.5%) underwent DBR. The DBR cohort had lower rates of small bowel (49.6% vs. 53.9%, p <0.001) and colon (46.7% vs. 49.7%, p <0.001) injuries, but similar rates of rectal injury (4.4% vs. 4.1%, p =0.166). Injuries to the liver (26.8% vs. 20.8%), spleen (28.2% vs. 23.4%), and kidney (12.9% vs. 9.0%) were more frequent in the DBR cohort (all p <0.001). DBR patients had an increased associated risk of mortality (13.0% vs. 8.5%, OR 1.21, 95% CI: 1.12–1.30, p <0.001). Small bowel injury was the only independent factor with decreased associated risk of DBR (OR 0.93, CI: 0.89–0.97, p =0.001). CONCLUSION: Delayed operative management for blunt HVI occurs more often in patients with solid organ injuries and is independently associated with increased mortality. These findings highlight the importance of early detection and timely surgical management of HVI. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic/Care Management, Level IV.

items.title: Persistent gaps in health-related quality of life measures for older adult trauma patients: A systematic review
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Older adults experience persistent functional and psychosocial consequences after trauma, but it remains unclear whether commonly used health-related quality of life (HRQoL) instruments adequately measure recovery in this population. This systematic review appraised psychometric evidence and risk of bias for HRQoL instruments used in United States trauma cohorts that included adults aged 65 years or older. METHODS: MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL were searched from inception through January 28, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Risk of bias was evaluated using an adapted Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies-of Interventions (ROBINS-I) assessment. Studies evaluating an HRQoL instrument as the target measure underwent Consensus-based Standards for the Selection of Health Measurement Instruments (COSMIN) Risk of Bias assessment for each reported measurement property. Results were rated as sufficient, insufficient, or indeterminate and synthesized by instrument. RESULTS: Of 17,195 records, 19 studies were included. Studies most often examined isolated orthopedic trauma (n=7, 36.8%), spinal cord injury (n=6, 31.6%), other injury populations (n=3, 15.8%), polytrauma or systemic injury (n=2, 10.5%), and burns (n=1, 5.3%). Frequently evaluated domains included physical functioning (n=16), emotional or mental health (n=13), overall life satisfaction (n=13), social functioning (n=11), and physical symptoms (n=10). Although all studies used at least one previously developed patient-reported measure, none explicitly adapted or comprehensively validated an eligible HRQoL instrument for older adult trauma patients. Ten studies evaluated a target HRQoL instrument, contributing 33 COSMIN measurement property assessments: 19 sufficient, 10 indeterminate, and 4 insufficient. Overall risk of bias was low in six studies, moderate in eight, serious in three, and unclear in two. CONCLUSIONS: Existing studies show that HRQoL instruments have been used in trauma cohorts including older adults, but they do not establish validity for older adult trauma patients specifically. Future studies should evaluate promising instruments in cohorts designed around older adults’ recovery priorities and clinical characteristics after trauma. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Systematic Review; Level III.

items.title: PIEZO1 activation alters membrane remodeling and aggregability of stored red blood cells
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Transfused red blood cells (RBCs) actively contribute to post-injury hemostasis due to surface phosphatidylserine (PS) exposure. We hypothesized that storage sensitizes erythrocytes to the PIEZO1-induced, calcium‑dependent, PS externalization through calcium and protein kinase C (PKC) dependent activation of the phospholipid scramblase TMEM16F. METHODS: Five units of type O whole blood were obtained for analysis at days 21 and 42 of storage. RBC PS was quantified by annexin V staining on flow cytometry at increasing extracellular CaCl₂ concentrations (0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, and 5.0 mmol/L), with and without the PIEZO1 agonist Yoda1 (0.2 μM), PKC agonist Phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA; 6 μM) and antagonist chelerythrine chloride (CC; 10 μM), and the TMEM16 family inhibitor niclosamide (2 μM). RBC aggregometry was assessed by multiplate. Data were analyzed by analysis of variance and mixed-effects modeling. RESULTS: PS exposure increased in a Ca²⁺‑dependent manner in both day 21 and 42 RBCs ( p <0.001). PIEZO1 stimulation enhanced this response to a greater extent in day 42 RBCs, with greater change in PS at 1 mmol/L (2.21% vs. −0.44%, p =0.021), 2 mmol/L (7.36% vs. 0.53%, p <0.001), and 5 mmol/L (12.09% vs. 6.40%, p <0.001) CaCl 2 . Compared with calcium alone, Yoda1 and PMA (+61.3%, p <0.001 for both) produced similar increases in PS externalization, whereas PKC inhibition (−45.6%, p =0.009) and TMEM16F inhibition (−4.6%, p =0.99) negated the PIEZO1 response. Yoda1 agonism preserved RBC aggregability after 42 days of storage (51.2±39.0 vs. 2.0±3.5 area under the curve, p <0.001). CONCLUSION: Storage sensitizes RBCs to PIEZO1-mediated, calcium-dependent, PS externalization through PKC- and TMEM16F-dependent signaling. Given its endogenous mechanosensitive properties, pharmacologic PIEZO1 activation highlights a potential mechanism by which mechanical stress encountered during trauma and transfusion through the injured microcirculation may promote erythrocyte phospholipid membrane remodeling and aggregability, contributing to the procoagulant activity of transfused RBCs.

items.title: Calculating trauma undertriage rates: Are we using the wrong formula—and the wrong definition?
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Undertriage (UT) is central to trauma center quality improvement, yet UT definitions vary, and no data-driven consensus target exists for interfacility benchmarking. We compared facility-level UT rates across four methods and assessed the impact on facility benchmarking. METHODS: This retrospective study included patients aged 18 to 89 from Level I & II trauma centers in the ACS TQP Files (2021–2023). Facility-level UT was calculated using the Cribari Matrix Method (CMM), modified Cribari Matrix Method (mCMM), Standardized Triage Assessment Tool (STAT), and High-Intensity Time-Sensitive (HITS) intervention-based definition representing trauma team actions. Paired facility-level UT rates were compared across methods. To estimate benchmarking impact, we calculated within-facility rank change (higher rank = higher UT) relative to CMM. RESULTS: 2,643,881 patients and 515 facilities were included. Median facility-level UT significantly differed by method: CMM 11% [interquartile range: 9–14], mCMM 60% [50–67], STAT 6% [5–8], and HITS 30% [22–40] (all P <0.001). At individual hospitals, the median range of maximum UT values between methods was 53% [44–60]. The median absolute facility rank change between the CMM method and other tools was 129 [54.5–236.5] for mCMM, 48 [17–90] for STAT, and 142 [62.5–252.5] for HITS. CONCLUSIONS: These UT data highlight a concerning level of variation and uncertainty in the calculation and interpretation of a key trauma center performance metric. Until a UT definition is standardized and data-driven UT target goals established, cross-center benchmarking using UT should be interpreted cautiously and may be better suited for within-center trending. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, therapeutic/care management.

items.title: From sirens to systems: Characterizing EMS and trauma care across America
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: State emergency medical services (EMS) and trauma systems determine prehospital triage, transport, trauma center designation, data reporting, and quality improvement, yet their contemporary organization has not been systematically characterized. We sought to describe state-level EMS and trauma system structures, policies, resources, and perceived gaps across the United States. METHODS: We conducted a cross-sectional survey of EMS and trauma system leaders in all 50 states and the District of Columbia from July 2025 through March 2026. A 56-item instrument utilizing categorical, Likert-type, rank-order, and free-text items assessed oversight, prehospital triage and transport, clinical protocols, trauma center verification, registries, quality improvement, and funding. Respondents were recruited by email and phone. Multiple respondents could contribute complementary domain-level information to a single state profile. Responses were summarized descriptively. RESULTS: All 51 jurisdictions participated. Most states reported a state EMS medical director (84%), statewide trauma triage protocols (84%), and mandatory participation in their state trauma registry (88%). However, operational coordination varied: only 29% had a centralized trauma communications center, only 6% of states reported a single point of contact for helicopter EMS dispatch, and 35% required a certificate of need for new helicopter services. Trauma center verification relied on American College of Surgeons (ACS) verification in 59% of states, while others used state-administered processes. More than half of states rated EMS financial resources in the two lowest adequacy categories, and 55% reported that their trauma system required at least moderate improvement. Rural populations were most frequently identified as underserved (96%) and as experiencing worse outcomes (92%). CONCLUSIONS: State EMS and trauma systems share broad adoption of national clinical standards but differ substantially in governance, coordination, verification, data integration, and funding. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE AND STUDY TYPE: Level V, Prognostic/epidemiological.

items.title: Resuscitation using fresh-frozen plasma is associated with improved contextual fear memory in a non-TBI mouse model of trauma and hemorrhagic shock
items.containerTitle: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cognitive dysfunction is a consequence of traumatic injury with lasting impacts. Even without direct brain injury, trauma and hemorrhagic shock (T/HS) can cause malperfusion, inflammation, and neuronal injury. Disruption of the endothelial glycocalyx (eGC), a key regulator of vascular homeostasis, contributes to trauma-induced endotheliopathy and may influence secondary neurologic injury. Prior work demonstrated that fresh-frozen plasma (FFP) resuscitation preserves eGC expression and reduces maladaptive vascular repair in a murine T/HS model. This study evaluates post-injury cognition and FFP protection against cognitive impairment compared with lactated Ringer’s (LR). METHODS: Male C57BL/6 mice were randomized to sham procedure or T/HS followed by a volume-driven LR or pressure-directed FFP resuscitation approach. T/HS mice underwent laparotomy, femoral artery cannulation, hemorrhagic shock, pseudofractures via bone homogenate injection, and hindlimb muscle crush injuries. Sham mice received laparotomy and femoral artery cutdown. Four days postsurgery, open field testing assessed locomotion, followed by fear conditioning on days 7 to 8 to assess cognition. Brains were collected to analyze hippocampal glycosaminoglycans hyaluronan, heparan sulfate (HS), and chondroitin sulfate (CS). RESULTS: Open field testing showed intact locomotion at post-injury day 4 in all groups. On day 8, mice resuscitated with FFP had significantly greater contextual freezing compared with mice resuscitated with LR, consistent with improved hippocampal-dependent contextual memory. Cued fear conditioning did not differ between groups. LR and FFP resuscitation strategies resulted in distinct hippocampal hyaluronan and HS staining patterns, without synthesis gene expression differences. T/HS+LR brains showed increased 4- O -sulfated CS (CS-4S), a neurologically detrimental sulfation pattern, whereas FFP decreased CS-4S and increased CS-6S. CONCLUSIONS: Goal-directed plasma resuscitation is associated with improved spatial memory and distinct eGC structural remodeling compared with volume-driven crystalloid resuscitation following T/HS. These findings highlight the potential for resuscitation strategy after hemorrhagic shock to influence neurological recovery, even in the absence of direct brain injury.

jama-2026-us-crs-heart-allocation-score.limitations: Finally, a limitation of match-run analysis is its inability to quantify potential impacts on posttransplant survival due to directing donor hearts to sicker candidates; a full simulation study, which could predict which candidates are likely to receive which donor hearts, is needed. If prioritization by US-CRS were projected to adversely affect posttransplant survival, an expected posttransplant survival score could also be included as a separate component of a composite allocation score. Overall, incorporating US-CRS into adult heart allocation would substantially reorganize the waitlist, increasing priority for the sickest candidates and potentially decreasing distance traveled from donor to recipient hospitals. Replacing the current 6 urgency statuses with the more accurate US-CRS could lead to heart allocation that is less susceptible to manipulation and saves more lives. A full simulation of a US-CRS–based policy that provides fair access to durable-LVAD and blood-type-O candidates must be performed prior to policy implementation.

Publications
A variety of publications and other educational resources are available through the Society and contain the latest information in cardiovascular anesthesiology. Discount subscriptions to the publications listed below are available for those who are members of both the SCA and the IARS.

SCA Newsletter
The SCA newsletter serves as a valuable resource for its members, offering updates on the latest advancements, educational events, and leadership messages relevant to cardiovascular anesthesiology. Each edition typically includes previews of upcoming conferences, such as the annual Echo and Thoracic Anesthesia Symposiums, important policy and guideline changes, and opportunities for professional development through hands-on workshops and scientific discussions. The newsletter also features announcements of society activities, member achievements, and committee updates, helping practitioners stay informed and engaged within the SCA community.
Read more

Anesthesia and Analgesia
The official journal of the International Anesthesia Research Society hosts three sections of interest to SCA membership: Cardiovascular Anesthesiology, Hemostasis, and Perioperative Echocardiography and Cardiovascular Education.
Discount subscriptions are available for those who are members of both the SCA and the IARS.
Free Access Articles

Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia
Aimed primarily at anesthesiologists who deal with patients undergoing cardiac, thoracic, or vascular surgical procedures.
The Red Journal features a multidisciplinary approach, with contributions from cardiac, vascular and thoracic surgeons, cardiologists, and other related specialists.
Emphasis is placed on rapid publication of clinically relevant material.
The journal is international in scope and encourages innovative submissions from all continents.

Guideline FAQs
How do I obtain copyright permission to use a table/figure from an ASE Guideline?Expand
To use images or tables from any ASE guideline (or JASE article) you must apply for permission to the JASE publisher, Elsevier. This is done via CCC RightsLink(opens in new tab).
A shortcut is to find the guideline or article you need on JASE (onlinejase.com) and then select the “get rights” link (which looks like a copyright symbol) and it will take you to the CCC RightsLink form for that specific guideline or article. Note that you may request more than one image/table from a guideline on the same form, but you will need separate forms for each guideline or article.
How do I submit an idea for an ASE Guideline?Expand
ASE members may become involved in proposing an ASE Guideline through participation in one of the ASE Councils(opens in new tab) or ASE Specialty Interest Groups(opens in new tab). ASE members may also login to the member portal to download the ASE Guideline Development Manual (updated June 2023) and download the ASE Guideline Proposal Template (see instructions here(opens in new tab)) for more information. Note that guideline proposals are reviewed, prioritized, and approved by ASE leadership depending on topic.
What is ASE’s Endorsement Policy? Expand
ASE supports collaboration with other medical societies and organizations that develop clinical practice guidelines, appropriate use criteria, position statements, and other communications related to echocardiographic imaging. ASE views collaboration as an opportunity to harmonize clinical recommendations, improve the delivery of patient care, and advance cardiovascular ultrasound to improve lives.
Guidelines and other clinical guidance documents developed by external organizations may be considered for ASE endorsement when they address topics relevant to ASE and its membership and meet the basic criteria for review, including:
Medical and scientific soundness.
Alignment with ASE policies.
Alignment with the ASE strategic plan.
At the discretion of the ASE Executive Committee, a request for review of a submitted clinical guidance document may not be accepted. Submission and review do not guarantee endorsement, and ASE endorsement does not guarantee publication in the Journal of the American Society of Echocardiography (JASE).
ASE Endorsement Process
ASE endorsement requires:
Formal review by the ASE Guidelines and Standards Committee to assess the appropriateness of endorsement.
Approval by the ASE Executive Committee.
External organizations may approach ASE to request review and endorsement of guidelines developed without ASE involvement. Although such documents may be considered, the likelihood of consideration is increased when ASE has been involved in, and has knowledge of, the development process.
Organizations seeking ASE endorsement must submit the guideline to ASE Guidelines staff for consideration and complete ASE’s Endorsement Letter of Agreement (LOA). The requesting organization should submit the final manuscript along with the endorsement request.
Categories of ASE Recognition
Clinical guidelines developed by external organizations that are relevant to patient care in cardiovascular ultrasound may be categorized as follows:
Endorsed
The guideline meets ASE’s criteria for endorsement, and ASE fully endorses the document.
Whenever feasible, ASE’s involvement in the development and review of an endorsed document should include one or more of the following:
ASE representation on the writing committee, with at least one member appointed by the ASE Executive Committee.
ASE participation in peer review of the final document.
The sponsoring organization’s written response to ASE peer-review comments and provision of the final document to ASE for review.
Affirmation of Value
The guideline does not meet the requirements for full endorsement, or ASE cannot endorse all of the recommendations. However, ASE determines that the guideline provides value in improving patient care as it relates to the advancement of cardiovascular ultrasound.
Not Endorsed
ASE does not endorse the guideline.
Dissemination of Endorsed Documents
If ASE fully endorses a document:
ASE may disseminate the document to its members with permission from the primary organization.
ASE may request permission to publish the full document, a portion of the document, or a summary on the ASE website, or to provide a link to the article after publication by the primary organization.
The requesting organization should submit the endorsement request and final manuscript to ASE Guidelines staff for consideration.

Clinical Practice Documents and Policies
Scroll to top
The Society of Thoracic Surgeons Workforce on Evidence Based Surgery develops clinical practice documents including clinical practice guidelines, expert consensus documents, and expert opinion/white papers to provide practical assistance to the STS membership. These documents are intended to assist physicians and other health care providers in clinical decision-making by describing a range of generally acceptable approaches for the diagnosis, management, or prevention of specific diseases or conditions.
Clinical practice guideline documents are thoroughly reviewed, and the conclusions and recommendations are based on a systematic review of scientific evidence published in medical literature.
Expert consensus documents represent the collective opinions of an expert panel on a clinical topic. The opinions expressed in the statement(s) are not generally developed in accordance with the formal evidence review process outline for clinical practice guidelines. The authors may suggest treatment strategies based on their collective knowledge and clinical experience.
An expert opinion/white paper is authored by leading experts on clinical topics with scarce data and significant uncertainty. These documents are intended to synthesize existing scientific literature, divergent opinions, and other treatment strategies, rather than provide recommendations.

Disclaimer: These guidelines are intended for educational use to build the knowledge of physicians and other health professionals in assessing the conditions and managing the treatment of patients undergoing ECLS / ECMO and describe what are believed to be useful and safe practice for extracorporeal life support (ECLS, ECMO) but these are not necessarily consensus recommendations. The aim of clinical guidelines are to help clinicians to make informed decisions about their patients. However, adherence to a guideline does not guarantee a successful outcome. Ultimately, healthcare professionals must make their own treatment decisions about care on a case-by-case basis, after consultation with their patients, using their clinical judgement, knowledge and expertise. These guidelines do not take the place of physicians’ and other health professionals’ judgment in diagnosing and treatment of particular patients. These guidelines are not intended to and should not be interpreted as setting a standard of care, or be deemed inclusive of all proper methods of care nor exclusive of other methods of care reasonably directed to obtaining the same results. The ultimate judgment must be made by the physician and other health professionals and the patient in light of all the circumstances presented by the individual patient, and the known variability and biological behavior of the clinical condition. These guidelines reflects the data at the time the guidelines were prepared; the results of subsequent studies or other information may cause revisions to the recommendations in these guidelines to be prudent to reflect new data, but ELSO is under no obligation to provide updates. In no event will ELSO be liable for any decision made or action taken in reliance upon the information provided through these guidelines.
